I'm going to recommend this game, although barely.  I'll break it down into pros and cons:
Pros:
This game does a fairly good job of putting the player into the shoes and mind of someone with clinical depression.  A lot of the descriptions in this game hit home for me.  Although I disliked the characters at first, they started to grow on me over time.
Cons:
The game makes it WAY too easy to make the right choices.  The biggest problem with depression is that it robs the sufferer of the motivation or ability to make good decisions.  On my first playthrough, I ended up fixing pretty much all of the main character's problems.  Yes, there are attempts to try and describe the precarious mental state and constant danger of backsliding, but it's just too easy to click on the equivalent of "suck it up and do the hard thing" every single time.
Also, the structure of this game just isn't very engaging.  It's basically a choose-your-own-adventure story, with the added mechanic that the character's current level of depression may lock out certain choices.
If you want a game that truly captures the hopelessness of deep depression, I can't recommend "Actual Sunlight" highly enough.

text:
Depression Quest is essentially a Choose Your Own Adventure book put into an electronic format. I wouldn't even go so far as to call it a visual novel, much less a game, because the pictures placed above the text don't add anything to the story. Basically, you play as "you", and you start out depressed. You have a bunch of first world problems going against you, and you have to manage all of these issues in order to get to the point where you're still depressed, but coping with it by the end of the story. I believe that the producer of this "game's" goal was to raise awareness for depression, but I don't think she really was able to do so. She made it seem much like the misconceptions that overpriviledged people who self-diagnose themselves were what depression really is, and it made the whole storyline seem a bit pretentious. I don't think it's really possible for anyone to get anything from this experience, because quite honestly, it didn't explain depression at all to those who don't have it, and only maybe convinced those with depression that it does help to get seek guidance and comfort from those who are close to you. And with all of this going against it, the producer couldn't even go through all the text walls to make sure there weren't any spelling or grammatical errors!
Overall:
Pros:
-Shows those with depression that they aren't suffering alone
Cons:
-No gameplay
-No visual aids
-Not a correct depiction of depression
-Grammatical/spelling errors all over the place

Before I begin, I will admit that the only reason I'm playing this game is because of the Zoe Quinn & her Five Guys scandal. And despite my feelings about infidelities, corruption of journalism, and the pack mentality of Indie Game developers, I will try to keep it out of this review.
Something I would not like to keep out of this review is my personal history with depression. I suffered for a few years, and at my worst was contemplating suicide. Seeing how this is a game about depression, I hope these experiences of mine can help with shedding light on this game.
The first thing I noticed about this game is its presentation. Though I have own a tumblr blog, I do not regularly browse tumblr or other blogging sites. However, if I did, I’m sure I’d find a striking similarity between the menus and greyed-out gifs at the tops of pages with their counterparts in tumblr blogs. I realize that this is a text-based adventure game, but for a Greenlit game I was expecting a game with more body to it. I felt like I was reading an article on the Internet, let alone engaging in a game, I wasn’t immersed.
But maybe that’s because when I was immersed I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at depression’s representation. The main character, in my first play through, goes through a downward spiral after his depression begins to take the better of him. The game represents this through staticy music and all color fading away. Granted, depression varies between individuals, and I’m sure others suffering from depression experience feelings of hopelessness and fatigue. But depression isn’t an easy thing to make a game out of without disrespecting it.
I’m competitive by nature. When I sit down and play Dark Souls or Team Fortress 2, I play to win. When I lose, I take it as a learning experience, and correct my strategy. It’s something I learned in my battle with depression. I fought, and didn’t let the common inconveniences that once disabled me slow me down further. This attitude proved useless in Depression quest, as even when I had all the chances in the world to fix my character’s problems, the game wouldn’t let me. The game wouldn’t let me do what I did in my victory over depression. It didn’t give me a chance.
I realize that many people wither under depression’s burdens without a chance of saving themselves. But a game is no place to toy with a problem that hurts millions. Depression Quest shouldn’t be played because of how it taunts a player with a chance of healing, only to cross-out the option to go to someone and get help.
A player can do a lot of amazing feats. They can save princesses, build worlds, and dominate the competition in their quests. But this is one quest that I recommend no player attempt. As a player, I was disappointed when my attitude to heal my character was worthless when the doors were already closed from the beginning. And as someone who suffered from depression, I was utterly disgusted with how a developer toys with a serious problem. Say what you will about gaming being a medium for art or a message, but this is one game that I feel is just worthless. Worthless to Indie Games, worthless to Steam, and worthless to the gaming world. Do not play this game.

A visually oriented psychological horror adventure game with rather shallow and unrealistic characters, poor dialogue, contrived and easy puzzles, crippled interface and finally; good art, atmosphere and at times sound. As an adventure game this game doesn't cut it. As psychological horror it falls flat on its face due to reasons laid out in more detail below.
I can't recommend this game mainly because it fails at what it seems to strive for: psychological horror and meaningful dialogue. The dialogues are extensive, and they consist mostly of filler back-and-forth bickering and unimaginative small-talk, sometimes attempting to be humorous despite the bleak circumstances and surroundings but practically just managing to break the immersion. There are lengthy pauses in the dialogue that you can't skip, and while I understand they were put there to put emphasis on lines and allow for a few seconds of contemplation, after you realize the dialogue is thoroughly shallow and void of depth they just become an annoying, arbitrary speed bump for advancing in the game. It is of course even more annoying if you go back just to get achievements.
Cursing is used with good taste for the most part, i.e. there's not too much of it, and the voice actors mostly manage not to sound ridiculous dropping the F-bombs here and there.
The interface is terrible. You play the game using WASD (up left down right) and enter. Space (and enter) skips a line of dialogue. Movement is in one dimension; you can either walk left or right. When you come across a hotspot, its name is displayed and you can interact with it by pressing up. This opens a list of possible actions such as "examine", "push", "open" etc., and you use up and down to select your action. To open inventory you press down, then left and right to choose item. Pressing enter on the item brings up an action list again, and you press up and down to select action "examine", "use" etc..
The problem arises from the context-sensitivity of the direction keys: To interact, you press up. To select action, you move up or down in the menu, and to exit you press left or right. But you enter the inventory by pressing down, and then left or right to select item, then enter, then again up or down to choose action. To exit from this menu and go back to inventory, you again press left or right. To exit from the
, you press up or down (left and right are for choosing item now). Then left and right are again for moving [the character] sideways and up and down for interacting and opening inventory. This all makes the interface very unintuitive and inconsistent. I wish they'd just gone with point'n'clicking instead.
The visuals in this game are very good. I liked the graphics throughout the game and they manage to create a nice atmosphere. All the characters seem to be the same height, which seems a bit strange. Animation is simplistic and a bit jerky but it didn't bother me.
The sound is up to par for the most part, although I thought some of the music (my apologies to the developer for using this word, but...), namely the "emo rock" sounded a bit out of place for this game. I would much have preferred something more reminiscient of Alexander Scriabin or - if you want to go modern - industrial or aggrotech. Teenage angst rock just doesn't quite cut it for a game revolving around the life and psyche of a suicidal woman in her forties. Voice actors are, in my opinion, surprisingly good and where they fall flat I would blame the director responsible or the dialogue.
Puzzles are few in this game, and didn't really require much thinking. Some of it is very, very contrived. For example, you have to make coffee one step at a time
. Didn't help me "get into the character" but made me frustrated that the game would bother wasting my time to supposedly make a poor attempt at that.
The game presents itself as dealing with mature and dark themes, but turns out there's not much dealing here, just putting nasty stuff on the table as a freakshow. There is not much analytical nor deep thought present in the dialogue, and the characters react to events in strikingly unrealistic ways, which is only indicative of poor writing considering how much effort the game puts into being taken seriously on other fronts. The content of the game is more juvenile, feigning maturity, and gets constantly caught for it through the aforementioned poor and unrealistic writing, for example;
. There's also a lot of arbitrary sadism in this game that is only mature for its violence. Nothing is really explained in more depth - the sadism, perversion and brutality just are there for people to "enjoy."
I tried to like this game, but entering chapter 4 or 5 I found myself speedstepping through dialogues because they just weren't interesting and felt like filler content purposely slowing me down, and there is a
of filler dialogue in this game. In the very end I would just skip the dialogue because the character weren't saying anything substantial at all, i.e. there's a lot of "yes", "no", "please", "no" verbal ping-pong that serves no purpose but to supposedly make everything more theatrical - if bad movie cliches are presumed as a good example of theatrics. I didn't find myself growing attached to the shallow characters and when the game ended I just said to myself; "Finally." There are a few OK scares, and I did enjoy the atmosphere briefly in some parts, but I feel the game didn't shine in the areas where it could and in my opinion should have, and deteriorated into a boring interactive gore fest.
There are also a few bugs and oddities: At least at one point the character seems to comment on something she shouldn't had known yet. A few times the game got stuck during or between cutscenes so that the only way out was to kill the game process. The dialogue options don't show the full text if the line is too long, so you're forced to respond with lines you can't even read before selecting them. Sometimes a character would skip her first line by herself after a pause or a cutscene. Nothing gamebreaking though as far as I can tell.
If you don't care about the quality of writing, think you can handle the bad interface and contrived puzzles, and just want some nice audio-visual gore and scares, then you might still be enjoying this game. If you're looking for mature handling of heavy subjects or true psychological horror with
behind it, or a satisfying adventure gaming experience, I'm afraid this game can't deliver.

I've just finished this game, and I rarely write reviews, but I feel this one deserves it.
I haven't really played games like this, but I was given this because I'm a bit of a crazy cat lady myself. Overall, I probably would have bought it myself anyway, from watching the trailer and the subject of the game, I was intrigued.
I first played this some months ago, then got stuck on Chapter 2 and left it. Susan annoyed me at first, complaining about things like not being strong enough to move something or not wanting to untie a knot because it would take too long. The slow pace of her walking and the sound of her monotonous footsteps as she walked were annoying as well, due to the fact there wasn't really much to do in the first chapter, but a lot of walking involved.
The graphics in this part were also a bad first impression, but I wasn't put off the game yet. I got to chapter 2, and got stuck in the Hospital. After many times being drugged and doing all but finding the name of a patient's mother, I gave up and didn't touch it until about a week ago.
I got stuck on a few of the "puzzles" in this game. Maybe I'm just not used to this kind of thing, but I found myself having to look at a guide at these points because I just couldn't progress. Some of them would have been obvious with a bit more direction, but others like the one in the hospital were kind of random to me, but I guess that fits with the nature of the game quite well.
The game follows Susan Ashworth who is depressed and commits suicide, but instead of dying, she is given immortality. She will only be allowed to die once she has killed 5 "parasites", serial killers who live off others' pain. Throughout the game, you learn about Susan's past, and things like the reason she hates flowers. Some of the choices you make through the game affect the outcomes, and there are alternate endings - I found this quite by accident when trying to pause the game during the last scene.
The storyline is very well written. You might say something a novel, movie or series would be much more fitting for this, however these mediums do not allow for the viewer to make choices which potentially alter the outcomes. The graphics aren't great, they remind me of old hidden-object games, but the visuals really aren't badly done at all. This game is somewhat gruesome in some parts, but I don't feel it's like other "horror" games where it's just thrown in for shock or scares. I ended up enjoying the graphics after chapter 3, so I'd say they're something of an acquired taste.
There are some small bugs with the game, like characters repeating lines randomly, but nothing game-breaking from what I've seen. There are 2 things to be aware of though: a) This game does not autosave, so save about every chapter or so, and b) You cannot pause while there is dialogue. I got a phone call while there was a whole lot of  dialogue going on in the last chapter and had no way to stop it except closing the game and reopening from my last save, so keep that in mind.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who knows a thing or two about depression, but this is sort of a textbook case, so I personally couldn't exactly relate to Susan. It would have been very different if she had things to live for but just couldn't face another day. She has every reason to feel the way she does, so if you can't relate, at least you can empathise.
I would still love to see this in a movie or series, but it's great as it is.

Some of the puzzles can be a bit tricky, but can usually be solved by "examine everything, pick up everything, and use everything on everything" logic. I didn't need any external help, at any rate (beyond the video series that brough me to the game in the first place, techncally, but I didn't seek it out because I was stuck or anything), and as far as I can tell it's difficult or impossible to actually fail anything and need to restart. Which makes it feel more like a visual novel with puzzles at times, but that doesn't mean it's not worth your time. Oh, and everyone seems to think it's a horror game, but, it really isn't. It did make me jump once, and there was one part where the audio was so creepy I had to take off my headphones after a while, but the rest of it is basically just piano dischords at random moments, to the point of being almost cheesy. It's not Amnesia or Slender or anything, to be sure. And it has a great sense of humor, too, everything from a difficult old man who has hearing problems and repeats himself to actually being able to call the police when you're in trouble instead of solving the puzzles to escape, but only to have them be complete government airheads and be no help at all to you anyway. It's wonderful and I love it.
I'd actually recommend people with clinical depression play this game. Which sounds weird, you'd think a game like this'd only make depression worse, but it has powerful messages in regards to that, especially the ending. It reminds me of a story I heard about a guy whose girlfriend recently broke up with him and the ending of Bastion helped him get through it. There's even a separate plotline that addresses flame arguments on the Internet. Are you really going to let some random nerd get you down, hm?
THINGS I'D LIKE TO APPEND:
Tech:
The above review was for the 1.2 version from their website (
), and there are definitely technical differences between that and the 1.4 version from Steam that I just played through recently. The verson I first played had no proper options menu and was locked to certain settings, including fullscreen 800x600 only, but other than a few engine quirks it was basically perfect, so it worked just fine. The new version has a basic options menu, the option for a windowed mode is particularly welcome, but it's still locked to 800x600, which makes the windowed mode kind of awkward. I also noticed some fairly terrible text bugs where both dialogue tree text and subtitles would get cut off, which got really irritating at times. There were also a few minor graphical glitches, namely with new user-friendly menu icons, and an item in my inventory was never deleted properly and I had it for the entire game. And on top of it all, I also got weird lag that would make the audio jutter for a second upon changing scenes. So yeah, I'm not sure if it's Steam vs. non-Steam or 1.2 vs. 1.4, but if you can get ahold of the older non-Steam version, I'd say that's definitely the better one, provided you don't care about a windowed mode/other settings, Steam achievements, and trading cards.
A few engine issues plague both versions, but they're not really game-breakers as long as you bear in mind that this is an indie game that doesn't come with triple-A smoothness. Odd music cutoffs, confusing graphics movement, inability to overwrite saves, occasional iffy voice acting and quality (some halfhearted laughter, minor normalization differences, really wish one of the voice actors had used a popshield), clunky arrow controls and menu navigation, can't skip cutscenes, things like that. For the most part these don't really impede gameplay, but hearken back to a more retro style of gaming; if you grew up in the NES/SNES/DOS era, you'll do just fine.
Gameplay:
It's a visual novel point-and-click thing that uses metaphors to tell the story of a woman's struggles with clinical depression. Apparently "puzzle game without failure states" was my way of saying "point-and-click" the first time around. A lot of people do seem to think it's a horror game, and while it is very grim and creepy with an occasional jumpscare, it's definitely more story-centered than it is scare-centered. The story is absolutely bonkers though, which is definitely a good thing, considering how slow and bogged-down it can feel with dialogue sometimes. Also the soundtrack is one of the best in any game I've played to date, with a good balance of passive atmospheric background noise and songs that actively grab your attention and really drive home what's happening on the screen.
Conclusion:
If you like visual novels that carve corpses up like pumpkins and don't mind engine quirks to do it, then why do you not already have this?

I've only tried Terrakin so far, who use hyperdrive, but other races use gates. There may be more forms I haven't seen.
Graphics are good enough, nothing to write home about. The ship battles are spectacles, though, compared to Sins. I also really really like the fleet system- capital ships form the backbone of fleets and automatically issue orders to their escort frigates and whatnot. You can have 60-120 small ships in formation and only worry about giving orders to the flagship unless you want to micro. They can also be set to auto-replenish with new recruits.
I also like the colonization system, you pick the planet and your homeworld automatically sends convoys of colony ships instead of one unit like most games use. I'm barely scratched the surface of planet development and economics but from what I can tell it's pretty in depth.
I'll probably have to post a more thorough review tomorrow when I have a better handle on the gameplay but my first impression is definitely very positive. Put simply it seems like it's a thinking person's Sins of a Solar Empire- besides having deeper 4X features basic things are also improved. For instance, you can actually do things while paused and the galaxy is more scientifically accurate and interesting to explore.
I can't wait to play more, it feels fresh and promising and I predict sinking a good bit of time into it.

You can only take two hits before you die. If you're going to be THAT rude, you should at least give me something as mechanically interesting as Volgarr at the very least. Castlevania-level quality would be nice but that game didn't need to two-shot you to be interesting.
Momodora Reverie just is not at that level.
It's bog-standard with only a couple of tricks: Lifted from Dark Souls was a silly refillable health potion and other buff items system that really isn't necessary outside of a Souls-style game (Insultingly, the refillable health potions don't refill enough of your health to undo the one hit you can take. But they aren't slow enough that you have to stop the fight to heal like you did in Souls. Why not just double my anemic health bar?). Worse, you have a roll. Don't get me wrong, if you're making an action game like Shank, Dishwasher, Streets of Fury, Aces Wild etc, a roll is welcome. But Momodora is closer to a low-budget two-hit-kill Mega Man than any of those games, and your roll never feels right*, it never ends up in the right position, and, combined with the ridiculous forward momentum on the melee, the combat feels graceless and greasy.
Oh, and that's all you do. Because like Momodora 3 the levels are just there to give you stuff to hop over, a bit like Kirby only less fun.
*Of course, thinking about it, your character's sprite is massive. There's no way you're dodging between or around ANY shots beyond one or two, so of course we need a roll with iframes rather than let you duck and weave like any other Mega Man-esque game.

I remember keeping up with this game since it was called "Momodora IV." The series has only grown bigger and better with each installment, and this game is a testament to that. Reverie Under the Moonlight is by far the most refined and fleshed out game of the entire series. At first, I thought that this was going to have the more linear structure of Momodora III, but then the game slowly but surely branched out into multiple paths. The combat is incredibly satisfying; the game does a great job of letting you know that you were damaging an enemy (and that enemies were hitting you). The soundtrack is beautiful and truly lends itself to the atmosphere of the game. The enemies are laid out to actually compliment the level design and to make you think differently about each encounter. Though the power-ups themselves aren't quite as satisfying as other metroidvanias on the market, I still got pretty giddy at times. Where this game truly shines is its boss battles (although at one point the pacing falters); they give you a very good challenge without being unfair, and they get progressively more difficult to reflect your progress. Between this game and Pony Island, 2016 is off to a very good start.

Risen 2 is a third-person RPG that made me spend a lot of time on it. You are a former Inquisition soldier that travels from nearly destroyed Caldera across the seas to various islands. The setting is quite immersive: Carribean-like islands, treasure hunt, grave plundering, pirate fights, the Creed....all of that you can experience here. The more you talk to the people in the game, the more details of story and quests you discover. From the drinking adventurer at the beginning to the captain of your own ship  in the end you will fight Mara using four artifacts that you have to get from each captain.
At first sight, the plot is distinct, linear but during the playthrough lots of interesting quests and events emerge. The goal of the game is to get all four artifacts to fight against the “she-devil” Mara. Each artifact has special means to be acquired. You will have to fight against titans, escape from the island after being marooned by one of the captains, build a raft with the help of gnomes and reveal the mascarade of another captain who killed the Inquisition soldiers and used their robes to gain trust from the Marakayas.  The game is filled with lots of side-quests.  A part of these quests suggest different wayouts due to your talents or your personal attitude. Points of glory that you get for fighting and completing tasks help you improve your skills. You can be a trickster, a fighter, a brute or a voodoo master. Better choose from the beginning what type of skills you will develop the most.  Hence, you can either intimidate or flatter people or simply do a point-blank shoot (if a script suggests) and many more.  Also it is worth mentioning that you can get such useful abilities as kicking over opponents, training monkeys and parrots to steal things and distract foes. There are some unique collectibles that require from you having certain of  the above mentioned abilities to get them.  Other abilities include the use of a voodoo doll to take direct control of other characters or rituals to weaken opponents. But the most hilarious tricks are breathing fire in the opponent's face, scattering sand in the eyes and dropping coconuts. This one was one of the highlights for me. Thorough exploration also awards you with unique items and treasure maps. The more gold you get, the more skills you can master from trainers all over the playground. Also you can use potions, parts of clothes and weapons that boost your skills. There certainly is a value in replay as the game suggests to play either for the Inquisition or for the local tribes. Personally I preferred learning cunning skills primarily and then slashing and piercing weapons because I rarely use magical skills in RPGs. This helped me open lots of chests, train monkeys and parrots, also complete quests using eloquent speech which was fun for me. The main hero could use sarcasm, jokes or steal gold. Voodoo is also a fun way. It helps you control people after getting some of their personal things and making a voodoo doll. And it unlocks another branch of quests.
There were enough animals and monsters in the game world. After killing them you can use their parts for trading or for magic. But not at once. You must get special tools at first: bone saw, ritual knife and others. The faster you find them, the better. This also encouraged me to explore.
Music and sound effects are decent, I wish there would be more ambient or combat soundtracks though. Sometimes it weakens the desire to play the game. From the other side, the main hero has his own voiceover, unlike in some other RPGs. This is crucial for me, adds an immersion. The best soundtrack is at the moment when the ghost of Captain Steelbeard appears at the Island of the Dead. Moreover, every companion that goes with you during the quests may also add some witty sentences in the cutscenes. Generally, the voiceover of the main characters is good. I appreciated that. Only the animations of body language repeat too much.
Graphics are demanding. It was hard for me to optimize the game to get normal fps. I sacrificed with draw distance and detail quality, downloaded a small fix that boosts fps from Steam community and changed some values in “ini” files. Then nothing was critical, the game can be completed at 20-25 fps, at dark and foggy places it drops to 15-18 fps on my old PC. I only regret that I could not pass shooting challenge in Antigua because it was impossible to aim and hit targets. Luckily, there was another quest to skip it and played on.
Another problem that I spotted is linked with achievements. Many of them are unlockable. For example, I definitely killed more than 20 giant crabs and unlocked more than 100 chests by the end of the game, but these achievements just do not pop up. Neither in game, nor in Steam and there is almost a dozen of them. Playing hours do not count properly too. My last save file has around 40 hours, Steam shows 19 or so.
Nevertheless, I kept hooked on this game because I tried upgrading the skills and wanted to see what if I tried to pass a certain quest having this or that talent. So, overall if counting the replays, the game will take good 60 hours approximately. If you like pirate themed RPGs, main heroes with a sense of humour and breaking the rules, this game is a good pick. Aye-aye, gamers!

A disappointing sequel to Risen, the devs tried to keep some characters from the first game to justify calling it Risen 2 but the story has little to do with what happened on the first game.
Other than that the game is decent, it's much more polished than Risen but at the same time it lost some of it's charm, the world feels more claustrophobic and small compared to the huge interconnected zones on Risen and the enemy variety is not very high, nor are the enemy designs very inspired since most of them are common animals. They also removed the mages and most of the magic abilities from the first game, and pretty much the most fantasy-RPG parts of the Risen.
The graphics are ok, it looks great on 4k but at lower resolutions the provided AA solution will not help much with all the blurriness on the vegetation (and there's a lot of vegetation in this game). The game still suffers from NPCs sharing faces and voice actors.
I'd still recommend it, but if you wanted a improved Risen 1, you'll be let down.

Gothic 1, Gothic 2 and Gothic 3. Risen 1, Risen 2 and Risen 3. What does Gothic series have in common with Risen series? Yes, you figured the question out - Piranha Bytes. Back in the days, everybody was looking forward Gothic 4, yes from Piranha, but instead we got Gothic 4 alias ArcaniA from Spellbound. But what Piranha did? They didn't fall asleep, they get back to work and came out with awesome Risen series. So basically we can say that thanks to no Gothic 4 we got Risen.
Anyway, there is not so much games about Pirates, and most of those are either old, animated, 2d and/or strategy games like Port Royale or Tropico 2. Except Risen 2, the big open-world game about Pirates I know and I have enjoyed that much as I have enjoyed Risen 2 is most definitely AC4: Black Flag. But without mentioning these two, there's nothing else for me, if so, let me know.
The actual topic about the Pirates, the story and point the game is all about, the place the game is set, dialogues, characters, Inquisition vs. Pirates, Kraken, Mara and of course Patty mixed all together makes this game absolutely awesome. I don't really want to get too much into the story as I never want to, but you as the let's say ex-member of Inquisition you are determinted to eliminate Mara - Titan Lord of Water to ensure peace in the Southern Seas. Story is pretty gripping and will last you around 20-30 hours depends on how you play it. 2 additional hours with DLC.
Southern Seas - vast expance of water - that is just place to be. Islands, grog, Pirates, ladies, palms, sun, coconuts, beaches, big boats, warm weather and OF COURSE THE MOST IMPORTANT THING EVER - RUM! What a time to be alive!
I still can't get over it, how awesome places this game actually have. From Inquisition Forts to so beautiful beaches you can imagine. Sometimes you even feel the sun on your face.
There is a lot of items you can use, but I believe almost everybody will stick to the combination of sword and pistol. I just wish there would be even more items you can use, like the bigger hunt for better clothing and weapons. Also if there would be more clothing, that would be absolutely brilliant. I like the selection of provisions and drinks, and even the options to do dirty tricks.
The way you progress and evolve is not pretty well choosen I would say and it is because you basically do not evolve with the experience, but by gold. Well, it is combined with experience earned + gold, but if it was two independed elements, that would be even better.
The game does not have problems with quest bugs, or some major bugs and if it had in 2012, I am sure it is fixed now. Lot of people said that AI is pretty low and most of the times it gets stucked somewhere, but it did not happened to me a lot, I would say twice or something like that. Even when I have abandoned them, it was all calm.
The fact that Piranha Bytes did not fixed bugged achievements, even after forum rants and petitions, is really sad. Yes, they completely removed 7 achievements that was unobtainable, but there is still over 10+ that is bugged because in game counter always reset to zero, when the game is closed. So either you play and let the game on and grind, or you will use command console. I do not even consider some of the achievements as grinding. Let me put it this way - If you kill around 400-500 monsters in one walkthrough, and you can do 2000 for an achievement, I would grind it, as I grinded few achievements like that. But when you cannot even leave the game to counter not reset AND EVEN IF YOU GRIND IT, AND GAME CRASHED FOR EVERYBODY AT 1500, then sorry, I am going to spam the sh*t out of command console, because it is not like I do not want to grind.
Now Piranha is making ELEX debuting 2017, and I'm really looking forward to it and I hope they do above average job with it. Most of the bugs and mistakes they did over Risen 2, they did not in Risen 3, so I really think that ELEX will be clean and I wish them the best with it. You can count on me, I am definitely getting it.
Before we get to the end of this review and the final rating, I would like to say, that not like the other reviews I wrote, this one will have one more rating. I hope you understand what I mean by the non-objective one.
DLC will be rated next time.

While it lacks the depth of some of the core entries of the Civilisation series, the setting, interesting approach to the technology tree and variety definitely makes it a worthwhile purchase.
I'd go as far to say it's a good entry to the Civi series - the diplomacy is a little simpler than in other games, the combat tends to be less one sided (until right at the end of the tech tree, you rarely are completely outmatched if someone is ahead of you in the tech tree). The AI on the normal/slightly harder difficulties pose a reasonable challenge, although it would be nice if they recognised your proximity to a victory condition. During a recent Emancipation victory (where you need to essentially contribute a unit per turn as a sort of economic victory), the AI made no effort to contest my impending victory, despite the fact I'd donated the vast majority of my army to the cause.
Overall, certainly worth the investment, and a must for any fans of Civi with a hankering for a sci-fi challenge.

This work of interactive fiction (this is not a game on the basis that a choose-your-own adventure book is not a video game because you read it online) fails on both of its objectives, that is a, to "show other sufferers that they are not alone in their feelings", and b. to "illustrate to people who may not understand the illness the depths of what it can do to people". Firstly, the concept of "Depression Quest" seems to be something of a text-based roleplay, but the protagonist has no definite identity other than a "twenty-something human being", presumably in an attempt to be politically correct for correctness's sake, which instead comes of as dismissive to "other sufferers" as the only thing i could tell you about the protagonist is that he/she/it has depression, the effects of which seem to be feeling sad sometimes and losing motivation after every few paragraphs based on my playthrough, which in no way illustrates to people the effects of the illness since it does little to differentiate depression from "being sad sometimes".
Furthermore, the "professional" reviews above seem to praise the game for being "innovative" and "artsy" however nothing In the game open to interpretation in the way a proper art piece should be, and it is impossible for this game to be Voyeuristic if the character himself has no identity, there is no intimacy between the reader and the character;the reviewers Effectively use the game to deliver the illusion of artistic critique.
Going past the recent social media uproar surrounding the personal lives of the developers, Depression Quest is still Ultimately a falied experiment at best and a dismissive publicity stunt at worst, delivering nothing that any site on depression You could find wouldn't give you. It is ultimately a cautionary tale about indie games that try to push the limits and be "edgy" Somehow becoming less artistic than games created solely for gameplay.

If someone had told me that they were thinking of making a short-form, story-focused party game that styles itself after choose your own adventure books, I would have advised them to find a better use of their time. Thankfully, the creators of The Yawhg did not receive or did not listen to such advice.
Each playthrough requires the player(s) to select at least two of the four available characters. The characters are unaware that the Yawhg, a fabled source of great destruction, is coming their way. The players get to decide how these unsuspecting characters spend their last six weeks: select one of eight locations and one of two actions for that character to take part in during that week. The chosen action, along with random events that might trigger, will alter the character's stats. One characters' actions might trigger or help explain events encountered by other characters; they might even begin a questline that can be followed or ignored.
The game has multiple endings based on all of these factors. Although there are a limited number of permutations, enough can happen that no single playthrough has felt the same as another. This is an excellent game, and I hope to see others like it.

Damian Sommer and Emily Carroll’s
is easily the most beautiful piece of choose-your-own-adventure fiction ever published. Carroll’s indie comics superstardom is immensely deserved and her work here depicts a wonderfully colorful world with a sensitive fairy tale look, defined not only by the setting, but by the flourish of the visual interface and of her distinctive hand lettering. Sommer and Carroll’s writing is whimsical, amusing, and mysterious, all in good measure. Ryan Roth’s shifting soundtrack feels perfectly of this world without being overbearing. As a production,
is an aesthetic triumph.
As a game, its success is tempered.
tells a story that would have benefitted from more prose. Completing one cycle in the coming and going of the apocalyptic Yawhg event takes only a few minutes. The random events are interesting but never deep, always dropping a choice in your lap before you know it. Every encounter is succinct to a fault, eschewing any sort of satisfying narrative exploration for an exceedingly quick presentation. Some choices and events will affect future encounters for other members of your party in different areas of the world, which is quite impressive. Still, the number of possible events is not astoundingly numerous, and given the short length of each “run,” events may repeat themselves as early as the second playthrough, before they’ve even vacated your short-term memory.
Playing the game with other people does somewhat alleviate the problems I’ve mentioned. It’s a joy to actually play a choose-your-own-adventure that actually allows for multiple people. Seeing the consequences of certain events weave between characters controlled by different people leads to some wonderful reactions. Chatter will do a lot to lengthen each go-around. As a social game, it’s quite nice. However, hosting or attending the right party that wants to kill an hour playing something like
is an uncommon occurrence at best. And when it comes down to it, I prefer to immerse myself in the twists and turns of a good narrative and the beauty of great visuals all by my lonesome.
For me, the pleasures of
are few – too few for me to heartily recommend. It is not a bad game, but it is a game that caters to a group of people who often play games and experience art together. It’s just not a game for someone like me.

Not the best game, but not the worst either. As someone that embraces additions onto a game but does remember the old ones fondly, I'm hoping I can put together a pretty decent detailed review for everyone.
Now, the pros of the game compared to the old ones is the sneaking. I love being able to sneak around the corners and get guards right when they least expect it. Guards do seem abit more attentive then they were in past games, so placing a body where it won't be exposed is key. However, if the body is seen they will look around for you for a little bit and then just walk over the body like it's no big deal. Eh. You still have your various arsenal of arrows and gadgets to help you get around with ease. Bringing a couple of new additions into the game as well makes things easier and the detail to the game is fantastic (the first time around seeing the same thing) but even that does grow a bit bland. I mean, how can you remember which window you snuck into when they all look exactly the same? Player detail can get a little annoying but the main characters in the game do pretty much have their own models. Did I mention there are prostitues everywhere that you can't do anything with? Yah, deal with it.
One of the biggest cons in this game is the map layout. It can be very confusing and isn't as straight forward as it was, say in the last expansion of Thief (which was my favorite) and you can quickly get turned around or end up running into a wall but the arrow to your next objective is through it. The game requires you to go through numerous windows and pick several locked doors, dodging out of sight. Even trying to use the map isn't very helpful because it stacks the different layers upon each other. I also miss the Brotherhood in there, forest guys, or even the main dudes in robes. Have yet to encounter any forms of mutants. The lock picking system is a new thing where you don't turn the mouse and line it up to the exact spot like the old ones. Instead it's rotate the mouse until a little bubble lights up and you can unlock it. No worries on your lock pick breaking though, it just alerts the nearby guard that has super hearing and can hear that little click. Does make the lock picking quicker but also a little less demanding and challenging.
Overall, it's got a pretty decent story, does keep you wanting to play more, and doesn't let you just go crazy with attacking things, actually making you do stealth like a proper Thief game should. The graphics do start to look the same and repetitve, but that's only something minor. I give it a 7/10 but only if you like sneaky games. Do not view it as a promising replay once beaten game, but if you take it slow can offer hours of good enjoyment.

First of all, let me start by saying that I think this game got critisized so unfairly that it's not even funny. Too many people comparing it to the orginal Thief games (which I have not played) and Dishonored. While I haven't played the original Thief games, I've noticed most of the reviews are bashing the game for not being like the originals, in other words, fan boys. And the other spectrum seems to be people comparing it too closely to Dishonored.
Let me just say this, it is -not- Dishonored. Not by any means. Yes, it has the first person stealth aspect, but to me personally, it plays completely different. Unlike in Dishonored, Thief almost requires you to rely soley on stealth, and as the name implies, steal as much as you can. That being said, there is almost no combat whatsoever aside from stealth knockouts so you can slip by guards. This is another reason I feel the game was unfairly rated, because it doesn't have all the combat sequences that most AAA titles today are loaded with.
This game requires -patience-. You can't simply bumrush your way through, expecting to cut everyone down in your path. You have to plan your approach, study guard patrols, and decide when and if you should slip by in that particular direction, or find another way around. For any true stealth fan out there, you will absolutely love this game.
Now, as for another one of my points about people comparing it to other games. Dont do that. I can almost guarentee you, that if you go into it expecting it to be something it's not, you will hate it. You have to appreciate the game for what it is, and not try to compare it or make it seem like another. And it is a wonderful first person stealth game.
Again, the object of the game is almost purely stealth. You're a thief, not an assassin, you're not supposed to run around killing everything you see. Doesn't mean you cant, but you're not going to have a good time as the guards are very tough and the combat it does have was clearly not designed to be used in open conflict.

It is the story that makes The Cat Lady outstanding. It is an original horror story that had me in its grip for the whole time to complete the game. The main protagonist is Susan Asworth, a 40-year-old woman who in the beginning of the game swallows a whole bunch of sleeping pills to end her life. Her suicide attempt hurls her into a world of supernatural, darkness, madness, violence and perversion. A lot of disturbing situations and imagery goes on throughout the game. The story also deals with themes like depression and terminal illness — themes that rarely are a subject in video games. Somehow the game reminds me of the 90's cult classic adventure games Harvester and Sanitarium.
Even though The Cat Lady feels like a descendant of the nineties point and click adventure games, the controls aren't actually "point and click" style, because the player uses a keyboard instead of a mouse. It can feel a bit clunky at first, but it's not something that the player can't get used to. Also, the characters can only move left and right on the screen — the areas are not "pseudo 3D" like in the classic adventure games.
The graphics might be a turn-off for some of the contemporary gamers. It's pixelated, and I couldn't find a way to change the resolution or the aspect ratio, and was stuck with 800 x 600 resolution and 4:3 ratio. I didn't mind that. The graphics and overall visual style of the game appeal to me a lot. Also the sound design is enjoyable. The music fits the twisted and horrific tone of The Cat Lady. Voice actors are doing a great job.
The puzzles aren't too frustrating and there's not much backtracking. The game's rather easy and it took me approximately seven hours to beat it. There is an annoying "feature" that won't allow you to make more than 50 game saves and you can't delete the saved games in-game to make more room for new saves. You have to do it manually in the saved games folder. Other than that, the game worked flawlessly.
I loved the whole gaming experience and The Cat Lady surely is going to be a cult classic of the future.

As a start, I want to say I don't have anything against the walking simulator genre. I think we're past the point where interactive art has to be a game to be worth time and/or money.
There are a few positive things to be said about TIMEframe.
First the premises are nice, if not originam. Being able to explore a dying world free of its inhabitants is the same pleasure that one can enjoy by rising early and taking a stroll in empty streets.
The art is quite nice too. Though minimalistic, it's style is used well enough that it doesn't feel out of place. The colour palette, though limited, does its job quite well, and while it's not the most magnificent thing I've ever witnessed, it possess indeniable charm.
The style in which the lore is written seems good, but english not being my native language, I can't really be sure.
Now I can't really recommend this guys for a few reasons.
First of all, despite the nice lore, and nice visual, the world that the visitor (I wouldn't call them a player) doesn't seem like a world at all. The places to visit are placed arbitrarily on the map which immediately make it seem artificial. Since the ambiance and wolrdbuilding are quite important in this kind of experience, I find it quite regrettable the immersion gets broken this quickly.
The place the visitor is set to explore doesn't feel like it had ever been populated. They're not seeing a place emptied of its inhabitants, it looks, and in fact is, a place sollely created to be explored by us. And it shows quite a bit.
The other sad thing, though I can't really blame the developpers to made it that way, is that the visitor has a short timeframe to visit the world before its destruction. It puts them in a bit of a rush to get from point A to point B, and puts a dent in the will to really explore. Not that there is that much to explore.
It looks and feel like a student project (which is not an insult by any mean.), and a nice one, but there is not so much more to it.
So there you have. I like this pice of interactive art. Not love it, I just find it interesting enough to believe it deserves a bit of your time.
But certainly not your money.

EDIT: Now for the real review!
Star Ruler 2 is a 4X-RTS game. There are multiple factions with different abilities and shipsets. There is heavy modding support and there is over 150 items on the workshop. There is complete ship customization(except for the look). You can test your designs in the design sandbox and still be able to use them in SP. You can only build more ships if you have a much bigger ship that can support them.Sorry, that last one was really wordy, I'll make it in better terms. You have larger ships such as the capital ships, dreadnaughts, and really anything larger than that. they each have a support capacity, and you can select ships that fit the support category to follow that larger ship. Hence the name "Support". all different saupport  ships have different support points depending on the weapons, armor, size, etc.  and different factions have different ships.
But not all of the factions have different ships. There is only 3 shipsets, but If you download all of the ones that arent copies of each other from the workshop then the count ammounts to around 53 shipsets. You expand by colonizing, and increasing the level of the planet by giving it certain rescources. Then you can build buildings on the planet and orbital structures. And you can have as many ships as you want! As long as you have the rescoruces to build them. YES!!!!! THAT MEANS THERE IS NO UNIT CAP!!!!!
In a nutshell Star Ruler 2 is an action-packed game with quick decisions that could kill you or make you win, and the enemy will be rutheless unless you stop them quick. This is a game that space game players will love A LOT if they take the time to learn the game and have fun playing it! I hope this was helpful! Now that Wake of the Heralds is out: it's a great expansion, only $10 as well! The new shipset is great and the mechancs of the 2 new factions are also really good. not to mention personalities as well, they can give you new bonuses while you're playing! there's a lot to say, so just check out the DLC yourself. You can figure it out a lot better than I can probably.
But to close off this review I have one more thing: Dont take forever on the tutorial since a lot of that info you most likely wont use until you learn a lot more, and so what I want to get across is that just have fun and build a really big fleet and watch it fight to the death! I did it with 30k size fleets on each side! AND IT WAS SO EPIC!!!!! I hope you all have fun playing Star Ruler 2!

The story line makes no sense next to FarCry3 which actually had a survival element to it. The missions are easily relatable to knock offs of the 3rd game. Character development has no depth and the main missions advance simply far too quickly to connect to any of the main characters.

FC4 feels like a well polished version of FC3, the mechanics and graphics look amazing, the landscape is more open and terrain a little more diverse with more vertical challenges.  I still think there is a lot of repetition in a lot of the villages and missions, overall a great game.  I give an 8/10.

A game that wants to be Metroidvania crossed with Dark Souls. and it almost gets it right. I don't think it fully understands either genre at their core.
It doesn't quite get the pacing of exploration and upgrades to call it a good Metroid style of game. the map is a bit too linear, with a few obvious shortcuts between areas, and marked inaccessible areas that you can backtrack to later for secret trinkets. Though there's only one ability that really matters for exploration: transforming into a cat. The rest is just finding specific keys instead of abilities, though the map doesn't give a clear sense of direction for the non-linear mid-game. You don't really advance in power very much, as even if you find a bunch of new items, they all must compete for your 5 equipment slots. You can swap them out in the pause menu, but it's so much of a hassle I didn't bother except during boss fights. however, the offensive upgrades are so ridiculously good that every other item seems superfluous.
And though the game goes for higher than average difficulty, it's no Dark Souls either. it's a little too easy to learn enemy patterns, since it's just a 2D platformer. for defense and maneuvering, rolling solves everything. honestly, most of the difficulty is in the damage you take when hit (on Normal or above). even with a lot of HP upgrades, you can maybe survive 5 hits instead of 3. the refillable healing items, though similar to Estus, seem more like a crutch than a feature. "I can brute force this many mistakes." In other words, it's an easy game that punishes you hard when you slip up, instead of a hard game that gives you some freedom for trial and error.
Despite all those flaws, I still really like this game and think it's worth it. From the above influences I mentioned, it also does so many things right. Boss fights are fun and intense, and feel much more balanced to the game system. The platforming and action are so smooth and fine tuned. The creepy atmosphere and feeling of isolation. Fragmented and intentionally vague storyline that requires some piecing together. Very minimal use of cutscenes (whew!) but still some interesting NPCs that flesh out the setting. Well, I wish you could interact with the NPCs a little more, such as when you're a cat. Missed opportunity, I demand more cat gameplay.
Do I even need to mention the graphics when you can watch the trailer yourself? It's amazing, and I'm not easily impressed. Far too many indie games go for ~rEtRo PiXeLs~ without knowing how to properly use them. some of them compensate with overly fluid animation that looks completely out of place... or worse, pseudo-minimalism. But this game is a genuine example of pixel art done tastefully. And to be honest, I really love the CaveStory-esque flat color sprites. I want more games in that style.
EDIT: In retrospect I think my review sounded too nitpicky and negative, so I wanted to clarify. I'm comparing this game to the very best, only because it strived for perfection. It's so rare to find a retro-style indie game with this much ambition! Momodora aimed for the stars, and while I think it didn't quite hit its goal, it's still light years above ALL the competition.
I have a feeling that the creator's next game will be even better.

is a pirate based open-world, role-playing, an adventure game that takes place in the fortress of the Inquisition. The main enemy of the Inquisition is called Titan Lords. Titan Lords are rather gods which have been cast into the sea . The gods became angry once pirates started turning on each other; now there is a great war between the Titans and pirates. In fact, a goddess named Mara controls the seas and the ocean currents. We could call her, the goddess of the seas much like Poseidon who sends judgment on everyone and causes the rainwaters to pour out from underneath the earth. Our mission is simple, go on the Black Betty which is a ship that takes you to Tacarigua, blend in with the prisoners, and mention nothing about us linked to the Inquisition. Our fate if we go back on our word is death.
The shipping area in Tacarigua houses prisoners that are taken away to slave ships and shipped out under merciless conditions. While
is a Caribbean pirate game full of adventure, enemy encounters, loot, and new discoveries through talking to non-playable characters, it gives you a choice through a set of dialogue options to control your path you take. You can become either a hospitable guy or you can become a smart aleck, arrogant fool in front of others that will quite literally, school you in the art of fighting, defense mechanisms. Others, you can steal from storekeepers storehouses, but you will be penalized because all of them will try to duel you.

In any open-world based adventure, role-playing game, the presentation is one of the most important features to determine whether the game can live on. In
we have a beautiful Caribbean outpost in the main game with a tower, well-done steps, a beach with caves here and there, an ocean full of war-like ships with realistic wave physics, build construction. It transports you to places you cannot always go in real-life but would want to see. For example, not everyone lives on a beach or a shore in their daily life. The main character is quite arrogant, and he can get drunk on some days. However, the majority of the presentation centers around going back and forth between non-playable characters and quest logs to find where to go next as well as any more information you may have missed along the way. Sometimes there are things you can collect on the beach such as provisions you can turn into shopkeepers in exchange for other goods and gold.
However, at times, as in the case early on in the game, they will be stingy and have you get the gold from somewhere else. One example is in the first area where we have to find the barrels and crates on the beach that were left over provisions washed up on the beach shore after a Kraken took one of the ships down  looking from the tower of the outpost with our conversation with Carlos. Hard rainwater falls down, and caves are silent with enemies hidden under its foregrounds such as the Sand Devils, the first enemy we come across. These Sand Devils are nasty creatures; they are low in the ground and act like beetles trying to thrust their weight in front of us only for intimidation. Even worse, is they hide on the side and usually appear in groups which can kill us easily if not careful.

Combat is basic as in most pirate games would be. You start out with a simple dagger and a pistol. The pistol is far less efficient on most enemies because, later on, as a pirate, you will either use your basic sword or a variation of the base sword you are given. We can parry back and forth between enemies and clash our metal on their thick skulls. One major drawback is our first enemy, the Sand Devils. Parry is non-effective on Sand Devils because they travel in groups. They will attack you with more force when you never parry, which this forces you to constantly attack until they all die which is a larger risk at times before you have any chance of leveling up in
.
The key bindings for keyboard controls feel awkward; it is tied to capslock by default for running, but you have to keep capslock on the whole time while you are running. Otherwise, it will switch off again. Then, you will have to reinitiate capslock to sprint each time again. Also, the sneak key binding feels awkward and unusual, more so, hard to reach. I recommend you try to invest in a good controller for this specific game since it is open-world; you want to be comfortable for when you have to either walk or run long distances when fulfilling mission objectives and side quests for people. Otherwise, the combat is relatively simple compared to other games in this genre.

However, the main drawback is the lack of capabilities with a variety of different compatibility modes for the personal computer version. I doubt that the developer Piranha Bytes will fix this since the game came out in 2012 on the personal computer.
It is a shame too because the textures are in very great detail; they look straight out of a movie which could be compared to
and
.

While
is a solid game within an open-world Caribbean environment, it falls short of being great. The storyline is solid but takes a long time to build up proper action. The earlier battles are mundane without offering the adrenaline based pumped action we would expect if this game was made into a movie with a similar setting. The voice acting is superb but is not movie based quality which I was expecting from a game published by Deep Silver because they have never disappointed in that field of work. However, Piranha Bytes does include some very nice tropes and notable references to other pirate theme games can be gathered through its exploration. This is a game you should not go buy on a whim on any particular day, but one you should check out if pirate based movies interest you.
It fulfills the need for a very niche audience and a fan base that, simply, will not be for everyone. Are you that person that wants a pirate fantasy open-world role-playing game, or better yet, do you prefer
because of its stellar combat, better settings, along with better voice acting and graphics when it comes to pirate themed games? The choice is all yours.

Alright, I finished playing Depression Quest, and I must say I'm heavily neutral/leaning towards negative. While I could relate with a few things in the game(which it really isn't, but meh using the term cuz it's easy), it felt forced. A lot of positive options were drawn through and unselectable as if people who suffer from depression are incapable of making those decisions.
More often than not I found myself forced to select an option I'd never honestly choose and that to me seems unfair in an "interactive" narrative which is apparently (non)-fiction as well. I'm pretty sure the story you're reading is fiction so not quite sure why the non, but it's in parentheses so probably referring to something else.
I could honestly relate with how having a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ job can emotionally and physically drain you, I know how social anxiety can be, and I know how it feels to go blank. Hence why I'm neutral. It's not bad, but it's certainly not good. In fact the reason why I'm leaning towards bad is, because the game feels more like it's trying to make you feel bad instead of understanding how a person with depression thinks and what he/she goes through.
Not to mention some options/areas were just blown up for no reason. It's ok to worry, but damn some were just why? They do add the disclaimer that not all people who suffer from depression experience it the same way, however I don't feel this game actually informs anyone more than just makes you feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥if you mess up.
I got a positive ending and that was nice, but it still snuck in stuff to try and say you're still feeling bad, and that you'd never escape depression. That you'd have to deal with it forever no matter how happy you get or do. Uh, I'm pretty sure there are people who have beaten it, and even if this was 100% true, why would you say that? If you're trying to convey a positive note don't say, "Hey you're feeling better, but you'll never escape those feelings. Have a nice day. 8D"
All in all while the game is relatable at points, the fact that the game focuses so much on making you feel bad more than understanding bothers me greatly. I suffer from depression and have been diagnosed by multiple therapists, (♥♥♥♥ off self-diagnosed Tumblristas), and it ♥♥♥♥ing sucks.
At points it seemed like the game would get how it is across, but if anything I think anyone who doesn't suffer would just look at this and scream at the computer because they think the person is just being mopey and making himself feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥ That he's making zero effort most of the time to even try to improve his situation. Hell, just picking the options to improve the situation felt like I was forcing the character instead of seeing it through his eyes.
You know what, I'm not neutral on this. Gonna just go with negative, because I don't think it did what it was meant to do. It's also just going to make some people feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥ and others feel worse.

The Review in short:
+ Some Levels are well-designed, both in regards to the aesthetics and the gameplay
+ The loot and collectables are well-designed and a fun to hunt down. Stealing stuff is fun!
+ Some of the Puzzles are fun!
- The story is horrible.

Overall I recommend it, because there are a few really good stealing-levels, burried between pointless cutscenes and linear corridors you must walk through for no reason.
Here are some more details for those interested. Spoilers for the Thief-Series as whole ahead:
My biggest problem with this game is the way in which the reboot is done. They kicked out all the memorable parts of the Thief-Lore, like the Hammerites and Pagans, in order to go for a more boring version of the same. On a basic level, the Thief-Universe is still about the conflict between nature and industry and rationalism versus occultism. But whereas the old Thief-Games executed this in a bright and colourful way, this Thief-Game feels like the best way to tell it's story is in shades of black. Everybody in this story is either a Moron or an awful person. They try really, really hard to turn Garret into the Hero by having everyone else be more awful.
This in itself would not be so much of a problem, if they had executed it well. But they have not. The story is largely told through cutscenes, during which characters show up in places they have no reason to be and tell stuff they have no way of knowing. For example: The Thief-Taker-General - a character which the game really wants us to view as the villain but who turns out a joke - shows up in the high-security area of TWO burning buildings in order to tangle with Garret. How the Hell does this guy even know Garret is there? Isn't this game supposed to be about Stealth?! And how did he get there? Did he crawl through the air vent too?
In regards to stealth-gameplay, nothing has changed since the 90s, really. Dishonored managed to put a little innovation into the series with it's neat use of various magic abilities for stealth, but Thief doesn't even do that. You get to play the basic game as in previous installments, only in much smaller levels. Those levels are sometimes fun and enjoyable, but it is not innovative by any means. Of course it doesn't have to be innovative to be fun, just don't look for anything new here.

If you can accept that this is not a sequel, if you can somehow separate the two things, than you will find a great game. It's a different Thief, but it still do things quite well. It has a great atmosphere, nicely working stealth mechanics, less combat options (which for me in this genre was an improvement), and quite a lot of stuff to do (haven't seen much of the main plot yet, though I liked it so far, because I was sidetracking a lot). I think this game would have been much better received, if they gave it a different name, because people nowadays have crazy expectations and amazingly whiney attitude, and feeding them hype is the worst thing to do for any game, almost anything is doomed to fail this way (just look at Watch Dogs, which is also a decent game in my opinion). So if you like stealth games with great atmosphere and lots to explore, I can really recommend this one, but if you want to pick up the story of that (ok, it's true, won't deny it) better and cooler Garrett of old and see what happens after Deadly Shadows, then you will be disappointed.

A few days after the defeat of Gwendyal, Edward's wedding day is marked by the fact that Lydia used a disguise to be his wife. And Mel is seeing a strange ghost, Nox, kinda looking like her. Given the fact that the Orb of Death has been completed, your young thief/spy sets her eyes on finding it on another island. However, her old team can't travel with her: Stella is convinced that it's a trap, Edward isn't even aware of her departure, Lydia couldn't care less unless she uses that fact to be the sole ruler, Ulf prefers to stay and learn, Galahad and Tej'Imal are living on his native hometown, though our dear ex-vampiress is sulking about the fact that she's not anymore a blood sucker and her man is very happy about that fact. So, when Mel finally reaches her destination, she will find new allies: June, an apprentice magician, Yvette, a shapeshifter and Spooks, a strange thief...
Aveyond 3 was fragmented in four chapters. This one is the sequel to the first two and as usual, the story is well-written and full of humor: animals can talk in another village, with their own fight, June is very joyful, Yvette has some sarcasm in her, Spooks is creepy and the other characters retain their personality, though Lydia revealed herself as power hungry. I would have preferred her in a role less darker and the fact that I've bought her robes in the previous game is making me regret to have a spent a cent for her.
The game mechanics are still the same, though now, you don't have any healer anymore: June and Yvette have offensive and defensive spells, Ulf and Edward are only using weapons and Spooks is leaning towards Mel's skills. You can still level up to improve yourself but now, June can also increase her spell powers by using them during the fight. Also, the HUD above the characters during the fight changed and is more visual. I've also discovered that you can swap characters during a battle, something I thing you couldn't do before. Also, in the animal village, you have an alchemist shop where you can mix ingredient to obtain potions, serums or even pies. You'll find recipes all around the world.
Some quests needs to be done in order to advance in the story, while they're appearing as being a side-quest just for the money. Others are just bonus. But given the fact that you need money to buy stuff or to fast-travel, any quest is worthy to be done. Besides, when defeating enemies, you can loot them and find also money or items. You have also chests to open or bags to find.
As you lost your pirate ship, your only way to come back to Harburg, Thais and any other town on the mainland is a special ferry. But you can also use warp eggs (the red is taking you back to the Moo Hatchery, the purple one to the animal village). The fast travel mirrors are still useful and when you're in the dead realm, you have also the Reaper that can connect you to the Vampire realm.
Aveyond comes also with three difficulties: Easy where you're stronger and where most of the enemies don't spawn again after a defeat (yeah, I'm playing in this difficulty), Normal where every is balanced and Hard where you'll die more frequently - though even in Easy, I've been wiped. Well, if a character dies, you can ressucitate them but if your team is wiped, it's game over and it's up to you to load the auto-save (when entering a new screen) or a save of yours.
And while I appreciate keeping my levels for my characters, I've lost all my money and all my gears. Just because Lydia made your life a little hell... So you don't have any good gear to begin with. Besides, even Edward didn't take Excalibur. I was disappointed.
Aveyond dates from 2009-10 and from an earlier version of RPG Maker but the graphisms are still good. Besides, the landscapes are still varied: while Thais, Stormbend, Witchwood and Harburg are still present, you're discovering now other towns: an oriental town, a medieval one, a eastern style, a port, etc...
I've spent 14 hours in it, showing that every Aveyond chapter takes time. However, strangely enough, I did felt like this was the shorter game. I don't know why.
Aveyond 3-3 isn't the best Aveyond out there. I largerly prefer the second chapter. Maybe because it was the lost of my gear, of my team (and my healer) and my ship that I felt like I wasn't going to like the chapter. It's still enjoyable, however, without Tej'Imal and Galahad, I've lost powerful teammates, without Stella, I don't have any good healer and many questions are still unanswered like Nox (though I've cheated and looked into the Aveyond wiki, well, I wasn't really far from the truth about her). Still, the game is worthy.
Continues the story. A little different than other three chapters.

Like the first one, combat is a lot of normal attacking. June's spells do get uesd, but mainly to level them up. Once they're all rank 5 there is littl reason to use any other than poison and confusion. Her normal attacks often will be stronger. Yvette's first form has a useful group attack. Other forms have some gimmicks. But she's not bad. If the allied effects were group cast she'd be a lot better off.
Traveling in this one is a huge pain. There is a LOT of back and forth between many areas.
Keeping your team properly geared requires a bit of farming. A bit too much for me personally. I don't mind it a little. It often means you're skipping too many mobs. But in this one you can kill everything between traveling points and still only get 25% of the gear you need at the next stop. Generaly left moving to the next area and trying to survive for the higher gold worth. Since combat isn't exactly anything special, this gets kind of dull fast.
The next new gimmick is Alchemy. Like gearing up, it requires a lot of repeated moving around. Luckly it's really not all that useful overall. There are a few quest points that require it and maybe two potions worth caring about(one for a quest, one for travel assistance). So it's not too horrible. But is kind of a let down for these reasons.
Overall the rest of it should feel like the last two. There's a less exploring to do, gearing up can be a chore. The rest can be ignored.

This is a story rich adventure game with very dark themes of suicide, depression and murder.
Visually it has a unique big-sprite animation style, I recalled an old Popeye game I used to play on my Spectrum.  But instead of vibrant colours the environments are almost invariably shades of dull greys, greens, blacks and blues.  Usually a huge turn off for me, I found this environment very comfortable to play in, in this game.
The controls are simple - cursor keys and enter, nothing more.  This gives the game the great pro of being 100% playable while the player is eating. It's so much better, not just with immersion, but being able to fully ride on the story's coattails without too much doggedness.
As I said previously, it's a rich story-based game where multiple choice dialogue leads the way throughout.  There is a lot of text and just as much voice - the latter being unskippable(?) which usually gets on my nerves quick in this type of adventure (thinking point and clicks) but did not in this game at all for some reason.  Maybe it was because there is so much of it, and the lines are so varied.  The voice acting is better in some places more than others - I liked the varied accents, it was more the rushed and mushy pronunciation at times - but the lead lady does a great job.  On the flip side, one of the slight annoyances I had during my playthrough was how easy it was to skip text on screen, would have preferred less sensitivity there - whether through assigning a different button, or through the programming itself.  The thing that didn't make this more serious a problem is that most of the dialogue was easy to repeat.
In general the game will make sure you get the right experiences at the right time, so it is linear in that aspect, but for me that was a pro in this game's instance.
I'd recommend this to mature adventure game fans and fans of story rich games.  A very enjoyable, sub-10-hour, easy to play adventure game with an unusually heavy dark tone throughout.

I love walking simulators. Dear Esther blew me away. I love atmospheric games. I love exploration. This game takes all that, puts a timer on it, and slaps it in the face.
Why would you make this excellent, atmospheric world, and make it so I can't explore? What does the timer add? I would so much rather explore the world at my own pace than retread the same ground time after time just to get slightly farther. I would so much rather take my time and soak in the (awesome!) underground crystal mine or the abandoned city than spend 5 seconds looking for the thing to click on before I move on so I can reach another destination before the stupid meteor hits. I would so much rather take my time reading each passage and pieceing together the lore than rush through it so I don't run out of time.
Why?
Just a frustrating game experience with so much potential from an art and worldbuilding standpoint.
