This is one of the games for which I'd really like to have a "mixed" rating option. Since there is none, it gets a very hesitant thumbs-up.
In TIMEframe, you freely explore a small map with 15 buildings (or similar structures) that are remnants of a vanished civilization. Each of them contains one artifact - usually a plaque, or an object that sticks out. Clicking on an artifact brings up a short text paragraph that gives a little insight in the lost civilization's culture. After clicking on all artifacts, and visiting the last building, you have discovered the entirety of the game and finished  the story.
Gameplay consists solely of walking around and looking for the 14 spots to click on. There are no puzzles, and the buildings and objects are very easy to find (you even have a map that marks the locations). The point of this game is not to challenge the player, but rather to tell a simple story and immerse the player in a melancholic atmosphere. The story elements are extremely short, but well-written, and showcase various facets of an alien culture.
There is a comet falling down on the map in slow motion. After 10 minutes of playing, the comet will hit the ground and reset the game (though the game does remember which objects you've already found, so you don't have to visit these again). The comet is a potentially interesting mechanic, and it does add to the atmosphere, but to be honest, it is almost pointless in terms of gameplay. All it does, is forcing you to walk some paths two or three times, since it effectively teleports you back to the center of the map when it hits.
The graphics are intended to resemble "early 3d playstation" looks. Personally I think that a ground made of blocky lines and distinct polygons looks rather ugly, but it might evoke some nostalgia among players who have fond memories of games with that look. Some of the structures and features are indeed beautifully designed, but the intentionally crude modeling made it harder for me to appreciate that.
The music, on the other hand, is truly excellent. It skillfully carries the melancholy throughout the game, without ever becoming annoying or overdone.
Do I recommend TIMEframe? Yes, but only to a small subset of players. Look at the screenshots, and ask yourself whether you will enjoy walking through this world for about an hour, while listening to melancholic tunes, and occasionally finding a short text to read that gives you a glimpse of a foreign culture. For many players this will not be an engaging experience, but for some it will. Personally I appreciated it, and I don't think it's a bad game, but on the other hand I played many explorative games that I enjoyed more than this one. I believe that the current price tag of 7,99€ is a bit too high considering how little content there is.

Fortunately for this game, you can try again in this game if ya screw up by Zoe Klein. But it's not worth doing it. Or even picking up to play in the first place.
To start, this is a choose your own adventure storygame. It's a game, but it'd be better off as a book.
The concept is interesting, but the format doesn't help much, as while it is harder to choose the right answer unlike other adventures, the way to a happy ending can still be seen. I made it through to a happy ending on my first run of the game.
After that, I didn't really want to get to the bad endings as they're probably easily predictable and it's manipulatable too. I clicked randomly and got a bad ending in no time.
On the topic of story, since I probably should have talked about that first. For someone who's read way too many books, the story is predictable for me. Positive decisions lead to positive endings, and vice versa. You have to choose some negative options first and then you move onto help, presumably because that was not the creator's intention and it would make a boring game if all the good answers were right in front of you.
The characters are also boring and cliched. Almost no one was very memorable unless you count yourself. You've seen these types of characters before. The one exception would be the main character, who is easy to project yourself onto if you've been through the experience, and hard as hell if you don't. It's a mixed bag.
On a side note, the main character doesn't really seem to have the despair and loss of hope in the darker storylines that I hear about in the media and know about from my friends.
A gripe I have with this game is that it's not explained where the depression comes from. You are told you have it. That's it. For me that is some real BS, as it's hard to sympathize with the main character (if that was the point), or more importantly understand him and some of his actions.
You're told on how you feel about certain situations and then given options on proceeding. One thing that's good is that the choices seem like possible answers and emotions shown also seem realistic, contributing to the atmosphere well. But unless you've been through depression, it's hard for a lot of people to experience the emotions that the protagonist feels by telling them. You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make it drink. I sympathized with the actions, but I'm sure that a bunch of others will look cluelessly on and then write a review about them not getting it.
This is compounded by the aspects of it being a game, since a player has control and must play. Depression Quest has this odd botched mix between choosing your own way and characterization that doesn't go well at all. You choose, but you're told how to feel. That does not work well because the idea of choosing your own adventure to "win" conflicts with emotions felt by a character you don't know. You aren't the character, you're God playing with a puppet.
The graphics are what they need to be. They contribute well to the atmosphere by being simplistic. I don't think the graphics changing would have made the game any better. The blurry effects are a nice touch, making things a lot more depressing and contributing to the atmosphere.
The music is something I can't comment on, since I played it without sounds without knowing it had a soundtrack.
The gameplay? Get real guys, it's choose your own adventure. What were you expecting?
Who is this game for? I'm not really sure.
Some depressed people may sympathize with it and others may use it as comedy material. It might even make some others saddened. Others will relate, but even others with depression won't. It's definitely a mixed bag.
"Normal" gamers probably will figure it out fast. Looking at the comments section, that wasn't hard. If the purpose was to educate them, all you have is a bunch of people asking why the options are chosen. Since the character's depression is not explained (if it is either I'm a moron or it wasn't explained well), there aren't really any answers.
Depression Quest is an interesting concept about a man with depression and his struggles, but marred by the conflict between game and story. The game just interferes with whatever this game tries to do, as games generally want you to win.
It left an emotional impact on me with its atmosphere and content, but that isn't good enough. For this to be good, it must be a book. Not a game, not choose your own adventure, but a book about a man with depression. And if the purpose was to educate people about depression, it needs for its characters to be fleshed out and to follow a story about a character, not you playing a puppet.
Read a book about someone's issues with depression. Watch a movie. Talk to someone who is depressed. If you want to know about depression, this game is not your best bet. The stuf listed may not be free, but your time is better spent somewhere else.
Perhaps if you've experienced the situations you will relate and find the game more appealing.
Thanks for reading my first review.

High recommended. Solid FPS and RTS elements, with a lower learning curve than say NS2 (which is also great). The lower learning curve DOES NOT mean that it is easy to win or dumbed down in anyway. If anything there are more options to choose from (each of the four classes has three different specialisations (Exo/Heavy has two), with unique abilities & tools to choose from), which complement different strategies well. There is also a degree of persistent levelling which allow new gadgets/'perks' to be unlocked as players progress.
Maps are pretty big with different play styles associated with each (some of CQB heavy, others more open sniper maps), all of which still require considerable team work in order to succeed.
Given Nuclear Dawn is built on the Source engine, the graphics are great and really add to the feel of battling it out in a post apocolyptic environment, with many buildings being able to be entered.
If you're looking for something different from the faster paced CS / BF / CoD one-man-army bullet fest, with a bit more strategic depth and a great community to boot, I would highly recommend Nuclear Dawn. One of the best games I've played in a while.

Telling stories around a campfire might seem antiquated, but The Yawhg replaces both the fire and the stories with its own tales of a civilization on the brink of the collapse. You and three friends take roles in the town just a week before ensured destruction. Attend a ball, clean a hospital, or even fight crime. The Yawhg presents imminent danger and allows you to forge a healthy backstory and stat sheet in only a few days. The real treasure is seeing how these actions affect your friends or the town itself. Once the town is overcome with darkness, it's up to you and your friends to triumph or despair with your experiences.
It's a superb bit of storytelling.

A quirky and quaint little game.  The story lines are funny and rather strange, but that makes them interesting.  They can also be unexpectedly dark.  The art is very bright and colourful, and the music, though only two songs, is pleasant.
Most people complain about it being too short (each round is about 10 minutes), although I think it's meant to be that way so you can play multiple rounds quickly, seeing as it can be difficult to save the town when you're still new to the game.  I wish there was more variation, though; once you've played about 10 rounds, you've basically seen everything, and saving the town becomes quite easy.
There are some typos in the game (I think I spotted about two or three), which is a little disappointing given that it's primarily text-based.  Also, I can't seem to run the game in windowed mode, although I know not everyone has this problem.  You can't skip the credits at the end, although they only last about 15 seconds, so I don't think that's a big deal.

I'd been eyeing this game up for a while because I was digging the graphics style in the preview and finally picked it up on sale.  Man... shouldn't have bothered waiting for a sale.  It's a point-and-click adventure game that is really not very hard at all - it's not meant to be difficult - but it is one heck of a story that drags you in.  When I first played this game, I only expected to play for about 15 minutes or so just to get a quick taste.  Eight hours later I've finished one of the story endings and the longest single gaming session I've done in years.  If Darren Aronofsky did video games instead of movies, he'd do something like this.
The main character, Susan Ashworth, is suicidally depressed and her depression is a driving factor in the story.  The depression is very tastefully and maturely handled and even while Susan has her 'woe-is-me' moments the game itself never falls into that trap.  Susan herself comes across as very real and not a caricature and it becomes very easy to care for her and what happens.
Replayability?  There's eight different endings if I remember right and a large number of steam achievements but it just doesn't feel right going back to grind the game for achievements, like that would be a disservice.  I'll let this sit on the shelf for a while but will definitely be back.

This game was flaming dreadful. But i was intrigued to keep playing. An awful, awful first impression. Holy cow it was ugly. I stuck at it, through the walking from one end of the screen, and back again, 100 times. I just stuck at it. It got worse, but i stuck at it.
I couldn't get past it's ugliness. It was just terrible. The music fell flat on so many occasions and made me cringe at some points, it felt very amateur and it just didn't fit right at certain scenes. Some of the voice acting was hilariously bad. Susan's voice wasn't badly acted, but sometimes it didn't quite 'fit'. It felt as though she was trying a little too hard on the sounding dreary and depressed tone that it became very monotone as the game went on. Even when faced with grosteque and terrifying situations, she was sarcastic and dreary.
I liked Mitzi, she was belivable and she was sweet. She was a well rounded character in a game that was otherwise devoid of them (think Pest Control dude, seriously...). Her voice actress was really great.
I was moved on a couple of occasions, (without spoiling anything) one involving Liz, and one involving Zoe. The scenes lingered for just the right amount of time for it to sink in, and it was touching. I thought it a huge shame that i felt unable to truly believe in Susan's depression and sadness. I felt that it was just textbook - bad things have happened to this woman, she's ended up miserable and depressed. Why not have it so that she's a woman with good prospects, a nice family life, living in a nice area, and yet she's burderned with depression? A story centered around her struggles with it despite her 'have-it-all' life could have been really interesting. People say 'what have you got to be depressed about?', unknowing that's not how depression works. It seems though that Susan Ashworth has a million and one things to be depressed about, and it's just too easy. Depression is much much deeper than what this game portrays it as. Mitzi asks Susan at one point 'What is depression like?' and Susan answers 'It's feeling as though all i want to do is die...but instead i have to live'. Simple as that apparently. And that is what the entire game is based on, Susan Ashworth being miserable because she is alive.
I wanted so much more from a game that looked so gritty and strangely dark. I wasn't expecting the gore and grotesque nature of it. I didn't feel it was justified, it was a little random if anything. It was a game full of bad guys, with Susan being a misery to play, i didn't connect with her as she took on a bunch of fairytale weirdos. Weirdos that i've seen a thousand times before in games and films. There was nothing unique or new about them, some even coming across as silly, rather than frightening. Mitzi was a small ray of light in a really really bleak setting, she brought a feeling of real life to the game (although i must admit her own story and motives were far fetched and not entirely realistic). The ending let me down - it summarised depression as something you just shutup and get on with. Something it seemed Susan HAD been doing up until she killed herself at the very beginning of the game! It was an ending without feeling, without real care for what happened next. You wrapped things up (kinda, i mean, half of it made no sense) and yet despite all of the disturbing and terrible things Susan had experienced, she spoke as though she'd just had a lousy week.
I was left with the question of 'what the hell did i just play?'.
I wish it would have been a game based on my original assumptions - Playing as a lady who lives with and looks after a bunch of cats. At least that would have had a deeper storyline.

I've been a fan of the series since the original CryTek Far Cry game.  Too bad many had (or still have) problems running it on lower-end hardware.   I am fortunate enough to be able to run the game at max settings and it was quite an experience, visually and from a gameplay perspective.
Pros:
- True open world gameplay.  There is a lot of s**t to do.  Blowing up Pagan Min's minions, hunting, exploring various locations, etc.
- Great graphics.  This game gives Crysis 3 a run for its money.  However, you will need serious hardware to push the Dunia engine to its maximum settings (I'm running the game on a Core i7 4790X and a single R9 290X 4Gb video card with zero issues).
- The Buzzsaw machine gun.  Just awesome firepower.  Once you unlock this baby, you'll be having the time of your life.
Cons:
- The campaign storyline is weak, Far Cry 3 was better in every way in that regard.
- The ending sucked.

First of all, this game has a great atmosphere, it's fantastic building tension. Throughout the game there were a number of sections where I knew what I had to do, but I really didn't want to because I knew it was going to be scary!
Although sometimes the story can get a bit 'out-there', the overall plot draws you in. Characterisation is fantastic, a great mix of disturbing and ordinary people with some good voice acting. In particular the two protaganists are really likable, despite their tragic stories.  Occasionally the voice recordings sound a little poor, but this doesn't pull you from the game.
I loved the orginal graphic style, which suited the atmosphere of the game, also making for some good use of colours. Even though it was a bit low-res there weren't too many "find the pixel" moments and the puzzles were fairly logical if you thought about them for a bit.
Overall, if you don't mind a story and text heavy game, you will be pleasantly rewarded playing this dark twist on what depression can feel like. I loved it!

Far Cry 4 was pretty fun. It captured all the open world freedom and country liberating mayhem that you had in the previous instalment and it throws it into a new Himalayan setting with a few new cool skills and twists.
Overall the story wasn't very complex but they do throw you a few curveballs by the end. The villain Pagan Min is probably the only likable character in the game, and unfortunately you don't interact with him all too much until the later portions of the game. Besides this however, the game plays great. You feel like an absolute bad♥♥♥♥♥once you unlock a few of the skills, and you can use many different tactics to take on any situation. The game gives you a few memorable set pieces such as driving a quad bike off a cliff-side runway, using your wingsuit to catch up to a plane that just took off, and then opening the door and throwing a grenade inside! Awesome stuff!
Far Cry 4 did not feel as refreshing and awesome as Far Cry 3 did when it came out, but it has definitely made some refinements and set this instalment in a new and great looking setting. Bring on the next one!

Despite some missteps, Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight is an easily recommendable game for your 2D Metroidvania-esque kick.
In case you didn't notice that in the trailers, the game looks amazing. The quality of the pixel art is one of the reasons why I become interested in the first place, but after playing the game I can easily confirm that artstyle, atmosphere, ambient music and overall presentation holds the bar pretty high thought the whole game with no major complains. Sprites are big, expressive and detailed (really loving the enemy designs!) and most environments are extremely polished as well. Decay and corruption is the name of the game here and It's realized masterfully by drab but beautiful locations and grim sound effects.
You can see that lots of thought went into level design. While the world isn't as big as in other games from the genre, it is planned very carefully. Interconnection of many areas allows for a quite a bit of freedom in tackling several areas in middle-game. Platforming challenges are also present, but they are tactful and not extremely demanding, so high skill isn’t required. Still, I would like to see some of the instant death spikes removed in few places. Those aren't viciously placed in particular but they are noticeable. There aren’t many upgrades and collectibles in comparison to other metroidvanias, but the gameplay is still well paced and there are few trinkets to collect. I need to mention a intuitive and non-annoying map and menus.
Combat is competent but very basic. You are given some melee attacks, dodges and ranged arrows, but I think that basic three-hit combo could use some company in form of few other melee moves and tactics. This isn't near being a deal breaker, since enemy encounters and especially bossfights, for what they are, present high excitement and pattern-reaction dodging action, which I really liked despite combat’s limitations. Still, there is a room for improvement.
The most glaring, wasted opportunity of the game is it’s story. This game is a prequel to the previous installments and it is implied that you don't need to know any events from previous Momodora titles to enjoy it. While this is technically true and story isn't nowhere near bad by itself, I'm afraid that game failed in giving enough lore and exposition for the new players. Fortunately, setup of the game is clear and you won't roam aimlessly not knowing what to do, but the game really could use some more flavor text in many places. Game sometimes takes benefit or you not knowing the basics of Monomora's lore, especially in the interesting ending sequence, but otherwise you would really like to know more about the world and characters. Worst offenders of exposition drought are the boss characters that appear and disappear without much explanation about their goals and whereabouts. Your opponents look like really interesting characters, but they aren't fleshed out, set up properly or they often leave the scene in undisclosed fashion. I would really like to squeeze more out of the game’s story, for example by NPCs changing their dialog depending on the plot events or optional story-driven locations.
While you can beat the game in 4 hours on your first try, it is ultimately satisfying adventure worth the asking price. There is a clear incentive of New Game+ mode and achievement encouraged challenges, so there is some replayability to the game after the initial run. I like to judge games based on the condition "Would I really like to replay the game again after finishing it". In that case, I can easily recommend this game. While flawed, it’s a wonderful little title with great presentation and honest effort. I really wish that dev will use experience from making this game as a base for new subsequent releases.

It's been a while since any 4x turn based game has held my attention for long. I had been looking for a good 4x game with a modern spin, but the current batch of popular 4x games just re-hash the same old mechanics that have been around since the dawn of 4x; the constant min-maxing, end-turn clicking, and save/reload experience that, to me, turn 4x games into something other than a game. They lose any kind of action feel and quickly the ADD kicks in; I'm moving on to something else.
Along comes Star Ruler 2, a 4x game in a sense, but more, with an additional RTS element allowing you to fully control time. It sounds novel and has probably been done in some other game(s) I'm not aware of. But it is expertly done in this game, to the point that I would like to tip my hat to the developers with a rare post of admiration. Truly, the thought put into the overall design is pretty genius. From the endless setup options, fully 3D galaxies, orbiting planets, ship designer and sandbox tester, the built in community page and IRC, tab UI functions, to the very awesome, imo, space battles. And even better, it all seems to be coded well; I have yet to experience any issues.
In the end it appears this game was put together by gamers and lovers of 4x, RTS, and space sims; they melded those genres very well into the fabric of this game.

Well, this is long overdue, and I still feel I'm going to do it wrong, but... better do it now and try to help out, I guess.
So, I'm going to start this review off with a bit of background information to explain just why I think this game, despite some shortcomings, might be the best thing that has happened to the 4X genre since its equivalent of sliced bread:
Its predecessor, Star Ruler, was characterized by the devs as 'a mod for its engine', with SR2 being said to be even more so. Indeed, if you stripped away all the stuff that could be read in a human-comprehensible form by something as simple as Notepad, the only thing left aside from the core engine's binaries (which presumably handle files, graphics, sounds and all that backend stuff no sane or insane modder would need to tamper with) would be textures, models, sounds and particle systems. (And you can change those, too - you just need proper tools to handle all of those except the particles, which are handled by a built-in particle editor.)
All of the game's logic and mechanics are exposed to anyone with an understanding of AngelScript - starship movement, AI, the Senate, even the code responsible for displaying the main menu instead of an empty black screen, for crying out loud! If Space Empires 4 and 5, Star Wars: Empire at War (not a 4X, but it gets some pretty significant mods anyway, and some of the teams there moved on to SOASE) or Sins of a Solar Empire could have been considered 'very moddable', SR2  probably goes off the scale.
Modding enthusiast's ranting aside, the base game is nice:
Customization: While it lacks the ability to write up your own lore for custom races (something that I admit I never took advantage of in Space Empires), racial customization is fairly meaningful, with 7 (more with mods) lifestyles which change the way the race plays in large or small ways, depending on the lifestyle. Governments have more of an early-game impact, while your choice of FTL method, like your choice of lifestyle, necessarily affects the way you run your empire. Another more subtle way of making your race stand out has yet to be released, and will (if the devs' plans don't deviate from my current observations) be arriving with the free DLC or whatever they called it, somewhere during this summer.
Customizing ships is much more detailed. With a number of subsystems to choose from, you literally paint the layout of your ship (not entirely unlike Space Empires 5, though more free-form), which is then reflected on the ship's icon on the galactic map. Needless to say, the design of your ship also affects its combat performance in ways both subtle and overt alike.
Diplomacy: The diplomatic system is simultaneously fairly underdeveloped (treaties and stuff) and quite well-developed. You only have a handful of treaty clauses with which to sign treaties, and you can go to war, make peace, surrender (doesn't remove you from the game, you now become a vassal and help your master win), and give various gifts. The main part of the game's diplomacy, however, revolves around obtaining various cards representing political actions - negotiation, abusing leverage, annexing planets... Doing all this stuff costs Influence, a resource which is generated in a fixed quantity and spread out amongst the empires based on their 'Influence Stake'. The more stake an empire has, the more influential it is, meaning one could hypothetically win a game through sheer power of influence. Bit of a long-term goal, though.
Economy: Past the initial stage of setting up your trade network, the micromanagement involved in running a star system is fairly minimal. Pressure from resources automatically instructs populations what 'civilian' buildings to use, and 'imperial' buildings are not something you simply spam whenever you can. There's a bunch of different planetary resources which contribute in different ways to leveling up your planets or producing global resources such as money, energy or influence.
Research: The somewhat chaotic, buff-driven (as opposed to giving new toys to play with) nature of the research grid has been criticized by some reviewers. I don't particularly have any feelings in either direction, and there are mods out there that attempt to change this, with Alarcarr's work on the grid in the 'Alternate Balance Expansion Mod' even being praised by at least one player.
Moddability: See the top of the review.
Scalability: With anywhere between 4 (or was it 5?) to over 1000+ star systems, and 2-28 (don't quote me on the upper limit, I just think I heard it somewhere) empires, the scale of the game depends solely on the desired duration and pace of the game, and the strength of your hardware. (I'm not from
, and more than 8 empires in a game is not recommended except on a LAN.)
The game is not without its drawbacks, though, as is always the case:
Combat: Yes, you can control your fleets in combat. (Which already tops all the Galactic Civilizations games! :P) You don't really get much out of it in most cases, though, as 'fleets' consist of an independent flagship and its armada of support ships, chained to the flagship. This is one of the things I dislike most about the game, really - it tends to just wind up as one supersized blob of ships flying in and fighting another supersized blob of ships until the bigger (or occasionally significantly better-designed) blob wins.
Unfortunately, it's too late to make it a turn-based game with real-time tactical combat, so there's (relatively) little that can be done to improve it, but I think making the combat closer to SOASE would already have been an improvement.
Ship customization: Well, one thing that people might complain about is that the layout of your ship doesn't entirely matter when determining the ship's physical appearance. This isn't Galactic Civilizations 2 with its 3D ship designer. :P (Such a thing was considered, if I'm not mistaken, but was scrapped in favor of optimization, multiplying the maximum ship count by a factor of 1000. I kind of have mixed feelings about that, as there are already more than enough ships to go around, but I must confess that a full 3D designer would make shipsets much harder to create.)
The vanilla game only has 4 shipsets, one of which is older and lower in quality than the others. (Also, it's the smallest one there is, with only a handful of hulls.) Some have said that there aren't enough shipsets/hulls to go around. This, for one, has already been corrected by various modders and their shipsets, and yet more shipsets seem inevitable.
Diplomacy: Like I said, the treaty side of SR2's diplomacy system is shallow compared to games like Space Empires 5. This, in my opinion, is still compensated for by the card side, but I felt I'd mention it anyway. (My pet peeve with it, though, is that you can only rename an object once. I have to find a way to make that work better. <.<)

You grab your giant blob and place it near the other guy's giant blob.  No maneuvering, limited AI settings, just a slap fight with lots of laser beams that stay on too long to look cool.
So no, I hella unreccommend this game.  It is a great pile of potential that just managed to suck all of the fun out of a giant spaceship game.

After completing the game, I have mixed feelings.
First, you can't take this game seriously. It's got intricacies and bugs like none other. Everyone talks like they're speaking sign language. You will complete missions before you are given them. At times, you will breeze through the combat. Other times, you will fire 180 degrees away from the enemies, roll into attacks, and instead of casting or shooting, the character will put down their weapon. Fighting is fun when it works. A lot of the time, it doesn't.
You are constantly picking flowers, and you can't help but look like a pansy. Cutscenes will skip without your consent. You can beat people up, rob them blind, and STILL they'll help you a few moments later. You recover healh slowly by eating food and quickly by drinking booze or sleeping on a random bed you happen across out in the open in the jungle. Auto-save will happen about once every 5 minutes to 3 hours.
You spend the whole game searching for amulets to defeat the ultimate evil... but in the end you don't really ever use them. The second to last boss will be unreachable for most of the game, but every 12 seconds will alternate between using the same predictable attack, and opening itself for retaliation... A leviathan monster, the Kraken, capeable of sinking ships.The rest of the time... you wait.
But, it's all-in-all, a pretty alright RPG. You have the leveling system, unlocking abilities, a choice between two factions, a gaggle of creatures with varying abilities, minigames. It's all nothing new, nothing you haven't seen plenty of times elsewhere. But it was still fun.

Clever, if very short, game that is strictly about exploration.
First, the soundtrack is excellent. My wife was watching me play and commented how she'd love to just listen to the soundtrack over and over (she didn't care much for the hyper-polygonal graphics).
I did have a few crashes when clicking on objects. The developers were very responsive, and I was unable to reproduce the crash on a second session of the game.
The game also seemed to randomly flash to "white" on me after a while, but it turns out this is intentional and part of the game's plot. The main problem here is that you have to be looking in the right spot to figure this out - I was exploring the "upper right" area of the map on my first few attempts and so didn't se the part of the map that clued me in until later.
As mentioned above, the game is very short. My stats say 1.1 hours, and that seems about right. You could probably get through this in 45 minutes or less if you knew what you were doing from the outset. There is a bit of cleverness to the game that is not immediately apparent, as I discovered when I went to collect the object that was falling off the 3 statues - this is what also clued me in to the real cause of the "white" screens.
With that in mind, know also that as far as gameplay goes, it is really just walking to a point, clicking on an object and repeating. There's not any depth here beyond that - it's strictly an explore-click type game, and a very brief one at that.
Rated 3 out of 5, if you enjoy a very short, very casual, very mellow experience. If you're not expecting more than that, you'll have a decent time.

TLDR: If you're interested in short, atmospheric pieces, download the free version and if you feel you want to sink a bit deeper then investing the money can very well be worth it (sales ftw!).
It's especially nice if you have no clue what it's about, so if that's the case and you're interested, don't read on, just go and play it.
I'm not sure why I'm so fascinated by this game (if that's what you want to call it; it's a walking simulator if I've ever seen one). Perhaps because it gives a glimpse of something that's lost and beyond saving. And the mood that comes with that is easily relatable.
Like in the original free version, you can explore what's left behind from an old civilization. Some locations were added, and, more importantly, some lore that gives an idea of what kind of people used to live here.
To me, the game is all about atmosphere which is conveyed superbly by the music and the simple, yet beautiful graphics. Add to that a feeling of timelessness and it's easy to get lost in it.
Ironically, the lore that was added for exploration also lessened the atmosphere somewhat. Whereas you could just enjoy the simplicity of the moment in the original version, here you suddenly have a goal to pursue, which creates a sense of urgency to actually use the time you have. And this goal is also emphasized by the game just automatically starting over, I'd much prefer it not to. I'd also like to be able to walk slowly, it feels too rushed at times.
But it's not that important when you've found your favorite tree to sit under, watching the leaves fall, enjoying the peaceful sounds in this still landscape.
A beautiful experience that feels all the better by not feeling like a real game.

Making an interactive story is not easy.  It is a lot slower then most games and takes quite a bit of paitence.  Paitence isn't my strong point, but I've sloged through interactive stories before.  I've actually had an engauging with them at times.  Playing a well made interactive story really is a lot like reading a novel, but better because of the added effects.
This isn't like reading a novel.  This is like reading bad Sadfic fan fiction.
So what is it that makes this story so taxing to get through?  It's terribly writen.  A good interactive story reads like a novel because it's writen like a novel.  This dumps a lot of information on you from the first page and doesn't give that information time to reveal it's self.  I got about three pages into the strory, and everything was just one massive exibition dump.  It wasn't even a good exibition dump because I have no idea who I am.  I have an SO, a job (which is unspecified), and family who cares about me,
No idea.
There are two other things that help make a good interactive story: music and visuals.  This game has poor of the first, and almost none of the second.
The music of this story is slow.  Incredibly slow.
It is repetative, tedious, and yet somehow is way to in your face.  It doesn't add to the mood, it's like someone is just screaming, "Sad!  This is sad!  Be sad!"  Over.  And over.  And over again.
The visuals are pictures.  That's...really all I can say, beacuse that's what they are.  Stock photos of things I could find on Google.  They are boring and add nothing, only serving to clutter the screen.
That's actually a really good way to sum up the whole experience.  This game is boring and adds nothing.  This doesn't make me more interested or give me an urge to understand depression deeper.  I'm sure that a well-made story about depression would be a good thing, but this isn't a well-made story.  I'm giving this one a pass.

Depression Quest as described by their website is an “interactive fiction game where you play as someone living with depression. You are given a series of everyday life events and have to attempt to manage your illness, relationships, job, and possible treatment. This game aims to show other sufferers of depression that they are not alone in their feelings, and to illustrate to people who may not understand the illness the depths of what it can do to people.“
Let’s talk about the code behind it… The game is written entirely in web-based languages, such as CSS, HTML, JS etc. It uses a node.js webkit browser to display said pages. There’s no problem with this, but it gave me a bit of a surprise as it doesn’t seem to be too suited to the task at hand. This also gave me a bit of trouble recording the game as I normally use DXTory but it didn’t pick the ‘browser game’ up. In my opinion it would be better coded in a different language as it didn’t even make use of any HTML5 features or any features to access websites which is kind of a waste.
Let’s talk about the game itself, it starts out with some story that didn’t explain why the character was depressed at all, it just seemed to drop you into something you knew nothing about with unfamiliar characters. It asks you some questions on what you would like to do and you can answer, 1, 2, 3 or 4. Except 1 is crossed out for no apparent reason other than to provay the story and lock it down to a more linearised path.
Suddenly after I clicked answer 1 to do work, I am very depressed for no reason other than to tell a story. Next my girlfriend calls me, Alex. It gives me a boring wall of text and 3 options. 1 is of course, as always crossed out because it is the most sensible option of them all - go hang out with your girlfriend and be happy, because that would be way too easy. Now we’re at a party, boring wall of text… and of course, option 1 is crossed off, which is the most sensible with ‘Enthusiastically socialize’. It really confuses me why the most sensible options are crossed off, I thought this story was Depression Quest and not ‘Let’s Try and be as Sad for No Reason and Silly as we can Quest.’
Now we’re back home and our mother has come over for a surprise visit, except we can’t choose the most sensible option again, which is tell her how sad we are, I’ll choose the similar option, number 2.
Sidenote: For some reason the crossed out options and the one just below them are nearly identical… This game is strange…
So, I decide to take up this offer with this person to get a cat as the other options to take the cat but enthusiastically were crossed out..
Anyway, the next scene is the character and their GF talking about some stuff I skipped because it was too long and didn’t seem too relevant to the plot when I speed-read it, anyway, you have options:
1. Tell her how awesome she is, explained with lots of words.
2. Tell her how awesome she is, explained with fewer amount of words.
3. Ask if she is happy with the relationship.
4. Do nothing.
I have decided to chose 3 as it seemed the most sensible. You know I’ve found a pattern; the highest available one seems the most sensible one to choose but usually ends up making you more depressed for no apparent reason.
Anyway, this carries on for some time. Eventually it just becomes “NEXT”, “PICK OPTION 6 AS IT’S THE ONLY ONE”.
Apparently playing with cats makes you depressed these days. I ended up after trying several times I managed to unlock the therapist and I talked to some guy called Attic who doesn’t actually live in my roof.
I skipped forward because I was starting to get more and more bored by the planck time. Infact the boredom turned into depression it was that lackluster and dull (in a boring way). Anyway, its now Christmas and this is where the game ends.
TL;DR
BORING QUESTIONS, PRETTY LINEAR STORY WITH FEW ACTUAL CHOICES, AND A STORY THAT MADE NO SENSE.
Overall: 1/10. Would NOT recommend.

I don't think this game can be recommended in any way. It's two years old now, and Steam are STILL selling it at virtually full retail price - £29.99 for the base game, and an eye-watering £46.99 if you want the two DLCs as well. And the game itself isn't good enough to justify those prices. I've played it with a friend on his PC, and even compared to the lacklustre Civ V, it seems dull and derivative. Many people say that Firaxis/Aspyr have simply taken the Civ V game engine, and replaced all the units and technologies with fancy-sounding sci-fi names to create a new cash-cow. While that may be a little simplistic, I think players definitely need to question the developers' motivations with this game.
If you're a previous Civ V player like me, what would I recommend for you? If you're rich and you MUST always have the "latest and greatest", then rush out and buy the new Civ VI. IMO it's very overpriced, but it's getting good reviews.
The more sensible approach? Well if you've never tried Civ IV (yes, four), I would recommend you get the bundle with THAT game and all its add-ons for a reasonable price. Although the graphics are a little dated, it has an EXCELLENT game system, with many strategies and alternative victories available. It also has a MASSIVE online community, and an ENORMOUS number of good-quality mods available both from the Steam Workshop, and other places. And it's quite easy to make mods yourself.

I admit that I don't really like horror games. At least, not the cheap pop-scare kind, nor the "creature is hunting you and you're alone and defenseless" kind. I never finished Amnesia, and I stay far away from games like Outlast or Slender. The Cat Lady is certainly a horror adventure: it's creepy throughout, and there's plenty of blood and gore and body horror. But the *point* of the game isn't to scare you. The horror is secondary to the story; and what a fantastic story it is. You could think of it as a sort of paranormal Kill Bill. You start the game committing suicide and getting caught in limbo. A creepy old lady says you can't die just yet, gives you immortality, and sends you back to the world of the living to murder five very evil people. It's more nuanced than it might first seem though. It's a story about depression and suicide, but also of friendship and hope. The characters are very well written and the voice acting is generally decent (the main character is thankfully very well voice-acted). If you like dark, interesting stories and don't mind some blood and guts, I would highly recommend The Cat Lady.

There are some minor flaws, like in every adventure game there are some puzzles that seem not very logical and few scenes that are not very convincing (like inside Pauline's flat when three persons spend far too much time deciding who's gonna open the door and who goes to bathroom with Mitzi), but theese things are not game braking in any way, just somewhat annoying. The last flaw that needs mentioning is animation of the characters (especially Susan and Mitzi). While the whole graphics beeing raw and ugly makes it at the same time very in place and atmosphere amplifying, animation of characters is very shaky and causes eye fatigue.
Nevertheless I highly recommend playing The Cat Lady for all those who are bored with naive and trivial game stories which we face in great majority of other games and seek something more convincing and interesting. You won't regret it.

It's easy to go insane, lose all your hope and push people away because you're scared of trusting them. I have trust issues and I bet that I'm not the only one who can relate. I was so suspicious of Mitzi before. I'm glad she wasn't one of the maggots. People take chances every time they decide to trust somebody. If Susan wasn't ready to take that risk, she wouldn't have learned anything from this. The ending is as real as it might get, so I'm not sad about it at all. After all, it's not just a tale. Susan is smart, she won't lose herself again. Not after she was lucky to meet such a great friend as Mitzi. Now, I'm not saying that she'll live in happiness till the end of her days. It's only the beginning. She has become stronger and she stopped running away from her past. She accepted the fact that the future is in her hands.
I really like the music, by the way.

This game has and still will be a wild ride for me.
I love this game to death, and it will always be my favorite fighting game.
Seeing the game grow and die was quite an experience, along with the little peaks of activity the game would have years after when all the veteran players would get on.
I do miss this game dearly, and I do hope that the effort of the members of the community *cough* Placebo *cough* pay off and bring back the game to at least a fragment of what it was.
This game seemed basic on the outside, yet when you played it you would get destoryed almost instantly and it was a shock at first. Then you would watch, see what people did, try to copy it and then fail.
You would fail and fail again until you got so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that you might ragequit, and many did.
However there were the people that would push on and try to learn how to play.
You would try to learn many techs such as Guard slips, Juggling, Jump Canceling, JLRs, etc.
And then you would finally pull them off. You would have done what you thought was impossible prior to this moment.
And that feeling was amazing.
You would become better, improve and grow, along with the community.
But then the devs announced that they would leave the game and everything stared to fall apart.
The community stayed a bit after, but hope was lost that they would ever come back.
You would only see veterans still playing or new players unaware of what happened to this game playing, unaware that it beame a relic of it's past.
But the game was still great, and fighting against the players still left was fun, but it wasnt the same.
You could feel in the community dying as you played and it was a dreaful feeling. Yet we would presist in hope that the community would make a comeback. But the big revival we wanted hasnt come yet. All that has come are little
hills while we wait for a mountain. Little by little though, we might just pull it back.
But bits of hope showed up for the game, the main person pushing the movement being the player Placebo and Raptor Jesus.
With Placebo's newest post on the announcements (10/10/17) being the biggest hope ive seen for the game in a long time I sincerly hope that the game made some sense of a revival.

Having played all 4 Momodora games, and after beating this one 3 times as of writing this review i have to say this one is now my all-time favorite. My favorite before this game was momodora 2 because of exploration alone. momodora 3 was a great title as it was closer to a megaman zero style of gameplay. But with all that said let’s talk about Reverie Under the Moonlight shall we?
**NO SPOILERS**
-Exploration/Environment/Details and Secrets-
Before this game came out i was very worried that it would have the same fate as Momodora 3, a great game that ended too short, due to little exploration. I’m glad that the developers took note on this issue and greatly expanded the world of Momodora 4. if you played Castlevania symphony of the Night you'll feel right at home with Momodora 4.This world is also filled with character puzzles to solve, Hidden passages, mini Quests which reward you with either a weapon upgrade or an item with an effect. This open world environment similar to symphony of the night is what the momodora series needed (momodora 2 comes pretty close though).
gameplay/references/art style
i can't help it but I’m getting the feeling that Momodora 4 borrowed some elements from BloodBorne (which is a good thing) . Even the first enemies in the game can still pose a threat if you don't respect them enough (very similar to the soul’s games). When seeing the combat/dodging system in the trailer i felt like it was going to be a useless gimmick of the game... boy was i wrong! Similar to devil may cry, if you don't figure out the boss/enemies attacks and you don't dodge them right you will die... A LOT! As for references to other games i feel this game borrows elements from: bloodborne, Metroid, castlevania , and megaman zero. On that note I have to say I’m impressed by the way I found NO GLITCHES in the game so far and the mechanics of the game run solid and smooth.
Replay value
This game has great replay value! If you beat the game with a “good ending” the game gives you the option to replay it with most of the items you picked up but from the beginning of the game! This gives the player a great chance to help a character they might have missed or choose a different method of doing things.
Religion?
Like it or not, this game is heavily religious based although it’s more of the “momodora religion” then something real. But this actually made me think “what would a priestess do?” as certain parts of the game had you choose in somewhat a religious manner. Being non-religious myself I had no problem with this element in the game.
Endings
Like other momodora titles you must achieve certain items by helping some characters (or if you find the item through hidden parts of the game) in order to get the True ending. This gives character design more importance and meaning as you take the time to understand each character and their specific needs.
-Music-
The music was great as always, I feel the music this time around tried hard to be bloodborne with a momodora sytle but that’s just my personal opinion.
In conclusion I have played many a game in my day and I have to say that this one is definitely a Triple A title! I feel this game was a great mile stone in the series and it will establish an even bigger fan base. I feel this 4th installment sets a new tone for the development team as before they were small and now they put a Big game out there and for many this is their first momodora game.
I don’t rate games this high often but I have to say this game is easily a 9/10.

The game is much like Far Cry 3. Same kind of play with similar goals. One thing I did find, and I don't know if anyone else has noticed, the terrain seems the same no matter where you go. I am still in jugle area but I seem to keep going up the same hills, following the same path, no every few hundred yards. I didn't notice this in Far Cry 3, at least not as bad. It seems the designers got lazy and just copied the same area over and over.
As for the game, I have found two major issues. One code related, the other more specific to game play. The big technical issue I've found is that there seems to be a memory leak. The longer you play, the more system RAM is used. I've had it fill up 16GB of memory which caused the game to load very slowly as it needed to manager the reduced memory. Once the game was closed, the memory was released and all was fine again. Poor programming and testing I'd say.
The second issue is with game saves. The game offers the choice to save during a mission but, of course, you loose all of your progress if you quit. If the save feature is not going to save the current progress, block it out or at least make sure you let the player know that the mission will be canceled. At least save to the last check point and let the player resume from there after quiting the game.
All in all, I'd give this a thumbs up though it lacks the true expansiveness that FC3 seemed to have. The story in FC3 was better also, at least in my humble opinion. Still, a good game and worth the money and time to play.

Now that the game is actually released, I recommend it. The AI is still pretty dull but it's "okay enough, I guess". It's worth knowing that multiplayer is solid and has an interesting feature: just go host a game and throw in a bunch of AI and start playing as if it was single-player. Other players will see your game in the list (unless you specifically lock it) and they can just join in, taking over for an AI. It means you can sit down for a single-player game and have a chance for some real brains to show up, which is a nice way to do it, versus having to sit around and hope people join at the start.
Anyway, the game is a real-time, space-based 4X with a focus on high level strategy. Battles occur somewhat like they would in Sins of a Solar Empire, but with less control -- you aren't meant to intensely focus on a particular battle. You are meant to primarily command the comings and goings of fleets as a whole, and flanking does matter (as many people design ships with most armor and guns to the front). This type of combat is what lets the real-time strategy component work and stay integrated into the main game (as opposed to some mini-game that it tosses you into, as in the old MOO games.)
Ship design is a primary focus and one of the most interesting aspects of the game. How you design your ship can impact how they will fight. You can get some pretty diverse ship styles.
Planetary management can seem complex at first but once you get the hang of it, it's pretty simple to work on the fly. Planets have resources that require a certain "planet level" to work. Raising the planet level involves importing resources, so you end up with a sort of support pyramid of minor planets exporting their goods to better planets which in turn export their goods to support a bustling capital, of sorts.
Really the two biggest problems I have with the game is that I wish the AI was more of a challenge and I wish more people played multiplayer! I think "early access" hurt the game because some aspects were very under-developed for a long time and people got bored. The 1.0.0 release added tons of new stuff, really fleshed out the tech tree and made the races distinct but for a majority of the early-buyers I think it was too late -- even though they mostly liked the game, they felt they played it out already and probably never even noticed 1.0.0 came out with so many changes.
Anyway, I think it's great. I'll be looking for you in multiplayer.

Star Ruler 2 is a unique spin on the whole 4X RTS genre that uses some new mechanics that I havn't seen before. Essentially, The game is a 4X RTS game with a whole new spin in the mechanical design. When you think 4X, you think of games such as Master Of Orion 2, Galactic Civilization, etc. These games all seem to be completely similar to each other (Mainly because most are based off of Master Of Orion, which was the most sucessful of it's genre in it's time). They all use turn based gameplay with turnbased combat, research was done by a turn by turn basis, ship movement was also turn based and so on and so on.
Star Ruler 2 does a unique spin on the original concept by making research based off how much of a certain resource you have, Planets need to import and export in order to be sucessful and lucrative, using a mechanic called pressure. Pressure is a varying counter that the higher it is, the more the planet produces and the more money you get. By importing certain resources, you can change pressure and the benefits it provides (For example, a resource might provide research pressure, which will increase your research resource on the planet in question).
There is also a very unique diplomacy system that uses "Influence". Influence allows you to buy and activate what is essentially cards. You can use these cards in votes, diplomatic agreeements with alien civilizations, or to benefit your civilization itself. You gain influence by the system above, with the use of pressure.
There is quite a large research tree, but a lot of the research just seems to be passive bonus' (Things like 20% more weapon damage, 20% more energy, etc) that doesn't have a whole lot of new things you can unlock, like new weapon systems, ship systems, buildings, and so on.
The game has a energy system that is, once again, affected by pressure that is producing energy. You can use this energy to purchase certain research projects, activate artifacts which give large bonus', and to use for certain diplomacy cards.
Star Ruler 2 has a system that is quite similar to normal 4X games with the idea of labor. Labor is essentially a planet's production that affects how fast something is built at said planet.
The game has a interesting ship design mechanic that allows you to make things like star sized ships and the like.
There is many many more things that can be said about this game, but now I will list a few negatives I find about it.
- Not a whole lot of variablity in how a ship looks, Sadly, unlike Galactic Civilization, this game doesn't allow you to customize the look of a ship
-Sometimes I found the enemy AI to be a little weird, as in, they declare war but I never seen them attack me. They essentially declared war on me just to lose. I only saw a fleet of theres maybe once, before it just jumped out of the star system.
-Why does a planet only produce 1 resource on average? How can a planet only just produce grain and meat, while another planet can only produce coal?
- Not a whole lot of race variety, and I havn't seen much of a story for the game, asside from a little bit of fluff on the race selection screen.
Thats about it. Overall, I sincerely recommend this game for a unique spin on the whole 4X genre.

The best game of the Risen series in my opinion.
If you read my other reviews, you may have noticed that I love atmospheric games. I love games with immersion and a fascinating storyline. And Risen 2 does a great job at delivering this.
First of all the pirates setting of the game is great. It's good to see that the devs have gone away from the magic theme of the first game and made something more interesting (I still like Risen 1 don't get me wrong). Instead of one big island there are now several smaller ones you can head for on your own pirate ship. There also are new weapons like pistols and muskets. Furthermore you can learn voodoo magic from the tribal guys in the jungle, unearth treasures, loot dangerous ruins, drink rum and grog - just pirate things. I love it!
The graphics and the graphical effects are stunning. It's not to colorful (
), not to grey, just right. And especially the creatures look great and realistic because of high resolution sprites. The only graphical letdown are the NPCs: Many of them look alike, their eyes are a bit too glossy and stuff like that.
The graphical and weather effects as well as the sound effects are doing a great job at adding to the atmosphere. Especially rain and storms are really heavy and atmospheric.
The main characters are charismatic. Every crew member has their strengths and weaknesses which makes them believable. Voice acting is above average.
But the combat system is crap and by far the biggest letdown of the game. It's worse than Risen 1's combat system (
). Ok, it's a Piranha Bytes game but still.. this is awful. But luckily there are companions in this game, so it's playable.
You may need some time but it's well spend, believe me.
All Risen and Gothic games have a certain something that makes them so extremly immersive. They are all great in some way but also have severe flaws. Despite the bad combat system, I think Risen 2 is a gem. The setting is great. The atmosphere is great. The story is ok.
Buy the Gold Editon! The DLCs are nice, you won't regret it.

Voxel-y polygons. Nice soundtrack. Color pallete mostly browns and yellows. No combat, sparse landscape. Not really considering a second playthrough. WARNING: Map not to scale. Buy it only if the price drops a lot.
EDIT: one additional feature would change my opinion to a Yes: once the game is completed, allow the player to roam freely without the world ending every 10 minutes.
Not so much a "walking" simulator as a "gather clues in bullet time before a comet destroys the world again" simulator.
There is insufficient time to gather all clues before the comet arrives. Each time the world is destroyed, you return to the central starting tower and your progress is saved. Yes, it does start to feel repetitive. Once you have found all the clues, your map reveals a new location. Go there to finish the game.
Produced by a very small team, TIMEframe can be finished in under an hour. The forced repetition of using the same terrain over and over again means this game really won't have much repeat-play appeal. It's also a bit of a design shortcut; since the player has only a set amount of time to explore, there is no need to build out much more detail or terrain.
Buy only if deeply discounted.

In TIMEframe, you walk around and find ancient structures and relics from a lost world and every ten minutes, the meteor that destroyed the society comes and you restart from the first temple. While this is certainly unique, its just feels a bit unnecessary. The idea for the game is really intresting and it had a lot of promise, but it doesnt hold up in the end.
Throughout your journey, you uncover clues about the ancient society and "The Nomad". Through the stories and clues, you can piece together that the society believes their ancient being/god is going to do something, and that their world may be coming to an end. You also can infer that "The Nomad" is a meteor coming to destroy their world. The way these clues are presented to you; through ancient artifacts and written passages by ancient scribes and scholars of the civilization, is really good. It helps you build a good sense of what this ancient world was like and how they acted towards the events of the unknown. The soundtrack was excellent and it really helped carry the mood. All in all the atmosphere was fantastic and I really did enjoy the calming, yet mysterious and slightly chilling atmosphere I felt in this game. The art style was really nice too and I enjoyed the polygon style graphics. Unfortunately, the other parts of the game REALLY took away from this.
This was a walker simulator to the point where it was too much of a walking simulator. All the things to discover were spread out way too far and it was nothing but walking through an open area in between each place. That was made even worse by the main premise of the game. The meteor crashing every 10 minutes was really just bothersome while playing. Especially when you could only discover about 3 places before you had to restart from the beginning. This grew very tiresome and made me start to lose interest. I also would have loved to explore some of the places a bit more but I didn't have time too because I only had 10 minutes to work. I also felt rushed to get through it, because I didn't want to spend forever starting from the beginning again. The meteor crashing also took away from some of the mystery of the game. Depending on what artifacts you found first, you may not have put it together that "The Nomad" was a meteor yet. But when it crashes after 10 minutes, you are pretty certain what "The Nomad" is. I feel the game should have had the meteor crash only once, at the end of the game. That way you could learn and infer things about the society throughout the game, and then see the true end of the society unfold with the meteor crashing down to end the game. This would have given you an answer, while still not blatantly telling you what happened so early on in the game. The game had promise but fell short and needed some changes in order for it to succeed.

Aside from commenting on if it constitutes as a "Game" or not, when I looked into Depression Quest, I looked onto it from the vantage point as a a councilor whom deals with clients with various levels of depression.
What I see is a vague, blanket statement of what depression consists of, coming from a rather mixed view point what barely tells a story of the reactions of depression, rather than the effects. Case in point, we see no concept of "Shaming and Blaming." Unless I missed it in my rather brief playthrough (As bad as it sounds, I couldn't continue with the story anymore without it feeling like a waste of time), I saw that the "player" has self-doubt issues, but there was nothing the self doubt is coming from, nor is the "player" shaming himself for feeling this way or annoying his partner (which was another factor, fine use of gender neutral...it the genders of both player and character weren't clearly defined as they were). Depression is a both mental and physical problem that hundreds of thousands of people face everyday, but depression usually is aided by something else, usually some sort of trauma from the past, as minute as it can be. The game takes you on a quest through a general, almost bland version of what depression commonly is seen as on a television commercial or Dr. Oz program, instead of the unique case by case basis that it actually is.
One other factor, if I can add my two cents in, is that the game does not offer any sort of "Help" to the player. There are hundreds of different programs, groups, different therapies, etc at someone's disposal, and this game again, picks a generic "Therapist" as a single option. The game is less of a way to show how people live with depression as well as try to manage their depression, and more like a choose your own adventure book, with every ending leading to not a single resolution. Yes, Depression may seem like a long dark hallways into nothingness to many, but it can be helpped, and Depression Quest if wanting to be seen as an educational tool, should've utilized some of those options.

Depression Quest is something I would not suggest to someone wanting to understand depression, or to use as an example or study for college-level clinical studies. Depression Quest tells a story about what depression should be, but not what it actually is.
My only good thing to say about Depression Quest: No Day One DLC.

As everyone knows, a game is entitled a fair chance. 'Depression Quest' is unique in its development as it brings forward the viewpoints and emotional curtains that define depression. However, it is only applicable to one scenario. It in fact plays through the possible actions of a single person in a very specific environment. The limited actions allow for smooth transitioning, but are generally lacking for what gamers consider to be a developing title.
With all else said and done, the game was fairly straight-forward in its guided direction. Did you fight through the depression, or did you succumb to what would be a vision-altering take on an individuals inner turmoil. With multiple paths to choose from which gradually became more and more limited as time progressed, one could feel restricted to their options, an argument which invalidates the free-thought that many gamers wish to experience. With no real graphical rendering save for a very contrasting back-drop to the text, I found my eyes hurting and straining, consistently reminding myself that this game looked more like a website than an actual game. There wasn't any Artificial Intelligence to interact with so the choices seemed rather stale in comparison to other titles. As for the images that did perceive themselves, the images were repetative and didn't give an ebb or flow to the text, so when it came up with changes in time, it felt much like a car slamming into a concrete baricade, and other times it felt like time was at a stand-still.
The music was a single repetitive track that played itself over and over again and was almost maddening in and of itself, so the feel was genuinely successful, but the music felt out of place at many points in the story line. As a fast reader, I was able to play through this game in roughly twenty minutes with all possible endings. On that note, the gameplay was very short, and the replay factor was damaged by my own personal abilities. That being said, it felt short and fairly lacking in immersive content. Credit shall be given, however, into the emotions that the game drew out. Having suffered from depression myself, a majority of the situations actually forced myself to review my own experiences in some self-reflection and as I am writing this, I can't help but feel emotionally connected to the game. However, I must remain clinical and give an honest review, and so my personal feelings will be directed in a more professional manner.
The last questions that come to mind are fairly straight-forward. Is this a game, and does it befit the genre advertised? The answer to these questions is an undeniable, "No." Depression Quest feels more like a book that you would select your choice, and then turn the page to reveal your decision's consequence, whether it be positive, negative, or neutral. As well, with Depression Quest having the graphical interface of a web-page or flash-based game, it did not feel like it belonged on Steam as a Green-Light. With all this said, it also cannot be considered a Role-Playing Game as it doesn't fit the criteria to be considered a game.
On a personal note, I feel that Depression Quest was fairly enlightening and would definately help others feel what depression is. As much as I can relate to it, I feel this would be better as a graphic novel or a short-story rather than a video-game. As a video-game, I stick by my rating of '2 out of 5" and would not recommend this game over-all, but on a personal scale, I feel that this could become something better if it were applied in a different application.

When trying to summarize my thoughts on a game, I usually ask myself "Was this fun to play ?". If the answer is no, I then ask myself "was this compelling and immersive enough to make up for the lack of pure fun, by providing a memorable and unique experience ?". If the answer is still no, then I can honestly not recommend it.
This is the result of my experience with This War of Mine, a game that tries to depict the horrors of war from the point of view of survivors caught in the crossfire. It is an indie title with a very fitting art direction, a good soundtrack reminescent of the first Fallout games, and some interesting crafting mechanics. It's relatively difficult and yours survivors will probably not all make it through the war, with random events such as raids, outbreaks of crime, and the harsh winter.
Despite my successful run, I quicky got bored as the days passed and the game became more of a routine, not to mention I had so many resources that scavenging became more of a chore than a thrilling escapade. Once you become self-sufficient, the game loses a lot of appeal. By the 20th day, I was wondering when the war would end. By the 40th, I was banging my head against a wall and listening to podcasts to keep myself awake.
So in the end, I cannot recommend This War of Mine. It has some undeniable qualities, and someone else might enjoy it far more than me, but in the end it didn't do it for me.

Very fun game. The game length feels just right, with a 100% playthrough on hard taking me around 4 hours. Combat is simple in a good way. You have a 3 hit ground combo, an air hit, arrows, and a roll that you're invincible in. The difficulty in combat comes from timing and knowing when to dodge attacks. Items allow for some customization in your playstyle, and the variety in them is great. The game gives some nice freedom in the beginning, allowing you to visit locations and fight most of the bosses in any order before the final two ares (unreachable until you get 4 crests by beating the bosses).
Speaking of bosses, the boss fights are great. Almost all attacks the bosses have are telegraphed before they come out, making it feel fair whenever you receive damage. Most of the bosses are pretty unique battles too, so there's some nice variance in those fights (though there is one repeated boss battle).
Story is... relatively light. Characters come and go rather quickly while not saying much, and the story itself is rather predictable. I'd say that's the weakest part but it is by no mean bad, just not as fleshed out as I'd like. The ambience is great too, most of the game has a very grim atmosphere to it. Easily recommendable, very fun, worth the money.

I'm marking this as not recommended game because of the single save slot. This is a stupid "feature" at best as it accomplishes nothing good and potentially lots bad. You can often work around these by backing up your save files independently of the game, but why do I need to do that? Again, there's no advantage, no sense of "fairness", etc. There's really no death penalty in the game, so there's nothing that a single save file does for game play.
What a single save file does in a long open world campaign is leave you at risk for corruption. This is particularly bad in this game because they've got a bug that will completely end your campaign that occurs at the very end of one mission just as you transition to a new area in game. I was 40 hours into the game (I tend to do many of the side activities before advancing the campaign missions) when I was bit by this. Many others have been bitten.
It would be an annoyance if you had multiple saves available. But with a single save AND the fact that it executes that save for you at various points means they built a game designed to have a lot of people abandoning it because they have no desire to repeat the grindier bits in the game.
Back up your files independently and frequently, especially before the "Willis" missions.
Single save is built for a world where there are no bugs. That's not the world we live in.
I am also marking this not recommended because Ubi forces you to sign into another system in order to play the game. I'm on steam, I do not need Ubi's garbage site.

I was pleasantly surprised by this VN. I thought it was going to be a lot more slice-of-life, but it ended up being a fantasy-themed romance VN with a lot of depth. The common route kind of "tricks" the player into thinking it is a lot more lighthearted, but once the character path develops, heavier topics are discussed/shown. Oddly enough, this is a ebi-hime game, and it is fairly different from their other work. Regardless, I highly recommend it.

I liked this game; however, I would not recommend it as an introduction to Ebi-hime's games.  I would suggest playing this after you are already a fan.  You may want to start with The Way They All Go.
Here's why:  there are four endings, each of which has a very long narrative with no choices to be made.   There are something like ten choices to make which set your course on one of those four tracks, and then you click and read, click and read, until the end.  If you *like* Ebi-hime's writing, there's a lot of fun to be had reading.  But I think of this more as a set of four (pretty interesting) short stories with a handful of choices rather than some other of Ebi-hime's works.

This World Unknown has charming character art, interesting personalities and detailed, imaginative text that the author clearly put a great deal of thought into. It took me 4 and a half hours to read my first play through, which is more than most VNs I've bought through Steam. Definitely, this game is worth the price.
While I generally enjoyed the game, I have a few gripes, some of which are due to personal taste. Please note that so far I've only played one route (Garrett's), so this is not a complete review of the entire game in any case. I may update this in the future if/when I play all the other routes.
(SPOILERS AHEAD)
- The background of Rhea and Clair's bedroom is the only one that doesn't have filters applied to it to make it look like it was sketched/painted. I found that really jarring and it would nag at me every time a scene played in their bedroom (which was pretty often).
- There were not just one, but three characters that had no sense of respecting personal space, e.g. taking the heroine's hand, or hugging her, or touching her without warning. I didn't mind it so much with Meirin because it fit her unsettling personality pretty well. But with Asa and Garrett, given they were romanceable characters, it came across as pushy and annoying. One or two characters with a penchant for unwelcome touchy-feeliness, sure, but three is overboard for me.
- Speaking of Garrett. Why would I want to date, much less spend my life with someone who treats life like a fairy tale and lies and runs away from responsibility so he can do what he wants, while completely lacking the perspective to understand the extreme privilege he has by way of his rich upbringing? Every time he talked about being a hero I wanted to roll my eyes and gag. I might have accepted going on a date with him if he really seemed to understand the implications of what he was doing. I accept I won't like every romance option in a VN. That's to be expected. But I actually felt disgust reading Garrett's lines and ended up skimming a lot by the time I realized I was on his path. The butler, though? Awesome. :D And Mina, too.
- This is probably not ever going to happen, but I would've liked to have some female dating options. I really was sweet on Selene and thought she would make an appealing romance option. I might've also pursued Clair, and even Meirin for the fun of it.
(END SPOILERS)
While this might sound like a "not recommended" review, I'm giving this game a thumbs up because I was clearly invested enough in the characters and story to build up intense feelings about it. That, I think, is the sign of a well-written and well-designed VN. :)
