Before you react, read this: This review is OBSOLETE. I now recommend this game as a lot of things have been addressed. For preservation and "I don't want my ratings cleared" reasons, I'm not switching it to a yes but my current opinion is now YES.
Note: I'm a big Momodora fan.
Note 2: I got the True Ending on Medium.
This game is kinda a one step forward, two steps back deal. If you haven't played Momodora 1, 2, and 3, here's a quick background:
Momodora is a series that follows a shrine maiden (or two) as she is sent to defeat an evil queen of ___ who is the source of a curse on their village by wrecking♥♥♥♥♥♥with a maple leaf. They are all platformers, and they all feature both a melee attack and a ranged attack. The first one was just a level based game, the second one (my favorite and imo the top of the series) was a metroidvania with permanent passive upgrades, and the third one featured two characters, a return to linear levels, and a new passive item management system.
This game is pretty much a mix of 2 and 3, with both passive permanent upgrades and additional charms you can equip for effects. It's also a metroidvania, but the level design is more linear than 2.
So let's talk about the goods and the bads.
Theme: Unlike the other games that were a bit more chipper, this game is rather dark. Yes it has cats, yes it has cute one eyed demons, but everything else is death and misery. It's a "feel like crap" ride until the end. If you're looking for anything uplifting or cute, look elsewhere, since you won't find it here.
The story is... honestly pretty eh. It doesn't really do much to change the Momodora formula OTHER than make it darker, which just isn't enough. I don't really care about any of the chars and they don't have as much personality despite them saying more. Really story has never been Momodora's strong suite, and for some reason I felt like I cared even less about chars in this game than the other. Maybe it's because in this one they were forced more, DevArt OC melodrama style. It just didn't work. Even the evil queens in the other game seemed to have more personality, in this one I just didn't feel anything as I was fighting her.
Graphics:
Gorgeous. Nothing bad to say here. I liked the cute chibi chars of the other games but style wise I see why the artist wanted to move on. I only have one complaints: For some reason the devs decided to turn the lights off, Binding of Isaac Curse of Darkness style, for half the levels (there's an item to get rid of this for a minute or so but it's one use until you hit the next checkpoint.) It's not even a spelunky "shroud of blackness," it's more like playing an original gameboy without a backlight. Either turn the brightness up on this game or you won't be able to see a thing. Seriously.
Platforming:
It's worse than the other games, honestly. Maybe it's the bigger hitboxes, or maybe it's the obsession with tiny platforms and one hit kill spikes in this game. The jump also feels shorter. There is a double jump, but it's Little Mac-level awful, and honestly I'm not quite sure why it's there. I feel like it used to be stronger when initially made but it was nerfed at some point, hard, and it really shouldn't have been. I often found myself jumping at a platform that I really felt I should be able to make but... can't. And it wasn't the metroidvania 'I'll get an upgrade for this later' (you don't) it was Maplestory Jump Quest level "why can't I just hit this?"
Combat:
It's both better and worse, and altogether more defensive. For the first time ever, you now have a roll, and though it's a bit finnicky and doesn't quite 'feel' right to be honest, it's necessary to deal with like 3/4 of what this game throws at you. Altogether the attacks switched from platforming style 'jump/run from the bullets' to 'just roll.'
Your maple leaf in this game is SIGNIFICANTLY slower and carries a whole lot less range. It also forces you significantly forward, which makes you often walk right into people's hitboxes. I mean, it's more interesting than the classic Momodora "stand and mash attack as fast as you can" but it's also more frustrating.
Ranged seems to be the way to go, honestly. For the first time ever, this ninja shrine maiden has a bow instead of charms, and she spams arrows as fast as the other shrine maidens spam melee. Of course they deal almost no damage, though, and it takes a while, but it's the safest option.
Difficulty:
Right onto it. This game is really frickin' hard. For some reason, starting from Momodora 3 this game took a turn for "you either get the easiest game ever or you pay dearly." If you pick easy, expect an almost insulting level of easy - you're practically invincible. If you pick Normal, though, prepare for what another game would consider Hard. It's not even a fun kind of challenge difficulty, it's a frustrating difficulty.
The bosses are meat shields that abuse the heck out of projectiles (roll often) or deal incredibly hard melee damage. They also seem to highlight all the issues with both platforming and combat. For example, one individual, the arsonist, cannot be attacked with melee. Why? Because though she has hitstun animations and it seems like the devs intended her to be melee-able, there is always fire on the ground around her. In other Momodora's you could stand and attack, but since attacking moves you forward in this game, you ALWAYS walk into the fire. Your only options are to either spam arrows and slooooooowly chip damage or wait for your partner (who's never elaborated on why she's there or helping you) to kill her for you (which takes a while.)
In fact, almost all the bosses in this game encourage you to just stand and spam projectiles. There's one boss with a giant sword that deals more than half your life in melee damage. I spent an hour trying to take her down the hard way, but the fact that she always broke in and out of hitstun seemingly randomly and avoiding her finnicky sometimes pixel perfect attacks was just frustrating, and I instead decided to just pelt arrows until she died. Not what I consider fun, and compared to the other Momodra's bosses? Bad.
There is also a specific collectible, the ivory bug, that is extremely hard to see. It's like 3 pixels or so and is often obscured by some foreground object. The challenge of collectibles should be uncovering the secret passage or doing the platforming challenge to get them, not seeing the dang thing.
Etc.:
There are some "it's 2016 and this is the 4th game in the series so why is this still a thing" problems with this game. See, I'm sure this was brought up before because Momodora 3 had the same issue: This game needs a serious epilepsy warning, when you get hit, it flashes bright red, when you die, it flashes red and black repeatedly and it hurts your eyes. If you fall into spikes prepare to get assaulted with both the flashing red of getting hit multiple times and then the death spam. Why can't we just do a pause and fade to black, Metroid style? Or just shake the screen? Anything but this works.
Also, there aren't any recongifurable controls. I personally found the keyboard controls questionable and there were things I wanted to switch (I'd love to use space or F to roll instead of the out of the way Q) and everyone has their own opinions, so why force us to use these controls? I used the xbox controls and it gave you a whopping two configurations that switched two buttons and that's it. Again, it's 2016, this is the 4th game in the series, this problem was here in Momodora 3 too, why is this still a thing?
Conclusion:
Do I regret the 6 hours it took me to beat this game? No. Would I recommend it? Well, if you're a Momodora fan, or you're willing to put up with some pretty questionable design decisions, then okay. But I expected better from this series. Buy it to support the devs, but don't expect gold like Momodora 2. Yet.

Oh wow, another 2D game with a Metroidvania-ish design and claims to draw design influence from Dark Souls.  It's a description you've probably read a million times before.  Now before you mentally checkout on this game, take notice that Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight is a legit very good game and one of the better 2D action games I've played in years.
In this type of game, the two things you're going to do most are running/jumping around as you explore and fight enemies.  M:RUM does both well.  At first, the controls might feel slightly deliberate, but you'll soon get used to them and by the end of the game you'll be flying across the screen with air-dashes as a cat and it just feels good.  The character mobility as you progress throughout the game is great. You're never fighting the controls, and the roll dodge mechanic is worked in quite well and it's not something you see in many 2D action games.
Combat is a bit simple.  You have your melee combo attack and a bow with infinite arrows and long-range.  Most enemy encounters are rather simple outside of their consistently strong character design and you're best bet is to rush and bring the offensive to them instead of sitting back and trying to gauge their attacks.  Despite that, combat just feels good.  This is completely a "feel" thing, but I never got tired of fighting regular enemies despite the general nature of encounters being rather limited in options.  It helps that no enemies are health sinks, as most enemies die after a few hits and never become a chore to fight.
The level design and interactivity is very well-done.  You can legitimately play a large portion of the game in any order you want.  You unlock power-ups by finishing each area that increase your mobility, combat ability, and give you the ability to warp, but there's nothing stopping you from doing so in any particular order.  This gives the game a lot of replay value.  Almost all bosses have unlockable shortcuts that place them right next to a save point.
Momodora has an equip/item system where consumable items recharge at save points.  I really like this mechanic in games that use it and here, it mainly deals with healing items.  Equipment is varied and versatile.  There's all kind of accessories that do things like add fire to your attacks, serve as a magnet for coins, give a beep if you're in a room with a secret item and much more.  There's a ton of mix-and-matching to do if you want to vary up your playstyle a bit.
Visually the game is quite nice, though I wish there were less dark areas.  Places like the forest and park look really nice and vibrant and I wish there was a bit more to the locale design color palette.  Animations are also great.  Things like rolling, notching arrows, attacking and using items look good and it doesn't look like any corners were cut.
Another big drawing point in this type of game is secrets, and there are quite a lot.  Don't want to spoil anything but there are a lot of little touches in the game that make it worth replaying.  As for replaying, there's a new game+ that lets you keep all non plot-skills and items you unlocked which lets you just blow through the game at leisure and I'm a fan of this type of NG+.
Finally, I'll get to some of the negative points of the game, which are mostly technical.  First off, no remappable buttons.  This is weird and is something I hope gets patched in.  Next, the in-game V-Sync seems to not work and there is minor screen tearing.  This is another thing that seems like it should be patched.  The "you got hit" sound effect is also quite harsh and shrill, and I wish I could tone it down.  Oh yeah, and a dedicated map button would be nice, too.
On the non-technical side, my major gripe is the instant death spikes.  These things are terrible in every game they're in, and they especially bad here, since it seems like they should just do some damage and let you leap out of them, but no, you just barely tap one and you're dead.  This is by far the most annoying aspect of the gameplay, especially when you cover a decent bit of distance only to hit a spike right before a save point.  Making spikes just give a percentage of damage would make the game much less artificially aggravating and not hurt the the level of difficulty at all.
Two lesser quibbles are that enemies do more damage then their attacks suggest, which will put you on the brink of death without you realizing it at times.  The last negative is something I touched on before, enemy encounters tend to feel rather samey, though killing stuff remains fun enough.
That's a lot of words.  In short, Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight is one of the better 2D actions games I've played in years.  Non-linear level design lets you progress in any direction you adventure with little artificial gating.  Character mobility is great.  The item and equipment systems are well-done and give a good dose of variety to the game.  There's no fat or filler to hit some predetermined playtime requirement.  This is just a very good, well-designed game I'd recommend to anyone that likes 2D actions games and/or Metroidvania elements in their games.
A bite-sized Symphony of the Night, Momodora is an essential purchase for any lovers of that game or people who want to get into the genre but are strapped for time.

Let me begin with the good parts of this game, because they are far less numerous than the bad parts.
The gameplay is reasonably fun, as far as stealth and theft are concerned. The controls are ok and the graphics are fine.
The rest is a hot mess.
The sections of the game that don't involve pure stealth are poorly executed, with comically bad AI, and a lot of long, boring treks through the same hub areas again and again. Some of the gear upgrades that would have been cool - like the rope arrows, are not at all cool since you can only use them in rigidly defined areas. The protagonist was apparently never trained to shoot at wooden things that weren't beams wrapped with rope. Wooden beam with no wrappings? Sorry!
The audio is soul crushingly bad. There are frequent sound and music glitches, which I may have been able to look past if I weren't listening to the eighteenth guard in a row asking what they put in the "sloop," which is apparently this game world's colorfully revamped name for soup. How clever.
I still don't know, by the way... The contents of the "sloop" are more frequently discussed by far than any of the game's actual plot points, but are never revealed.
It's worth noting, while we're on the subject of audio, that I was at one point attempting to sneak past two guards, who - due to some cruel glitch, began to have the same inane conversation, not once, not twice, but three times simultaneously. Each instance of the conversation was staggered by about one second, which created a cacophony of poorly written dialogue that smothered all other sounds. When the conversation concluded I breathed a sigh of relief, only to hear them start it again just moments later... and then again, and again. I was forced to murder them both or risk losing what little sanity the rest of this awful game had allowed me to preserve.
Then there's the plot. It starts out with an intro sequence that wraps up by demonstrating that both the main character and his rival / sidekick are childish dim-wits who would rather get into a slap fight over who has cooler toys than pay attention to the occult ritual that is about to doom them all. I wish I were joking about this...
The bulk of the game from there on out is filler plot, with silly excuses for mysterious things to happen and the occasional pointless character who is given way more screen time than they deserve. The main character's chief rival, for instance, really never goes anywhere from a story standpoint. He dislikes you, and apparently that is enough reason for him to relentlessly hunt you, even after he has lost any reasonable motive to do so.
The ending was one of the worst I have seen in a game. Ever.
To call it merely bad would be criminally understated. It was absurd... laughably absurd. A half-witted attempt to infuse a bad story with cryptic meaning, executed by a writer who could only have done so after suffering a traumatic head injury and enthusiastically huffing paint fumes.
If the ending of this game had a face, I would punch it.

This was a tough one for me. As a long running fan of the Thief series I was very excited for this game, and it left me feeling a little mixed. The game seems to take place several years after Deadly Shadows and while that isn't a bad thing, they seem to use it as an excuse to discard a LOT of the Thief series staples...pagans, keepers, hammerites only got the subtlest of nods, nobody uses Taffer anymore, though it is mentioned oddly, elemental crystals are gone for seemingly no reason and Garret isn't quite the cynical anti-hero he originally was; he openly elects to be the hero this time around which is stupid; all to save his new spunky girl sidekick!....it actually hurt me to type that. The plot is ehhh.. at best and they forgot Garret's mechanical eye. Just as weird they went about bringing up a lot of other things..Basso from Thief 2 returns, they even recall his marriage, you actually stumble into Keeper ruins once or twice they even give a nod to insane widow Moira in the form of a chapter Moira's Asylym. In short from a Lore standpoint, they wrecked this game in the most puzzling of manners.
Gameplay is another issue however. Disregarding the mauled lore, the game is actually a lot of fun to play. The levels are of good size, not nearly as sprawling as classic Thief levels but certainly a dramatic improvement over Deadly Shadows small spaces, with multiple points of entry and progression such as the game demands. The downside is this game actually features points of no return; which is baffling. A game that is heavily about exploration actually has points where you can't backtrack from....really at a loss for words there other the quick-save is your friend. The City itself is open to exploration again like in Deadly Shadows, but unlike Deadly Shadows it's actually awesome! The City is large, gloomy, tightly-knit with a plethora of doors and windows you can break into, rooftops to explore, and all sorts of hidden nooks and crannies. Inbetween chapters you can pick up simple thief missions that take you around the city to find and steal various trinkets as well as whole, albeit small, individual chapters in the form of client jobs. A nice touch as well is you're able to go back and replay any chapter you just played without needing to load an old save to do so in case you want to try again or missed some loot. They did this aspect at least very well.
In the end if you're new to the Thief series and looking to try your hand at stealth games, I imagine you'll find this one a lot of fun. If you're a Thief veteran you'll be very disappointed in the butchering of the lore, almost as if they basically said they don't care, but you'll still find a lot of enjoyment in the gameplay despite it's few hiccups in that regard. It's fun but it's no Metal Age.

Having only ever played a very little of the first two Thief games, I found this new Thief reboot to be pretty faithful to my impressions about the feel of the originals from over a decade ago. Lots of slow stealthy creeping around watching guard patrol patterns and getting the timing right on swiping loot, avoiding and disarming traps to get to loot, and picking locks or turning combo lock dials to get to loot, all before the guard gets back or turns around. The guard AI, while too stupid to notice the missing loot, will notice and react to doors being open (or closed) that were not, safes being open, candles and torches being out (even lighting them again), et cetera.
While Thief does allow for a variety of play styles from full stealth to just flat out killing everyone, unlike other modern stealth action games combat is absolutely best avoided. Guards while maybe not as skill full as the player controlled Garrett, are certainly much more lethal, making direct combat a thing to avoid by design. Overall game difficulty has a lot of options, between a normal assortment of standard pre-built difficulties, but Thief also offers a custom difficulty option to tailor many additional options to add handicaps for those interested in a greater challenge or higher score. Thief's gameplay takes place in multiple connected open world hubs of the different districts of the city, with lots of opportunity for spur of the moment breaking and entering and larceny that are purely optional. Missions take the form of three tiers of activity, with the main plot existing in its own map spaces off the main hubs, client missions that are similar, but smaller and optional, and simple theft missions from the fence that are very small one offs more within the open hub spaces. These open world hubs are not large enough to make the lack of a fast travel system very annoying, except maybe related to getting to the Beggar Queen.
Graphics are nice and high in fidelity, art style is pretty good, though suffers a bit from a not terribly interesting color palette. Voice acting is good with lots of chatter between civilians and guards, with the occasional clue to the whereabouts of particularly valuable pieces of loot, but they often seemed far too quiet on my computer, while cut-sceen and Garrett's own voice when he has something to say about the world around him were just fine.
Plot-wise the story is pretty straightforward, with no plot changing choices available to the player, and the ending is a bit weak and unsatisfactory, but the asylum level is very nicely done. The backdrop of a mysterious and deadly plague in the city of the games setting might have been less cliched if it was not similarly used in Dishonored.
Many comparisons between this game and Dishonored come up, but they fill slightly different niches of the stealth game genre. Dishonored is more combat and killing focused, in a slightly more mutable plot, while Thief de-emphasises combat and killing placing all the focus on finding and getting all the stuff. Overall, Thief is fun and good at its narrow focus, but Dishonored is the overall better game experience.

The best adventure I've played on Steam so far besides Primordia.
+ Great - deep, thoughtful and clever - writing
+ Great characters
+ Great voice acting
+ Lots of mono- or dialogues, all fully voiced
+ Lots of dialogue options and some critical point choices can be made to alter the way things turn out. Can't tell how far it goes yet as I've done one playthrough only, but from the looks of it there are at least two different endings)
+ Great ambiance
+ Nice music (louder and more calmer tunes)
+ Good puzzles
+ Interesting style and design (I especially liked the thoughtful use of colored objects in contrast to otherwise gray ones, possibly working as a symbol for the darker and brighter sides of life and how the protagonist may see them)
+ Easy controls: WASD or arrow keys and ENTER. Objects of interested are highlighted when you get close to them. I prefer this over tediously examinating every pixel on the screen with a mouse as it otherwise often works in adventure games.
- Minor bugs and design overlooks (voice acting and text not always being identical word for word, voice acting in a few instances repeating the same lines even though the text is farther, voice acting sometimes cutting off prematurely, one or two lines the game skipped even though I didn't want to, a few text misspellings, voice acting sometimes including atmospheric recording noise - couldn't tell how to avoid it though, I'm no sound engineer, but it's sometimes easily noticeable especially since the game itself has little sounds, for most parts its walking sounds and random ambiance sounds mixed in and put on loop).
- One severe bug/technical oddity: You cannot save more than 50 savegames. If you try to save more slots the game will tell you saving was successful, but it actually isn't. Overwriting older files isn't possible (the game will simply create duplicate files, shown in the game with same naming). And since the game has many dialogue options and some critical point choices one is encouraged to save, load and test around with his possibilites unless one knows very sure he is gonna do multiple playthroughs. Could be fatal if someone decides to do a one-night walkthrough and only notices very late that his +50 savegames don't actually exist. Can be avoided by simply deleting/moving some of the savefiles one has (C -> Users -> Your Name -> Saved Games -> The Cat Lady)
? The game is about depression. Those who suffer from it may struggle with some aspects shown to it though, because some of the situations and happenings in the game will hardly ever happen this or in a similar way in the real life. It's not totally far-fetched, but it could be seen as an overdramatization of the otherwise rather sober and to the outside world unspectacular hardships to overcome it. Ultimatively I think there is no way it could have turned out the great adventure game it is had it sticked too close to dry facts of reality though. If one
to he could break the whole game apart arguing this way, but what good would that do? For a game I think it did very well in showing some aspects of depression and how to possibly deal with it.
? The violent situations in the game are possibly morally questionable. The game tries hard to make you not sympathize with any of the people that die by your hand and to drive you with your back to the wall (expect for one situation where you can apparently kill someone for "minor" reasons), but in the end even the worst sociopaths in our society have a history and there are reasons why they become who they are. *The Cat lady* is a dark, creepy and quite gory adventure game, that centers around a depressed woman named Susan who, after an attempted suicide, meets “The Queen of Maggots” (basically Death). The queen gives her a mission to rid the world of evil and dangerous people, who hurt and kill others for their own personal gain or amusement . As Susan wakes up from the incident, we get to know her as a person and learn to understand why she've made the choices she made during her life, as well as experience with her the atrocious events the occur afterworlds. She also gets to meet a young woman named Mitzi, who seems to be on a mission of her own...
The game plays quite similarly to a point and click adventure game, but you actually don't “point and click” so to speak, but use the arrow keys to move the character around. During the game, you'll also have to make a few choices, which influence how the game ends. I personally found this to be a very interesting and nice touch.
The game has a wonderful soundtrack, if you like this kind of music. It includes some creepy and atmospheric tracks, but also some great punk and metal songs, that really fits the feel of the game.
As for the graphics and style of the game... well, I think the art style is what will put some people off. You might find it a bit grotesque, but as you play you'll come to realize that style fits very well with the rest of the game, as it conveys the trauma and the emotions of the characters extremely well. There are a few instances where they could have done a better job graphically though, as at times characters or things can look disproportionate.
The game also has voice acting, which is a bit of a hit and miss. Sometimes the acting is quite alright, but other times it's extremely flat, over the top or simply to obvious and stereotypical. Even so I actually enjoyed the voice acting quite a bit, and I don't think I'd enjoy the game as much if it wasn't included.
So yeah... Even though the game has it's flaws (like most games) I totally recommend this game! At least to people who like dark adventure games. It has great music, great sympathetic female lead characters (well I've gone through a depression of my own, so maybe that makes it easier for me to sympathize), great character development, some really dark and twisted scenarios as well as an amazingly creepy atmosphere.
To be honest, it's one of my favorite adventure games of all time.

My one regret about Star Ruler 2 is the lack of publicity it has gotten so far.
Star Ruler 2 is a very well made and polished game with several unique features that all come together quite convincingly. I'd say much more so than Star Ruler 1 ever accomplished.
The game focuses on the macro side of empire maangement but you can still build key facilities on planets and plan out your empire in some detail. The best new feature of the game is definitely the empire growth side of things. In essence, you are trying to advance a few key planets by supporting them with many less developed ones. It creates a very intricate chain of supply and demand that is also nicely automated enough that it doesn't get tedious.
Diplomacy is very well done and actually a big part of the game. This is the first diplomacy system in a long time that I wanted to dig into. There are diplomatic actions not only by competing empires, but by the general galactic community as a whole. And each faction gets to vote, and attempt to sway votes from other factions as well.
The combat and ship building have been redone and are now very much more coherent. Combat hinges on massive flagships supported by multiple smaller ships which can play differing roles and tactics in combat.
There is a lot more to the game, but I'll just stop here and say that this is a title very much worth checking out if you like 4x RTS games or just space empire games in general. Give Star Ruler 2 a try. You won't regret it.

Star Date: Wrote this on Patch 1.0.0
------------------------------------------------------------------
Captain's Log: Have been playing 4x Space Games since I was in elementary school starting with MOO, SE, Gal Civ, Stars!, etc. If there's been a good 4x game, I've probably at least tried it.
------------------------------------------------------------------
Combat Systems Ready:
(+) Diplomacy - Faction on Faction diplomacy is simple enough. All of the basic functions are there. What really stands the game out is the innovative card system. Use influence to purchase cards to suggest new universal regulations such as annexing a rival's system or declaring your own homeworld as the home of the Galactic Senate. Buy other cards to support your own proposals while rejecting those of your rivals. Manipulate other empires to join your crusade against your enemies lest they remember your wrath in their future proposals. The possibilities are extremely deep and I'd place this as the #1 innovation for SR2.
(+) Ship Building / Planet Building - Ships you build tile by tile. The larger you build a gun and it's subsystem, the stronger it'll be. Place armor around vulnerable areas such as the front but don't forget to neglect the rear lest the enemy sends in a pincer fleet. Planets have building room dependent on size. Each planet also has unique terrain features that seperate from other worlds. Depending on the terrain, buildings such as research labs and farms cost less so you'll have to plan accordingly to maximize your credits.
(+) Fleets - Most games you'll command 20 ships in the late game. Some give you a hundred. Here the basic unit of combat is the fleet. You build a capital ship and then attach up to hundreds of smaller support ships to that capital ship to fight. What results is hundreds of laser beams, missiles, cannons firing off at each other. Each ship is rendered and simply put, that's just awesome.
(+) Economy - I'm hesitant to label this as purely a strength. I find the economy a bit simple but more on a positive note than a negative note. For those who are used to the complexity of games such as Distant Worlds, SR2 will be a big downgrade. Each planet usually produces 1 resource. You then connect those resources to other planets that produce more complex resources to level them up and then you ship those complex resources to a major population center to level them up so they grow more and are more productive. What results is many resource worlds and a few concentrated centers in each empire. Now this does provide interesting opportunities such as allowing an apt leader to focus their attention on those major centers  to deal the biggest damage. On the other hand, perhaps the regional capital is too difficult to assault and  knocking out all of the food suppliers might be a more effective way to neutralize the population.... Overall, I'll label this a positve because for new players, it's simple enough to get into and only the most diehard captains of industry will feel bored with the economy of SR2.
(+) Tutorial - There's a lot of games that do the tutorial wrong or make it super confusing. SR2 did it right. It explains all you need to know to get started and does so in a UI-friendly manner.
------------------------------------------------------------------
Out of Supplies
(-) Empire Customization: Yes you can customize by assigning your empire a unique government / space travel method and a few other features. You can also give your empire a portrait and which set of ships to use but that's about it. I'd have liked to be able to pick more bonuses for each empire such as maybe I'll take +10% budget but my ships do -10% damage or some trades like that. These are usually basics and for the game not to have them available was a bit of a let down.
(-) Tech Tree: The tech tree is a bit convoluted to look at. There's simply too many options being thrown onto a beehive grid that just disorients the eyes. Oh I need more budget, let me find how I can get to more business techs. Scan, scan, scan, oh there it is. Now I need more budget, oh the next tech and it's prerequisites for more budget is up here. It's just a bit too disorganized, especially for new players.
------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall I'd give this game 8 fleets blowing up out of 10. You'll find some new features that are unique to this game such as fleet design and diplomacy done right. I didn't touch on this but moddability will surely fix some of the weaknesses such as the lack of empire customization so that's why I didn't weigh too heavily on that part.
Anyways, fleet battles are epic and hopefully we can see thousands of thousands of ships fighting one day over some backwater planet that was only made important because multiple fleets decided to clash over it. That's my dream and the dream of many 4x space lovers!
------------------------------------------------------------------

I will be honest, I only heard of this game because of the contreversy surrounding the creater. But amid the turmoil, I found myself somewhere I didn't want to be -a particularly hateful state of mind. I've said things I am not proud of and decided to cool off and approach the axis of this whole ordeal with the presence of mind to be as objective and purely observant as possible, and leaving behind any intial personal feelings and bias so that I may gain a perspective. I am not a professional video game critic in the least bit, but I do write and edit people's stories as a hobby, so I like to think that I have a credible right to review this.
With all that said, and after playing through, I do no recommend this game.
Foremostly -and this critical point has been brought up before- can this really be considered a game? It is a digital choose-your-own-adventure novel that feels like it belongs to a site dedicated to ametuer fiction or to an art blog like Deviantart -not a video game distributer. I feel Depression Quest would of been more appropriate and more well received if it were distributed on an art site where skill progression and opinionated pieces are welcome. But Steam brings with it a great expectation, and you can be hard hit by the community if you fall short of it with even the greatest intentions. There just isn't a place for a glorified book in steam, and I feel that alone warrants my negative recommendation.
But beyond where and how the developers chose to distribute Depression Quest, the game falls flat in a number of ways. Despite a fairly strong start, the protagonist becomes insufferable and I find it impossible to sympathize half the time, and this is due to, for the most part, the constant repitition of the same theme of "I'm sad". The chapters blend together as a blur of melancholy and it becomes increasingly difficult for me to go on as it progresses to the point that it is so dull it becomes a chore to keep on reading. Each page felt like a rehash of the previous with a different background and theme like a depression Madlib. My determination to see it through to the end to gain perspective on the situation was the only thing that kept me going, and I otherwise would of just stopped half way through if this wasn't the case.
Then there is the sporadic grammar mistakes, colorless style, lackluster attempt at scenery and visuals, bluntness in the expression of emotions and feelings where I'm just told how he feels and am expected to just accept it -not a sight of subtley to be seen. And there's just a general lack of direction, with what would seem obvious to be the main goal of being 'not depressed' always being touched upon but never probed. Without the going into detail of the process of recovering and coping with depression, all this is is page after page of complaining and whining, with brief breaks to choose between an obviously good choice and the obviously bad one -which brings me to my last point.
Literally the only gameplay mechanic the game provides is terrible. There is no critical decisions to be made. One is always the best choice with the rest at varying degerees of bad, making the story linear and defeating the purpose of a choice system, and therefore effectively turning this into a book entirely. The only reason to choose the bad decisions is just to speed through it again to see how it ends differently -and spoiler: it isn't suicide. Yes, what you would expect be the greatest and most terrible end the character could possibly find in game about depression is not that. Not to say that I was hoping to see someone, even fictional, lose themselves to the struggle with depression, but it would add such a greater depth when the reppercussions of not being able to solve your issues with depression is ultimately depth at your own hands.
If this game achieved anything, it definitely looks like a depressed person designed it, but it needs a
that can bring across the feeling of depression and have it seep into the reader with the protagonist's actions and thoughts without the writer themselves getting absorbed in self-pity. If this was a story I received from a upstart writer, I would praise him/her/whoever for what they accomplished, but would stress that they put asside a few more months to work on it and make it everything it could be. However; this is a professional, million dollar site that I and everyone else expects a higher standard from, and this game is below that standard. Its only saving grace is that it's free.

I've decieded to give this a bash because I saw Isaac Schankler was involved with the project and I really liked his work with Analogue and Hate Plus. People have been bringing up the controversy with Quinn, but here's the thing: it has nothing to do with Depression Quest so I could care less about someone's personal life simply because it was never my business to begin with so lets move away from that and actually talk about the "game".
Depression Quest is simply a choose you own adventure kind of ordeal touching upon the subject of depression and I have mixed feelings on how the subject matter was handled. I do like on how it simulated the feeling of depression since there is a sense of hopelessness in the world, but what also irritates me is that they crossed out choices that makes a real positive impact in your life and forces you to remain in a state of depression for the entire run, which for those people who are currently or formerly depressed might not find this helpful in any shape or form (at least they gave us a warning about suicidal thoughts). You are basically just some guy in his twenties who currently is in a state of depression possibly because of an inferiority complex constantly comparing himself with his friends and family including his significant other.
Unfortunately the soundtrack basically consists of one track on a loop the entire time and for me, it did not deliver much of an impact so that was pretty disapointing because if Depression Quest wasn't good, (which it wasn't) I was hoping the music would at least make up for it.
Despite having multiple "endings", I had no desire to go back and find out what they are because I feel it would be similar to one another, which is falling into despair with no chance of self redemption with the best "ending" is continuing to assess your condition which in no way it feels reassuring which is the purpose of this "game" and it acheives it.
I do not know much about depression other than it negatively affects the relationships of those around the victim, so to end this, I can only say to those who is or knows someone that is depressed, try to be patient and get assistance as soon as possible.

This game is great for a group of friends who love playing games together.
The Yawhg is not your average multiplayer game, however. It is sort of a multiplayer choose-your-own-adventure game. Each person chooses a character and then chooses where they want to spend one of their 6 weeks before the Yawhg arrives. The beuty lies in the amount of variation you can get therein. Will you stay at the bar and get drunk all week? Will you go to the palace and dance the nights away? Will you don a mask and fight crime in the back alleys for the slums? All these options are available to you.
After choosing what you will be doing that week, a small story is told to you for that week, maybe while fighting crime you meet someone who turns you into a vampire! Maybe during your work at the hospital hundreds of leeches break free! While they are limited, the story elements of each location are different from each other and highly entertaining. During the story part, your stats will change (Physique, Mind, Magic, Finesse, etc). These will be important after the Yawhg arrives.
The most interesting thing about the story elements is that they have a chance of crossing over to other areas. If the aformentioned leeches break free from the hospital, they may spill over into the slums! Or maybe even the lake! The dryad you met in the woods may show up in the arena! The combinations are truely interesting and make the game even more fun to explore.
After the Yawhg arrives, you are tasked to rebuild by taking on one of many important (or not so important) roles around the town. Will you band the remaning townsfolk together and lead? Will you try to use your might to build? Will you use your magical aptitued to brew potions? Beware, though, because if you do not have the proper stats (gained from the story parts of the game) you will fail in your attempt to help, and you will hinder the rebuilding.
After everyone has chosen a role they are given their last story segment and you are told if the town will press on after the Yawhg or if it will ultimately fall to ruin.
I would like to see more stories added or mod support so that the community could add their own stories.
The game is overall fun for a group of friends, and trying to get the best ending can be challanging and a true team effort. I would highly reccomend this game with 2 or 3 friends that are will to experiment in gameplay and work together.

Ok so, here's the thing. The Yawhg isn't a bad game, in fact the ideas behind the game and the execution are very sound. The problem is that this really shouldn't be a paid product. The Yawhg feels and plays like a free flash game, and ironicly is no where near as good as other Flash games of this type.
Unlike the interactive fiction games you find on Kongrigate The Yawhg isn't really a single player game, rather is basicly a digital Cards vs. Humanity type experience (i hope that makes sense). The Yawhg is turnbased, with each turn repersenting a week Players take turns selecting what they will do on any given week, after 7 weeks a great disaster (the titualr Yawhg) will befall the city and using the skills you've learned throughout the last 7 weeks will try to repair the town in the best way you can. the idea being that the event's pre-Yawhg will be so wacky that players will be able to laugh and have a good time and all the post-Yawhg stuff will be really sad and dramatic. In practice though it's horibly broken, the way the game is structured with it's stat system means that after about one playthrough you'll have no problem easily maxing out a stat to win at the end. This would be fine if the random events at the core of the game kept you guessing, but they don't. Not because there bad or anything but because there are so few of them. I bet that if you played the game with four players one you would see everything this game had to offer. So in other words the game has no replay value what so ever and in the end for a game that costs $10 that's unacceptable.
It may sound like The Yawhg is the worst thing ever but it's not. It clear that the developers put a lot more heart and soul into it then... other games *cough* Call of Duty *cough* and i would love to see a game like this with a lot more random events. But The Yawhg just feels unfinished, both as a regular video game and as the party based experience it WANT'S to be. Meaning i can't recomend playing 10 or even 1 dollers on The Yawhg, becing as it clearly shouldn't be a paid product.

TIMEframe – A short story on Art vs. Games.
There are games in this world that border on art, and this would be one of them.
This game is equal parts Journey (art direction)if it was first person, The soundtrack of a triple A title such as Halo (just what came to mind when I was playing) and a world to explore.
I honestly didn’t know what to expect when I first hit play on this, but this wasn’t it.
There is a narrative here, that you discover in pieces. You can’t possibly do it all at once. There isn’t enough time.
Even knowing that there isn’t enough time though doesn’t stop you from pushing forwards. You can feel time running out as you go to the next location, needing to hear more about this world.
And much like our own world, we’re looking at it as it was, trying to avoid what is to come. I like to think that when I played this, I was able to get a story of my own. That there is no clear narrative to this game outside of the pre-determined factors that are known. Your role, can be as trivial, or as important as you can imagine it to be.
It’s not often that a world so small, can feel so massive. This world, frozen into a trickle of time, flames slowly licking the air, flowers slowly spinning in the air and water falling slowly. It tells a story of The Nomad, which for sake of the story itself I won’t tell anything about. The first time I played, I didn’t know what would happen. Then there was a moment of realization. It takes you on a journey through this world, but you’re in control of how you get there.
I found myself often exploring just to get another screenshot, one more picture for the library. There is a dream-like quality to the game, and it’s a great dream to have because of the beauty. It’s not about the end, but how you get to that point.
This can be  a small, short game, or it can last you days. How much time you want to put forth is your decision.  Is this a game I would recommend, yes. If only to support these artists in their work, and to have something, an experience to show your friends when they come over, because after having finished this game, that’s what it was. An Experience.

I've never been so delighted by a game before. I was expecting a walking simulator based around the concept of exploring a forgotten world. But there's this mechanic that gets introduced, and I don't want to spoil it, but the emotions that is conveyed when it first happen were so vivid and real- it was amazing. It's an exploration game with, and in all my years of gaming, has one of the most endearing and interesting mechanics with beauty in its simplicity. I've already said too much, please, go play it.
The idea is Impermanence. It flips the whole walking simulator / exploration genre on its head. I fully expected to explore the world looking for hidden secrets. In fact, I was kind of upset at the inclusion of this abstract map because I thought it hindered exploration. But as I neared the first landmark a twang of an acoustic guitar picked up and a subtle pacing began. I explored the landmark, checked out the plants growing, and was scaling up this hill when I was admiring this unique mosaic-esque art style the game has. Then I looked up and saw IT. A giant meteor seemingly breaking through the world leaving shattered pieces of the sky trailing behind it. I stood in marvel as it came closer and closer. I felt completely helpless and isolated, but endlessly intrigued. And then the screen faded to white...only to reapear at the beginning of the game.
You see, here's the catch: you're expected to explore as much as you can of this world within a ten minute limute (or 10 seconds slowed down as the description says). That's why you have the inclusion of the map. Each "cycle" (as you later discover) has you frantically searching the different landmarks. And it creates this atmosphere of beautiful impermanence. I WANT to explore everything here, the setpieces are beautiful and evoke a sadness of a recently deceased civilization. But I can't explore everything...not with doom lingering overhead. You'll start running to land marks finding the text each one boasts piecing the story together all while looking over your shoulder at the, at first, blank sky that evolves into a dot, a circle, and a meteor crashing through.
It's wonderously exerimental and, sorry to use the term, a bit avant-garde for this new genre of walking simlutaors. It shows what can really be done with them and the themes and emotions they can convey. The ending of the first cycle is one of my favorite video game moments in recent history, and the game became even more engaging afterwards.

Garrett is back, and better than ever!
After Looking Glass was absorbed/dissolved/disbanded/exploded whatever, it was thought we'd never see another good Thief or System Shock title again. Although the Bioshock series (particularly the first one) had been applauded for being the 'spiritual successor' to System Shock 2 to the point of ad nauseam (not entirely justified either if you ask me); there had been nothing for the Thief series. Granted there was Deadly Shadows, but even ex-members of Looking Glass being part of Ion Storm couldn't change the fact that it was missing something. Maybe it was the 3rd person perspective? Console to PC port? Whatever the reason is, it missed the mark ever so slightly - but I digress.
In the simply titled Thief we are finally back in the shoes of Garrett sneaking around town relieving the 1% of their trinkets. The world which he inhabits is rich and detailed as are the various ways one can get around; whether it be rooftops or streetlevel. Noticeable improvements have been made to AI in relation to their awareness and detection as well as methods to avoid/distract enemies and victims. But the thing that really shines for me is the storytelling through inner dialogue and voice acting and audio in general; and the atmosphere... whew... I remember crapping my pants during those zombie missions in The Dark Project - and for this one the Asylum is doing the same. Some may think 'how is that different from the originals?', simply put - it's not. That's the beauty of it, they've somehow captured all the elements that worked in the first two games all the while bringing the graphics and technology up to speed.
I've been waiting a long time for another installment in the Thief series, and so far with this one I haven't been disappointed.
The original First Person Sneaker is back and in full form.

Yomawari Midnight Shadows improves on its predecessor without breaking the mold. You are playing as a little girl wandering in a Japanese town at night, while ghosts are roaming around, and there is a dog involved once more. This could feel like "more of the same", but the game adds enough little things that it's a significant step up from the first game:
- Outside of a specific area (and for good reasons), all of the ghosts are brand new, which means new strategies to figure out to survive
- You now have two protagonists instead of one, and even if they both play exactly the same, that gotta count for something, right?
- You can now enter some buildings, which makes for more variety in the environments you explore
- The game is bigger than the first one, and it's a brand new town for you to explore
- More bosses!
- And last but not least, more twists that will leave your soul scarred!
If you liked Yomawari Night Alone, you are sure to love this one. And even if you did not, you will probably enjoy it if you enjoy things such as a nice blend of horror and cuteness, when your heart bleeds, ghosts, quiet little towns, scissors, and trying to run away as fast as your little girl's feet can carry you.
I recommend playing Yomawari Night Alone before playing this game if you did not already.

I'm severely cynical of all sides in the recent social justice craze. Individuals must be objectively judged for there to be true justice, regardless of their stance on (insert prejudice or cause here), and hopping on a indignation hype train is not the way to do it.
Criticism of the development staffmembers involved aside, there is some good information to be had from this project. Do I believe it belongs on Steam? No. Do I believe it could potentially assist the general public with becoming more educated about "depression" as a whole? Sure.
It feels disingenuous to call this a game, when it's more like an after-school special, or a pamphlet you'd find at a clinic. Having had to live with and help many people in my life come to terms with and work through their issues, I understand exactly the message trying to be conveyed, but also fully understand that the only people who would benefit from a run or two through this "story" are practically non-existent: simultaneously open-minded and ignorant.
A person with depression doesn't need this to understand depression, because they live it.
A person who deals with depression in others doesn't need this to understand depression, because they live(d) with it.
A person who honestly believes depression is not a real illness doesn't understand depression, and this won't convince them otherwise.
This belongs on a website, which I believe was its original form. It must be easily and publicly accessible, and distributed, to be truly effective.
I recommend talking about depression to raise awareness, but can't recommend this on Steam because it (and mental illness) isn't a game.

Depression Quest is about a chap who can get a kitten...
His psychological problems seem to mostly stem from both, a lack of sleep, and feeling everything is too easy; and attempts to deal with it via a misguided imposter syndrome. (freudian slip of the developers, perhaps?)
Anyways, in the story you can get a pet kitten. Highlight of the game.
On that note, it is not really much a "game" as much as a "take some mostly irrelevent choices that we think reflect depressed people's thoughts" sort of thing. The design is mostly text and images with links. This is closer to a choose your own adventure book, a shallow one at that.
The imagination here is very paint by numbers and does not portray depression as anything other than a woe is me dithering, to the point where it's downright insulting to the science behind depression as well as misrepresentative of depression in sufferers as a whole.
But umm... kitty... going in between people's legs... (The writers are oh so cleverly subtle)
I, by no means like freudian phychology, but this game's writing makes a very compelling argument for it.
Conclusivly, this choose your own adventure book (because calling it a game is highly demeaning to the gaming industry, forsooth, it is insulting to adventure books akin) comes off as an abusive exploitation of the depressed, and is downright offensive to the reader's (player would suggest gameplay) intelligence, shows and pervades a contempt for humanity, and portrays the depressed as unlikeable slobs who are to blame for their own issues.
Cons
-Choose your own adventure book pampered up as a "game".
-Insults your intelligence.
-Demeaning to men and women alike.
-Comes off as abusive.
-Taunts with choices you cannot choose.
Pro
-Kitten.
-Wonderous example of irony.

I'm sorry, but this hardly deserves any of the publicity, interest, or credit it has recieved. If you had told me that this was a browser game, I wouldn't doubt you for a second. I've seen browser games that put more effort in. Bare graphics, some piano music, and overall poor and unrealistic writing.
I can't say much on the game's subject. People I know with depression don't normally act in the way the character in this game supposedly acts, but that can be written off as coincidence. The word pretentious comes back because it simply feels like it's trying to be more than it actually is. These websites that reviewed it made it seem like something that would stun me and blow my mind with how thought-provoking it is. It wasn't. At all.
Not to mention the recent controversy surrounding this game. I have some not so positive words surrounding the developer and her boy toy- er, friends (HINT: Pretentious is one of them).  Quite frankly, I don't want to say them because I'm horredously afraid of Phil Fish and his threating twitter tweets.  Needless to say, this isn't about her as much as the game.

The only thing depressing about this game is the despicable regime of lies, slander, and cover-ups that were used to not only destroy an unrelated internet community and a program specifically designed to allow women to ability to make games, but also to push a game through greenlight based only on the perceived "abuse" of the developer rather than the actual merit of the game. Not only that, but while I won't make the accusations here, there is significant reason to show that the media coverage of this game has been based on personal "favors" for journalists covering its development, and not on any significance in the development of the game.
Beyond that, the game fails to contribute in any meaningful way to a person's understanding of depression or other mental illnesses, and as someone who has had personal experience with friends and family with said illnesses I can say that with confidence.
The only positive point I can come up with to describe this game is that its content matches its price level. There is almost nothing that you can do gameplay-wise, the wording of the options is tacky to say the least, and the sound is poorly balanced, even when it hasn't been altered.
I can objectively say that this game does
deserve to be played, and I would not recommend greenlighting any further content by this developer.

The rationalization this game uses for the anthropomorphization of the Manga artists is weak, to put it mildly.

One of the screenwriters is the very astute DeXPeri. This game's “believe in yourself” message is borne out, in a perverse way, by the very fact that it even exists. - At least as far in as I got, you don't have much of a sense of objective. The game starts with an objective for you, but then it just feels like the average day in the life of this weird bulb kid in this weird world. You're stuck in rooms doing regular, daily activities. There's a puzzle room to get something to eat, then a puzzle room having to do with going to the bathroom after you've eaten. Then there's intermittent puzzles that are flashback memories of casual activities you had with your grandfather. They feel like filler. The whole thing kinda feels like filler. I think these things make the game feel less satisfying.
- The puzzles themselves can sometimes feel particularly random/illogical. It really relies on just clicking what's available and trying everything. That should only be a last resort in point-and-click adventures; not a starting off point.
Anyway, it's not horrible at all. I could've happily finished playing it, but I got it on sale for half price, and I still felt that was more money than I wanted to pay for the game. So after 45 minutes of playing, I put in for  a refund and wrote this review. If it sounds fine to you and you're really into the cool and humourus art style (it IS funny in its Garbage Pail Kids way), then by all means, look at this like a positive recommendation.

Bulb Boy is a very interesting game about a boy's search for his grandfather, who has been abducted by a mysterious darkness. The game is tremendously odd in that you control a cartoonish little boy and his dog, but yet it is horrifying and disgusting. I appreciate that it is very unique and not just the same old thing, but I didn't actually enjoy it much and can't recommend it.
Pros:
+ Very unique theme and art. The game combines cutesy and grotesque in a really interesting way. Kudos to the devs for doing something different.
+ Point and click puzzles are fairly well constructed. Solutions make sense, for the most part.
Cons:
- The game is too gross. If you don't enjoy being grossed out, you're not going to like fighting poop monsters, getting eaten by worms, using vomit to propel yourself forward, or riding around in the carcass of a giant spider.
- The game is very short. It took me about two hours, and I wasn't going particularly fast.
- The puzzles are very straightforward and not very interesting. There are very few things to click on, and so the solutions are often very simple. Unlike many point and click games, you really don't need to switch on your problem solving skills for this one.
- The ending left me disappointed. It seemed very cheesy, didn't fit the theme, and didn't explain anything.

Reading the other reviews for this game I see huge walls of text expounding upon the philosophy of the game and the deep thoughts it provokes. I'm not really going to do that here because honestly, I can't see myself spending more time writing about it than I did playing it. Plus I'm not that deep of a thinker.
It's a very pretty game, very stylized with a sort of triangular texture applied to everything. The soundtrack is simple but effective, becoming more elaborate with every new discovery. Basically, you're wandering through a landscape looking for various locations that will present you with a bit of text or information about the inhabitants that once lived in this area. By visiting all these areas you unlock the one last location on your map that implies where everybody went to escape the giant meteor that's getting ready to obliterate the world.
Yeah, that meteor. I hate that damned thing. After a few minutes you see it in the sky, getting closer every minutes until ten minutes have elapsed and the screen whites out, starting you back at the big tower in the center where you started. Thankfully your map still shows the locations you've visited so you can continue on your merry way, so it's not that huge of an obstacle. The reason I hate the meteor is because it turns a game that could be a relaxing contemplative exploration into a race against time to find the next location before you have to start over.
Still, this is a damned nice game, worth the money and I can think of a hundred other worse ways to spend an hour. Admittedly I got the game for free for supporting the author's upcoming game Lacuna Passage but having played it I would have gladly paid for it.

Imagine you appear in a world where there are 12 different wonders of a civilization that has been destroyed, or perhaps they have vanished. Now imagine that there is a comet, or perhaps it is simply a prophetic encounter that seems to have occurred, and that you will experience this event as well.
In TIMEframe, you are not going to be running around, talking to people, you are going to be take a soft music journey to uncover what was hidden about these 12 wonders, and perhaps unlock the power of an object left in this world. There is one catch, however, and that is that you shall find yourself constantly returning to the spire, which is where your story begins, but have no fear, the actions that you take in those 10 minute increments will be retained.
One of the ways that you will know that time is almost up is hidden in the music, now you might not catch it the first couple of times but it will be the harbinger of your position in the world resetting. In so regards this can be a good thing, mainly because it is possible to get lost in the world, and to restart back in a centralized point, can get you back on the correct path that you need to be on.
You will find that by pressing the Spacebar you will reveal many dots on the screen laid out in an infinity pattern. You'll also notice that if you successfully reach one of the wonders in this world that that dot will change into a symbol. If you unlock all the symbols you will be able to progress the game into the ending.
I'm going to be totally honest with you, when I first heard about this game I was told it was in the same vein as Dear Ester, and in a way it is, but it also isn't. Dear Ester seemed more like a guided tour, this game at times seems like a blind journey. Now that's not saying that this game is lacking something, but it does take a little bit of time to get used to, and it also takes patience, ESPECIALLY since you might find yourself within a stone's throw of a wonder, and the special music is playing, and you know that you're not going to make it before the world resets again.
That can be frustrating, and to add to matters you are going to be walking the entire time, there is no run or speed walk button, you are going to be taking in the sights, you are going to be walking through this little window in time, and although at first I didn't know if I was going to be able to hang with this game, I've got to admit that once I accepted the reset, and the natural pace, I got hooked into wanting to see what would happen when I visited all the wonders.
This is definitely not a game for everyone, but this is a kind of meditative game that one can definitely lose time in. I do kind of wish that when you interacted with the wonders, and you got that small quote or bit of history that it was spoken in some kind of interesting accent, but at the same time I don't know if that would actually end up hurting the experience, either way this is something that in the end I enjoyed, and to be honest part of me was a little same to see the credits roll, of course there was a part of me as well that felt a great deal of accomplishment after finally seeing this game all the way through. So in the end I think I'm going to have to give this game an 8.2 out of 10.

It looks great, the music is absolutely awesome, controls are nice, there's good atmosphere. A lot of elements are on the right place but it fails to give me an engaging experience, and the main reason for that is the lack of depth in the game.
You'll start playing the game with, for example, a wizard. So you'll start to walk around, shoot fireballs, collect coins and keys. And you'll keep doing that forever with very little variation. Very rarely you'll update your character to change some stats that you'll hardly notice.  Enemies are all more or less the same thing. It's not very challenging, the few times I die was because I got bored and reckless. Your only concern is with what's on screen at the moment, which always require the exact same strategy, and occasionally backtracking.
From the top of my head, some things that could help this game out are management of resources, the good old levelling system, different abilities, (more) different enemies that require different strategies etc. There's a good reason these things keep showing up in games, they add a whole level of gameplay the player needs to be aware of, it adds a layer of complexity. The player is not only moving and shooting, he's always thinking about these other layers, and that influences how he plays the game. Too many moving parts and the game becomes overwhelming, too few and it lacks depth which is the case with hammerwatch.
On a side note, I only played the single player campaign and I'm starting to get the impression that the game was intended as a coop experience. This could explain the simplicity, as it makes the game more casual and easy to play with friends without any prior skill.

A very fun metroidvania game that challenges you all throughout the game. It take a rather decent step away from Momodora III in most ways. Most notably is the art style. It's damn good. Everything looks fluid, colorful, and realistic for all animations making it a very pleasing to look at. Another change is the difficultly. I feel like the Dark Souls and Bloodborne was being played while making this game. The amount of dodge roll, the amount of damage you take, and the flower animation stand out to me the most but there are pleanty of other things you feel is very Dark Souls about the game and while 90% of other games try it as well, this is one of the few that does it right. Enemies feel placed in a way that punishes you for trying to rush and with the amount of damage that is done, on hard at least, makes you slow down to a steady pace that's neither too slow nor too fast. Another nice change of pace is the length of the game. Momodora III takes only 1-2 hours on your first run and can be speed runned under 10 minutes while Momodora 4 took me 5 hours on the first run and I'd imagine the speed run being around 30-40 minutes.
My only real complaints is the music and the items. Most of the music is just ambiance that doesn't stand out except for bosses and 2 areas and while the boss music is okay, the area music is forgettable. I actually only remember 2 pieces and one of those is because I died like 15 times on a certain boss and the other was the final boss fights. My other complaint is how the items aren't exactly balanced and a lot do the same thing. There's like 5 ways to boost your attack but once you get to the end, you have a deadly dou combo that makes the game too much easier. I feel like Momodora III handled these two much better and hopefully in Momodora 5, we'll get a combonation of the two games.
Overall, it's a huge improvement over Momodora III. If you're a fan of the series or have just looked at the game and thought "that looks interesting" then you won't be disappointed. Very solid 4/5

Momodora is an interesting Metroidvania type game. I'm not usually fan of this type of game, but the cute artwork and beautiful music drew me to it. I have a soft spot for cute female protagonists, what can I say? I've completed 100% of the map, but still have plenty of challenges to do, like a pacifist run and a run without dying. Not to mention collecting Ivory Bugs & completing Insane difficulty.
As mentioned above, the art and music is beautiful. The gameplay itself is also smooth and responsive (I am using a keyboard and the only issue I have is forgetting which buttons do what). Transition between the various rooms is fluid and feel rather nice. The bosses are unique and have a variety of mechanics, but for the most part you can look for a pattern and beat them.
Speaking of the bosses, they range from mini-bosses to full on kick-your♥♥♥♥♥bosses. The hardest boss for me so far took me around 10 tries to kill it, while before that one, I averaged about 3 tries. For the most part, you will encounter the bosses in a linear fashion but occasionally you can fight them depending on your preference. (I probably killed that hard boss before I was actually supposed to)
While exploring the map, you'll encounter areas you can't reach yet. You will unlock these as you progress (obtaining new abilities), kill bosses, or obtain keys. You'll be backtracking a few times, but there is a lovely little map feature so you can keep track of where to go.
In your travels, you will encounter various characters that give you information or background about the world. It is a nice way to give the option of learning about the world without forcing you into too many forced-reading sessions.
All in all, it is a pretty decent game. I was able to complete it in about 7 hours in my first run, so it is definately worth the $10 price.
**As a side note, after completing the game, it lets you start over, and keep most of your items & your HP increase. You lose your upgrades and key items. In this "New Game+" mode, I was able to complete the game in little over an hour. (I should add at this point, I'm playing on Normal difficulty)

I finished the game. As most people know I am a big fan of this franchise. Rather than doing a normal review, while playing the game I kept notes of the thoughts that occurred to me, and thought I'd share them for those who've been asking me what I think of the game.
• No taffers, no Hammerites, no Keepers, no Pagans. No mention of the builder, one mention of the trickster in passing. The "rich vs poor" meme is not a good substitute. UPDATE: there is one reference to the Hammerites at the end.
• This is not Garrett. Different voice, different face, different clothes, different personality. Same name.
• Looting is fun
• Sneaking mechanics are pretty solid, they fixed issues from previous games where guards never looked up and where you were always invisible in doorways. However it is annoying sometimes, you'll be sitting still they won't see you, but then they start "seeing" you more, and suddenly shout out "IS THAT SOMETHING MOVING?"
• Graphics are fine. Very good performance.
• No distinction is made between killing and knocking out??  There are no blackjacks, you sneak up behind someone and press an action key to perform a melee takedown.
• Contextual controls are dumb. I'll decide when I want to jump, thanks.
• The paintings are pretty... interesting.
• I missed the old thief-style cutscenes
• Lockpicking minigames are terrible in all games, this one is less terrible than others.
• The city in this game is better than the one in Deadly Shadows, and I like the sidequests.
• Rope arrows are limited to only specific anchor points, they seem to disappear when you reload the zone and the arrows cannot be retrieved.
• Much of the humor and personality of the city is gone. The humor that does exist isn't nearly as funny or clever.
• No more crate stacking, and no jumping
• Hate the name, we already had a Thief. This is Thief 4.
• The city lost a lot of the steampunk vibe.
• I enjoy the rooftop navigation, but wish there were fewer loadscreens.
• Windows are annoying. You have to go through a button mashing process to open one to get into a house, then the window immediately closes and you have to do it again to get back out. It quickly becomes tedious.
• The asylum seems like a less-scary ripoff of The Shalesbridge Cradle.
• If a guard sees something has changed, like a door open on their patrol route, he will investigate. This is great. I also noticed on occasion they will investigate every time they pass that open door. If the room is fairly big this can mean you add a significant delay to their patrol, which is strategically interesting, if not particularly smart AI.
• On the hardest difficulty, when playing passively, Thief is more difficult than Dishonored.
• Some fun puzzles for getting to loot
• Why is Garrett collecting a  bunch of crap in his home now instead of selling it?
• Be very careful about hiding in wardrobes as it forces the game to quicksave.
• It seems like the new developers only played Deadly Shadows
• The story was mostly an incoherent mix of cliches, and ends unsatisfactorily.
• The Thief-Taker General is pretty ridiculous.
The game is not horrible, but given the source material and what it could have been, it is very disappointing. If you want a true Thief expierience, Thief 2 and 1 (Gold) are still perfectly playable, and still the best games ever made.

I've never played a Thief game.  This is my first review on Steam.  I got this game because a lot of people were comparing it to Dishonored, which I loved.  However, this game is *nothing like Dishonored*, in a very bad way.  The only reason I've played for ~5 hours is because I keep pushing through, waiting for the game to get fun, and it has yet to do so.
My biggest gripe about the game is the combat.  Combat is terrible - absolutely *horrible*.  I know, I know - it's a game focused around stealth - but, that doesn't mean the combat mechanics should be completely ignored - and by completely ignored, I mean you have one melee move you can do, which is to keep hitting the guards with a club until they fall to their knees, then you have to hold down a button and wait for this meter to fill up and then you do a takedown move.  Dumbest mechanic in the history of games.  Who beats someone almost unconscious and then stands there like an idiot for 2-3 seconds before taking them out?  A serial killer.  Not a thief.
I've played for around 5 hours and as far as I can tell, there's no real story.  I've just been sneaking around stealing stuff for ~5 hours and it's really getting old.
The levels seem much more open than they actually are, too.  They're much more closed off than Dishonored.  They're actually quite linear - at least, so far there's been a clear path that I've had to follow to get to each checkpoint.
The game encourages you to eavesdrop and overhear conversations.  Fine.  But give us more than two or three scripted conversations that just play over and over on each level?  Sometimes you can't even tell where the voices are coming from - it's as if they're just coming out of nowhere, then you realize "oh.. it's coming from inside that building which is completely unaccessable."
Lastly, there's been more than one instance of a guard getting stuck along his path and just spinning around and around.
The only way I could recommend this game is if you really just don't like combat at all (because if you're detected, you might as well just reload your last save because the combat is so horrible) and if you don't mind a complete lack of story, at least for the first ~5 hours.

This game, sigh. Where to start?
Let's start with the good. The graphics are really good and atmospheric and, well...
