First and foremost, I want to say I'm writing this as a beta player, and subscequent two year player of DotA, as well as a five-year-long League of Legends player, so I'm very experienced in the MOBA genre by now.
So when I was given an early access copy of this game by a friend so he could have a three-man team going, I was quite confident in my skills going in.
It was very misplaced.
Battlerite is a much faster game, cutting out leveling, laning, or anything you would recognise from the major MOBAs, like League of Legends or DotA. It is a game that very much focuses on the "Arena" portion. Everyone takes control of one champion and fights it out together, and unsurprisingly, this can get very addicting and very, very fun.
Battlerite, if the previous statement hasn't already informed you, is fast paced, multiplayer online battle arena game (
) created by the good folks at Stunlock Studios. It was released back in September 20th, 2016 to Early Access, offering full access to all of the game's champions current and future to early access purchasers. A nice deal, given that the Early Access purchase came to around £15 (or about $19 for US players) for all of the characters instantly as well as a few extra bonuses and perks such as extra cosmetics and titles. As well as, of course, playing the game early.
It was then revealed that on November 8th of this year, Battlerite would go Free-to-Play, expanding the audience massively as well as introducing premium currency to use for purchases such as cosmetic chests - which seem to be far more generous than most - as well as other features to be later added.
Since not too many people seem to care about artsy junk, I'll keep this consise. Battlerite looks really nice. It's polished, round and cartoony, and all of the characters have their own distinctive silhouette, way of moving and aesthetic in both graphical flourish and sound choices. To give an example, Blossom, a nature-loving, cheerful deer-lady skips around, leaving flowers behind her. All of her skills trail magical, soft, natural-looking colours, and are backed up by her giggles and playful vocalisations. (
) In a nutshell, it's very easy to identify the characters at a glance.
While I'm at it, I'll say that the character diversity so far is pretty wide in many regards. There's multiple body types, a good spread of male, female, god-gifted monks, bandits, elementals, monsters, human-hybrids and much more. It's not quite at the kind of crazy selection League is at just yet, but given some time to go through it's next year of F2P release, I'm very confident enough to say that Battlerite's cast is going to expand ever further.
The game is very soft on the eyes and nice to look at, even on lower settings, looking appealing and running stable on most machines. I would certainly never call it ugly, and the aesthetics of the randomly-chosen arenas you fight in always allow the abilities and their area markers to remain as clear and identifiable as they always are. So, I guarantee you that you won't be messed up by some horribly innacurate indicator.
As I mentioned before, Battlerite is all teamfights within an arena. Battlerite's gameflow goes like this:
Long story short, it's simply: Get in the arena, fight with friends, and win, and try not to miss.
In case I've lost you with this title, I'll explain. This will be covering the big thing most people will be asking: "So what
I have to pay for now that it's Free to Play?"
Well, first of all, the only current DLC available (at time of writing) are a few packs:
- The
- which gives you everything the Early Access offered, but at a little bit of a higher price, about £5 and $7 extra: all current and future champions released are yours instantaneously.
- The
- giving you a nice bundle of goodies, including the following:
- The Soundtrack - which, erm... gives you the soundtrack of the game.

Subsection:

Like League of Legends and many of it's contemporaries, like Smite, the currency system is split into two main currencies- one being from gameplay, and the other is premium; Battlecoins and Gems respectively. However, it also features a third currency, exclusively for cosmetics: Tokens.
Battlecoins are used to purchase champions and silver chests, as well as other smaller functions added down the line. Gems are optionally used for everything else and require purchase with real-world cash.
Gems are used to purchase Gold, Legendary and Special Event chests - which guarantee varying qualities of items depending on what type you buy - changing your player name, and other features to be added in future.
The third currency, Tokens, is gained through chests - either through duplicates or just unboxing large amounts - or possibly from certain events. They're used exclusively to unlock cosmetics; costumes, weapons, mounts and poses - which is a nice consolation knowing that even if you don't get the item you want from chests, once you have the tokens for it, you can buy it. A nice little addition I whole-heartedly applaud.
Keep in mind that chests can also be earned from daily or weekly missons the game sets you. 100% Free.

this game was essentially far cry 3 but with two new mode of transportation, which are mini-helicoptors and a climbing with a grappling hook. the story in my mind was pretty lack luster, and the ending was of a more philisophical nature. i personally like philisophical endings, however as mass effect 3 showed, most gamers dont like endings where the ending isnt spelled out for them. the story itself was pretty lack luster, you could skip most of the games quests and you would still be fine with your understanding of the ending. that said there are choices throughout the game and perhaps its just my choices that made most of the games story pretty boring. i would give this game a 6 out of 10 due to its boring nature and rehashing of far cry 3's gameplay, but then you have to consider the bugs i ran into. i finished a mission that took me 15 minutes and then after it was complete the loading screen got stuck. now as a programmer i know that spinners are a sham, but the fake loader added a small chunk every minute to make it seem like its loading.  i actually waited 5 minutes for the bar to finish because i thought it was just loading a custscene or something large. once the loading bar had filled i waited 10 minutes (i walked away from the computer), and when i got back it still hadnt loaded so i had to restart the game and redo the mission. there were also a few other bugs like screen stuttering and eagles cawing rapidly (they caw when they lock on a target, but perhaps they relock on the target when they cant find a path to the target, but i often cant find them so its just this bird really loudly cawing over and over again). the third main issue was the screen stuttering, this game is the same engine as far cry 3 and as such there shouldnt be any issues on my computer, but you can just see the general choppyness as you move through the world. these three issues persisted throughout the entire game and while they didnt hinder me (as in stop me from doing whatever i was doing) that often (except the loading issue, which happend to me about once every 2-6 hours), i still think they are an issue that warrents inclusion on how i rate this game. in short ubisoft needs to get thier♥♥♥♥♥♥together and stop releasing♥♥♥♥♥♥poor ports on pc and rehashed old games in general (my point that this was basically far cry 3 with a different color pallete and two small features added). this is probably the last far cry game i buy, unless they actually change something about the game or actually take some time to write a good story, and even then ill have to worry about them just releasing it as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port. one last word to the wise, i regretted buying this game, if you want this kind of game but havent played far cry 3 then buy far cry 3, if you want far cry 4 then wait till its at least 50% off if not 75% off (i found far cry 3: blood dragon more fun, and its far cheaper). in short, bugs included, rehashed gameplay, reused engine and textures, and it being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port, i would give this game a 4 out of 10.

I have played maplestory since early 2006 and I've kept playing since then. I have 6 level 200+ characters amd will continue to make more. I am an MMORPG fanatic and I really enjoy the 2D side-scolling games. I recently got Maplestory on steam to avoid using the horrendus Nexon client.
This game has a lot of grinding. A lot of grinding. Much like WoW, in Maplestory you constantly grind and are trying to level up your character to get better gear, a new job advancment, etc. That is one of the aspects I love the most about this game. In a game such as WoW you get new abilities every 4-5 levels depending on what level you are, in Maplestory you get things called job advancments. Basically, you have a certain moveset with certain abilities, you can upgrade these abilites until you reach a certain level, and then you get a new set of abilities. This is one of my favorite aspects of Maplestory and it really makes it unique. The player base in Maplestory is also awesome, everyone on here is extremely nice and it can be really fun to just talk to other players rather than grind. There are many other things for you to do besides grind of course; You can do "dungeons" where you are sent to a certain area for 10-15 levels and do quests for the NPCs there and have a lot of fun learning the lore, you can also fight massive bosses with other players (this is much like a raid in WoW). There are so many fun things to do in Maplestory which is why I have played the game for so long and will continue to do so.

For some reason, I've always had a weak spot for source mods. Some of my favorites being Zombie Master, Synergy, and this game. I remember playing the free weekend for this game around 2011 or 2012 and remembering how much I liked it. The gameplay is pretty cool, combines elements of both FPS and RTS, the commander gets an RTS Eagle-Eye view and can place a bunch of structures and so forth. The FPS gameplay is your standard shooter, point crosshairs at baddies, destroy enemy structures and so forth.
However, one thing really bothers me about this game: How come there aren't that many people playing? The game is fun, and with the addition of trading cards and Steamworks support, you'd think the game would be a little more popular. That's not to say there's absolutely nobody playing, while the community is small, it seems to be a very dedicated one. You should be able to makes a few friends pretty fast on here.
The game creates a nice twist by incorporating RTS elements into the mix, anyone who is a fan of team-based, squad combat shooters should feel right at home with this game. For $10, you can't go wrong.

Cons:
1. After 2-3 runs (which is about 7-9 hours) you basically have seen it all, there are only 2 types of "Home" maps and the rest just seem to cycle.

3. Collecting resources after you cleared a specific "level" gets boring.  One of the techniques of scavanging in this game is to collect everything from the level and stack it all in 1 pile next to the exit.
So what happens is that you keep coming back to the same level just to fill up your inventory from the huge pile of materials you stacked near the exit.
overall the game is fun for about 10-15 hours and definitely worth its price on sales.

This is the most depressing, hopeless version of The Sims I have ever seen. You control your people in a doll-house style game play. During the day, you improve your home and prepare for the night. During the night, you venture in to the warzone to gather resources and hope things go well back home in your absence.
It is an amazingly entertaining walk through surviving a warzone as a civilian, not a super-soldier, not a hero, just a civilian. The Cat Lady takes thoroughly simple gameplay and puzzle mechanics and uses its incredible story and atmosphere to turn itself into a highly tense and gripping game.
The Cat Lady's gameplay can perhaps be best described as side-scrolling adventure game, with a focus on puzzles but also featuring some other mechanics, such as simple stealth and combat (although these themselves take the style of a puzzle). Giving that solving puzzles is at the core of the game, it's good to see that although they vary widely in difficulty, and are well integrated into the game's progression.
The world of The Cat Lady is highly immersive. The use of sound effects and a top-notch soundtrack really create a sense of dread, but also of distance and detachment, which reduces as the game progresses. Coupled with a distinct art style, one truly feels that one is exploring the dark underworld of everyday society. Many envirnments are almost entirely black and white, reflecting the drepression of the protagonist, but occassionally the colour-pallete shifts to immense saturation, representing hope.

Originally I had low expectationt for this game. I saw some screenshots, I read a few reveiws, and I came away feeling like it was just an overhyped indie game. I caught it on sale and thought, why not. Once I finally started it up I found I had severely misjudged the game.
The art style I originally thought looked clunky and awkward in screenshots actually does wonders to setting, the tone and mood for the game and looks much smoother in motion. Everything feels dark and grimy and unpleasent, and highlights the ending quite well. that said the game also does a fantastic job of being unsettling and creepy.
The story is intriguing, but the charcters are the most interesting. The depiction of people. their struggles and lives, and the way they form interactions is really the meat of what makes this game fun. Walking in the shoes of a woman who's lost everything she loved in life and severed herself from the world, seeing neighbors and life through her eyes. It's very well portrayed, and they don't ham fist any 'lessons' into it really.
The game's puzzles are also a plus. While it follows the traditional formula of 'find x item and use on y thing' they're pretty simple to figure out and don't require you to preform huge logical leaps to solve them. They give you very clearly defined goals, and logic can carry you through how to accomplish them. The game is forgiving in that sense too, there's no puzzles you can just screw up and be unable to finish the game. No items you needed to grab in a room before you left because you can't get back into it later either. They devs developed the puzzles with the idea that they wanted you to actually progress it seems.
The downside is it's essentially a point and click adventure. Lots of moving around clicking on things, and listening to dialogue. There's some places you can make multiple choices, but alot of it is set on a specific plot line. This means you won't find alot of heavy mechanics in this game, and you don't have any real form of combat.
I was a tad unimpressed with the end of the game, but that is forgivable.
However if you're looking for an interesting, horror, point and click adventure with some really unique art I'd reccomend checking it out.
Easy pick up and play game, if you could do multiplayer its a very nice time filler.
ah this game is really fun and cool. The dialogue is clever and funny and the art and music is beautiful. its really fun to play with someone else too

The Cat Lady - 9/10
I have over 200 games on Steam but none seem to keep my interest for that long, but The Cat Lady has!
Every night I've been making myself a nice cup of coffee, sitting down then progressing further into the dark story. Voice acting is fantastic, especially between our main character and her room mate (Mitsi) It feels like I'm watching a really good thriller but I'm controlling the actions.
The art direction is really good, the music is great (I especially like the main menu music when you first boot up the game)
The story is really what grabs you, whilst most games revolve around the gameplay whilst there story is lacking, The Cat Lady is the opposite in that it is the story that takes the front seat, This isn't to say the gameplay is bad, the gameplay is similiar to a point and click although you use the keyboard keys to move your character in a 2d fashion (WASD being the main keys)
This is where my one complaint comes in, and the reason I scored this Masterpiece a 9 rather than a straight up 10. The controls do feel clunky, pressing down (or S) brings up your inventory, this feels sluggish and not as snappy as it should be.
I really wanted to sit back in my chair with my nice hot coffee and play this using my pad... The game should be perfectly suited to a pad, move left and right, select objects, open inventory, but whats this? No controller support?
I'm sure it would of been a simple thing to implement partial controller support, even a slight vibration feature on the pad when something jumps out (or even to reflect your characters heartbeat in the more tense sections)
I know there is 3rd party software out there to be able to map keys to the pad but this would of been a nice inclusion from the start.
But enough of my grumbling because that minor complaint is the only thing I can think of, This is one of the finest adventure games I have had the joy of playing since Grim Fandango & I look forward to future releases from this developer
+ Fantastic Story
+ Dark moody atmosphere
+ Great Voice acting & music
- Lack of controller support
- Slightly clunky Keyboard controlls

Well, first off...this is a point and click, but not in the traditional, click on everything on the page sort of way. Rather, it is set up in 2D scrolling fashion with interactive objects along the way.
Also, there is an in game disclaimer stating tha you should be at least 18 years old to play this. I would say that is mostly accurate. Consider it to be similar to a rated R horror/suspense flick. If you would watch one or allow your kids to watch one, then this game should be fine.
The visual style of the game is jarring, graphic, and quite lush in a minimalistic fashion. The images can really evoke a strong reaction from the player. It was truly effective in setting the dark, oppressive, and downright shocking (at times) atmosphere that the game relies on to get its point across.
The actual story is all of those things...dark, jarring, oppressive, shocking, hopeful, sad....a roller coaster of emotion....which is appropriate since the protagonist, Susan Ashworth, starts the game by commiting suicide via sleeping pills. She is cast into a sort of underworld where she finds that she will not be allowed to die until she performs five tasks...namely the execution of five "parasites" (aka serial killers). So begins her journey of self discovery  and as she progresses, she slowly unchains the shackles of mental illness (in her case, clinical depression).
As sick and twisted as the game can be, it also carries an underlying beauty to it, as seeing the worst humanity has to offer and overcoming that also helps Susan in overcoming her depression and start seeing the world in a hopeful light.
All told, I think the game took me about 5 hours to conclude, and I would recommend saving often if you intend to get all the achievements in one playthrough, as many of the scenarios have two possible outcomes that each come with an achievement. I kept forgetting to do so, but if it's important to you, the 100% achievements is very easy to come by. Speaking of which, there is some replay value here due to the fact that there can be more than one outcome to vaious parts of the game (or rather, more than one way to get the same outcome).
I would also note that chapters 5 and 6 in particular did drag out a bit too much in my opinion, but the pacing, while slow overall, was still pretty stellar in my opinion.
I definitely recommend this game, but not if you are squeamish or particularly sensitive to tense and dark scenarios.

I haven't made it to EndGame material yet, but from everything I've experienced so far, this is the one. I have played every big 4X space game out there and this one takes the cake.
PROS:
+Entirely unique diplomacy feature. It is complex and a little difficult to pick up at first, but it is very unique and advanced. Have only discovered a couple of games with this amount of diplomacy actions.
+graphics. Very smooth graphics. I have a lower-end PC and I haven't experienced below 40 fps even with 10x speed on.
+Interface is great and easy to use. The game is built on tabs now, for major interactions at least. There is the visual galaxy tab, diplomacy, research, designs, planets, and a community tab (which allows you to view the game's wiki and player-submitted ship designs). The overall flow of the interface is great, allowing you to jump between these tabs without losing where you left off in them.
+Combat and fleet management is much smoother than the first SR. Instead of building a large number of different ships and assigning them to a fleet that then gets deleted whenever you retrofit or do anything out of the ordinary, you build a single flagship. Once you have that flagship you start building support ships, which you can customize and design like a normal ship. You can then recruit them using the flagship and it'll automatically add them to your fleet. I very much enjoy this.
+Ship design system is amazing and very user friendly. The process is more visual now and is even better than the previous SR. I have only played with it a little at this time but from what I've seen so far it is very nice.
+New Planet Management system is unique. Have not experienced it before in a 4X game. Planets now use a hierarchy system, allowing them to level up and down depending on what resources the planet has access to. This allows for a more complicated gameplay and using real strategy when it comes to planet management. In a terrority of 5 systems with roughly 4-5 planets in each system you'll only be able to maintain 1-2 Level 4 planets (0 being worst; 4 being best). It is very easy to learn as well.
Neutral:
--Sound needs some work. The sounds are good and the music is good, but it is all pretty limited and gets a little repetitive.
--Research I feel is limited. I like the new system and how it works, but there doesn't appear to be many technologies you can unlock at this point. Many of them are just repeats that stack. Looking forward to new additions as development progresses.
Cons:
NONE! I'll let you know if I find any.

I do not even know where to begin.   There are some amazing ideas in this game, and it seems a lot of polish even during early access.  The diplomacy is unique and very complex, with influence and interactions that feel very very real.  The planetary resource systems are fascinating to me, as is the resulting trade networks that grow organically.  The ship builder is actually better than the first Star Ruler, which had an amazing ship builder.  FTL was weak in Star Ruler 1, here there are 5 different methods each unique and tactical.  Combat seems solid, manageable, and interesting.  The flagship system means that you are ordering around fleets, not ships, but you still have a nice amount of control and the ship numbers are amazing.   Everything is . . . perfect.
I'm a highly critical gamer with jaded tastes.  I've been disappointed by one 4x game after another.  MoO3, Endless Space, Sword of the Stars 2, all sad memories.  Even Galciv and Distant Worlds weren't quite good enough for me.  I have never been so completely blown away just playing a tutorial, realizing the depth of the systems I'm seeing laid out in front of me.  Assuming there is nothing horribly wrong with this game that is hidden from me currently . . . well damn, I'll say it, this might be the game that surpasses Master of Orion 2.
It's an overused cliche, but it fits with this game.  Things could go wrong, the AI may turn out to be useless, or some other chronic mistake, but I don't think so.  Star Ruler 1 was visionary and flawed, fascinating but clunky.  It seems they learned a lot from that game.  Seeing this come from a small studio . . . I hope it gains the accolades it deserves.  I also suspect modding will be amazing, since Star Ruler 1 had a wonderful modding scope, and I suspect they did the same here.
Buy this game.  No seriously, if you like 4x gaming at all, buy Star Ruler 2.  This isn't a game you buy just to support the ideas of the devs, though those ideas are amazing.  This is the game I wish I had paid more for, because I think I cheated the devs and got way more than I paid for.
:::Post-release:::
The game remains very strong, with several major improvements over the beta.  The ship design remains the high point of the game, and sadly the AI remains a little weak.  The AI is competent, certainly.  It does know how to play the game properly, but it lacks aggression.  On the other hand, it is smart enough to know when it has lost.
I won a game recently without actually taking a single enemy planet.  I out-expanded them slightly, and while they fought wars against each other, I offered surrender to whichever side was near to losing.  Most of them accepted subjugation, since I was a friendly power that was roughly 10 times their strength.  After I did this three times, I turned on the one remaining AI.  I declared war, sent my massive ships.  Three of my ships arrived in their systems and I received an offer of surrender before they could reach the planet.  I think they just saw the ships blotting out the sun and said "Nope, this is not winnable."  That is smart design and saved me a long slog to a certain victory.
Recent improvements to the tech tree have made it far more understandable and elegant.  Technology in general seems far more unique and useful as compared to the beta tech tree, which was somewhat repetitive.  Performance remains very good, I've yet to see a bug or crash in any of my games.  The races and various FTL methods have vastly improved from the beta, and the AI knows how to play every combination without error.
The modding community is rapidly expanding, as predicted, and has already furnished several very solid mods.  The devs have already incorporated some of the best additions as core gameplay, which does not surprise me.  I still recommend this game highly, it remains a very original and solid 4x game.  I have high hopes for the future, and I do feel they have delivered a solid game as it currently stands.  Of course, I always yearn for more.

I will star off by saying that star ruler 2 is an excellent game. If you like sci-fi empire building games this is one you will enjoy. So of this review will be things that I think the game needs and other complaints that is because the game is early access. First with the things I liked.
The galactic senate is an excellent addition to the game. It adds the ability to have tons of different options and effect. A creative change from just the simple allience and war options.
I like the fleet setup, which works around a flag ship that does not force me to command each unit individually. Creating your own ships has kind of lost some charm for me now that it is becomming more common, but I still welcome the feature.
The colonial developement system is cleaver. In a way it reminds me of the anno games but a bit simplified. In order to level up a planet you need to import specific resources. Depending on the variety of resources depends on what the consumers produce. But because a resource cannot be used on the same planet that exports it you will develope major centers. This helps differentiate one territory from another, something many games lack.
Now for the things I need to see changed:
I need a way to tell which empire is which. The empires are identified on the map with colors and that is it. In a game with more than just 3 or 4 players this becomes very confusing very fast. There are not enough colors or portraits to identify all the players. I need names to display on the planets when I hold over them and and maybe large names over the empires when I zoom out.
I have never seen the AI accept a trade agreement or allience or anything. The game lets you give treaties fancy names, but gives you next to no options with them. The do have a vassal status, which I see more and more. But like games such as space empires V or europa universalis I want some neat terms. Creating neutral zone, creating new states and trade tarriffs, and long term payments.  While I do not see it happening I always like it when games differentiate between occupations and integrations. I just am happy in a game where there are other resolution to war other than the endless conflict untill one empire completely conquors the other.
In the senate I'd like to see more options that could be tacked onto a vote. You have the rider, but I like to see some larger item that could be tacted on like the annex planet. It should be exspensive but interesting. I'd also like to see the option to force a player to release a system to be a new player. The new player of course would be their vassal. I also like an option to push for a vassal to become independent.
I would like to establish more uniqueness between the various player. This could be in the form of more race trait or in the form of different technological paths. The players just do not feel different enough to me.
I know this game is early access, so I should comment on bugs. Occasion I have more influence than my maximum, but I've encountered almost no bugginess. Although the AI may do all kind of weirdness I do not know about.

Oh wow. So, like almost everybody else, I've heard about this thanks to all the controversy surrounding Zoe Quinn and I went into it quite negatively biased. Anyway, I wanted to see what all this fuss was about and I'll try to sum up my thoughts as objectively as I can in this post.
So, with all that out of the way, is Depression Quest a good game? First of all, it's not much of a game. It's done in the classic choose-your-own-adventure style, but it's not done very well. Your choices don't affect the main course of the game very much - they mostly just affect your character's status.
Generally you just get a wall of text and a few options (which options you get depends on your character's status) and you choose one of them. This may cause a change in your character's status, e.g. it can make you more or less depressed. Then you get another wall of text which is a reaction to you choice and then you move on to the next event.
And that's it. Most of the game follows exactly this formula and you shouldn't expect any extensive branching - there isn't any. The only change is right at the very end, and that's simply not enough.
The other problem is that it's quite easy to get a good ending - just pick the choices that make your character actually DO something. And of course it's equally easy to get a bad ending - just pick the choices that make your character do nothing. Usually the choices are even ordered from good to bad, so you really don't need to think about them too much.
Unfortunately all the above means that there is not much replay value. You may go through the game two or three times just to be able to read the different endings, but you really will not be reading all the stuff before that.
Technically the game is alright. Although for some weird reason it has to run in three processes which in total use more than a hundred megs of RAM. I guess it's got something to do with the fact that the game is using Webkit. There's a graphical glitch when the text is shorter than what fits on your screen, but that doesn't cause any problems.
There are a few typographical mistakes, but nothing serious (there will probably be more mistakes in this post than there are in the game :P). I haven't noticed any bad grammar or misspellings.
What is kind of annoying is the sound. Basically, it's just a single repeating piano track which gets boring quite fast. There are some ambient noises for some of the events but nothing major.
And finally we get to the last part. This game obviously deals with depression, which is quite a strong emotional theme. So, did I feel depressed when playing this? Not exactly, although it did show me how a person with depression might feel - or at least I think so.
All in all it's not a great game. The mechanics are weak and the depression part just doesn't do it for me, but that is most likely subjective.
Finally, I do feel that it doesn't deserve all the publicity it's getting, but hey, at least it's free.
tl;dr: I felt more depressed when I couldn't find the bloody keys in Doom.

This has one very dissapointing thing compared to the original series:
When you encounter a challenge to surpass, does it feel like you're **inventing your own** solution to the challenge, or does it feel like you're **discovering** the pre-made solution to the challenge that the level designer put there?
This new game makes it feel like your job is to discover the solution that was implemented by the level designer.  In the original games, it felt more like you were inventing the soluton yourself by applying the tools in your theiving skillset.  Even though you can turn the hints off that still doesn't change the feeling that there's a single solution hardcoded by the level designer - it just takes the clues away to help find it but in the end you're still following the method intended for you.
This isn't about the plot, the graphics, or the glitches.  This is about the basic game engine design.  In the older games, Looking Glass studios hooked your thieving abilities directly into the low level behavior of the game's engine.  Whether or not the environment allows you to peek around corners, shoot a rope arrow, or jump, were all the responsibility of the game engine to decide.   If the person designing the level wants to make a jump possible, they have to abide by the rules of the game engine and make the jump the right length to make it possible.  If they want to prevent a rope arrow from working they have to abide by the rules of the game engine and make sure no surfaces are made from shootable materials. In the newer game, however, they took the lazier design of doing that all backward.  They made it the responsibility of the level designer to TELL the game engine where those abilities work and where they don't.  The game engine isn't in control.  The person who wrote the level is.
And that means inventing your own solution to the challenge isn't possible anymore because there is no such thing as "the rules of the universe" that you can work with to create your solution.  Every solution that works works because the level designer allowed it to work at that location.
And that ruins a lot of the feel of the game for me. Eidos Montreal got the rights to the game's name but ignored the entire design philosophy that made it good, and stole control away from the player.
It's a shame because using modern computer hardware you could have made a game with the "game engine in charge" design and gotten something a lot cooler than what Looking Glass did with 1999's limitations.  But instead they ignored that part of the game design and managed to make a game that was somehow worse despite using modern technology that makes everything prettier.

As for the length, this is the most subjective area. While it is relatively short (3 hours for me to 100% the game), I enjoyed the entire experience I had with it.
I can sympathize with people who want bang for their buck; there are plenty of $10 games on Steam that will give you 100+ hours. I bought this game through a Humble Bundle, and at the pricepoint I got it (~$1-$2), this game is a no-brainer.  This is definetly a quality over quantity game, and I recommend purchasing at a discount and beating the whole thing in on shot.

Far Cry 4 takes Far Cry 3's excellent gameplay and refines it to near-perfection. One thing you will notice when running around is that the game feels a lot like Far Cry 3, but a lot of the annoyances are fixed. Falling damage isn't nearly as brutal, and takes a longer fall to trigger it; simply jumping while running on a slight slope will no longer take half your health. The driving physics are also much-improved, and the vehicles, though similar-looking, are more useful and a bit more capable off-road. The pickup trucks no longer look so generic, and actually strongly resemble older-model vehicles of a particular US brand. You also get access to a wider variety of powerful weapons much sooner than in FC3.
Skill progression in FC4 is much more open than in FC3. There's fewer restrictions based on where you are at in the campaign. Sometimes you do have to accomplish a particular feat or task to unlock a skill, but it always tells you what you have to do so it isn't hard to figure out. Side missions are much more varied and rewarding.
The biggest problem I've had is that the game tends to stutter a bit randomly, for no real reason, and my machine exceeds the recommended hardware in every way. I am sure a future patch will fix this, but it is a bit annoying at times.
Overall, if you enjoyed Far Cry 3, you'll love Far Cry 4. It takes everything great about Far Cry 3 and improves it.

I'm casul Hearthstone and Paper Magic player so take this review with this in mind.
Clear recommendation for the great experience and reward structure this game got to offer compared to many competitors in the digital TCG market.
Magic Duels comes with an interesting deck building limit which seperates it from the traditional trading card game (TCG). You can only put 3 uncommons and 2 rares with the same name in your deck. Mythic rarity cards are limited to one each. This results in a deck building environment which I personally as it discerns itself clearly from the TCG. As a result the size of boosters containing 6 cards instead of the 15 cards you may be used to weights lighter. A booster comes with 3 common, 2 uncommon and 1 rare or mythic cards. Sets are smaller than in the original game because the developers don't invest too much time adding mechanical overly complex cards to the game but still big enough to promote many different deck archetypes.
You can easily get 2 boosters for 300 gold with the multiple daily quest rewards and some wins probably while completing the dailies on Versus Mode against other players. In detail a win or an enemy forfeit mid-game rewards you with 30 gold while daily quests give you 60-120 gold depending on the complexity of the quest. Matches against random NPCs reward you between 5-20 gold depending on difficulty level. You get 2 new quests daily and have 3 quest slots at hand. Many daily quests can be completed in NPC matches as well.
If the enemy forfeits in online matchmaking, an AI takes over giving you the choice to continue the game. Rewards remain the same if the enemy did not leave immediately upon connecting to the match. It is funny to see people quitting because of bad draws and me getting then royally ♥♥♥♥ed by the AI because my draw also was not good. Getting them gold while losing a hard match is fun for me personally but might not be up everyones alley.
The NPC content is throughout with multiple campaigns which grant you prebuild decks and show you the different mechanics the card sets in Magic Duels got to offer. Completing a campaign rewards you with a selection of pre-defined cards of the specific set you completed the story for. I don't know how long random NPC matches might satisfy players not comfortable playing against other players but as of writing I have you to beat a hard difficulty NPC.

This is a simply-designed game - hand-drawn graphics and handwritten text. Instead of yet another game that showers you with blocks of preformatted lines, this is an adventure, two of them. This has an enchantingly human story. The player chooses the course of two lives, how they build, how they grow or how they fail. It's not another high-budget super-graphical story like any of a thousand roleplay games, instead it feels much more like a choose-your-own-adventure story. The music is heartfelt, and the storylines feel involving, despite this being a relatively short game. The closest similarity I could find is with the Stanley Parable, but that does The Yawhg a disservice - the choices for the lives of the characters really do matter and they affect what ultimately happens at the story's end. I found myself really enjoying this - it's rare for a game to have a hand-crafted heartfelt sort of feeling to it, but The Yawhg has this from beginning to end. Excellent. Rare. Interesting.

I played the Yawhg a couple of times, and I must say it is quite an amusing game. It's all pretty straight-forward: you and/or your friends each choose a character (you can also choose characters yourself and play the game on your own) and choose a location you wish to go to. Each location has a couple of options on actions you can perform, such as cutting wood, tending to patients, and yes, even getting drunk! But beware: each choice you make might positively or negatively affect your stats. After a couple of turns, the mysterious Yawhg happens and each person will have to choose a role which fits their character's stats best (or you can do the opposite, and watch the outcome!), after which you'll get to know whether your town survived, and -more importantly- how your characters pick up their life again afterwards.
The Yawhg is a funny little game which you can play with friends. The graphics are all really fitting and nice, the music is simple, yet suits the game and the absolute highlight of the game is the amount of choices you can make, and the randomnized events you'll encounter. However, the game is VERY short. Almost too short. And that, in my humble opinion, is the only thing where it falls short, for me personally. However, the replay value is very big.
Get it during a sale, or if you like experimental choice-heavy little games like this one.
All in all, 7/10

Don’t get me wrong its a good game but If you have been playing Star Ruler 1 and think this is an improvement to that stop right here.
Lets first go over the things missing in Star Ruler 2.
Economy: You no longer have a galactic bank with credits, food, metal, electronics, advance parts and luxury items. Nope your planets basically run themselves without the need for these in fact what they need are items you have to import from others in a glorified connect the dots experiment.
Your income doesn't pool up instead your on a budget that resets after every cycle.
Research is capped in that you cannot level a type of research over and over instead there are x amount of research options with x amount cost involved in unlocking them.
Some changes in shipbuilding schematics:
Firstly now most support ships don’t have a power requirement unless you research shields and give them those.
Schematics now called designs abandon the old way of doing it and now use hexes that you place on a hex grid. While this sounds good at first you will quickly be asking yourself, why can I specify size of my ship then still have to scale things on the hex-grid compared to adding different size components in like in Star Ruler 1.
Additionally this system is a bit strange in my opinion. If you create a probe using 3 hexes it will cost more than a fully fledged out scout ship?
Mining asteroids is your fancy? Well give up here you wont be making civilian ships anyway... yip no more miners, traders, colonizers, repair ships, scanning ships, heck military vessels don’t even have boarding parties.
All this aside the game gets you in combat quickly and fleets are controlled by flag ships that replenish their support ships which make the game allot easier to micromanage so you can get straight to the combat.
Overall I understand many gamers are put off by StarRuler 1 however Star Ruler 1 is the most unique game in its genre and the most complicated. Its  a jewel that this game is not even close to.
As for this game I personally think Sins of the solar empire is more fun. Want space combat? That game has awesome graphics too!
Now only if Star Ruler 1 was on linux like this game is I'd play so much more. 1 up to the developors for supporting another OS in this build!

A hidden gem in the space RTS genre
I haven't had much time to put into this game as of yet but so far I am loving how everything fits together. This is a complex game that doesn't have a big learning curve and is extremly addictive. Below i will describe the elements I like and some improvements that could be made.
Empire Management:
In most space rts games your star systems are pretty much self reliant and doesnt require reasources to travel from one system to another. Here, if you want to have a powerful industrial/economic/science system you will need that primary stystem to have trade connections to other systems. Each planet can level up, increasing the population and amount of structures that can be built on them but to level up the planet must meet certain reasource requirements (example to get to level 1, a planet must import food and water from both a food and water planet). What this does is allows the player to have multiple home worlds that have a specific purpose (industrial,economic,science) thus opening up a wide range of tactics an enemy can use to damage an empire. It's difficult to explain but once you see it for yourself it makes perfect sense.
Fleet Management
the combat in this game is all about building fleets and the start of every fleet begins with a flagship. Once you have a flagship built you can link multiple support ships, the only limit being the number of support points a flagship has and that number gets bigger the larger the flagship is so a size 100 flagship may only support a size 300 support fleet whereas a size 500 flagship can support 3000 using the right modules. Which brings us to....
Ship Design
Like other space RTS games you can design the internal specs of your falgships and support ships (weapons, armor, shields, command and control modules ect) which allows you to change your tactics when approaching an enemy. Maybe you want a flagship designed around amassing a huge fleet, or a flagship that is a WMD, its all whatever you make of it.
Combat
Support ships will always stay in formation with the flagship so managing which supportships go with which flagship is not an issue as they are linked. This makes it easy to coordinate offensives and defenses with multiple flagships. in combat your flagship targets an enemy flagship (or whatever target you specify) and the fleet engages. It's very simple with the fleet management that is implemented here and it looks epic when you have massive fleets duking it out.
Diplomacy
This is the crown jewel imo. In most space rts's diplomacy takes a backseat with very limited options. Here it's a card game.... Not kidding, it's all about using influence (a reasource you aquire from specific planets) to buy cards that pop up from time to time. Certain cards are very desirable and your enemy may buy them before you do if you aren't quick enough. For example certain cards allow you to capure an entire solar system without ever firing a shot. Such cards when you use them bring up a galactic vote where you can use negotiation cards to win favor and it turns into a game of who has the more votes wins! It's pure genius and much like how politics works in real life. (it's all about political capital)
There are some things that could use some improvement but i expect some of these things could be handled with mods. For example there could be more ship designs and different ship formations. The graphics are also not stellar (no pun intended) but that also allows for bigger fleets and smoother gameplay (I haven't run into any latency at all). A storyline would also help not only get new people into the game and learn the mechanics but also immerse people into the lore of the game.
I think that's enough from me, this is a must buy for any fan of the space RTS genre that crushes others like it. I'm suprised I only heard of this after scrolling through page 10 of steam's top sellers in the strategy section.

If you're a big fan of fleet combat and the like, don't buy Star Ruler 2.
It seems to over-emphasize setting up your economic links between systems/planets in order to "upgrade" your home planet (or other chosen planet).
By the time I got my home planet to Tier 4, it was connected to over 20 systems, and I hadn't even built my first combat fleet (I didn't set it to have an enemy during this playthrough to see how I could manage my empire).
It over-emphasizes this element of the game, at the expense of the fleet combat. What was the point of the ship-designer if you're going to rub the "logistics" of your Empire into the player's face constantly?
Here's the TL;DR pros/cons:
Pros
Diplomacy System is a fresh take on the concept in RTS games.
Ship design system is robust
Combat is nice to watch
Cons
Feels like it emphasizes the economic side of things far too much
Feels a bit too clicky for a game that's supposed to be 4X, for me anyway.
Like I said before, the economy system is a big hassle for me to work with, and it's not my thing at all. Let's say you wanna upgrade this planet to Level 2? You're gonna need to get several other level 1 planets supplied with the things they need, and then have them export their goods to your targeted system in order to get it to level 2.
Now imagine this workload increasing almost exponentially with each level up to level 4. As a level 3 planet, you've already got a fistful of Level 1 and level 2 systems connected to it, but it's already asking for even MORE level 1 and level 2 systems before it can get upgraded to level 4. You're looking at over 15 direct connected planets to your level 4 planet, and that's not counting their subordinate feeder planets.
After a couple of hours of trying to get a hang of this, my wrist is already hurting from all the clicking. NOT FUN.
I bought and enjoyed the first Star Ruler because it took a more simplistic approach to the economy system, and gave me control over what kind of resource exports I wanted to produce. Star Ruler 2 completely takes that out of your hands, and instead demands that you set up a logistical network to feed your empire's needs. All of the planets are randomized in what they can produce, but you can't change what they produce at all.
The result? Your empire is a lot, LOT more vulnerable to having its supply lines cut. While that's certainly nice, I'm a player that likes to be able to control the circumstances of his Empire, and that means consolidating key, valuable production facilities within pockets of my Empire that can be protected. Star Ruler 2 does not allow for this.
This is a 4X game, and it puts a bigger emphasis on the economic side of things. While a nice change from the average space RTS, I feel that they could have done a better job with the design. The way it is now, it creates that perception that it involves a bit more management than it should require.
It sucks that the Star Ruler series is almost practically the ONLY series with the ability for you to custom-design your ships' capabilities. Now, if it were Sins of a Solar Empire with your own ship-designer element to it, I would be loving it to pieces.

There are a lot of progressive and enjoyable features in the game. How fleets work, having alternate paths of research for much of the research, how diplomacy works (and how powerful it is), and just the good 'ol ship designing.
However the commodities system seems overly restrictive and a bit convoluted. The UI can be a bit clunky as well. While there are a good amount of subsystems and research there is not a LOT of subsystems and research.
All in all it's an imperfect but enjoyable game. This review has been edited to reflect my new opinion and is now thumbs up instead of down.

While dressing itself up as noble, it probably doesn't give the average person a better insight into depression. It certainly doesn't help by describing the antidepressant medication as something that's wonderfully free of side effects, but maybe questionably effective.
Depression doesn't come from any one source, but this seems to be the case in this game. The main characters tedious job seems to be the main thing getting him down- his insecurities and poor confidence being another contributor. A rude mother, a small part of the MCs life, is arguably also part. These three would rarely amount to "deep depression", something we're told via cop-out status bars that we're experiencing. The main character has a social circle they're satisfied with, a stable girlfriend and all in all a great life.
The main character recovers and stays well. This is rarely the case with real-life depression.
All in all, don't pay for this. Go read the wiki article about depression, talk to someone who has experienced depression, and donate to some charity if you want to. Do not let people profiteer off of an at best okay work in the guise of raising awareness for depression.

Here are some of the things I ran into with my experience with Risen 2:
Sexist character writing.
No, really, the first island you travel to with steelbeard as you hunt down Crow, the guard at the natives camp says something like "You sound like woman. Women talk, men act!" as he chastises you for talking too much after being accused of having hostile intentions as a pirate. He wasn't even written as a villain, just a regular passive-aggressive guard that you cannot kill or interact with beyond this.
Broken Map Markers.
When it came time to duel Slayne, I did not actually know where the blood square was which is where we had to duel. I checked my map, and the red objective marker simply lead me in front of the Admiral's house, when in fact Slayne was waiting for me a ways off to the side instead. This is but one of many examples where the map is flat out broken with some quests like here, and simply nonexistent with others. Another quest had required picking up multiple items, but the objective marker disappeared once you picked up just 1, so if you did not realize there were more to find in that area, and you cannot remember where it was, you wander aimlessly for a very long time, pulling your hair out.
Idiotic Movement Mechanics.
No, seriously, there is NO stamina bar, and rolling is by far a quicker means of on-foot travel than simple running. There was no sprint feature, even though npcs had the sprint ability which they occasionally used to catch up to my rolling being faster than their jogging. Why not just give the player that same ability!?
Sloppy Level Design.
Many, many, many many many times did I come across a stone staircase at a temple or tomb that did not actually connect properly with the stone floor at the end of the staircase, allowing players to see massive gaps into the game world void. This also happened a bit with terrain, such as at Garcia's Treasure hiding spot.
Lazy Design.
So becoming a ghost pirate is just you putting a filter over the player's screen, and changing a few detail models in the exact same environment, huh? Yeah, you disgust me Pirhanna Bytes. Also taking screenshots hard-crash the game to your desktop more than half the time based on how long you have been playing. It's unstable and sloppily coded.
Vague/Stupid Quests.
Certain story-required quests require the player to locate specific npcs to talk to, like normal. However, these npcs do not always show up on the map as an objective marker, and as the npc is only referred to by name, and some game areas have dozens of npcs, it's annoying to have to run around and check every single person's name just to find who you are supposed to talk to to continue the quest.
Even worse, certain quest objectives themselves are just stupid. A gnome on Isle of Thieves wanted something only defined as "round and black", but there was no map marker to locate it. Again, this is a story-required quest. Round and black made me think bullet, cannon ball, bomb, lead pellet, or black pearl. Seeing as I had a black pearl on me, but no new dialogue showed up, I assumed it was something else. Little did I know, there was a hidden gnome in one of the caves that gave me a "pitch-black pearl". Each cave has only one bed, suggesting there is 1 cave per gnome, and there was already a gnome outside of this cave I had already talked to, which is why I ran all across the island for an hour and a half, checking every nook and cranny for another "round and black thing" instead of going inside.
Are you serious? He didn't want a black pearl, he wanted a "pitch-black pearl" that can only be gotten from a concealed, non-map-marked npc? Yeah.... No.
The list of problems do NOT stop there by any means. There are literally over a dozen other topics I could complain about and provide examples to but the review character count does not allow it, just trust me from the above citations from my experience, this is a garbage game that only people with low-standards and an abnormal admiration for RPG games should even bother with. It had a few moments which weren't really played up to their full potential, but even if they were, they would be far too few and far too far between to justify the passionless mistake that is this game. Risen 1 was a bit better, but not by too much. This was just desperate, stupid, rushed, sloppy, and an overall embarrassment of a product, which becomes blatantly clear when the customer really spends the hours to sink their teeth into it only to be greeted with a rancid waste of their time.

I tried very hard to like this game. But there are simply too many problems with it. Everytime the game did something good, it was too little and too late into the game. The controls are very awkward and stiff. You can peak around corners which is a very cool mechanic and is actually necessary in order to carefully navigate the hallways. Vertical movement is limited to specific ledges and ropes that you are meant to navigate, and levels are very small and offer only a few different paths to navigate that all end up bringing you to the same place with hardly any advantages one way or the other. You are equiped with a variety of arrow types that can be used to help you move throughout the levels. The water arrows allow you to douse flames from a distance which is helpful for distractions. Rope arrows are useful for accessing hidden locations, but they feel more like they are required in order to collect all the loot rather than it being a fun optional path. Sneaking around is fun, but getting caught is never fun to escape from like other stealth games. You're better off just quickly restarting from your last checkpoint because the combat is terrible and the penalty for getting caught is so frustrating that there's no point in trying to hide. Other stealth games like "Hitman" have fantastic combat that is fun to play out when you end up getting caught.. but thief's combat is just garbage and not worth the waste of 5 minutes before you reload your save. The saving grace of this game's gameplay is the stealth itself, which is good because this is a stealth game after all. You can quickly glide from shadow to shadow and you have to pay very close to attention to many fine details to avoid detection. I especially liked having to walk slowly on broken glass and carefully move around animals to avoid the guards getting suspicious. It's a shame this kind of effort can't be found in any of the other aspects of the game.
The graphics are bitter sweet. The lighting, shadows, physics, and texture work is fantastic, but the environment itself is just BORING. That thumbnail of the game's coverart... that basically summarizes exactly how the ENTIRE game looks. Misty... blue.. dark... that's it. Just lots of grays, dark blues, black, gray, gray, and more gray. I get that the game's setting calls for rather dull colors, but it just doesn't translate well with a game that has you slowly sneaking around. It's just an incredibly boring game that is just barely kept alive with some decent stealth mechanics.
The sound is pretty simplistic and badly done. You'll hear the same guards saying the same things from beginning to the end of the game and it's more repetitive than usual. Sometimes the same guard overlaps himself with the same phrases. It really breaks the immersion and gets annoying quickly. The music is a strange modern day adrenaline techno sound that just doesn't seem to fit the games setting at all, and the exact same music plays every time you get caught... but that's it. No other songs in the game, no ambient music, nothing. The city just sounds dead, like the people living there just got bored of it themselves and left.
The story is just a play and forget typical video game story. No characters are memorable, and the character you play as sounds terrible. He constantly chimes in with corny one-liners that feel so out of place and unnecessary. Garret has a very cocky attitude that just doesn't translate well to the type of person he is. The story calls for him to be emotional, but you just can't take him seriously when he never takes his actions seriously. It's a very confused character and I just learned to ignore him completley after the first few missions.
One thing that really came out of left field was Chapter 5. Out of nowhere, the entire game changed into something else. I won't say what, but I wish that the entire game had just been Chapter 5 and it would have been a lot more enjoyable. But then, right after that, the game goes back into it's boring rut of locations that all basically look the same.
Overall, the game does what it's meant to do very well. It has great stealth mechanics and has a good length. It's a great game for hardcore stealth fans, but anyone else should avoid this like the plague. It's boring, stale, lifeless, and plenty of other stealth franchises do what this new Thief game does far better.

Bulb Boy is a Point-and-Click adventure game that's part David Lynch, part Japanese School Girl. Possibly the only game to come out this year that's simultaneously cute and repulsive, don't miss out on it!

Ever wondered about Tim Burton making games on crack? No? But if you want to see what could happen in such combination, please buy "Bulb Boy", it will probably ruin your "sweet dreams". Don't get me wrong, it isn't "scary" game, it's just sick fairy tale about Bulb Boy, who is fighting his own anxiety and nightmares.
When you was small, you probably saw something innocuous, but during dreams the same "innocent" thing appeared in twisted, horrifying way. This  is what "Bulb Boy" is about - fighting child's inner fears about every-day reality and about happiness and cohesion of a family.
Anyways, "Bulb Boy" is a rich source of messages for every headshrinker:-D
Be aware, this game isn't standard point'n'click adventure. Certainly, there is objects combing and normal inventory, but the tasks are very simple and there's a lot of arcade elements. It's just casual game, where you want to see some  abominable, nasty, gross, but funny things, but not really tricky puzzles, or riddles.
Check this game out, if you want to see some disturbing, but good graphics, working mechanis, and black, twisted humor. Avoid it when you're looking for a top notch, classic adventure game in Gabriel Nigt, or Monkey Island style.
Nevertheless, Tim Burton should be proud:-)
PS. This game has a one, but significant flaw, it's too short.

Pro Tip: When you start the game, go into options before anything else. There are a bunch of optional settings turned on by default, and more experienced players will definetly want to turn those off. Even if your brand new to the game however, make sure to turn off "Combat Animation" or whatever it's called and "Auto Resolution" (And no, that's not a graphical thing). On to the actual review.
The first time I played this game it was called Magic: Origins, and it took me so little time to decide I didn't like it, I wasn't allowed to make a review. Back then, it had several issues spanning from the fact that there was only Origins cards in the game to the fact that the deck builder customization was extremely limited.
Recently however, I found myself on this page again, and after learning that four other expansions had been added into the game, I decided to give it another shot. I'm very glad I decided to do that. Daily quests have been added so you can earn coins to unlock more cards.
The deck builder now gives you free reign to do whatever you'd like with whatever you have unlocked. If you're newer to the game, there is however an in-game system that will build you a deck.
There are nine story campaigns in the game that allows you to explore the story of MTG's last five expansions whilst also unlocking bonus cards and coins. The Origins campaigns let you learn the backstory of the Origins Planeswalkers, with the campaigns for Battle of Zendikar, Oath of the Gatewatch, Shadows of Innistrad, and Eldritch Moon giving you a starter pack of cards from those expansions, in addition to enough coins to buy a booster pack.
Let's talk about coins, the game's currency. Each booster pack costs 150 coins to buy, allowing you to choose a booster pack from either of the game's expansions, with a meter telling you how far away from owning all of the cards you are. Obviously, the game has a microtransaction system in place for buying more coins, but that's completely optional. If you choose not to buy coins with real money, everything in game rewards you with coins. Beating a campaign for the first time will reward with you coins for every segment, all of the segments totalling at 150 per campaign. Versus battles reward you with 30 coins per victory, and there are AI battles which reward coins based on difficulty. There are also the daily quests, and a community quest.
Considering this is a free game, I will absolutely recommend it, and I will rate it at 10/10.

Even being in early stages this game is a pretty solid game. Stable, fun to play, and has a neat and unique twist of strategies for a 4x game.
My Thoughts:
-Game is pretty stable for being early stages. Though I did not have any crashes or show stopping events, I did notice a few places where the UI could be corrected. Nothing major and I am sure the developers will solve this in time
- You will either absolutely love or loathe the planet resource sharing system. It is very unique and different from anything that I have played. In their current version you must obtain a bunch of smaller, low level planets and share a single resource per planet in a web that eventually all points to a main planet. (The tutorial really helps explain this more)
-Research, research, research. Though I can see the cause and effects of the different system, I really enjoyed the system from SR1. I personally love LOTS of research, unlocking all kinds of new stuff, being able to do super awesome things. Again this is early access, so I am sure there will be more things to come.
- Though the game is good AND in early stages I feel like the game is missing a deep element. Space. I use to love being able to build a legit mining fleet, sending them to an asteroid belt, build an outpost and send those resources back to my empire. I loved the idea of building the space stations that had different features and reasons to be built. I loved the immense depth of SR1 with all of the things you could (or could not) do. I feel that even though this game is still in early stages it is missing some fundamentally sound building blocks. Everything has been streamlined, we took the ability to micromanage away and replaced it with a simple ‘Right Click – Build mining outpost – walk away and never think about that asteroid again’ mentality.
Overall I think it’s going to shape out to be a great game. It has many new and exciting features and in time will turn into something as fun as SR1

Being a long term fan of Star Ruler, I picked up Star Ruler 2 out of sheer devotion to the developers. Thankfully, after playing the game, I can say that the loyalty was well deserved. Where Star Ruler was a game of potential, but lacking little polish, Star Ruler 2 is a game that has ample servings of both. Wether you are looking to build a massive empire, or just see glorious battles of sheer carnage, Star Ruler 2 will sate your cravings.
Still in Beta, the game already has most of the groundwork that will enable it to be played for hours on end. Be it the designing of ships from the bottom up, the beatiful beams of light sending ships to their oblivion, or the much more accessible UI, the game is a testament to developers who have a vision, and though they have made mistakes along the way, aren't above learning from their mistakes to create a better game. They have taken what works from the original game and worked it into a much higher quality version.
The accessibility of the developers is also a huge plus to this game. Whereas many titles on early access have a hit or miss relationship with the developers, often times devolving into sporadic comments on a monthly basis, the Star Ruler 2 team has taken the initiative to integrate an IRC into the game, allowing instantaneous, or near to depending on work/sleep schedules, interaction with the developers.
If you are interested in playing an Early Access game done right, and want to see your own ships, or the enemies, blowing up in the process, Star Ruler 2 is the game for you.

To give some context, I've been playing on/off since Beta. So I have a nostalgia for this game I cannot shake. Therefore, at the time of writing this review, I have 912 hours of this game on my Steam account. But don't get me wrong. Most of this was just me AFKing overnight to sell things, because if you want to have a shop that you can leave open without playing the game, you have to pay a crazy amount of money. I think it's like, I dunno, $3 for a 24 hour shop. Yeah. Meanwhile, it's only $1.80 for a 3 month permit to do the same thing, but you have to be online. Seems fair, right? Yeah. Anyways, here's the review lmao
+ Surprisingly fun combat
+ Consistently updated
+ Several different classes
+ Levelling is straightforward and easy
+ Reboot server takes the pay to win out of the game (but also removes other features as a result, encouraging people to keep playing on the P2W servers as well)
+ Very cute style, have had a lot of fun customizing my character with gear.
~ Simple Crafting system (Both good and bad, because those who don't like crafting in MMOs typically won't have trouble using it, but it also makes it boring for those who love in-depth crafting systems in MMOs.)
- Pay to win out the♥♥♥♥♥ People sell their godly weapons and armor on Paypal. Anyone with a few hundred dollars can become number one in a day.
- Outdated, constantly lags and crashes, built on old framework and needs updating. The sequel, Maplestory 2, looks fun but will probably never come out globally.
- Once you reach a certain level, your daily routine typically involves fighting the standard bosses for about an hour or two then keeping your shop open overnight to sell more and buy more gear/cosmetics. It's a massive grind til the very end.
- Pay 2 Fashion. You have a very small, if even any, selection of hairs/faces at the beginning. The only way to change them is with NX. No joke, you have to pay real money to change your hair and face. Of course, you can just pay people to gift you a coupon with in-game money, but if you want to have enough in-game cash to pay someone to do that, you either have to beg or pay real money to get gear to grind for these things. In short, unless you're insanely patient or have wealthy friends, you're going to be coerced into buying NX with real cash. Because looking ugly in an MMO sucks. Oh, and not to mention, the best hairs are in Royal Coupons and the likes, which have a RANDOM SELECTION of 6-8 hairs, of which at least half usually look terrible. This game wants your money. That's why it's still alive. And it works.
Overall: Giant cash grab. Still fun if you have the money. If you don't like looking decent and don't care about bossing, then sure, I can see how you can enjoy this game, but honestly, who's going to go to this outdated MMO and do that? There are better MMOs out there. Don't waste your time here.

Alright, after reading up a few things (which I won't dabble on) I decided to sit down, download, and...at a current loss for wording, "play" this "game". I have not been able to finish this "game"
I'm using "game" loosely as this isn't a game in multiple definitions. This is a choose-your-destiny, interactive novel where on several pages you are presented with options that may (or may not) alter the flow of the story being portrayed through the use of hyperlinks that lead to the various branches of the story. Another point is that this is just a downloadable copy of the original website (
) that has added functionality, such as Xbox controller support. As to why you would need a(n) Xbox controller to "play" a digital novel is beyond me. Pressing the arrow keys or using a mouse is more effective. Though the same could probably be said for Dating Simulators, though those usually have more interaction than just pointing and clicking to advance plot. Just a bit of a quip, but that's just me.
Either way, onto the review.
First and foremost - why on this planet is there a "game" that's about depression? Depression depicted in this game is just from one point of view. While the point is to show depression in its basic form, there is many, many different triggers to how depression begins, and how one goes through with their life while being depressed. Every individual is unique in how depression affects them.
The story has been...well, depressing. I guess that's
Though for myself as someone who doesn't sit down and enjoy reading pages upon pages of books, it's hard for someone as myself to put myself into the role of the character in question. I guess that's why I don't read books very often, if at all. Not rating until the story is finished, if I get to that point from the audio - more on that later.
Graphical use is extremely minimal, displaying a picture within a set of three photos that appear that have been shot by an older Kodak camera, along with GIFs of snow static (reminiscent of tv static) with text of apparent famous quotes from other people,  or at the bottom with the - I'm assuming - current status of the character. Other than that, no real fancy use of graphics. No 3D renders, photo-esque landscapes. Just simple photography to bring the point of the story with each page. For what it is, simplistic. Not going to rate that.
Audio, a poor choice. I get that the audio is supposed to be ambient, but when wearing a headset (or in general from computer speakers), it was VERY loud. Along with the audio being loud, it was mono. Imagine listening to your favorite song with your earbuds/headphones/whatever you use to listen to music (if you do). You can hear some instruments in your right ear, that you cannot hear in your left, and vice versa. This is Stereo. Mono is hearing all instruments in both ears at the same time. As limited as the soundtrack was in this digital novel, wearing a headset hurt my ears less than 5 seconds from just booting the game for the first time, and after adjusting the volume in-line on my headset. The soundtrack itself was simply a strike of (a) piano key(s) three~five seconds between eachother - along with a few pages in, the sound of "static" along with the piano. This "static" (or "glitch" sound as a few other reviews have put it) is not as loud as the notes from the piano, but I had to turn off audio because  of the audio cue being both loud, and monotonous (and mono in general). While I could continue the story without the audio, it would detract to what the author's message would be. However at this rate, the audio doesn't change much, which would do more harm than good to the story in question. As someone who's psyche is influeced by music (feel more energetic with some, mellowed with others, and variances inbetween), this just made me want to chuck my headset across the room in hopes to make the sound of nails-on-chalkboard stop. A for effort. F for execution.
Gameplay is simple. Point, click. You can also use the up/down arrow keys to scroll up and down the page, use Tab to select an option, and hit Enter to select that option. Alternatively you have the option to use a(n) Xbox controller to navigate through the story. I don't have one on me, so I'm unable to say if that's feasible or not. Options (or Settings) allows you to toggle audio on or off (no volume adjustment), toggle fullscreen or window mode (Or you could just, you know, use the max/window button next to the minimize and close button on the top right of the window if you're using Windows), and you can restart your "game". Otherwise nothing else to mention.
All in all, the story may hold some ground, however the audio keeps it on leash. The audio tears the story apart when making an attempt to read. Again - this is NOT what is generally definied as a "game". This is a digital novel.
Would I recommend this game? Probably not. This can be found online (as stated previously) without having to have Steam installed, the only thing that would really be missing would be controller support. Along with that, allowing others to live another day instead of hearing the nails-on-chalkboard soundtrack.
Along with my lack of recommending this so-called game, why would you play a game made to show you what depression is?  There's thousands of other games that have more potential grabbing your attention than a game about depression. Heck, there's probably some good time-wasting games on your computer right now, like Minesweeper, or Klondike Solitaire.
