Risen2: Dark Waters is an open world RPG game based around the theme of pirates. Its the sequeal to the original Risen game developed by Piranha Bytes. Risen 2 was released in early 2012 on the PC and then later released on consoles. Even today, the game is still popular among PC gamers with at least one million people owning the game on Steam alone.
This is an action RPG where you play in a third-person perspective to explore the world. You complete quests and customize your characters abilities and equipment through leveling up and assigning glory points. This takes RPG games back to their routes, allowing you to customize your character exactly how you want to play with the amount of abilities and talents on display. The combat much like Risen 1 is not exactly a strong point; it seems clunky at times, and you will often find your self dying through no fault of your own other than the strange combat system. You have two weapon slots, a melee weapon and a range weapon. You aren't able to use the range weapon unless you are within melee range of an enemy oddly yet your enemies have almost laser guided aim against you with their spears and guns.
A nice little change I found was the infinite amount of inventory space you have, some will think this removes some of the challenge of the game, but for me I have always found a limited inventory space to be a chore which is not always needed. Obviously this means that currency is never a problem once you reach the latter stages of the game since you are able to just sell everything though.
The graphics in Risen 2 are certainly an improvement on Risen 1, however there are a few glaring problems I found. The main one being the terrain pop-in throughout the open world. As you are roaming around the jungle, all of a sudden you will quite clearly notice trees and plants suddenly expanding before your very eyes. It's clear this is done to try and reduce the strain on systems for loading the world, but it is done in such an obvious way that sometimes it can ruin the immersion. I also found the game to be very very dark. The day/night circle while adds to the realism, the game is sometimes virtually unplayable in the night hours due to how dark it is. I found myself actually having to turn up the brightness settings at times to keep playing.
While the game is completely voice acted, it does have some very bad acting in it; some of the lines which are said are very out of place and just don't fit right. That being said; there are some absolute classics such as "...off, before I put a banana on your c*ck and call for the gorilla" being easily the best line I have heard in a video game.
Risen 2 is a hard game; as you begin your adventure you will die a lot of times due to being under geared and under trained and having no money. A lot of the early quests require you to have certain training in sneaking and lock picking, which all require gold to learn, so the game starts out very slowly. I would say the first three hours are the hardest part of the game due to the speed in which you are able to carry out even the smallest side quests.
This is a well designed open world game. The world is full of life and plenty of items, weapons, buildings and much more to find. You are able to go mining, or skinning animals as well, which reminded me a lot of the MMO type games.
Risen 2 has so much content to offer, so many side quests, worlds to explore, everything. I have put almost fifty five hours into this game, doing all of the side quests, a good amount of grinding and of course the main story. It's very rare these days to find a game this good that gives you that amount of gameplay.
I had a few little technical issues which were random frame drops in certain areas, as well as long loading times but nothing that can't be overpowered by either using a SSD or a DIMM drive.
1) Stay away
2) Only recommended when on sale
3) Recommended
5) This is a must play

I was laughing for the last hour, reading negative reviews for Risen 2. Well, what can I say?
There will always be some problems with Piranha Bytes games, mostly of the technical origin. I can foretell you that, being a fan of them from the year 2002, when I climbed on the highest and almost inaccessible tower in the first Gothic game... and on the top of it a chest which contained a mysterious item with description in German, the only use of that was breaking my save file... So what?
Piranha Bytes may not be code wizards, but they do an impressive work over the years. They bring passion, dedication, soul in the every game they making. For that I'm grateful.
Down to the Risen 2. The most user-friendly, most casual in the progress compared with the previous games... And with embellished and fancy pirate theme. Surely it attracted some new players to the franchise. Aaaand... some of them were distracted! That's that I felt, while was reading all those complaints about awkward controls, unbearable skills elaboration system etc.
For my part, I got that for what has come into the game: an interesting adventure. You know the kind where you explore new lands, meet new people, kill some of them, getting better in the process...
I had some downsides, too. For first, game was far more narrative than before, and exploring part was less than usual in favor of major quest line by saving the world. Second, famous tech issues of the developer made a process of gaining achievements far more complicated. And for third, my pride suffered a bit from the shooting mini-game, where I cannot hit any bottle!
All of those minuses are tolerable, of course. For the luxury of being a pirate captain with your own ship and crew... Risen 2 is surely deserved its cost.

I personally regret buying this game.  I was truly expecting so much more and I was left disappointed.  I watched some videos of game play and foolishly decided too quickly that this game was something incredible.  That was my mistake, and I'm simply writing a review to hopefully prevent someone else from making the same mistake.
The storyline had promise, but it was very poorly put together and very difficult to follow.  This continues until the very end of the game and you're left feeling as though nothing was resolved.  By the end of the game the only thing accomplished is stopping Orion from turning everyone into monsters and saving Erin. ‘Nothing’ in the city changes. Gloom is still running rampant, people are still dying, the city is still corrupt and now it has no leaders...
The side missions are a catastrophe.  They are bland and unrewarding.  You simply enter the location steal an object and your mission is complete.  There is never anyone inside the house to challenge your sneaking skills or anything at all.  You don't even have to deliver the object after you've stolen it.    You simply get a tiny description on the mission and that's it.
The full map and mini map are extremely lacking with barely any detail put into them whatsoever.  Certain areas of the city are mission locked and the areas that you can explore never change. It's a very boring and bland place to explore.  All of the accessible ‘houses’ are rundown and every room looks practically the same. Really, you don’t get to explore houses as 90% of the house is always off limits and no one is ever inside either.  I also hate how you can't fast travel.  That is extremely annoying, especially when everything about the 'free roaming area' of the city is repetitive.
The population of the city consists of possibly at most four generic AI faces.  There are never any events in the city other than the occasional hanging which consists of a crowd between three and four people.  The city doesn’t feel real at all.  Gossip between AI’s never change either even if you’ve stolen the loot they’re discussing they just keep looping forever.  They even follow the same path after the events of chapter six when their city is on fire burning around them! They don’t react AT ALL.
There are so many features that could have been implemented into this game that would make it incredible.  But, aside from stunning visuals of the game it really has nothing else to offer.

This reboot of Thief is an "alright" game in itself, but if you are a fan of the previous games, this pretty much rips out most of the lore of Keepers, Hammerites and Pagans etc. All gone apart from small references like when you enter an old church in one of the chapters which bears the Hammerite symbol.
Game mechanics are flawed and some things are just plain stupid. Prime example thats really obvious from the first hour of playing; if I jimmy (break open) a window to nick a house which requires quick-time event button mashing, I should not have to do it again when leaving! Master Thief my♥♥♥♥♥♥ Getting around the city is quite clunky and sluggish in terms of animation; although I do like the immersive first person view (you can see your body when you look down etc) you are given where Garrett physically reaches out into the 3D space and picks up the item. Hard to explain in mere text but you feel truly like you are nicking something rather than "*boop* you've stolen a candle!".
Sound aesthetic can vary from well done to "why the hell can I hear conversations being held indoors three blocks away as if they were standing in front of me?" or "Okay, if I hear that 'sloop' conversation one more time I'll bludgeon that guy to death". Voice acting also ranges from good to downright woeful with Garrett somewhere in the middle of that. For some reason certain cutscenes are too low, in others some characters are too loud while others are so feint you can't hear them etc. What a mess.
Performance wise, the game frequently stutters since the latest patch in order to stream in textures "better". Visual aesthetic is spot on though I'll give them that. Dark and gloomy and infested with vermin; who are not necessarily rats but of mankind too. Plague is rife, beggars line the streets, hangings are amidst and generally this is where you see a lot of effort has been made to make it authentic. What a pity that the gameplay is just lacking in every department. I'm pretty crap at reviews but take it as a someone whos played the originals; its a dissapointing "No" from me.

Ok, I'd like to start out by saying that the older Thief games, mainly the first 2, are some of my favourite games, they were so story rich and emmersive with the amount of detail to the areas, they were always very atmospheric, what with the sounds as well. Depending on where you were, you would hear different sounds. In an old abonded house? You'll hear creacking wood and mice scurrying across the floor. In an old cathedral? You're gonna hear rubble, and wind. In the older gmaes, they always had some very good villians and heroes, and also some very nice side characters. The heroes were always loveable, the villians were always hateable. and with that being said, let me start my review. Ok, so not the best game ever made, but comparing it to some of the greatest games ever made, thats not too bad. Just like the old ones, it's as immersive as ever, still very atmospheric. There is an entire mission that builds up suspension in a haunted prison/asylum, as you creep around to see what happened, to suspension of what actually DID happen builds up, with hearing things behind you, seeing ghosts at the ends of halways, and an occasional jumpscare. In the sense of good characters, Thief doesn't fail, but compared to the older games, all the characters are are good. Garret seems a bit emo, the villian is, so-so, not really that hateable, more annoying than anything. as for story, it is good, I won't lie. It's well thought out, and executed well, with AMAZING plotwists along the way. Gameplay wise, one of the greats. Definatly one of the most immersive games ever made, what with when you steal a glimmering piece of shining loot, Garret will actually reach out and grab it, rather than it just getting sucked twords you such as in dishonored for example. Everytime you look down, you can see your body and feel, and the headbob is minimal, but realistic. As for the soundtrack, to be perfectly honest, I think thats one of the things that this Reboot does as well as the originals, some of the best, atmospheric music in a game. Very well done, but if you're trying to decide weather to get this one, or the older ones, no question get the older ones, they're cheaper and overall better, however, this is a truly fantastic game aswell. Overall, an 8/10, very nice!

Thief is a good stealth game, despite criticism, has been enhanced in some spots since launch, and since I did not play the old titles, my opinion is only valid for this title.
The gameplay is good for what the game intends, stealth, the mechanics are solid and well implemented and there is the option to customize the difficulty for a challenge that most pleases you. You are induced to be stealthy, the combat is shallow and ineffective against multiple enemies, the AI has been improved since launch, despite some caveats, is efficient and react convincingly to disturbances in the environment. At first I thought the level design a bit limited and linear, but over time it changes, there are several choices of routes and you can choose the one that best suit you. The city has a good size and a great atmosphere, enough places to explore and side missions to make, although at times the city appearing to be very dead. The graphics are excellent, with great lighting effects, textures, in overall the game is very good looking. There are good sound effects too.
The game disappoints in the plot, the development of the story was not efficient in getting me involved, gets to be cliche in some aspects. the characters are not striking, especially the Garrett, despite its darker atmosphere, I was unable to have an affinity for him.
Anyway, I recommend for those who like the genre, but I think wiser to wait for a good sale.

One of the best indie games I played in 2013. Tha Cat Lady is a fantastic sidescrolling philosophical/adult adventure with a really good voice acting, a perfect soundtrack and a story extremely engaging.
Definitely recommend.

The Cat Lady took me completely by surprise.  When I first heard of it, I identified a few primary adjectives that applied to it: dark, horror, atmospheric, indie, adventure, interesting.  The "interesting" bit was why I decided to torrent it out of a casual curiosity.  I bought it after having completed it, because it absolutely deserves it.
If you have not yet watched the game's trailer, then I highly recommned it before proceeding in this review in order to really get a feel for the game's style and theme.  After having seen the trailer, I was immediately interested, but the game's tremendously heavy tone was a little worrisome at first.  Of course, it was one of things that drew me to it in the first place, but at the same time one of my greatest fears for the game was that it would end up being an overly grimdark puddle of emo for emo's sake.  Thankfully, my concerns were completely unfounded as the game surprised me with the depth and dynamic qualities of its story and characters.  The quality of the game's protagonists is incredible.  They feel tremendously real despite their extreme circumstances and their growth and development as characters is one of my very favourite things about the game.
The art and music are also both consistently top-rate.  Some may find the paper-cutout animation style a bit off-putting, thinking it primitive, but I could not disagree more.  Its brilliance lies in how beautifully it expresses the game's core themes.  The player character, Susan Ashworth, is a sufferer of chronic, even suicidal, depression.  To her, the world is a dark, colourless place and people are hated reminders of her own prison of sorrow and alienation.  The game's bleak depictions of environments and unnatural, eerily-jerking character animations express this perfectly.
The game's soundtrack is simply superb and the game does an incredible job of using music to convey emotion and intensity within the narrative.  It doesn't serve as a backdrop to fill dead air as it so often does in other games, but really, truly contributes to the strength of the narrative in wonderful ways.
The only area I honestly think the game could be improved is the audio-recording quality for one or two of the minor characters.  If you have read other reviews, this issue will surely have caught your attention, but don't let its significance become overstated.  The main characters are voiced and recorded expertly and the overall game really isn't detracted from by these few technical failings.  Once you have played the game, you will think back on the wonderfully realized characters, moving story and consistently powerful conveyance of theme and emotion, not the odd technical hiccup of inadequate recording equipment.

I loved the first, though it had its problems and I love this iteration even more.
Star Ruler 2 takes the good things from SR1 and makes the great.
Diplomacy? Redone and changed entirely from the now 'staple' civilization-style diplomacy system, for the better in the extreme.
Ship Design? Early in its design but the overall idea is far better and really only needs more hull types and subsystems to be better than SR1's system.
Economy? Truly beautiful. This is Sins Of A Solar Empire on crack! This is the best 4x space strategy I have ever played. It is only limited by what your computer can handle. Unlike SOASE your fleet size is unlimited, along with galaxy size/number. You can also create war machines the size of the galaxy, although that would probably take a year to build in real time, you can do it! There have been major improvements since Star Ruler 1 that make this game easier to play. One thing I hated about the first one is the AI players would always out expand me and therefor wipe me out after about 4 hours of playing. This one encourages rapid expansions and makes it fun and not just something you have to do to keep up with the AI. It also gives you a home base to build the best stuff instead of having many home bases to protect your systems. From what I have seen so far you really only need one or two massive armies to protect yourself with the FTL system. Instead of spending 20 minutes watching your ships snail their way through space you can just have them warp and be there in a few seconds.
It is very hard to learn at first but becomes easy after you understand the basics. The tutorial is not very instructive when it comes to resources and planet leveling and I had to watch a youtube video to understand it. I honestly do not know why this game is not as popular as some of the other 4x games out there. I think this game would rival Civilization in terms of enjoyment.

Oh the mixed bag which is SR2. (as of now since it is a beta). Star Ruler the original is still installed on my system and still gets some play time. I love that game, it is awesome. All this said, I do recommend Star Ruler 2, however, I hope they make a few more changes.
Pros:
Diplomacy, the “buy a card, play a card” system is actually rather interesting
FTL, there are several FTL technologies, each race dependant.
Graphics, ships and weapons fire looks amazing.
Territory and FoW, both systems are done quite well.
Mixed:
Budget system, everything is built using “money”. It is a little simple for my personal tastes.
Planet management, (I don’t hate it… completely) some planets have food, some have water and some have a resource. For a planet to grow at all, it has to have food AND water. You have a few options to do this, build a farm or hydro collector, which normally costs more to maintain than the planet makes in income, or trade it from one planet to the next. Here is the clincher, if you trade off a resource, that planet can no longer use it. The way it is tiered, once you have a level 3 or 4 planet, you have about 10 level 0s trading their resources off to support it. This does keep the computer from colonizing everything, but it still feels strange to me.
Power, Energy, FTL and Research, the way you stockpile and earn these is a pain. Power is used to buy and play diplomacy cards. Energy is used to activate artifacts. FTL is your empire’s pool of FTL crystals, any ship using FTL will deplete from this pool. Research is … for research. There are bonus ways to get points in these categories but the basic way is from left over “budget” allocation.
Cons:
Ship control, capital ships … that’s all you can control … Well, capital ships and scouts, but that is seriously it. You build a capital ship, tell it what to do, and it is followed around by “support” ships. A few of my largest battles to date were between a handful of ships and their supports. To me, this system is somewhat lack luster.
Ship design, do you like rail guns, lasers and missiles? I sure hope so, because that’s pretty much all the weapons there are. There are only about a dozen modules total and you only have to research a few of them.

The Yawhg is a choice-based adventure where you must select a character and await the arrival of the deadly Yawhg.
I played a little over 80 minutes, and thoroughly enjoyed the game. First, let's discuss it's strengths.
The Yawhg is beautiful. The artwork is all fantastic and fits the theme of the game perfectly. The music and soundtrack of the game is haunting and wonderful. The gameplay is interesting and, at first, exciting. The story is enjoyable and satisfying.
And now, the negative sides of the game. It's short. Not such a bad thing, but when coupled with the retail price, the sense of worth is a little low. I got 80 minutes of gameplay out of the game, which I did enjoy, though the price is a little high for my taste.  Next up, again, the gameplay. After one or two playthroughs of the game, the mechanics are no longer exciting as you can kind of see what's happening quite easily, meaning completion of the game can be easily "gamed" (if you know what I mean). The game also lacks achievements. Woah woah wait, that's not a bad thing right? Actually, I think in this case, it is. Achievements mean nothing, it's true, but I think, had The Yawhg had achievements, it would have added a heck of a lot more replayability as the achievements could direct your play, asking you to complete sub-stories, professions, and multiple side ideas which, after completion, many will not revisit.
Either way, a really charming and lovely game. I enjoyed it thoroughly.

Let's forget about all the controversy surrounding this game's promotion and look only at the game itself for this review. Not that I think it would quite be right to call it a game—Depression Quest is more a Choose Your Own Adventure novel than a video game—but I don't think that means it doesn't belong firmly in the realm of digital, interactive storytelling.
My initial reaction to Depression Quest was, unsuprisingly, "Wow. This game is depressing." But as the game went on, I found myself inextricably drawn into the story, attatched to the characters and caring more than I thought I would about the wellbeing of my player character. Maybe I'm lucky since I know more than what the game assumes the average person knows about depression, so I found it quite simple to make the choices that provided a reasonable amount of improvement and I certainly don't think I want to replay it "to get all the endings". However, it often managed not to feel like "find the right choice" so much as genuinely considering what I think my character would and ought to do, which was a feat I think worth mentioning.
The soundtrack is also just the right level of relaxing and lethargic. Actually, I'd go so far as to say the soundtrack was one of the game's greatest strengths—it absolutely sets the tone and helps you to connect with the story in a way I found particularly effective. It's also genuinely beautiful and I found myself reaching the end of the game and not wanting to close it because that would mean the music would stop.
Don't get me wrong, the game has its downsides. I found the amount of text surprising and, whilst I enjoy reading and am quite the fan of CYOAs, I was simply unprepared for it and found myself skimming sections without realising. Likewise, I found the use of presenting options that could not be chosen tiresome after some repetition, especially when they wouldn't have been options I would have chosen anyway, regardless of the gimmick. Maybe on replaying the gimmick may become less (I imagine some options become unusable the worse you are doing) but one of the game's major downsides is that after completing the game with a positive(-ish) ending I cannot bring myself to replay it. This might have been different had I sunk deeply into depression, as the desire to see my character recover would bring me to replay, but overall this game has minimal replay value and the one playthrough I had lasted less than half an hour. It is a one-off experience and whilst it is one that teaches important lessons effectively and has genuinely touched me I cannot deny that I would feel deeply cheated if I had been required to pay much money for this at all.
Overall, I think the game has chosen the right medium to set across its intended message, and I think it has done so with a reasonable level of effectiveness. It is, of course, not everyone's cup of tea, but if you feel like you'd like to know more about depression and enjoy the occasional Choose Your Own Adventure novel, I cannot recommend this game more. And whilst I will I admit that that is quite a select group of people, I don't think that makes this any less a reccomendation.

Hot Tin Roof: The Cat That Wore A Fedora is really charming game even though it's sometimes extremely frustrating.
To start off with what really works: the graphics, the atmosphere, the music. The plot of the crime-solving part of the game is complex without being offputting, and figuring everything out actually felt rewarding. The multiple endings actually depend on your choices and whether you choose to be bold, meticulous, etc. in your investigation, and the writing is witty, and often funny.
The world of Hot TIn Roof is a strange mix of stuff that I never expected to mix well together. 8-bit music and jazz. A typical noir setting with a kitty trying to lead a class war. Also, talking rats, one of whom is the kingpin of the underground. And that's without going into spoiler territory. And yet this whole world feels cohesive and entertaining. I only wish there was more: more NPCs, more side quests, more locations...Instead, there's the 3D platforming.
I do appreciate the attempt to mix a puzzle-platformer with an adventure game, and i think it works in some regards. It certainly helps make the world feel more expansive, it's sometimes justified by the narrative and some of these platforming sections are nice (imo, the Penthouse and the Works). However, the nature of an adventure game means you often have to run around the world and retrace your steps to find clues, so at best, the platforming sections felt like a chore I had to go through in order to go back to adventuring and crime-solving. At their worst (towards the end of the game), they felt frankly unfair, especially since the controls weren't nearly smooth enough to follow that difficulty curve.
[Side note: the developer did suggest cheat codes in the forums to help with the platforming.]
All in all, I'm glad I stuck with the game throughout these painful sections, which is why I recommend it, with these caveats. I really hope the developers will give adventure games another try because that part is a true success, and I'd love to see more quality writing like this.

Bought this game for Android a while ago when it was part of the Humble Bundle. Thoroughly enjoyed it on a mobile device, though I wasn't particular good at the game. Since it was fun I added the game to my Steam Wishlist and when it was released today, I straight away bought it.
In the game you fly a mecha robot "on a rail" shooting down invading aircraft. In between the flying parts of the level your robot lands on roofs or roads to combat enemies walking or flying around him. In other sections your robot drives a fast vehicle through streets. Each different combat section requires a different play style adding much variety to the level design.
Having just completed the first level, which incorperates all game play styles stated above, I have moved on to level 2 which is in the format of a traditional space shooter game. So again, a different kind of gameplay experience.
The game is fast paced, and at least for a fairly new player like me, quite difficult. I died a lot. The game is forgiving however, ending up being "Game Over" provides the option to restart the game at the last save point.
Despite having spent limited time in the game, I had a lot of fun playing my way through the first level, and for the cheap price would definiatelly recommend it to players who like casual shooter games. Specially given the game can be played from the couch with a controller.

This game is absolutely a hidden gem especially for the more seasoned gamers.
Ok first impressions were not that great, the inability to go fullscreen and the web-like UI had me mentally kicking myself for buying it.
However, after remembering this is early access I persevered and to my surprise the more i investigated, the more good things i found.
Pro's:
Multi-Platform
Highly original diplomacy not personally seen before in this genre.
Solid game mechanics and AI, although still room for improvement.
Customizable Races for you and your AI.
Massive, fully customisable Ship designer, with shareable ship designs
Ingame IRC chat direct with the Devs, dont like something about the game? then tell them :)
Create Mods ingame. The use of text files for settings and ai make this a modders paradise.
Easy to use UI.
In-game wiki.
Customisable Autosave feature.
Fully customisable Key Binds.
Cons:
Graphics are not finished, expect some rather dire pixel art in places not finished yet.
Tutorial could be better.
Lean documentation.
Summary:
There are plenty of places where the game needs some improvement, but the game flows so well, there is nothing to my mind that sticks out as an obvious con, other than the unfinished graphics and some bugs in graphics device area.
In regards to the tutorial it gives a good overview of setting up your planets and the basics of setting up your colonies etc. but Diplomacy is hardly touched on and you only get a fleeting glance at the ship design feature.
The documentation could be better and leaves a lot of the detail to figure out yourself which can be good/bad on your preference. Although, the Devs are very approachable and the IRC makes for a good read even while playing solo.
Overall though, if like me you have fond memories of SupCom Lan parties and the like, this game is an absolute "Must Have" in your library. The fact this game is unfinished and still in active development only adds to the credit due to the developers, for this game surely shows a great deal of promise.

So, another FPS stealth game that relies purely on stealth, with no superpowers or weapons(the weapons are more like tools in this game), sounds right up my alley!  I said count me in.  Oh what a mistake...
First off, let's talk about the biggest and arguably dumbest design decision I could think of, the controls.  For starters, you cannot free jump.  Let me reiterate again, you cannot freely jump.  What kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥brain at Square Enix thought this was a good idea?  Let's just take one of the basic mechanics of all FPS games and exclude it.  It makes Garret feel and play like an utter gimp.  What kind of a thief can't jump on his own?  So how does he actually get around?  Well, the game dicatates where you can jump.  As in only certain platforms or boxes can be climbed.  Only specified platforms can be crossed or leaped across.  It makes traversing the already clausterphobic levels frustrating beyond belief.  Too many times have I thought I could jump across the roof top only to jump straight down into the street, right in front of a guard and get killed.  Only too many times have I have been cornered, and the obvious route is blocked off by arbritrary obstacles like a pile of boxes or debris that any other game would simply allow myself to climb or jump over, but in this case since the object is not specified, I can't do anything with it.  This doesn't apply to just platforms either.  This also applies to climbing roofs and walls.  You have a tool called the claw, which allows you to climb high walls.  But again, only designated walls which are few and far between.  This also applies to leaning around corners.  A normal game typically used Q and E to lean left and right retrospectively.  But no, this game you have to go up to a corner, and press E and Garrett will grab the corner and peak around.  Why couldn't they just assign different keys?  Too many times have I wanted to grab an object on top of a box or table, press E and wind up peeking around the edge.
My second biggest problem is the level design.  It's so cramped and maze like.  The open city of the previous entries is gone, replaced with narrow, winding streets cut up into small areas with too many loading areas  that take away any immersion this game had.  There are multiple smaller routes that can be explored, each with different loot than be stolen.  It's routine design when it comes to these type of games to allow replayability.  Some routes require certain tools to be explored.  However, there's no real reward to all the risk to going near guards because of the next biggest issue...
The combat.  Now, combat has always taken a backseat in the Thief games because it's main emphasis is on stealth and avoiding being seen in the first place.  I wouldn't mind this, but because your jumping and movement is so castrated, combat is almost always inevitable at some point because you either slip up or because not on purpose you jump down instead of jumping across a roof.  You get cornered and can't run away because of arbirtrary game rules.  So running away isn't always an option.  Garret is armed with a bow and a tool called a black jack which is used for striking.  The bow is a typical bow, equips different arrow types and the whole shebang.  However, the black jack is a worthless piece of garbage.  First off,  you press R to swing by default.  Yes, freaking R.  Left click equips your bow and V is for dodge.  So, take yourself throw a scenario where combat is involved.  You have to press V to dodge, and R to strike.  By default, this is extremely awkward, the black jack does minimal damage and your bow is too clumsy to be used in close quarters.  Remember in Dishonored when in combat, parrying and striking with your sword felt smooth and responsive?  Well, take all of that and throw it out the window in this game.
The AI for the most part is passable for a stealth game, if they get alerted they will search around corners and shine their torches into shadows.  They have their routes and can be distracted with blunt arrows, throwable objects and snuck up behind and knocked out.  It's your typical stealth game AI, nothing too remarkable and nothing too terrible.  However a big flaw I notice is if you are in combat in the middle of the street with a guard, the civilians fail to react in any way shape or form.  They just continue standing in their awkward, repetitive idle stances.  It takes away the immersion, and reminds you again that you are playing a video game.  This doesn't happen 100% of the time, but it happens enough where I had to make note of it.
On the other hand, the graphics are quite nice.  Especially the lighting effects.  The dreary gloomy feel of the franchise is as present as ever.  Garrett has full awareness, and looking down shows his legs and hands so he feels more than just a floating camera with arms.  On the other hand the animations are stiff, awkward and flat.  Garrett has a little animation for everything including opening draws, grabbing loot, picking locks, turning the dials on a safe, pressing buttons, opening doors and more.  I can appreciate this, as it makes me feel more in the shows of the protagonist.  But, this comes at a draw back.  You cannot quickly rifle threw draws or cabinets, as Garrett has to straighten out, look down and open every single door and draw.  This little times it takes to watch the animations add up, and more than once have I been stuck opening a window or draw and caught by a patrolling guard.  So you really have to make sure the coast is clear before sifting through every draw and dresser in a room.  So trying to be a quick, cunning thief is harder than it has to be.  Unlike Corvo who could pop easily in and out of sight to grab a key, Garrett has to go through an animation which takes away your control for a second.
The sound on the other hand is busted.  The voice acting is atrocious, with lines awkwardly and poorly delivered.  Dialogue contains many strange pauses in the conversations and combined with lip synching issues, makes cutscenes cringeworthy.  At least cutscenes are rendered in games instead of FMVs though, minus one or two.  NPCs constantly repeat the same few lines over and over, leading to immersion breaking design.Another big issue with the audio is the depth of sound is all sorts of wonky.  For example, if you are standing on the roof top and two guards are talking on the street three stories below, the voices will be loud enough as if they were right next to you.  This is a constant issue I notice throughout the game, and while it's a small quirk, it leads to moments where I would have the volume up and all of a sudden two voices will be blaring through my speakers even though there's no NPCs near me.  However, the audio is not all bad, as sound plays a big factor in being stealthy.  Walk faster, louder footsteps.  The typical stealth sound routine is all in place but to great detail.  Walking across broken glass renders your footsteps very loud, same with walking in water and such.
The game gets a few things right.  Garretts sprint and swoop moves are very welcomed.  The levels are littered with beautiful little details like hidden rooms, hidden safes, traps and alternate routes, which makes exploring every nook and cranny and must.  Paying attention to surroundings is a must, as broken glass, traps, puddles of water and creaky wood planks are almost everywhere, so speed running is ill advised.
The game also contains a fair of customization, such as upgrading your abilities and gear.  Also included is a load of gameplay options, like optional warnings, object highlighting, difficulty settings and how much information you want on your HUD.
All in all, too many clueless design decisions hinder what could have been an enjoyable stealth game.  This is not a thief game at heart, so don't let the name fool you.  2/5 stars, and that's being generous.

As a long time fan of the series, I was really excited to hear Eidos was making this game (especially having enjoyed Deus Ex Human Revolution so much so I expected good things).  That said, this a pretty sorry excuse for a game regardless if you are familiar with the previous titles or not.
First of all, let's start with the awful storyline.  Not only did I find the story completely predictable, it was not even remotely well written or interesting at all.  There really is not much else to say about the story, moving on.
The number one complaint I have against this game was how little it actually felt like previous thief games.  Sure there is a sneaking mechanic, but the rest of the gameplay completely falls flat when the AI is asked to anything other than move from patrol point to patrol point.  The second you are detected, the horrible AI reveals just how bad it truly is.  Expect to see guards running into walls and unable to show any signs of intelligence in trying to track you down.  When I was detected, the simple act of clambering up onto a dresser or balcony is enough to evade them for good so long as you wait for them to give up.
If I was not getting annoyed over how easily I was able to sneak wherever I pleased with little to no resistance, I was facepalming my way though all the parkour driven rush sequences which feel completely out of place in this game.  Hey Call of Duty does these types of sequences great, that does not mean I want to see it in a game like Thief Eidos, COMON!
When there actually were brief moments in the game when I thought it had a chance to feel like the Thief games of old I love, those moments were quickly erased and forgotten amidst the horrible dialogue, out of place action sequences that you are forced to endure, and laughable AI that was about as challenging as pressing DELETE from my installed games...

This game has some flaws but is also just brilliant.
First off the lack of settings (like turning down volume or monitor settings) and several typos (for example switching "he" and "she" on occasion) are slight annoyances.
It is also quite easy to figure out a "winning" strategy which gets you the "flourishing" ending almost every time. This would make the game very boring, if that were actually relevant, which it isn't.
This is where the game's brilliant aspects come in. The random events through the game provide witty, at times completely unexpected (and being genuinely surprised is something I very rarely experience in games) and simply hilarious moments. You will find yourself just playing through the game (which takes less than 30 minutes in single player) time and time again trying to discover new random events, possible outcomes and resulting consequences.
And then there is the ending. All your choices tying together to decide the fate of the village, followed by (perhaps more importantly) the conclusion of each character's own story based on the chosen tasks and random events, once more providing several outcomes to be discovered.
In this regard this game, with it's "choose your own adventure" feeling despite the preset timeline, is exactly what alot of the bigger RPG titles are lacking realized on a smaller stage.
Expecially the multiplayer (which is limited to hot seat, but quite frankly a online multiplayer wouldn't make sense anyway) adds even more excitement and laughter to the game. If you have the option it is very rewarding.
All this combined with a lovely animation and very soothing soundtrack in my opinion make this game most definetely worth the time and money.

I really liked Risen 2.  When it was over, I wished there was more. I really liked the story, I liked the characters, and I loved the locations. Risen 1, on the other hand, was an ok time waster, but by the time it was over, I was really ready for it to be over (because I had gotten bored).  Get both if you can, but if I had to chose I would definitely recommend this game.
Risen 2 is set in gorgeous island jungles that feel a lot more open they actually are, and there are a good number of islands you get to visit.  Early on you are allowed to fast travel so you don't have to keep running the same paths over and over - and OVER - again (like in Risen 1).
The pirate aspect of the game is only to get a ship for transport between locations and to hold your crew (you can chose between most of them for traveling/fighting companions when you leave the ship)...there are no sea battles.  It would have been great if there were, but they had no part of the story.
There's a crafting system is based on the skills you decide to acquire and the recipes you find/pay for...you gather the materials as you play.  Money is really hard to come by in the beginning, frustratingly so...and every skill has to be bought.   I am not really thrilled with the skill system, most of the skills aren't as useful as they should be.  A number of them are really useful once or twice, but then you never need them again.  Others you want to max out as soon as possible...but you don't know which till the end of the game.  (or unless you look at a game guide)
I am also not thrilled with the fighting system.  I ended up hack and slashing despite the fact I was also supposed to be able to parry and riposte...I don't know for sure that I ever managed to...I can't swear that they actually work.  I had the same problem in Risen 1 though.  I was never sure if I was doing it right, so quit trying after a while.  Have lots potions and grog on hand.  I lived and my opponents died though, so in the end it worked out.
The game has faults but none that ever made me yell at the screen.  It was quite an enjoyable ride while it lasted.

bulb boy's kinda like binding of isaac if it were a point & click adventure instead of a roguelike. it's got the same kind of gross and disgusting aesthetic with liberal use of poop imagery that i know a lot of people, including myself, aren't really into. furthermore, the use of only a single color (green or red) at a time is something i appreciate as an idea, but i'm not too big of a fan of how this game does it. it feels more like a way to mask the newgrounds-y level of the artistry, rather than something genuinely pleasing stylistically. on the other hand, the sound design is top notch, though i'm not a fan of the tune that's supposed to represent pleasant moments — it's kinda grating more than soothing.
the adventure is mostly slow and linear. the puzzles aren't too difficult to figure out despite the lack of dialogue, and there's a hint option available at every step just in case something's a bit unclear. there's a boss battle at the end of each section to add a bit of tension; while these are mostly not frustrating, misclicking into the same drawn out death animation repeatedly and having to wait until the game lets you restart can be a bit irritating.
i hesitate to call the game horrifying; the monster designs are creepy, but they lack detail in-game compared to what is shown in the concept art on the store page. the adventure parts without them are kinda boring and tend to overstay their welcome, even despite the game's already short 3 hour length. in all honesty, i enjoyed the cute and heartfelt moments of the game more than anything else — which there were quite a few of, thankfully. the final boss is also hilarious.
i've mulled over how to end this review for a bit, but i can only really muster up an "it's okay." so, yeah. bulb boy is okay, and his dog and grandpa are okay too. thanx 4 readin'

This game is one of the best detective games I have ever played. It is thoughtfully laid out and every single detail is answered in the end, and that shows that real thought and effort has gone in. I do not intend to spoil the end but I am sure you will be satisfied with the end, because I know I am!
While the start can seem a bit slow, and eventually you may feel a bit of repetition going on, each of the characters have real personalities. Each character contributes in some way to the story, and the detective skills are very much required to look at the dialogue being spoken and to cross reference them with your notes. While it is not essential, and the game will help you out if you need to, this game has a lot of complexity to it, which allows you to get involved with the story and make your own investigations - this is something that I really like - you do not need to follow a set path and while the story is, inevitability, linear, the game does not say “you have to do this in this order”.
The level design is very well made and I especially like the use of the contrast between simplistic tessellations of objects and their detailed textures. The levels make good use of 2D and 3D elements, such that the world appears 3D while the camera is fixed on a 2D plane.
The cat model for your detective friend is a nice addition, and even helps you out where necessary.
There is some plat-former type elements to the game which is further developed with the use of the gun ammo, which you pick-up along the course of the story. Though, I must admit, this can be very frustrating, especially when there are no save points around!
Another main part of this game’s composition is puzzles; there are a couple different types such as finding hidden levers or trying to time your jumping and coordination skills to perfection. Each puzzle fits nicely into the theme and is another great addition to liven up the game.
Further more, I like the way that, when you go into a new area or a new layer of a building, the previous layer disappears and only the new one remains, which makes the game not only less resource intensive, but really resonates focus on the layer you are one and not the other layers/background.
A really nice touch and to emphasize on the cleverness of this game, the title itself is actually a play on words for a phrase called “like a cat on a hot tin roof”, which really impressed me at how thoughtful the developers were!
If you intend to buy this game, I advise you to take one thing at a time and not solve all the little details at once, ever-wise, you can get overwhelmed and confused. (Remember to talk to your chief for clues if your stuck!) The story is complicated and may seem overwhelming at times but if you have read a few detective stories recently, then you should be in the mind set for a complex story. Some people have critiqued against the game for this but as Hercule Poirot once said, “Every murder has a simple solution behind its lies”.
All in all, this is a great game and while not too long (my first complete run through took about 7 hours), it is really well polished and I hope for a sequel some time in the future. Great job developers!

This is my first real review, but I feel that this game is missunderstood and underappreciated so I hope to improve on that.
Beyond Earth is similar to other Civilization franchise games, but different enough to feel fresh. It's like a new game that you already know how to play. With aliens. And lasers.
It is not as profound as classic Civ games, but I like the fact that the average game is shorter, with this game a quick skirmish doesn't last weeks. I feel that because of this they removed the cost for upgrading units, changed the evolution tree and made affinities...
Without the DLC the game feels like it is lacking, but with the Rising Tide complexity rises considerably; I adore the new hybrid affinities, the new diplomacy is ok, personality traits are awesome. Connection to Sid Meier's Starship is also a neat bonus, ehich enhances immersity in the game universe.
It also runs well on non-gaming laptops and steam cloud save works seamlessly; to me this is of a paramount importance, because I like to play it on my gaming PC as well on my laptop.
A Steam controller is almost a must have for Civilization games, after a quick personalization it makes everything so much quicker and effortless...
The main CON of this game is it's full price. If Beyond Earth, Rising Tide and Sid Meier's Starship came on the market as one complete game I feel it would get the praise it rightfully deserves. With it's current marketing system...well...buy it on sale, as have I.

By itself, it's an incomplete game. I wouldn't bother buying it unless you get the Rising Tide expansion as well. Once you do get the Rising Tide expansion however, it's so much better and is worth playing. Combat at on water is pretty much ignored, in fact, just about anything that has to do with the water is ignored. This is fixed in the DLC. I feel they could have added more in terms of the satellites. You'd think, with this taking place in the future, that air/orbital supremacy would be a little more important. Yet, you only get one type of air based unit, and the satellites are largely not worth producing. Furthermore, the AI is stupid. Even on the most difficult settings, it's very easy to beat, unlike Civ 5, where it was actually challenging. Maybe I'm just really good? But, I doubt that. Diplomacy is seriously non-existent. Again, this is something they improve upon in Rising Tide, quite significantly. It's also a shame that there's no technology that reveals the entire map. Exploring every inch of the map on quick or standard game speed is near impossible. This is even more of a nuisance when you have the Rising tide expansion. ARC's civilization bonus is OP. Lastly, the naming of the technologies and buildings needs some work. They literally just stuck nano- or xeno- in front of half of them and called it day.
As for some positives, I like how it takes some time for outposts to grow into new cities. The technology tree is non-linear, allowing you to research what you want to fit your favorite game style. The aliens can be very troublesome, especially the colossal units. This adds some difficulty to the game, that is lacking elsewhere. The affinities are unique and have different buildings, units, and perks, also the victories associated with them are cool.
All in all, don't get this game by itself. You're gonna want to get the Rising Tide expansion to make this a complete game, hence why I'm not recommending this game. They should have released a complete game to start off with. It really is almost unplayable by itself. If you are interested in this game, try to wait for it to go on sale or for it to be bundled with the DLC at a cheaper price.

In August last year I made the mistake of buying this as my first Civ game. At that time, it seemed really cool to me because I liked the theme and watched some videos on it. I still enjoy it, but it has many more drawbacks than Civ 5.

Cool sci-fi theme, great graphics and awesome music (if you really care about those things)
Affinity system makes for different playstyles and can be diversified (unlike ideologies)
There is now one air unit which can perform all three functions (attacking, air sweeping, and intercepting) and doesn't use oil/petroleum (no logistical nightmares involved with building an air force)
Cons:
No anti-air, helicopter, or anti-cavalry units and naval melee units only appear in the DLC
Embarked units only have 2 movement--and this can never be improved. Come on, it's 2600!
Melee cavalry only have 3 movement and can't move after attacking
Research takes a painfully long time at the start of the game and can quickly devolve into a race for affinity levels
Air units are only effective at intercepting for the most part
The best starting bonuses are only available through quests and victories in Starships (biggest problem of all in my opinion)
Overall rating: 5/10. Wait for a sale or until the price drops again.

This game is a fantastic exploration of some of the deepest life's problems and strongest emotions. Susan Ashworth is The Cat Lady with a very deep seated rage which has created her morbid depression. Her own depression saves her in a strange way when she commits suicide but comes back to life.
Facing her deep rage she confronts the most wicked people in the world, those with a sheer hatred of all things good, and engorging themselves on the destruction of the most precious in life, people (in fact, literally in some cases). In this point-and-click adventure game, solving puzzles to deal learn about the truth of life and the truth of evil, Susan grows and becomes a stronger person, until she finally finds her calling in the world, which redeems her and finally gives her hope to live... a thought she was entirely convinced could not be possible.
This game doesn't deal with evil in the ways most other pieces of their genres do. Most games have ruthless villaines that do more than just be an irritating jaugernaut. Rather, it deals more in depth with what evil truly is. The people she must face are true bona fide psychopaths.
The gore of this game makes sense. I wouldn't ordinarily play a gory game, but because of the philosophical nature, it's excusable. It's rather shocking however, throughout almost the entire game. A user only gets a brief relief from the horror.

I decided to re-review this to properly express how much I enjoyed it.
Be aware, this isn't just another horror game, it's an experience with a capital E!
You fall into the shoes of Susan, she is depressed and with a reason, she survives day to day until it's all over, Then amid the waking nightmares someone enters her life and everything changes, the nightmare is only just begun >:D
I loved this game when I first played it, it's dark, twisted, surreal and downright disturbing, it dares to do what very few dare to do, and I like that, when a company pushes and pushes till the barrier breaks!
I still love it now as I prepare to replay it all over again and re-renter that nightmare with an eagerness that comes from satisfying actual horror instead of wannabe horror :D

Just started playing the early access and I'm very impressed. While many of the systems are not fully completed (graphics aren't final, some UI quirks etc) this game definately has the trappings of greatness. In particular, I like the new planetary leveling system. Each planet has 1 resource and they require a combination of resources to level up. So you might have 1 or 2 crown worlds at level 4 (the max) and several smaller worlds which are supplying the goods to those planets. This type of internal trading simply doesn't exist in other 4x games.
In addition to the internal trade routes, there is a pressure system. If I supply a planet with materials for energy (plutonium etc), then small civilian structures will be built based upon energy production. So some of your planet's construction is done automatically based upon what resources you supply. This gives a very organic feel to the planet's developments.

Imagine, if you will, a 4x game. a 4x game, that, on the surface, looks like any other. You know. Colonize, research, diplomatize, exterminate.
now, imagine that 4x game without any limits. Imagine a 4x game that lets you research... forever. Imagine a 4x game that lets you build a carrier fleet with 10,000 ships. Imagine a 4x game that lets you design a ship larger than your homeworld.
Imagine... Star Ruler 2.
The first Star Ruler was a game that had so many great ideas, but was weighed down by lack of style. SR2 is the game the original wanted to be. Lasers from 20 systems away? You got it. Complex diplomacy system unheard of in any other game? Oh yeah. Scale that literally no other game can even come close to? Par for the course.
It's Early Access. The developers are literally an IRC channel away and are always willing to listen to ideas and suggestions. THE GAME LETS YOU MAKE A PLANET BUSTER THAT IS LARGER THAN MOST STARS.
Look, let's be real here. 4x games are all the same. you start, you colonize, you research, you slog out some battles, you win eventually.
But what if you won by sheer ridiculous scale? What if you won because you fed half the galaxy's economy to your homeworld? What if you won because you have a ship that can ruin fleets from 3 systems away? What if you won because you blew up the black hole in the middle of the galaxy? Isn't that better? Isn't it all better?
YES, YES it is. Give them your money. Do it.

Thought I would update this since the game is 1.0+ now.
All the things I liked about the first one, with pretty much all my issues with it fixed. SR2 easily my favorite space 4x. If you've played other 4x space games, here are the main draws:
* Properly 3d space, that is, things can be above or below
* Actually interesting and useful diplomacy!
* Civilian ships! You can actually do real commerce raiding, and you blockade by actually attacking shipping
* Very good ship design, but ships can be any size you think you can build. Placement location matters! Where you place armor and so on is important to combat.
* Very unique and interesting FTL that can vary between empires and act quite differently
* Battles are interesting, and not too fast
* Multiplayer!
* Native Linux support!
* Reasonable pricetag!
The tech tree is the weakest part of the game, but compared to the standard 4x these days its not "weak". There are some fantastically cool things deep in that tech tree but I haven't got them yet. :(
This game plays a lot differently than others, you spend a lot of time moving resources, colonizing worlds because you need the resources of that world rather than "just places to put things" like other 4x games. By that I mean worlds have different "exportable resouces" that you can ship to other worlds, that they'll need to become bigger and better.
Now, this game is really good -- but its complex to play. Expect to spend your first few games just trying to figure out how it all works before you really get a handle on it. The AI is challenging.
Bottom line, this is the 4x to get, the rest are fluff compared to this one.
PS. Check out the growing modding community! Badass.

Original 4x Space Sim games like Masters of Orion and Ascendency have set the standards on how a 4x game should be.
Ascendency has even gotten a Game App update.
People who are fans of this type of game can find Star Ruler 2 less like the modern 4x Space Sim's that they expect after seeing Star Ruler 2's graphic interface. Even the method of colonizing planets can seem backwards.
In truth however Star Ruler 2 (even still in Beta) has a play mechanic that is more suited to Multi-Player Online mechanics then the coveted original 4x Space Sims.
Take it from a veteran Master of Orion player like myself. Balancing a game like Masters of Orion for online use has been tried many times but IMHO no one has gotten it to work out well. Part of the inventiveness of this Real Time 4x system is the use of influence points that are used in Diplomacy. Add the 'Pressure' mechanic along with auto colony ships and you have the closest thing to a Masters of Orion-Real Time mechanic. It feels like my 100+ hours of playing Maters of Orion but with better graphics.
You can just think of it like seeing someone who has 3 tons of lemons and is screaming about it to you (the Boss.) Pressure amounts the computer deciding to make lemon aid without screaming to you about it or worse just letting them rot. A welcome and novel idea that balances out the Real Time while keeping to the origins of 4x.
It's still in Beta but this is the 4x to watch

Superb, free, action-packed MOBA for anyone seeking to hone their skills or just have some fun.
Battlerite is an excellent example of just about everything I want in a MOBA. If anyone is a fan of other MOBAs like League of Legends or DotA; I absolutely recommend Battlerite, as in my opinion, it takes all the best of what makes a MOBA and takes it to the next level. The quick deathmatch style matches bring about heart-pounding intense action, while pushing you to constantly better your mechanical skill and decision making. The in-game models; their movements and style, and the maps (with audience and background and all) are expertly crafted, and you can really see the work and care the developers put into them. The cosmetic content is available without paywall through opening loot chests, or saving up the appropriate in-game currency to buy whatever you fancy.
I consider Battlerite to be a highly 'player skill' based game where winning or losing is decided by the player's ability to decide on an appropriate loadout, stay co-ordinated and work with their team, and mechanically outplay their opponents.  While other MOBAs may leave you feeling hung out to dry after the enemy gets a minor lead causing a "snowball" for perhaps the entire duration of the match (15-30+ minutes), Battlerite is without this issue and in the unfortunate circumstance that you find yourself outmatched or simply with a disfunctional team the matches are short enough that you won't be stuck wondering "Why am I even playing at all?".
While other MOBAs have up to minutes inbetween any real action taking place, Battlerite brings the action right to you. Having been an old time League of Legends player I can honestly say that after playing Battlerite; playing LoL simply feels boring, lacking eventfulness, and not mechanically challenging. This may partially have to do with what I consider to be League of Legends golden age being long over and it's continual "fall from grace", but I digress, and I believe that even in LoL's prime, Battlerite would certainly be a worthy rival.

I'm enjoying Hot Tin Roof so far, having purchased it as part of the Humble Freedom Bundle. I will confess the interface took some getting used to. Everything you pick up or hear about is considered a "clue", even if it's not relevent to solving the current mystery in question. This can lead to some convoluted interface using to give something to someone. I can see what the developer was aiming for, something similar to Blackwell's "notes" system I think, but they've merged it with a traditional game "inventory" and it's a little confusing.
Other reviews have mentioned that the gun needs to be reloaded manually but they obviously didn't play far enough in to find the character/contexual command that tells you to hold down the reload button and your character will do a full reload. This way you only need to access the reload menu to switch ammo types.
It has taken me a little while to get used to the 3D-grid system the game is using for its maps but again, once it clicks you can actually position places in your head in relation to other places and you're away. So when I was given a task I was able to work out "I need to speak to this person at the end of the town" and off I went as the map system had 'clicked' for me.
The characterisation is funny with some very amusing lines and references to other classic adventures including classics from the Lucasarts stable.
I'll happily keep playing this one right until the end.

It's an FPS, with some classes that resemble those from TF2, also, huge maps and mechanics that resemble those from Battlefield. There are no vehicles, this is because each team has a "Commander" who builds structures and researches upgrades for the team whilst playing the game Real Time Strategy style. Teamwork is absolutely required to win, which leads to genuine gratification. The maps are urban and very detailed, definitely some of the best and most memorable source maps I've ever seen. The game developers claim they are the biggest source maps ever. They did a great job on it and I not going to lie to you, this game makes my dong hard.

It's pretty cool to play with an experienced team and commander. So make sure to find a team or clan for you. Sometimes you can get angry because your team play badly and you constanly die trying to win. In such moments you need to relax and don't try to win, find a spot where you can hide and  destroy structures or kill enemies. Even in a situation when your team will surely loose you can have much fun killing enemy Heavies (EXOs) with armblades (invisible guy) or sniper rifle.
I'm not a good RTS player, so it's hard for me to be a commander. Besides maps are very complex and detailed, there are so many pathes and ways to build in every map that I get lost. RTS gamers will probably be interested in playing as a commander, but for me it's hard. It's also inconvenient for me to use RTS camera, I can't see what's happening on the map.

The game has some issues which make it less fun to play:
- performance problems. Frame rate drops significantly (from 100+ fps to 25 fps)  when there are 32 players and lots of structures on map.
- sounds bugs. when looping sounds are bugged. for each looped sound there are 3 sounds playing, and even if structure is removed the sound remains. Can be worked around by deleting looped sounds from game's installation
- misc little bugs here and there. Like structure teleportation, server crashes etc
- Stuckable points. You can stuck in static props and buildings.
- The annoying sound when hit by explosion. Can't be turned off. And it can sometimes become permanent. snd_restart removes permanent
- Annoying effects of blood all over the screen when took damage. Can't be turned off.
- The FPS part is generally not very fun. I think it's because they wanted to make it Call of Duty(COD) like but added too much HP for most classes. So in COD you have fun killing enemies with 2 bullets, but here you have to use 2 mags. E.g. EXO needs 7 head shots to be killed.
For me the most annoying thing is the frame rate drops.
In spite of these drawbacks this game is currently the best FPS+RTS game on the market as for me.

First up, I bought this in a humble bundle and I'm still annoyed at the 20p or percentage of the price I paid went to Risen 2.
I must say, this game has to have the most relatively worst combat controls I have had the unfortunate experience to suffer through. Combat feels totally disconnected from pressing buttons, more akin to ordering the character to perform an attack which he will then perform on his own time. Attacking is limited to just spamming the left click, which is mired by long wind up times, as well as enemies not being staggered by your attacks, while they are more than capable of stunlocking you should they even lightly cough on you, which they will do so, far quicker than your attack animation. The only way I felt I could actually attack enemies was to rub myself up against an enemy and clip through them when they thrusted.
Animals are even worse, as their attacks are unblockable, as well as un-staggerable. Not only that, but skills that reduce damage taken are limited to only effecting human opponents. So not only can you not block animal attacks, they do far more damage than is feasible, forcing you to hoard potions in order to just soak enemy attacks until you grind them down.
Animations are in themselves janky and poor quality, and recycled to a horrendous degree. Human characters talking merely flap their jaws as if they belonged in the 90s, while the camera and characters noticebly constantly reset themselves every line of dialog, causing them to visibly spawn in every 5 seconds during cinematics. Texture and model quality, while not everything is to do with graphics, the level of quality is most definitely sub par for a studio as old as this.
Voice acting is poor too, it's better than average in that it actually uses British actors, but they're still pretty pants.
Overall a poor and infuriating experience not worth investing in, even if you are desperate for a pirate game like I was.

Then I found it on sale on Steam, for dirt cheap, and having progressed farther than I did when I had rented it, in hindsight I would now say that that $40 might have been well spent.
If you are going into to it looking for a triple-A title like Assassin's Creed or Skyrim, you are probably going to be a little dissappointed.  However, if you go into it not expecting it to strictly adhere to standards set by other titles, looking for something similar to Skyrim but focused on pirates and voodoo instead of dragons and magic, you might be rather surprised with what you find.  I find the voice acting somewhere between entertaining to quite good.  The tropical ambiance, settlements (Inquisition, pirates, and savages), and wildlife look great.  The story is interesting for the most part (I found myself to be more inclined towards free-roaming and side-questing).
So in conclusion, if you are like me and actually enjoyed Two Worlds 2, I think that you would also have a great time with this.  Ironic to end a review by compairing it to another game when I just tried to impress upon those reading to NOT do exactly that when going into it, but there you have it. :D

The Risen 2 development team's discussions must have included lines such as these: "It doesn't have to actually look like the player character is jumping, so long as he is moving through the air." "The player doesn't need to feel like they're controlling the combat - we'll just have them try to press buttons at enemies until they die." - "Explain the game mechanics to the player? Meh, Dark Souls doesn't do that, either."
There is one word that perfectly described Risen 2: "curde", as in "crudely made". So why am I actually recommending this game? Well, because it's crudeness is sort of a "Mount & Blade"-like crudeness.
Yes, Risen 2 is crude. But it's also charming and captivating. How captivating? Well, I was really pining to play Dark Souls again while playing Risen 2, put I decided to put it off. The dialogue in this game is well written, though not always well voice-acted. The characters are all you'd expect from a pirate game: drunks, thieves, ruffians and weirdos litter the various islands of its world. But its biggest asset is the sense of exploration that it gives the player. It always makes you curious for the next thing. I don't know how they did it, but ever since Gothic 1, Piranha Bytes has been able to make running around and picking up random stuff off the ground an intriguing passtime. But that is not all that Risen 2 is, of course. There are many interesting conversations to have, talents to learn, quests to undertake and enemies to slay, despite the abysmal combat system - seriously, it takes the guy like 2 seconds to execute the input! Could be that I'm playing with a controller, but it's just so much more fun.
Get the game on a bargain and enjoy!

Let's get this out of the way from the start: Thief 2014 is not as good as the original Thief trilogy.
The story isn't anything special, nor is the writing, but I felt the voice acting for Garrett was decent, though it's no where near as good as Stephen Russells performance as the original Garrett.
That said, I still found it to be an overall enjoyable game. The sneaking works well, with it being fairly easy to know how visible you are at any given time thanks to the light gem. A specifc noise plays if an guard has detected you which gives you a chance to get out of sight before being spotted, as well.
The difficulty of the game is also highly customizable, and you can turn off practically every element of the HUD to up the challenge, as well.
There's a Focus mode that can be upgraded to allow you to perform other abilities, but I found the most useful function it had was highlighting interactable objects and locations for collectibles.
WHile not a perfect game, and not as good as the original games, I would recommend Thief 2014 to fans of the stealth genre.

1) After the first main phase of the opponent, and before he enters his attack phase, there is only a very short window to react if you want to cast a spell or ability that would tap a creature. IMO there should be a five second timer, allowing the other side to react with some more time, and enable them to stop the timer, before the opponent can make his choice of attackers.
2) The matched games don't appear very matched to me. As a rather new player who did not open that many boosters yet, I seem to get players with ranking way higher than my own and decks thus much stronger a lot. Of course this does not help to win and improve your own decks if you are way more often than not outmatched.
3) You seriously need to work on the system randomly drawing cards. 8 out of 10 games I lose because either I just don't draw any mana at all, like seven rounds from the start hand not a single mana, allowing the opponent a huge advantage, or I draw NOTHING but mana, which also makes a good start slow down very hard all of a sudden if you simply have nothing to cast. And it really is frustrating if you know your deck is good enough to win a game, but you are being manipulated by the game mechanics and keep losing games just because of this randomness. It can happen, yes, it happens in real life duells as well. But NOT 8/10 times, and I am serious here. It happens way too often.

Probably the closest to playing "real" magic next to MTGO or even Shandalar.  I've played most duels of the planeswalkers games including the one for android, and they all seem to suffer from shoddy game dev.  The developers are learning from past mistakes with this version, and are closer to having a user friendly interface that lets you respond to most situations.  However, the timer method they use is at the bottom right corner, and unless you're always watching it closely, you'll miss the trigger to react  (like when you're distracted by what your opponent just played), even if you predicted your opponent's move ahead of time.
If compared to a very successful online card game (ie Hearthstone) Wizards/Stainless should take some notes, because it really is a more fun setup.  Besides, Blizzard copied a lot of what Magic is, so why shouldn't Wizards copy Hearthstone (if it's going to benefit users in the end anyway).
Pros(+) / Cons(-)
-Slow interface and gameplay in general
-Difficult to respond to opponent (ie Hourglass not obvious enough)
-Difficult to tap specific lands/auto-tap sometimes taps down a land you wanted untapped
-Interface unforgiving (ie <alt-[something]> to go back 1 move)
-Gold is a little pricey and no rebate for buying lots at once
+Much improved from previous Duels of Planeswalkers games
+You can play Solo / versus / and even two headed giant with real opponents
+Decent prize structure for getting gold to buy packs without paying real cash
+Good rewards for daily quests
+Great quests that relate to the newest expansion, with equally good rewards
To the developers:
All in all, great work!  It's a way more playable version of duels, but don't stop trying to improve this version. Thanks!

So, i'm writing a review because the game keeps on pestering me to do so, between one match and the other. Probably because the developers think that if i'm playing it i'm obviously enjoying it, right?
No, not at all.
First things first. The game still has stability problems, meaning that it crashes, some times often, other times rarely, but it's still really annoying when it happens. Recently they changed the questing system (through which you gain gold to buy booster packs) so that roughly 80% of the quests are for versus pvp only, whereas before it was a bunch of generic quests that you could do in pvp or pve since they required specific decks to complete them, and that's it.
Not only this is a butchered version of magic the gathering, with mythic rares limited to one copy and most rares limited to less than 3 too, a lot of cards are missing altogether. It's like playing limited all the time, which is not bad per se, but after a while it gets boring (i can't bring myself to play more than 3-4 matches at a time, and i often switch decks to try to keep things interesting).
I guess my biggest frustration is that this game could be so much more. Yes, i know there's MTG online out there and yes, i know that this has to be different because people spent loads of money on virtual cards on the other one. But then why does this thing exist? Why does MTG online still has an awful graphic quality compared to this one? Why don't they just merge the two into a decent game capable of competing with the other online card games? Just to be clear i dislike all the current alternatives, namely casualstone and similar ones; i'm a devoted mtg fan, but this is just not enough.
All in all, if you want to play without spending money i guess this is a good compromise.
