This is based on a single playthrough with 2 enemies and the standard galaxy.
I'm a fan of the 4X genre, I really liked MOO2, MOM, Pax imperia 2, GalCiv, Space empires 2 - 5, SOTS, Eclipse and a few others.
This game is named somewhat badly, it's not that similar to the first game. I'd say you might like the first one even if you don't like this, or that you might not like this one if you liked the first. Although this game is not complete, I think they won't change the idea of the game that much, regardless of how much people cry about it.
I'd say this game is more oriented towards the multiplayer experience than the first one.
Being different doesn't make it bad though and although seemingly simplistic, it doesn't lack in depth in most aspects of the game. In combat micro management is almost non-existent though, But there is lots of other stuff to do.
Planetary management seems simple, link planets to make resources to turn your homeworld to level 4 and get the wonder thing. But the game does become quite complex when you start to think about what each resource does and how to best use it. Stacking every kind of resource on a single planet quickly fills the planet and you can't use all of the Pressure to you advantage. The game at it's current state doesn't try to make the resources too different, but I could see how the devs might start messing around with them to make them more varied. Maybe more can be added via modding at some later date? Also note that it seems to be possible to have multiple resources on a single planet. You really have to know how the game works in order to understand what this means, but don't worry if you don't.
Diplomacy is quite unique in this game, best described as a card game. Already there are quite lots of different cards you can play in the diplomacy game, but as same with the resources, I think the devs have made a choice to only add the ones that are quite balanced. More might come later, and maybe even modded ones? Inter - racial diplomacy seemed a bit lacking, peace or war seemed to be the only choices? Maybe I somehow missed it?
Ship design has been simplified in this game, I think it makes for a better multiplayer experience, since designing ships is a bit faster now. I rarely made mining ships in the first game because designing a balanced ship required quite a lot of tweaking I would never have had the time to make them in a multiplayer match. And note that when you research upgrades to components, you need to design it again to get the optimal design, in the first game. In this one the ship components don't change in the various resource consumption ways, such as power and command. This makes it so that the ship designs stay optimal. I play kerbal space program, but in a game like this, I actually prefer simplistic ship design mechanisms. The game might need a few more components, but I don't see the point in having weapons (or other components) that are just better in every way to others.
Combat is the one area I find a bit lacking, The visual effects currently clutter everything and the only thing you can make out is two blobs diminishing in size. There isn't any combat micromanagement to do either. Two blobs go in, one leaves. But this is not that big of an issue since the game provides other stuff for you to do. If you like space combat micromanagement games, you should really check out "Nexus: The Jupiter Incident".
Research is quite boring right now, but I hope it's due to the fact that the game is still in development, although I quite like the Insight mechanism.
Exploration of the map is quite interesting since you are looking for artifacts and resources. For quite a while 4x games haven't really made a big deal about the exploration.
So all in all, this isn't a space 4x simulation game, but I don't think that it's bad because of it. I'm really waiting for them to finish it an try the multiplayer.
I bought it to support the development and because I had the loose money to do so. Don't buy it to play it, yet.

So far Star Ruler 2 has me extremely concerned....  I'm not going to condemn it quite yet because I understand it is effectively in beta the same way Star Ruler 1 was when I purchased that game, but even in its beta I absolutely LOVED Star Ruler 1.  In comparison Star Ruler 2 just feels like a step backwards in several departments but I will try to sum up my opinions in point format.
Pros:
1.  So far the audio that I've heard makes the audio in SR1 look like completel garbage, awesome job guys.
2.  The graphics are current about on par with SR1, better in some regards, worse in others but I'm sure after they refine everything this will be like the audio making the graphics of SR1 look like crap.
3.  Ship movement seems to be better in SR2 thatn SR1 so far and I can only assume it will improve.  I liked ship movement in SR1 but sometimes whatever controlled ship movement in SR1 would do silly amusing things that would require intervention.
4.  While I've never been big on dealing with the diplomacy side of games as it isn't my thing, I can say thus far SR1 practically has no diplomacy in comparison to SR2.
5.  Ability to not only add additional systems to a galaxy but to have multiple galaxies! I wanted this in SR1 so badly!
Cons:
1.  Ship design - Okay, maybe I will condemn SR2 just a little bit.  SR2 has a ship design similar to other games I've played in the past and I absolutely hate this style.  SR2's ship design feels like the beta for a game that came out 10 years prior to SR1.  I'm sorry, I absolutely hate this new ship design method.  In my opinion you guys nearly had it perfect in SR1 and has been the best method I've used in any game to date.
2.  Colonization & Planet development - I spend far more time in SR2 finding the planets I need and setting up routes than I would ever care to, this is such a huge complaint for me as it is a massive boring time waste to me and I don't to customize my planets nearly to the extent I could in SR1.  I end up searching through multiple systems on a constant basis trying to find all the requirements I need to set up a trade route to level up a planet and on a regular basis end up never colonizing some planets simply because I can't use the single resource they have and don't want to pay any upkeep for the stupid planet.  In SR1 no matter how small the planet was I could find some use for it, I could make a planet dedicated to research or producing food for my empire or just make a multi-purpose planet, I was truely the ruler of an empire where as in SR2 a planet is marked as 'fish' and that is all it can and ever will be.  I could go on about all the flaws of this system but suffice it to say I am seriously let down by it in comparison to SR1.
3.  The research page is just bleh, I wish I could give more constructive examples/reasonings as to why I dislike it or how it could be improved but I honestly don't know at the moment.
Others: (I'm like 99% sure these will be resolved overtime but I feel I should mention them anyways)
1.  Race portraits - Small selection and no where near as good as SR1 in my personal opinion, way to cartoonie
2.  Racial traits - Very small selection limiting your ability to create a custom race
3.  Unless I'm missing something I don't see anywhere to pick a ship set (what your ships will look like)
4.  Very few sub systems to put in your ship designs
5.  Lack of detailed descriptions for various items/objects
I am still hoping with all my heart that SR2 will be a great successor to SR1 and will keep playing SR2 throughout its development, but as it stands right now I honestly couldn't reccomend this game to anyone as I just don't see the designers completely redesigning key parts of its system that I have such strong dislikes for such as the new ship designer.

I've played sins and AI war, neither seemed to grasp me as this game has. Sins is certainly enjoyable, and has a slight one up when it comes to combat. However sins is a fully realized game and is complete. This isnt, and thats what people need to realize when it comes to early access games. AI war in my oppinion was a mess. Comparasins aside:
The diplomacy, from what I've seen, Is very orginal and fun. It keeps you on your toes and makes diplomacy a real part of the game, and not so much as a side mechanic. It has you buying cards. The cards are used in a multitude of ways, from an eco boost, to the annexation of an entire star system.
Economy is in my oppinion very fun. Planets need resources from other planets to help your population grow and become more andvanced. There are tierd resources that go up to 3 and range from common to uncommon. There are even special resources that you can export to certain planets for an added boost to a certain stat. Research is a bit lack luster. Dev's can correct me if im wrong, but I've heard that they will be working on it more and making it more intresting. It's one of those few games that you may love or hate, but personally I love it. I have a thing for good stories; no matter how awful the gameplay. However, I'm not saying this game has awful gameplay, rather the contrary. Its the perfect genre to tell the story of Susan Ashworthe; the suicidal Cat Lady. This game makes you understand that depression can happen to any of us. That all we really need is connection and a purpose in life. The writing is simply top-notch and the voice acting is generally good with a few misses. Especially, with a story centric game like this you've got to have an amazing story to tell and indeed this game does so with flying monochrome colors.
Graphics wise, the game looks like newpaper cutouts mixed with black and white paper dolls w/ clipped, low reso, & blurred animations from the 90s. However, this rugged look adds to the game's atmosphere of insanity and depression very nicely. Color is also used well to evoke mood of otherworldliness. The old-school look really adds to the horror aspect of the game; if silent hill 2 was in 2D, this would be the perfect look.
Music wise, the game it top notch. The industrial clanking, the heavy rock guitars, and the slow piano melodies on the touching moments; everything just amplifies the immersion. Again, can't help but compare it to Silent Hill since the OST has the same feel.
Gameplay wise, it's your typical point and click adventure minus the point and click. Instead, you use the directional keys and the enter key. Puzzles are straightforward and logical, which helps with a game as story heavy as this one. There's also clever use of dialogue, especially parts where you choose answers for Susan. An example would be a dialogue choice which cleverly makes you shape her story based on your personal struggles.
If there was a complaint with this game, it would be the audio. Sometimes, music would clip and voice acting of some side characters is like listening to them speaking through a can. Don't worry it doesn't destroy from the immersion, but just a nitpick. Still, I'm forgiving about it considering the indie aspect of this game; may be they don't have the budget for recording some lines in a studio?
Overall, I simply must recommend this game to you if you love games more than just something to pass time with, and something of an art form. This game is indeed not for everyone, some age old topics about what makes a good or a bad game may surface, but to me it doesn't really matter; if you got a good experience out of it (happiness, life lessons etc.) then it's good enough for me.

What a masterpiece of a game. Wow.
Art, original music, and writing are all superb. Graphics could have been more detailed, but the art style makes the graphical detail (resolution) not as important, and even more fitting in a way for the darker and grainier feel to the game. Voice acting is some of the best I've heard in a game making all the characters believable and worthy of your investment in them. Especially the main female protagonist, who is very unique for the gaming world and isn't constrained by the typical gaming tropes.
The writing and character dialogue is by far the most mature and believable for any game I have played. You are getting adult level dialogue and script writing here with very few, if any instances of the kind of cheesy video game writing we have grown to expect from video game writers.
This story will present some very dark themes. Depression, suicide, murder, and any other dark thoughts you could have. It's not technically a horror game, but it is psychologically creepy enough to feel like it at times. Something that most of us who no longer feel any fear from the "horror" genre are more likely to find unnerving in parts due to it being much more about the emotional level of the characters and their mental state rather than just seeing a ton of  gore. This game does have several  strange and gory scenes in it, but that isn't really what makes it great. The depth of the characters' thoughts and emotional upheaval is what makes it shine in the end.
The atmosphere of the game as well as all the set designs capture the mood of the story and the characters perfectly. The grainy sadness of the entire game keeps you in a perfect mood to enjoy the tale you are presented with.
For anyone that has experienced sadness, or depression on a deep level, this game will be relateable to you in many ways I'm sure. Living with the inability to properly address negative emotions that keep you in a state of sadness is perfectly presented here. Living with depression has never been shown better in a video game that I have played. You feel like you really know the main character, and you feel like the writer has a deep understanding of why she is the way she is.
There are well designed puzzles along the way that adventure fans expect. It is definitely possible to get a bit stuck and not be able to figure out a puzzle as some are a bit unorthodox, but if you look hard enough and think about all the interactable items in every stage eventually you can figure it out. Nothing too difficult, however.
This game deserves far more recognition than it gets. It is a truly great work of art, and it is quite apparent that the developer put a lot of deep thought into making this game. It absolutely had to have come from personal experience with the things presented. I don't think you could make a game like this unless you understand, or have studied many of these themes in depth.
10/10

Wow... just, wow. I wasn't expecting much from this game, but I was absolutely blown away. The writing is excellent. The story really makes you think. The style is incredibly artistic and incredibly creepy. The puzzles are pretty intelligent, and logical enough that you shouldn't be stuck for too long.
At first I thought it would be nice if the game ran at a higher resolution, but part-way through I realized that it turned out to be part of the charm of it all for me--the jaggedness of everything helped me to invoke certain feelings throughout the game.
The Cat Lady deals with mature themes and things that most games don't touch upon (like deep depression and suicide). There is plenty of blood and gore for those who like that as well. Oh, and drug-fueled (and sober) hallucinations? Check.
It's going to be tough to play another game now that I've finished this, because I can't imagine it will leave me feeling this deep and thoughtful.
Highly, highly recommended for anyone with the stomach for a little creepiness and gore.

I started playing Maplestory in June of 2005, just weeks after its was released to the North American region. Man, the memories I had wasting my time on this game. Even though I stopped around early 2007, I will never forget those two years where I wasted my life playing the game. The summers of 2005 and 2006 where I played non-stop with friends, those cold-winter days where I did quest runs with randoms, and those Saturday nights playing the game while watching the Boondocks on Adult Swim.
Even though I had a lot of fond memories of Maplestory, it was not that good of a game. With the arrival of the NX-Shop in late 05/early 06, the game's model turned from Free MMO to Free to Pay. It might have been the first instance I have experienced F2P. At first, the Nexon Shop offered cosmetic upgrades and various useless as fu
ck trinkets; it was fine at first. Slowly but surely, the OP game-breaking weapons started pouring in. By the start of 2007, Maplestory was littered with alternate accounts/players boosting from low levels to ridiculously high levels in the matter of a few hours; all they had to do was shell out a couple of dollars. It was at this point, the Maplestory community turned toxic. If all the xXAzNnAbuGo1995Xx names didn't ruin it for you, the di
ck measuring contests and the constant fleecing might have.
Naturally, I took a break from the game for a good year and a half. I came back in the summer of 2008, and what do you know? Still the same bullsh
it as last time. From that point, I completely gave up on Maplestory, uninstalled it from my computer, and tried blocking anything MS related from my head.
Fast-forward to 2016. I was browsing the Free-Game section on Steam, saw it, and thought to myself "why not? Let's see if it changed a single bit." So I downloaded it, had to restore my Nexon account, and renew the credentials in order to play it. Got it up and running, and played it for a bit. Here are my thoughts.
THE GOOD:
+ My account somehow survived 8 years of inactivity. Though my character names got fu
cked in the process. (see THE BAD for more details)
+ My friend's list remained intact, even though most of my friends had their names messed up too.
+ All of my items, equips, weapons, and quests - including completed, finished, and in progress - were retained too!
+ It's really easy to level up. Some long-time players think this is a bad thing, but not me. It used to take so long to level up back in the early days. To give you some perspective: it would take 2 hours to get from level 41 to level 42 (no matter your character's profession) in 2005/2006, now it takes 4 hours to get from level 40 to level 50.
+ Dat music doe. It hits me right in the nostalgia, and it's pretty rockin too.
THE BAD:
- Character names on inactive accounts were changed into a long-string of numbers. If you had not logged in since 2013, your characters will have fu
cked numbers for names because Nexon purged some useless data from their servers.
- There's only 3 screen resolutions in the game: 800 x 600, 1024 x 768, and 1368 x 768. Trying to modify the screen resolution will result in a ban from Nexon, so don't even think about it. It's 2016, and Nexon can't even be pressed to provide support for 1920 x 1080. What the fu
ck.
- The game still runs in 16bit color mode. I understand the sprites were created as early as 2001 or even 2000, but it's just inexcusable to see those color dots all over the screen.
- Main function keys are still not rebindable. I'm sorry Wizet/Nexon, I do not like moving my character with my right hand. Can you at least allow us to rebind it to WASD?
- The world map is still a bit
ch to navigate.
- Game still has spotty netcode. Those iconic hiccups were you might teleport from one side of the map to the other is still here.
- NX Shop has an even stronger presence than before.
- The community is effectively dead; no one is playing anymore. It's really weird to see the Scania server have open slots in their 20 channels.
THE MIXED:
~ Controller support. There is finally support for game pads, and unfortunately it's very spotty (my PS3 controller's d-pad was not recognizable). However, your standard console pads do not have enough buttons to accomodate various functions, especially when you get into the higher levels and need a lot of hotkeys.
~ Cut-scenes. I don't think there were cut-scenes in MS when I started playing, so it's a nice addition. However, most of these cut-scenes are unskippable and a pain in the a
ss to watch.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game for newcomers, but I do recommend it for old-timers who want to get back in and play it for old-time's sake. However, the game is on its deathbed. Nexon is contemplating on retiring the service by the end of this decade. Before that happens, Maplestory 2 will have more than likely be localized to the states. For those who are wondering, yes there is a Maplestory 2, and yes it is garbage. It has Maplestory aesthetics, combined with isometric ARPG gameplay with Minecraft's voxel influence mixed in.

I feel like a traitor for writing this as a long time Civ fan, moreso because I do believe the team put an awful lot of work into making this game. Unfortunately, however, I cannot recommend making a purchase to others. It's hard to place my finger on exactly where this went wrong...it's more that nothing really stands out as being 'right'. There just doesn't seem to be any flavour between factions, no interesting boosts or unique abilities besides +2% trade gains or -0.5% pollution and other uninspiring traits.
There is no real sense of wonder or excitement exploring this new world. Just a feeling of a reskinned Civ V with all the resources named something else so you need to remember the new names. The technology web is confusing as there is no organisation allowing that pushing in one area will benefit military or integration or science. Just drawn out periods of scanning the web for something...anything...that interests you. Generally you just end up picking something that won't take too long to research and hope you'll have a better idea what you want the next time you look.
For me, the whole game just becomes an aimless series of clicking one thing to do another thing and move that thing over to that place. This goes on for several hours before you realise the addictive nature of Civ is still there, but the fun just isn't. It just feels more like a well polished time sink than a game and I haven't bothered to finish a single campaign after starting several.
There are plenty of positive things to say...but they are only things that can be found in the far superior Civ V and I won't praise this game for copying its predecessor.

Hammerwatch is a Dungeon crawler that takes you through 4 levels or “acts”. There are several different classes you can play as. The game feels like a throwback from older 8bit video games, while enjoyable to play occasionally, to try to power through the game was a bit excessive for my tastes (the game play was very repetitive).
There isn’t much of a story, you start the game out separated from your companions because “the bridge is out!” Because you simply couldn’t jump across that stupid bridge you had to wander throughout the four acts for several hours until you get to the last boss. (and at that point, I really hope you got all the planks, or else you’ll need to do it… AGAIN!)
Hammerwatch requires excessive spamming of my forward key (it would work better with a controller, or maybe rebinding the attack keys from the keyboard default). I understand that it’s my own fault for not taking the care to get a controller or rebind the key. But I preferred the default set up. I really got tired of spamming my forward arrow, while kiting around and holding down the space bar to strafe.
After my 10th hour, it stopped being amusing and fun. I only played as the Ranger class; those of you who know me know I like to play Range classes in video games. In Hammerwatch the ranger seems to be rather over powered as well. There are several other classes that are really fun to try out though.
Many dungeon crawlers the dungeon changes shape as you play, or they’re so big you cannot remember where anything else. I found myself getting very bored wandering around trying to get every single thing inside the dungeon. Worse yet; when you play the story mode a second time the dungeon doesn’t change at all. That made “exploring” pretty impossible for me, and finding secret area’s I had missed my first time playing only gives me so much of a thrill. Simply put: I felt like I was grinding, not playing a game.
The achievements are pretty straightforward. I earned all of them aside from two: don’t plan to get the last two “Slay the Lich achievements” until I have help, or I’m really, really bored with time to burn.
The achievements are three categories: 1) Beat the game/boss on _____ Difficulty. 2) Find the secret area. 3) Grind the ____ Amount of NPC’s/Gold. There are good guides in the steam community that assist with the secret areas, which for me was the most work. I had to redo the story mode part of the game Three times.
Hammerwatch’s standard price is $9.99, I really didn’t enjoy playing this game solo that much. I’m sure it’s more fun with friends. I guess $9.99 is a fair price, but I think you can get a better game with more enjoyment out of it for that price. I would skip this game unless you really want to try out new games. My recommendation is to wait for a steam sale before you purchase the game.

Pro’s: The game was a fresh idea, it was fun to play through once and leave it alone. It was very easy on my graphic’s, I could play it on my laptop (most people could probably play it on their phone).
Con’s: The game is very grindy in nature, I was quite tired of spamming my forward key to do attacks, I had to repeat the same story at least three times with no real dynamic differences between the dungeons or NPC’s I fought.
I’m not sure if I should be giving this game a recommended or not recommended. I wouldn’t be telling the truth to say I was unsatisfied with the game. I don’t think that most people will get as much entertainment out of the game as I did, and like I’ve clearly outlined I felt like I was grinding most of my time. I would like to say I’m uncertain which way I lean.

As a person who suffers from depression and has to deal with the hardships on a day to day basis I can honestly say that I am offended that this title is trying to say that it recreates such difficulties in any way. The writing barely skims over daily challenges, makes it seem like therapy and medication are miracle cures, and that depression is just easily overcome. Yes, at the end of the story it says some fluff about this being a lifelong struggle, but the story never delvs into anything more than superficially. It feels as though the warnings of possible triggers were only put in place so that persons who actually suffer from this condition don't see this and point out how absolutely flawed it is.
Putting the subject matter aside, I am offended that this somehow managed to get through Steam's Greenlight program when so many great games do not. This is arguably a game, and it fails on all accounts even when it comes to interactive fiction. The audio is abysmal, coming across as annoying more than saddening, what little graphics are present are blurry and come across more as product placements, and the interactivity is so minute that I felt the need to write this review to get the value from my time spent.
Depression Quest should be avoided, removed from Steam, and the developers should be scolded for ever releasing it.
tl;dr

Linear and poorly written. Only representative of mild depression, yet suggests taking SSRIs, despite the fact that SSRIs  are not recommended or safe for mild depression. The medical advice contained in this game is dangerous, it should contain a disclaimer of references to medical treatment are fictional and hazardous to one's mental health, or make such a disclaimer more visible if it is already present.

I heard about this game from all of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that last few days revolving around its creator.  I was diagnosed with severe depression in high school and went though several anti-depressants and therapists. I'm now in my last semester of college and all is going well but High School was rough on me but mostly on my family.  So, I was thinking that I could possibly be able to relate to this game because of my past experiences.  I could not, this is not a good representation of depression and it is not a good representation of video games, hell it isn't even a game.
Ok, so what is the game?  It is a text based adventure where you are given a set of text and then have to choose a reponse based on that.  These response are in the form of hypertext and this could basically be a webpage and there would be no difference.  Whatever, the actualy gameplay is bland but it is text based, what would you expect?
My core issue here lies in the representation of depression and the way the "adventure" is set up.  So it starts you as a depressed person with not much context as to how you got there.  Then, it throws you in with a cast of characters who seem  to want to help you but no matter what I did my character was constantly in a downward spiral.  It seemed like the creator was under the impression that a depressed person can only be helped by therapy and SSRI's (anti-depressants).  This game perpuates the idea (which is wrong) that all depression can be fixed with drugs and that all depression is basically the same.  This is anything but though truth, there are thousands of factors that can influence depression.  Diet, excersize, lack of vitamin D, getting a blood test to test for lack of SERT (serotonin transporters), or drug abuse.  You do not have the option to explore any of these.  No, you are on a downward spiral and you can't get help to get better.  It is a terrible representation of depression because depression is something that simply can't be represented in a video game.
There are reasons that doctors spent years and years studying depression and mental illnesses because there are millions of factors and millions of solution and possiblities.  This game is not just an embarrassment to video games but to people who are unlucky enough to suffer from depression and or anxiety.  How this game got past greenlight simply blows my mind.  I can not recommend this game at all, to anyone.
If you are suffering from depression, know this, there is help and there are people out there who care about you.  I was lucky enough to have my parents and they are the the primary reason I graduated highschool and made my way into college.  Please to remember,  It gets better, I promise.

EDIT 10/13/2017: Apparently years after its original listing on Steam, the aformentioned modding community is now the official developer with Codebrush gone with the wind?  Idk how any of this happened but it makes a good chunk of this review out of date.  Will come back and touch this up maybe.
EDIT: 10/30/2017 Okay, nothing changed.  Game is still in the pitiful state it was before, with only 1 server that is frequented by the "main guys" still being played.  Its just now the mods are more official than they were before.  Still won't change this to a positive review.
-Developers ditched this early access game to work on another F2P title that they ended up getting sued over for including copyrighted material/parodies.  Before doing so, they added a P2W system and then subsequently removed it after a community backlash.  Honestly, the outfit system could have been done right, but not with these guys at the wheel.
-Another last minute decision, they made the console publicly available.  Where once before, cheaters were not a common sight, the vanilla servers were flooded with constant console cheaters and the game was ruined.  It would have died right here, if not for some of the long time vets putting in effort to mod the game, adding balance updates, unreleased content, and anti cheat functions to the game.
-Unfortunately, because of how the master server worked(ie: it never had modded clients/servers in mind), the improved mod became a huge divide between the already shriveled-up community.  Even more people left after this, leaving only a small chunk of vets to maintain a game that only they would play.
-You can see this small group in the forums, treating the general discussion like its a *chan image board.  I’ve never seen such a pool of toxic degenerates on official Steam discussion.
As for the game itself, you have the aforementioned easily accessible cheats on vanilla.  In both vanilla and modded, the game is heavily centered around stun locking and teaming up on individuals to win.  Before you criticize me for “not being good”, I’m not complaining that this isn’t fair.  I’m saying its just a really dumb design for this genre.  The game plays like a third person MOBA kind of deal.  Teams can consist of 2 to 7 players, and their abilities/combo strings are inescapable in 2v1 situations.  The fighting hybrid aspect of this is lost, as most of the time you die from being put in a bad situation, rather than an individual opponent having skill. I guess that is part of the design, because even the advanced techniques(if you can even call them that) are brain dead easy.  In the vanilla version, Ridika has an infinite combo involving air juggling.  She is by far one of the best characters in FFA matches, because of her escape ability, guard pressure, and for being able to guarantee kills with little to no meter usage.
The game runs in Unreal, and honestly doesn’t need good specs to run.  I am a bit irritated at the graphics options however.  It takes the game from looking appealing on high to washed out play-dough world on medium.  You get no significant performance boost from going all the way to very low, but your eyes will wish you never did.
The community has always been toxic, filled to the brim with a contradictory collection of elitist comp players and casual scrubs.  If you win, they hate you.  If you lose, they hate you.  People would complain about your character choice, regardless of who it is.  You basically cannot enjoy the social qualities of this game.  I assume by now that only veterans exist; judging by the forum posts, you probably only need to worry about elitists at this point.
Card drops are bugged for some players.  You were expected to get 1 card drop for every $10 spent on items in the now nearly empty in game story.  If you bought the early access packs before they were taken off the store, you will have 2 card drops available, but for some they never will drop.  For these users(myself included), they will never get a chance at booster packs, despite technically being eligible for them.
TL_DR: Scummy devs, non existent vanilla community, grumpy toxic modded community, bad game design, card drop glitches.  Stay smart; don't start.

Hot Tin Roof: The Cat that Wore a Fedora is an unfortunate blunder that had a few things going right for it, but a lot of things going wrong. To start, the game has a lot of platforming and physics puzzles which would normally not be an issue but the controls for moving and aiming make them an absolute chore. There’s no map system to assist you with knowing whether you’ve fully explored areas and the lack of fast travel means you have to walk all the way to each locale at a snail’s pace. The gun reloading and custom bullet system is pretty cool but I kept wishing the gun had more than 4 chambers on many an occasion. Solving multiple bullet type puzzles was a real chore since you have to load the chambers the exact right way to have the necessary bullet ready within a moment’s notice.
Sadly even with a seemingly-cozy detective noir aesthetic, Hot Tin Roof fails to land on its feet and becomes yet another forgettable indie title.

Hot Tin Roof: The Cat That Wore A Fedora is a funny little adventure game where you take the role of former firefighter, now Private investigator Emma Jones and her partner Franky (a cat). The game's plot revolves around Emma investigating a chain of criminal activities through out the city. You have to explore the city, find clues, ask people about the case, get a search and/or arrest warrant, collect items, etc. To do all this, you have your trusty revolver which can shoot different types of bullet, i.e. grapple bullets, bubble, knockback, etc. Each has their own unique use in the gameplay.
The world is not too big but interesting. I love how the animals (cats, rats, pigeons, etc.) are members of the society in a way that they are treated almost like people. I mean, we have a cat running for mayor, rats going on bad deals, a pigeon trying to get his life together, etc.
The way the game is presented is good, they give the audience an idea on what kind of game it is.
The graphics is well done (in my opinion anyway). It's not the realistic type of graphic but more of a minecraft block type (but more cartoonish) and that really makes the game more alluring. The colors used are somewhat dim and that compliments the solving mystery vibe of the game.
The sounds used in the game are the classic detective movie music. The ones where a detective enters a bar and a guy is playing a clarinet type of music. This gives that "Im a classic detective" vibe for me.

Gameplay wise, the game only allow you to walk left, right, up, and down. You can also jump and climb stuffs using your revolver. The game as an adventure game also feels like a puzzle, but the easy kind. You have to use your tools in order to progress further. Your health bar is symbolized by a flower in the top left of the screen. Each time you take damage you lose a petal. You have a default of 4 petals and as you progress, you can gain more petals.
There are also dialogue choices present but I find that they give no significant changes in the story, I think they are just there to let you give Emma and Franky some sort of personality. Although some dialogue are funny and from time to time the game makes my giggle. Another thing about this game is to save, you need to use the toilet. This was a very clever mechanic and made me love the game even more.
Now for the bad bits. There was one instance in the game where as I was going down the camera didn't follow my character and so I was unable to see my character. I can still here them walking and jumping but I can't see them. This forced me to load a previous save. Another this with the camera, sometimes it goes crazy. Like it goes left and right, but this is on specific areas.
Additionally, there is a part in the game where you kind of need to grind to earn some bits(currency) in order to purchase some tools but it isnt that much of an issue.
Overall, I give the game an 8/10.

text:
Review for Royal Heroes
Royal Heroes is a casual game with suprisingly great rpg mechanics and progression. It has an impressive array of features that make this game truthfully entertaining and it is very apt to suck you into its easy to use interface and solid strategic mechanics for a casual game.
-------------------------------
Full Review and Features
The following will rate the games mechanics, sound, graphics, replayability, and value for price on a 1 to 10 score.
A score of 1 being do NOT buy the game if you value this feature. 10 being you MUST buy this game if you value this feature.  5 is a completely average score meaning I have no problems with it but at the same time nothing about it impresses me.
Mechanics: 9
This is a simple casual game that really gets itself in front of the rather large and dull pack of casual games on offer.  The premise of the game is direct. You simply hire units, put them in a formation of your choice, and start a battle. You watch your battles commence for the most part as their is no direct control of the armies. However the meat of the game is setting up your armies equipment, skills, squad size and strength, spells, and so on. The strategy comes in on how you set up your formations which will vary based on the types of enemies you will face. Some control of your armies will begin when you obtain mages for your party as they can use AOE (Area Of Effect) spells that you may place on the battlefield for your advantage.
The game gives you the ability to craft weapons, armor, trinkets, and other stuff using a minecraft-esque system of loot management and crafting on a 3 by 3 grid. You can obtain recipies as loot that will show you how to craft a specific type of item, however you can also experiment with your crafting items and learn how to craft items on your own in case you want something before you find a blueprint for it. You can also recycle unwanted gear in the crafting section which will give you a chance to obtain a different peice of equipment that may be more useful.
Once you unlock the mages guild you obtain access to a spellbook, as you unlock more spells and spell slots you can equip any combonation of the spells to your spellbook. As you use the spells in battle they will level up and become stronger. This is highly customizable to your playstyle and allows your mages to take on versatile roles.
The games overworld is setup in a familiar mobile game like style where each level has sub levels where you can obtain 1 to 3 stars based on how long it takes you to defeat the enemy army. Getting three stars will let you obtain more gold and loot. You unlock new levels by defeating all the sub levels in each level. Obtaining 100% of the stars in a level can unlock special levels that are more challenging and will require more strategy on your part to defeat them.
Sound: 6
There is not much to say about the music and effects in this game. The overworld music is rather relaxing and nice. The music in general is high quality for a casual game you won't be wowwed by anything but at the same time there is nothing here that will annoy you or grate on you over time.
Graphics: 7
The graphics are about what you would expect from a casual indie game. The entire feel of the graphics would suggest this game was ported from mobile, or meant to be a mobile game originally. However the graphics do have a certain charm to them. They definitly fit the overall style of the game and there is nothing really to complain about graphically. Some assets get reused a bit too often however there is a decent variety to the types of units you can hire. The amount of units that are fielded at one time in battles gets quite impressive and is a real treat to watch.
Replayability: 9
This is the kind of game that will keep you coming back for more when you are bored. It is easy enough to pick up and play even after an extended period of time away from the game. The game does give some incentive to come back and play again after a day as it will give you goals to complete once in a while that will grant you loot and gold. There are no microtransactions at all which is refreshing for this kind of game. It is great fun wrapped in a neat package.
Value for price: 9
At 2.99 for the content and replayability of this game on the steam platform it is extremely reasonable. You will get hours of entertainment out of this game. This game however does have free versions on websites such as kongregate. However the web version has lower quality graphics and music. It also has less features, updates, and an inferior interface. The 2.99 price in this case is extremely justified. If this game did not have free web versions and they were selling it on steam for 4.99 I would still consider that a very fair value.
Changes from free version
-  Graphical improvements
-  Audio Improvements
-  Mechanic improvements
-  Added features
-  Steam trading cards
-  More frequent patches and updates
-  Very active development staff for Steam platform
-------------------------------
Overall: 8.5
If you are looking for a great casual game to sit back and play frusteration free yet still challenging if you take on its special challenges this is the game for you. If you prefer a deeper and more interactive experience in your combat instead of pre combat strategy then you may want to stay away from this game. I personally highly reccomend this game for anyone who wants something to fill up some spare time, or have a game to casually play while studying, web surfering, or doing meanial tasks. It will keep you entertained but not overly distracted.

First Review ever, so I just thought I'd throw in a few of my thoughts:
Imagine a world wrought with conflict, exploration, and an attractive appeal unlike any other. A world of vast snowy mountains, civil war, and dangerous wildlife. A world where nature itself can be your greatest friend or your worst enemy, and the decision between life and death lies between the choices one makes.
Such is the world of Far Cry 4, the vast, over the top open world first person shooter developed by Ubisoft.
With a sense of adventure unmatchable by many games to have recently come out, Far Cry 4’s diversity of utility and sense of exploration easily make it one of the most enjoyable games of the year. Yet despite this, the lack of direction and focus, along with the confusing narrative aspects of the game, restrict it from being something truly outstanding.
Probably one of the most mixed aspects of the game lies in the story’s plot and characters. It’s a typical, if not cliche, storyline. The player plays as Ajay Ghale, an American of Kirati descent who comes to his parent’s native land of Kyrat to scatter his mother’s ashes. Along the way, he is swept up in a civil war between the country’s charismatic dictator, Pagan Min, and the rebel group which oppose him, the Golden Path.
While one of the positive aspects of the game’s story comes in the form of being able to utilize choice in order to determine the outcome of the story, a negative aspect stems in the lack of clarity that some of these story missions have. There’s not really a sense of explanation about why something happens, such as Ajay’s remarkable ability of suddenly being able to use an elephant as the world’s largest battering ram, and as a result it leaves players muddled and confused.
Furthermore, the inconsistency with the performance of the game’s characters inhibits the flow of the story.
One of the most noticeable would be Pagan Min, the self proclaimed dictator of Kyrat. He is as insane as he is logical, as civilized as he is barbaric, and because of this easily becomes of the most memorable characters within the game. Despite this, he doesn’t get enough screen time to truly flush him out as a character, and his inconsistent appearances truly dampen his amazing qualities.
Fortunately though, regardless of the lack of direction and unclear characters that Far Cry 4 introduces, the massive and jaw dropping world of Kyrat for which the game takes place in more than makes up for these faults.
There’s always so much to do in the fictional landscape, whether that be exploring the snow capped mountains of the Himalayas, hunting in the dense and dangerous forests, or even attacking enemy bases to take for oneself. All of this feeds into the game’s remarkable ability of having these events matter, as the rewards for accomplishing side tasks lead to a more memorable game experience. Pelts taken from hunted animals can be used to craft tools which help aid the character, while money looted from enemy outposts can be used to buy new and more destructive weapons. In fact, many of the off hand missions which don’t necessarily follow the main story are the ones that players end up really remembering.
This transitions well into the game’s online aspect, as cooperative play with friends and competitive
multiplayer carry the same insane, never ending action seen in single player.
These events truly showcase the world of Kyrat which Ubisoft wanted it to be, and what a world it is.
From the mountainous lakes and unpredictable events which occur in the game’s wilderness, to the humble villages and simple tribesmen who inhabit the land, the world of Kyrat is not only memorable because it’s gorgeous, but because it’s a living and breathing embodiment of the game’s uncivilized spirit.

All in all, Far Cry 4 is one of the more enjoyable games to come out this winter.
Despite the inconsistent qualities within the game's characters and narritive, the colorful and interactive land of Kyrat is an interactive advenure which shouldn't be missed.

This game has the single best diplomacy system I've ever seen in a strategy game. The diplomacy revolves around influence and influence cards. Influence ticks up depending on the resources and research your empire has aquired, and can be spent on cards such as "negotiate", "annex planet", "protect system". These cards appear in a queue, and every empire has the option of spending influence to snag the card for themself, or to keep it away from someone else. Cards refresh quickly, so keep an eye on the queue if you're playing the diplomacy game. Some cards can be played for immediate effects, such a "protect system" protecting a system from hostile takover for some number of minutes. Other cards, such as "annex planet" require a vote in the galactic senate before they can take effect. Each empire can then play cards for or against the proposition. "negotiate" simply provides direct support or opposition, while cards like "rhetoric" have a greater magniture of support or opposition, but provide benefits to anyone who takes your side. This can lead to interesting situations where two empires you really don't care about are duking it out in the galactic senate, but you want to get in on the action to get the benefit of a "rhetoric" or "bribe" card. Overall, the system is fun, and gives diplomacy some real teeth, without it being overpowered.
Another system that is done very well is the economy. Every planet has a core resource that it can export to other planets, and every planet needs resources to grow and level up. Some resources need a certain level planet to be utilized. So the economy game revolves around creating chains of trade to funnel the right resources to the right planets. It's very steamlined, and provides tangible effects without much micromanagement. Additionally, most resources have secondary effects that can interact without other resources. So while it's easy to just get a planet up to a high level by giving it whatever it needs, you may want to save that grain for your homeworld, and find some fish for your asteroid mining planet. On the downside, the game currently lacks any kind of filter mechanic, so it can be difficult to find that one resource you're looking for in the late game. This being an alpha/beta game, I expect the issue to be resolved before launch.
The two systems that are still farily lackluster are research and ship design. While the core mechanics of ship design are great, the game currently lacks enough variety in ship parts to make it really interesting. This ties in with the very small number of research options. Interviews from before early access seemed to indicate that the research system is still in a very early stage. However, the devs are very genuine in their desire to make a great game, and I have no concern that these features will be fleshed out significantly before release.

A beautiful and very atmospheric game. It combines photo-realistic imagery with subliminal flashes of scenes, characters, objects, etc. that remain imprinted on the back of your eyes long after they have presented themselves on the screen. If you looked up examples of games that personify and exhude the emotion of "melancholy", this would be at the top of the list. Everything is dark, gray, dreary, much like the UK's weather, indeed it takes place there (London, I believe). Everything is muted save for the interesting and visceral color schemes of the "other side" and the blood that is inevitably spilled by one character or another. The themes are adult, dealing with murder and suicide as well as the Susan aka The Cat Lady's ongoing depression. At times the visuals are like a bad acid trip or something out of a mad artist's dabblings in an Adult Swim commercial, "wrong" in a couple of ways yet at the same time...interesting.
The music and sound effects are always on par, setting the chilling and thrilling or grimly determined tone of the scene to be played out. The controls take some getting used to (Enter to select a prompt, and down key to access your inventory) but that's neither here nor there. There are quite a few ways to take this story and the choices you have concerning dialogue can take your character quite a few ways, even if in the end it doesn't ultimately amount to much save for a few key spots, but I can't complain about that.
Susan, the main character, is someone that I know will stick with me long after I have finished this game. Not only because of her unbreakable spirit, or perhaps petty defiance in the face of everything, but because I have also been touched by depression and this game perfectly reflects how I sometimes still view the world: Shifting, blurry, rough around the edges with mechanical people that you'd rather not deal with and little to no color or pleasures to seek out and revel in.
I highly recommend this game based on the story it has to tell and the method that it is told, namely with the soundtrack, characters, ideas expressed and executed, and of course the visuals.

This game was not only satisfying, but very deep and thought provoking at times which is something I don't often expect in games that aren't made by well-known people. The atmosphere is great, the art style is a nice change and it's so simple. The puzzles are odd at times but it's nothing that is impossible to solve. Just search everything twice and attempt an item on everything and you'll do just fine. My only critique would be that, for a game that seems to center around making your own choices (seen throughout the achievements and conflicts in game), your choices don't seem to have any real consequences or impact. Which is a real shame because it made the game seem a lot less like I had control and more like it was playing itself at times. I'd give it a 4/5 and do highly recommend it to those who like the... dark and grotesque side of humanity.

So, i'm writing a review because the game keeps on pestering me to do so, between one match and the other. Probably because the developers think that if i'm playing it i'm obviously enjoying it, right?
No, not at all.
First things first. The game still has stability problems, meaning that it crashes, some times often, other times rarely, but it's still really annoying when it happens. Recently they changed the questing system (through which you gain gold to buy booster packs) so that roughly 80% of the quests are for versus pvp only, whereas before it was a bunch of generic quests that you could do in pvp or pve since they required specific decks to complete them, and that's it.
Not only this is a butchered version of magic the gathering, with mythic rares limited to one copy and most rares limited to less than 3 too, a lot of cards are missing altogether. It's like playing limited all the time, which is not bad per se, but after a while it gets boring (i can't bring myself to play more than 3-4 matches at a time, and i often switch decks to try to keep things interesting).
I guess my biggest frustration is that this game could be so much more. Yes, i know there's MTG online out there and yes, i know that this has to be different because people spent loads of money on virtual cards on the other one. But then why does this thing exist? Why does MTG online still has an awful graphic quality compared to this one? Why don't they just merge the two into a decent game capable of competing with the other online card games? Just to be clear i dislike all the current alternatives, namely casualstone and similar ones; i'm a devoted mtg fan, but this is just not enough.
All in all, if you want to play without spending money i guess this is a good compromise.

Thief is not just a game, its an experience of the dark and there have been none more darker themes for a Thief game than this one. A city in terror, penetrated with a disease, greedy merchants, sinister politics, scared guards and a traumatized Garrett, there are only questions and so few answers.
GamePlay - 4/5
Thief plays like any other Thief game, a true stealth experience (and it is intended to be played that way). There are shadows and enough of them to get past guards, pick pockets, complete goals without getting spotted. It's in this gameplay that Thief fans and stealth players will find maximum satisfaction. At time, you will need to knock them out or kill them but it is not necessary since Garrett is not a killer. There are multiple ways to approach the goals and Garrett is free to choose the path he wants. It highly satisfying when you stumble upon a secret path to your goal. Upgrades and weapons are available from dealers around the town.
The best feature I like is lockpicking. Just turn off the damn assist and you will know how thievy you will feel picking locks. Its one of the best lock picking I have seen in games. (The fingers move ever so slightly letting you know when to click, its a satisfying experience)
Jumping, climbing is context sensitive and Garrett cannot climb places which the devs do not allow. In my gameplay this was not a big issue but might not provide the freedom which certain players want to enjoy.
Garrett has the ability to "Swoosh" for a short distance which is a quick dash through the shadows. The feature has been cleverly implemented and swooshing over noisy surfaces will get you heard/spotted. Players will definitely use this a lot.
The problem for a few people will arise from the map and navigating the city since it is very confusing at first (If Waypoints are OFF). I had a hard time figuring it out for the first 2 chapters, now I have a hang of it and I know The City, all exits, entries and secret paths to tranverse between various parts. Once I figured out The city, I felt that the devs did this in order to provide the player a sense of being lost and discovering the city by themselves, but still the map is not implemented well (no reference points to orient the players).
Graphics - 5/5
This game is eye candy. I have played it on PC with Very High Settings and it has top notch graphics. The dark shadows, lighting of lamps, night sky, Garrett's clothes, in-game textures are all well done. However, it is a dark game and most colors seen are grey and black, it just adds to how dark themed this game is.
Story - 3.5/5
The story (without spoilers) is mostly about a disease ridden city, an exploitative authority, some supernatural elements and Garrett's confusion. The game has a decent start sequence to throw Garrett in a confused state. There is no clue why things happened the way they are and Garrett is supposed to figure it out. There are foes and friends and the game makes them clear early on. I havent played the entire game, so lets wait for the ending sequence.
Environments/Discovery - 4/5
The environments are superb. There are hidden passages, underground tombs, rooftops (sort of) etc. The game shines when you find these secrets. The experience is exhilarating, Thief is about discovery. It is game for the patient so take time to look at the environments, they are your friend.
Try to find the side missions, they are extremely satisfying and provide great additional gameplay besides the main story. Also, the more gold you earn, it is good for getting upgrades.
One thing where I believe Thief misses out is populating the city. You will hardly run into people in the city. I understand its a diseased place but the city should have more people. It just feels that something has been stolen from the Thief :)
Music/Sound/Voice Acting - 4/5
Sounds are an integral part of any modern day game and Thief does a great job at this. The music stays low and slow as Garrett sneaks through the shadows but as tension mounts, guards discover and chase Garrett. the music picks up and adds on to that excitement superbly. You run through the streets, climb ladders and try to evade them, its an intense feeling. As you discover secrets, a satisfying chime adds to your accomplishment. In the dark corridors of tombs, the sounds are murkier and deathly. Voice acting in this game is just fine, I would have liked better voice acting specially for Garrett. The villain in the game does a far better job. NPC dialogues are best ignored, they can be absurd as well as astonishing at times.
Overall, it is a superb Thief game and I am loving every moment of playing it. There are moments where the AI is not upto the mark, but it does a decent job of keeping you on your toes. I would advise to play this game on Master difficulty with Lockpicking and waypoints OFF. I bought this game on Steam for $14.41 on sale, its worth much more than that.
Note: The game can be approached with a lethal way of killing everyone but it is not recommended since Garrett is neither very agile nor skillful at wielding blades, also it spoils the experience of the darkness.

GRAPHICS- Absolutely freaking beautiful. Very gloomy setting to the game. With graphical settings on high, this game is most definitely eye candy. Only one issue with this and it just involves video quality and rendering at one of the cutscenes towards the end of the game. It appears to me that it is just the result of rushing the scene for whatever reason. It caught my eye and I'm betting I'm not alone. Otherwise flawless and fantastic experience.
GAMEPLAY- Very responsive controls with a gamepad, no problems whatsoever. Engaging combat system which allows you to map inventory as you like, small upgrade system, just enough to keep you out of any customization menus for too long  and allows you to focus more on your creeping skills.
STORYLINE- Interesting story that kept me grinding to see what was next( a good 20 hours even without secondary quests, no complaints here (although I cannot compare this with previous Thief titles as this is the first I've played). Regardless, i thought the game in itself did an extremely good job of morphing many story cutscenes directly into gaps of gameplay.
UPDATES/SUPPORT- I know there was a save game problem due to a technical problem with time zones a little while back but the devs were quick to fix this problem and that is the mark of a good team. No problems I am aware of since that.
OVERALL- To wrap it up, this game is definitely one to check out and not let slip through your fingers. I would recommend to everyone who loves: a good story, beautiful graphics, sneaking around, killing things, sneaking around, shooting arrows, blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up, burning♥♥♥♥♥♥ sneaking around, putting out candles, peeping through keyholes, picking locks, lifting loot while being sneaky, the dark, breaking bottles, and ummm...sneaking around ;)  Great Game, highly suggest checking it out.

I would recommend this game to people who have already played and enjoyed PB's previous games in the Gothic or Risen series. This is probably not a good place for newcomers to get introduced to the studio's unique style of RPGs.
Risen 2 could have been so much more. For every step forward from the excellent Risen, there are several steps back. Combat, while functional, is clunkier than it should be and plays like a low rent version of The Witcher 2's combat. Parts of the game seem unfinished—some of the skills, like the promising monkey training and intimidation skills, are poorly implemented into the game. Worse of all, the dialogue and character animations seem like they came out of a game from the 90s.
So why the recommendation? For all its faults, Risen 2 still manages to capture what makes PB's games so enjoyable. Few developers craft such lush, believable worlds that are fun and rewarding to explore. While there are a ton of quests of varying quality, the game really shines when the player is just exploring new areas, with the danger of coming across enemies more powerful than you.
Unfortunately, technical issues still plague this game. Nvidia users are advised to uninstall any 3D Vision components, as it's been known to mess with framerates. Also, a simple "Anti Warp" mod is needed to fix the awful and emersion-breaking foliage warping problems.

Hammerwatch is a very modern version of Gauntlet under the pixel graphics, and is just as challenging without the dumb "always needing food" mechanic that the old arcade Gauntlet used to coax more quarters out of players. There's a campaign mode, survival mode, and a mode that is sort of like a tower defense, but the game supports custom content, so it really doesn't end there. Hammerwatch supports couch co-op (so it's an excellent Steam Machine candidate) and online co-op.
The classes are: Warrior, Wizard, Archer, Warlock and Thief. They all have their own upgrades that can be purchased in the various modes that improve their specialities, such as the Thief earning more money to use for skills, and the Warrior being able to upgrade their projectile blocking radius. Character upgrades persist through a campaign, but when a new campaign is started players start from scratch. The average campaign time is a few hours, and progress can be saved mid-campaign and resumed later.
The game is fun as a single player game, but it's at its best when when friends are involved. Any group of players looking for a modern, challenging Gauntlet with a couple of modern mechanics should look no further!

When deciding on whether or not to buy Hammerwatch, you need to be clear on what it is. Because for what it is and what it does, it does well. It's an achievement hunter game. You want to get it for cheap and then grind it out for some rare achievements and steam levels, maybe some steam trading cards. It does deliver there, as you can relatively easily obtain the (at the moment) 0,09% achievement.
First, if you don't have a gamepad I would strongly recommend either getting one for Hammerwatch, or just not pick up the game. It's not a necessity, but the quality of your time is seriously lowered with a keyboard and mouse.
Secondly, where the game starts to fall short is in the actual gameplay aspects. There is very little replayability as it's the same dungeon, same enemies in the same places every time. That in of itself isn't necessarily damning, but seeing as how you do the exact same strafing and shooting for every enemy all game long, you will get bored. It's the same even with the other classes, as you quickly find "the way" to abuse the non-existing AI, and after that you just do that ad nauseum for the next couple of hours. There are not enough skills or abilities to make you feel like you're accomplishing anything, and there's no diversity in enemies, puzzles or dungeon design to keep you interested.
The music and sound effects are fairly good, but way too short, few and repetetive for prolonged gameplay. During my grind for kills and gold, I turned the music and effects off entirely in favour of my own playlist.
The difficulty depends on which class you play, with the archer being the easiest and probably paladin the hardest simply due to being melee. Setting the game from medium to hard doesn't really matter, it's negligible. Playing the archer, I'd put the game at medium going on easy. There are a couple of hairy situations that you can find yourself in, and the Lich level can get frustratingly unfair at times, but doing dungeon runs you'll mostly be spamming your shoot key all the way between bosses, maybe racking up a couple of deaths due to losing patience or focus. You get tons of lives though, so there's no risk of ever actually running out entirely, and there's an all too easy way of cheating the death counter by just exiting and reloading if you're dying.
Finally, when it comes to the achievement hunting itself, be aware that the game is unstable to the point of crashing and ruining entire attempts. You can tell when it starts to slow down and lag, eventually insta-closing with an error message window popping up. Doing the crystal lich achievement on hard I had too many enemies activated at the same time with the lich at about 50% hp and it killed a sure win, which really soured my opinion of it.
You can definitively get all achievements in two dungeon runs and two lich runs, clocking out at perhaps 20 hours if you're doing all secrets and figuring stuff out as you go along. I went four dungeon runs and did a whole lot of lich fighting, as well as doing the soul crushing grind achievements, clocking out at 69 hours.
I would not recommend Hammerwatch to your casual gamer, your hardcore powergamer looking for a bullet hell or insane roguelike. I would barely recommend it for completionists who want the rarest achievements. Barely. The 1 million gold and 250k kills achievements aren't hard to get, they just take hours upon hours of mind destroying grinding to reach. If the game is on sale, and if you can get a couple of friends to play it with, you could pick it up when it's on sale and you have a couple of hours to laugh away with crazy antics.
That, however, is not good enough to warrant a recommendation from me.

The music was also very good! I'll be listening to some of the soundtrack later to get what was going on, but, going with the nasty looks, the music has some weird sounds and modulations going on. And it also sounds good, with a great rap song in the credits.
The gameplay itself, for me, is the weak point. I mean, it's okay, for the most part. Some of the sections were somewhat frustrating, since you move slowly and rather imprecisely... if there are enemies around, you may make a mistake and have to restart the section. The checkpoints are very frequent, but since there's absolutely no variation to the gameplay, any repetition is too much... Not too much of a problem, honestly.
You go from scene to scene, each a short, self-contained puzzle. They're mostly linear and you don't really have much choice in the matter, so you'll go through the interactable objects in order and get things done.
Didn't get much out of the story either. Maybe other people disagree?

After seeing the Gamespot feature of this title pitted against Bethesda's Dishonored, one would have an uneasy feeling of having invested on the title. I was a bit conflicted to say the least - I loved the time I spent being Corvo, and honestly speaking it was one of the few stealth titles that I got really immersed in. On the other end, Garrett, the master thief is also an icon to be recognized - he is the hero of the game series that built the foundations of the stealth genre. How could a reboot of the classic title for the the current generations gaming not stay faithful to the original? A bleak picture was already painted for me before even getting a chance play it.
But we play on. Maybe at this point, what I really want to say is: take everything you read and hear about with a grain of salt. I know Gamespot is an authority when it comes to games but the best judge is still yourself. (Or putting it more humorously, I already bought the damn game, what other choice do I have but playing it?)
Lo and behold, some of the things I watched and read were dispelled once I started playing. Let me first tackle the four points where Gamespot compared this title to Dishonored:
1) Authentic World: Both worlds are beautiful. While Dishonored does a great job of utilizing the Steam Punk overlay on a Victorian inspired city, I wouldn't really say that Thief doesn't do an equally good job by creating the The City more realistically. The gloom-stricken city of Thief is as beautiful in its own foggy London town way. The shadows around the corners and the residents' whispers are both functional and gripping, if you care to listen intently. Details were worked on well and this is coming from a player using a low setting laptop, as the GPU capability is quite gimped. The only losing points of Thief is the loading time and the navigation aspect. Continuity, which is technically the end product of both is not as preserved as Dishonored.
2) Creative Choice: Ah this one is a pickle. Dishonored really packed the title with a lot of choice from freedom of movement to the tools and magic the character can make use of. Thief doesn't have this full luxury of this but if you think about it really, being a thief with a limited set of tools and somewhat contract driven, I would have to say the limitation is the very challenge the game offers. The game obviously is single minded as a thief should be - you have something to steal, and too much freedom of choice can become the master thief's undoing.
3) A City Under Chaos: Gamespot says that Thief's City is somewhat under populated for you to feel the Chaos ensuing. I can't really say much for this point as I've only reached the fourth chapter. I haven't seen the full extent of any riots or street fights, if the narrative turns to those events. But the lack of population save for the patrols of the City Watch and underworld gangs should actually serve as reminder to the player that you are a sore thumb in all that is happening. Here is a city under lockdown - and save for the occasional hanging, a ♥♥♥♥♥ displaying her goods, gloom victims, and bystanders - the streets should really be empty. The emptiness of the streets evokes loneliness and a certain level of dread.
4) First Person Immersion: Garrett's gloves look really fetching, don't you think? Kidding aside, Thief manages to do an excellent experience in my opinion. The stealth aspect is laid out more in detailed compared to Dishonored. And the way Garrett interacts with objects like Windows and Frames make for an authentic experience. However, it can be overdone, and I would have to agree with Gamespot, as it makes for a redundant experience in some cases. (How different will be this window to the one on the next rooftop really?) The Swoop is a really neat move for the character as it makes you feel really sneaky. Aside from the physical hindrances I've mentioned in Creative choices, I really can't complain much about the way the first-person design was developed for this game.
To me, the game is really beautiful in its own respect. While I haven't completed it, I would have to say that still offers the kick that it should for a stealth title. Dishonored, to me, is a slightly different animal. The things Gamespot mentioned that are the losing points of Thief should be inspected in a more positive view, as the lack or absence of some freedoms and features offer the challenge or flavor the title needs. I can't say much for the story yet but so far the journey has been immersing. One of the best features, I think, would be the custom difficulty setting of the game. You can pump the highest difficulty setting of the game with truckloads of additional restrictions to really test your skills. I believe that limitations drive your creativity further, and in a sense creates an atmosphere that being an infamous master thief is a hard life underneath all that stolen glitter and gold.

Thief is the fourth installment in the classic "Thief" series of video games. The franchise has been known for its outstanding contributions to the stealth genre and is favourably remembered by the majority of the gaming community. Thief, rather than serving as a sequel, is a reboot for the series. This is a new start for the series, and it should be stated that the purpose of this game is to reinvent the series for the new generation, rather than build on the successful formulas used in Thief, Thief II and Thief: Deadly Shadows. This game shouldn't be compared to previous titles; with that said, in this review, I will treat Thief as a completely new game and will not judge it based on earlier titles in the series.
Thief lets the player play as Garrett; Master Thief and one-liner delivering badass. He's been in the trade of stealing goods for years, and the game opens with Garrett on a job that almost immediately gives him a "bad feeling". This provides a set-up for the events of the game, most of which doesn't make a lot of sense from a writing point of view, and leaves the player feeling confused and a bit disappointed with the lacklustre and muddled story.
Fortunately, the actual gameplay in Thief is far better. You can crouch, sprint, walk, scale wales, climb ropes and peek around corners, all of which feels really fluid and genuinely makes you feel like a trained thief. Hiding in the shadows gives you the best advantage over roaming enemies like Guards, and you can also use the 'swoop' ability to fly from one shadow to the next without being spotted. You can also climb walls and certain objects to obtain a higher vantage point over your enemies. These enemies can also be distracted with a variety of tools such as water arrows, fire arrows, rope arrows, smoke bombs, and small breakable glass objects. This all makes for a diverse stealth experience and really sells the role of being a Master Thief.
However, the level design of the game often makes it difficult for the player to fully embrace these options. Level design is often linear and constrictive, and often misleads the player by being inconsistent with climbable and non-climbable objects. The level design is repetitive and somewhat bland, and doesn't really allow the player to be adventurous or explorative. The only exploration to be found in the game is the constant scavenge for loot, which while fun, doesn't make up for the overall limiting design.
Additionally, enemy AI is also quite poor. Guards sometimes spot you from a fair distance away, and sometimes they fail to spot you even when you are two feet away. This kind of inconsistency feels frustrating and lazy, especially from developers who are known for producing excellent games like Deus Ex: Human Revolution, which didn't feature any of this laziness or inconsistent level design and technical flaws.
With that being said, I really did enjoy this game. It has beautiful visuals, and the lighting effects look fantastic on any graphics setting. The game was a very enjoyable stealth experience, despite the lack of innovation, and offers loads of replay value and additional challenges beyond the short 7-hour campaign. Pick up this game if you like a decent stealth game reminiscent of Dishonored, although lacking the polish. This game deserves a solid score of 7.5 / 10.

The Yawhg is a game of stories, stories that the player travels through randomly, forever hoping that they will survive the eponymous disaster.
I shall not beat around the bush here. The gameplay in The Yawhg is incredibly minimal, with the only real player input being what actions the characters take during the six week ingame cycle. The game instead focuses heavily on the story and world interactions your choices create.
The in depth details in The Yawhg are astounding with many in-game events big and small, hidden in obscure event pathways, based entirely on the skills you have bult up for your characters.
But because of skill and day limitations it may become extremely tiresome for many players to try and see some of the Yawhgs more inner secrets, as they may accidentally trigger a event to occur earlier than they wished, or even a different event than what is wished for to occur.
The main thing to keep in mind though when purchasing this game is this: Do you have any friends who live near you?
If yes then The Yawhg is a great game to play as its couch co-op focus can make for a fun and eventful time. If not and you also have no means of streaming events to friends and playing that way, you will find yourself playing a game for four on your ownsome, and as fun as the game can be, playing it by yourself can be a very tiresome experience.
Basically buy this game if you like fun storytelling and have friends.
