This War of Mine is a survival game made by 11 bit studios, who used to be known mainly thanks to the Anomaly series ("tower offence" games). This time they went with something completely different, as you'll have to get into lives of people who try to survive in partially destroyed house, in the middle of a war zone.
To survive all the terror outside your house, you have to keep people in healthy state (to the extent possible) - you have to fight their hunger, thirst and depressions, but also keep them prepared for raids - being armed is helpful. From morning to evening, you'll be taking care of all basic needs of your characters by reasonable use of your collected resources like herbs, meat, wood and metal. It may seem complex but the whole crafting system is pretty simple and there isn't a huge amount of items you can have; you'll get known of most items in first hours. But where you'll get all those important resources? At the beginning, you'll find them in the ruined house you try to live in, but sooner or later you have to send out your characters to scavenge the other houses during the night.
That's the phase where the game swaps from resource management to 2D stealth game, where the whole outcome is only up to you. You can try to rob army deserters, or you can be afraid of them and rather pick the house where ill and old people live. But what will you do if somebody finds you and protects their property? There comes the important part of This War of Mine - all your scavenging brings even more depression to all characters that you control. Even though they have pretty limited amount of dialogues among themselves, you'll still feel the emotional press coming from your actions. Let's say that you won't mind killing other people for food - congratulations, character who kills will get truly depressed and other will be disgusted of him. And what if you don't kill? Congratulations, character will feel depressed because of stealing other people's things, and other will also get disgusted. Or you can just let them die, if you feel that's the better option.
Graphic style of the game is a great one, it doesn't require a strong hardware to play it since it's a combination of 3D models and drawn textures and effects with a really specific style (
). Low HW requirement is also the positive fact for players not just on Steam, as This War of Mine is also ported for mobile platforms (Android, iOS) - that seems obvious from the controls, as they are really touch-friendly, maybe too much for PC standards. All movement is done just by clicking to a specific place, and all actions are done by clicking on small icons over every object that you can interact with.
This War of Mine isn't overall much complex and isn't even long (few hours for a single scenario is enough), but the game's quality tops at the atmosphere and story based on despair. You may think that you can survive without hurting others (somehow) but you'll be forced to compromise pretty soon. There's no good way, there's only "wrong" and "somehow lesser wrong" way, but at least you can manage to survive the war.

I understand why this game has mixed reviews.
CONS:
1.  First the worst part of the game: the combat mechanics.  Clunky and frustrating, but can be 'finessed' by levelling up your Blades skill and getting used to the controls.  (It's also much easier once you can bring a companion.)
2.  Boring Game Design:  I understand why game designers want to prevent grinding, but gameplay and atmosphere suffer when there's little to no monster regeneration.  Clear a map and all of a sudden this once dangerous jungle is now...  empty.  Six days later- still empty.  Better game design would've been to regenerate the creatures and lower the amount of experience you get.
3.  Unbalanced Game Design: My favorite part of a RPG is getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked at the beginning and slowly becoming stronger- better skills, better armor, etc.  The beginning was hard, exploration was fun, keeping track of locked chests to return to unlock later- great, but pretty early on, I acquired 90% of the equipment that I used for the entire game.  Boring.  Chest after chest and nothing good.  Tons of gold, jade, gems- but you didn't need it.  No skills that you were dying to upgrade.  No equipment to save up for.  Nobody wants to finish a RPG with 10,000,000,000 gold and 99 health potions, but it happens.  There should always be a struggle- especially towards the end.

You have all these empty crew slots and it wasn't until the very end that I realized that those slots are for DLC characters. Game designers- It's poor game design to put a hint in the game to visit a location that's only available through DLC.  Eff you.

For someone without depression this may be the heaviest hour or so you'll go through. For someone with it, this is the experience of your life across an hour. Except that you don't get to stop when the game is done.
Depression Quest is not fun. What it does do is communicate the experience of depression in a way that makes it feel empathetic to those who suffer from it. There were points during playing it that it felt ripped from my life. It uses words and choices (or lack of) to communicate what feels impossible to verbalize. It's an intelligent example of using the medium to provoke empathy.
It is painful and heartrending. It rings true often and isn't easy to experience. That's important because that's exactly how it should and does feel to be depressed. Play it. Discuss it.

Touching. And while I do not suffer from depression I could certainly empathise with some of the feelings communicated in the game.
I hope it serves to help other people with understanding and dealign with despression.

Quite a short game, only played once so far but I think there are multiple endings. While not a "fun" game (the developer mentions this in the first screen) it was definitely a worthwile experience.
The game doesn't try to impose an understanding of depression, it lets you watch it as your character wrestles with things like socialising and staying motivated. The character goes through a lot of things that are relatable to or are actually happening in my life, which makes the struggle a lot more real. In some parts I could feel the character's frustration (mainly because some of the choices are "blocked" depending on how depressed the character is and understandably so since some actions aren't realistic when depressed) and in other parts I was honestly happy that he was making progress in battling depression.
I like that it helps the player keep their expectations realistic - that people with depression can't just "feel better" or "do something about it" - it shows that the struggle is definitely real.
I'll be playing this a couple more times and try to explore the hesitation and discomfort that comes with having depression.

Simple and decent, the bland interface and slow piano music definitely delivers the whole depression aspect.
I played through twice in one sitting, the first time choosing options that improved the situation, the second time I dragged the character through the dirt.
I felt relieved that the character had improved their life so much by fighting the depression and helping themself and those they interacted with on the first playthrough.
The second time, I felt like ♥♥♥♥ when they lost their grasp on their social life, let his girlfriend give up on him, neglected their job, and lied to people to hide the fact the character is struggling. At the end, I felt really bad they couldn't even give an answer to a simple inquiry into their life.
If you have the patience to watch someone's life improve/fall apart in about an hour, I'd recommend running through this at least once. It's free, and you're reading a dumb game review right now, you clearly have time on your hands.
Accurate and emotional portrayal of the choices and decisions made by a person with mental health problems.

As someone who has experienced depression, I decided to go into this picking the most honest answers I could, as if I was actually IN that situation. Much of what I saw hit very close to home, and the game made me tear up. It's a very simple game that sticks you in the shoes of depression and you walk through the turmoil and turbulence of being stuck in life. The choices in the game are done brilliantly, as while you do have choices in situations, there are choices that you'd like to make, that you are unable to no matter what the choice is or how good it would be for you, which is so like depression that it makes me cry just thinking about it.
I think that games like this are great not just for how it shows what it's like to have it, but to enlighten those that masking emotions is a huge part of it.
This is a bit of a ramble, but these are my thoughts after just playing it, and I hightly recommend it.

This game requires the Rising Tides DLC to be truly worthwhile. It can be fun without it too, but it depends a lot on your expectations and how much you're ready to spend on a game for hours played. Other than that it's basically Civilization V without any of its gameplay perks like interesting and unique leader abilities, or great design of technology and social policy progression.
The DLC makes Beyond Earth stand out as a full-fledged Civ spin-off with its own unique diplomacy system, quest system (better than both Civ IV random events or Civ V city-state questing) and innovative naval play. If you already own this game or are able to find it with a great discount, I recommend only playing it when you can find the Rising Tide DLC with slightly reduced price tag. The vanilla Beyond Earth is not worth 40€.
tl;dr: Buy Rising Tide if you own this game. Skip if you don't.

Compared to what some of the other reviewers had to say, I don't believe that this game is absolute trash; it actually has a lot of different interesting mechanincs as well as a new UI, which feels good considering that the mechanics are similar to its predecent Civ 5. None the less, this game has failed in two different categories, categories that are deemed essential for every Civ game: diplomacy and warfare.
First of all, the diplomacy in this game is absolutely horrendous, and frankly insulting to the casual strategy gamer. The system of interaction with other leaders is based off a 'respect' value system, which depends based on your civ's development in various different categories {culture, military and science as well as others}, but does not matter in any way to help the direction of the game. The AI will tend to nitpick the very littlest of your problems/accomplishments, so as a player, you pretty much end up ignoring all of the AIs' issues with your Civ. {Example: If an alien were to pillage one of your farms, and you had to wait on repairing the farm because the alien were still there, the different AIs would condemn you for being not caring for your territory, which reduces the relationship between the two different powers} Even with the relationship status going up and down, it won't matter, as there seems to be no point to interact with other leaders, who are by the way hopelessly bland.
This would lead towards the military side of things. As you tend to ignore the stupid comments of the other leaders, some of the relations might lead to a sudden declarration of war {there is no denouncing in this game, so you pretty much have no clue when the AI will decide to screw you over}. While the player might then start immediately preparing his defenses as well as armies/navies, the opponent will immediately begin the training of two {or if you're lucky three} little pathetic units to invade your heavely fortified cities. Of course, when they invade, their movements strategies are so terrible that they fall easy prey to your units and citites. But due to there being no care for military, once you destroy one of their units, they panic and then retreat to the outskirts of your territory; this would only end once the AI offers a peace treaty with no strings attached, or she/he believes that the destruction of his/her one unit means that they owe you an incredible amount of resources. As previously stated, due to the crappy diplomacy in the game, these sudden wars as well as there outcomes will happen often.
Like I said, this game has a lot of interesting material, such as the development of your civilization towards a certain ideology related to the alien planet, or even the upgrading system of your units. However, these are overshadowed by the terrible diplomacy and pathetic combat AI, which should have been improved upon with the latest expansion. Unfortunately, the expansion was more for show and only added material instead of improving material.

This is a visual novel in the same style as Monster Loves You. The game involves choosing where to go each turn, then responding to the randomized event that happens there. The event and your response to it will have positive or negative effects on one or more of your character's stats, which in turn influence later events and the end of the game. It's sort of like a dating sim, except instead of trying to get the girl, you're trying to survive the apocalypse.
The music and the writing are top notch, which makes the game a joy to play through several times over. Events are randomized to give the game more replay value, but they also interconnect with each other in surprising and delightful ways, so you're likely to see something new even on your tenth time through the game. Each run only takes about ten minutes, so finishing it multiple times is more fun than frustrating.
Though enjoyable as a solitary experience, the game really shines when used as a party game. Grab a few friends and try to stave off The Yawhg together - or don't, and see if your character can fare better than the others after the apocalypse.

T H E     C A T     L A D Y
.   .   .   Suicide is not the end.
Imagine your life in it's darkest moments, trapped in a bleak, meaningless circle of dead ends and false hope. You wake up every day, only to realize it will be the same as yesterday. Only to realize that the life you have been living for the last ten years means nothing anymore. You have no friends, you have nothing to motivate you, and you have no one to care about you. Happiness now seems like a dark puddle you sometimes see your face in on a rainy day, stripped of any emotion.
You think to yourself:
So, that evening, as you prepare for your last night on this planet, you reflect on your past - who you've hurt, what you regret, the mistakes you made and wanted to change. You come to the conclusion that the world is not meant for you. You are not meant for it. Dying is now your only friend. It tempts you, haunts you, sings to you. You give in once you see the sleeping pills. All thirty four of them. Swallowed. In moments you can no longer see the dim lights of your apartment. You fade, in a blur, out of reality. A moment later, you vanish. You have killed yourself. No one will miss you. No one will care...
. . .But. What if you were offered a second chance? A chance, not to exact revenge on the people you hate most, but to change your very life and it's purpose. What if someone offered you the keys to fulfill what's been missing in your life. To truly find the happiness you once held, long ago, in those brighter, long forgotten days.

You think this over. Question the morality of the offer. What have you got to live for anyway? Why would this... "person", so to speak, even give this type of chance to someone as pathetic as you? As worthless and miserable and unforgiving as you? After all, YOU were the one who took those pills to end the torment and suffering, to be free of the hostile pain that has swelled inside you for so long. Why even bother? Holy ♥♥♥♥ this is one of the most underrated games of all time, I'm dead serious, this is one of the best things to come out of a movie tie in and for it's position, a movie tie in in the 2000's and one by disney of all people, it's simply one of the best.
alright, let me take a breather here and tell you why this small little game would provoke such a responce out of me. this game as I've said befor is a 2000's era movie tie in, usuallly these are compleat shovelware, and, uppon it's release, it was surrounded by shovelware compatriots, crappy one trick games that did nothing new or special, this game, however, DID do something special, be origional. origional story, origional music, origional gameplay.
Treasure Planet: Battle at Procyon is a naval combat simulator set to continue the story told in the movie, Treasure Planet, it follows Jim Hawkins uppon graduation from navel acadamy and into service of the royal navy. a new threat, however, has arrisin in the far reaches of the empire, Ironclads. these formidible ships sail with no sail, leave no trace, and no survivors. it is not up to you, however, to chase these down, you are to report to the admiral and obey your commands, sail the seas and follow through this game's impressive single player storyline. the single player and the story of this game are inseprable as every mission shuttles you through, wasting none of it's time on pointless sidequests or grind. Treasure Planet: Battle at Procyon earns a great recomendation in the singleplayer/story department for it's well designed layouts filled with a impressive amount of unique hazards, obsticles, and beautiful scenery as well for a story put together extrodinarally well I am very impressed.
In the gameplay space, there too is an suprising amount of complexity and a fair ammount of depth. you, yourself don't command a fleet, but rather a flagship that commands the other ships in your armada. this is very unlike other naval combat simulators where you controll the whole fleet from a god's eye perspective. in Treasure Planet: Battle at Procyon, you control a flagship from which you order the fleet under your command around. the controll of your flagship as well as your fleet is where half of the depth and complexity come from, micromanaging is at whatever level you want it at, controll every ships course and plot or just orde them all into a "v" and everything inbetween, it's up to you. movement is nice, ships have momentum and a speed and size determaned turning radius, combat is engaging with a suprining amount of weapons that all function in ther own way with some weapons getting a unique targetable aoe charge. dammage and stat are more that just a healthbar, your ship state and even how well you can operate is fully fleshed out with dammage dependant systems. and even beyond that there is ship and fleet costimization allowing for compleat controll over not just what ship and what guns, but also the crew  and captian itself. a points system is in place with better crew, guns, ships, and fleet size costing more from the sae shared pool, forcing critical thought and disision about your how you wish to play.
the systems, however ahead of their time are by today's standards, above avrage, but for the 2000's? amazing.
the solid gameplay foundation earns an applaud from me. I am impressed with a bonus applaud.
in presentation, there is not much to say but the ui is competent, graphics  themselves may not hold, but the ammount of detail from sea(space)gulls, sea(space)whale, islands decorated with sand, trees, shipwrecks, you know what, now that I think about it, everything is deatailed. all of it, from spaceports to spacegulls, the presentation earns a rating of moderetly impressed to very impressed with towns and spaceports taking a notible exeption and earning a very impressed. (side note, the main menu itself is rather underwhelming, being a vague picture layed behind some high quality buttons)
side-sidenote, the tutorials are topist of top notch for seperated experiencees. (like the tutorial from the origional half-life, where you have to click a menu option to get to it)
in the sound department, everything is a 9 or a 10, music is very fitting and well composed as well as well sounding. voice acting is some of the best I've heard in a while, all of it is very immersive. the enviromeental effects are absoulutly amazing. the blackhole sound effect being one that stands out in my mind, it's encreadably eariy and fitts them to an astounding degree.
ui and menu noises are short and satisfying. I'm very impressed.
multi-player is everything it aimed to be, just perfect. available in lan and internet. shame no-one's online, even so, with many maps, well made bots, and the astounding gameplay to back it up, this mode can afford to live off of it's dm only note. a well made compliment to the main story mode. I'm impressed.
overall, Treasure Planet: Battle at Procyon is not a hyper platnum best of all time revolutionize everything omgomgomg, but is it a gem of outstanding, unbelievable quality and should be a must play and must play again for any hidden jem hunter. I'm very impressed
tl;dr one of, if not the best hidden jem on steam, yes, buy it, even if it's not on sale.

Another free game down.   Review time.
So....Long "Tutorial" on what job you want.   If you're even hired, then you'll think "Okay, I guess there's a job I get to do based on my training.  My training will actually mean something."   .....No.   Dead wrong.  You're an anonymous placeholder that is just along for a ride in a game that barely acknowledges your existence.
It's a game about being part of a manga translating team.....that does no translating, but continues to procrastinate on a project while getting butthurt when someone else chooses to take on the project herself.
The humor is bland, the grammar is bad (Hell, I've proofread a giantess comic before release and even I know this), and the story?  Let's face it....what does a girl in underwear, an undressed bunny girl, a punch-happy girl, a middle-aged con artist, a science nerd, a girl with emoticon faces, and a pointless winged dragon-girl(?) have anything to do with a manga translating team?
It's a fist-full of randomness done in an amateur-ish way that shows an obliterated project scope.   Almost as if saying "I forgot where I was going with this.  But you know what WOULD be funny?..."   It's like ad-lib.....on a day that a college speech is due.  Not a good experience.   Oh, but it wraps up with a "But friendship is what's important" ending all of a sudden....   (BTW, the game is a week long in game-time.  You'll finish in an hour)
To be perfectly honest, I was hoping most of the characters would just die in a fiery explosion given their bland and useless nature.  (Only characters I found engaging were Malia and Valilla)
Pros:
Short
Skip button
Programmed decently as a first attempt at a visual novel
Achievements
Free
Cons:
Bad Grammar
Disjointed and irrelevent story points (The narrator says after each day how useless each day basically is)
Uninteresting characters  (In the end, I really couldn't tell you who's who outside of "Anime girl 1", "Anime girl 2", and anime guy.    I can only name Dex, Alex, Malia, and Valilla from memory.)
I know it's a free game.  I know I sound harsh, but I cannot see how this game was greenlit.  Should the developer continue his...."Story", I suggest he takes a while longer on his....."Manga translation".  It's a nice start....but it does feel slapped together.   I understand "It's not easy to make a game" and I can understand it takes a lot to make a game.  But it just does not feel tested.
If you want achievements, dive right in.   If you want to ignore this review, that's up to you.
If you are looking for an actual story or something that actually has something to do with the end objective and the scope of a project?  AVOID.
2/10   (Generosity for Malia and Valilla.   Without them?  1/10)

This War of Mine is a survival game made by 11 bit studios, who used to be known mainly thanks to the Anomaly series ("tower offence" games). This time they went with something completely different, as you'll have to get into lives of people who try to survive in partially destroyed house, in the middle of a war zone.
To survive all the terror outside your house, you have to keep people in healthy state (to the extent possible) - you have to fight their hunger, thirst and depressions, but also keep them prepared for raids - being armed is helpful. From morning to evening, you'll be taking care of all basic needs of your characters by reasonable use of your collected resources like herbs, meat, wood and metal. It may seem complex but the whole crafting system is pretty simple and there isn't a huge amount of items you can have; you'll get known of most items in first hours. But where you'll get all those important resources? At the beginning, you'll find them in the ruined house you try to live in, but sooner or later you have to send out your characters to scavenge the other houses during the night.
That's the phase where the game swaps from resource management to 2D stealth game, where the whole outcome is only up to you. You can try to rob army deserters, or you can be afraid of them and rather pick the house where ill and old people live. But what will you do if somebody finds you and protects their property? There comes the important part of This War of Mine - all your scavenging brings even more depression to all characters that you control. Even though they have pretty limited amount of dialogues among themselves, you'll still feel the emotional press coming from your actions. Let's say that you won't mind killing other people for food - congratulations, character who kills will get truly depressed and other will be disgusted of him. And what if you don't kill? Congratulations, character will feel depressed because of stealing other people's things, and other will also get disgusted. Or you can just let them die, if you feel that's the better option.
Graphic style of the game is a great one, it doesn't require a strong hardware to play it since it's a combination of 3D models and drawn textures and effects with a really specific style (
). Low HW requirement is also the positive fact for players not just on Steam, as This War of Mine is also ported for mobile platforms (Android, iOS) - that seems obvious from the controls, as they are really touch-friendly, maybe too much for PC standards. All movement is done just by clicking to a specific place, and all actions are done by clicking on small icons over every object that you can interact with.
This War of Mine isn't overall much complex and isn't even long (few hours for a single scenario is enough), but the game's quality tops at the atmosphere and story based on despair. You may think that you can survive without hurting others (somehow) but you'll be forced to compromise pretty soon. There's no good way, there's only "wrong" and "somehow lesser wrong" way, but at least you can manage to survive the war.

Maplestory is an online anime-chibi-styled MMORPG made by Nexon. The game is very widespread and has a cute and colorful design to it. With over 40 classes to choose from, you'll definately find the class you want in there somewhere, with unique classes ranging from Xenon, a cyborg that can dish out quick and powerful hits, to Evan, a magician that fights with the help of a mighty Onyx dragon. Then there's classes that feel...rather similar to one another with the generally same playstyle, such as Bowmasters and Wild Hunters. I find that this game has a lot of replay value, and if you find some friends and a guild, it will be very worth your time to play.
Pros: Many classes to suit yourself with. Cute and colorful graphics and fun platforming. Multiple updates that keep the game going onwards. Lots of customization options, and amazing in-game storyline for an online multiplayer game.
Cons: Very laggy at times if you do not have a very powerful computer. Terrible hackshield that tends to kick innocent players while leaving actual hackers untouched. While there are many classes, many of them have near identical playstyles to one another, and the somewhat shabbily-made tutorials may leave new players confused.

Throwing in with a Piranha Bytes title, at the best of times, is a bit of a crap shoot.  Their games have been plagued from the start with programming issues and frustrating gameplay (like enemies that can just repeat-charge you to death), and yet the stories are consistently engaging, the worlds large and accessible, and the variety of progression rich.
Risen improved SOMEWHAT on the poor combat model of the Gothic franchise and Risen 2 is even more polished.  Taken by itself, it is probably the most beautiful and professional game Piranha Bytes has produced to date (Risen 3 is due out soon) and it's genuinely fun to play.  Skills are extremely varied, from having your own parrot/monkey to do your bidding to various attacks to using guns, rifles and even voodoo; Risen 2 really throws a lot of gameplay options at you and surprisingly doesn't screw up any of them.  My biggest complaint was that if you choose rifles over voodoo there isn't really much in the way of skill progression available, but that's a minor issue.
So to summarize, the game has pleasing visuals, solid gameplay and an interesting story that will take you to multiple islands and require much exploration and adventure to complete.  If you enjoyed Assassin's Creed: Black Flag for the setting you will likely enjoy this game.

I'm quite impressed with this sequel to the highly enjoyable Risen.
Not only have the graphics and controls been improved, but the feeling of freedom and exploration remain in tact. I'm not a huge fan of the pirate setting and quite honestly I prefered the more late medieval setting of the original, but it doesn't really hurt anything and provides an excuse to change up some of the mechanics like replacing crossbows with muskets and magic with voodoo.
What I continue to like about this game and series is that if feels realistic overall, while providing fantasy elements in appropriate quantity that it still feels fantastic. Magic isn't blasted around like it's mundane, and strange creatures like giant crabs and ghouls will assault you between duals with vicious pirates or a hungry jaguar.
The combat system still feels a bit rough, but it's an improvement over the last game. Musket blasts and sword slashes feel like they are hitting and making an impact, but there is still a level of random unavoidable damage from enemy attacks that can frustrate you during combat that feels a bit too fast at times and a bit too glitchy at other times. You will need to save often, because like the original Risen, you'll die from enemy encounters...a lot.
Now of course the most important aspect of a RIsen game is the roleplaying element. So far, I'm happy to say that you'll be running errands, playing people against each other, and choosing factions and training paths as in the first Risen. Because it's a sequel and events were established in the first game, there at first appears to be less choice of your overall direction, but that fades away as the game continues. Allies are made and play a larger role in your adventures this time as well (although they are invincible and hiding behind them during encounters will almost feel like cheating). It does add the illusion of story driven set pieces in an otherwise extremely open-world type adventure.
So far, my overall rating of Risen 2: Dark Waters
♠♠♠♠♠

What is the Yawhg?
It's a terrifying catastrophe that occurs in a medieval city after the entire population attempts unsuccessfully to spell it.
Yahwg.
Yhawg.
Yawgh.

If we follow Sid Meier’s definition of a game as “a series of meaningful choices”, then The Yawhg is indeed the gamiest of all the games. It is all about the choices you make. Still, there might be people out there who will think that there’s not enough, uh, game in this game.
In the end it doesn’t really matter though, I have no problem whatsoever with thinking of this as a “mood piece”. I enjoyed it immensely. Sometimes it is rather straightforward, sometimes it is deliciously dark and twisted. It is an astonishing, unique thing and I am very glad that it is out there.

For those who love an interesting narrative and playing games with friends, the Yawhg offers a unique experience that I have found to be very memborable. While the game can be played alone controlling multiple characters, it is best with friends. There  are some very creative stories within this, that I definitely do not want to spoil. A wonderful soundtrack and gorgeous art complement the 'choose your own adventure' gameplay.
The biggest question for you will be is it worth the price? I have played the game four times now (roughly 30 minutes per playthrough) and have seen some repeated stories (but not always the same outcome!) but have enjoyed every time. The Steam release makes me want to play it again. For such a memborable experience, I say it's definitely worth the price. If you are unsure, how about check out the start of a playthrough (I have one linked below) but don't watch too much, as the best part of this game is experiencing it for yourself!
My friends and I filmed a whole playthrough of the Yawhg, the first episode is available here:
Simply designed yet amazing game. The music, art, and writing are top-notch. Watching events from your own turn unfold in other player's turns can be pretty heartbreaking at times.

Don't pay more than a few dollars for this game. Not only is it about 10 minutes long, it's broken, and froze multiple times. Even if you manage to finish the end is rarely rewarding. Sure, it has mildy clever intereplay between your choices but it is ultimately too repetitive and unoriginal with every playthrough. This should have been a free flashgame. This is the age we live in where pretentiously artistic individuals devalue the medium of gaming by overcharging for shallowness.

The Yawhg looks simple at first, but after a few play sessions, its depths become apparent. There’s a ton of replay value here, and it has amazing potential as a party game. Get The Yawhg if you love storytelling, humor, and a vague sense of foreboding.

What can I say? It is very, very good, but also a brief experience. With a few friends the tales you weave will cause fits of raucous laughter, but they will be short-lived. A play-through takes around 10-30 minutes, and the end phase offers no real-resolution.
A folk music style soundtrack interweaves the basic, but charming presentation of the game. Both are lovely, and compliment one another well.
The Yawhg puts me in a tough place because I really enjoyed it, but I question its worth at $10. I don't usually draw comparisons between price and longevity, but if I paid $10 I can't help thinking I would feel a little let down. There are multiple play-throughs here, but even by the second play you will be seeing the same situations again.
Buy it if you are looking for a fun, memorable experience to play with your friends, and don't mind the longevity issues.

For you youngins, this game was meant to be a spiritual successor to a game known as Alpha Centauri. Alpha Centauri is still an incredible game worth checking out by the way (and that's where the problems begin). This game gets a thumbs down not only for not being able to live up to its progenitor, but also because it fails to live up to its real parent, Civ 5.
Why it doesn't live up to Alpha Centauri:
Alpha Centauri had a functional elevation system, you can even change elevations through terraforming later in the game.
Alpha Centauri had a more robust troop customization system. Units were 'Chassis' that you could add 4 components to making for thousands of potential combos.
Alpha Centauri had a virtues and ethics system that made a little more sense. Rather than pure unlock bonuses, various political philosophies had benifits and drawbacks and colored the ideology of your civ.
The aliens in Alpha Centauri are an actual threat, not only that but their difficulty and agression scales with the progression of the humans based on a pollution mechanic.
Why it doesn't live up to Civ 5:
People have made too big of a deal out of this, but Civ 5 feels more immersive or rather the context is more relatable due to the history. There is always going to be something amusing about Jewish Germans allying Poland that BE will never replicate. That said the personalities, techs and designs of all the civs are so super boring in BE it really made this problem stand out.
The AI seems significantly dumber to me. I had to raise the difficulty higher to get the same level of challenge in BE. This makes no sense to me because Civ is always going to be a much more popular and mainstream game, BE should be MORE challenging not less, for people who love civ and want more.
By far the weirdest problem that BE has vs Civ is the fact that in Civ each type of point you acquire (aside perhaps from strategic resources) has a lot of utility. If you go science, culture, military, money, these resources are always useful and put you on a path to winning the game. Civ is interesting because of the way these different resources can interact. You can leverage your science to focus on culture for example, and this was expanded and refined in the expansions. In BE however there are a number of resources that just plain max out and become useless. Health can't benifit more than a certain cap (unlike hapiness in civ) and the capital resource becomes more useless even though you get exponentially more as the game goes on.
Final Thoughts: What went wrong? I think when it comes to failing as a spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri, this game showed a failure of imagination to look at how to take the creative aspects of that game and bring them into the new Civ formula. It looks like they didn't even bother trying to be faithful to the source material in a lot of key areas, including the aliens and pollution, the elevation mechanics, the ethics system, and most importantly unit customization. It seems whenever they had the opportunity they chose to err on the side of Civ 5 and that resulted in basically everyone agreeing this game was a bad reskin. They aren't wrong.
The more curious question is, if all deference was given to civ 5 how could they possibly fail in that regard? Really the only explanation I can come up with is the Civ formula of expantion packs. Whether it was an intrinsic part of the design plan to wait on developing certain content for expantions, Firaxis genuinely needs more money, time, and player feedback to develop the game further, the designers have gotten complacent in their ability to deliver a half-finished product that can ultimately be fixed through expansions. Players had no patience for this in BE because Alpha Centauri and Civ 5 both already exist and boast a number of features BE clearly just didn't have. I think Firaxis was planning on weathering this criticism like it did with the civ series and hoping that it would iron out the flaws, however with critics panning it, fans hating it, and new people seeing all the negative reviews on the basegame won't even consider buying and expanding it. Their gambit failed and after one expansion it looks like Firaxis won't be speaking about BE again.

It's a MOBA in the very sense of the word.
Teams of 3 (or 2) are pitted against one another in a best out of 5 competition. It's a fight to the death (no respawns, minions or objectives, just 3v3 arena style battle). It has enough dept to keep it interesting (something I don't say lightly) and is still simple and streamlined enough so that it doesn't become an einstein project to get good at it. The control is fluent and easy to get used to, while the champions range from straight forward ones to more complicated ones with a higher learning curve, while all of them remain viable (somewhat).
What's awesome is the business model. You can either play the Free to Play model (which isn't pay to win) and unlock the champions one at a time with in-game currency. You can spend a few bucks to speed up this process if you like, or you can buy the all champions pack for 28 bucks and you'll have them all (including the future releases). It's an exemplary way of doing things that other game devs should look at and learn from.
This game has my compliments.

First off, I should point out that this is a visual novel, not exactly a game, regardless I highly recommend the Fault Milestone series. Playtime (before going back for achievements): 4.6 Hours
That being said, on Fault: Milestone One, I made a claim that you should only buy the game on sale--while I still stand with that opinion on the first one,
Considering the gameplay time is roughly the same and its a continuing of the previous game, the question as to why I would pay $15USD is kind of important so let me try to explain this through my
.
The world of science and magic is still fascinating, and although there were times I felt were awkward science lessons shoved in for the sake of plot, the story about the characters and the overall philosophical questions the games addresses and boils down to is not only beautiful, but uniquely handled and complicated.
The problems faced in this game were so vastly different than what was handled in the last game, yet it still boiled down to what it meant to be human--in a slightly different sense. Less of "what makes a human different than a non-human" and more "what does it
to be human." What does it mean to be in society and to have that society influence you and for you to influence it. Is it inequality if people don't know they're being discriminated against? Is it the place of outsiders to even go into developing places to encourage change?
Fundamental questions that are even so recently being thought about and discussed.
It's truly unique and handled amazingly well.
The characters are dynamic, 3-dimensional, well-rounded, and
and that's all I could ever ask for from a kinetic novel.

Indisputably one of the higher-quality VNs with a genuinely delectable story. The slight touch of thought-provoking philosophy represents itself here as well. Overall, a definite improvement over the first Fault game (which was already impeccable)

I'm not sure I've played an adventure game quite like this one before. Despite a couple of minor bugs and an occasionally clumsy interface, it's one of the most uniquely-presented and interesting games I've played in a long while .. and one that actually lives up to its 'for adults' classification, too. Terrific soundtrack as well. I'm fully on board with whatever this developer chooses to come up with next.

The Cat Lady is an unique experience, it could be considered a point and click adventure game, but the game is entirely controlled by the directional keys on the keyboard: you can move around, interact with the scenery and check your inventory just using these.
The art style is wonderful and very artistic, playing around with black and white scenes with coloured ones to change the mood. The story knows how to mix gore-ish scenes and melancholic, surrealistic ones. The game is long for an indie adventure game and has no filler, every chapter brings something new to the gameplay, one chapter has you just guiding Susan through her house to make her feel better and before you know it another one is an outright homage to LucasArts' Maniac Mansion.
The only thing that bothered me is that later in the game there are some references to the developer's previous game, Downfall, and as I didn't play it I felt a bit confused at first, but it's just a secondary plot line, so it doesn't matter too much to the main story. Downfall is on Steam Greenlight, so vote for it to get a remastered Steam version!
If you like point and click adventure games with a dark atmosphere you NEED to support this

This game is very much worth playing if you enjoy darker games.
One of the best horror games Ive played in a while.
Confused me a little at first but after a few minutes of gameplay I fell in love.
Story line is amazing, and the graphics are just awesome :P

An artistic platformer adventure game that gives us a fresh journey in the form of classic click and point adventure style.
You'll only need the arrows on your keyboard and a spacebar and the enter button.
A graphic interactive novel, Players will play as Susan Ashworth, a 40 year old single woman, dwelling in a flat with local cats and clinically depressed. She is visited by a bizzare figure who suddenly blesses her with a dark ability to rid the world of parasites. Why? How? and Who? That's up to you to discover.
The game is dialog heavy. You'll be reading many subtitles and lots of voices too if you cant keep up. While the voice acting is a bit loose and sometimes lacks the realistic emotion of the current scenario, It's made up by the developing story that unfolds during her adventure. You'll learn about her past. Her current life and even some of her world.
The enviroment illustrated in its own unique way is complimented well with the music soundtrack.
Surrealist images in backgrounds, calm piano fills with grungy guitars and saturated colours amongst the play through give an experince of dream and mystery.
But the most impressive part is the accurate experince of manic depression and suicidal symtoms. Personally, I was moved by the third chapter and impressed that the people behind this must of sat down with people who have been ill before and taken the time to understand how they respond and react with their world. A highly mature game that will push you to think well about mixing items with other items to solve some puzzles. The Cat Lady is a dark and thrilling game that can be enjoying by anyone.

The darkest adventure game I've ever played. It deals with some really heavy stuff... cancer, depression, suicide and of course... death, but what's really impressive is that while also doing all that it manages to remain a really a gripping game, that keeps your attention until the very end. The Cat Lady is all about interpretation, there are dream sequences, some storylines remain completely open and overall a lot of weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ where the explonations aren't fed to the player, and that's the beauty of the whole thing.
The Cat Lady is an adventure game, although not of the point&click type, you control everything whit the keyboard (just a few buttons actually), it seemed weird at first, but it worked perfectly here. The puzzles are mostly easy, so the game is basically closer to an interactive movie like The Walking Dead game, but since the story is as good as it is, I don't see a problem with that. The atmosphere is... Silent Hill-esque... rain, darkness, thick fog combined with misery, torture and lots of gore. I wouldn't exactly call this game horror, but there are quite a few scary moments, mostly achieved by the fantastic sound effects and music.
If it wasn't too obvious until now, I say it here: I was blown away by this game. I didn't expect it, I wasn't waiting years for it, it just happened, I'm definitely looking forward to whatever the devs are doing next though.

The Cat Lady is one of the best adventure genre games I have ever played, and I write as someone who has played a lot of this genre.
This game will not appeal to everyone. The story is based around a suicidal woman who has been overpowered by depression for years. Some reviewes have criticised the game for being depressing, which I would suggest is unfair considering that is the focal point of the story, and as described in the game literature. Rather, this game will appeal to those who enjoy dark and surreal stories. Surreal is the best adjective here as the path the Cat Lady is taken on is by no means ordinary, and the situations and characters she engages with are saturated in a dark surrealism which I found very pleasing.
The second bone of contention may be the format of the game. You control the Cat Lady by using the arrow keys and she moves in 2-dimensional fashion across the screen. For me, this was a perfect choice to represent the flatness of  her dark and depressed world and adds also to the creepy ambience. It is therefore not the same as a conventional point-and-click. In the same comparison, while there is a fair amount of acquiring items and using them to progress, it is not as heavy as the average adventure game, and is far more logical and functional than some games of this genre. That is not to say that solutions are immediately obvious, in fact as the atmosphere is mysterious and quite scary, it was enjoyable to feel fear just walking around to find an item.
The story is very good and the introduction a fantasic way to become accustomed to the game and to be made to feel a little jumpy. The story is surreal as I have said, and is also mysterious. Without risking spoilers, the main story is taken to a satisfying conclusion, however some of the characters, the first one you meet in particular, remain mysterious and give you just enough to hint at what they really are. This is definitely a story and you have to want to absorb it. If you prefer fairly shallow gameplay where you don't have to deeply engage with the story then this is not for you and you will find it unsatisfying - you have to concentrate to join the dots sometimes - and you have to interpret the events and dialogue in the depressed, dark and surreal context intended. It is also dark and adult, the Cat Lady finds herself in several truly horriffic situations. The voice acting is good and I did not feel it ever pulled me out of the game.
A final issue that annoyed some reviewes is that the game does not run in a full widescreen resolution. I do not defend the creators decsion but likewise I did not find it had any negative impact on my immersion or enjoyment.
For me this game was an engaging, dark, and adult creation which I really enjoyed playing. It made a refresing change from token 'comedy' adventure games, or games trying to be 'dark' and completely failing. There are few well made dark adventure games and I think it is just as important to experience dark mature games as light and happy. If you're a little dark yourself and have the depth of character and intelligence to enjoy this kind of story, then you are likely to enjoy this game.

The Cat Lady is simply put..a story of a depressed 40 year old that kills herself. But of course there's a lot more to it than that..otherwise it wouldn't be such a well received game.
The horror elements are very well done. There were things even I have never seen before (and I am a big fan of horror movies/games/the genre in general). In this game you WILL care about the characters you meet and find yourself having a bit of an emotional attachment. This will drive most of the decisions you make.
Now with that being said, this won't be a game everyone will enjoy. There is A LOT of reading involved, and it can be a bit slow at times. There is some nudity, and some sexual themes and vulgar language. Stay away from this if you find that sort of thing offensive..(you're missing out though! ;]). If you're into achievements, this isn't hard to 100%. If you're into stories, then this one has a really good one that you may like. :) Definitely worth the price in my opinion!

On the surface,
seems like a competent enough game. It's a
clone with power-ups, boss-battles, and several types of aliens to destroy. The controls work like they're supposed to, and the game doesn't randomly spaz out or explode into dust if you look at it wrong.
Is it a good game? Nope.
I would go as far to say that this game isn't even as good as the game that inspired it. Let's pretend that it's the year 1978. The funkiest of space-time distortions causes
cabinets to appear in arcades everywhere. I don't doubt that a few people will spend some quarters on this game, for curiousity's sake. But before long, they're going to draw the same conclusion:
This game is boring.
works because it has an interesting concept. Not only are the aliens trying to destroy you with their lasers, they're also rapidly approaching. If you can't destroy everyone, then it's all over. This added dimension gives the game purpose beyond "shoot stuff".
isn't nearly as inspired. It is a little more creative in terms of enemy variety, but that's about it. Without the whole "invasion" element, the game doesn't have any tension.
The lack of tension is apparent from the very start of the game. You're given 13 lives, which is just plain silly. Surprisingly, this doesn't make the game easy. It just means that the difficulty is poorly balanced. The surplus of lives will slip away very quickly due to a combination of lousy hit-box mechanics and frustratingly random enemy-waves. A lot of bullets get thrown around, and your ship isn't all that capable of dodging them. Even if you're familiar with the enemies and their unique qualities, there's always the possibility that a random UFO will appear and mess everything up.
Randomness in an arcade game is not particularly welcome, and this game is a stunning example of why. Whenever you destroy an enemy, there's a tiny percentage of a chance that it'll drop a power-up. If this power-up is something that actually benefits your current situation, then congratulations! Your luck would make lottery winners envious. Most of the power-up weapons are useless, because they don't last longer than a second. If you receive a shield, you probably already cleared most of the wave.
1ups are also randomized because of freakin' course. I mean... seriously? 1ups are always nice to have, but they're supposed to be awarded for specific actions. If their appearance is left entirely to chance, players get the wrong idea. I know that when I receive five or six 1ups in my last game of
, I'll expect to get a similar number in my next game. I develop my play-style around this expectation, and get frustrated when I don't recieve any extra lives. If I wanted to subject myself to the whims of the RNG, I would have played one of the millions of rogue-likes available on Steam.
When all of these negative aspects come together, they result in an incoherent game. Things just sort of happen, and the player gets frustrated trying to figure them all out. This frustration quickly gives way to boredom. Before long, everyone is going back to playing
.

I first picked up this game at a Scholastic book fair when I was about 8 years old, I then spent about a year getting pretty religious about, but then something else inevitably came along and I fell off completely.
Not that long ago I rediscoved this game on Steam, and you know what... it actually holds up pretty good, though both it's age, and it's orgins as a tie-in game to an early 2000s disney movie are really obvious:
- alot of the artwork is terrible, like off-model direct to vhs terrible.
- the voice acting varies, i'm fairly sure the cast is all soundalikes, they all manage the voice part pretty well, but there are a few that stumble on the acting part, no ones great, but some are definitely bad.
- the script seems like it wasn't proof read, at least not very thoroughly, spelling and gramatical errors begin to pop up very early on, though none of them are that egregious.
- by default, the game doesn't allow resolutions above 800x600, you can use modern resolutions by modifying the config files, but the UI was made for lower resolutions and dosen't scale up very well as a result
- the UI, in addition to scaling bad, is also bad. It looks like it was slapped together in less than an hour using a couple of leftover assets. But more importantly it fails to provide basic information; there is no way to determine the firing arc of a weapon other than feeling it out; a selected ship's health values are displayed as three not immediatly obvious meters just off the bottom center of the screen between some camera options and a chat log; unselected ships only display a rough approximation of hull strength in the fleet window, no information relating to weapons or sails are dsiplayed.
- the game's speed is also an issue, often campaign missions will ask the player to travel across the map from point A to point B taking about 2-3 minutes assuming the ship is both very fast and travling at maximum speed, during this period of time absolutely nothing happens. This issue could be corrected if there was some way to change game speed during play, and it would only need to be there for singleplayer, I can't really say anything about pacing in multiplayer, but I assume its fine.
- not that many keybindings, you can cycle through ships or change a ship's speed and thats it, everything else can only be accomplished with mouse clicks.
- unskippable cutscenes, but dialog in cutscenes can be skipped.
- most of these issues and then some would be fixed if the game had a better modding community, there's alot of potential but it dosen't have much of a follow through.
tl/dr: game's good, not great.
- maybe get it if you like AssCreed BlackFlag, but wished it was more strategic/focused/involved.
- must buy if someone manages to mod some anime boat girls in.

In Treasure planet, battle at procyon, you play as an older Jim Hawkins, who decided to stop being a little thug and joined up with the navy he sailed with in the movie. The game gives more depth to the treasure planet universe and, to be honest, is a bloody damn good example of a RTS ship game. You can board and steal enemy ships, set up skirmishes, and play a very well put together campain.
It kills me this game didnt end up a classic in the minds of all gamers. People should scoff at new games and say "Dear god, why couldnt you do what a disney game thats demo was given away for free with kids meals at mcdonalds do, why cant you even manage to be as good as "Battle at Procyon"
In the main game you can only play as the Royal Navy, as jim hawkins, however in skirmishes you can play as any of the three factions (Navy, pirates, or "Procyons" the raccoon like massive military empire that specializes in badass warships) and you can individually construct your fleet and crew with the minutest details under your control.
Just some examples of the things you can have happen in this game, often at random
Lure enemies into a nebula where their sails stop providing energy and they must be tugged out or be left as easy prey.
Steal enemy ships and use their talents to help you win battles.
Stick a "REALLY BIG GUN" on your warship and blow anything within 10 parsecs to a billion pieces, you can fully customize your ships firepower
Defend forts in space and use their guns to aid you
Command everything from a torpedo boat to the impressive Fast Frigate
Get sucked into a black hole and legitimately be scared to death as you watch your ship vanish from reality, or even better, get sucked into a supernova and have the same experience, but on fire
Amelia is back for all the people like me who had a crush on her in the movie! she leads you through the campain
Big ship thinks your torpedo boat is whimpy? knock out its engines (Yes you can target specific places) then launch a line into it and tow its♥♥♥♥♥over to a black hole, or better, to your own fleet and let them ravage it.

Is the game any good?
Short answer - Yes it is.
BUT, the game is plagued by a long history of expectations from previous really good games in this series, and also by troubled development, which makes it much more complicated to talk about. A lot of reviews gave this game a low score, and even though I do understand that point of view partially, I also think it is unfair most of the time.
Why? Well, more on that later.
So what is good about it?
It has very good stealth-mechanics. It has fantastic options for customizing your experience. It looks really great. Movement is smooth. It feels great to sneak, run, jump, and swoop. Good atmosphere in general. Hub-world is quite large and filled with many secrets. Many, really great side-missions. Great voice acting overall.
What is not so good about it?
Story feels unfinished and does not make much sense - it is also really cheesy and out of place. Audio is badly optimized at times. Frequent loading-screens in hub-world break immersion. You need quite a powerful machine to run it well. WEIRD April 1st bug, making it possible to complete the game, because of looping the chapter you are currently at. Bypassed by changing your date on the computer, but WHY???
Control:
Mouse and keyboard is the better experience - and it is excellent . Some controllers have fun rumble feedback, but it is not entirely worth it.
So, why are some reviews unfair?
Because of nostalgia:
Some people have spent so much time into the older games, and they had such a good time playing those games, that they expect exactly the same experience again in later installments.
Reboot-hate (stuck in the past)
You simply can't repeat  an experience - it is not the same game - It is not the same you. The feeling we remember when we played a game the first time is mostly a nostalgic memory, that is probably a little warped from reality. And with that somewhat warped memory we search for the same feeling in the new game, which we never get - hence we become upset.
I see so many reviewers critiquing the game from this angle, and so the critique is not objective in my mind. Instead of objectiviley looking at the game, everything gets judged as bad, because it does not fit the past. and many seemed to have decided in advance to hate the game no matter what it did. Another reason it is judged badly is partially because the game should be played slowly (I think) - Rushing through the game in order to write a quick review, and I think the essence of the game is mostly lost.
Do we really want the game to be the same as the older ones?
I would be really disappointed if they made Thief the same game as before with just better graphics, which I feel a lot of people are asking for.
If that is what you want, I say go play the old games instead. I'm serious. Those games exist here on steam and GoG, they are still great (and MUCH cheaper), and they have tons of mods, updates, and fan made missions that make these games highly enjoyable.
Devs. Damned if they do, damned if they don't.
And, how do you create a game that is both enjoyable for someone who has hundreds of hours invested, and for someone totally new to the series?  It would, for example, not be commercially viable to create a game just for the SMALL devote thief-community. It is also interesting that most players who are not familiar with the older games really like this new Thief.
Is this game a true thief-game?
You hide in the shadows. You can sneak, you can explore, both vertically and horizontally, you have all the interesting arrows and gadgets. The game-mechanics are really good. There is lock-picking (best in the series). The AI chatter is better than ever, even though buggy at times. The atmosphere is very tense, dark and scary. You are weak and vulnerable. There is lots of loot and hidden areas - The game is quite long and re-playable. There is aspects of the supernatural, and the world is kind of steam-punk-medieval.  Sound design is really well made (a part from the bugs), and an integral part of the game.
So, yes, it is absolutely a thief-game.
Problems?
Yes, there are quite a few. The most noticeable one is sound in general. Sure, at times the sound is really great, but it just does not seem to be mixed right. Sometimes you don't hear what you should hear, because something else is too loud. Sometimes you hear NPCs that are not in the same room as you, still as loud as they were right next to you. On occasion the music cuts out which makes you wonder if someone saw you, or something happened.
The guards seem to get stuck sometimes, but there is always a way to get around them if you have your wits around. But then there is also the occasional issue of some NPCs being completely frozen, or "glitching out". None of the problems are game-breaking, a part of the April 1st bug that truly was a mystery. (You were kept in a loop and could not exit the current mission, when you reloaded a save you always started from the beginning.)
What I don't like:
Oh the story... In a way, it seems like they put some real effort into it, and the voice-acting and cut-scenes are nice. But, it also does not seem to head anywhere - Some cut-scenes just did not feel like they fit the situation you were in previously or after.  You get the sensation the story was quickly put together before the deadline, using various ideas all mixed together. You don't care for anyone really.
Also, the occasional 3rd person wall climbing, even though not a problem at all, it just doesn't fit in the game - there is no point for this mechanic either. Also, I wished there could have been a little more space for "inventing your own path". All options on how to finish a task or path, were pretty obvious (to me). For example, you can't just use a rope arrow where you like, only at specific places. Frequent loading screens does break immersion - It becomes mostly apparent when you are trying to reach a specific location. The loading-screen times are not awful, and not too frequent, but I was hoping that it would be a little better, considering that was Deadly Shadow's biggest flaw, and I'm a little surprised it's needed with today's hardware - Aren't there ways to load stuff in the background as you progress? At least there are no loading screens during missions anymore (as in Deadly Shadows).
Verdict:
I say that Thief is a very good game despite its problems. The stealth mechanics, atmosphere and immersion are all fantastic, and the fact that you can highly customize your experience is just icing on the cake. Hopefully patches will come soon to correct the flaws, but the story and direction can't be patched, and it is unfortunately a real mess. But the main mechanics: thieving and sneaking is actually really well done, and the levels are atmospheric and fun, sometimes truly great. The side-missions are really worth your time as well. Then you can of course compete with your friends in terms of how fast you can complete a level, how much loot, knockdowns, ghosting etc. All this clearly makes the game very much worth it.
If the other thief-games did not exist, if we did not compare with our sometimes questionable nostalgia, more would probably see this game as a really good and unique experience. But some people just decided to hate this game no matter what it is - haters are gonna hate I guess.

Sid Meier's Civilization Beyond Earth + Rising Tide DLC
Being a huge fan of space exploration and sci-fi fantasy games, Sid Meier's Civilization Beyond Earth fits my taste perfectly. It has enough new content to feel fresh, while also keeping the familiarities of the series at heart.
+ Gigantic tech web where you can research new upgrades for units and buildings, which grant affinity points. These points further your progress in a particular affinity - purity (human focused), supremacy (machine focused) and harmony (alien focused). Each affinity has unique combat units and a different appearance for said units. With the addition of Rising Tides DLC, you can create hybrid armies with multiple affinities.
+ Many victory conditions exist, from domination to contacting aliens and liberating humans on earth, to name a few - so you'll get multiple playthroughs.
+ The introduction of artifacts and research pods at the beginning of the game is great. Sending explorers to derelict settlemens, sunken colony landers, crashed satellites, alien ruins and more results in the chance to discover rare artifacts. Such items give either an immediate benefit or can be merged with eachother to produce a powerful building schematic.
+ Graphics are good, considering Sid Meier games are typically birds-eye.
+ I really enjoyed the atmosphere of Sid Meier's Civilization Beyond Earth and how this changed between map types. The terrain detail was superb. Depending on the map selected, you'd have desert or tropics, perhaps a frozen ice world scattered with tiny islands. It changed the way you approached the game and how you felt about it. Variety is important to maintaining interest.
+ Another part of Sid Meier's Civilization Beyond Earth that I thoroughly liked were quests. Small decisions which influenced how you built your nation, which resources you acquired and which affinity you would lean towards. Do you choose to eradicate local alien wildlife or study them? There are probably well over 100 of these quest decisions in the game, meaning each new game can take a new direction.
~ Combat between nations is really fun but not very challenging once you've built a foundation for yourself (even on higher difficulties), it's usually the first 100-150 turns which you struggle in.
- Really hard to find any cons with this game. Extremely solid across the board. The one thing I would say is that the highest difficulty tends to result in unrealistic diplomatic backlashes, where it becomes unbearably hard to manage relationships and you have enemies on all fronts. I was really keen to try and finish this game on Apollo after beating every other difficulty, but it's too much of a chore than balanced strategy. The AI bonuses are so huge it's stupid.
Overall Score: 9/10

This is a fantastic game, whether you're a noob or seasoned pro! Between the clear and concise tutorials, gameplay animations, and card information, this is one of the best ways to learn Magic. Magic Duels includes all the best features of the previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, plus a veritable cornucopia (lol) of features the old games lacked, such as: a wider variety of cards, the ability to "buy" booster packs with gold you earn in the game (or actually buy as a microtransaction), online battles with both friends and random opponents, and total control over deck customization. New and interesting gameplay modes in the single player campaigns are also a welcome addition; my favorite so far is Liliana vs. her four demons in the Origins campaign.
I have very few problems with Duels, and most of them relate to the clarity and functionality of the GUI. For example, when assigning blocker order, if numbers appeared next to the creatures as you select them, it would be easier to tell the queue order. When making card selections as part of a spell or ability, I am often confused by the buttons "confirm" vs. "finish", as well as which cards are selected. The specific functionality of each button should be clearer - perhaps "confirm [X cards selected]" and "skip" or "finish without selecting". Also, some visual indication of whose turn it is, besides simply the "opponent's turn"/"your turn" text, would be most welcome, but that's mostly my own laziness talking. Visual shorthand is often more effective in video games than text. I also wish each set had all the cards from its paper counterpart; it seems like that would be extremely simple to do, but it's possible there's a non-public reason to which I'm not privy.
Overall, Magic duels is fun, educational (at least about Magic - though I suppose you could argue for logic and game theory too), well tuned, and highly addictive - just like paper Magic! Quite unlike paper Magic though, Magic Duels is free (and it's tough to beat free)!

Nuclear Dawn is another source engine based mod that made into a full game. And, it is one of the better ones.
First, lets see what is so good in this game. The mechanics are great. The use of weapons feel natural and easy to handle. The arsenal is also acceptable. Core maps are well designed allowing multiple playing styles and tactics to use. The classes felt balanced and competitive against each other. There are some unlockable customization options also which can be used to earn a little bit of advantage, but they are not that much they could ruin the fun. Strategy elements are well implemented requiring a good commander and teamwork.
I also need to mention the worse parts of the game. The content is somewhat less than it would be ideal, but since release the developers made tools to aid the community, just before they abandoned the game for good. But, you can now have some good custom built maps and stuff from workshop. However, now comes the worst aspect of the game, its current playerbase. To be able to play this game ideally, you would need one applicable commander and at least five people in your team. Also, teamwork is necessary for success. Now, when the game has only a minimal amount of regular players you can hardly play a match in normal circumstances. Bots can be deployed in both online and offline play, but they are only half-solution. Also, they cannot control the constructions, so someone will still need to take care of the commander duties.
This game had its time in the competitive multiplayer scene, but it is surely one of those games that should not be forgotten due the amount of fun that it can give those who really spend time and effort to it.

Note: I'm only commenting on the single player. I don't multiplay with strangers and none of my friends have this game.
Background: I loved the Magic: Duels Of The Planeswalkers series that I had on the Xbox 360. I was hoping this would be more of the same. It isn't.
In the previous DotP games, in single player mode you had some control over your deck. The starting card set was usually pretty weak, but you could unlock cards by playing and winning the single player games, so if you found you were getting stuck, you could go back to an easier encounter and grind out some better cards. You could also customize the deck (e.g. go heavy on direct damage and chump blockers to counter an enemy that likes to summon big creatures). None of that is possible here. In single player mode, you're stuck with whatever crappy deck the game gives you. No editing, and no way to grind out better cards. Using these subpar pre-made decks, you get to duel against the CPU which is wielding some of the greatest cheese this side of Wisconsin. Think the Elf deck from the original DotP. That level of cheese.
Honestly, I don't understand why Wizards has made the single player mode such an exercise in frustration. It *is* possible to beat the incredibly slanted odds, but it's pretty clear pretty quick that it's all up to luck and not up to skill. Yes, single player does earn you a few of the in-game "coins", but if I was interested in farming coins, I would have played a random battle against the random CPU with the deck that you get from finishing the tutorial. I just wanted to get a chance to experience the game "lore", but it's not worth the aggravation.
I'll probably keep the game around to play the random CPU battles when I feel like tinkering with a deck, but I doubt I'll ever bother finishing the rest of the story mode. And I'll certainly never give these bozos a nickle of my money.

Context:
• I've only played it with Rising Tide.
• A few days before I bought it I finished playing Civilization V one last time before waiting for Civilization VI.
• After about 60 hours it still seemed new and interesting.
• As I approach 100 hours its flaws are showing.
End of Context, Beginning of Review.
From what I've seen so far I consider CivBE (with RT) to be a deeply flawed game.
There are more ways to customize the way you play, which increases the replayability. There are a lot of ways of approaching the tech tree and I've only scratched the surface of the ways to leverage that.
It's now lost that one-more-turn thing.
There's more going on in each turn than in Civilization V I think. The choices are more challenging, but once you've made them once a replay won't show you anything new nor add much challenge.
One major downside is the diplomacy. The vast majority of the deals clearly aren't value for money. Diplomatic capital is so much more useful for personal traits, but by the time you've filled those up it's doubtful that your opponents will deal with you and it probably won't be clear why not. The diplomacy is a perpetual drivel of stuff you only care about if you either want war to be declared on you or want to avoid it and the politics itself is so one-dimensional that it's pointless. Build up your army to avoid war from the natural aggressors and the others won't deal with you. That's about it in one sentence. The only other way you deal with your neighbours is through trade routes and they are always a significant nett benefit to your opponent. There's no indication of how you're doing compared to them, though they know everything you're doing, which is unfair. In short the diplomacy is pointless, a frustratingly impossible balancing act that's no more complicated than a litteral balancing act, and so not fun that I've started reducing the number of opponents. Maybe then I'll be able to make some sense of it. To make it worse, unlike in Civ V, you meet them all very early in the game because the map sizes are way too small — The 'massive' map seems to me like a below average map.
Now for the dealbreaker, the reason I'll be uninstalling it: I hate the undersized maps. The largest map should be about 8 times the width and height, but instead an opponent can land a quarter of the map width away and they're virtually in your back yard, on a 'massive' map.
I dislike the one dimensional aliens. Either they all like you or they all hate you. Each nest seems to spawn multiple different species of alien, which is scientifically ridiculous. Why would they not make separate nest types? And why do they stop spawning aliens after a while? Also the aliens are a frustrating nuissance from a gameplay perspective – navigating out of a nest area is a huge waste of my time, during which I'll often just hit space because there's no way forward – not exactly deep gameplay.
I like the enhanced exploration.
I love the customisable faction stuff.
I like the movable floating cities. I used one to great effect where it started and then moved it to retask it, but they're a gimmick really.
I like the story elements.
I like the quest decisions and the quest system.
I dislike the balancing. I've loaded up a mod to deal with that, but I've lost interest before I've had time to find out if it's really helped.

This is a classic semi-open world exploration based action RPG in the Gothic/Arcania tradition, except that this time you get gunpowder, voodoo and pirates instead of magic, inquisitors and orcs/demons. The backdrop is nonetheless equally epic (you could interpret all this as the events taking place in a different part of the world of Gothic, somehwat later), and you still get to make significant choices which  influence gameplay based around factions selection. FInally, there are memorable characters with whom you will share many sarcastic conversations.
Two playthroughs are advised, you'll see why!
NB: Some reviewers have complained about the combat system taking a while to get into the flow, and this is understandable. This is partly a Gothic legacy, and partly a reflection of modern RPGs where too many of what should be basic moves are only unlocked gradually throughout the game - presumably because players are otherwise assumed to be bored too easily. The difference is, here it is up to you how urgently you address the matter. If you like fencing, then you need to work on it. This is one of the reasons I suggested two playthroughs. In one, focus on muskets and thievery/exploration and side with the inquisition you begin with. In the other, side with the ... um, other guys, and focus on their special voodoo secret sauce and swordplay.
