"The Cat Lady" does two remarcable things: it manages to turn a horror-themed game, filled with ghosts, corpses and psychopatic killers into a heart-warming experience, and it does it so naturelly that it makes "The Walking Dead" look like a drama queen. (I think Mr. Michalsky may be one of the few people in the industry able to pull off a stunt like this).

Chapter 3, where you return from the hospital as a "recovering suicide victim", and slowly, hesitantly, almost painfully resettle in your own life is one of the best bits I played in a
long time.
Also, I found refreshing its new take on horror. At its heart it is a game about depression and grieving and learning to deal with loss and other true to life themes, only presented in a horror setting. Horror is nothing more here then a subtle setting for the story it wants to tell. Usually in horror stories the protagonist is taken out of his everyday life and put to deal with some exterior intrusive unconceivable thing that threatens to kill him horribly. In The Cat Lady the horror comes from within and poor Susan Ashworth has no way of escaping it other then slowly learning to live with herself. The horror here is the form depression and self hating takes in a poor soul dealing with it every day, year after year, as life silently and hopelessly goes on. A story about what it takes for a soul to leave the darkness it cast itself into and re-learn to slowly bend itself towards the sun.
One of the best adventure games I've ever played. Riddles are really reasonable and you can figure it out without any guides.

There's good and bad in this game. I got The Cat Lady as a gift from a sibling. Upon first playing the game I didn't expect much out of it- in terms of looks, the character design sometimes has an odd, unpolished look (proportions are often unabashedly off) and speaking animations are often odd South Park-esque head waggling. (I'm not sure if these issues were intentional, and meant to make them puppet-like, or not.) The titular cats look like their running/jumping animations were done by an alien who never saw a cat, and was just guessing.
Additionally, some of the 'missions' can be frustrating- sometimes it can seem less like a puzzle and more like a dull back-and-forth at the beginning of the game. The music with vocals that they got is also eye-rollingly wannabe-APC. It's less annoying than MCR, but takes itself far too seriously- juxtaposed with emotional scenes, it detracts more than it adds. Sounds are often looped poorly, or too quickly, and random lines of subtitle are all-capsed or just ill-fitting to the voice acting, which is pretty good- they had a surprisingly large cast for such a small game.
On to the good: I wouldn't be so hard on the game if it wasn't one that I really liked, and this game has one of the most honest portrayals of depression that I've ever witnessed in a game, and a storyline that was refreshing and relatable. It doesn't hit everyone in the same way, but I personally felt invested in the story and sympathetic to Susan, who, though you can play her in several different ways, has a storyline that always makes sense. I felt, despite the supernatural elements, that she was a fairly realistic person and I regard the game fondly enough to get my friends to play it.
TL;DR, mediocre visuals, good plot. Quick play and definitely worth it.

An adventure game about death!  If you truly enjoy indie films (not the so-called indie films of today) you will enjoy this adventure game.  Beware, some puzzles may not be as straight-forward to solve but you will keep plowing (clicking) through to the next chapter to see what'll happen next.
The game's theme is very dark and heavy.  It deals with depression and mental illness.  You experience these afflictions as you guide the Cat Lady while you help her cope with her trials and help others cope with theirs, too.  The art style is visually-striking and it does a good job at conveying a sense of uneasiness and suspense as you walk from scene to scene.
The user interface is very basic.  No mouse clicking, just arrow keys and Enter key.  The interface is text menu driven.  Hint: Use your spacebar to advance dialogue you wish to fastforward.  A technical downside occurs when you save your game.  There is no way to overwrite your previous saves within the game.  You will have to go into the game folder yourself and delete extra saves you do not need.
Fans of the old point-n-click game from Lucasfilm Games involving a hamster in a microwave will be in for a treat of their gaming lives.

Very fun to play and beautiful to look at. It doesn't boast anything "ground breaking" like Destiny or Advance Warfare, it has built upon Farcry 3 and has more content and a different location. I really enjoyed Farcry 3 and this is a polished version of that, meaning all the improvements they've made I've greatly enjoyed. All the new features are great and easy to get adjusted to. I still wish they would allow you to skip cutscenes, but then again it forces me to get into the story.
Some new features I really enjoyed:
-Being able to disable brakes outside the vehicle; place on a hill and watch em go.
-Grappling hook makes scaling mountain sides much faster so you can jump off em. The grappling system works surprisingly well, being able to swing around and ungrapple. It is very easy to learn and adapt to, but there are only certain grapple points which can be frustrating to find, especially if one entire mountain side doesn't have one.
-Throwing knives are awesome and satisfying
-The physics are the same from FC3, i.e., bullets shoot straight and gravity's hold on arrows is ever so slight
-There are a lot of cool little caves to explore that are fairly detailed and different, I spent a bit of time crashing into mountain sides trying to get near a cave.
-Vehicles have an auto-drive which is AMAZING. It allows you to actually shoot back at other vehicles and people rather than raining bullets into the air.
-The mini helicopter is awesome and gets you where you need to go and over those pesky mountains.
-Outposts are replayable. This is a great feature and gives you something to do after you beat the game. I've done so many varieties of outpost clearing because of this, throwing knives only, melee only, shotgun only, desert eagle only, grenades only, etc
-The location is amazing just to look at. Similar to Skyrim for it's vast appearance when you reach the top of a huge mountain or are just cruising with the auto-drive and able to see some great sights.
-Side missions are great and add a bit of variety and random diversions.
-Map editor is pretty cool and people come up with some great maps. It isn't the hardest to use, but requires creativity and patience. Worth checking out.
Those are just a few of the new features I enjoyed, there are plenty more. All in all this game still brought a crazy amount of randomness and hilarity. My first hour playing I accidentally machete'd a civilian in the face who was getting attacked by an eagle; the eagle few away right as I was swinging. I felt terrible cause their husband watched me brutally kill them by accident. I saw three of my rebel buddies I just saved in a firefight get mowed down by a civilian speeding in a van.
I highly recommend this game if you want something that is just fun to play, this won't revolutionize the way you see gaming, but it will keep you entertained.

I first got my hands on this game via a demo disc from McDonald's back when it was first released. The disc came with a trailer for Kingdom Hearts, a music video for I'm Still Here from the Treasure Planet movie, and some images/desktop backgrounds. Needless to say, I wasn't expecting much from an incomplete, licensed game demo bundled with a Happy Meal.
Boy, was I wrong.
I played the demo for many, many hours. It defied my expectations with thrilling action, simplified but tight strategy mechanics, and an above-average soundtrack that really puts you in the mood for, well, being in a ship out in space. I remember being astounded the first time I sailed through a nebula, eager to find whatever mysteries lay behind the pink clouds. I remember watching in fear as a black hole swallowed ships, tearing them asunder. All this in just a demo!
Jumping back into the full release, I thought that nostalgia would have dulled my senses, or maybe I wouldn't remember how to play, or maybe I would be biased. Again, I was wrong. I jumped right back in (speaking to the ease of the gameplay) and was immediately surprised to find that it was just as fun as I remembered! That's something that can't be said for many games.
To sum up, I really enjoy Treasure Planet: Battle at Procyon. It enhances the story of the original film and raises the bar for licensed games everywhere with stunning space combat done correctly, solid voice acting, graphics and sound that really put you in the world (or in space, if you prefer), and just being plain fun to learn and play. I wholeheartedly recommend it for fans of action-strategy games, space combat, or video games in general.

One Manga Day is a revenge story that is perhaps like any other- a son's quest for avenging his father's murder. But it has been said that nothing is new under the sun. All stories are old and familiar, and it is the telling that raises it to the level of a masterpiece. Love, lust and hatred, those indispensable elements of every story, are discovered anew in this timeless classic. The drama pulls the reader into an intimate engagement and One Manga Day's tragedy becomes the tragedy of every individual. No nation is a stranger to political intrigues and love affairs. Scandals in the court are scintillating without being surprising. With the words "something is rotten in the state of Japan", DeXP underlines the universality of 'rotten'-ness. The emperor of Japan is killed by his onii-san, who lusts after the crown and the queen. Dex, the prince, comes to know about this and vows revenge.
Social/Historical context:
One Manga Day was probably written between 1599 and 1601. The story is based on popular legend, but in spite of being completely embedded in the 16th century, it is a tale that has a universal reach- across boundaries of time and space. DeXP tries to communicate a message- and thoughts of staging a performance with ease take a backseat, which is why this play is regarded as the ultimate challenge for any actor. One Manga Day has even entered the English language and is a part of public memory- people quote from the play unknowingly. DeXP takes the old tale of a hero who sacrifices himself in the cause of justice and turns it on its head. Dex is hardly the popular hero- he is confused and indecisive, he is unable to act and he procrastinates. He achieves something only when some external calamity forces him to react. He is preoccupied with thoughts of death and suicide. His intellect and erudition are very unusual for a royal personage. He is no weakling- but his fencing skills are hardly of any use while his anger is misdirected. One Manga Day is not a revenge story at heart, it is a quest for identity and self-knowledge.
Writing Style:
It is unnecessary to say that the verse is superb- the fact that it stays with the reader for a long time is ample testimony.DeXP uses rhetoric to convey many kinds of meaning with just one line, which makes every line very intense and open to a variety of interpretations. Ample use of puns and metaphors put forward ideas about identity, female sexuality, etc. It is interesting to note how DeXP treats love. The oedipal overtones of Dex's love for Lap have been discussed for centuries. Laiby's ill-timed love affair has been dissected in the light of midlife crisis, menopause, etc. But there are other kinds of love that have received comparatively lesser attention. The extremely low-key treatment of the relationship between Dex and Lap is startling when one considers the tragedy of Lap, which is as magnificent as the love story of Desdemona or Juliet. Filial love forms the basis of the play, and ideas about parental supervision and imposition run as an undercurrent.
My Thoughts:
One Manga Day changed the way I look at life. I cannot explain why I fell in love with the most flawed character in English literature. Perhaps because it is not easy to recognize flaws for what they are and accept them.

Although it pains me to do so, I do not recommend this game. The primary reason being that it is simply a downgrade to the original, there is no money in the game, no crew, just race to gain fans. I don't even know if fans do anything as of how far I've gotten, they just kinda stack up.
Now a short bit on gameplay, the automatic transmission sucks, it shifts up too late, and doesn't downshift when it needs to. There is another 'mechanic' in the game, fatal crashes. The idea is that if you crash your car hard enough, pop goes your brains against the wall and you fail and lose the race. I tried for at least 2 minutes of constant high speed crashes to get the car to stop working, after caving in the engine by a few inches, the worst of it was my car veering slightly to the right. I call it a 'mechanic' because it doesn't seem to work. To clarify, yes I am certain it was turned on, as there is an option to turn it off. Why is this so bad? In this high speed game, crashing isn't a threat, if you're too lazy to turn a corner, just grind against the guard rails and you'll be right as rain. This is one of the downsides from the original Grid. In the original grid, crashing was scary, slipping slightly and seeing your car get snapped in half and losing the race was interesting, it required braking before turns.
Let's talk about the AI. It cheats. On the higher difficulties on regular races, they still aren't much of a challenge, maybe it'll take a few tries so that's manageable, if you ignore their impossible traction of rounding a corner without sliding. The problem is in activities where points are involved. One such event is known as Overtake. The idea is simple, pass cars without crashing, get points, the further you get without crashing, the more points you get. Even on the Very Hard difficulty, the ai is going hella slow and in the time they pass a single car, their multiplier would be at 0 and that would net 100 points. While the player blasts past them scoring thousands of points and spends a minute gaining 10 thousand points in a perfect lap, the AI says 'oops' and gives themselves a magical 12 thousand points for passing basically 3 cars, while the player just passed 20-30.
Finally, let's go over the 'Ones to watch.' These guys are considered the Elite, they are the pros, the ones to be careful around - before you blast past them. These Elite seem to have the same AI as the other drives, so they take corners insanely slowly which is generally when you'll pass them. The only threat they pose is when they're hogging the road and stopping you from passing, or when there's a long stretch of road and it's race of top speed instead of skill, because these  'Elite' have slightly better cars for some inexplicable magical reason.
To conclude, one of the few times I truly smiled while playing this game was when I remembered the original Grid. If it's available on Steam when you're reading this, buy the original Grid, NOT Grid Autosport. Those are different games.

In many ways I find Thief 2014 a very enjoyable game to play but do feel that the storyline is somewhat thin.
The basic game mechanics are fairly the same as the original 1998 game, or at least they feel that way, and I find that the AI has not really improved much. The graphics and game dynamics though are upgraded as suspected from a "new" game and are up to standards (PC version).
Storyline:
Apart from the thin storyline the storyline missions were not as hard as I suspect them to be from a 'Stealth' game and feel somewaht linear. As said earlier the storyline could have been way better and all the graphics in the world could not make up for it in my opinion. The story just didn't feel finished in the end, and left me with a very unsattisfied feeling (I don't mean the feeling of longing for more but just sheer dissapointment). It seems to me more and more game developers seem to be forgetting that the story is more important than the graphics and only if you get the story right people will look forward to a future part in the series (and pay another silly amount of cash for it).
Almost roam freely:
I did enjoy the other part of the game where you were able to, almost, roam freely through the city and accept a range of different 'client jobs' and it's very cool to swing high above the ground from rope to rope on route to your next mission, especially when you get to know the city better and better. It's not a open world as most of us would like it to be but it certainly gives you many ways to reach your next mission or job to keep enjoying it for a while.
Replayability:
After finishing the storyline, and a few client jobs, I started the game over on a harder level but I don't think I'll finish it. Not that it's too hard but I feel like "been there done that" and don't feel like I enjoy the game as much as the first time I played it. Mainly because the storyline feels the same as the first time I played it. I just doesn't challenge me enough to play all the way through them again, even on a harder level. I might just replay a few client jobs but thats it.
Bugs:
Although this is a somewaht gray area because this also depends on what kind of PC you have I did experience a few bugs.
At chapter 3 suddenly the game crashed on the intro movie. I had to down the resolution a few steps before it wanted to go through (probably my Radeon 6800 is a bit to old to handle certain graphics on low quality but full HD).
Secondly there were a few times the Guards got stuck on one place and weren't able to move anymore (they kept spinning around).
There were some problems with the audio in the cutscenes, unable to hear what they were saying.
Conclusion:
Worth playing, nice city and a few nice challenges. Storyline is enjoyable but very thin, especially in the end. (7/10)

Longer Version:
Okay, I want to write a review about Civ Beyond Earth again, as I seem to have found good words to describe this game.
The game itself is not really bad. Actually it's rather good. The biggest flaw of Civ Beyond Earth is, that is has to compete and to be compared with Civ IV, Civ V, Civ VI and Alpha Centauri.
While the 4 mentioned games all would have scores around 9/10 points, maybe +- a half point, Civ BE would get 6.5/10 points from me, maybe 7/10.
And right there is the problem. When you compare it to your Civilization game of your choice, no matter if it's Civ IV or Civ VI, Civ BE will always lose and look terrible.
But it isn't. It's a fun game with a lot to explore. Maybe you wont play it as much as other Civ games, but it still can be fun and entertaining. The overall setting and many of the features are really interesting and it's something different to your normal Civ game.
Oh, and the Music is absolutely the best thing about this game. At times I only keep playing because the Music is so fricking good.
To sum it all up: when you're interested (and when reading random reviews on steam about this game you very likely are) buy it when it's on a sale. Maybe around Xmas or on the Summer Sale. Just, don't try to compare it to the Civ game of your choice, else you will be disappointed.

With Risen 3 just over a month away, I thought I'd add my input for anyone who might pick this up, expecting to get an impression of the series. Warning: this is a long review, so for a brief summary, just skip to the end paragraph.
The original Risen was, fundamentally, a sound, well-executed, and generally enjoyable fantasy RPG experience, if a bit unimagined and simple. It had everything that made the studio (Piranha Bytes) known in the fantasy RPG market, including memorable NPC's with dynamic behaviors and daily routines to give the game world an organic, living setting. The combat system was decent, but a bit glitchy, and magic offered an interesting, varied complement to combat and exploration. While mostly taking place in a single outdoor landmass, the game also transitioned (seamlessly, I might add) to deep, ruined dungeons which stretched from brief to expansive, and all very nicely designed.
Risen 2: Dark Waters lost a lot of that. Abandoning the medieval fantasy theme for a pirate setting, and giving up the single landmass for individual islands separated by loading screens, it's not wrong of you to expect a game with a lot of open-sea activities and exploration and loot-filled adventure. That's not what you get. You find yourself on foot the entire time, running around tiny islands that you soon realize are even smaller than they appear due to deliberate landscape design, turning what could be immersive wilderness exploration into a boring run along pathways between mountains and rocky cliff faces. Dungeons are small, tubular caves or cookie-cutter ruined hallways that rarely yield memorable loot.
Whereas previous games from Piranha Bytes gave us NPC's that we could laugh at and remember, there's very little to make us like the batch of characters in this title. Patty, the supposed "love interest" of the player character, is the most expressive NPC by far, but is still a pretty generic representation of a typical pirate fantasy trope of a female character trying to prove her strength and independence amongst the tough, grizzled men in the piratey world. The follower Bones offered a bit of humor, but apart from that, I couldn't care less about the characters. Only four NPC's (including Patty) make the crossover between Risen and Risen 2, and two of those characters only appear in the DLC's, and none of them truly reflect their former selves, so anyone whom you might have loved and hoped to see from Risen won't be here.
The combat system is what drives many people to complain about this game. In the beginning, I can certainly agree with them - until you get some of the upper-tier skills, which allow you to parry and counter enemy attacks, you're left only with the ability to spam the attack button and hope that everything else dies before you do. The bigger problem is getting those skills. The opening area of the game, Tacarigua, encourages you to invest in a wide variety of skills, but there is no chance of you getting them all so soon - learning skills requires not only levelling up your stats, but paying teachers a huge sum to instruct you, and gold is not easily acquired this early in the game. By the time you get the upper tier combat skills, you'll be used to spamming attacks and depending on your followers, so you may never actually discover how useful parrying and riposting really is.
On the topic of skills, you can safely ignore about half of the skills the game offers. Many of them have such selective usefulness in so few occasions that they aren't worth investing in at all. Partway through the game, you're forced to make a decision that decides what skills will be open to you later - either being able to use muskets, or voodoo magic. Voodoo may sound like the more attractive option, but in my experience, it's almost completely worthless. Many enemies later in the game are immune to the spells, and potions are such short-term buffs that they're a waste of time to fuss with. Still, it hardly matters which side you choose, because even if you forego muskets for voodoo, you can still use shotguns (or 'shotgun,' since I think only one exists in the game), which function exactly the same.
The only one thing I can actually give credit to this game for is the "legendary items" feature. Starting with the expansion for Gothic II, Piranha Bytes has included a series of hidden treasures in each of their games to seek out and dig up. Risen included pieces of broken weapons that could be reforged into powerful swords. This was included in Risen 2 as well, but the game also featured legendary items that could be read about in books found throughout the settlements of the world, and offered clues leading to special items giving passive perks to your character. This feature was the only thing that made the islands truly worth exploring, as the majority of loot you found in dungeons and the landscape was little more than fodder to dump onto a vendor for a quick buck.
All in all, Risen 2: Dark Waters fails in its promise to give us the first true pirate RPG. It fails to give us an endearing RPG experience of any kind, in fact. Calling it "streamlined" is too forgiving, as the whole game is woefully shallow; with an assortment of useless skills to waste money on, small, unimagined islands that offer little incentive to explore, and characters that, at best, are simply mind-numbing caricatures of the common stereotypes of Hollywood pirates. This title is an offense to the legacy of Piranha Bytes, and it fills me with dread to know that the developers of four quintessential RPG's could sink this low. Here's hoping Risen 2 was a bitter lesson for the studio, and while I expect RIsen 3: Titan Lords to have some of the same flaws (with their shortest development time so far, I can't expect it to be a complete turn-around), I can only hope we see some signs of life in the future to indicate that they can provide us with another beloved RPG for the ages.

You play the same guy from Risen 1, but come on, this game isn't fooling anyone. Badass sword/magic wielding guy is now a drunken one eyed pirate due to the end of Risen 1? No. This feels like they had a game in mind and just let it piggyback on Risen.
Go play Risen. It was so good that I had to look into the Gothic games.

Now let me start off by saying I loved the premise of this game, and I went into it expecting all the bad stuff I heard to just be talk, how could a pirate RPG be bad, right?
Now, maybe 55 minutes isn't enough time to get a true idea of the game, and hey, it probably isn't, but 55 minutes was all I could bring myself to spend. Now most times if I play a game and it's not great at first, I wait it out, and keep playing, and generally, I tend to enjoy them after a few hours. But I couldn't even get 55 minutes into this without having to stop. Everything about it is just so... stale. The combat isn't enjoyable, the story is generally boring, the enviroments in the game look like something that was rejected from Pirates of the Caribbean, the list goes on.
If you're going to buy this game, get it on sale if anything, don't buy it full price, you
feel like you've wasted your money.

This isn't anything like your Amnesia: The Dark Descent or Fallout games; it's a simple point-and-click with graphics and voice-acting that are very reminiscent of visual novels. It's a fantastic, mature horror game of which the story contains a relatively accurate portrayal of depression, and the whimsical harshness of the tracks created for this game (of which I also must highly recommend) hit home just as hard. It would be nice for everyone to give this game a chance, especially those who are heavily affected by depression; however, a word of warning must be given for its often macabre images and blunt presentation which can be upsetting.

A very interesting game which depicts depression very well, I feel the game is quite relatable and I often see myself thinking similar to the individual in the game.
The game supports a suicide help service by donating donations to it and is quite an honorable thing to do, not only did they make the game a compelling and relatable experience, you can see they tried to make it as realistic as possible without going to far, I have only played one playthrough and felt very compelled and effected by the different choices and the outcome that would await me.
If you suffer or have suffered from depression, I feel this would be a great experience due to its relatability and may help you make choices in regard to said depression, but be aware the game can be dark and can trigger.
A compelling game which is relatable and realistic, with a modern touch, I feel it is a brilliant game with it's feautres, not every developer can make you tear up at a wall of text. :)

This is not "fun" Nor even a game really. What it is, is a look into the life of a depressed man who could be almost anyone, and it's the players job of directing there life. Havin suffered from depression from various things in the past i can relate to some of these things and playing brings back distant memories of those bad feelings. The story and dialogue are amazing and can be very absorbing. Overall though the game is not like most other games. The final boss isnt an actual thing that can be seen and fought physicaly, it is the main characters emotions. Even before you go into this you should know there are only 2 true ways this can turn out if you know anything about clinical depression. The game feels real and relateable as you are tasked with guiding this man to a beter life or down the spiral of darkness he curenty rests in. This game doesnt have any replayability (unless you feel like going through the same situations but with different actions). But still deserves a play, weather you want something storybased and sadening, or you're perhaps someone who can relate to the concept. It's not very long and shouldnt take more than 10 minutes to instal and an hour to experience

Far cry 4, is a major improvement from far cry 3. While far cry 3 is still a fantastic game it was missing some immersion aspects that far cry 4 has hit the head of the nail on. let's start with graphics.
Far cry 4's graphics are almost movie-like. With fantastic animations, great foliage and shadowing, the game looks simply brilliant. It has a nice Game look to it without it looking fake, unreal and Non-immersiable. while i have only played a miniscule amount of the game, i can already tell that it will take off to become on my top games.
Gameplay, Far cry 4 started out fantastic. the characters are great, connectable, and you can really imagine the reality of them. Even the main antagonist is fantastic, honestely i would totally be on his side of things, and that would be a great twist. The talking amongst various NPC to NPC's is also not terrible. You don't necessarily hear, "I used to be an adventurer like you, until i took an arrow to the knee" a thousand times until it becomes hardy-har funny. It uses a fantastic amount of realism and is overall a very immerseful experience.
Hunting, the hunting in Far cry 4 is fantabulous. It's honestly. I can't get enough of it. It is too easy to be walking along see a deer and end up on the other end of the map wingsuiting down from a bridge following a river all the way down to a small lake that i can fish at, well more like unload on the water until stuff floats up. But, the point is that it's great.
Co-op.  The Co-op in far cry 4 is exactly what i hoped it would have been in far cry 3 only better. It has a fantastic selection of things to do and if you run out of things to do because you and a friend are simply too badass, then reset the outposts.! It's amazing how that can restore the fun back into the game and keep you coming back for more action packed hunting, killing, looting, driving, and exploration.
Rate 9.5/10 - fantastic game. very well done. Bravo sir.

a lot of people compare it (and rightfuly so) to far cry 3, but i choose to compare it to far cry 2. just like far cry 2, this game is riddled with bugs, glitches, it will crash every so often and everything and everyone wants, and will go out of their way, to kill you. just like in far cry 2 you use beds to advance time by sleeping. and just like in far cry 2, your seemingly obvious choice makes people's lives worse. if far cry 3 was far cry 2 in a new dress, then this is fac cry 2 with new shoes as well. tap dancing shoes to be precise, as almost every few minutes you'll be pulled into an adventure of your own making. if you can find a friend that bought this game as well (or bought the god awful crime of a game assassin's creed unity and was reimbursed by free far cry 4), you can get so much fun out of this game, as the overall chaos and stupidity can get doubled.
storywise however, this is where this game really wants to shine, yet drowns in typical far cry storytelling. you will never fully understand who the characters are, as they are just thrown at you and then they kick you out to do repetitive killing ,honestly, it took me almost six main missions to start piecing together the characters and their motivations. you want to know more about kyrati customs and traditions to better understand the world? run around that very world for hours, reading scraps of paper scattered about to realize why the little girl you only see three times is so important. you will never care for the kyrati people ,as there simply aren't any, it's like everyone was eaten by omnipresent wolves and eagles or shot by the army. all you'll ever care about is getting more of pagan min (brillianty voice by troy baker), the most sympathetic, charming, smart and well written character of the cast, partly because every time he shows up you remember that this game has a story, not a bad one at that, hidden somewhere between recycled bits and bytes of this beatiful and vast world (if ubisoft can make something besides trailers, it's open world maps).
in short, while i do recommend it, especially in coop, i strongly criticize the price tag. this game should not cost so much, as it isn't worth it and definetly cost far cry 2 budget, or less, to make

Someone who wants a bone dry simulation, with realistic handling and professional racing is wrong with this title. Everybody esle, who wants a fun and exciting racer - even tough it is now 5 years old, will love this game.

By far the best mode in this game is the Touge mode, having probably the best touge tracks of all racing games, being tough and punishing but very rewarding at a high difficulty level.
The story is a typical "From the bottom to the top" style one, but a nice addition to the progression system.
As contra points, the race engineer is annoying after some time (can be turned off) and clean racing being almost impossible due to the agressive AI.
For only 2.99$ during a steam sale, it is definitely no wasted money.
Tip: Turn on some Eurobeat during touge to enhance driving skills.

Do you enjoy listening to Hansen, MC Hammer and Vanilla Ice?  Do you enjoy throwing away your loose change?  Do you enjoy watching bad movies from the 80's on VHS?  If you answered yes to any of these questions I'd recommend you stop reading my review and immediately purchase this game, you'll love it.  For the rest of us do yourself a favor, click not interested and by all means, even during a steam sale, when you see it for 49 cent... don't buy it..
So my warning wasn't enough and you want to know what this game is about.... well aside from trying and failing to be a video game anybody on the face of Earth will like, you are an Astronaut who has found yourself floating in space...  We'll ignore the fact that no spaceship, capsule, satellite or anything needed to keep a human being in space alive, seems to be anywhere in sight, and the fact your character floats freely through space asleep and oblivious to everything around him....
Out of the dark recesses of space come the P men....  or as I like to call them... PU men, cause they stink just as much as this game...  They strike your character sending him hurling towards what looks to be Earth...  Instead of burning into a crispy little ball of flame (which I'd have happily handed over my .49 cent to see) you somehow manage to come down unscathed, bounce a few times and then somehow wake up in the magical land of...   WTF were the developers taking when they created this World.  or CashGrab Land as I'll call.
Inside CashGrab land you float from one point to another, using arrows, messages and other assorted random things to find your way around.  If you ever played an 80's game when you would spend hours wandering around the same dungeon looking for your next objective you'll understand this game...  The only difference is you'll be floating past PU creatures for no apparent reason, searching for beach equipment....  Why!....  Who knows why, I suppose the developers thought Space is like a vast ocean and tried to put some hidden message into their game..... NA they just didn't care...
So wander around this CashGrab Land for a few hours, find your beach stuff and enjoy this game...   err well actually no enjoyment will be found or had with this game,  it just drains your soul.. much like a succubus after 3 hours of playing the only thing left to do is drool on yourself until someone comes along and frees you from it's sucktastic grip.....

Great multiuser dungeon. Single player mode is also beefy.
Choose your character out of Wizard / Knight / Warlock / Ranger and increse its abilities with powerups you find / unlock / buy with coins; said coins are found randomly or in chests, you also get coins by killing mobs.
There is no player name and no player level.
You have 4 acts, each with its own final boss and themed setting. Each act is subdivided in levels. You can go up an ddown levels freely within the same act.
There is a LOT of replayability as the game features "crutches" (infinite lifes, hp auto regen, etc) and "challenges" (1 life, 1hp, no sp regen, etc). To either make your games easier or harder to suit your skill level.
Finally, there is a map editor, so you can build your own adventure if you are into it !
UPDATE: After hundreds of hours more: It is still as awesome as day one ;-)

You will hear a lot of complaints about this game; it's relatively shallow, the characters lack personality, it's essentially a clone of Civ V, the settings are ugly, etc., etc.. That said, this game does feel quite a bit like Civ V, and that is not a bad thing at all. Consider this a review of Rising Tide, because without it I do not recommend the game, but with its additions (floating cities, the new diplomacy points system, the increased effectiveness of Spies) the game feels less like a clone with a new paint job and more of a very clever total conversion mod. If you find this game on sale with Rising Tide and have already logged your hundreds of hours in Civ V, go grab it! You will not be disappointed, assuming you've already heard all the (mostly undeserved) negative press. It's a fun, addictive, sci-fi Civ game that really will suck you in if you're willing to give it the chance.

fault - milestone two is the second installment in the fault series of visual novels, and as such, this review will contain spoilers for fault – milestone one. I highly recommend reading the first novel in the series before reading any further.
milestone two begins directly where milestone one left off: Selphine, Ritona, and Rune are confronted by Melano, one of the mysterious assailants that attacked Rughzenhaide the night Ritona whisked herself and Selphine away, leaving themselves stranded in the Outer Pole. Melano isn’t the focus of the story here, though, and before long, Selphine, Ritona, and Rune are left to continue their journey back to Rughzenhaide.
The basic premise of milestone two is very similar to that of milestone one. The girls arrive at a new city with different social norms and values than what they’re used to. They meet some new characters, and just like in the first installment, there’s some vague tension between them as they all try to get to know each other a bit better and reconcile cultural differences.
However, whereas milestone one focused on Rune as a character to explore themes of identity, milestone two is much more plot-driven. But that’s not to say that milestone two has weaker characters than milestone one just for the sake of advancing the narrative. If anything, this novel manages to have some very interesting developments for both the characters and the story. It takes a little while, but once the ball starts rolling, the story becomes very engaging, and hints at some very interesting directions for the characters and the story to go. But in the interest of avoiding spoilers, I won’t say any more. The fun is in finding out for yourself.
milestone two continues to add world-building details throughout the narrative. While I found a lot of it to be somewhat dull in milestone one, I think the writers handled it much better in milestone two. It might just be that I’m more used to it by now since this is the second novel in the series, but I think the details about the world, each character’s backstory, and how manakravte works are all doled out at a much better pace in this story. These details are also (usually) much more relevant to the plot at hand, making it a much easier read since it’s directly involved with the story. Over time, I actually started to become very interested in the world the writers created. It seems they put a lot of effort into making it feel very “real” and consistent with all the details across the two novels.
Overall, I really enjoyed reading fault – milestone two, and I think it’s a significant improvement over the first novel, which I already liked. I highly, highly recommend this novel if you read and enjoyed fault – milestone one. I’m very much looking forward to the next installment of the series, which seems to be a prequel to milestone one, and is actually a point-and-click adventure! I already played the demo, and enjoyed what I’ve seen so far. I hope the writers continue to improve and impress from here.

I first played maplestory maybe 7 or 8 years ago and at first it was fun. (Note: my main interest is quests.)
I remembered it was a game that, if you are a casual player, got harder and harder to progress as you went on. Eventually I stopped playing because it would take far too long to level up and make any sort of meaningful progress. Plus items like scrolls to increase certain traits of a weapon were pricey and overall the game was just slow.
Fast forward to 2016 and I am back! It's a lot of fun now. Nexon have made certain parts of the game painless and have introduced new niche areas. Not interested in monsters or mapleworld? How about becoming a star/celebrity over at Star Planet? Want something different to the world of monsters and magic? Check out Friends Story, one of the alternative dimensions that's set in the modern world where you play a student!
If you just want to do quests and wander about - the game now has a very good guide that will recommend the quests that are right for your level. I followed this guide and levelled up quickly, giving me more options to explore other parts of the game and even take on a big boss or two.
Improving your weapons and equipment is now simple to do and doesn't take long at all.
My main criticism of the game is that it seems like a neverending mess. Little to no structure and if you were looking for a main storyline to follow there isn't really one. Instead there are lots of short story arcs, or series of quests (one leading on to the next), which is great while it lasts but leaves you thinking - now what?
Playing alone is fine, and I mainly solo, however playing with friends is a lot more fun.

Note: I'm only commenting on the single player. I don't multiplay with strangers and none of my friends have this game.
Background: I loved the Magic: Duels Of The Planeswalkers series that I had on the Xbox 360. I was hoping this would be more of the same. It isn't.
In the previous DotP games, in single player mode you had some control over your deck. The starting card set was usually pretty weak, but you could unlock cards by playing and winning the single player games, so if you found you were getting stuck, you could go back to an easier encounter and grind out some better cards. You could also customize the deck (e.g. go heavy on direct damage and chump blockers to counter an enemy that likes to summon big creatures). None of that is possible here. In single player mode, you're stuck with whatever crappy deck the game gives you. No editing, and no way to grind out better cards. Using these subpar pre-made decks, you get to duel against the CPU which is wielding some of the greatest cheese this side of Wisconsin. Think the Elf deck from the original DotP. That level of cheese.
Honestly, I don't understand why Wizards has made the single player mode such an exercise in frustration. It *is* possible to beat the incredibly slanted odds, but it's pretty clear pretty quick that it's all up to luck and not up to skill. Yes, single player does earn you a few of the in-game "coins", but if I was interested in farming coins, I would have played a random battle against the random CPU with the deck that you get from finishing the tutorial. I just wanted to get a chance to experience the game "lore", but it's not worth the aggravation.
I'll probably keep the game around to play the random CPU battles when I feel like tinkering with a deck, but I doubt I'll ever bother finishing the rest of the story mode. And I'll certainly never give these bozos a nickle of my money.

„The Cat Lady“ is an adventure game in horror style. You can find different objects which could maybe useful for the story later so you should remember what you see and what the characters are telling you!
I don't want to spoil so I can't tell you too much, but what I can relate is: the protagonist is called Susan Ashworth, a lonely 40 year old woman. She has a sad life with no friends and nothing which makes her happy instead of her cats maybe. The game deals with themes considered mature and dark such as depression, suicide and loneliness. You have to make decisions like in life… do you trust people? Or do you kill them? Maybe you see a friend in someone… and later it will be a mistake. You will meet psychopaths and people who need help. How do you act? Do you run away? Or do you help people who don’t even care about you. But maybe just you think no one cares about you – maybe others love you. Some moments of hope break the dark but to find out the whole story and what really happened to Susan you have to play the game!

This story is very dark and dreary, but it really pulls through in the end. There are some unanswered questions left over, but nothing that would really change anything. The game can be a bit misleading for any alternate "paths," but the story pulls through, along with a solid soundtrack. The game has some technical issues, as it was made by a lower-budget indie studio, but given what they had available they do manage to pull off a great experience. I would love to see what this team could do with a full budget and some real team backing behind it. If you want a dark and dreary story with an uplifting message, stick through this. As I said, it's not for everyone, but it can be powerful if you let it sink in.

If you treat the game as a faithful sequel to the original three games, you are going to disappointed. If you treat the game as a new reboot, you're going to like it. The game itself plays between a mixture of Thief 3 and Dishonoured. (Which isn't really a bad combination, though this game is quite linear)
The graphics, animations and audio are great, which does a great deal for immersion. Not to mention the voice acting is pretty good.
Bad points: The story writing is poor, and it is not as slow paced/tactical as the previous games in the series.
Does this mean the game is bad? No way, it's actually pretty good. A bit buggy, but it's a solid game in its own right.
Should you buy it? Yes,  but make sure you buy it cheap. It's always on offer because of the mixed reception it's getting.

Hammerwatch is a really fun game that follows closely to the methods of past games it pays homage to. So much so that it will more than likely only appeal to the generation of gamer who grew up playing those past games and in that one niche move, Hammerwatch has, in a sense, alienated itself from being a truly great game.
Hammerwatch plays a lot like Gauntlet, there are hordes of mobs that appear from spawners. The dungeon has you zigzagging from one floor to the next and back in a winding trek through traps, hidden doors, and other general death dealing tricks. You will need to find keys in order to unlock progression further in the game. You have a shared life pool that all players respawn from. Once all your lives are expended you have to start from the beginning, no savesies. There are even certain times when the game goes full-on bullet-hell. Bosses are a mix of tactics, luck, and putrid frustration that, once beaten, gives you a high sense of accomplishment rarely felt in modern games; yet amid all these great gameplay features lies Hammerwatch's Achilles Heel.
To truly enjoy this game you
play co-op. Single player is possible, albeit arduous and really slow. To progress deep into the dungeon you really need a coordinated team effort or else you'll find yourself spending a lot of time fleeing and waiting around for perfect opportunities to strike. Two man teams still make this game challenging. To really get progression you almost need 4 players.
Team play is great, but
if you have a well managed team. Players who have never played games of this type quickly become a liability and ruin gameplay and progression. When the 'newguy' runs through all your lives, while the rest of the team manages to stay alive, it means none of the 'veteran' players can die or else the whole team could wipe.
All the loot in-game is displayed for all players to take; so you have to be willing to share success with your team. Therefore you really need a team of players who are all ranked about the same and can cooperate with each other and not go around ninjaing health, loot, and gold. When you've managed to stay alive with a sliver of health for 15 minutes desperately hoping to find a health potion and someone on your team, who died 2 times in the same 15 minutes, decides they need to top up their 90% health bar with the
health potion you've seen in that time, it can lead to quite the rage face.
These are all issues that old-school games experienced and many newer games have found ways to prevent such frustrations by giving each player their own loot, allowing for individual lives, and scaling difficulty for the number of people in your team. Hammerwatch is great fun, but only under a specific set of conditions: 4 veteran players who look out for the team not themselves and have the time to group together for long play sessions. Finding those conditions can be difficult for mature
players. It's sad really, because I have owned this game for 5 months and my friends and I have only been able to find time to play Hammerwatch together for 2 hours.
So I do recommend Hammerwatch, it's fun, nostalgic, and difficult. I do wish they didn't go so old school, but my own experience is not what a review should be about. It's about the game and this game is great!

Plays like a mediocre civ mod.
Despite the relatively low scores this game got I was pretty excited to play it when it went on sale for the Steam summer sale. I've played a lot of the civ games and really enjoyed alpha centauri. I figured even if it wasn't the best game in the series I'd still enjoy it. In the end while it wasn't awful it really didn't live up to my expectations.
A few observations from my first play through:
- I figured for my first time I'd play 8 player, large map, standard difficulty, pace and world type (i.e. "terra" type planet with continents)
-Game pacing felt all off: some things seemed to progress pretty normally such as leveling up the virtue trees with culture or having your cities grow, but otherwise a lot of stuff just felt to go at an uneven pace. I didn't feel like the tech trees were set up well. Also the progress to victory conditions felt waaay too fast. I normally turn those types of things off on my first playthrough of a civ game but somehow missed it on this one. I don't really find it fun to suddenly be faced with the game wrapping up because one of the AIs decided to start a space program or trying to get elected in the UN, forcing me to do the same or lose (in this case it's things like finding alien signals or opening a portal to earth). I found myself having to start my own game ending project around turn 250 and at that point I hadn't even made contact with all of the other players. By the time I won I still hadn't explored but about a quarter of the globe.
-Somehow despite being a "civ in the future" type game progression still seems really shallow. Basically it feels like there's less progression and not more. Like I said above I barely got to explore the map, this is in part due to the fact that unlike other civ games you don't ever really get progress on unit movement. There's for example one type of land based explorer unit, it's extremely weak and can only move a max of two spaces (only one if you're doing something like climbing a hill). I think the unit with the most movement is a naval one that can move 5 spaces a turn. You'd think that after mastering the non-trivial task of interstellar space flight our colonists would be able to develop a technology to let their explorers move faster than on foot, like, I don't know a car maybe? Other bonuses such as those from wonders seem uninspired, basically boiling down to things "get +10% production in this city", making them either basically worthless or OP. There were plenty of other things like the artifact system and satellite system which seemed tacked on half finished.
-Alien ecology balance seems really off: so basically the alien fauna is the "barbarians" of this game. The game explains that they're a collective so attacking one alien unit decreases your standing with all of them, and makes them more likely to turn against you. I think my biggest gripe here was the alien activity didn't ramp up over time like it did in alpha centauri. You're just kind of there on the planet with all these aliens and "miasma" (condition on tiles that does dmg to you). I decided to play nice with the locals on my first playthrough but they still seemed to randomly attack me. Early on I got not one, but two high level kraken aliens pillaging the crap out of my first city which was on the coast. Luckily they couldn't raze the city and I was able to eventually bombard them to death, but for what seemed like forever I had to just stop making improvements in the water. By the time I finally got the technologies to make them friendly to me it didn't really matter anymore, even on the few occassions I fought wars with other factions who were hostile to the aliens they would steamroll my little green friends.
-Certain things still felt very obtuse and unintuitive: I've played a lot of these games. It still took me a while to, for example figure out why my explorer couldn't do any more excavation sites early on. I had to look it up and it turns out you have to resupply them back at your city every time do that. A popup saying "hey your explorer needs to go back to town now" would have been nice.
-Combat is awful: I saved the worst for last. I'd have overlooked all of the other stuff but combat is abyssmal in this game. It's due in large part to some of the things I mentioned above, such as the progression tree for units being really shallow and not being able to do things like upgrade unit movement very far. There are other things that they have in other civ games that it just doesn't make sense they didn't include here. There's no stacking of units for example, no general type of units etc. Also the overall balance is really off. For example I built one of the "ultimate" melee type units, a golem, only to have it get trashed by opposing infantry because they had a lot of veterancy. It would by like having spearmen take out a tank unit in civ V just because they had a lot of experience. The way cities are taken doesn't make a lot of sense either. When you attack a city you fight and do damage to the health of that city rather than any units stationed there. When you reduce the health of the city to zero it just automatically kills any units previously on that tile and turns control over. It also for whatever reason instantly destroys all building in the city even if you're annexing it. I started just razing every city I was able to capture, partially out of spite and partially because I couldn't see any reason to do otherwise.
In summary: the game had a lot of promise but in the end it feels unpolished and unbalanced to the point where it really diminished my enjoyment.

As with all multi-part VN's, you should always start with the first entry, even if it's the worse of the two, as several things will make less or no sense without it.
I won't go as in depth as with my review of the first, just going to go over some thoughts as of just finishing this one. This will be a short summary review since, unlike Sol, I have a job to go to. :P
Some more involved side-story, but far less main story than the first game with roughly the same amount of screen time.
Too few CG's, though the ones that were there were, as always, very nice. Basically no focus on the main story. Thrown in excuse to keep the main characters in the same place too long. Weirdly grew far more attached to Reghan than Selphine. Maybe this should have been a RPG/VN hybrid like Tears to Tiara or Utawarerumono with the way a fair amount of the scenes played out. The art for adult men is just not good, regardless of age. The introduction of the characters in another location was not interesting to me, and they certainly were not interesting enough to go back to several times. Couldn't empathize with Sol at all until near the end, and even then it seemed like a cop out for why he did the things he did. Sound and music far less grating and made more sense. The attempt to talk about imageboard culture and then say there's nobody just posting stuff for fun even if mildly at the expense of others pulled me out a fair bit.
But as always the most damning part of this VN is that it is far far far far too short for the asking price. Until I start seeing stories that last 10 or more hours for the same price with the same or better quality of everything else, I won't stop repeating this criticism. Like I said before maybe this is the state of VN's right now but 2-3 hours of play time is simply unnacceptable for the price, and had I not gotten this game in a bundle I wouldn't have ever thought the asking price was worth it for anyone, unless VN's are pretty much all you enjoy, or unless the price gets down to below $5.
Just like always I enjoyed the story and now most of the characters (Misha and the rest are so trite and banal that I sighed the third time I was expected to pay attention to them) but I cannot understand what their intention is by taking so much time to tell what we must already assume is a full story about the kingdom, the world, the planet, the universe, the way we observe it, how certain characters are aware of how we observe it, and why we are given the power to influence it by those characters only at very specific moments. How many 2 to 3 hour entries will there be, each priced so highly, before some actual plot advancement happens? The intro to this game is as strong as it was to the first, but for a different reason which will need to be explained in full eventually. I'm feeling a strange sense of déja-vu reminiscent somewhat of many other VN-style games, most recently the Nosurge line, from fault 2's intro here.
Lastly I'll say I think robbing Sol of his chance to viciously, suddenly emotionally emerge/grow was a mistake, narratively and in/for the fiction itself. No matter how the story tried to paint him in the same light as another young character we were told about in the first game, it's quite obvious he's very different and does possess the capability to empathize with others; there's plenty of evidence for this but the most obvious is were that not the case he would not care for at least one other person the way he does.
The last few images we got were very sweet... But I couldn't help feeling that, regardless of what was being shown, there's a reason we never saw Sol's face again, a gnawing, worrying feeling about how perhaps being witness to what had transpired without being aware of all the facts will inevitably lead to more repression, and the potential for even more despair to those around him than what existed already. And I know this was not the intention of the story at all, based on the music and what had happened just before.
Thanks for reading my rambling and have a good day.

This game really forces you to think, unlike many games that are out on the market right now. Imagine yourself put into these freakishly realistic scenarios, a strained relationship with your significant other, alongside, your dead end job. What are your options? Depression Quest does a very good job at forcing you to ponder over the choices you have made and ponder over whether or not you have the right choice. Even if these (non)fictional choices strain the relationships you posess or even the job you hold, the game still makes you think within the psuedo-mindset of being this depressed character. One aspect I really like is the use of multiple options, when prompted. In the beginning of the story, you have, say, 4-5 options available as a response to the "What do you do?" question. As the story progresses and you make your choices, there is a point in the story where your available options dwindle to 2 or even, in one case, 1 mandatory option as a suitable response. This aspect of the gameplay really mimics a human being's lack of response during his/her bout with depression and gives a very good insight as to how depression really hinders our minds to think positively, negatively, and even neutrally, at some points.
Read.
Respond.
Think.
Repeat.
These four actions alone make this game a must play.

As a fan of Magic: The Gathering, having the ability to play whenever, wherever I like is convienent- not to mention, having the freedom to connect with friends is also nice.  Magic Duels provides an exciting magic experience and is free-to-play- win-win.  There are pros and cons to this game, however.  Below are some of the key features of this game that I like and dislike:
--PROS:
A very easy to navigate set of GUIs that are very artistically created and implemented.  The effect is that the gamer feels immersed in the world of Magic upon entering the game.  The GUI, honestly looks very professional, and needs no improvement as far as I can see.
A helpful, search-powered deck-builder and card collecting system makes the efforts of strategizing and amassing cards a pleasant experience.  On that note, it would be stellar if the gamer were able to search his stash of cards for key words too.
A very fun single-player, story mode that shares some of the lore of the MTG universe with fans.  In my opinion, this is one of the very unique features of the game that should be explored more by the developers.  The backgrounds of many of the characters/planeswalkers, the invasion of the scittering Eldrazi and the like are actually quite compelling.  I recommend better backgrounds (instead of foggy purple), music and more campaign missions with each release; a map that shows the movement of the given character would be classy too.
The game's versus mode is fun and easy-to-use.
A unique take on the game.  A card's rarity in this game determines how many of them one may use in this deck.  While some may find this a Con, I personally find this rule balances the game more between the beginners and free-to-players versus the experienced and play-to-winners.  A powerful deck is still a powerful deck, but they don't seem to be so powerful that a beginner has no chance at winning.  This is why I believe this is a Pro for Duels.
The game continues to progress!  With each real world set release, Duels also has a similar release.  This effectively keeps the game fresh.
--CONS:
Although the background music isn't terrible- in fact, sometimes it feels quite epic- I would encourage the developers to seek more variety in the theme and motifs, else it ends up feeling like Duels is caught in a slow elevator that won't stop.
There is no economy to this game- no way to trade.  Unfortunately, I believe many Magic fans may be deterred by this feature.  The inability to trade and sell cards is something that many enjoy with the tangible version of the game.
There is a game mode called "Two-Headed Giant," which although fun is very squished graphically and tends to be a chore to play through.  A sectioned background or perhaps a environment where the gamers can pan around the tabletop and zoom in/out would make the experience more enjoyable.
There aren't multiple competetive modes.  This is something that will likely change down the road as more sets are released.  I imagine the developers will have a mode equivalent to "Modern" in the the tangible version of the game.  I do hope the developers plan to release the older sets!  (I want my Pack Rats and Necrotic Oozes! ;))
--
Overall, I give this game four out of five stars, and only half a star is given because I plainly enjoy magic.  I would and do recommend this game to friends.

Oh where to begin. Most people had heard about this game once big youtubers played it and with the sudden interest, it gained enough attention to get greenlit on steam. One thing that bothered me watching them play is that I feel they didn't take the game seriously.
The Cat Lady is about Susan Ashworth, a woman suffering from depression who has decided to commit suicide. Susan is given a second chance (and immortality at that) to find a reason to live, but along the way she will meet "parasites", people who pretty much make you lose faith in humanity and are the most disgusting individuals. It is Susan's job to eliminate those parasites.
The game is made by a developer known for dark and twisted games. That style fits perfectly here. A word of caution if you did not look at the rating, there are very mature themes and sensetive material which may trigger some people. Please keep that in mind before purchasing. At times it can be hard.
The gameplay is basic like a lot of adventure games for the pc along with puzzles.
Now as for the story, it really hit home for me. As one who has struggled with depression and suicide before, I really synced with Susan and was absorbed with her tale. I wanted the best for her and I shared in her hatred of the parasites. I didn't want to stop playing until the very end. The game takes maybe 5-7 hours to finish, but keep in mind there are multiple endings and multiple choises for most situations. I have replayed several times.
I have recommended this game before to friends who didn't understand depression and how it affects someone to give them an idea. You see the suffering, the negativity, the toll it takes on someone and how it can affect their life. It can be an eye opening experience.
And I must say at the end at the final screen, I cried. I will not spoil it, but it really resonates and the end made the entire experience worth it. Highly recommended.

Ever played Silent Hill 1/2? Ever played Fatal Frame? SCP-087? Spec Ops: The Line?
These are horror games in the proper sense of the word. With the exception of Spec Ops, these are games that pit YOU, the unarmed, unequipped player against the antagonist. And in these cases, the antagonist is a fragmet of your psyche. All the machine guns in the world won't equip you for that (which is why Spec Ops is forgiven.)
How about Dark Seed? I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream?
These are "adventure," games that pit you against an unknowable and all-powerful force. This is horror, in the classic sense. You can not win. There is no victory to be attained here, the force that is against you is God-like in power. What chance is there that you could hope to win? None. Just remember that when you die, to aim your corpse in some meaningful manner.
Then there is The Cat Lady...
Then there is The Cat Lady...
You want horror? You want dark? You want real? You want a metaphysical hand to tear through your computer screen and pull your heart from your chest? It's $10. I clicked the "YES" button for my recommendation, but take that as you will. The writers of this game know fear, hate, loss, pain, addiction, suffering, suicide, alchoholism, schizophrenia, PTSD, physical and psychological abuse, and they do not dare treat these subjects with kid gloves. They dive right in.
You will not feel good during or after playing this game. You will feel bad. You will hurt, or you are a sociopath.
Find me a place I can spend $10 and feel more emotion than here, and I'll give you a ♥♥♥♥ing medal. This is Video Games as Art. As a gamer, this is our Van Gough, our Kurt Cobain, our Sylvia Plath.

The Cat Lady - while for some the name of the game might sound weird considering its theme, it is, after all, a horror game with psychological influences. You get to play Susan, a woman who attempted suicide and through some bizzare event got the superpower of immortality as she goes on to kill serial killers.
While the plot in itself might not sound that strong, the level of detail with which the events are detailed is amazing and truly realistic. The characters are quite believable in what they do and make you either love or hate them according to their actions and what they say, so the game does a fantastic job in immersing the player in it. In the end, due to this level of detail the story is saved and becomes rather interesting. The element of danger and the plot twists really complete this experience.
The graphics are not amazing, but this is a more of a 2d horror game after all. There is gore however and some nudity, so be prepared. Especially for gore, which is all over the place. So the game is 18+ (though we know you won't care about this even if you were under 18, isn't that right?)
In terms of sounds and music, I belive they fit with the theme of the story and the music usually starts at the right time and only helps you get into the story even more.
Overall, The Cat Lady shows an attention to details and an interesting story due to said details. This makes it a good game worth buying.

Level design is horrible, requiring the player to trial and error there way through to various objectives- In fact I would liken the level design to the worst parts of classic adventure games: half an hour of "is this where I need to go? No? Repeat".
Sound design may actually be worse than level design. I can put up with poorly designed levels as long as the soundtrack/scape is decent enough. Sadly, that was not the case. The game features no music (save for the few seconds of relief after completing a checkpoint worthy event) and the sound effects of "busy city center" and "bugged out generic jetpack noises" can only be listened to on continuous repeat for a maximum of five minutes before you feel like committing ear-seppuku in front of your moniter.
To sum up:
Concept is bad, level design is bad, sound design is bad, and now my ears breath their last breaths with honor intact.

I'm really enjoying Thief - I still have 2 Chapters and a handful of side missions to go.
Deadly Shadows and Dishonored are 2 of my all time favourite games; there have been a lot of comparison between Thief and those 2 games, saying that Thief falls short. But if you simply take this game for what it is, then it's still a highly enjoyable game.
The stealth game play is great; the city has a fantastic feel to it, you can customize your options more than in any other game I've played. There's masses to explore skulking around the city doing side missions, scouring every inch to find little nooks and crannies you'd previously overlooked, different ways to traverse an area, and eavesdrop on conversations for hints and clues.
The main story is slightly lacking in originality, and there are inconsistencies with the AI (sometimes they'll notice an opened chest, sometimes they won't etc.). But I'm thoroughly enjoying the game. Like I said, take it for what it is and it's a whole load of fun.
But if budget is an issue, I'd hold out until it's on offer.

So I just beat Thief (not the Bank Heist dlc) and I have to say I love the game. Not sure what to make of the ending but if it means what I think it means then I don't like it (the ending that is). The ending aside there are a multitude of ways to complete objectives (you can go pure stealth-no knockouts/kills/being spotted, hybrid-knockouts and not being seen and/or Predator-killing and taking names) and to find loot. Just keep in mind that this isn't a fighting game so if you get 3+ enemies attacking you at once..you may not survive. You can replay missions over and over again building up money (or that perfect score) so you can afford the most useful/expensive items. New items from the merchant are released as you complete missions/chapters so don't bother hoping a good one will show up randomly.
At times killing/knocking enemies out is...broken. Some instances you can knock someone out and everyone nearby will hear it while other times they can be easily within ear shot and no one notices. You'll have to experiment (save a lot in this game so if/when you mess up you aren't screwed) to find a way that works for you. Some enemies are supposed to patrol certain areas but end up bugging and not moving which can mess up a perfect run (you'll have to log-out/back-in to fix this). If you do decide to kill with bow/arrows (your blackjack(melee weapon) is also an option) make sure you're accurate because certain ammo doesn't grow on trees if you know what I mean.
Although you don't need it to play/beat the game I suggest buying the players(strategy) guide because it will show you were 98% of the loot is (yes it still misses some here and there). It does show you were ALL of the "collectibles" are (I found all of them in one run during my playthrough).
If you really want a challenge you can turn off a lot of the help thats offered in the game and add more difficulty to the game. I won't bother listing all of the options just know theres a lot you can alter.
All in all I recommend this game to those who like stealth/stealing/puzzle-solving/action and a decent story. You will enjoy yourself.

However this is at best a bland re-skin of the Civ games, lacking innovation and left me feeling flat. It's not without merits, the tech web was a great idea and I hope to see it return.
I can't recommend the game either buy one of the standard civ games which feel more cohesively designed or if you want the science fiction angle search out a copy of Alpha Centuri in my eyes it's still the superior game.

I like being able to play Magic any time for free. I don't like the timer - I have lost many a game when I had my hand off the mouse and unexpectedly needed to pause the game to cast a spell and missed my window because of the timer. I know you can't simply give players all the time they want, but dang that thing is fast. I'd suggest at least doubling the reaction timer. Also, the mana tapping is stupid. I know there *is* a way to choose what mana is tapped for each spell...but I don't know how to do it. It is not at all intuitive. I have also lost games because I trusted the computer to pick the right mana. It is often pretty good, but on occasion I get screwed. Make the game more casual-friendly by giving a little more reaction time, and a little more intuitive on the mana. What's wrong with simply clicking what lands you want to tap to add mana to your pool, and then paying all spells out of your pool rather than having the game auto-tap your land for you?

So, recently I have been on a Visual Novel trip, trying a lot of different ones. I saw this game on the front page, its free and I wanted to check it out. The art wasnt to my liking, but sometimes you find gold under a rough surface. Therefore I downloaded the free game and tried it. I havent finished it yet but im sure I will. I stopped playing and went to the forums to look how the "obvious" reactions were gonna be.
I will tell you two my honest opinion about the game, it might be hard but dont get discouraged!
Obviously the game is made by two people that just started with programming or creating a game in general. Obviously people will hate on it, give it a bad review and despise Greenlight for letting it on Steam. Its your opinion, I cant change that, even though I think it is wrong in this case.
I dont know the creators, but to me it seems like they are two teenagers making a game and showing it to the world. Therefore I can value the game as it is, a beginners project.
On to the game itself, the characters dont have much animatio (its a Visual Novel), no Voice Acting, they are mostly stereotypes that you would choose if you are interested in Anime and Manga, the English translation is kinda crappy, the characters lack depth in personality. The gameplay resolves around some dialog choices which sound crazy sometimes, the Art isnt that good and maybe just Stock Art.
All this shows how its a beginners project and in my opinion its brave to show it to other people as it will, as mentioned above, get critized for everything.
But, they shouldnt get discouraged from that and get better to realize their dreams. I still had fun while playing the game, even if it was more for the funny characters and stereotypes that I recognized.
What advice I would give is:
You can expand the game, make each job bigger and let the player actually choose different options, such as translated phrases, scans and stuff. This will add some depth to the game.
Develop the characters with more depth rework the storyline a little bit so that the story doesnt evolve that fast. As an example, there is a scene at the party after choosing a job, where like 3-4 confessions happen. It was funny due to the clichee of Anime confessions, the typical girl reaction and the frequence of them. Still its a little much for a story plot. If you want to let the player choose who gets together with who then let it start slowly over the days, which requires you to tie up all loose plot ends at the end of the game.
Rework some of the background and let the characters stand on something to not make them float around on the background. Maybe change some colours to match Items you put on them as the military hat.
Voice Acting is nice, but really, really, really hard. So just skip it at first. Rather no Voice Acting than bad voice acting.
Maybe read up on some things about Anime/Japan/Manga and make the stereotypes more subtle as in not that obvious.
As a general advice!!!
Dont let the haters get to you. Learn a programming language! Maybe befriend some young artists to get some art and continue to work on your dreams. I critized a lot, but dont let that drag you two down and keep working on your skills!
At the end, its a funny game that is free to play. Dont hate on it!
