What am I doing here?
I'll go past the glitchy black bars, the flickering paper-thin trees, and the inability to remap the controls I've experienced so far in this buggy game.
After 4 hours of play, I have to ask myself, my character "what am I doing here?," "why am I being shot at?"
You come to an island to get rid of your mom's ashes, only to be almost-killed on numerous occasions. Then, it tuns out your now-dead mom knew that would happen all along, but without a warning she planned your visit. The supposedly-insane and wild villan treats you to a nice meal and a place to rest your head, but you don't get a chance to enjoy it as a gang of gun-slinging dudes come in to "rescue" you.
After that point you are thrown into the broken world of annoying mountains and obstacles. Fighting for a goal you couldn't care less.
What am I doing in this place? Why am I helping these people? Why am I risking my life for all of this?
There's no motivation for my character to be in this place. None at all. I'm just throwing myself into battles because the game wants me to. At one point I found myself being shot at by "hunters," and I had absolutely no freakin' idea who they were or why they were trying to kill me.
All the basic elements of the genius Far Cry 3 are rehashed in this game: the towers, the outposts, the plants, and the animals. But there's no decent story, no motivation, no plot. You're just thrown into the place.
In Far Cry 3, right from the start, you were given no choice: you were forced to move on, to get stronger, to save those close to you because they were too big a part of who you are.
In Far Cry 4, you're meant to care about a dead woman you never knew, who supposedly knew you were going to meet danger but did not bother to warn you. You're meant to fight against a villan who loved your mom and who treated you nicely. It's just.... weak, dumb, and pointless.
I feel I can leave the world of Far Cry 4 at any second and nothing in my character's life would change; not for the worse at least, only for the better. Why should I care to scatter some random woman's (main character's mom) ashes in a warzone? Why should I care if some random guy (main characer's dad) was supposedly a badass at this place? Why does my characer constantly agree to risk his life to rescue a bunch of "hostages" simply because a random guy tells me to; while himself doing nothing for those hostages?
Just like Skyrim, Far Cry 4's positives are nothing by nostalgia whiffed off the previous iteration that ignore all the glaring bugs, plot holes, and lack of characterization.
I'm glad Far Cry 3  was great. It was amazing. It's the only justification I can give myself for spending $100 on the buggy, rushed, and barely-thought-through Far Cry 4.
All good things must come to an end, I guess. Far Cry 4 is the coffin of Far Cry 3.
--------
After waiting for critical bug fixes and buying a new, 16:9 monitor to fix the black bars issues, I've actually played and completed this game.
I suppose 60 hours of entertainment (and more, since I'll likely play it again in the future) justify the $100 I paid for the full super-duper edition. But it's an incredibly lazy re-hash of Far Cry 3 and it shows and that's what annoys me. It could've been an amazing Top-All-Time game if UbiSoft spent another year on it.
I've came across many bugs and glitches that look like problems swept under the rug by the devs/quality assurance team. The unlocks are incredibly unbalanced: you get a ton of unlocks at one time, then nothing for a long period. You get the best guns almost at the start of the game, so there's no point in getting any of the other ones. And the best and most fun gun to take out the outposts with is locked until you've completed 23 out 24 outposts. Ridiculous.
The writing is abhorrent. It serves no other purpose than to interrupt your pillaging of outposts. I didn't hate the villan: he was just a dictator, subjugating the people I didn't care about. I suppose it's bad, but should I do something about it? I didn't like the protagonists: they're obnoxious, ugly, and incessantly cry for help. Most of the missions you're told to do something while they all sit somewhere comfy. You're supposed to care for Kyrat because it's your birthplace, but you're constantly being told that you left when you were very young and you don't remember any of it. Should I care about a piece of land that was proximate to my mother's womb when I was born? Please!
The choices you make with the two supposed leaders of the Golden Path are non-choices. At one point I had to decide whether to side with Amita and keep the drug fields to make money to rebuild Kyrat or to side with Sabal and burn the field down because it's "not who we are." But that's a non-choice! I'm not given any alternative on how to rebuild Kyrat if we destroy the drugs. Amita says without the drugs we'll live in poverty and Sabal makes no counterargument!
The details of the choices are moot, however, because they have absolutely no impact at the end.
Speaking of the end, what a load of manure it is! You can definitely find the various endings on YouTube, but the one I ended up with didn't even resolve the initial conflict. The very reason why my character decided to stay in Kyrat instead of legging it! I killed the bad gun with a boring shot to the head from a pistol during a cutscene and instantly it faded and I was shown "FIN." What about tea-bagging the guy? Good grief!
Lazy. Obnoxious. Pallid. An overpriced reskin of Far Cry 3, to be enjoyable by people who loved Far Cry 3.

This game's not for everyone. It features violence, nudity and gore to some extent - despite the graphic design, it's still rather extreme. Use caution when playing with kids or underaged teen.
That said, the game also is good at presenting story, helped by good voice actors (notably Susan Asworth - our protagonist, and Mitzi) that perform and convey emotion of the characters they portray very well. The Cat Lady brings a good plot from the start and it revolves over time the deeper you go.
Gameplay is simple as it's a basically a point and click game. Some puzzles, however, made me scratch my head. With the ultimate weapon called walkthrough it's not a big deal though. :)
If you're going to do full achievements, do note that basically it's almost impossible getting everything in one playthrough, especially since you have to choose the dialoges/options at the correct time at the correct order.
Also there's an annoying bug as this time of writing: The caption is not complete. After Chapter 5 ends, there's no more English sub. If you're not an English native speaker like me this can be troublesome, as the main point of playing is following the story. Being unable to read what the characters have to say can be irksome as you'll be unable to understand the story. I hope this will be fixed with patch.
Edit: It's confirmed that pressing 'T' disables/enables subs. I am yet to check as I already uninstalled the game so can't confirm with my Chapter 6 saves - will check back later.
Replayability... almost none. Unless you want to see different outcome at the end of the game or, as I said, get achievements. Even then, only last chapters that matter. The game's quite fast with saves, so use this for your advantage: save as many times as possible, so you can quickly revert to the old saves if you want.
The game would've been taking benefit from full controller support. What's better than sit back and relax with controller in your hands and play the game? The Cat Lady is just perfect to be played that way. Sadly, there's no controller support, but you can utilize Joy2Key which is fairly simple to setup and get you controller support in game. You only need to setup directional buttons, confirm and cancel. That's all.
All in all, this is a niche game. As I said, not for everyone (kids included). But if you want a deep, engaging story, with good characters development game, this one is for you.

The Cat Lady is a brilliant game, a true work of art, and an experience with the potential to be quite affecting. As a survivor of depression, I can say that the atmosphere of the game is spot on, and my gaming experience was incredibly uplifting - though I would warn others to think carefully about their own triggers and current mental state before diving in, as the depictions of depression and suicide are very realistic.
It's an intense game that speaks to the deepest parts of the human psyche, and a powerful example of the potential of computer games as art.

The Cat Lady tells the tale of Susan Ashworth, a woman pushed to suicide by the events of her life. However, once dead, she meets up with a mysterious figure called the Queen of Maggots who has bigger plans for Susan... namely, pitting her against five serial killers, aka Parasites. Susan really has no choice in the matter: in fact, she cannot die until she kills all of the Parasites. With that, The Cat Lady begins, a macabre little game that is surprisingly touching while still being spooky.
Above all else, The Cat Lady's art style is one of its best features. Objects are put together in a collage-like style, with color used to set the mood (and often effectively). Combined with the soundtrack, which ranges from death metal(?) to eerie creaking, breathing and heartbeats, it's all too easy to set the average player on edge for some of the scarier scenes. Make no mistake, this game doesn't rely on jumpscares to get your pulse racing. Rather, your own unsettled nature becomes your own worst enemy. For a game with an unkillable protagonist, still making a player scared is quite an accomplishment.
Still, those worried about the scariness shouldn't pass up this game. Underneath the 'horror' aspect is a moving story about death, depression, and the various ways of coping with both. Both Susan and sidekick Mitzi are highly empathetic characters and it won't take most players long to get attached to both of them. The game does suffer from a few moments of melodrama, but they're short and easily forgotten.
Overall, if you're looking for a story driven game with plenty of the macabre, and you don't mind a little horror mixed in, The Cat Lady might just be for you. And if not... pick it up anyways.

There are almost always multiple ways to progress and the game allows for many different playstyles. The story is really what keeps me playing though. Each new situation is like a game of chess, you need to move this way as a guard moves that way. As I am about to complete my first playthrough I realize how much fun this game when it's challenging. I turned off most of my HUD (except lock-pick indicator and waypoint marker)  and I highly recommend it if you want the advertised feeling of true immersion.
To conclude, this game can be great or bad depending on how YOU want to play it. Want to play on normal difficulty? Prepare for a mundane, short, less rewarding experience. Want to challenge yourself on Master and turn off a lot of the HUD? Then you'll have a dangerous environment filled with scares and strategies each time you open a door or turn a corner.
This being said, I encourage those who enjoy a challenging, first-person singleplayer to check out Thief!!!

Thief is a very solid and enjoyable game. BUT here's my advice: don't play it with the default settings (they are too "handholdy" and the source of much of the criticism it got).
You'll get a very immersive experience if you turn off all the HUD elements (well, maybe except the bow aiming reticule and the mini-map), and try to use Focus Mode only when you're really stuck. That way the experience is much more open, as you'll have to explore carefully your surroundings to advance, and won't have to worry about the game telling you constantly what you can or can't do.
Another good idea is to turn down a bit the brightness setting. The guards won't be able to see you even if you put your nose in their eye, but at least the darkness looks a bit more realistic.
And my last advice: turn off the music!! It's not that great and in my opinion it takes you out of the immersion. Also, you'll be able to trace the guards listening to the sound of their steps.

As a fan of the series I was very worried by the early footage of this game and felt pretty sure they were going to ruin the series.  Fortunately they do seem to have corrected a lot of issues such that I feel I can recommend the game, but it's definitely worth noting there are problems.
For those who want a brief summary, here's the short version first.  The game lacks polish, the level design isn't always up to par, dialogue gets repetitive at times and the story is just annoying and thoroughly awful.  It feels like 30 different people all want to tell their story and you get an incoherent noise where you can pick up some ideas from different stories.  That said, the game is still at its heart a Thief game.  If you want a traditional stealth game you can definitely find it here, especially with the remarkable amount of customisation available, and the actual gameplay itself is sufficient that I would recommend looking past the problems.
So this Thief game is a series reboot which means that there is no story you're missing if you're new to the series.  There are some nods to older fans but nothing particularly relevant.  There is a central hub city where routes through open up as you advance through the main missions and there is a reasonable amount of exploration and side missions to be found.  The missions, and bigger side quests, all take place in separate levels you access by finding them around the city.
The design of the mission areas is hit and miss, with some fairly competent design let down by other areas clearly influenced by the earlier path the game was taking and, frustratingly, late in the game there are boss fights which is never a good thing in a stealth game.  Given they don't break character by forcing an actual altercation it isn't as terrible as it could have been, they all the same feel frustratingly out of place and should at least be a consequence of gameplay rather than something you just have to live with.
Another, more significant addition to the game is focus mode.  With this you can look around your world to highlight loot, hidden buttons or things you can use.  It can also be upgraded to provide a lot of additional upgrades in pickpocketing and lock picking, combat and stealth mechanics.  Whilst I welcome the mechanic being available to help people through the game and make it less frustrating, if you're really in to stealth games you're going to find it makes things a bit easy as the game goes on, especially as you can use it when your focus meter is empty whenever you want to get a lingering highlight of the important things in the world. Fortunately it can be disabled, but only when you're selecting starting difficulty settings.
Customisation is really the strongest part of the game and really sets a standard I'd like to see in more games.  First the PC port of this game has a great options menu with everything you could really want.  The options continue though in the difficulty of the game, with 3 base difficulties but also custom options you can use to tailor the game to what you want.  A few examples include disabling focus mode, no kills or knockouts, no alerts allowed and many more up to even Iron Man where failing or dying means you have to start from the beginning of the game.  The game continues though, with every single element of the HUD being able to be turned off (including loot glint and lock pick help) or being given a timed fade away for things like health bars.  You really can set this game up how you want it and it's remarkable in that sense.
Several other aspects of the game are done very well; the character feels like they're really in the world, with the use of limbs and the way the character interacts with things giving a real sense of there really being a person there.  You can learn quite a bit about the world by eavesdropping, spying on people and some reasonably well written documents and it feels reasonably organic.  The swoop feature (where you quietly dash forward) also feels really good to use and actually adds rather well to some tense stealth sections.
The AI in the game is sometimes quite good, noticing things on their patrol route have been opened and being reasonably consistent in its detection of you or otherwise.  Other times though it will bug out, will get stuck on doors, not notice really obvious things, or notice really unobvious things such as you, through a wall, one floor down, in the shadows.  It's usually alright but sometimes feels a bit under-polished, which is a phrase that would describe a lot of the game quite well unfortunately.
The world sometimes feels a bit lifeless, people have set paths with very limited dialogue options that repeat annoyingly often - you will sometimes hear 3 or 4 guards in a row repeat the exact same thing.  Some rather useful information is hidden in loading screens, such as pressing X to let go of ropes, which leads to perfectly functioning aspects of the game feeling annoying.  Sometimes your character will drop off ledges; sometimes you need to use the drop button.  Sometimes you can leave vents; sometimes you will need to try repeatedly.  Sometimes you will loot the draw with a context sensitive button; sometimes it'll move away and look around a corner with the same context sensitive button.  These kinds of things give the game the feeling of just not quite being finished.
Finally, the biggest problem with the game is the story, it damages the game.  For one thing it starts pretty bad and just gets worse every single time there is some major advancement in it.  It's so focussed on someone it's very difficult to care about that it is annoying to experience, and to make things worse because you're driven by it you're not so much going to places to steal from them, you're stealing from them on the way through.  As a result of this approach you spend a lot more time stealing cutlery than planning a big heist.  The bank heist DLC comes the closest to this ideal and really shows the potential the game really did have when unencumbered by the mess that is the story.
I appreciate this review sounds quite negative; indeed there is a lot to be negative about.  It is the weakest game in the series, but with its great customisation options you can still find a Thief game in it.  It is, at its heart, a rather competent stealth game and if you're a fan of the genre you will definitely get something out of it.  You do need to look past its rough edges though.

For a person like me, who first played Gran Turismo as a kid, up to this point, I wasn't sure what to expect of this, except...The visuals looked pretty good. I would be understating this game. Oh, yes. So, here I'll give my opinion of the game, of what I've played so far, and make what you think of it, take my word or not.
-Firstly, the Graphics.
Forza 4 has some pretty solid graphics, as a comparison, and though it came out before this did, I'll say that is holds up well in that respect. But this is better. MUCH better. Even when I played this on my older laptop, on a lower setting where the shapes and oddities were of quality expected in something from the early 2000s Racing Games....it's not of that level, not even close. Believe me, the shine on the car, to the reflections of the streetlights, the crowd....It's breathtaking to the eyes.
-The Sounds.
Probably the strongest suit Grid 2 has to offer. Taking this as an example, the RX-7's rotary sound in-game...it's the closest engine note i've heard to the irl thing. And I'm not saying this out of bias, because Gran Turismo covers the sound good, too. BUT when the car is idle....It sounds realistic. Engine sounds are a plus here, and the atmosphere of the various fireworks...I literally have not had another Racing game like this where they've taken the time to get the engine note down to the wire like this.
-Price
I got Grid 2 when it was on sale, and that's what you should probably aim for, in case you want it. Not saying it's worth cheap, but it'll help, because the DLC in this game is pretty nice, considering you get to unlock all of the in-game vehicles for Online mode. Which is great with friends, btw.
-Physics
A friend of mine was pointing this out, and...despite the great sounds and graphics....the cars still tend to flop around aimlessly. Like...that's understandable in Dirt Rally, because that particular sport is crazy already. Heh. But in here, it's mostly circuit racing and various styles as such. So having a 3000+ pound vehicle toppling side-over-side off of a cliff like as if it was a Domino? Eh....No thank you.

This review will contain some spoilers. They will be marked with the spoiler tag.
As with my review for fault: milestone one, I should preface this review by saying that, generally speaking, I dislike visual novels: I usually find the writing in them to be ear-gratingly awful: bland, gutless protagonists, dialogue that points out the obvious, characters who announce their feelings, and unnecessary flashbacks -- these are among the visual novel-isms that I truly loathe.
And yet fault: milestone two manages to commit none of these missteps. In fact, it vastly exceeded my expectations.
If fault: milestone one is a diamond in the rough, then fault: milestone two is where the writing was tempered and then honed to a fine edge. I am incredibly impressed with the leaps and bounds by which the storytelling has improved -- particularly the development that Selphine's character undergoes.
fault: milestone two isn't afraid to ask the questions that matter, nor is it shy about bringing its strong ideas about culture, ethics, and politics to the forefront once more, letting the unyielding logic behind the world the characters live in drive them to think about, discuss, and act upon the implications of this world's rules where human nature is concerned.
Instead of a lot of meaningless dialogue, characters often speak concisely and say interesting things that -- gasp! -- only hint at what's really on their minds instead of saying it outright! Imagine that. Certain character interactions even give you the strong impression that the two characters are intellectually duelling with one another, which makes for engaging and subtle characterization.
I think I may be in love with her.
Some dialogue in fault is genuinely horrifying and all-too-real -- in good ways. There's a grounded verisimilitude throughout the visual novel, despite the fantastical setting. If a character was unsettling, I felt my blood run cold; if a character was downtrodden by circumstance, I felt their justified anger; if characters had a heartfelt scene, I was tenderly moved. I cannot praise enough fault's skilled use of dialogue in characterization.
The music is as good as the first chapter -- if not better -- and the sound design is impressive. There are background sounds that add some real cinematic ambiance to certain scenes.
I am happily delighted with how wonderful -- and oftentimes surprising -- fault: milestone two could be. If you like stories with likeable, interesting characters and intriguing, complex concepts, you will enjoy this visual novel.
Like it even more than the first game.

Because this is a long review, I will stick a TLDR at the bottom.
fault - milestone two side:above is a sequel to fault milestone one. If you have not played fault milestone one, I strongly recommend that you play that game first, lest you risk being completely lost in what is going on. fault - milestone two side:above is a medium length kinetic visual novel (very like fault milestone one). When I mean kinetic visual novel, I mean that there are no choices in the game, and you simply click and read as the game progress. However, fret not, because fault milestone two does a very good job in many regards. fault milestone 2 side:above was actually meant to be half a game, but for game length and pricing concerns, it was split up into the first half of fault milestone 2.
The story follows the travels of Selphine, Ritona, and Rune as they try to return home (Okay no more otherwise I'll be spoiling >:), and I wouldn't want to do that). The storytelling improved in fault milestone 2 from fault milestone 1. The pacing got better at times, and once again, there is a great deal of world building. In fault milestone 2, Selphine and Rune both really recieved a great deal of further character development. Selphine's character development really stood out in the second half of the visual novel, be it her or not her (you'll see what I mean). It is hard to tell some more without spoiling certain parts, but I will just say that the story deals with complex and deep things while still staying true to the series. There is a bittersweet story near the end once again, and at the very end there is a rather heartwarming mini-movie (a couple of drawings paired as a story). Overall, the story of fault milestone 2 did not dissapoint, and I will look forward to more great things from the next installments.
Aside from the story, fault milestone two side:above also features a great upgrade to the art. There are more scenes, that are better quality, and with more variety. The art is only going to get better in the future. Oh, and what about the music? The music for  this game was even better than fault milestone one in my opinion. Some of the scenes were very fitting, and I enjoyed the last song the most (the one that comes with the mini-movie, it's really good in a calming way). It is really nice seeing the staff responsible for creating the fault series improve as people like me and all the other people who played this game support them. We can only expect even better installments.
Speaking about the staff and developer, it is also worth mentioning that the Alice in Dissonance community is also starting to thrive. I joined their Discord around one year ago, back when it was still relatively small, and now it has grown to a much bigger level. Same goes for the Steam group. There is a community of people sprouting around this game, supporting it, and supporting each other. This doesn't always happen with many games, and for all I care, this is great.
TLDR: You lazy♥♥♥♥♥ well here it is. fault - milestone two side:above is a great sequal to fault - milestone one that has a good story, art, music, and community

I've always been known to be depressed since I was a teenager and tonight was another sleepless night. It was 5am when I started this game. I picked options similar to my own thoughts and all I could think was, "Wow, stay out of my head, Charles." What I like about this game is how it shows that depression isn't always as obvious as showing sadness. It can simply be apathy or coming to the conclusion that everything feels pointless, nothing is going to improve. The characters you interact with are archetypes of those I've had to deal with(or avoid.) Another thing the game helps to show are the preconcieved notions one may have about others from ruminating so often. There may not be much leeway with the options you are given and how things turn out, but the basics are there. Be aware that there are people out there who have worse things in life to deal with that aren't showcased in Depression Quest. This game just conveys one person's journey, but I think the main point it's trying to get across is that even a person that you think is normal may become depressed.
Not exactly a fun game nor one filled with entertaining graphics or sound effects, but it gives plenty of insight if you're willing to take it seriously. It's mainly just text, so don't get too excited. If you've never been one to be depressed, you might think, "Wow, what a whiny little sap!" Stop. It's people like you who make it harder to say anything. It's an interesting read and it's free. I'd make my parents play it, but they're not fluent in English and I doubt they'd want to understand. This War of Mine is a micromanagement simulator. You are given several survivors and a shelter to maintain and upgrade. You must manage survivor's health, food supply, shelter heating, and supplies for crafting to further your survival. Crafting is a huge gameplay component and you spend half the game scavenging materials from various locations outside your shelter. Outside your shelter, different scenarios play out presenting the player with decisions; decisions that greatly affect your survivor's moral compass, happiness and health.
The goal of the game is to make the player feel the sadness and rawness of war. To this end, the game employs a heavy, dark shading filter that works hand in hand with the music to provide a solemn ambience. Combined with the character's happiness meter and moral compass, decisions to kill or rob for survival cannot be made lightly.
I believe This War of Mine excels in achieving this goal through the scenarios, the semi-realistic dialog and difficult choices. Through these, the player must live with the consequences of their actions or inactions.
10/10.

What blew it, however, at least for me, was the endless loading screens you had to get through in order to travel in The City.

A > Travel for 20 sec - reach gate, game pauses, get asked if you want to proceed to next area > 30 sec Loading Screen > B > Travel for 20 sec - reach gate, game pauses, get asked if you want to proceed to next area > 40 sec Loading Screen > C > Travel for 20 sec - reach gate, game pauses, get asked if you want to proceed to next area > 30 sec Loading Screen > D > Finally Arrived.

It's an interesting and fun current generation stealth game, but it definitely could not achieve what the original series did. It simply does not live up to it in many key aspects (main character, story-telling, player freedom). I don't say it is a bad game, because it is not. I'd even say that it is a good one, but potentially it could have been so much more. It is very apparent that the game was developed with love and care and lots of enthusiasm, but it feels like the developers wanted to grasp too much and wanted to please too many kind of tastes. Also it feels a bit of a product which was constantly pushed and pulled between different producers with totally different ideas about what it should be (it shows especially in the script-writing department and on some level in the gameplay-design). But again, it is entertaining, fun to play and I hope that they will continue the series after learning from their mistakes and the reactions of the critics and the gamer community.

The Cat Lady succeeds in engrossing you where so many AAA titles have failed in the past in a way in which baffles and confuses me even an hour after finishing the game. It's one of those rare experiences akin to Gone Home that has a snowball effect when it comes to character and plot development, taking you on a rollercoaster ride of emotions that seems to only build on itself faster by the minute as it comes to what I considered a timely conclusion.
Another aspect of this game that reminded me of Gone Home was how it managed to make me somehow relate and feel connected to the protagonist, even though I myself am a 27 year old male with a fairly positive outlook on life and the character is a middle aged woman with rather sad case of depression (for good reason as you will find out later in the game). Adding to its ambiance is an exceptional soundtrack, that while being a bit rough around the edges is so in such a way that lends itself to the art style of the game.
The way in which the plot revealed her background story kept me intrigued, and is delivered in such a way that you are thrown into a situation wondering "what the hell just happened" but don't have to wait too long to fill in the gaps and arrive at the "Aha!" moment.
The game is obviously not without its quirks, many times I was presented with duplicated voice loops and the setup utility/screen resolution options are largely useless, however none of these problems ruined the atmosphere for me. I personally would have like the use of the mouse in the save menu and did have the game crash once during my play through.
In summary I would recommend this game to anyone that considers a great video game experience to be more than just a sum of its parts, what the developers have managed to do with an outdated game engine, low res graphics and a keyboard only control scheme has somehow evolved into one of the best gaming experiences I've had in my life.

It's no surprise that horror games are dark and morbid in nature, but Cat Lady affects you on a more cerebral and emotional level than the average horror game. Certain aspects of the game will haunt you and really stay with you, even after you're done playing. The themes introduced in this game are heavy and highly mature. Never before have a seen a game which deals with suicide and depression in such a personal and well-informed way, without being exploitative, either. This game doesn't need a huge budget or fancy graphics to convey its message properly; it has a powerful style that shifts between surrealistic art and dreary black and white photography. The voice acting is well done (most notably with Susan and Mitzi), which is a big positive considering the game itself is very dialogue-based. The puzzles are challenging, while fitting naturally into the flow of the gameplay. Can't recommend it enough, and I'm looking forward to what comes next from Harvester Games!

I think this is important as part of the allure of the other civilisation games is reliving the centuries with the discoveries, units, etc.  Because this is Sci-fi and based on the future, it removes allot of familiarity with the playable races, but it also means it has an oppertunity to be more creative.
-Unlike Civ V, Diplomacy is more than just a trading of goods and safe passage.  Diplomacy feels more fleshed out, and in ways you are more/less in control of it as your choices reflect the happiness of other races, but you can also control to what degree.  I feel that Civ V, though a great game, was not so much a diplomatic game, at least not without it's expansions.
-PVE is more a thing in Beyond Earth as it's more than just barbarians, there is a multitude of alien creatures that may (or may not) attack you.  This makes exploration more dangerous, but also more thrilling/rewarding.
My only concern of this game is that it only had one expansion, and although the setup was amazing, I feel it required allot more fleshing out than what it recieved.  Arguably I feel that would of been the same for Civ V, but as Civ V was more famliar due to its connections to the other Civ games, it didn't suffer as much as Beyond Earth did.  It's a shame because all in all it was the same game but different theme, and if more investment and time went into this game, it could of becoming a very fascinating game to play and arguably may of achieved a similar rank to Civ V.
I would definately say the biggest downfall of this game is that it's the future, so immediately it loses its familiarity in playing the game, identifying characters, scenes, and basically our history.  Because of this it had to be exciting enough to have the mechanics of the other Civ games but be entirely different at the same time, and it was just a gamble that people did not wish to explore.
It particular saddens me that Civ VI is out and again it's gone back to using our history and familiarity as the theme content of the game.
Give the game a try with an open mind, it' is Civ mechanics, but the theme is one that is more out there than our history.
this being the next game in the series after civ 5, it is incredibly disappointing =[

Here’s the best way I can describe Civ BE. It’s like you’ve just won a science victory in Civ V but could only take Modern Era tech with you, and only to discover that other civs that lagged behind in science caught up and made the trip as well, bringing the variety of conflicting ideologies with them. So you have to redevelop planes, satellites, missiles and navies even if that wasn’t what got you a science victory. These technologies are obscured by separation and by the attitudes that would develop within communities that have had to adopt an alien world, fully aware of the consequences that industrial development had on Earth. So rather than simply research a new technology exactly as a person on Earth would have in its particular history, you discover it within the context of this alien place that can preserve the old way of life or reject it outright, and it will be this balance between accepting or rejecting Earth that will decide the shape your units will take, and the ways you can effectively 4X. Besides Domination, every victory type is tied to not only researching a given technology and building a particular wonder, but also the way in which that wonder will demand you construct your society a particular way to fulfill its victory conditions.
(If you already have Beyond Earth and were bored with it, I can't recommend Rising Tide enough. The game's diplomacy has been revamped, there's an artifact system that is begging to be to turned into a fully fledged inventory/crafting system, and water combat makes it feel like more of a futuristic Civ, as you can cozy up to your rivals by moving your cities right to their border. If you haven't played Beyond Earth at all, this review is a reflection of the game as a whole now that Rising Tide has been added.)
If you liked combat in Civ V, and are willing to spend a bit of time learning a made up sci-fi tech tree where a lot of the complexity is buried, then I have to believe you’ll like Beyond Earth in its current form, though like Civ V that does involve also buying the Rising Tide expansion.
The reason why I say you probably need to like combat is that at least on moderate to higher difficulties, you can’t win if you don’t at least understand how to defend whatever map you’re expanding into (which often have a lot more impassable terrain than a Civ V map would have). I suppose this is how every 4X works, but because combat gets so versatile in the late game you just can’t ignore it. Cities are sacked very easily at first, though it’s easy to buy defensive buildings right after it’s settled. Once hover vehicles and orbital attack/healing platforms become available, you can effectively deploy anywhere on the map, which also means you can be attacked. So even if you bottleneck navy or ground forces, you can’t neglect air and space combat (which is where another expansion should focus) though it does seem limited and shallow with the options available to you early in the game.
A problem I’ve always had with Civ is how little happens in the early game for how long it takes. In Beyond Earth, you’ll face a lot of the same drag. So many turns seem to be dedicated to revealing the map and navigating alien life, deciding if you want to clear them like barbarians or keep them around as a buffer and eventually a domesticated asset. This would be fine if it didn’t feel like having to jump back to the Ancient Era with its tutorial pace, if there was some diversity to exploration or conservation. But for the most part every Civ will play very similarly until they’ve started to diverge through affinities, at which point the real character of the game has a chance to take shape.
There are two kinds of unit diversity: the units themselves, and then the upgrades they get that are unique to each affinity. The order in which you research new technologies determines how these affinities develop, with universal bonuses for each level. But upgrades for your units will become tied to which affinity levels are reached first. If you balance your research, you can hand select the kind of upgrades you want, but if you try to rush a particular victory type or tech, you’ll develop an affinity sooner than you do the others and this will limit the upgrades you [must] choose, which also changes the way your units play. Things like detect invisible units, damage bonus for adjacent troops, passive healing, extra range, ability to carry planes, etc. If you focus on certain affinities, you will begin to reflect the particular characteristics of that ideology down to the way your units and cities are presented aesthetically.
I wish there was tech trading, either through whole units or just modular upgrades that you could acquire from other cultures, but as it is I do like the way you develop shapes the gameplay.
Finally, the Rising Tide expansion is necessary because in addition to naval cities that can secure territory by moving along coastal tiles, it revamps the diplomacy system in a way that makes the use of force seem like a bargaining chip. If you can destroy someone’s infrastructure to the point they surrender, you literally decide what spoils you want to take from them — including outposts/cities — if you have a high enough war score, which you gain by killing units or capturing outposts. So even if you’re not looking to dominate your opponents, you can use combat to coax them into giving you other things you didn’t focus on.
Also, as mentioned above, there is an artifact system that adds variety to what wonders you can construct if you're willing to explore and find the components. The system is pretty basic, really just exploration site bonuses, but it seems like an easy place to start modding, which the developers have provided a tool for the game in general. This is probably where we'll see the game get new life going forward, but that's not always a bad thing. There's arguably more combat unit diversity in Beyond Earth than there was in Civ V, and it wouldn't be hard to implement Great People or something akin to missionaries. The game isn't Alpha Centauri, but I have to believe it's only one big expansion away from being something else that's even better.
Suggestions (or my bucket list of mods to make since the toolkit included with the game seems pretty useful):
-Automated movement of orbital units similar to trade convoys and/or orbital units that actually follow orbitals into other territory
-Polar transit
-Canal building and landfilling
-More impact from climate and more variables to affect surivivability, perhaps according to map type
-Multi-map carryover [I have not played Starships so can't speak to the integration]
-More military automation

Hammerwatch is a great top down dungeon crawler if you're into fast and easy gameplay. There is no inventory to manage, no skills to juggle and the visual style is clean and easy to parse. The gameplay moves fast, and each of the classes is unique enough to keep the game fresh enough to replay. Chaining combos gets really fun and exciting, especially at higher levels.
The music is really nice, but does get a bit repetitive after a while.
Local co-op is possible, but kind of a pain unless you and your buddies stay fairly close together. Online co-op is a little confusing at first, and I see that others have had issues with it, but my friends and I have been sucessful and getting a party together. Once you're in the game, it's smooth sailing.
I suggest that you play the game with a controller. Keyboard controls are kind of uncomfortable, but this may just be my personal preference.

The first two milestones in the fault series have been a fantastic ride so far. The story and artwork are beautiful, the stakes feel real, and the cast really grows on you over time. It should be noted there are no choices to be made in this series, and it isn't so much of a game as a several hour anime almost, meaning there's not much replayability; this makes you wonder if it's worth the relatively hefty price (at full price). If you can get the game on sale, it's definitely worth a buy, and that gets you into the story; at this point, when milestone 3 comes out, I'll probably be happy to drop the full price to continue the journey.

I do wonder whether it actually achieves the goal of allowing people who have never dealt with this to get a better insight, but I'm still glad it exists. And I'm especially glad that emphasis is given on allowing outsiders to get a glimpse into how the "spoon theory" (wiki it) affects people with depression in their every day life. This War of Mine is a micromanagement simulator. You are given several survivors and a shelter to maintain and upgrade. You must manage survivor's health, food supply, shelter heating, and supplies for crafting to further your survival. Crafting is a huge gameplay component and you spend half the game scavenging materials from various locations outside your shelter. Outside your shelter, different scenarios play out presenting the player with decisions; decisions that greatly affect your survivor's moral compass, happiness and health.
The goal of the game is to make the player feel the sadness and rawness of war. To this end, the game employs a heavy, dark shading filter that works hand in hand with the music to provide a solemn ambience. Combined with the character's happiness meter and moral compass, decisions to kill or rob for survival cannot be made lightly.
I believe This War of Mine excels in achieving this goal through the scenarios, the semi-realistic dialog and difficult choices. Through these, the player must live with the consequences of their actions or inactions.
10/10.

The play style of The Cat Lady is simple and intuitive. The entire game is controlled with the keyboard – left and right arrow keys to move, up to examine objects and areas of interest, down to select items in your inventory, and enter to select an option. The interface is minimal as well, with just a bar across the bottom of the screen to display items you’ve collected.
I really enjoyed that this game was side-scrolling. The ability to actually control Susan, rather than scanning a cursor all around the screen as in traditional, point-and-click adventure games, made the game a much more engaging, organic experience. This isn’t♥♥♥♥♥♥talking point-and-clicks in any way – the ability to navigate Susan through the nightmarish environments just made the game feel a lot more personal, and less zoomed-out, which works since The Cat Lady is more about your interaction with others than solving elaborate puzzles.
The Cat Lady is not a game about ridding the world of evil. It’s about accepting that sometimes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s rough, but you have to find your happiness in spite of it all. It’s about learning to smile in the face of horror, and realizing that your fear of others is just a result of your own weakness.
I don’t have much of a conclusion other than GO GET THE CAT LADY. It’s a unique and engaging experience that I would hate to see fly under the radar. It’s definitely in my top games that I've played this year. If you like adventure games, cats, horror, good writing, and stuff with explicit content warnings at the beginning, this is the game for you!

Let me say that i am not a big fan of the adventure genre. But this game... Dear god, it is amazing. From the diverse cast of characters, to the cleverly crafted riddles all the way to it's sick and disturbing story and atmosphere, this game will grab and hold on to you untill you finish it. If you do not like the Adventure genre, do not be afraid. This is more of a Heavy Rain type of game, like an interactive story but will puzzles and riddles that, although not always easy, only require to use logic to solve. Kudos to the creator for bringing something different in terms of story and visuals to the genre.
The Cat Lady is a Mystery/Horror Adventure game. I will not go into much detail about the story, but i must warn you that there is a lot of violent and disturbing imagery that you rarely find in a video game, but there is a reason for all of it, and it is so expertly crafted that your heart will keep pounding until the next chapter, and will keep you wanting for more.
The visuals have a unique personality, a good blend of black and white and various other colors to flesh out specific images. They do an extremely good job at giving you a sense of depression and decay, adding a great deal to the atmosphere of the game. The characters and, especialy, the backrounds are well drawn, however the animation could have been alot better. But it is understandable, since this game is the work of one man for the most part, and animations are very hard to do.
The music and sound effects are also excellent, creepy and eerie, keeping you on guard constantly. From creeking doors to footsteps from the floor above, they create a feeling of constant danger, never letting the player rest.
I highly recommend this game. Even if you do not like the genre you should definetly take a look at this, since the gameplay and story are unique and can be played by everyone, not just hardcore adventure fans. Give it a shot and i am sure you will be pleasantly surprised.

The Cat Lady is a point and click style game designed for use with arrow keys or wads. The game offers a bizarre yet emotional story line with puzzles (that are mostly straight foward) and randomness with lots of dialogue. The more you play the more you start to paint of a picture of the main character, Susan Ashowrth (The Cat Lady) is a deeply despressed, troubled, suicidal and lonely indivudal who gets hurled into a world of madness, make believe and death.
It took me just over 9 hours to complete my first play through and I believe I would play it again in the future. My playthrough was personal and depended on answers that I opted for during the game. Though for the most part the story is the same there are times that the story changes depending on your answers and replies, this makes for great individual gaming though being similar enough to follow a walk through if needed. Also depending on which way you go you have the opportunity to unlock special hidden achievements.
While this may not be the most active game and patience is a virtue I believe this game makes wonderful weekend playing or in-between games. For some you can feel free to sit back as though you are watching a film, with the odd click here or there as to your dialogue choices. Other times your solving puzzles and walking back and forth trying to deal with Susans new found crazy life. I woulc recommend this game to anyone that is interested in heart felt, moving games that doesn't mind dealing with a lot of dialogue. For such a cheap price I'm sure you will find it worth the chance of playing something worth while.

This a review for both parts of Fault Milestone released so far.
As much as I love adventure games, I’m not too hot on VNs. Most are cliché-ridden fap-bait and the genre’s overall quality is so abysmally low that even some of the ones people laud aren’t even that good to begin with. (*coughdanganronpaandzeroescapecough*) But Fault Milestone is one of the few that I feel is good. Mind you that it does dip into the anime trope well heavily, but this isn’t a detriment for the game in how it uses them. It's rarely ever creepy and there are no high schools in sight for example.
Fault Milestone is a fantasy story and right from the start it goes in fast and loose with seemingly amateur hour fantasy terms (It’s Manacravt, not manacraft), but it gets better from there. Fault Milestone’s strengths is that it has a likable cast and an interesting world. It’s pretty slow paced too, but I kind of like that, the main plot is always looming in the background, but Fault Milestone goes out of its way to develop is characters and world. It’s not mindblowing stuff or anything, but it’s engaging and entertaining. Neither part really moves the main plot, so keep that in mind, but as I said they take their time exploring everything else so it’s not a really bad thing. The character art is a little bit stock sterile modern anime, but the enviroments look good. The music is really good too.
So in conclusion, if you’re actually looking for a good VN look no further than Fault Milestone. I just hope the next part actually comes out…

Short Review
Gameplay: 8/10 (better than most)
Graphics: 10/10 (stunning)
Mechanics: 7/10 (best played with a controller... keyboarding a selection wheel is a bit awkward)
Music: 4/10 (annoying as hell unless you have a red dot on your forehead)
Co-Op: 7/10 (needs more but works pretty well with what it has currently)
Attacking killer eagles: -5/10  (fuq those eagles)
Long Review
So no surprise, FC4 is exactly like FC3... which is not at all a bad thing.  First of all, the game is gourgeous... long gone seem to be the days when beautiful cutscenes gave way to dismal graphics during the actual gameplay.  This game, to say the very least, is visually stunning. The new environment seems to work well (although you do have to suspend reality a few times-- crocodiles at high altitudes in the Himmalayns?)  Gamers with moderate PCs will be pleasantly surprised by medium graphics settings but of course, to truly take it all in, the highest settings are where it's at.
Gameplay is good, although its a bit buggy-- especially with the online co-op.  There seems to be a problem with syncing some of the casual encounters that the game offers such as taking out roving patrols and courriers between you and your co-op companion at times making these missions difficult, if not impossible to complete.  There are also issues with loading (especially after fast-traveling or completing a quest) in the SP mode where the game fails to load properly and you get a blank screen with sound.  Although this has happened a few times, it doesn't occur all that often and isn't anything that should keep you from buying the game.
So far, the biggest dissapointment of the game is the co-op mode which has fairly limited accessibility in terms of what you and your partner can actually do and the progress that can be saved.  Co-op mode only allows the joining party to save money, weapons, skins, etc... no quest progress is saved.  This means that aside from collecting new weapons and such, the joining partner will not really get all that much accomplished within their own campaign leading to a lot of play overs.  Additionally, there are many things available in SP that are no available in co-op.  The hosting party will not be able to complete any campaign missions while in co-op mode, and thus will be unable to advance the geography while in a co-op match.  This would lead one to conclude that co-op should be undertaken after one has already completed a good portion of the campaign and has unlocked many of the locales and side missions that can be undertaken together.  This is a little dissapointing compared with games like Borderlands which allow both parties to advance simultaneously.  Not sure why they didn't go in that direction but nonetheless, I'm happy to have the co-op in any form.
The biggest complaint I have about the game so far is the inability to replay things in co-op mode that would allow for a longer, more satisfying experience.  My co-op companion and I are obsessed with stealthing everything and were dissapointed that we were unable to replay fortress and outpost captures within the co-op mode.  That is something that I certainly feel needs changing.
Other than that, FC4 is an extremely solid game that rewards players for almost everything that you can do within it.   Hopefully in the coming months and expansions they expand the co-op mode a little and this game will get a lot closer to a perfect score.  For now, I plant this game at a solid 8.5/10.  Absolutely worth the money.

I just realized recently that I hadn't written a review for this milestone, so I thought I might as well now. If you couldn't already tell from the hours I've invested into this VN, I'm a super big fan of the fault series, so I'm always trying to get more people into playing this series. So if you're interested in hearing me ramble on about what I love about fault, be my guest!
One of the first things that caught my eye about fault was the story: it's incredibly well-written, and you can tell that the team behind this really put forth a lot of thought into the universe it's set in. On that note, the characters are arguably one of my favorite aspects of this series; it's very refreshing to see female characters that are portrayed realistically in this genre, that I as a female can relate to. Ritona, one of the main protagonists of this series, is someone who I can really resonate with, and I'm grateful I had the privilege to play this VN to discover her wonderful character. All the countless other characters have a wealth of depth to them, so you will hardly get bored just reading about predictable "flat characters" that lack an interesting backstory or motivation.
In relations to the visual aspects of the series, the art is absolutely gorgeous and it blows my mind every time when Hare-san, the artist behind fault, manages to capture a scene perfectly. Her art truly breathes life into the characters and world of fault! The backgrounds are also very vibrant and immersive, which really improves your playing experience even more. Another thing that makes the visual portion of this VN different from the rest of market is the "3D camera" they have implemented-- it adds another layer of depth to the scene by giving you a full cinematic experience, effectively deepening your perception of the emotions and intensity of a scene.
The soundtrack is also a key component to the enjoyment of the fault series. Each track masterfully expresses the specific feeling that a scene is supposed to convey, and the OST is very catchy to boot. I've lost count of how many times that Rune's theme got stuck in my mind ever since I've played fault, loool. In my opinion, there's definitely little to complain about concerning the musical score of fault.
In regards to this specific milestone, I most certainly enjoyed this one more compared to the first one. While fault milestone one spent most of its time detailing the history of the Zhevitz family and explaining the intricacies of the fault universe, this one focused more on character development and the Harthager twins. The main trio leaves the Outer-Pole at the beginning of this milestone, and then reach the shorebanks of Viscanta on ship. After spending more and more time there, the realization starts to dawn on them that the inner workings of Viscanta's society is in shambles--class discrimination runs rampant at its very core. As such, they soon discover that not all is as pristine and luxurious in Viscanta as the underwater city of Neo Sasary...
All in all, I would say this VN is a must-have to avid collectors of visual novels. Or if you're perhaps looking for something to get you started in the genre, this series is a nice choice to kick off your delving into the VN environment as well.
As for any complaints I might have had, there are a few that I can think of at the top of my head. Since this series functions in "milestones", you have to wait awhile for the next installment to come out following the most recent one. It also tends to have cliffhangers at the end of each milestone, so that can get a bit frustrating for some people. If you would rather read a whole VN in one chunk, then maybe this wouldn't be the best choice for you. However, if you have the patience to wait for the next (amazing) installment, then you should buy fault without delay!
The VN is also not voiced, so you have to read the characters' lines without any voices to listen to. From what I recall though, I heard they will be considering adding voice-acting when fault is finally completed. So if you're willing to play without any voices at this current point in time, then this shouldn't be much of a con for you.
I guess that I'll wrap this up right here, since this is getting somewhat lengthy. Please play fault if you're still interested in it after reading my review! The next installment in the series, fault - Silence the Pedant, is releasing in both English and Japanese soon, so you won't have to wait long for the next one after you finish this milestone.
Thank you for reading, and vilserio! :^)

I have been a fan of Piranha Bytes since Gothic 2, and have played and beaten all their games. For some reason the Pirate theme and look of this game put me off; it seemed different, and worse than previous titles. After picking it up for just a buck during the Humble ReBundle, it pleasantly surprised me. I'd rank this right up there with the rest of their games. Adventuring in their open world maps, stealing and beating up NPCs is great fun. The game is also VERY pretty on max settings. I actually thought the combat was an improvement over previous titles; it was still difficult, but learning an enemy's patterns and fully utilizing your abilties (leveling up your 'player skill') proved fruitful, and that's satisfying. The voice acting was decent - nothing incredible, mind you, but I tend to be picky and felt the actors were pretty good; their manner of speaking reminded me of Game of Thrones a couple times.
If you take your time with each island, exploring it throroughly and completeing all the quests, this is actually a reasonably long game. My first (very thorough) playthrough was over 50 hours, and the game is constructed so that you cannot get all the skills or experience all the content in a single playthrough. I don't know if it will hold my attention for a second go-around, but I could see my clock hitting nearly 100 hours if I do, and that's great bang for your buck.
Another reviewer complained that training and items were "too expensive" and the game was "too difficult". I couldn't disagree more. Too often, loot and gold are meaningless in games. You hoard hundreds of thousands of gold and have nothing to spend it on! In this game, you need to choose what gear and training you get with care, and that gives a real sense of value to loot when you get it. As for "too difficult"? Maybe my opinion is different as a fan since Gothic 1, but the challenge in these games are part of the experience. Why should you be able to go anywhere and beat anyone willy-nilly? One of the most memorable experiences of Gothic 2 was when I faced a situation in which I found myself unable beat a crowd of Orcs guarding the enterance to a city, and was forced to make a break from my "kill everything" mentality, and instead find a way to sneak past them and then proceed to RUN FOR MY LIFE! This was such a breath of fresh air! Furthermore, if you use all your resources in this game (proper gear, potion use... strategy) you can prevail in any fight, and overcoming the challenge makes it all the more satisfying when you do.
This game might not be for everyone. There are bugs, and quirks, but looking past those you have a very thoughtfully and lovingly made game here. I definitely recommend it. If you like Risen, or Gothic, this should be a safe buy, but you may want to wait for a sale.
All said and done, I really enjoyed this game, would have paid more for it, and would like to pick up the DLC when it goes on sale. Looking forward to Risen 3: Titan Lords, for sure!

TyranoBuilder draws you in with the promise of being an easy-to-use and intuitive interface, promises you simple drag-and-drop scripting, but falls short of these promises due to it's glitches in audio-looping (audio files will not loop without producing a delay between track end and track beginning), lack of functional 1080p interfaces, an incredibly buggy configuration screen which does not work in 1080p without complete redesign, bugs with fading out music tracks while trying to fade-in music tracks, causing you to put your music on the "sound" channel which can cause other issues, etc. etc. etc.
This program would be great if it were free, because then all of it's bugs and lack of features could be explained away as "well what do you expect, it's free!?" but this program is $15 which may not sound like much but considering their main competitor, Ren'Py is a free program which does not have ANY of these issues, it is unacceptable for them to charge money for this unfinished product.
Only buy this if you do not intend on making a professional, polished looking game. No matter how good you are at developing, this software will hold you back. Just download Ren'Py instead and deal with writing your game in a text document instead of a drag-and-drop interface. As someone who switched from Ren'Py to TyranoBuilder I feel like I was completely misled by their software which I expected to have basic and rudimentary features such as audio looping without delays between loop, 1080p interface support, etc. Heck they don't even give you a functional options menu to start with.
BUYER BEWARE, stay far far away from TyranoBuilder if you have any intention at releasing a professional, polished game! This is for amateurs who don't care about audio, graphic glitches and no 1080p support only!
I will revise this review if they ever fix these glaring issues but until then, I cannot recommend this software to ANYONE.
Go download Ren'Py for FREE.

I've seen a lot of negative review that all basically say the same things:
1. Software is buggy
2. Doesn't come with a butt load of free resources
3. It's not easy. . . enough.
I'll address each of these a little, then I'll give my own personal review.
As for bugs, yes, there are some bugs.  You know what else there is?  There is someone almost constantly checking the discussion board in order to help you through your issues.  jay_rab works seemingly tirelessly to answer questions and look at issues to provide the best possible experience with the software.  One might say that there shouldn't be bugs in the first place, but in a software like this, which is frequently updated with new features and options to make it even more user-friendly, things will sometimes happen.  Any developer worth his/her salt knows this going into a project.  There's also human error on the part of the user, and that is frequently the culprit of the so-called bugs.  If you aren't willing to be thorough with your own work, don't cry about it.
It's also true that TyranoBuilder isn't brimming with resources upon first launch.  Do you know what it does have, though?  It has a dedicated thread on the discussion board that's filled with links to free and pay for use resources, including sprites, music, and backgrounds.  In fact, that post is stickied right at the top.  There are also people in discussion who offer their services, some free and some pay.  So, while the resources aren't bundled with the software, they are readily available.  If you find they aren't "good enough", then I suggest you take some art and music classes and show us how it's done.
The complaint that the software isn't easy enough to use is frankly ridiculous.  Having no coding knowledge at all going into this software, I found it extremely easy to get a handle on.  The official tutorials are exceptionally straight forward, and there are plenty of user-made tutorials that focus on specific elements if you'd just take the time to google and watch a video or two.  What seems more of an issue is that so many people bought this with the expectation that the software would create the game for them.  Sadly, this is not a fully self-aware piece of AI.  It's a game dev software, which gives the user a ton of tools with witch to make amazing games.  It is entirely up to the user to make the most of the software.  The drag and drop features list really does already practically make the game for you, you just need to put them in a coherent order.  Everything is customizable.  Everything is functional.  You can even use coding on top of the ready-made functions to make something completely unique and astounding.  To me, it feels like a lot of people want to blame the software for their own shortcoming in comprehension and creativity.
So, now that I've laid out my wall of text regarding the common complaints I've seen, I'll give a quick rundown of TyranoBuilder as I see it:
This is a constantly evolving, yet somehow comprehensive feeling VN software for which no coding knowledge is needed in any way.  However, by referencing the TyranoScript tags and learning some VERY BASIC coding techniques, this software opens up an entire world of creative possibilities for those willing to work hard to see their story come to life.  Tyrano boasts so many tools and features that it's hard to believe it's available for $15.  The most important thing, in my opinion, is that TyranoBuilder has some of the most dedicated and invested devs I've ever seen.  They strive, constantly, to give the user a fantastic experience.  Whether it's answering tech questions, or giving quick but effective coding advice, or even just encouraging creators who share their progress.  I, for one, am willing to eat a few bugs and errors to be able to have that at my disposal.
And to be clear, it won't matter how intuitive the software or how abundant the resources, you will always have to take the time to learn and be patient, and you'll always have to work harder than you thought you would, and you'll always have to suffer setback after setback, if you want to make a game worth playing.

Depression quest is a free to play, text based, choice driven game. The thoughts, experiences and research of three developers collaborate together to bring you this title. I urge you to download, boot it up and go through it. This games aims to open the common view on depression from "just being sad", providing greater depth and insight into this illness. Choices to some scenarios have been deliberately left out to portray the thought process of individuals battling this illness, and symbolically represents the common perception on depression which combatants cannot simply choose. The music reflects current situations, creating further immersion into the plot perhaps evoking an emotive response from the player. The plot reveals and demonstrate the thoughts, feelings and reactions of an individual experiencing this illness. The decision to craft this plot in first person allows for a more personal playthrough as though the player has been hit with this illness. This War of Mine is a micromanagement simulator. You are given several survivors and a shelter to maintain and upgrade. You must manage survivor's health, food supply, shelter heating, and supplies for crafting to further your survival. Crafting is a huge gameplay component and you spend half the game scavenging materials from various locations outside your shelter. Outside your shelter, different scenarios play out presenting the player with decisions; decisions that greatly affect your survivor's moral compass, happiness and health.
The goal of the game is to make the player feel the sadness and rawness of war. To this end, the game employs a heavy, dark shading filter that works hand in hand with the music to provide a solemn ambience. Combined with the character's happiness meter and moral compass, decisions to kill or rob for survival cannot be made lightly.
I believe This War of Mine excels in achieving this goal through the scenarios, the semi-realistic dialog and difficult choices. Through these, the player must live with the consequences of their actions or inactions.
10/10.

Well, to start I want to clarify one thing – the game is not bad, it’s just mediocre.
While I have played all previous instalments (and The Dark Mod) I’m not going to judge Thief developers for the level of fidelity to its predecessors. I don’t mind changing the backstory and getting rid of the known and established lore, the conflict between the Pagans and Mechanist etc.
The thing is – new Thief fails in creating something equally interesting on its own. It just has this generic XIX century steampunk vibe, that didn’t manage to tackle my interest.
I will just try to explain why I’m rather disappointed in this game. There is no single game feature that would make it mediocre in my opinion, it’s just the sum of little things, that create this rather bland experience. I will try to explain it giving just some points as an example.
Lack of the ability to jump – it’s not that limiting as I initially was led to believe, because you can mantle practically on any surface you would like to, with only few exceptions, so I’m ok with that.
Contextual rope arrow – I can live with that, but implementing that solution causes the rope anchor point to stand like sore thumbs and screaming invitation – “look, here you can climb, this is the way further to something interesting”.
Sound design – now this is a big letdown for me. Original Thief games had wonderful sound design that let you place characters and objects in 3D space. Judging by the sound of footsteps you were able to determine the surface someone is walking on, but also whether someone is closing up on you, or getting away further.
In new Thief it’s hardly the case. Footsteps really doesn’t give you good sense of direction, and to make things worse – they are often muffled by generics speeches that persons give. About♥♥♥♥♥♥rings. From the other side of the stone wall. With audio repeated twice. And alas, that happens frequently, especially when you load new area (which also happens frequently). So often what would be a tense moment of hiding from a patrolling guard will be ruined, because you will only hear repeated generic guard chat (to loudly, even from the other side of the wall (sic!)) ad nauseam that will muffle the footsteps.
As for the random chats and guard lines – they have a big variety of them, but it seems like every person you encounter has only 2-3 limited lines, that they repeat constantly. So you creep for long minutes around the guards that are having the same conversation over and over. Occasionally you will encounter a scripted exposition conversation that shed some light on the world, characters, or even gives you clues about hidden loot. But Karras forbid you raise their suspicion level, because if you interrupt them, there is no coming back (except for a load long before you encounter such situation).
Staying with that – voice acting is pretty decent, albeit there are some issues with lip-sync, and Garret on liners are sometimes over the top.
Speaking about conversations we go to another element – the writing. It’s not that good. I don’t know how the story was butchered and changed in its turbulent development process, but the outcome is average at most and sometimes straight out laughable (so the protagonist is a Thief – lets name his nemesis Thief- Catcher General). Conversations imply sexual things in not very subtle style, like it was written with teenage audience in mind. Plot is uninteresting and cliché-ridden, not to mention that it bears unhealthy resemblance to Dishonored (city dying of plague, you are the only saviour, your allies betray you).
Going back to gameplay – City hub is divided into many districts, all separated by loading zones, and sometimes having loading zones in them. It’s painfully boring to navigate, especially if you have explored most of it on the beginning, because some side missions are available only after finishing main story “Chapters”. So, one mission requires you to go through 3 separate loading zones before you get to the mission area, and there is nothing to do on the way. You have to sneak (or fight) past the guards with, well known by that point, patrol routes, listening to the same conversations.
The City itself seems lifeless.  I didn’t expect crowds on the streets by night (and the plague is a poor device to justify keeping NPC’s of the streets), but even if there is a public event, like hanging  there are 2 persons performing it, and just 2 citizens watching.
Main story is divided into Chapters, but they are designed rather linearly, with multiple loading sections (cleverly disguised, I admit). They just feel like a scripted set of arenas you have to complete in order to move forward, to the next arena. And what’s worse, they feel even more limiting than Dishonored. Admittedly, there are some missions, where you can freely roam big mansions, and they gave me big enjoyment and this “Thief” vibe I was longing to feel. The plot sometimes acts as just to give you a pretext to move your character to a different setting.
The graphics are nice, and lighting is especially good looking, but not always working well. For example if you hide behind a crate with only your head sticking out and the passing guard will have a lantern, the screen will flash to indicate that you are fully visible (another not good design decision), but you will still remain hidden. Or you will be spotted on the other side of the fence, even if you were hiding there (maybe the can see you through the space between planks?). But those are rare instances. Other than that, the bluish tint in everything, and the repeating window textures for rooms that you cannot get into got me bored after some time. On the other hand, interiors are sometimes exceptionally well designed, and underline the differences between mission locations.
As for exploring the City – almost every breaking and entering will be proceed by a loading screen, which takes form of your hands working a crowbar animation, paired with a QTE. Also – your hands are almost constantly visible, and you can see the animations for doing almost anything – looking for a hidden switch, working a lock pick, or taking the loot. But since the most common loot is a pair of scissors laying precisely in the middle of a drawer, it quickly gets boring, and rather brakes immersion, because you know that behind every pair of golden scissors there is an 1-2 second long animation, that you can’t do anything about. I don’t know why they just didn’t go for stacks of coin here and there.
The AI – while they seem competent, when alerted, it’s painfully easy to lose the chase, even by going around the corner and hiding behind a crate, or changing the climbing up or down. Other than that, the change their patrol routs on the basis of your current location. So even if they have no indication of you moving to a different area, they will go and do their routine over there, because the game says so – also a poor design decision.  Other than that they react rather properly to you dousing the lights, or making too much noise.
Now for the good things. Side missions proved to give me most enjoyment so far, and some have really brilliant moments. They are well thought out, loading screens are better incorporated (talking about bank job mission here), the gave me the thief experience I was hoping to get.
But, alas, those few great moments drown in the sea of mediocrity.
And that is why I don’t recommend buying this game for its current price. I’m rather disappointed with the experience, and while I’ve spent around 30h, I had to fight boredom on much more occasions that I wished.
So, to sum up – while not a bad game, it’s not good either, I would recommend waiting for a 50% sale before buying it.
