I'm a huge fan of the original Thief series, especially Thief 2 the Metal Age, so I was really looking forward to the new Thief game and at the same time dreading it a bit because of the large span of time since Thief 3 Deadly Shadows and the sluggish, overbuilt quality of the same. So first off, the new Thief game is not the modern version of Thief 2 that most of the older fans have been hoping for. It is not a bad game; the controls take a bit of getting used to and the player interaction animations bog the gameplay down, but once you get used to these the game is pretty playable. It is beautiful and atmospheric, with great lighting and an excellent musical score. It is also tragically broken, and was obviously not ready to be released yet. The biggest problem is the save game system, and I want to state right up front that you should manually save your game often. I just lost three days of game play because I tried to restart a mission midway through and the game erased all my save game data except a manual save I had done earlier, and if I hadn't done that I would be starting over all the way from the beginning. The background conversation system is also a mess. In one waterfront area a couple of guards glitched out and had the same bawdy exchange about a prosititute over and over and over again until I finally moved to a different map; and when I came back, they continued to glitch out and repeat the same tired dialogue. Once these issues are fixed, I think this will be a pretty decent game; again, not the modern Thief 2 remake I was hoping for, but hopefully another chapter in the story that keeps the saga alive a little longer.

I spent a lot of time mulling over what can be said about Thief.
Unfortunately, nothing in the game is particularly bad, or good. There's very little of anything actually interesting to do or to see.
Gameplay is standard 1st person with stealth elements. Hiding in the shadows, breaking into buildings, stealing loot. Picking locks gets repetitive after the 100th time, like most of the content in game you will be repeating over and over. The fun part is plotting your method to break into a building, most of the missions will give you multiple ways to do so.
Graphics are fine, but performance is poor. Frame-rates dip when entering new areas. Sometimes characters glitch out and start spinning in a circle or textures take on a strange rainbow-like flashing colours. The city is a gloomy, depressing place and the visuals reflect this very well.
Audio is weak. Half of the time, I can't even hear what characters are telling me. The other half, I can hear people through solid walls as if they were stood right next to me. Add to this there isn't any noteworthy music or voice acting.
The game is relatively bug-free. Aside from the rare graphical glitches and framerate issue I previously mentioned, I did not encounter any game-breaking bugs during my time playing.
In conclusion, it's a very "meh" game. Not bad at all, but it fails to impress in any area. If you can pick it up for 50% off, I would recommend it. Again, it's hard to think of anything to say about this game because it manages to straddle the "average" line so accurately.

So, I've played this game since about as early as the developer allowed players from his other games to play it, so my time logged is vastly undercounted on Steam, but I felt this game deserved a review, in order to help other players judge it's worthiness of their time.
Firstly, this is NOT going to be a game you sit down to play for long sessions. This will be one of those titles you sit down for 5-10 minutes at a time, a few times a day, to see how things play out and act accordingly.
Secondly, while it can be a PvP title, it is not necessarily a PvP game. A lot of time, especially early-game, players will coordinate and work together, planning out constructions around thier areas in order to complement constructions other places, sometimes on the opposite side of the map.
Thirdly, given that this is a one-man show (yes, there's 1, count them, ONE, developer), it has been updated at the slowest, once every other month, and at the fastest nearly twice a week. The developer, Tom, is putting his all into reacting to player suggestions, fixing bugs, and generally making this game the best it can be, in a way that puts a lot of indie developers to shame.
So, if you're at all interested in a light-weight, casual, few times a day for a few minutes, type of game about strategy, betrayal, cooperation, and struggling against the nearly-impossible, you should give this game a try.

Technically, The Cat Lady is a deeply-flawed indie game.  The engine is absurdly antiquated, clunky and unstable. The sound mixing is at times amateurish.  It's a point-and-click adventure without the point and clicking, as all interactions are done using the keyboard's arrow keys and space bar.  The game also runs at 800x600.
Creatively, though—artistically—The Cat Lady is wonderful.  Well, wonderful may be the wrong word.  This is grindhouse horror.  Bloody imagery, rusted machinery and deprecated rooms accompany its muted tones and grim environment.  Nothing's 'wonderful' in Susan Ashworth's world, a fact that leads the protagonist to her suicide attempt in the game's introduction.
No, the Cat Lady isn't wonderful, per se.  It's captivating, provocative and memorable.  It's also dark, unrelenting and austere.  That's usually how it is for sufferers of depression.  That's how it is for Susan.  But as she drifts throughout her despair, the story provides her with the ability to put matters into her own hands—whether she likes it or not.
The Cat Lady is a worthwhile, fantastic experience if story-driven horror/adventure calls out to you.  Though its design is decidedly rough around the edges, its vision and its story do make up for it.  Those rough edges are nevertheless a shame, as they diminish what I feel could have otherwise been a masterpiece of its genre.
Perfect journey into raw human emotions.

Vision of a non-paying player:
This game succeeds at the "Frustrating New Players Formula": put new players to play against experienced opponents right at the beggining of their multiplayer experience.
Yes, there is the matchmaking system based on the rank of players, but that doesnt prevents a low rank like me to play against other low rank people that have a full of rares in the deck while I can make a deck with maximum 5 rares in it by farming that few gold every day and hoping to get something good at the boosters and make a decent deck. The result is obvious: 8 of 10 matches I get stomped and the "hidden message" in the game gradually becomes  cleaner: -BUY COINS TO GET NEW CARDS AND HAVE A CHANCE OF WINNING!
Then I realize this game is exactly as the physical card game (in the majority of the cases): Wins who has better deck --> To have a better deck you must have plenty of cards to be able to make challeging  strategies --> To have plenty of cards you have to spend a lot of money buying it!
At least in the physical card game I have the possibility to buy cards individually and spend less money rather than being locked to boosters and rely on my luck to get the cards I need.
In my country I have to pay R$121,30 to get 50 boosters. And now I ask you: How many other nice games could I afford with R$121,30??? And the worst of all is that there is a chance that I won't get good cards to make challenging decks in those 50 boosters, so I would have to spend even more money to have another chance to get good cards!!!
I really like MTG but got so frustraded with Magic Duels that I don't have any other option unless stop playing it and hope that in the future devs create other mechanics to encourage new non-paying players  to have fun playing this Pay2Win game (yes I know that what they want is the paying players who will give them the money, but free players always can turn into paying players depending on their excitement with the game and I dont think I'm the only one who have this opinion).

What should i say about "This war of mine"?
Its a good game. You control a few civilians in a war raged city, survivors of bombardments, crimes and a lot of attrocities. Your goal is to keep your civilians alive while the war is running or until a ceasefire.
Your situation is dire, city running low on food, medicine, "winter is coming", raiders and armed looters taking of the life of others, desperate times what really could happen anytime with us as we can never forecast future. There were allways war and there will be wars until the end of mankind.
You need to handle sickness of your survivors, battle wounds, beat the hunger, the cold and eventually the sickness of the soul.
Most of your survivor have a special ability, an exsoldier is good in fight, other one, a prewar engineer could require less materials for items and some better in running or scavenging, various abilities what you need to profit from if you want to stay alive until the arrival of the peacekeeper forces.
The game isnt easy, its challenging, you'll never have enough resources and you will have allways hard decisions.
Will you scavenge ammo or weapons at the time when raiders invading homes on daily basis or you will go for medicine for your sick party member?
The decision is yours, but there are no good decisions! So now stop reading and try to survive, you will fail before you will win but then the win will be even sweeter:-)

TL;DR:
PROS: levelling with quests and not just grinds, a lot of classes, findable good equips, great for new players (and old ones if they can get over the fact that the game isn't the same as it was 16 years ago)
CONS: quiet community in-game, some party quests are completely dead
I see a lot of reviews talking about how much the game has changed and how there's no nostalgia left for us older players. As an older player myself (I've been playing Maple off and on since 2006), I disagree. What brought me back to Maple after the last four year haitus I had was the nostalgia, but what kept me playing was the complete rehaul of the game.
When I was a kid with dial-up internet, getting to the first job advancement was difficult. Fast forward to today: I have played almost every class through into the fourth advancement. Yes, it's been made a lot easier, but it's also reasonable now; any player can get a good diversity  of content regardless of experience or skill. The endless 10-20 level grind on the same map is gone, now theme dungeons and quests offer the best leveling chance, which is loads more fun. In fact, quests used to be altogether useless, so this change is super awesome.
There's so many classes now! I was super happy when I came back to all the new classes. I actually can't wait for more to come out so I have more skills to try out. (I'm hoping there's an all-new class soon with new clothing equips and not just weapons.)
The addition of spell traces and the equip enhancement system actually reduces the pay-to-win aspect that has ALWAYS (as in FOREVER, as in THIS IS NOTHING NEW) been a part of Maple. It offers people the chance to have good equips but without the ridiculous cost and rarity of scrolls. Equipment drops have been completely rehauled and now have hidden potentials, allowing players to find their equips without having to spend mesos or real money and to make a decent bit of mesos that help in the later game with pots and the like. (Side note: I remember the days of the scrolled out sauna robe, can't nobody tell me the new equip drop system is bad.)
Us older players are not the major target of this game anymore and that's OKAY. It's for those kids coming in at the same age when we started back in the day. It's not entirely Maple and Nexon's fault that the previous audience left, a good deal of people left because they got older and found other games, particularly MOBAs. (Admittedly, the game community has gotten quieter and some party quests are dead, but, again, see previous point.)
All-in-all, it's not right to make a crappy review on the game because it's changed over the course of over a decade and a half. The game is different, even easier, and that's totally cool. I think it's a great choice for new, young gamers with its cute graphics and background music. And if older players approach it as a different game than the one they remember, it can be really great for them too.

First things first. This is going to be very long and very detailed. So I will give a short answer for all those who hate reading or don't feel like you have the time to read a very detailed fanboy review and then a long answer for those that are curious of the opinion of a person who considers the Thief franchise the greatest single player franchise ever.

Yes. This game is worth getting. If you're a new comer to the Thief series then this is a game you should check out if you are a fan of the stealth genre. If you're a fan or fanboy of the Thief series, this is worth adding to your collection regardless of if you end up liking it or not so you can complete your collection of Thief games.
~~!!!POSSIBLE SPOILERS!!!!~~
This is where it's going to seem like I'm contridicting myself. It's going to seem like I should by all rights HATE this game by the things I'm going to say. However, I'm going to be intellectually honest and tell you in the same breath, the game is still worth getting and playing. I wouldn't blame you either way if you paid full price for it, or wait until it's on sale. I'll give my list of reasons I feel the game is good with the positives and what I think is wrong with the negatives.
Exquisite Ambiance. When it comes to the actual gameplay, there has never been a game that has sucked me into it's world as much as this one did. When you turn down the lights, crank up the volume you really get an absurd realization of this game. From the city to each and every mission... especially the Moira Asylum!
The addition of new Thief Tools. Your original tools in Thief were basically just lock picks. In addition to the lock picks, there is a wrench, wire cutters and a razor for your thieving adventures. All these are crutial to become successful and to fully experience the game. Each one offers a new unique experience to the game that I found to be an excellent addition.
The Swoop. This is such a cool feature that it makes me want to smash partical board with my testicles in a single thrust! It's a unique ability that gives you a visible / physical sense of what sets you apart from your average thief. It's EXTREMELY useful in almost every situation and in some cases, is not without risk. So use it wisely!
The addition of collectible loot. I just found this to be a cool feature they added. It's a visible accomplishment of your work that gives a sense of accomplishment.
Customization. There is so much customization from the HUD to the difficulties in this game, it's almost overwhelming. You can add everything that's important to your HUD so it's easier for you to keep track of, or make it 100% dedicated to gameplay. As far as the difficulties goes, there are 3. Rogue, Thief and Master all of which adjust the AI of the npc's and also certain restrictions as you increase the difficulty. All 3 of these difficulties can have custom addon's added to any of them. There are too many to list here, but know this, there is quite a few. So if you're looking to personalize your experience, look no further!
Focus Ability. This was another good addition to the game. As with the swoop, this is another visible ability that really helps you feel / understand why you are considered the master thief! This ability highlights area's or objects that might be of interest or things you can interact with. Garrett's ability to recognize things that would be invisible to most others are the stuff of legend. As well as being able to see in the dark far better than others.
Upgrades + replayability. I felt I should include both of those in this one. Because you can't purchase every single upgrade there is in your first playthough. Unless you hack the game, it's just not possible. There are a lot of cool upgrades from weapons to stealth to armor and focus. This game has extremely easy setup for replaying. So when you've earned enough money to upgrade what you wanted. Head right back to the mission you want to play and load it right up with your new stealth boots or massivly powerful bow!
Not using Stephen Russell for the voice of Garrett! I will
forgive Eidos Montreal for this! Their rebuttal for this was they wanted to have a 100% geniune experience of motion capture with the stuntman they used for Garrett. While this is a corporate rebuttal that sounds pretty and looks good on paper, it still holds no weight with me or with purists / true Thief fans. Why? Garrett was never a face. Garrett was a voice... or a shadow with a voice, however you choose to look at it. This is the utmost WORST possible betrayal to the Thief franchise and to us fans of this legendary series.
Bad writing, lip syncing, storyline and very unlikeable characters. The lip syncing in so many cutscenes is just way off which makes it pretty annoying to watch and really pulls you out of the immersion of the game. The storyline was just extremely bad... I don't want to go into too much detail so I don't give away the farm with spoilers. However, the storyline really has no satisfaction where there should be highs and lows. Nothing about this story sucks you into the storyline to give you the rollercoaster of emotions that a good story gives you. The writing in this game creates extremely awkward interactions between characters. You find yourself saying "Umm... why did she do that? Why did she say that... wait, what???" The closest thing I can equate this feeling of awkwardness to is when you walk up to a random group of people in a social situation, and try to include yourself in their conversation with a lame joke. Or talking to a woman, who's clearly not interested in you or what you have to say, about why you believe Elvis is still alive. The characters emotions and their lines are just... lame. Between the bad audio that overlaps other audio and the bad lines each characters are given, instead of getting normal dialogue, you end up listening to a symphony of weirdos. The main character Garrett is very noticibly inexperienced and, I dare say, a grade B voice actor.
We were lied to. Eidos Montreal said in several interviews that they were trying to stay as true to the original series as possible. If you played the original games or know anything about the original games, you'll quickly realize how much of a bold faced lie that was. I imagine it is the similar feeling that you would have when your wife tells you that you are the only man she's ever been with. Then when your baby is born, it's a different color. It turns out that there are bits and pieces of the original game spread out as... I guess you can call them cameos? They kept the names of some of the original characters, Garrett, Basso, Erin... You see a hammer on a cathedral, a tip of the hat to the old hammerites. Out of 183 hours of gameplay I heard the word "Taffer" twice from listening to random conversations near windows. There is a drunk by the name of "Lenny", an indirect homage to the old character "Benny". The Trickster was mentioned one time by Garrett. Without playing the original games, nobody knows who the f*** the trickster is, which is another example of the bad writing, because it makes people go "Who? Wait... did I miss something? Who is the trickster?" While there are a handful of others, the point is, nothing about this game is "true to the old series" like we were told. Utterly disgraceful.
New game mechanics. Gives a clostrophobic and linear feel to the game. Like your hand is being held and told exactly where to go. While I do not dislike these new mechanics, I perfer the old mechanics better.
Well I'm out of room to type. I didn't realize I had limited characters. There is a ton more I could say, so feel free to add me to find out more.

First off this game does not compare to the original Thief series (which is one of my all time favorites) once we get past that its actually kind of fun. Sure the story is a bit flat mostly due to boring characters, but i rather enjoyed it. The graphics are nice and the animations smooth, although i think there are too many of the latter which can become annoying. But they do a great job of level design and the ambiance really sets the mood for any particular level. The in-level puzzles are fun and intruding and sometimes challenging making the game similar to the new Tomb Raider in that respect. The game is designed with different play styles in mind and even encourages playing the levels differently increasing its replay value. I like the idea of the open-world city (which doesn't actually have a name) between missions ,its packed with some extra side missions and lots of loot and easter eggs to find if your a completionist. This also allows for a “store” out of mission meaning your items and weapons carry over between missions as well as character upgrades are available to purchase. All together this makes this fun but not excellent game.
Where it really falls flat is in comparison to the original series. You are limited in the use of your specialty arrows allowing them only to be used on specific objects in the game which destroys the creative problem solving that made the originals so fun. They have also made Garrett look weird he looks like a skinny Gothic dude who's into S&M. And i also really miss the gaurds calling everyone a taffer.
Overall a decent game thats fun to play but nothing exceptional. Grab it if its on sale.

I really enjoyed the story of the game, it's definitely got adult themes but they're not shoe-horned in there to be edgy or shocking, it has to be there with the story being told. It's got some fantastic ideas in there, I was skeptical about the main character however, but it may be me being a bit picky because of the range of quality in the voice acting that sometimes hit or missed for me. A couple of scenes or conversations made me think that maybe some lines needed re-writing but in truth, that's my only problem with the writing here. Susan Ashworth, as a character, as much as it pains me to say this, was not someone I as rooting for but I'm being picky. I did on a few occassions say outloud to my laptop "Why aren't you saying this?!" I'll refrine from plot spoilers but, as it is with every adventure game with a dialouge option, they won't say the bleeding obvious. A lot of hard work has gone into this and I can see that in the characters and level design. I just wish the quality of mics were even across the board, it sounds like some people did either their lines over skype or right before they went to bed.
The game play is around puzzles and logical/lateral thinking and there were a few I were stuck on but as I don't play a lot of them, I was surprised that the puzzles were fresh, solvable and quite original which made me want to see the next puzzle there, the next thing I had to do. All in all, the game has its moments where you feel tense and excited and it was a good experience. It's full of ideas, it's full of life, funnily enough, for a game about death. For me this is why I kept coming back, your experience with the character may vary but she wasn't totally unbearable to me but never had her moments where I laughed.
The sound design on this game is an incredibly mixed bag. The music is great and you'll want to listen to more of it, it'll build and it'll be effective but then just cut out when they need it to and it abruptly stops. There's one sound that plays for multiple effects, but hey, you don't play this for the sound do you? The sound is a mixed bag but the graphics and attention to the levels and story is where the most focus has gone I feel. Although hard work must have been made to record and mix all those lines of dialouge, I don't feel like it's on par at times with the game world they've created.
All in all, this is a good game, buy it. Even though I have a few negative points about it, there more production points than gameplay points. The way the game plays is solid and it never gets boring or repeats the same idea over and over again.

As a huge fan of the Gothic series I was reasonably excited for when the first Risen game was announced. Although it was mostly just a copy of Gothic 2 and its gameplay systems I still very much enjoyed it. Risen 2 tries to innovate on that formula. And I am thankful for that, since it was getting a bit stale towards the end of the first game.
Risen 2 is a bit of hard game to get into, even for a fan of the developer. You really need to put a few hours into the game to get it going, as it has a very slow start. I'd say that'd be once you're past the first island as a pirate (yes the game has multiple islands which you can sail to anytime you want once you've discovered them and once you get yourself a ship), but it does take a good 4-5 hours to get through that.
The game's biggest problem is the combat system, it is just badly designed, while the previous Risen/Gothic games had no great combat systems either, they had a lot of different ways you could approach it. In Risen 2 you are much more limited for most of the game. You can use swords, muskets or voodoo to vanquish your enemies, however you only get access to the the latter two much later in the game and they are painfully underdeveloped. As a result you will mostly just try and melee your way out of everything, and the melee system is quite bad.
Piranha Bytes did a fine job with world building in this game, and they made sure there are interesting quests here also. And once you're past the initial slog, the game just keeps getting better. And at a fine length of about 20-25 hours, you will most certainly leave satisfied if you can manage to get there.

When playing This War of Mine I notice something. After spending a lot of time trying to figure out the mechanics in the game I started thinking "I should restart". Under normal circumstances that way of thinking isn't weird or odd but... This was different.
One of my characters; Bruno, died. Soon two more would if I couldn't fix bandages to one and medicine for the other. Its kind of hard to find those things at the same night. But not only that. They have both been struggling for a long time already. Meaning even if I would find the items it might be to late. But...
Starting over would help me as I had already played for some time now and understood the mechanics better.
"Start over" - My head said to me. Each night I saw everything going to hell. "Start over. Then you will have it better chance".
I started wondering "But how could I?". This is war.
"For some people this is real. Not all, but many.". I have tools that tells me what I will get. Hell! Tell me to do a rainwater collector on a random day without me knowing and see how far I would get. No Internet. No library. No neighbors that might have that knowledge. Its honestly a chilling thought.
"Start over". I can't. In real life these people wouldn't be able to start over. Life doesn't have a restart button.
Depressing, isn't it?
But I feel like this is actually a great game mechanic that might be looked away from. The unknown of doing something for the first time. Not knowing what is right or wrong. Pretty much just hoping that what you did is the right move at the time.
As in life.
Thats why I continue on playing with these characters. I need to see them through.
One of my characters Emilia comes back home from a night of scavening. She comes in and sits down.
Staring.
Staring blankly into nothing.
Someone raided the house again. This time with brute force. Pavile died during the night from the wounds that Emilia bandaged him with before I sent her out to scavange.
I gave Katie meds to survive through the night but after this night she left.
Only one person lives in the house now. Emilia. Still staring.
With no hope left in her.
Even later when someone bangs on the door yelling for help she doesn't move.
I press on the button to make her open the door to see if there might be something to help her, some hope left... but... She just sits there.
Broken.
The day goes by and night falls again. My only options is to let Emilia sleep. She's too depressed to do anything else.
Next day comes.
A picture of someones feet hovering just above the ground flashes infront of me.
Emilia, is dead.
Suicide.
In the end, not every move you do turns out to be the right one. But you learn. Take it to heart and try again. And again.
Life doesn't have a restart button as this game has.

I used to play Maplestory around 2005 while in highschool, and to me it was extremely difficult to get to level 120 as a Bowmaster. Every couple months since 2006 I wanted to play the game as a game I could sink some hours into just to get the grind out of my system, but due to compatability issues, I could never ever return to the game unless I went through these ridiculous changes to my OS and when I did, the game was so different and I felt I missed so much and the learning curve was so drastic at the point of where I was that I simply was dettered from rejoining the game, so my Maplestory experience so far ended there.
Fast forward to 2015, I find out that Maplestory is now accessible through Steam. So I decided to do a little research and see if I could pull up my old account and start up my Bowmaster and just be higher average in the game. I get my archer back, but man EVERYTHING is different, but in a good way.
Game was much easier to get into, the learning curve and leveling process was MUCH easier, there were a lot of classes to choose from, all with their own style of gameplay and storyline, and each as good as the last.

Cons:

- The social aspect of the game is near none, so it's very hard to get a group or make ANY friends at all
- Some microtransactions are neccessary to get min/max unless you play for a LONG time
********
TL;DR
********
Easy learning curve, a lot of classes to choose from and each one is as good as the last. Big numbers everywhere, but very grind intensive. Be prepared to play this game alone, as there's no socialness here.

This War of Mine is a game like no other, taking a surprisingly real (well, ish) look at what it would be like to have war engulf your home. It's a survival management game full of tension and atmosphere that is worth playing through completely at least once if you're even remotely interested in the concept.
During the day time you are restricted to your shelter due to the conflict and can build new tools for survival and see to the needs of your survivors such as food, sleep and trying to keep their morale up. During the night phase you have the option of sending one of your survivors out to scavenge for building materials and vital resources. This is an essential part of survival, but an increasingly dangerous and intense undertaking. Your goal is simply to survive, but there is no way to know for how long, and as the game progresses resources become more and more scarce.
As far as replayability goes, you can opt to start with a random selection of different survivors and the locations may be ever so slightly reshuffled, but on the whole the game takes you through the same scenarios every time so you're likely to get two or three playthroughs at most out of it.
I look forward to "The Little Ones" expansion when it comes out for PC, which will hopefully add some interesting new content to explore.

In this review I'll try to be concise but deepening the major aspects of the game. (°ロ°)☝
♦ The difficulty
♦ The graphics
♦ The gameplay
♦ The lore
♦ The difficulty
First of all, and probably the reason why this game is so famous (or infamous), is the difficulty.
This game ain't that hard, it punishes every single mistake the player makes, often with death.
I often read people complaining that this game is so hard only becase it's artificially made so with bad programming or ultraoverpowered enemies.
It's not true.
This game forces to learn (sometimes killing you 5 billion times in a row) the mechanics, but once you have learnt them, you can "easily" kill almost every single boss (made exception for 3 or 4 in which one you will just need patience or luck).
I said that this game punishes mistakes. But not only the player's ones, even the one made by the AI: there is always a easier way to kill stuff than running onto them (because 90% of the time it will end with you respawning at the last bonfire).
It's a challenge. No more words needed.
♦ The graphics
The graphic comparment of this game is simply beautiful.
Maybe is not that pumped, but it's so cured that literally gives the feeling of running in a world made of anime and mango.
The textures are a bit gross and at a closer look, ugly.
But the way they are implemented in the world, with every collapsed building, grass growing in the wild or every strange liquid in the deepest areas of the world, the textures are just perfect.
The light is not that well done but when it's kawaii, for God's sake, it's really kawaii. Not kawaii like "meh, i can barely see stuff", kawaii like "Where the hell am I going? Where the hell is the road? Am I still alive? Was that a damned arrow?".
♦ The Gameplay
This game is definetely not indicated for people who like the classic RPG game with quests, NPCs and maps.
It gives only two directed suggestions:
-"In One Manga Day, level up and kindle at bonfires"
-"Translate two sentences and GTFO"
STOP. No more instructions. no one will tell you where to go or what the hell is happening. You're alone in this dark and shattered world. People will trick you, people will invade you from their world, people will ♥♥♥♥ your game up killing NPCs. The only way to know where you have to lead next, is reading everything. On every item there is a description that tells you everything you need: where to go, where to look and what are the weaknesses of the senpais.
Every single weapon has a unique moveset that goes well against certain enemies but against others are better other weapons. And i'm not saying that every weapon class has a moveset. Every. Single. Weapon.
Don't ever try to do a 3v1 in an area (unless you're overleved), you will probably get rekt, or finish without manga (potions).
This game is divided in areas, at the end whereof there is a boss fight. Until the final boss is killed, people can invade your world trying to kill you for figurines and animes. In the other hand, until the area is freed, you can provoke players.
Last but not Least, when you die a blood stain will appear on the floor, cointaing the figurines and the animes you had.
You can pick them up restoring everything you had. But if you die again trying, sayonara figurines.
USE A CONTROLLER.
♦ The lore
Some people complains that this game has no lore. This happens because just like what you have to do, no one says what the hell is going on. But items, ambientations, enemies, will scream out loud what happened and what is going on.
Quoting the director of the game: "A well designed world could tell its story in silence."
Watch THIS video. NOW.

Only with very..."special" games do I ever scrutinize the contents displayed on my monitor, rushing my fingers through my hair as I ponder on what gave me the strength to just contemplate finishing the game. This just happens to be one of those lucky games. Devised by some amateur Russian with the help of the haunting ComiPo! software, "One Manga Day" (Which will be abbreviated to OMD for most of this review) has a distinct charm that is better avoided than one to fall victim too.
Discussing OMD will not go without mention of the aforementioned ComiPo! software that the developer utilized to produce the fascinating cast you will see on screen. All the characters featured in this novel are 3D, chibi-esque dolls which look rather disturbing, and the reader/player's eyes will tire terribly soon from the same, unpleasant poses they'd display themselves in. It is understandable that one might not be able to feasibly procure the funds necessary to have more agreeable art in your game, but in this case it just accentuates the almost revolting overall presentation of the novel consisting of royalty-free backgrounds, redundant insert music and occasional spine-chilling voices. The ComiPo! software is a convenient, cheap tool, but it is also unrefined and in need of graphical polish if the creators of this application desire more usage of it in games, which is probably not the case. This is not to the fault from the guys responsible for this kawaii software, as this is ultimately just a poor design choice by the developer of this novel.
Here, you will take position of a nameless protagonist as he suddenly joins a manga
team that has a considerable amount of catching up to do as they are behind on their projects. After learning a thing or two about the translation process, you will be granted the choice on deciding what branch of the team you will want to occupy yourself in. Don't worry or think too much about it, however, as this is an inconsequential choice that neither adds or removes anything from the rest of the plot, just like the majority of the choices you will make in this game, as they will but toss in extra line of dialogue. That is, if you even have the delight of reading an extra one at all as other variants of these trivial choices include the effect on the actions of other characters or simply nothing at all, just a click on the alternative choice bar.
Decent writing has been an intrinsic part of literature as a whole since all of time. If a conglomeration of text fails to entertain or just satisfy the consumer, the piece of art failed completely. It is a shame to say that OMD had more than just a slight potential as it contains an intriguing premise, but the developers of this novel (
) shot themselves in the foot considering all the different elements that make this brief reading experience just plain boring to endure. It is evident that the frivolous encounters of the protagonist with the rest of the staff is essentially the aim of the entire script, and this inane atmosphere would have been appreciated wholeheartedly if any one put minimal attempt to spice the script with some clever writing. The attitudes exhibited from all of the characters are so effortlessly insipid that I'm convinced myself that none of these Russian dudes enjoyed themselves in writing any of this. Many of our cherished personalities here spit out corny one liners that serve as nothing but a way to augment their painfully conventional quirks. It doesn't end there, however, as there are many situations these characters are placed in that prove the many blemishes in the abominable writing. In the 7 in-game days the reader gets to partake in, most, if not all, of the staff members are skirmishing about all around the office. Many shenanigans the personnel participate in have the tendency to stifle the pacing and compromise the novel's sense of objective, and they manage to gnaw on my patience too, as they feel very pedestrian and off on a tangent.
This mischief subsequently becomes tiresome bickering between the translation group on how they don't get anything done or haven't done much at all, just after running amok, engaged in lame diversions. Is this an episode of Another? Those who read will put on a puzzled smirk throughout the duration of this novel, as things start to lose their significance and simply stop making sense. Before you know it all the misconduct has ceased and the credits roll after an ending with such an absence of conclusion, having the power to drive some to beat their heads against the wall in profound frustration as a result of all the
fun that has occurred in the past hour and a half. Describing how this novel was rushed like a time trial is limitless, most of the scenarios featured here were out of place from all angles, all accumulating to disappointment.
There is a tease at the ending of the true and of the game suggesting a sequel, but the damage has already been done and it is ensured that most people that have played this will not seduced by any of the crap this next game brings, let alone download and play it. "One Manga Day" (Which should really be called 'week', but sure.) is an A1 materialization of deplorable execution of a decent concept. This game has been taking a beating by a handful of users here on Steam and it sure deserves it. I bear no malice towards anyone involved with the game, but what a mistake this has been.

Battlerite is everything fun about MOBAS without the excrutiatingly boring early game, which would normally consist of 15-20 minutes of last hitting creeps and having meaningless slap fights with your lane opponent(s). The characters are more complex and fun to play, and the WASD movement feels incredible after playing years of League of Legends. I love how I don't have to invest 20-45 mostly frustrating minutes on a single match, sometimes ending in failure and bickering amongst friends (not that this game doesn't end in bickering sometimes). The ~6 minute or less match time is very satisfying when I'm feeling impatient. Battlerite, to me, is a truly innovative title that brings out my usually non-existant competitive side.
Due to the style of game, I was expecting mouse movement akin to Dota or LoL, however I quickly adjusted to the new controls. This control scheme allows you to constantly aim where you want (the enemy/your teammates for a heal), without having to perform two actions with the mouse in two different places. It also allows for good dodging should your reaction time permit, especially on more agile characters with speed amplifiers.
The condensed, fast-paced combat is incredibly gratifying and visceral, each character coming with pleasant surprises to their abilities through modifiers called, shockingly, 'Battlerites'. This is one of the only learning curves that the game has to offer aside from learning your character's abilities and Shift abilities, as different builds of Battlerites will vastly alter your success rate at your desire goal, whether it be healing, survivability, damage, etc.. As a healer/tank player in most games, I'm happy to see a game which has interesting and fun supports who are able to contribute damage if necessary, sometimes outdamaging their ranged teammates. Different Battlerites allow supports to take on an aggressive role if they choose, which is successful more often than not.
Rounds last 2 minutes each, with arenas perfectly sized and shaped to allow escape, or to corner your opponents. The maps are diverse enough where preferences can be formed based on your favourite champion, some providing more cover or walls to leap over. The 'Death Vortex', a damaging mist that covers the map and encircles the middle, forces those who would flee to engage their opponent, which is a fun mechanic when you play a character with knockback, panic, or mind control (looking at you pestilus), otherwise your best bet is to kill opponents who possess those abilities quickly once the Vortex sets in.
I have recommended this game to those of my friends who I think would enjoy it, and all those who have tried it have liked it a lot. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys competitive games and is willing to give something new and unique a try; I promise you won't be disappointed.

From the PoV of a gamer that enjoys modern stealth fps game (e.g: Deus Ex HR & Dishonored), Thief offers a unique experience with high in-game graphic fidelity. Unlike the examples I've mentioned, Thief does not provide players any form of superpowers (with the exception of focus power to help locate objects or enter slow-mo) that help players to breeze through areas. The main objective of Thief (is to steal and), aside from doing the plot, is to explore the area surrounding your hideout which is not greatly done in other stealth games.
There are sure to be negative reviews for a title that has a long running history from fans of the original thief which is dissatisfied by what Thief (4) has to offer. A valid point that was made by these die-hard fans is the lack of alternative paths in most areas.
The biggest charm of this particular stealth fps game, other than the explorable city hub, is the collectibles, which are not only well designed, but gives a satisfaction feeling to me personally as I complete each sets of collectibles. The collectibles itself have intriguing mini back stories.

As a game on it's own it has both good and bad aspects but overall on par with most modern first person titles from quality point of view in most areas but is not without it's flaws.
Firstly the visual graphics are decent while in keeping with the style of game...perpetual night feels odd to me in any game and the city feels perpetually dark in general not just because of the lighting but this also makes the game feel depressing to me as opposed to being much on the way of uplifting content but it is in keeping with the theme of the story and setting so it is understandable and maybe credit should be given that they managed to express that story/setting depression well.
The audio was good enough, at first the protagonist seemed like a complete jerk to me but he grows on you with aid of the soft toned VO and nonchalant dialogue regarding his bleak view of humanity...but the Erin character I felt was just bad in general on many levels. The bad guys in this game such as the Thief Taker General or Orion at times are quite well done on the other hand. Combat feels in line with what would expect in a stealth based game but at times can be slightly tedious later in the game for myself so I switched to just knocking everyone out by the end so that I would not get stabbed in the back as I progressed. Some of the side/main quests are quite good like the bank heist, the brothel, the asylum, clockwork mission to name a few but overall many of them are mere open a window or door pop in and grab something which is pure and simple lackluster fetch quests.
The story is not good overall, I won't lie the most positive spin I can put on it is it's messy to say the least but has some nice parts within that mess from time to time. It is just a shame the main story feels to me so disjointed and badly paced plus by the end lacking any real closure in my eyes, maybe this has to do with the players ability to carry on living and doing things in the city once completed even if no more story to it or the element that the story is so messy and some major characters stories are left completely unresolved regarding what happens to them. The game has the desire of being adapted well for completionist gameplay standpoint, with so many collections, trinkets, candles you can light for reward or almost everything in it being linked to some arbitrary number you can collect in total even down to so much being ranked or scored based on performance trying to provoke people to keep retrying till got 100% on everything.
There are some flaws to the game I feel such as how amazingly tedious it becomes to traverse the city given there are no quick travel options between objectives whether main story or side mission goals. This leads you to having to go on foot across the same places over and over and over again even though you may well have cleared and done every single thing possible there the very first time you went through it...passing the same empty locations over and over, killing or bypassing the same respawned guards for the millionth time. It's game time padding taken to the extreme and given how convoluted the city is and how depressing the setting and city is by purposeful design, this has a negative impact on enjoyment. On top of this things like every time  want to open a window or door etc you have to go through the same animation leading up to actually doing it which is more time padding gameplay.
The map too is poorly designed on some levels such as while you can move it around and zoom in and out, you cannot change elevation, you cannot see any entrance or exits between sections of the city and have to rely mostly on memory of where there might have been a door or window leading to one or the other. This too is missing from the map such as locations of any doors or windows accessible to the player. The mini map had a tendency to also disappear every time entered a window or moved to another part of the city and this annoyed me as I had to keep turning it back on to keep my bearings on where I was heading over and over.
The economy is bad, after short period things get so expensive it would seem your expected to have completed the game multiple times before can afford much of whats in it first time around. All those trinkets and plates, necklaces, candle sticks and such are really nothing more than gold coins but with different appearances and each being worth so little it seems pointless at times going around trying to find them all. The non generic items are much more interesting to find behind traps and tricks, hidden passages and such but the generic loot seems a waste of time.
There are bugs and glitches in the game but the only major one I encountered was memory leaks from time to time which led to game freezes. I have a top of the range custom built PC so performance wise I expected no major problems but this memory leak is a software issue that I wish they had sorted out before released the game to retail. While this problem did not happen enough to make me throw a tantrum of sorts it was very annoying when did happen. Other than this I hear and read people have found many problems with quest items, or missions, dialogue and other such things but each seemed minor at most and not everyone had such issues.
Overall I would say this game is okay. It has some nice elements to it and some bad ones. Some of the major complainers I have seen are ones trying to compare with the openess and freedom of the first Thief titles but if they took off the rose tinted nostalgia blinding goggles they would not be so eager to use them as a comparison. I believe no-one should compare old titles against new ones yet solely relying on nostalgia and decades old memories as basis for it because nostalgia is not reliable and often taints your perception of that previous games actual quality or lack of to be exact. If they want to compare such old games with the new one then they need to play the old one again just prior to playing the new one if they want to offer a fair and reliable comparison not tainted by nostalgia.
I do not like giving games scores but if I was forced to do so then this title would be around maybe a 6.5 out of 10 if push comes to shove, being above average in some areas, very good in a few but below average in others. I do not regret preordering it though especially given I only paid around £20 and at that price I feel it is worth it for quality of graphics, quality of a some of the story missions, some of the side missions and mostly because of the gameplay in general which was fairly solid most of the time...also given the amount of time played but keep in mind a lot of that time was pure padding such as the fetch quests that lacked any depth whatsoever or the fact most of my time playing was spent traversing the city for no other reason than being forced to because of no quick travel options.
It's a bit like Diablo 3 in one aspect, the thing it does well is allows for enjoyable bite sized chunk gameplay when feel in the mood for some sneaking around finding often pointless loot, taking down some guards for giggles or do some exploration and such in order to complete another trinket collection. There is enough quality elements to the game which leads me to give a thumbs up rather than thumbs down despite the games annoying flaws or poor design direction on some aspects. The game is very short though (8 main chapters/missions) if remove all the padding mentioned above from pointless replay of animations leading up to things like opening windows or the tedious fetch quests, the majority of time traversing same locations multiple times and also if remove the completionist collecting/scoring elements.

Thief places players in a sprawling steampunk metropolis known as The City, which after a mysterious ritual is interrupted by Garrett and his protege Erin, is ravaged by a plague known as The Gloom. When Garrett comes to, he finds that Erin perished and the city is at it's knees with the citizens united under a man named Orion who is trying to rid the city of The Baron who oversees it and eliminate The Gloom. It's a bit of a remix of the elements that made up the narratives of previous games with corrupt politicians, shadowy occult orders and, of course, plenty of shiny stuff for Garret to get his hands on. The problem is that Garret himself isn't exactly a silver tongued swindler, instead he dryly pontificates on the city's woes and his predisposition to lift anything with a luster. The plot itself unfolds in an uneven manner with the final act unfolding quickly and clumsily; making it similar to watching a racing thoroughbred breaking a leg and tumbling fifty feet from the finish line throwing up clouds of dust and leaving it's jockey a bloody, crumpled mess. There is never a satisfying build to the major plot points in Thief, they are just thrown out without much in the way of foreshadowing dramatic flair. Ultimately, both fans and newcomers will likely not list the plot of Thief among it's strong points.

Like the previous entry, Deadly Shadows, this installment allows players to explore the city between story missions as well as tackle side missions and steal anything of value that isn't bolted down. From the clocktower that Garret calls home, the city is split between districts that unlock as players progress. A jaunt around the city quickly shows players that Garret's kleptomania isn't his only character fault as he is also prone to eves dropping. Loose lipped denizens give players clues to secret loot as well as adding a few narrative flourishes. The City is also host to a number of secrets and keen players will find themselves stumbling across hidden passages, bookshelf switches, wall safes behind paintings, tunnels and traps to boot. Maps can be located that point players in the direction of some cleverly concealed spoils. All of this makes early exploration of The City a real treat but it only takes a mission or two for the luster to fade. Many secret areas don't really seem to lead to any kind of exceptional reward. The game makes a point of letting you know that you have discovered something intentionally tucked away with an audio cue but the rewards are often the same stupid trinkets that populate every other area in the game. Also, over the course of the game navigating the same streets, dodging or bludgeoning the same guards and visiting the same landmarks becomes tiring and tedious. Many players will pick over each and every home before receiving a specific job from Basso, Garrett's contact, necessitating a return trip. More vexing is how lifeless the city feels. Thief makes a point of trying to explain it's empty streets away with the Gloom and a city wide lockdown but nearly every home that Garret finds his way into is unoccupied. Those who are in the streets often stand in one place or follow a very short path. Many of them don't even speak making your time wandering the streets seem like you are taking part in a steampunk parody of Westworld.

Missions are generally a bit more engaging, offering greater challenges and more intriguing environments. Missions are linear, at best offering a few paths to the next objective. Series fans will mourn the more open areas of past titles but there are a few sections which evoke someof the older game's design like one late game mission that has you infiltrating a huge estate and making your way to it's study. It's here that another disappointing flaw rears it's ugly head, while guards can be dangerous, they never feel cunning or autonomous. Guards can be three feet away staring in Garrett's direction but so long as he looms among the shadows, he will remain undetected. Likewise, the simple patrol paths that guards follow makes stalking them and discreetly taking them out really simple. Being discovered in Thief is usually the result of not seeing a pet bird of dog that draws attention to your presence or bumbling on a surface littered with broken glass. If you happen to be detected while in an elevated position, guards will founder around in the area below in a flustered alert state. Levels are designed around this unsatisfactory AI, so there are still some challenges while playing Thief but they are anything but satisfying. Thankfully, Garret's toolbox is better suited for stealing than fighting, so combat should be avoided at all cost. While players can easily pummel a single guard with Garret's Blackjack, facing more than one foe is usually a death sentence. Garret's bow is also a better tool than a weapon with it's long draw time and limited supply of lethal arrows, that is until he get's his grubby hands on exploding blast arrows...

Thief does make some major strides forward when it comes to giving players control over their game experience, and the importance of this innovation for the stealth game genre cannot be overstated. The menu features a number of UI and difficulty options that can be toggled to provide players with and unprecedented amount of control over how much or how little information they have concerning their surroundings. An icon that tells players whether or not they are completely concealed in the dark can be toggled, the mini map can be turned on and off, how health is displayed can be altered, objective markers can be turned off and even the glint given off by trinkets can be turned off. Also, the new focus feature can be turned off as well. Focus helps highlight traps, collectables, switches, breakables and obstacles. With a few upgrades it will also allow you to deliver punishing blows with the backjack, hasten you lockpicking, move silently and even slow time. It's a handy tool for newcomers and even those familiar with the series will find it useful for things like disarming traps. Also, easing newcomers in is the swoops ability which lets Garrett move swiftly and silently for a short distance. In addition to upgrading the focus ability, Garrett can buy upgrades for his bow and clothing as well as perk bestowing trinkets from a Walter White-esque merchant.
Thief isn't exactly the reboot fans had hoped for but there are some flashes of brilliance among the stupid AI, performance hiccups, lame narrative and repetive trips through the city to your next mission. There is plenty here to suggest that a sequel could provide stealth game fans with what they are looking for. Make your decision to purchase accordingly.

I never played the previous Thief games, so I had no predetermined expectations about what the franchise should be. My only hope was for a good game, but unfortunately for every part of the game that I enjoyed, there was something else that I didn't like.
The player takes on the role of Garrett who, as the title suggests, earns his living as a thief. When one job goes wrong, Garrett stumbles into a conspiracy involving high society and a touch of the supernatural. The following story is okay, but it never really excited me, and I didn't find any of the characters interesting.
Thief's gameplay is primarily focused on stealth. You'll want to stick to the shadows and either avoid guards/civilians entirely, or sneak up behind and perform silent takedowns. One very good design decision is that the player decides how forgiving the stealth system is, in the difficulty options. If you want detection to mean instant failure, go for it. If, like me, you prefer to have the ability to fight through your mistakes, you can do that too.
However, the combat is terrible, so you should avoid it unless you have no choice. Both the bow and the melee weapon are slow and weak, and Garrett's armour is paper thin, even when you've bought their upgrades. Taking on more than two enemies simultaneously is almost certain death. This may be realistic, but its not fun.
There are three types of missions. Story and client missions are mostly enjoyable. These require you to break into a unique building and steal a special item which will advance either Garrett's story, or a smaller arc for one of two friendly NPCs. The buildings tend to be quite large, have multiple entrance points and hidden paths to reach your goal while providing excellent stealth opportunities.
Side missions don't have a purpose beyond earning extra coin, which you can also get by stealing from random houses along your path. These all take place in the City hub areas, which is the weakest part of the game. The level design here is very narrow, full of dead ends and only one or two paths through. Even if you ignore these minor missions, you still have to travel through the City to reach the story missions. There's no fast travel option, so the amount of times you have to bypass the same respawning guards, while listening to their one line of repeated dialogue, quickly becomes tedious. You'll also notice that most houses are empty, which makes the City feel lifeless.
It wouldn't be fair for me to comment on graphics because I'm currently below recommended spec for gfx card, so I had to do some tweaking to get a reasonable framerate. Controls are fully rebindable and work fine with mouse and keyboard. Most elements of the HUD can be customised to find your desired balance between functionality and immersion. It took me 17 hours to finish the main quest, and I skipped some side quests, so value for money is good.
Overall I don't think Thief deserves a thumbs down, but I also wouldn't view it as an essential purchase.

If you are into stealth games, Thief might be the game for you.  However, do not be confused in thinking that this game is similar to other popular stealth titles like Splinter Cell, Dishonored, or Hitman.  Thief is a game for stealth purists, that is, the only truly gratifying way to play this game is to remain invisible for the entire time.  Otherwise, Thief is a rather bland experience.
While Thief presents a fairly solid all-around stealth title, there are a few things that I would like to point out that contributed to me rating it as low as I did.  There are two major categories for these gripes.  First, are the problems with the storyline and characters.  If you are looking for a Tom Clancy storyline, an epic struggle of good and evil, or a heartpounding journey into darkness for the main character, you are going to be sad you ever bought this game.  Plain and simple, the story sucks balls.  It is extremely bland and underdeveloped.  In contrast to titles like Dishonored which had a very deep and compelling storyline, Thief comes off like corn flakes without milk-- just stale, boring, and hard to swallow.  Add in the terrible voice acting and this feels more and more like one of those Japanese titles that was voiced over poorly and never quite communitcated the storyline that the devs wanted it to deliver.  Still, depsite not caring about the story at all, the game can be quite enjoyable which speaks to the level of difficulty involved in stealing as much loot as possible while remaining completely hidden.
The second major flaw is concerning basic game mechanics.  There are several issues here that really ruin the fluidity of the game and cause the player to undergo unnecessarily frustrating moments trying to get the game to do what it should do.  First, the mapping system sucks.  As a quasi-open world title, it is important to have the ability to quickly get the player where they want to be.  Good luck with that.  Each sublevel is designed like a maze with almost no help (other than an objective marker) to guide you.  The map has symbols on it, but there are no legends telling you what each symbol means.  Also, you can have a popup map in the corner of the screen, but it only shows the local area and is relatively useless when trying to traverse from one sub-level to another.  This can mean spending tons of time simply trying to figure out where the hell to go to get to where you need to be.  Annoying.  This game desperately needs a Dishonored type system where an arrow appears and points you in the right direction and allows the player to keep their bearings.  Hopefully this is something they patch in later.
Another flawed mechanic, is the way in which some of the windows, doors, and secret passages operate.  Activating some of these doors will instantly push you through them and then close the door behind you in a mini cutscene-like experience.  This can be very frustrating when trying to dodge soldiers looking for you as if you enter the wrong area you are essentially locked out of retreating right away.  Windows and sewer grates often close behind you immidiately after you enter them, which at the very least makes it extremely annoying to go back and forth.
Lastly, whenever you pick up special items, there is a mini-cutscene where you cannot move your character.  This is extremely annoying when you are trying to grab an item in a room where enemies are present as you have to account for an extra 4-5 seconds after you retrieve the item because you just stand there looking at it like a schmuck after you pick it up.
All in all, this is a good game but I shouldn't have paid full price for it.  Pick it up for $25 and it will be a good buy if you like stealth.  If not, stay far away.

The Cat Lady is one of the few games I would actually consider to be a work of art.

The Cat Lady also features an unusual and refreshing visual style which uses a sparse colour palette and even though it sometimes doesn't look very nice I believe this is intentional choice by the artist. The game also has an excellent soundtrack that perfect compliments they different areas of the game.
The game, however, is not perfect. For some reason every save creates a new save slot, preventing one playthrough from using just one save slot. The game also lags slightly and occasionally crashes, although this may just be because my computer isn't very very strong. Overall, I would recommend The Cat Lady for anyone look for a good story or horror experience in a game, or who just wants to try something different.

Risen 2 improves on certain aspects of Risen 1, but takes some pretty serious steps back in other areas.
First, graphically, the game is pretty great and an improvement, voice acting is much improved, the story is way better and follows a much more coherent arc, and the general atmosphere is much, much improved. The pirate setting is generally well done and there is plenty of humor.
NPC teammates are a nice addition, but one of them is so much better than the others that I doubt most players will spend much time switching between them. A couple of them are painfully boring, and one of them seems to be something of a jarjar binks ripoff in terms of irritating accent, total failure at humor and racist undertones.
COMBAT and CHOICE are where this game really fails.
Risen 1 had punishing combat that was at first really difficult, until you figured out the enemies' attack patterns and were given proper armour (that game's "soft" invisible wall in terms of exploration), at which point all combat pretty much became trivial and tedious. Risen 2 takes any feeling of real flow out of combat by making most enemies' attacks unblockable, which makes combat revolve around spamming attacks and hoping to beat them to the punch. Once you get a rifle, pretty much all combat involves cheesy "hit and run" and/or using your teammate as a distraction/tank, while you spam the fire button.
There are lots of choices for off-hand weapons and tactics, but because of enemies' total lack of AI and frustrating attack spamming/swarming, none of them are particularly useful.
Combat is, in short, broken, tedious and not fun. There is also a lot of it.
CHOICE is this game is thankfully not broken like in Risen 1, but rather pointless and badly implemented all the same. You pick a "faction" close to the start of the game, but neither has much of an impact on the story other than some changed dialogue, and one different NPC on your ship, neither of which is interesting enough to use throughout the rest of the game, IMHO. This choice also locks you in/out of using either Rifles or Voodoo. Rifles are SO MUCH better than Voodoo that choosing Voodoo amounts to purposely gimping your character. This is a big problem, since Voodoo powers are lots of fun and open up 90% of the (otherwise extremely boring) crafting system. Muskets make all combat extremely easy, however, so picking the fun of voodoo just doesn't make sense since you end up with much more frustrating combat. It would have been great if the devs had allowed you to learn all talents and mix the voodoo with the rifles.
Character progression is nicely handled, but other than the Voodoo/Musket choice, I think most players will end up putting points into exactly the same skills, since a handful of them (lockpicking especially) are necessities, and the rest are no-brainers. In the end, it's a very shallow system, but could be a template for a great skill system in the hands of better developers.
This game will really leave a "low budget game" bad taste in your mouth. There are lots of corners cut, the devs don't seem to have a very easy time using the game engine (i think it's based on unreal engine) as there are some awkward animations, draw distances and fake physics, and while certain aspects of the voice acting are great, others are horrible and/or too repetitive in the Morrowind kind of sense of every non-major NPC having one of 2 voices. Walking into deep water causes the screen to briefly go black before you're teleported back to where you're standing, certain kills have a Fallout 3 style slow motion finish in which your weapon will never actually make contact with your victim and most textures will be see-through, and NPCs in general have too few lines and don't react to your exploits/the changing world in any meaningful way.
I'll also mention that, while the devs are known for "open world" games like Risen 1 and Gothic, this game is painfully linear for the first 35% of the game, then gives you a bioware-style choice of what order the next 3 small "hubs" will be tackled in, follwed by the final 20% of the game being linear.
I left this game running accidentally overnight at one point, and would estimate that game took me in all about 20-25 hours to beat, including the DLC.
A special note regarding the DLC: The "Air Temple" is horrible and tedious, while "Treasure Island" is simply below-average, boring DLC. Niether adds anything to the game (air temple is so bad that it actually takes away from the rest of the game, in my opinion, even though it adds an NPC from Risen 1 who some fans might appreciate).
All in all, I can only recommend this game if you've replayed Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyborn so many times that you're sick of them, have multiple playthroughs of all Bioware RPG's and Witcher games under your belt, and don't have any higher quality or more original games in your backlog. Of course, if you're a HUGE fan of pirates, by all means try it out.

This is a great way to play Magic the Gathering for free. Magic Duels can provide a fun MTG experience and never spend a single penny.
It is also a great way for new players to get started. You get to build your own decks, or have the game help you. You can test decks against bots instead of going straight into PvP. Also, the game does a pretty good job of explaining things like phases of a turn, priority, how to interact with the stack, etc.
One downside is that this game is watered down a bit. It kind of had to be. It would have been a programming nightmare to put every single detail of how MTG works in this game. Also, not every card in the real expansions are in the game. They took some of the cards out and included some cards not in current standard. That's not necessarily bad, but it makes the experience not exactly the same as your local standard constructed FNM.
Lastly, this game is a little buggy. the developers have acknowledged that the game is buggy and they have done a kinda sh*t job of fixing the bugs. In earlier versions of this game, some cards just didnt work the way the card said it did. "Greenwarden of Murasa" is one example. That card had two abilities, the second one was just broken in Magic Duels. It literally didnt work properly. In a later update, "Abbot of Keral Keep" didnt work properly. It could make you skip phases of your turn without you telling the game to do so. Little things like that made me quit Magic Duels for long periods of time until they were fixed.

I absolutely loved Far Cry 3. I beat the singleplayer, the coop campaign with 3 buddies, and hit max level in multiplayer. You can see my Far Cry 3 pvp videos on youtube, including "Rambo Mode", named by PCGamesN as one of the top 10 entertaining FC3 videos. Based on my love for Far Cry 3 I went ahead, on blind faith, and preordered the deluxe edition of this game.
With that said, what a massive disappointment this game is. There isn't any one single aspect that breaks it for me. Instead, I would call it death by a thousand cuts.
First off I want to address the absolutely undebatable. Something that has nothing to do with personal taste. This game is BUGGY AS ALL HELL. Several times I've randomly slid backwards up hills as if an invisible force was dragging me backward. I've died from 5 foot drops, and in the next moment fell 30 feet and didn't take a single point of damage. Birds constantly land in midair. I've seen up to 4 birds all perched in the sky, and it's not due to draw distance -- this happens even a few meters away on ultra detail. If you skin an animal and your inventory is full, that animal is forever broken and cannot be skinned, even if you drop items to free up space. To add insult, they still glow white as if lootable. Small bugs like this are absolutely pervasive, and affect nearly every mechanic in the game.
Looking past the bugs, this game is also riddled with poor design decisions. Perhaps the most outrageous and baffling is that there is a constant tiny radius around you during every single mission where if you walk 10 feet out of it, you lose. I thought this was an open world game? An early game example is when you have to pick between two quest givers and there is a propaganda poster less than 50 feet away from them. But you can't pick it up. If you do, you'll fail the mission for being out of bounds, and you'll have to watch the entire mission intro cutscene again which is several minutes long. You might say "well, damn! That's not a big deal! I'll just turn around if the message pops up!" Good luck. All the most fun ways to travel (wingsuit, gyrocopter, handglider, etc) move so fast that you'll get game over'd a split second after you see the message. This game is an open world game that arbitrarily decides it doesn't want to be open world anymore. It wasn't such an issue in Far Cry 3 because a) it was far more rare, b) the boundaries were far less confined, and c) there were clear out-of-bounds lines shown on the map when this type of rule applied. Not here.
In coop, we experienced falling through the world. Respawning and instantly dying as if falling from a great height. Terrible syncing issues, such as seeing whole groups of enemies and vehicles that my coop partner did not. This was not a consistent issue, but it's something we never experienced in all of our hours playing Far Cry 3. The most ridiculous death I had was getting teleported to my buddy because he had wingsuited off a cliff. It teleported me close to him in mid-air, in my own wing suit, headed straight toward a cliff wall and I promptly died.
The PVP is so bad now I'm not even going to waste words on it.
A lot of people complained about Far Cry 3's story, but this story is just flat and lifeless. Pagan Min seems entertaining enough, but your character's motivation -- what we're supposed to relate to -- is meaningless. You're here to spread your mother's ashes -- so logically you might as well stay and instantly transform into a super soldier. Criticise Far Cry 3's Jason Brody all you want, but at least he had an easily relatable motivation -- revenge, and a modicum of development. He changed, however unlikely, from a terrified kid into a guerilla leader. In this, your character literally goes from being a bored sounding tourist with no desire to be involved in the war, to hanging up on the rebel leader offering you backup and telling her you are going to destroy the very first enemy outpost in the game by yourself. Why? "Because I can handle this." And your character still sounds incredibly bored about it all. I can't stress how bored your character sounds at every moment of the game.
I am scratching my head trying to understand how they could take a solid game like Far Cry 3 and break so many aspects of it. The grappling is cool. Some of the new wildlife is cool. The graphics are gorgeous. But everything else? I'm just not happy with my purchase at all. I should have loved this game, but the only emotions I felt while playing coop were boredom and anger, punctuated by an incredibly rare moment of "wow, that was cool". Those rare moments were not worth $60, let alone $90.
