Risen 2: Dark Waters is a very glitchy and at times very tedious pirate RPG game. If you are honestly wanting to play an RPG, I would suggest you try the Witcher or Skyrim, as your time would be better spent with those games. In regards to Risen 2, I will say this: the combat is broken and frustrating for the most part, there are all manner of glitches which break any sort of immersion you have in the game, the story is incredibly bland and unexciting and most of the characters you meet are devoid of personality. In essence, the game is unpolished and truthfully not worth the time investment. It is sad, because the pirate setting seemed interesting, the voice acting is remarkably good at times, and even the music (though repetitive) is enjoyable. The idea of scourging for hidden treasures, finding legendary artifacts and the different ways to buid your character are great... but in the end never really amount to anything. If you enjoyed the first one, you will probably like or at least tolerate this game. But having so many incredible RPG jewels out there, Risen 2 just isn't worth the effort. Ultimately, you can enjoy this game and it does have its moments, but only if you keep your expectations low.

Let's see... Risen 2 is a classic Piranha Bytes game. So what's a Piranha Bytes game like? Well, it is an open world rpg which presents a fabulous world to explore and has ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fighting mechanics.
I am a fan of Gothic series, especially Gothic 1 & 2. So I liked Risen 2 very much. Tough beware if you are not familiar with Gothic. This game may not be the game you want or think. Or it may be.
Risen 2 presents very very very beautiful lands to explore. Besides the models, the graphics are very good and the only thing that prevents you to feel you are actually in that tropical island is the lack of wind on your face. The short but adequate soundtrack also plays it's part well.
So if you like open-world RPGs I definetely recommend the Risen 2. Just keep in mind that Risen 2 is a little "different" game.
Overall game mechanics may be and will be awkward sometimes. The fighting mechanics are broken as in every Piranha Bytes game, especially for the first 10 hours in the game (But don't give up, it gets easier and enjoyable after you get some skills and stuff). The progress is slow and painful. The story is not strong but the cheesy characters are somehow enjoyable.
So it's like a negative review. Actually it is not. The point is, Piranha Bytes never learn from their mistakes. Yet their all games has a kind of strange charm in them. They make you angry, but they make you happy more. Those bad gameplay mechanics that you will complain, you will get to enjoy them after a point. At least, you will ignore them. The "charm" that the game possesses makes you enjoy the game. Besides, Risen 2 really puts you in the world, as Gothic 1 did back in the time. Maps are so lively. You can play and enjoy the game even just for that.

While this game is both singleplayer and multiplayer, I found it more fun to play it coop then singleplayer.. I have played and seen all the classes. Each ofcourse has his own advantage. The paladin can block arrows, can heal later in the game and hits quite fast, but is bad against stronger or many mage class enemies. The ranger has enough range to kill most spawnpoints without getting near, but has avarage health and mana. The mage has an AOE fireball, but has little health. The castle is the same every time you go through it, so if you want to have a different map each playthrough you're out of luck. This said, the maps are big. You need a lot of time to clear them and then some more time to find the secrets in this game. These are well hidden and you need a good eye. Also, while there is only one campaing at this time, the game has a leveleditor to make your own maps. Futhermore, the enemies are more of the same all the time. You have ranged, melee and caster enemies, each with certain abilities (faster, poison etc.). One might find this repetitive, but then again this is a hack and slash game; they are always repetative. The coop game I played lasted about 7 hours for me.
In general I would give this game an 8 out of 10.

I've got something now like 8,000 games logged on Heroes of the Storm; rightfully I'm an all-season-repeat Master+ player. I was drawn to Battlerite from the word of a couple friends, and even the occassional random advertisement.
I can say, fairly safely, for a game that still more or less clasifies itself as a BRAND NEW release, this game has more time, care, effort, aesthetic, and so on than I could have ever imagined. The indie gaming branch "Stunlock" has, in my opinion, managed to so grossly outdo the genre and competition from companies like Blizzard and Riot that it's seemingly miraculous.
There is no pronounced "meta". There's no overdone systemic flaws in maps or game procession. There is you, one or maybe two other players, a big circle, and an all-out skill versus skill slaughterhouse competition of grueling 2 minute rounds.
Perhaps the greatest part of this whole game is the "All Champions Bundle". Take, for example, a game like Overwatch. You pay to buy the game around $60, in return, the content (of course outside of loot boxes and cosmetic appeal) is free to you from the moment you buy the game onward. Stunlock gives Battlerite players the choice of the "All Champions Bundle" which unlocks every character in the roster and every character future.... for $30. You have to understand, you can literally still play the game entirely free without ever dropping a cent, but if you want to talk about the most iconic deal you've probably seen in a game - consider this the "game's price". $30 unlocks all of the critical content, specifically the champion pool, and allows you to direct your attention towards grinding in-game currencies to unlock cosmetics and appeals that you'd like through work and proper effort. I've honestly felt more inclined to buy in-game loot boxes knowing that my money is actually well spent here.
Battlerite is a colorful cast of memorable characters, awesome fights, conscious consumer choices, and a caring team of developers that obviously take great pride in their work. An amazing game, and I'm eager to see where it goes from here.

okay, so I've played this game on and off probably since I was 10 or 11 years old. I have put countless hours into this game and it will forever and always hold a speical place in my heart.
That being said...
The Good
This game is MASSIVE! By virtue of it being such a long standing MMO, it has more conntent then I could ever hope to see.
Grinding (And ooohhhh yeah there's A LOT of that...) has some suprising little challenges that make it more tolorable.
It has a unique artstyle and gameplay as compared to most MMO's.
It has a lot of charm if you're willing to sit through the other stuff.
The Bad
Um... There's a whole lot.
The comunity seems to have fallen appart. I've heard of MMO's with toxic comunities. Maplestory's is non existant. There's a group of max level players that seem to... enjoy? them? Selves? (They sit in cities waiting for people to "fame" them.) I Actively attempted to have social interactions with other individuals, and failed. Miserably. They're just... not there. Or they simply seem to not care. At all.
It's so borring to do anything after a while. I've been playing since I was ten, and it probably took me 25+ hours just getting one character to level 100 (Which is less than half-way to max level) and... it wasn't fun after the inital 20 or so. I did it just because it was like my childhood dream to have a character at the final job advancement.
Also, balance is non-existant. Certain classes are just WAY more fun and WAY stronger than other classes. That's just part of the game. (I guess that's not nessisarily bad. It's just something to be aware of)
The Ugly
It's... it's an old game. It shows. It feels like they keep trying to put more and more paint on it, and now it feels like it's just that... Paint. A facsimile of it's former self. Almost like someone has taken a dead relative and taxadermised they're corpse and prettends like they're still alive. (A bit of an extreme example, but acurate nonetheless.)
The end.
I am done with this game, it's not fun for me anymore. If you decide to play it, maybe you'll find something I didn't and have more fun then I did. I sinceerly hope you do. But I honestly suggest you play a different game. or wait for Maplestory 2 to come out. I know I'll be giving it a shot, haha. (Seriously, it's a thing give it a look.)

The game is made up of a ton of short levels in which you're thrown into an arena with some walls, platforms, enemies, and sometimes other things like conveyor belts, doors that are opened with electricity, or other more unique objects. You blast your way through all the Target Enemies using powers picked up in the level, then repeat for each other level. Variety comes from being given different weapons, fighting different enemies, the occasional boss, and of course, the worlds' unique gimmicks. The basic gameplay flow may sound repetitive, but the game generally stays pretty fresh, largely thanks to its great weapon variety, when considering how many ways there are to mix weapons.
Since both characters are dramatically different, including in how their weapons act when they have the exact same weapons available, and since stages are completely redesigned for Hard mode, it's perfectly reasonable to want to fully clear both difficulties as both characters, which added up to about 28 hours for me. This included a enough of a dip into endless mode to unlock some bonus stages that required it, but not even trying everything available in endless mode, doing much with custom stages, or playing much with some of the gameplay modifiers that are gradually unlocked.
The writing of the game is decent enough, but mostly wisely stays out of the way of you destroying more robots.
The game's difficulty felt fine to me. It's a decent challenge, but not amazingly difficult. My deaths per stage stayed within the single digit range, with my overall average even including normal mode remaining below one.
A few too many controls and a bit too chaodic but fun all the same. The extra character is simply a hassle to control though with not a lot of clarity.

It's one of those games that you have to play just for the experience itself.
I still remember that moment where I stumbled upon this guy who got shot by a sniper. He was hurt and immobile. He was out getting medicine for his kid who was sick when the sniper got to him. I ran through the sniper fire with relative ease, hiding behind an object here and there until I got across the street to the man's residence. When I busted through the door, I heard his baby start to cry. I had to stop for a minute. The fact that there are millions of children out there right now who spend their childhood in this environment dawned on me. Dammit, I wasn't gonna let this kid die because of this senseless war so I unlocked this passageway that was out of the sniper's line of sight so the father could get through safely. He gave his child the medicine and promptly gave me a reward. I didn't really take much as I thought that the child's reunion with his father was reward enough for me. I strolled out of the building feeling like a champ. It didn't last long as time was running out and I foolishly hurried my character to leave the area and head home. What I didn't expect was for my character to run across the street like an idiot til he got shot.
Very much over hyped. While the atmosphere and "story" are immersive, it is a potentially good game ruined by poor combat system, limited scope for exploration and absence of save system.

Never have I ever felt as depressed as this game has made me.
Odd sentece to start this review, I know, however, allow me explain why this still a positive review.
This War of Mine is an amazing execution of the roguelike genre that uses that overused theme of War that most of our games now a days seem to have grown fond of using, however, they delve into things we generally do not think about, the civilian aspect of war. What happens to those who are not soldiers.
This game is one of the few games that have made me stop for a second and consider the moral implications of my actions. Do I starve to death, or do I kill to survive? That is a question that made me stop playing the first time I played this game.

It's one of the best thought, best designed games I've seen in a while, with a sound track that will get into you.
This is a game you simply MUST play at least once in your life.

Risen 2 follows the original Risen and Gothic 1&2 as entertaining and challenging 3rd person rpgs.  I enjoyed it about the same as Gothic 2 but with an ease of use not found in the Gothic games.  The controls have improved IMMENSELY since Gothic 1&2 and combat is more intriguing compared to Risen.  The story isn't the most engaging, but it is fun, including a few surprise moments.  The voice acting is good, but accompanying hand movements can be silly and repetitive.    I encountered some minor graphical glitches (swords not being in NPC's hands, for instance) but no major crashes.  The environmental graphics were quite a bit better than I expected.  The characters and their animations seem to be a slight step up from Risen.  The HUD is unobtrusive and allows for some sense of immersion.
Now, I am comparing it to Risen and Gothic 1&2 because of the setting, protaganist and system.  It is not an action RPG.  It is not Diablo, Skyrim  Choices can matter to how the quests resolve and the story progesses.  There is action and prompts for traps.  Combat isn't the easiest, either to use or to survive against the monsters until a few tricks are learned.  All in all, I recommend the game if you like RPGs or wish to try one.

I so wanted to like this game.  Here's what's wrong:
1) Too many aliens.  At the start of the game the entire planet is covered in randomly aggressive aliens.  With the starting soldiers you can't kill them quickly enough to get to the nests (spawn points) where you can only temporarily stop the spawning.  The Seige Worms can one shot most every one of your units until you've really improved them.  If they started the game with only one alien unit at each spawn point (like barbarians in Civ V), you might have a chance to explore before your explorer gets killed.
2) Your units are too weak to take out another civs city.  I attacked a city early on with two soldiers, two ranged units, and three seige units.  I couldn't scratch the city.  In Civ V, I would have taken the city in at most three turns.
3) It's almost impossible to keep your civ healthy (happy) if you expand quickly.  And there are so few buildings that keep your health (happiness) on the positive side that once you fall behind you're stuck there for 40+ turns.

This review concerns potential consumers who have yet learned to code Java:
TyranoBuilder is a tool kit designed for aspiring game designers / programmers who wish to start small. It's designed to simplify the process of creating a visual novel under the assumption that its users have minimal knowledge of the code tucked behind its interface, and what a wonderful interace it presents.
Each function is shown as small "icons" that the user can drag and drop onto a timeline with ease. At its surface, it does what it advertised. But at its core, it leaves too much to be desired:
The icons themselves are simply shortened strands of code that the user is free to drag along the timeline, but without proper knowledge of using Java (which is free for the user to code onto the timeline) caused a laundry list of frustrations that will hinder the user's experience as follows:
1. Character portraits do not have the freedom of adjusting their size / position without duplicating multiple versions of a character portrait that has different dimensional sizes.
2. Without proper knowledge of Java, functions such as puzzle-solving, inventories, characters (or narrator) remembering custom-created names / identities (from the player) and the like are nigh impossible in this current build. One way of manuevering around this dilemna is by duplicating the same scene multiple times per unique criteria (this will fill up a lot of unnecessary space for the visual novel)
3. It's impossible to edit sound effects and background music from where the user wants them to begin (in the middle of a sound effect / song) and where they want them to end.
4. It's common to experience the preview funciton / exported visual novel build to crash without being given an affordance of <what> causes the software to crash in the first place. (Edit: This tends to happen when the user reaches an undisclosed threshold of too much code within a single scene)
The list goes on.
Despite these flaws, it is in the best interest for potential consumers to be aware that this product will <not> create proper visual novels without additional coding knowledge, but it has potential to be a compelling experience for newcomers to learn how to make smaller, simplified projects nonetheless.

This is a game by its most basic definition; A system in which a player makes meaningful decisions to meet a defined goal, whether that goal is defined by the system or the player.
Playing through this game once took around 70 minutes of my time, and was decently impactful. The situations and feelings depicted are ones I have and do deal with, even if not to the full extent of diagnosable depression. At the end of each playthrough, there is a reflective slide which generally details a number of decisions you made, and definitely gets you to think about the choices you as the player made in each situation.
The game plays out as scenarios, which are each well written and common enough that almost anyone can see themselves there. You are presented a situation, and, at the bottom of the page, after a detailed but not at all tedious narrative, you are given a list of choices. One of the more impactful parts of this game is the list of choices you can make. Each are presented in the form of the narrator's thought process, and there are ALWAYS choices in red text and crossed out, which should be read, as they represent what a fully functioning, non-depressed person could and likely would do. By presenting these options, which, are clearly better than the rest, but making them unavailable to select, it brings home the point that the narrator, or the player knows what they SHOULD do, but, as the narrator is literally incapable of choosing that option, so is the player.
This is 80 MB of hard drive space and an hour well spent. Further thanks to the developer for addressing an issue which is rarely addressed in such a manner. 10/10

The art and music were just fine, but those are the least of your worries when it comes to a good game. What makes a good game "good" is the story and gameplay. The gameplay is less important and can be easy to ruin if not given a bit of thought. Thankfully, this game doesn't do that...a lot. The gameplay was multiple-choice answers to questions and I don't mind that. Full disclosure: I am a beta tester for this game.
Copy Kitty! What is there to say about it? It's got a lighthearted plot, good character design, and big, shiny explosions! If any of that sounds like good times to you, you're in the right place.
Considering the price point, this game throws a LOT of content the player's way. Two campaign modes, each with two difficulties with enough differences to arguably be called entire seperate campaigns themselves. An endless survival mode with a bunch of environmental variants. Modifiers to make the game harder, easier, shinier, squeakier, or just plain weirder!
Then we get in to player-created content! Copy Kitty comes fully equipped with it's own level-building mode, so the party never stops! Build levels, slap your friends in the face with them, race for the best time! Or don't! Maybe you want to make a puzzle level! Those can be done too!
Gameplay-wise you're looking at a 2D platformer/shoot-em-up with plenty of weapon choice, and it revels in it. Will you use the Planet Breaker? Maybe the Paradox Blade is more your style? How about Orbital Laser? They're all in there, with plenty more weapons to choose from!
My sole complaint is that certain points in the game can get slightly visually overwhelming, but the pacing of the game means it's never for very long.
TL;DR: If you're here this game probably has something for you. Pick it up, you won't regret it!

Disclaimer: Steam only logs hours played while online; my in-game records show as almost 50 hours played, and that timer only goes up while in levels and such; it does not account for the time spent in the soundtest or gallery. And believe me, I've spent a few hours in those, as well. Worth noting that in those 48 hours, I am still not done Savant's hard mode (Only done up to World 6) and am still missing 5 or 6 achievements, mostly related to endless mode.
Copy Kitty is, quite frankly, an example of Early Access done right. The game has been in development for a long time, and I first learned about it in 2012 when an LPer by the name of Raocow took a look at a much, much earlier build. Yet, it only came out on Steam in 2016, showing the dedication to making a good game instead of looking to make a quick buck like so many other Early Access titles. As of the first Steam Release, there's easily enough to rival many full games, and they're still working on additions.
The first impression is strong; your first time playing, it launches straight into the Tutorial - a Tutorial that serves to kick off the story, no less. Right away, you're launched into what the game has to offer, and what an offering it is! While it can best be described as "Kirby ate the Gunstar Heroes," I realize not everyone has played Gunstar Heroes, so allow me to explain in slightly more detail what I mean.
In GH, you could get up to two weapons, and combine them or fire them individually. Copy Kitty takes this idea up to 11 by allowing you to combine up to three weapons. Although these weapons have finite ammunition, I do remind you of the "Copy" in the title; you're always getting more. Even one of the playable characters (Boki Lamira, the titular "Copy Kitty,") comments on how more enemies just means more powers to copy, and how it's a rather neat advantage to have. But that's not to say that the fights against fewer enemies are bad, either. Of particular note is a boss known as Arikan, who basically pulls a Meta Knight and gives you a sword for a one on one duel - a sword with a bunch of neat abilities you don't really get from other weapons, making it a popular enough boss that it got it's own music after it had already been implemented. It's always a good sign when the developers listen to the feedback and build on it.
What really makes the game memorable, however, is simply it's personality. And I don't just mean how flashy the game looks, but the explosions do help. The banter between Boki and her uncle, Savant, is just the right mix of silly and serious. Many levels (most notably bosses, but not always bosses) will also provide hints after you lose one or more times, and some of these conversations are amusing - and without giving too much away, all I can say is... "Freakish Experiment on Hard Mode." Anyone who's died to that boss knows exactly what I mean. I love it.
I also need to mention the soundtrack; I'm not normally a fan of techno, but considering the setting of the game, it just works, and I find myself going back to the Sound Test regularly just to play it in the background as I work on other things. There's numerous variants of songs for specific situations (Such as the more cheerful music from World 1, and then a subdued version of it for a mission when you don't want to go in guns blazing.) The standard "Low HP Beeps" from many games have actually been worked into the soundtrack, with the song adjusting based on how damaged you are. The Sound Test even lets you toggle these damage thresholds to see how the music changes. It's a great way to get your attention without being infuriating within a short time.
Between two very distinct playable characters and over 40 hours of gameplay (Unless I just suck, which is admittedly a very real possibility - I did beat Boki's Extra World on Hard Mode, but it took me a few tries!) there's definitely enough here to keep you playing, and I basically reccommend it to anyone who likes this kind of thing.
Pros:
- For an Early Access title, there's a LOT of content.
- Tight controls and frantic action.
- The artstyle is nice; flashy, but not gaudy.
- A fleshed out setting via the Encyclopedia and Bestiary.
- So much personality.
- Goldeneye-style cheats: Infinite ammo? Invincibility? Sure, but it's just for fun, can't unlock anything with them on.
- Fun achievements, like "Kick this thing in the face!"
- The soundtrack, quite frankly, rocks.
- Robust Level Editor lets you save and share entire level packs.
Cons:
- Sometimes, the dazzling explosions can make it easy to get hit since it's hard to see!
- A few enemies, like the Paradox Yinmiro Delta, can go die in a fire for all I care.
- Controls can take a little getting used to; Boki doesn't shoot straight up, for example.
- Some bosses can feel unfair, but at least Hard Mode lets you skip up to 5 levels.
Reccomendation: If the trailer looks appealing, you'll probably like it!

Far Cry 4 follows a very similar formula to FC3, you will still hunt animals for weapon/ammo slot upgrades. You will still liberate towers and enemy camps. There are a multitude of small improvements though that really add to the formula. I don't want to spoil them, but just know that the game conceptually is very similar, although improved over the last version.
The graphics are great, set in fictional country that seems to be modelled off of Nepal, the change of landscape is much appreciated. There are lots of new vehicles, weapons and different enemy types this time around. There is also a pretty impressive grappling mechanic with some cool rope physics.
This game does a much better job than FC3 of making a direct assault with guns blazing a more viable approach. In FC3 they made it seem like you had the option, but really the reward system sort of forced you to go stealth. Not so much in this game. You will need stealth at times definitely, but going in guns blazing is much more viable.
The different enemy types also add a lot to the strategy. There are now different types of heavies, as well as a bow wielding "cloaking" enemy that cannot be permanently marked.
There are a lot of small changes like that which make the game really enjoyable.
This game gets a solid 8.5/10, well worth the playthrough.

I'm a huge fan of Risen, so although I expected a reasonable game, I really didn't expect to enjoy Risen 2 more than its predecessor.
Both are third person adventures, both have solid stories that generate cause and effect with a beginning, middle and end.  In Risen 2 you play a pirate with a number of companions available who are actually useful.  I'm not a fan of using companions.  I play Skyrim without them unless forced by a quest.  In Risen 2, the fact your companions get stuck in and not stuck in your way is a bonus.
Risen 2 is an exciting game.  With Patty, Captain Steelbeard's daughter from Risen, you journey across the sea to various islands, tracking down legendary weapons, digging up treasure and deciding which faction you want to side with.  You have plenty of choice regarding how you develop your character and teachers are to be found in every port.  I've focused on being a thief and just love the trained monkey.  NCPs talk to it, ask what its up to, does it want a drink - silly detail, but wonderfully immersive.  Parrots also feature and are fun as well as useful.
General control of your character is straightforward but fights are another story.  Combat in Risen 2 has been slated for being poor but, like Dungeon Lords and Venetica, you need to use timing and avoidance to make the most of your abilities.  You also use both hands.  Your right has a sword, spear or voodoo doll, your left a pistol, coconut, knife, parrot, sand/salt.  Plus, you can kick an enemy.  The only two handed weapon I've found to date is a musket.  The Boss battles are hard, but enjoyable.  This isn't an easy game, the combat is difficult to master, but very satisfying once you have.  I've also noticed there is often more than one way to complete a quest.
Yes, I did say a voodoo doll is a weapon.  Rather than using magic as we gamers generally understand and know it, Risen 2 has voodoo.  At times it's quite brilliant and has given me some of the biggest laughs I've had from a game for a long time.  There is a lot of humour present in the dialogue.  Combine this with taking someone over by waving a doll at them and..... well, I'll let you find out.
The dialogue also contains a fair amount of cussing - but then you're amongst pirates.  Joking aside, this is not a game you would want your children listening to, the language is very adult.  But, if you enjoy action packed, third person RPGs, have a look at this one.  It's very enjoyable and I'm totally hooked.

I love this game because it is a very unique take on the rts genre. If you are looking for traditional base building, resource gathering, and specialized counter units, you should look elsewhere. This game is very simple and easy to learn the basics, but difficult ot master. Only 2 ground unit types, 2 air, and 2 sea. Each is 100% equal in strength to the other, so a $3.5B Bomber will be on equal footing with a $1B infantry unit. Once a battle starts there's not really much you can do to affect the outcome other than throw more units in. The key to this game is maneuvering. If an enemy is more poweful than you, the only way to win is to find where he's exposed and use faster, more expensive units, to go around their stronger forces to capture cities and hurt their economy, or attack isolated units before their main force catches up to whittle him down. I promise every single scenario is beatable if you find the right strategy.
PROS
Very unique
Very simple yet still challenging
Pretty good value, especially if on sale
Multiplayer
CONS
Honestly won't be very fun until you get to the large scale scenarios, which can take a while
No campaign
Multiplayer never has anyone on it

So, with  War, the Game one gets the basic RTS package, with the twist of your map being the entire earth and you having the topdown view on a sphere instead of the obligatory 2d map. Unlike many other games of this genre, War, the Game does not offer a main story-line, but instead various scenario missions - some also in multiplayer - which will reward you with a certain amount of stars when you fulfill specific extra conditions (these may vary from the time you required to the amount of money you spent etc.)
Also unlike many other RTS games, this game offers no possibility of base-building, and does not give all players the same starting conditions:
In the game you take control over one of the Earth's many nations, controlling their cities and armies. Cities have a certain income (I couldn't really figure out a pattern - for example Sydney with 4.6 million inhabitants generates 8 billion $/year, whilst Munich with 1.4 million inhabitants generates 16 billion $/year), so when you start with a great or a rich nation, you automatically have a headstart since your income over time and your starting army differs from other's. In multiplayer missions this leads to great imbalance (America for example has 14 starting cities (with a total income of  137.8 billion $/year)- all of them providing buildings that allow the creation of units - whilst Australia is stuck with 2  (with a total income of 16 billion $/year) ).
There are five building types, which are all preset, which takes away a great amount of flexibility and individual strategy since one usually has to resign to one of the very few tactics that always seem to work out fine.
In multiplayer getting to a lategame stage could get very interesting for sure, but the problem is that the game is very slow paced, resulting in the multiplayer games dragging on for hours - and without the option to save it's very hard to pull off a full game.
Now in singleplayer you can for one speed up the time and also save, but this mode really suffers from it's nonexistant versatility -> most of the missions have one and only one way to be beaten, whilst in the large scheme world wars the AI always goes back to their
strategy, making the game very monotonous.
The gameplay itself also is very basic, there are seven unit types:
Infantry, armor, jets, bombers, battleships, transporters and carriers. Now whilst all of these have their little twists about them, they all share the same firepower, resulting in the battles strategically devolving into 'Who can send more troops?'.
Now since the fighting is based around this strategy, the game's early stage is basically building units into a massive stack and waiting for money to be able to build more units to throw onto that massive stack.
Overall I give the game a 3.5/10 - for it offers no more than any other RTS game, has poor amount of
content and thus gets stale very fast in addition to it suffering from too slow gameplay.

Depression is not a thing one can explain easily. An allegory of you, laying down in a dark room, with a dim light just out of your hand's reach is as close as I can get. You could reach the light if you could stand up, but you can't. You blame yourself for this, adding more fuel to the dark that surrounds you. The light, other people, whose lives seem to be all right, is the most disheartening thing of all. You just can't seem reach it, because it's just impossible to stand up. I claim not to know what depression truly is, for I am not or have been depressed, but that's how I see it.
Depression Quest is a text-based game that emphasizes on choice. Even if the choices aren't "hard" in the traditional sense, DQ made the choices hard on a wholly another level. No other game has ever made my mouse feel like lead. It's just emotionally hard to click the button that leads to the next part of the story. Even if the choice before you seems to have an obvious good and bad answers, actually clicking the good answer is an challenge in on itself. At least for me it was.
Playing this game hurts. It hurts because you can, for a little while, see what it really means to be depressed. See through your own eyes what life looks like to another person. See, and also feel a little bit, how hard it can be for some people to even get out of their bed every morning. How even the most obvious of answers become hard when one just cannot anymore.
The way the game works enforces the feeling, and it is the intention. You are given choices, of which usually some are ruled out, but still readable. This gives insight on the fact that depressed people often DO KNOW what they could do, but they just as often CANNOT do those things.
In short, this game lets you feel the doubt and anguish that depressed people go through every day. The fear that what if the right choice is the wrong one, and what if everything goes into s**t even if you try your hardest. The frustration towards the people who do not understand, but also the relief when some do. It is a game that one should play... I was going to say "if", but it's not necessary. This game is free, and it gave me stronger emotions than any other game has, in that short half an hour that it lasted.
And... If you are depressed, remember: there are always people who don't understand, but there are also those who do. The most important part is: you are not alone.
It is a good game. But I can't complete even one game because it depresses me too much.

TyranoBuilder may not be perfect YET but what it CAN do for you, outweighs what it CAN'T

I was featured on CinnamonToastKen's YouTube channel with a game I built (Deadpool Dating Simulator) using TyranoBuilder. This is an amazing piece of software. It makes building a Visual Novel incredibly easy. I have experience with everything from flash to gamemaker and this is the quickest way to build a game and tell a story. Very user friendly. I had my first game completed in around five hours, most of which was just spent writing and creating graphics. Love it and recommend it to all.

Easy enough to require no scripting, flexible enough to create traditional VN to mobile VN to kinetic novels.
Of course, to have more advanced features scripting is recommended, and there is a good library of tags for Tyranoscript including examples.
The tutorial is well made and the support is amazing. Every update brings quite a lot of new features to the table. Customizing the GUI is crazy easy, creating galleries and extra title screen items can be done with little work.
The constant drag and dropping can become more tedious then double checking indentation in Ren'Py, but that's the price to pay.
Recommended despite the flaws (Android export doesn't work for Lollipop, preview can be funky).

According to Steam, and as of writing, I spent about 1.4 hours using this program. When I first bought it awhile back, I was pretty excited and positive about the click and drag features. But recently, I've tried out Ren'py for the first time, and after spending about a good week now using it, I can no longer look at TyranoBuilder the same way I had previously.
I won't really go on a rant about how much I prefer Ren'py since deciding to try it out, but I will bring up my complaints about the programming. First of all, the font text that is displayed in game, looks drawn on, and doesn't resemble what you would expect to see from a visual novel. There are also plenty of random crashes when performing an action too quickly, the screen when starting up randomly positions itself, and scrolling down in coding is odd.
These are just a few of the problems the program has, but overall, it's pretty unprofessional for something that's $15. Still, with the program being new, I look forward to seeing how it develops in comparison to other VN engines.

Very easy to operate, has comprehensive tutorials on website, and the creators are actually extremely helpfull. When i asked a question they even made a specific video covering exactly what i wanted to know! Its incredible!

One Manga Day is a very special kind of game. It is a game I recommend. Not because it is good. Oh no, of course not. I recommend it because it is SO BAD. And it's free too. What do you have to lose?
My initial impressions were bad, as it was plainly obvious that the character models were generated with the ComiPo! software, and I gave the developer some criticism about that on the Steam forum. But that is truly the least of the game's problems. The fact is, this is one of the most disjointed, nonsensical, poorly-written pieces of fiction I have ever come across, and I read Bleach.

It doesn't make sense. Really. You are introduced to a team of Manga translators (and it's plainly obvious that they are translating Manga illegally. Not that it really bothers me, I just thought that was amusing) who each have a job in the process of translating a Manga from Japanese to
English. You are offered a job on the team and I ended up taking the "Typist" job (which is called a Typesetter by actual English translation groups, by the way) and I was presented with absolutely nothing related to typesetting whatsoever in my entire runthrough of the game. My job was completely irrelevant to the progression of the plot.
Speaking of the plot, it makes no sense. The general idea seems to be that another rival translation group has decided to pick up a project that your group left abandoned for several months and you basically declare war on them for daring to finish what your group refused to finish. But most of the time, it isn't even focusing on that. Instead, we are treated to completely random, disjointed, incomprehensible scenes of absolute nonsense. In the span of my playthrough of what I assume to be one small route, I watched our group talk about translating manga, engage in get rich quick schemes, perform random acts of violence on each other, go to a dance party, go to space and meet God, eat lunch on a Kotatsu in the middle of the park whilst a bird poops on them, deal with "chemists-satanists", and speak to an unexplained entity named Spicy who appears out of nowhere to offer random sagely advice that usually amounts to "Google it". There's also a Dragon-Girl for... some reason?
It just... doesn't make sense. There is supposed to be a flow to a story, yeah? One scene is supposed to lead into the next. But this game completely ignores every established concept of a story. There is no sense to any of it. It's just one random event to the next without anything tying them together whatsoever. And it certainly does not help that the author's native language is Russian as opposed to English, and it clearly shows. There are many, many scenes where the dialog can barely be described as Engrish, much less proper English. And even if it was in proper English, the plot structure is a complete mess and probably still wouldn't make any sense.

So... why am I recommending this game?

Because this should be a prime example of what NOT to do when developing an indie visual novel. It's a learning experience. Don't be this guy. Don't be a chemists-satanist. And shame on you, Steam, and shame on everyone who voted this through Greenlight, because even though it is free, this sets a bad precedent for the kind of content that can be on the Steam storefront.

OK review time.
I've played about 6 hours fo far. The game is definitely good; no doubt about that. I recommend it.
First is gameplay. It is indeed a lot like Far Cry 3. Most of the animations (if not all) are identical. Like they couldn't be bothered to change them? It feels like I'm playing an expansion than a new game. That's not necessarily a bad thing. CoD does that every year and nobody panics. But then Far Cry does it everyone looses their minds.
The gameplay is typical Far Cry. Open world, with radio towers outposts and side missions. The crafting is almost identical too. You hunt animals and you get their pelts to craft stuff (like more weapon slots) or sell them for money. The weapon system is also identical. You get 4 slots but you have to craft them and so far one of them is for sidearms only (I've only unlocked 2 so far).
Next is the main character and story. I've read other reviews and they all said that he's boring. In my opinion he's similar to the character from FC3 but without the tattoos. Just a guy that has been put at a situation he doesn't want to be in. He's in Kyrat to bury his mother's ashes in the middle of a civil war (or a rebellion) and he decides to help them a little bit in thanks for saving his life. And that's all I know about it. Too early to say if it's good but so far it looks like the typical help-the-rebels-against-the-oppressing-ruler kind.
Last is the graphics. On my system (i5 3470 @ 3.2Ghz, 4GB ram, Sapphire 7850 OC 2GB, Windows 8.1, and Samsung 840 ssd though the game isn't installed on that) the game runs great. At very high (but not ultra) and without Anti-aliasing and Ambient occlusion it runs at 40-60 with vsync enabled. And here comes the elephant in the room. They say stuff about black screens and bad optimization and crashes but I've had none of that. On the other hand I have had stutters. Every couple of minutes or so framerate drops at 10-15 for a couple of seconds. It is indeed annoying but I can deal with that. After the horrendous bullcrap some call video game and other Assassin's Creed, Far Cry 4 this is actually pretty good.
I haven't tried multiplayer yet and I probably never will so I can't say anything about that.
If I had to rate it it would be 7/10. Despite it's fun gameplay, the story is mediocre, it stutters a bit and it feels like I bought Far Cry 3 by accident.
It also needs uplay. Of course it needs uplay. Stupid thing I hate it. I nearly rated it 6/10 for this bullcrap.
And one last thing. It doesn't have support for 16:10 resolution screens (or anything else other than a 16:9). It just covers the top and bottom of the screen with two black bars in order to maintain the 16:9 ration without stretching the game. What is this bullcrap? I've just about had it with Ubisoft.

So, here we are, Ubisoft's last chance to redeem themselves from their crappy year.  Did they succeed?
I think so.
While Far Cry 4 feels and plays alot similar to Far Cry 3, it has alot of new features that make up for that.
First off, as most people probably know, you can ride elephants and gyrocopters, which I find really cool and fun.  The elephants are great for taking an outpost very agressively, and the gyrocopters are a great mode of transportation.  I find both of these useful, as their an alternative to a car or ATV like in Far Cry 3.
Along with new vehicles, they made driving even better.  Ever been shot when your driving?  You had to get out of your car to fight back like in Far Cry 3?  Not anymore, if you have a one-handed weapon (mainly pistols), you can look freely and shoot from the inside of your car.  To make this easier and better, they added Autodrive, by pressing shift, you car will automatically follow the road and drive at a decent speed, while staying on the road and not curving off.
They also added a few new weapons which are incredibly fun and useful.  You might remember the knife throw takedown from Far Cry 3.  Now you can throw knifes whenever you want.  They also have the one handed grenade launcher, and, yes, you can shoot it from a car or gyrocopter (strafe runs anyone?)
They also added the grappling hook, which is used at specific palces to climb/swing to an area.  Honestly, it seems a bit uncessesary, but it's cool none the less
They also added some little things, such as when you want to make a healing syringe, you would have to pause and manually craft it.  Now it autocrafts when you have 2 green leaves, which is very useful.  They also change the weapon wheel slightly, now there's 3 normal slots, and one slot reserved for a one-handed weapon.  It sounds annoying, but I mainly use it to have a one-handed grenade launcher, and I haven't changed that slot since I unlocked that weapon.  They also made the wingsuit is available from the start, for really cheap, which is really nice, instead waiting top get it half-way through the game like in Far Cry 3.
While this is all great, it has it's faults:
The optimization isn't perfect.  It's not horrendous or anything, but it could be better. (Atleast it's not like Watch_Dogs or AC Unity)
There is mouse acceleration turned on, and the slider doesn't change it, you have to manually change it in the config files. (Apparently they have 2 mouse acceleration options in the configs, the slider changes only 1). And it sometimes doesn't fix, from what i heard.
You don't connect to the main antagonist, who is Pagan Min, as you did in Far Cry 3.  Most of us who played Far Cry 3 agree, Vas was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, none of us liked him, we wanted to kill him.  I can't feel that same hatred towards Pagan Min.  It's mainly because you really only see him in the prolouge, I've done about 10 missions (only a guess), and I haven't seen him since, you really only here him when he calls you occasionally after beating a mission.  He doesn't seem that evil either, at least comparatively.
EDIT:
Just saw him again after the end of Act 2 in the storyline.
Also, only one sound slider for all volume, not cool.
Overall, the game is fun, the gameplay is good, just the optimization and settings annoy me.
8/10.  If you liked Far Cry 3, and wanted more, you'll love Far Cry 4.  If you weren't a fan of Far Cry 3, you'll probably dislike this aswell.

Though Thief is a reimagining of the series, in a way, it's not. There are many options to choose from, from what you'd expect, to even altering the game itself. Don't like being able to kill with arrows? Remove the ability to use broadhead arrows. Don't like being ble to kill everyone and skip the stealth? Make it a penalty, as small as returning to the last checkpoint, or as devilish as taking you back to the menu and deleting your save data. Small changes, to large ones, each added change will add a certain ammount of points to an overall difficulty score. Each standard difficult comes with it's own limitations. For instance, the hardest difficulty punishes you for knocking out or killing any innocent individuals, not to mention altering the cost of gear and upgrades to sky-high costs, choose wisely.
Thief carries an FOV slider of 90 to 110, a very good thing to have that isn't seen near enough.
This game also features full body awareness.
As far as the story goes, I found myself more confused than anything, more questions than answers, and very few explanations. This, however, could just be me. When the game is completed, however, you can freely return to each mission to replay it with different gear, and try a different style of play. Who doesn't want to return for more free loot?
For some negatives, I've constantly encountered audio bugs. Strange sound levels where people in another room sound like they're behind you, and people in front of you sound as muffled as whispering through a luxoriously fluffy feather pillow. There seems to be a constant bug where audio lines will replay themselves while the line is already playing, layering two very loud lines while you're trying to focus on other things, the fact that random voice lines trigger far too often doesn't help this. Another issue I've seen appears to be a huge drop in framerate when you run around in areas with a fair bit of light or other objects to render such as patrolling guardsmen and the various smelly homeless people grunting at you go through the entire game. I questioned if it was just me, but one of these slowdowsn seems to always happen in the exact same place at the exact same time in the game like clockwork, and I've seen it happen with another player. Again though, this could just be a coincidence. Last issue sort of lies within the full body awareness and animations, and is subject to personal taste. I actually enjoy it as it adds challenge, and feels realistic. Looting things requires Garett to reach out and snag what you're aiming at. You have to wait for him to finish before getting the next item, and sometimes you might mis-click, and he'll cower down behind things near him, such as the chest you were looting, as if the loot inside startled him with its shininess. Keys can be rebound of course, so this isn't too much of an issue I suppose.
All in all, comparing the positive with the negative, I personally feel this game is worth a try for anyone who takes stealth seriously in their games. So if you feel like scooting around in the dark and stealing letter openers and candle holders from sick people, this is worth a try.

I heard that this game got a lot of bad reviews, and didn't sit well with the press.  My freinds, i am here to tell you that they are wrong.  This game is pure stealth, and sneaking around the streets of the "City"(no clear name), is just pure fun.  I have never played the other Thief games and i didn't know what to expect when i started it, but as i went on playing, it made me want to play the other Thief games as well.  You are Garret, a master thief who could steal anything if he set his mind on it.  He does a job for his good freind Basso.  His former hot headed apprentice Erin, accepted the same job, and doing the job with her makes Garret remember why she was his former disciple.  She is arrogent, and kills without a concience, taking no thought to stealth.  The job goes horribly wrong, and Garret finds himself with a bounty on his head, and Erin dead.  But the accident caused him to have a "focus  power".  A way to see everything in the enviroment.  Garret must find out what happened to him, and gets tangled up in a struggle for power and control.  Now that the storys out of the way, what is game like?  This game is meant for people who love the stealth genre, and also looking for a good way to pass the time.  The game itself is structured well, and you feel Garrets every movement.  A really good first-person perspective.  Each job you take on can take from 20 to 40 minutes, depending on how you want to play it.  You can go weapons blazing, and killing everyone.  Or, you can sneek pass them.  There are so many possiblitys it made me play the missions again to try out a different style.  You steal everything in this game, from jewled medallions, to golden forks.  After the mission, it tells you how much loot you collected, and what play style you played doing it.  The combat in this game, is very bad and is really kind of weird to master.  But i like that they are not good, because it makes you not want to get into confronation with the guards.  Play the game it's meant to be played.  Plus, you can turn off things you don't want in the game within the options menu, from the enemies detecing bar, to the entire hub.  All depends on the player.  Health and your Focus ability is non regenerative, and finding resources can be hard, so be careful, and use the focus wisely.  The graphics in this game are good looking, and beutifal to look at, i would suggest buying this if you want to have an alternative to the runnig and gunning games.  On a scale of 1 to 10, i would give this game a 7 out of 10.  I plan to do more reviews in the future, so hope this helps!

My fingers hurt.
That's probably a big indication that I'm enjoying myself; I'm willing to play until my digits are threatning to go on strike. They're kind of protesting me typing this, but hell with it. This is a game I picked up on a total whim and that you could reasonably describe as an indie gem.
Enter Boki, a... gem-eating 'copycat' with... crystalline feet who... can kick a laser buzzsaw in half, who appears... despondent that her objectively awesome ability to fuse stolen projectile weapons into much scarier projectile weapons is not 'unique,' and as a result, is... thrown into what is ostensibly a... combat simulation by her dapper... mantis... uncle...
Eh, screw it. The story is a pile of mildly adorable videogame nonsense, but it doesn't really get in the way. Very quickly, you'll be immersed in a visually-offensive riot of glorious color making robots explode, and you won't care.
It's a 2-d shooter-platformer made of bite-size levels; they're anywhere from about 45 seconds to four minutes long and basically are all the same premise - Murder specific robots on the level. There's powerups and pickups and all the sorts of things you would expect; the game's USP is that is that the 10 main weapons that make up the game - any 3 of which you can hold at a time - can all be fused in any combination of two or three to produce a unique effect with a button press. On the simple end, a grenadelike weapon and a force bolt weapon combine to produce a homing rocket, for example. On the 'ridiculous' end, you can create room-clearing atomic tornadoes that spew wall-piercing razors or cascades of fragmenting explosives. There's a few on the 'useless' end - if it uses those stupid fiddly remote mines and doesn't clear a friggin' room, what's the damn point?! - but overall it does enough neat stuff to keep you wanting to try out other combinations.
The game aesthetic is garish; a shiny miasma of digital rainbows, lasers and explosions coupled with cartoony character models; like you'd just done Ecstacy while playing Mega Man while watching The Matrix. Fortunately for the game, I like garish. If you don't, options do exist to tone it up or down a touch - but there's even a Shiny Mode in the options I was delighted to discover. The explosions - and you will be creating many - have enough of a thwack to them to do the job, and the soundtrack is bouncy with echoes of 16-bit chiptunes; a suitably chipper mood-setter.
It's fun. It's flowing runny shooty double-jumpy fire-in-all-directions nuke-stuff fun. The game has apparently been in development for something like 5 years, and it kind of shows; a lot of potential niggles have been ironed out of the gameplay. I'll update this review as I find any, but the only glaring one is that swapping weapons out when you already have 3 is kind of clunky compared to the rest of the usually solid controls.
Ultimately: Give it a whirl if you're after some joyous vaguely felinoid robot smashing violence.

Let's be brutally honest here games like Mega Man have a magic that is very difficult to capture. Mighty No 9 proved this as it was panned by most critics and was an utter disaster from Kickstarter to release. I personally know fans who still worship the ground that Mega Man X walks on. Praising the music, gameplay, game structure and so on and so forth. If you are looking for a fan base that is rabidly passionate and dedicated I would put Mega Man fans up near the top ten.
Well I am more then happy to say that Copy Kitty is FAR from better then nothing.(See what I did there?) This game hits all the right cords when it comes to a side scroller action title. Now if you're paying attention you will note that the game is in Early Access but to be honest I forgot that it was by the time I decided to do this first impression piece. The game is exceptionally well put together for an EA title. The game has two playable characters with drastically different combat styles. Over a hundred levels, an endless mode, bosses, hard modes, custom levels and that is just Early Access. It's rather impressive and there is more to come which is exciting.
The game play itself is an homage to Mega Man but it plays with the formula a bit. You have all that buster cannon shooting, weapon stealing/combining action that you know and love however, the levels are all bite sized. Most levels can be completed in less then two minutes with boss fights taking up to four at the max. This leads to very fast, very chaotic gameplay that can become very overwhelming at the beginning. Once you settle in though the action becomes a fluid dance of explosions and mixing and matching.
Kitty our hero, can take up to three weapons/buffs from her enemies, then combine them into a super weapon of sorts. This leads to an endless variety of weapons that all have spectacular use and visuals to match.
Sadly, you lose the combo of weapons you have at the end of the every level and start over again in most cases. Sometimes you are allowed to bring one weapon of your choosing but getting familiar with everything is going to take a while as more weapons are added. I found myself just spamming the combine weapon attack and not really caring about whats around. This will do the trick most of the time but future bosses and levels will prove difficult with this strategy. I think dedicated levels to certain weapons would be an excellent idea. This is present in the game but isn't very in depth currently.
Copy Kitty has its ducks in a row graphically and musically. There are times where I wish the colors were more vibrant and areas more detailed like the cut scenes  but the level design is suffice and explosions a plenty for me to not really notice.
Of course there is a cadre of robots ranging from  self destructing, bunny tossing, shield bearing, the robots can get pretty crazy and the bosses even more so. Enemy design is exceptionally well done here and I never got tired of blasting robot enemies to bits. Now one thing I did feel was the levels were very short, perhaps too short. The length at which some of them can be designed seems almost limited in space. Lack of longevity could be due to the ability to create your own custom levels but those who enjoyed long robust levels in classic Mega Man might find a gripe with that.
While most of the features are already in place and I could definitely go on and on about this game. There is still more to come so I will reserve my final judgement for release. Copy Kitty is an impressive title and gives a strong showing straight out of the gate. Any fan of retro-action titles is going to love Copy Kitty. The games price will be increasing once final release hits. The developer plans for more levels, polish to levels, and general upgrades.
That being the case I still feel highly confident in saying that there is already a game here. So buy it now if you like what you see as more is coming in the months ahead. If you are unsure feel free to try their free Demo.

Copy Kitty is a game about thrilling destruction and sensory overload. The main character, Boki, has a pithy, weak weapon, but the player is able to absorb up to three powers from enemies and combine them in any which way, leading to powerful and often gloriously fabulous particle effect destruction.
The story is a bit forgettable, as Boki's uncle, Savant, is using the program to explore the title "Copy Kitty's" powers with a simulation. The story mode, I would classify as almost a puzzle game. You are supposed to destroy specific enemies, and there are various obstacles to prevent Boki from just steamrolling anything in your way. Certain things your weapons can't go through, or you yourself can't go through, etc. Marked enemies act as keys to green doors as well. There is a lot of visual information on the screen at any one time, but visual cues tie you in to the important elements of the level.
The bosses of story mode are all unique experiences, even considering the persistent midboss that keeps following you around. Each one feels unique; sometimes Boki will leverage the copying ability to gain an upper hand halfway through the fight, or often the course of the fight will completely change at some points. They are very rewarding experiences in terms of varied gameplay.
The endless mode is more a pure arcade game, where the element of chance and randomness are there to thrill the player with brief tastes of their favorite weapons in an environment that constantly changes.
The controls are servicable but can feel a bit stiff at times. Boki has a lot of moves, and her kick attack is very important because it can destroy some terrain and deflect or even reflect bullets. Practice is key to mastery, but I can see how some people may get frustrated early on. Boki lacks certain abilities like a pass-down jump, which is easy to forget, and some of her moves have both a button and a dual input command, like her dodge roll, which takes the command normally used in other games for a pass-down jump.
The "feel" of the game is marvelous. Inspiration is taken from Mega Man, Metroid, and Kirby, as well as sprinklings of other video games, and the varied effects are memorable and charming. If you are a fan of video game explosions, this is a game for you. The music is a bit repetitive but energetic, and has layers for things like invincibility and low health (the siren of which is not annoying, thankfully).
Overall, I would highly suggest you play this game if you love both nuanced action games and the feeling of being on a power trip. Copy Kitty does a great job at feeling both complex and simple at the same time. There is a lot of content, room for mastery of levels (with appropriate markers to tell you what you've done), and even a completely different way to play with Boki's uncle Savant; he feels a lot different and not a mere "pallete swap".
To sum up, give Copy Kitty a try. It's meowvelous.

I played this game for 17 minutes and 42 seconds (my steam profile says 21 minutes but that was mostly spent testing the game, navigating the menus, and waiting for the animation that pops up after you attempt to quit the game (for some reason...) to end) and, unless the overall design of the individual missions drastically changes, I don't think I'll be putting in any more of my time. Because to me, this game failed at one of the biggest things it was trying to accomplish: it isn't satisfying to kill enemies.
NOW HOLD ON: When I got to the first boss, I couldn't believe I was even playing the same game. The introduction to the boss itself and the entire second half of the fight (once I got that crazy Super Sayain power-up) were some of the most satisfying feelings I've felt fighting in a sidescroller since Symphony of the Night (I dont play a lot of side-scrollers...). I understand why the whole game can't play like this, but... let me explain.
The regular levels of this game, in both navigation and fighting, were both remarkably unsatisfying and almost embarrasing to play out. So much effort goes into making each hit and explosion something wonderful, but at the end of the day it isn't. You can dye a vanilla cake to look like a rainbow, but you wont be tasting skittles, if you know what I mean. Most of the levels i was able to complete without even looking at the screen. i spent a majority of my play time just holding down the C button (and if nothing was happening, the X button) and left or right. Because I couldn't care, because the game didn't try to make me care. It almost felt like it was just going to assume I found all the explosions and text boxes neat enough to carry my interest, but it didn't. The attacks had no weight to them, happened so frequently they never felt impactful, and often times the screen was so cluttered I wasn't even sure who's attacks were hitting who. There was never any real time to focus on what I was doing or why. The whole time I played I almost heard the game developer's voice, telling me how exciting all the action was and how much fun I was having. Because that's what it all felt like to me: an experience designed to look like it's a fun and exciting time, without actually being a fun and exciting time. Like a haunted house that turns out to just be your uncle's scary basement.
I had a few other points I wanted to make (the jump arc is way too heavy considering how floaty the game is, the momentum is ridiculous and makes precision movement almost impossible, I'd say etc. but that's really it), but really, the big think I wanted to touch on is the lack of any real sense of danger, as well as the complete absense of a feeling of reward (okay that's not true... I already said my shpeal about the boss though). It felt like a very superficial game, that focused more on cosmetic details in favour of finding the source of what really makes games like this fun to play. The shooting was boring and flat, i never felt like I was really shooting anything, was unable to become immersed in the experience, and overall found myself wishing for better things. And that's just not what a game should do.
(in my opinion, at least.)

War, the Game is a deceivingly simple video game at first sight, but as more operations open up, the player will be surprised by the circumstances and how the mechanics interact with one another and will have to carefully plan his actions in order to meet the mission objectives.
Each nation that the player controls has units, which can range from infantry and tanks to nuclear missiles and aircraft carriers, and production facilities that can be used to create them.
The gamer is in charge of choosing what and when to build, based on the money the cities he controls are generating, and on moving his forces across the map in order to engage the enemy, defeat him and then capture his urban centers.
The actual battles do not require any sort of input and they are only based on the power of the units that are taking part, with both infantry and tanks contributing one level each when at full strength and with air units offering the same strength but with some special rules attached.
The initial scenarios seem simple, but the game quickly ramps up the difficulty level and it takes a lot of tries and restarts in order to complete the later mission objectives.
The best way I have found to create a solid path towards victory is to find the nearest enemy divisions and focus as many of my forces on them in a coordinated attack.
The trick is to keep your own units in War, the Game together as much as possible, while making sure that the enemy is scattered and unable to mount a powerful counteroffensive.
What makes the entire experience more difficult than it should be is the fact that the entire game moves a little too fast and sometimes the AI, with its unlimited attention, simply makes moves that the player cannot respond to in time.
War, the Game does a good job of teaching the player, via a virtual assistant, how to play the game and it’s always easy for gamers to understand what they need to do in order to succeed.
The game shows that indie developers do not need to try to compete with big companies in the graphics department and only have to come up with an interesting design choice in order to capture the attention of the player with a simple, clean, efficient look.
-Solid real-time strategy structure
-Interesting art style
-Limited tactical options
-Limited units
-Sound design is less impressive, but it does mesh well with the rest of the game.
War, the Game is a title that all strategy lovers should try out at least once in order to see how smaller teams can innovate by taking the classic concepts of the genre and turning them into something new

This War of Mine is truly an excellent game. The premise is one I've never experienced before, the visuals are fantastic, the soundtrack is simple yet moving, and the concept is simple: survive.
You don't really win this game, it just ends eventually, whether your characters are alive or not. This is one of the few games I've played where I really care if my characters die, not just because I know it's going to be harder to go on for the others, but because I probably could've done something to keep them alive, but didn't.
The day-time survive/craft/trade time, mixed with the tense, nightly scavanging for supplies along with the random events and consequense-based decision making all combine to put you in a situation where you can never quite relax. The game is always hanging on the edge of a bad situation and can be tipped over by a stupid choice or random chance very easily, irreparably changing how the game will progress, and what your characters have to deal with.
Overall, it's a fantastic game. Would recommend, 10/10.

It's too bad the entire game is executed so poorly.

I played the Thief demo when it came out in the late 90's. I bought it as soon as it came out. I bought Thief 2. I bought the third "Thief". I bought Thief Gold when it came out. Then I repurchased all three on Steam. Suffice to say, I really REALLY like Thief. Needless to say, I had high expectations for this game.
It didn't disappoint! This iteration is addicting, despite some issues. To avoid a tl;dr, I'll summarize:
The good:
Love the bow. LOVE the bow.
Ambient sound and music is spot on (a cornerstone of the originals)
Rich environments and some "feels real" settings
At least one level that will make you want to curl up into a fetal position and weep in shame at your fear
The bad:
Can't jump, except for under certain circumstances
Some levels feel small-ish, some feel abnormally large (i.e. a wooden ship that seems to have acres of square footage)
The map. It's nigh useless, especially if you're trying to track down the level entrances once you've beat the game.
The ugly (spoilers?):
The story. That's not to say it's a bad story, because it really isn't, in my humble opinion. It's just incomplete. Garrett was out for a year, and there's loud hints dropped that he was in an asylum. Why? How did he get out? The Gloom is gutting The City. Why? What is it? Where did it come from? Is it even connected with the plot? What happened to Erin? Who IS Erin, anyway? And oh my! Garrett's eye is part of a mysterious crystal! Yet nothing comes of that. His eye remains intact and the crystal seems to get put back together without it. So why bring it up?
Square Enix and Eidos Montreal have created a great platform that could see some very epic gameplay, it's just a shame they didn't spend a wee bit longer on fleshing out the main story.

Surprisingly good modern stealth game.
First person perspective is done well, movement is fantastic, the way you can edit the difficulty in so many different ways to customise the game to how you want to play is just awesome, and the AI is.... good. It's not great, but then AI for stealth games is usually laughable. This is as good as you usually get, if not slightly better.
You can't sneak right up to people in the dark and have them not notice you, as you can in games like metro last light or splinter cell blacklist. You can't scurry all over the place, since different surfaces will make more or less noise depending on what they are; water splashes, glass cracks and breaks and so on.
The atmosphere is great, the mechanics are very well implemented.
There are some niggles, such as no dedicated jump key. It's well known already that you can only jump when you are in a specific place.
Same with rope arrows. You can only place them on certain beams hanging near a ledge, with rope on the beam for the arrow to stick into. It's restrictive and nonsensical, but only a small problem really that mostly hardcore thief fans will whine about to any major degree. The rope arrows are always useable in a place where there will be some otherwise unreachable ledge or something, so you never waste an arrow.
The thief vision is pretty useless for the most part I found. You get poppies to replenish the vision meter. But I just sold the poppies, since when the meter is empty and you hit the vision key, it flashes on and off quickly, while still highlighting useable objects, traps, doors and loot for a couple of seconds, which is more than enough.
The thief vision should have been used just for this, because I found it far better than using the vision with a full meter, with a horrible humming noise and terrible sepia-toned colour scheme while you are looking around.
Also, the character faces look very rushed. No real detail, they look like waxwork models. The lip syncing is terrible as well.
These are small problems though, that have no major impact on the gameplay, which is mostly great.
I have 25 hours or so in the game, and still have some side quests to do, and am halfway through a story mission that I believe is the penultimate one. So another story mission as well, which will be around an hour or more, and if there are only 3-4 side quests, that will add at least another hour, depending on the type of side quest they are.
Some side quests just have you enter a building in the city that is your hub between missions, while some quests have their own large area, and are almost as big as a story mission. In this instance they can last up to an hour, and are as good or better than any of the story missions I have played.
Speaking of the story; ignore it. It's tosh. But it doesn't matter, as it is just there to give you a reason to go thieving in this city.
All in all, great game, with some small problems that are easily excusable.
If you like first person stealth at all, this will be for you.
If you are a thief fanboy of the first 3 games, you will probably complain about these small problems much more, as this isn't an exact clone of the previous games.
If you find yourself focusing on how it isn't like the previous games, I feel sorry for you, because you are denying yourself a very good stealth game by having such exacting standards of exactly what a "thief" game must be.
Get over that, and you can't help but enjoy this.
And let's face it, there aren't many good stealth games around these days, so let's make the most of them when they are fun like this.
