Disclosure: I got this game on the Groupees Greenlight Bundle for about $1 and I've known the developers and this game for quite some time.
Copy Kitty should be a really great game, considering it takes inspiration from some of Treasure's finest games (Gunstar Heroes, Bangai-O) and has a great concept at the core; take Gunstar Heroes to its logical extreme and have hundreds of combinations of powers at your disposal. Unfortunately, the game suffers from cluttered level design and obnoxious graphics and an overall unrefined experience.
Based on world 1 and the first half of world 2, the level design is fairly bland and uninspired. Aside from world themes (which based on the screenshots and trailer seem fairly typical) levels just seem to be a mesh of blocks and enemy oversaturation; there does not seem to be any real rhyme or reason to the layout. Often times most of the challenge would just come from enemy spam rather than clever placement or AI. However, this may have been tolerable if it weren't for the horrifically noisy graphics. Even aside from the less than decent enemy and character designs, the sheer brightness from the bullets mixed with the glowing enemies and platforms makes it difficult to comprehend what is happening on screen. Many times I've found myself damaged by an enemy I couldn't even tell was on screen, so it just blended into the screen. The worst case of this was the first water level, where I didn't notice either air meter while underwater until I started seeing my health drop dramatically because it was just a few more elements added to the clutter.
This also brings me to my next point: a lot of mechanics are not introduced properly. I will say that the tutorial stage is done well and I do understand that the newer mechanics are relatively self-explanatory. However, the game seems to not acknowledge features like talismans, solo powers, or enemy spawners at all, making the elements feel a lot more tacked on. Players should at the very least be aware that these items exist, and, in the case of water, at least a mention at the beginning of the stage would be nice. The beginning stage banter is a simple way of rectifying this. The default keyboard controls are also fairly obtuse; arrow keys for movements feel really outdated, and there were times where dodging was somewhat annoying to pull off. While customizing keys and controller options are there, a "simple" control setup should be improved enough for players who don't want to fiddle around. Also, jumping feels somewhat off; it feels like your character is too heavy and falls back down too fast.
While none of these other issues are as major, there are still a lot of improvements that could be made. The music is passable, but does not stand out particularly well; it's not something I'd listen to outside of the game. The story feels fairly uninspired but at the same time it probably isn't the vocal point of the game anyway, so it's not that big of a deal. The power-ups also feel relatively standard, but they all seem to work fine and the three-power combinations do feel fairly satisfying to use (though I feel that with the large amount of power-ups it will be inevitable that only a select few are useful, compared to the more refined few available in Gunstar Heroes). Personally I think the enemy spawning powers and the solo powers are more trouble than they're worth, but I'll give the benefit of the doubt that other players may find them enjoyable. And while this is a particularly minor complaint, I do wonder if all the enemy names are just randomly generated.
I haven't played much of this game, though I played some of the demo a few years ago, but personally I don't think the story is compelling enough for me to go farther in story mode, and endless mode sounds self-explanatory that I don't feel I need to play it. Honestly I think I got pretty much everything the game could offer in the time that I played, and unless there are some serious improvements to the graphics and level design I won't be checking this out again.

(Note, this review is written after playing the original itch.io version and a work-in-progress build of the Steam release early)
A genuinely excellent platform shooter, reministcent of many of Treasure's best (especially Bangai-O: Missile Fury and Gunstar Heroes), with tons of content and lots of replay value, admittedly at the cost of having a fairly lengthy learning curve for an arcade game. It's loud and satisfying and everything blows up *just right*.
The main gimmick of Copy Kitty is that (for the main character, at least - there's two with entirely different weapon systems) is that you can hold up to three weapons at once, and every single combination of two or three also generates a uniquely named combination attack that has properties from all three components. Each weapon has limited ammo and every level has a different set to find, so you're going to constantly be juggling your arsenal and never sticking to one set of attacks for any length of time.
On top of the hundreds of ways to shoot stuff, there's also a basic melee attack that can be used to deflect attacks (or return to sender if timed perfectly) and a dodge-roll, meaning that skilled players can pull off some very technical play, although all of this means there's a lot to learn. Even moreso when you consider that there's a second character with an even more technical combat style, and also a 'Hard Mode' that continues the story and completely remixes the levels and bosses.
If I had one grumble about the game it's that it's locked to a 4:3 aspect ratio, with any remaining space on a widescreen monitor just being black. Even if the game itself isn't going to make the jump to widescreen, it would be nice to see that space being filled with the HUD or wallpaper.
Don't be put off by the early access badge either. The game is 'complete' now, and ends on a massive setpiece battle (if not a complete story resolution). The developer plans to extend the story a little further in later updates, but there's more than enough to chew on as-is.
Highly recommended.

I had been playing this game off and on up to version 1.61, and have loved every bit of it. Really, the only reason I had stopped playing was just because I was waiting for the Steam release that was in the works. :P
Of course, I bought it as soon as I learned that it had come out on early access, and I don't regret it for a moment. The hard work that's gone into even just the last 2 years of development (out of 5+ total) is very apparent; the primary issues that I had with the game back in version 1.61 (telling Boki's shots apart from enemy shots, switching between powers in real-time being a pain at best, having to replay every level several times to reach 4 oftentimes conflicting targets (time, score, enemy, and damage targets), etc.) have all been addressed completely.
Savant is playable, with his own set of abilities and playstyle. Cutscenes have been added for both characters' story modes. Even more "solo abilities" have been added. Existing bosses have been refined and have entirely new tricks up their sleeve. New bosses have been created, including a recurring thorn in Boki's side. ;) Some existing levels have been re-ordered, many have been refined at least slightly, and entire worlds have been added. There's now a lore encyclopedia in addition to the (improved) bestiary. Ability switching is now done via a slick side-menu that pauses the action, which makes strategic usage of them much more viable in the heat of battle (especially when it comes to "solo abilities"). Instead of 4 different "perfection" targets being set for every level, only the "damage taken" one exists now.[1]
I don't know how much of the above was added to the freeware release(s) since version 1.61, but I do know this: Copy Kitty was awesome back then, and it's at least 200% more awesome now. So awesome, that I had to leave this review, which is something I rarely do for anything, because words are hard. :P
In short:
Is the game "worth it"?
. It has many hours of enjoyable and genuinely fun content even in "early access". I'd have easily paid up to 30 Canadian Dollars for it, although admittedly that's because I would have known what I was getting for the price. Still, even without that knowledge, the current price of CDN$ 10.99 almost feels like stealing. :O
Would I recommend this to others?
. Strongly. Stronger that a dragon summoned forth to destroy the [virtual] world and all the Constructs that reside in it! \ :D /
Side note:
[1] That last point might sound like a bad thing, but the game has so much content as it is, that the multiple playthroughs per level that would often be needed to attain every target ended up feeling excessive and draining even, in my experience. Limiting it to one clear "extra" goal per level (take as little damage as possible) was a smart move, and additionally shows that the developers have already learned one of the most crucial lessons of game design: "Knowing when to stop." Trust me; I've played a lot of fan games, and it's not as common sense as one might think... ;)

I'm a fan of pirate scenarios and naval combat.  Unfortunately, despite carrying that theme, Risen 2 is stylized and plays like an Elder Scrolls Lite title, but without the support of the absurdity of ES modding communities to provide and/or refine all the needed elements.
The basis of the game is "Yay Pirates" combat, which while it can occassionally be entertaining, is often nothing more than frustrating due to the mechanics.  Melee combat has two modes: attack and die.  If you block on a melee character, you're awful and need to reevaluate your life choices.  Blocking is purely useful to ranged characters, because on melee, blocking an enemy attack staggerlocks you, which causes you to delay before being able to counterattack, allowing the enemy to hit you again to interrupt your counterattack, or to blockbreak you.  You can tumble away though, allowing it to be viable to ranged combat.  The problem with ranged combat though is the limited resource of bullets.  Bullets are fairly rare, and must be conserved for boss battles and duels, because entering into melee combat in those situations is suicidal (mostly due to bugs: bosses can't be staggerlocked, you can, so you lose in a melee slugfest), but going ranged trivializes these encounters.  Easiest example?  The very first "challenge" duel in the tutorial area: if you melee him, he outdamages you, staggerlocks you and you lose.  That fight is designed for you to lose, give up and come back later when you're on his level (he hits ~4x as hard as you do at low levels).  But if you block, tumble back and hit him with a pistol shot, then kite until he catches you, rinse and repeat?  You can complete the fight without getting hit.
The skill trees, while entertaining in theory, are plagued by a very clear "Best path", due to the alternatives not being viable. For example, pursuing the Monkey skill requires you to forgo combat specs (making the game harder), but the Monkey is awful, so there's no reason to suffer through a path with no benefits for the first half of the game, when the big payoff is a complete letdown.
The game also lacks naval combat, so it's not truly a Pirate game.
Every day is Talk Like A Pirate Day if you're playing Risen 2.

Fault Milestone 2A maintains all of the strengths of its predecessor while ironing out much of the flaws.  If Fault Milestone One was a 7/10, this would have to be a solid 9.
With much of the initial worldbuilding complete, there's a good deal less raw exposition than before.  It's not entirely gone, of course; not by a long shot.  This world is huge, and the characters of Fault are moving.  But at this point, it's more welcome than anything; the details given in Fault Milestone One are enough to provoke your imagination, and at this point you actually want the information to help fill in the blanks.
The art and soundtrack continue to be amazing.  The 3D camera system is used to much, much better effect in this installment, particularly
.
The old cast continue to be amazing.  Rune in particular takes the spotlight again, when our narrator is
.  Substantial character development is shown from Rune's thoughts and personality, and we learn quite a bit about Selphine.
New protagonist characters are introduced; and in one of the glaring disappointments of Fault Milestone 2A, I don't really like them.  This is mostly because I was too enamored with the original trio, so I'm not sure how much of this criticism is actually valid.  But, anyways, I don't really care for them.  Thankfully, they don't take up much space at all.
We're left with the plot and the way it is presented now, which was the glaring weakness of Fault Milestone One.
Fault Milestone Two solves this problem.
First of all, the story is now told in the present.  As the backstory of Rune has been thoroughly established, we move on to more present character specifications; like Selphine's
and the limit of
.
The plot as a general thing is moved forward well; the pacing is excellent, because the mix of social commentary, exposition, plot, and character interaction blends very neatly.  That's all that really needs to be said, I think.
The social commentary expands from Fault Milestone One; the concepts of humanity and morality are massively expanded, as are the gaps between the poor and the privledged.  Compassion, revenge, and emotion as a general topic are heavily involved in the series; this installation of Fault Milestone is far more emotionally thrilling and breathtaking than its precedent and are what make the series shine so brightly.
Fault Milestone 2A vastly improves upon its precedent, and the series will only get better from here.
If you liked Fault Milestone One, you'll love Fault Milestone 2A.
If you like the first, you'll like this too. It's shorter though, probably due to the less time spent on explaining lore. The formula generally hasn't changed though.

Alright.
I was surprised by its gameplay because i tried out Thief Gold before this and clearly there were a lot of changes to how the mechanics work. (Well it IS a reboot.)
Oh and before i go further, stop comparing this to Dishonored. In Dishonored, you are an arcane assassin.
In Thief, you are a Thief. You are there to steal stuff stealthily. You are discouraged from fighting because you were there to steal things. You have arrows so that you can avoid direct contact and close quarters combat.
Sure, you can kill and steal and you're in First Person View but still.
There are similarities but that doesn't make it a clone. Thief came before Dishonored. That's like saying every fighting game that can kick and punch is a clone of Tekken. See? That sounds absurd yet people still keep ♥♥♥♥ing comparing this to Dishonored.
Seriously guys. Stop.
Anyway, It runs great on my system so i have no qualms when it comes to PC optimization
(Ah the beauty of the PC, easily patchable.)
The camera bobbing can get annoying at times especially when grabbing things but hey, they're trying to immerse you. Trying. The first mission of the game set the tone for how i felt for the rest of the game. It was a great first mission.
There are some glaring issues like the save system. It needs work, it needs to be changed. I like the quick save format of Max Payne 1 and would have wanted that in this game. no? Okay, fine. The game is playable anyway.
Sometimes i feel underpowered as a Master Thief when it comes to dispatching enemies who have seen me but that's a plus in my book cause you were never meant to come at them head-on. You were meant to sneak, knock out or kill in the shadows. You were supposed to feel scared and have this feeling of dread when you feel that you're about to get caught and will have to engage in close quarters combat. As a Master Thief, you should never have to be in that situation in the first place. You're a Ghost. An Opportunist. A Predator. But not up close.
On the other hand, I love knocking people around with the BlackJack. Never gets old.
The Focus feature is a cool mechanic but i kinda wish they had added more oculus themed abilities. (You know, since its his eye, why not have some sort of Stone Gaze or something like that? Cool. but yeah. I know. He's a thief, not an arcane assassin so we can just forget about this particular idea.)
The Third Person sections of the game fit in well in my opinion and you get to see Garrett if you're really that keen on seeing him. The cloth physics make his cloak really flowy and i just really wanted to put that out there. Great cloth physics.
The selection of arrows is okay, but it kinda makes me wish i could craft more. Like maybe steal a secret blueprint so you can craft a different set of arrows. Hopefully they'll patch in the ability to make more kinds of arrows. (Shock arrows sound cool.)
The Claw Tool could have seen more action (There should have been an option to use the claw instead of the blackjack when engaging opponents.)
The AI has its shining moments of brilliance when it comes to them tracking you, its funny when they don't happen to catch you even if they are just standing in front of you.
The city feels alive and dead, hopeful and miserable but never dull.
Great game, it satisfied me and i'm going to continue playing it (so i can finish some quests)
I hope the future DLC's will be more arrow types or maps or a new story. (ERIN'S story perhaps? or the story of what happens after Garrett's ending?)
I also feel that this game would benefit from adding a multiplayer option. Think Payday: The Heist or Payday 2 but more on the stealth and sneakyness that we come to expect from the Thief Series. I'd like to have my friends play as other thieves and we'd do a heist with arrows and blackjacks.
That would have been great.
I simply recommend this game for you or anyone else to play because i enjoyed it.
Not because someone told me to enjoy it and not because i'm blackmailed to, but simply because i enjoyed the ride.
I would play again and again til someone overwrites my save file and i rage quit and then play again.

My experience with the Thief games started originally on the Xbox playing “Deadly Shadows”. I rather enjoyed that game despite some of its flaws, and more importantly it inspired me to go play Thief 1 & 2. My experiences with all three games was very positive.
When I heard that Thief 4 was coming out I was very enthusiastic to play it. I watched for screen shots, news etc... The developers said that it would be a great fit with the classic thief games. Multiple ways of getting in and out of a mission area. A wide open city filled with interesting things/people, challenging maps and big heists.... oh boy time to get my inner childhood kleptomaniac on.
Initially I could not play it. The game was unplayable on a dual core... although granted my dual core was about 8 years old. So technically I was seriously overdue for an upgrade. Once my processor was properly upgraded, ran it in 32 bit, the game ran beautifully. Everything maxed out even the shadows, the only two settings I kept off where Vsync and Super AA.

The good:
Play style. At the end of each main story mission your performance determines your play style. A ghost means you tried to leave no trace. Opportunists use distraction and interact with the environment. Predators simply knockout or kill everything that moves. Having this type of feedback encouraged me to try other play styles or challenge myself by trying to get 90-100% in any one style. I have found over all ghost to be the most challenging. Especially when you pick up every piece of loot.
Combat. Many reviewers have complained that enemies in this game are OP. My response... This is a stealth game. In a stealth game your approach to combat should not be a front attack. Your approach should be sneaking up and bopping them on the head. Or sitting high up and blasting an arrow into their brain case. Or setting an oil patch on fire and listening to them scream in agony and keel over dead. I understand accidents happen, you slip up and get caught. But attacking head on is writing your own death sentence.
Stealth. I rather liked the stealth in this game, the shadows are really well defined. In prior games mostly due to graphics, it could be difficult to tell where it was truly dark. I really liked the “swoop” feature, it saved my butt a couple of times.
The bad:
Enemies. I am not talking combat I am talking enemies in general. SPOILERS. There are really only 4 enemies, 2 of those don't count. Humans, freaks, dogs and birds. When I entered this game I was expecting what I found in the previous 3 games, a variety of enemies. That was not to be had, there is not even any mention of giant spiders or zombies. I found the same generic NPC to get rather tedious, and freaks... yeah scary at first but once you have been there done that, they are cake compared to humans.
NPC dialogue. If I did not need sound to play this game I would have put it on mute. The one liners start to make you want to murder the speaker, after you have heard them for the 100th time. I would rather listen to “I used to be an adventurer like you...”, then have to listen to another NPC fap his mouth in this game. Also why is there only one conversation about taffers? I like being called a taffer, and I didn't even get to have that... or Benny the drunk guard. I miss Benny.
AI. The gloom also blesses everyone with stupidity. Because you saw me, and you didn't alert your superior officer or even your buddy in the next room. You know that silver tea cup you were just drinking from? Aren't you curious why it just vanished? No? Okay. Oh and hey I happen to be standing right next to you... but you can't see me, also I just touched your butt and stole your gold.
Focus. I call this my shiny locator. That is all it is for really. Focus burns up quickly, your required to keep it on to do anything cool with. Even when its at zero, you can still tap it to find the shines. I did not understand the point of this ability, except for emergency situations really.
“Parkour”. Garrett can't jump anymore. Or rather, you the player can't just repeatedly hit the space bar over and over again. No Garrett can only transverse a gap if it is scripted. He can only climb certain crates, and never barrels. Also his sense of balance or my sense of aim really sucks. Rope Arrows are also relegated to certain posts limiting your access everywhere.
Certain Animations. I can't tell you how much picking up a collectable♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. For a full 5 seconds Garrett sits there fondling a piece of loot, preventing me from shutting the damn safe before that guard turns around. Opening and shutting doors I also found to be tedious, along with cranking open windows and sliding between crates. It is not necessary for me to repeatedly press X. In addition I found him scaling pipes/grates to be unfair. Why can't I scale such pipes/grates everywhere?
Modern Day Menus. Irritated me. This is a steam punk universe. Get better designers, match the menus with the genera.
Map/navigation. Difficult. Easier to memorize everything then use the map.
Missions. I have positive things to say about missions, but the cons out weigh the good. I was told that I would have several options for entering/exiting areas. I found that at most I had 3 maximum and usually only 2 otherwise. This counts walking in the front door. Most missions are so linear that it makes me wonder if they even allowed level designers to be creative. The other thing that irritates me is static doors. Doors you cannot open inside of a mansion... I can understand and embrace these doors in the city. But it screams laziness when I see a static door inside of a level. Its implied there is a room behind that door, and I want to loot it damn it! The only level that made me feel like it was classic thief was the bank heist and sadly that is DLC, and not even a story mission.
Speaking of the story...
Story. Was lacking. I did not mind the supernatural primal element, or the gloom. What I did find irritating is that the story is not about the character. Its about Erin. A character I found right from the start to be grating and annoying. She quickly dissolved into the whiny, aggressive, helpless female who needs to be saved. I did not understand how someone like Garrett would ever have worked with her in the first place. I also honestly felt that we needed at least 2-3 more missions that focused on what, where, when, who? Because most things are left up in the air.
Characters. Underdeveloped. Who is “The Queen of Beggars”? I don't know. Some crazy blind lady who is out of her mind. How did Basso get into this line of work? I don't know. Why is the Thief Taker General such a♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't know. Why does Garrett not leave the city? There is a plague here, if anyone can leave he can. Oh wait he has to save Erin, because she exists only to be saved...
Conclusion.
I am not a good person to ask if this is a good or bad game. Because I just listed more cons then pros. But my verdict in the end, is that yes I liked this game. I recognize its flaws, and I hope for better. If this game even gets another installment, I hope the Developers listen to the reviews and fix many of these things. Would I recommend  it? Yes, but I would wait until steam has a sale, or the price drops down to 15.00.

OK lets get a few things out of the way. Yes there are some issue, with the worst being sound bugs (hopefully to be patched) and the couple of non thief like areas like the "exciting"TM rooftop chase scene. Is it annoying? You betcha but since it is a 2 minute sequence in a 40 hour (YMMV) stealth game you will hardly notice it before you go back to creeping in the shadows trying to avoid guards, lights and search for treasure.
One of the best things that SE did with this is that they really do let you customize it to make it feel the way you want it to. For thief veterans I would recommend turning off all visual markers (waypoints, alert etc) and turn off focus and playing through on master. Unlike other games this is honestly viable and even encouraged, and I'm currently working through a non violent ghost run. Finding 100% of the loot in a level is exhilarating.
The key thing is that you can tailor the game to your playstyle. Do you want to spend 40 minutes trying to find a secret entrance or do you want to be able to fall back on focus and let it mark it for you? Is the game still too easy? Make rope arrows cost 700 gold each, or set fail conditions if anyone gets alerted by you.
The game is crafted by people who get thief, and I can’t wait until they make another.
PS make sure to pick up the bank heist mission :D

Fairly streamlined interface to help you learn how to play magic the gathering (MTG) or get a quick match in.
The annoying

Also, as the game is trying to streamline and speed up the MTG rule set, it can be VERY easy to miss a critical play which can be VERY annoying and frustrating.  You have to expect to screw this up early on, but trust you will get better.
The interface is also not very intuitive or obvious.
All in all, a pretty good way to scratch your MTG itch, but I would recommend people new to MTG to also find people to play with outside of the game as some of the more complicated plays are not as obvious in this games interface.

This game is like playing a fun old school Need for Speed but with a lot more emphasis on drifting/power sliding. Not on the extreme like Ridge Racer, but it's there and the prefered meta for high speed cornering.

+++Nice and fun arcade styled racing

+++Takes an interesting minor cinematic approach to racing that doesn't detract too much from gameplay

Good for those days when you want to avoid something demanding (of time and/or mental effort), Battle Group 2 is more or less a clicker game - a good one at that, if I may add, and it looks alright for this type of game too.
You click to shoot, and by shooting down enemy ships and buildings not only do you save the day, you also accumulate oil, which you can later on use to unlock new ships and upgrades and to buy power ups. Battle Group 2 is a pretty safe purchase if you like this idea (or enjoyed Missile Command before) and the game is on sale.
I beat the game in less than 3h, then played maybe 1h more to get 4 stars on every level (it's rather easy with stronger ships and power ups). Afterwards, I took some time to unlock and upgrade all ships. There are 31 levels, and each can be completed in a few minutes, making it good to play in short bursts.
If you're going for the achievements: they're easy but grindy. In the game's menu you can open Player tab to see the statistics and how much progress you've made.
As for the ships and power ups:
There are 3 power ups - one which makes time pass very slowly and is expensive, one which immediately destroys all incoming missiles on the screen, and one which reloads the support functions (so you can use them again without waiting for the cooldown to pass).
You can unlock 3 primary ships - Ticonderoga, Arsenal, and Iowa. Ticonderoga is un upgraded version of your first ship (Cyclone), and you can play the entire campaign with it. Iowa is the strongest one, and it plays different from the others - it makes the levels easier to beat, but you will get smaller streaks because it always fires 2 shots and a missed shot resets the streak. Arsenal feels pointless, only buy it for the achievement. Both primary and secondary ships have support functions (I describe them below).
You can unlock 4 secondary ships - Armidale, Huchuan, Hazard Perry, and Invincible. The support ships provide automatic aid upon pressing a key or clicking the respective button on the screen. I spent most of the game with Hazard Perry, which has artillery and a helicopter that blocks incoming missiles. Armidale (the cheapest) only provides artillery. Invincible releases a figher that is good at destroying ships, but does not block incoming missiles. I did not spent any time with Huchuan.
Again, overall a pretty safe purchase if the game is on sale and you like this idea or enjoyed Missile Command before.

Excellent game. The game features two modes to play the game, story and endless. In story mode you play through premade stages, each with unique terrain, where you have to destroy all the target enemies or a boss. Since there are different enemies each stage you always have different powers to copy and combine, which makes the stages even more varied and fun. At first it is not very difficult, but it can be challenging before you get used to the controls, however, after you beat normal mode you can play hard mode, which continues the story, has new enemies and new bosses, the terrain is based on the normal mode equivalent stage, but is often altered in some way. While the game can be difficult at times, these times are often the times when you can become the most powerful. Also, if you lose a boss battle multiple times you usually get tips on how to beat it from Savant, this also applies to some stages that the dev suspects the player might have trouble with.
In endless mode the terrain is always generated and every tenth wave (11, 21 and so forth) you switch to a different biome. Here you also have to destroy the enemies, with the fifth and ninth wave being minibosses and the tenth being a boss for every biome. The big boss is set for every biome but which enemies and minibosses you face is semi-random, it picks from enemies fitting the biome. If you want to mix things up from the standard endless you can either play in a set of four themed biomes, or you can play pandemonium, where every enemy has new randomized attacks for each session (it does stay consistent during the session).
You can play as two characters, Boki, our main hero, can hold and combine three base powers into very powerful combinations, she is the more straightforward of the two characters and has the most raw power, she much more likely to fill the screen with destruction. Savant, Boki's adoptive uncle and in-universe creator of the simulation they play, can also hold three powers, but can only combine two, but the order matters, which means that he always has many different combined powers to choose from, you have to choose the one that fits the situation best. All his powers originate from a window, or sometimes multiple windows, which window you get depends on what base power you use or combine. Savant can fly, teleport and create barriers for a short time, while Boki gets a double jump, a dodge roll and kicks (including a drill kick, which works a bit like an aeriel dodge). The characters both control well and are very responsive, but sometimes it can be hard to aim with them because you only have one set of direction buttons which both aims and moves them, but that is one of the game's only flaws.
The music is very good, there aren't very many base themes (11), but there are many variations of every theme and the music flows seamlessly between them. Every variation is different and has a new feel even though it shares the same base melody and length with other themes. Furthermore every theme also has extra layers which are sometimes added to the main track, these include the game's low HP warning, which has a different version for each theme that is incorporated into the theme, which makes it awesome rather than annoying, there are also other extra layers but these don't play very often, they're usually associated with an enemy or a rare power.
The game has an extensive encyclopedia and bestiary which holds a lot of lore for the game's setting. It also has an art gallery, modifiers (which alter the game, like cheats) and a sound test which allows you to listen to nearly every variation of ever track in the game. You can take in game screenshots and the game records your playing for replays, it saves the ten most recent ones and the ones you choose to save forever. There are also gameplay stats if you're interested.
Overall, the game is fun, varied and has a lot of content, it also does many things right which other games do wrong (such as the implementation of the low HP warning). I strongly recommend this game.

At this point in time, having only put in 7 hours of play time into the game, I feel confident in saying that Copy Kitty is one of the most underrated indie action games currently on Steam. While I won't say the game has the highest production values, being an indie title with a small development team... the polish and thought that's been put into the mechanics are quite refreshing. I'm taking some shots in the dark here, but it would seem to me the developers have been heavily influenced by Treasure's 2D action games like Gunstar Heroes and Bangai-O. And if that is indeed what they were going for, they nailed it, all they while providing their own unique spin on things.
In Copy Kitty's main Story Mode, you traverse a large variety of stages as one of two playable characters: Boki, an immensely powerful catgirl training to be a superhero; Or her genius insectoid uncle Savant. While both of them play extremely differently, chaotic action is the order of the day. In each stage, as you defeat enemies, they drop power-ups that you can combine together to create an enormous plethora of destructive weapons. While the weapons you have access to will depend on the current stage, a whole bunch of explosions filling the screen is entirely normal here. As you progress through the game and become familiar with the mechanics and weapon combinations, the game will start to feel like your own personal playground of destruction. Although with that said, that's certainly not to say the game isn't a challenge. Sometimes the screen will up with enemy projectiles, and when combined with your own it can be tough to tell exactly what's happening. Thankfully, the game is quite generous with its health system, so you don't have to worry about making a few mistakes here and there. There are also quite a few bosses and minibosses to contend with as well as you make your way through the campaign, and pretty much all of these are over the top and a blast to fight against. Top notch marks on that!
Aside from story mode, the game also has an Endless Mode which turns the game into something more akin to a roguelike. You navigate constantly shifting landscapes as you eliminate enemies and bosses. As you might expect, the difficulty ramps up the longer you survive. There are two difficulties for this mode as well. In general this mode is much more freeform than the story mode, but it's certainly interesting in its own right and gives you an opportunity to mess around with everything the game has to offer. Once again, I'm compelled to call the game a playground of destruction.
Aside from the two main modes, the game also has a level editor, and a surprising amount of unlockables. It's got everything from a bestiary where you can find interesting and often adorable information about the game's many foes, to unlockable modifiers that can greatly change the way the game is played. It's actually pretty surprising just how much content this game has given the seemingly small size of its development team. On top of all that, I'm constantly charmed by the game's surprisingly well done dynamic soundtrack. As you run low on HP, there's an audible warning that integrates itself uniquely into each of the game's tracks. As you transition from a regular stage to one of the miniboss stages, the music will dynamically shift to a more intense version of the same theme. Your mileage may vary on this one, but I love the attention to detail that's gone into the soundtrack.
Sure, as I write this the game is still in early access... but as it is now, it is more than worth your $10 if you're looking for a compelling 2D shooter. It's certainly not perfect, the main issue being visibility as explosions and projectiles fill the screen... but the game is just so damn fun that it's easy to forgive, and there's more than enough content to hold you over for many hours. And hey, if you like Treasure titles like Gunstar Heroes and Bangai-O... go buy Copy Kitty!

It's psychedelic, totally adorable, and an absolute blast to play.
The core concept is pretty straightforward. Go into a level, and blast all the enemies in it or reach the end to win. In that sense it's like a regular platformer. Our heroine, Boki, can shoot the "Boki Beam" which is a pretty puny looking blast that doesn't do a lot. Once you kill your first enemy, that's when you're introduced to the meat of the game. As you could assume by the title, there is a copy system. Much like Kirby 64, you can absorb powers from fallen foes and gain completely unique abilities by combining them. You can store up to three powers from a possible 10 base powers, and there's a unique function and name for each one. I didn't even mention the particularly fun "Solo" abilities, which consist of things like Street Fighter dragon kicks and summoning little minions to attack for you.
Discovering every possible combination is part of the enjoyment, and being able to blitz through a level with a combined ability called "Aurora Star" is probably the most satisfying thing ever. It is from here that this game plays like a crazy psychedelic Metroid or Mega Man X, and man is it FUUUN. Throw in some giant robots for good measure, and you've got a solid game on your hands. The game itself is tight and responsive, and the sound and visual effects really make you feel like you're doing something. And you are, after all.
Luckily there's quite a bit of content here. There are a LOT of levels with more coming soon, and then there's an Endless Mode and an alternate campaign for a second character you unlock later. On top of that there's a little database containing information on the enemies (as well as how many of that particular enemy you've killed or lost to) and the characters themselves.
The graphics themselves seem to consist of pre-rendered 3D models, but it doesn't look as awkward as you'd think. It looks quite nice, and there's all sorts of pretty particle effects for the explosions and your abilities, allowing you to create one helluva lightshow with your powers.
I'd say the controls are really the only falling point, as they're a little hard to get used to and sometimes the action gets way too fastpaced for what you need to be doing.
+ Colorful and interesting visual style
+ Fun fast-paced gameplay

+ Solid music
+ Plenty of playtime and replay value
+ Boki is adorable
+ Boki's bug-uncle has a really nice suit

After waiting for eons for updates that were much needed for the program, I can now post a legit review.
The program itself is BEAUTIFUL. The design of the program is perfect and has easy drag-n-drop features that help EVERY user make the perfect Visual Novel.
While there are still updates (some of which, I, myself, am very excited to see!) I highly recommend users getting this program. I used a program called Novelty for well over five years, and I admit, it has never been as easy and as smooth as TyranoBuilder has made it out to be. Even compared to Ren'Py, which has high customability (a feature I really love about that program), I would prefer TyranoBuilder over Ren'Py. What's more is that, unlike Novelty, TyranoBuilder is continuously gaining constant updates and suggestions for the program, and every day, it becomes just that much more easier and better to use.
If you are NOT a programmer, that is perfectly fine. You can make a legit visual novel of your own, and you don't even NEED to go through training just to be able to use this program. I have been able to make a visual novel on my own, and I didn't even have to take a look at any tutorials to create one either.
Above all, TyranoBuilder is user-friendly, which, in my opinion, is a great quality to have for a program. I have almost completely converted from using Novelty to using TyranoBuilder, however, with the upcoming updates, it won't be long before TyranoBuilder takes over my life and becomes my #1 program tool to use for creating visual novels.

This is a cute way for beginners to get started with creating their own visual novels. However, the limited amount of customization of the interface means that I can't really see a viable commercial game being made on the engine. The engine is far more limited than Ren'py, not having a settings menu and offering limited UI customization and animation.
I am still giving it a thumbs up because I suppose it fills a certain niche but if you are considering serious game development then try out the free Ren'py before buying this.

This War of Mine is truly an excellent game. The premise is one I've never experienced before, the visuals are fantastic, the soundtrack is simple yet moving, and the concept is simple: survive.
You don't really win this game, it just ends eventually, whether your characters are alive or not. This is one of the few games I've played where I really care if my characters die, not just because I know it's going to be harder to go on for the others, but because I probably could've done something to keep them alive, but didn't.
The day-time survive/craft/trade time, mixed with the tense, nightly scavanging for supplies along with the random events and consequense-based decision making all combine to put you in a situation where you can never quite relax. The game is always hanging on the edge of a bad situation and can be tipped over by a stupid choice or random chance very easily, irreparably changing how the game will progress, and what your characters have to deal with.
Overall, it's a fantastic game. Would recommend, 10/10.

What this game is:
A decent entry point into Magic: the Gathering universe and ruleset. While it only shows a tip of the MtG iceberg, it is completely sufficient for a new player to pick up the basics. At last but not least, unless you can borrow cards from a friend and have someone teach you, it is the only real option to try the game for free.
What this game is NOT:
A good videogame. It still has technical issues with certain cards. You will also occasionally be disconnected from the game. The interface could use some work too, as it gets pretty chaotic the moment there are more than a couple cards in play.
I cannot but compare it to Hearthstone. Magic Duels has deeper and more complex systems hidden under its rather unattractive presentation. Unless you know the cards and their artworks, you will spend time reading what is completely obvious immediately in Hearhtstone. It also lacks the audiovisual polish of the Blizzard game.
On the other hand, the actual card game that Magic Duels is a digital version of is undoubtedly richer, more interesting, engaging and varied on strategical and tactical levels.
To sum it up, while Magic: the Gathering is a better card game than Hearthstone is. That being said, Hearthstone is definitely a better videogame than Magic Duels, which leaves a lot to be desired, especially its technical state.
Give the game a shot whether you've played Magic: the Gathering before or not. If you didn't, it gives you an insight into what the game is like.
If you've played Magic: the Gathering before or if you're an active player, give it a shot, but don't expect Magic Duels to be a full-fledged replacement of playing with actual cards and actual people.

A very simple top down type shooter where your in command of a fleet which needs to get from point A to point B while taking on waves of enemies. Again a very simple and time killer game.

I got this game in a bundle and was interested to try a grand strategy title that looked very reminiscent of Risk, one of my childhood rage-inducing board games. I was satisfied with my gameplay experience, although I routinely got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me.
If you like Risk-style grand strategy and simplistic mechanics, then you will enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are nice - the amount of detail is very simple but in no way boring or unpleasant. The game takes place on a map of the Earth's globe that you can rotate at will, and visual effects that mimic a radar occur periodically as you play. For example, there will be static feedback at times, and at others the world map will colourize. The music and sounds are good, however, I eventually muted the music in favor of my own. A female-voiced artificial intelligence helps you as you play, and will sometimes remark on different things, including a particular game track being her favorite, which I thought was a charming touch. The story is fairly basic - you play as a General-for-hire and will have to aid different nations in their conquests for world domination.
Controls are not too difficult to learn, however, it may take a bit to get accustomed to using the right mouse-click to select and left mouse-click to deselect/cancel unit movement and building production. There is a series of tutorial missions that will help you understand the mechanics of the game, however, the in-game tutorial dialogues pause action and can take a bit too long. Fortunately, you have the option of turning these off and on - I prefer having them off because sometimes you may speed through the dialogue (spacebar) back into gameplay, and spacebar is also used to speed up action by one day; bad design choice in my opinion. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with real-time strategy and grand strategy games.
Gameplay consists of you building forces (slowly), generating income (passively), and taking over territories to expand the first two goals. There are a small number of unit types - infantry, armor (tanks), two aircraft, three navy, and a nuclear missile. Each unit moves at a certain speed, and you can stack different units together to move as a single entity (they will move as slow as the slowest unit in the stack). Every unit is exactly the same across nations, so an armor unit at 100% will fight another undamaged armor unit until they both die around the same time. You cannot heal units, however, you can merge units to refill their health (ex: merge three infanty at 30-40% health each to get a 100% and a 20% unit). Only infantry can capture structures. They are also the land unit capable of entering transport ships (a design choice I find weird because it grounds your tanks and forces you to slow your island invasions).
Aircraft are extremely quick and can help turn the tide of battle, however, you must keep them supplied with either an aircraft carrier or airpad - they will only fly within a certain supply radius.
During combat, units will fight to the death, and pulling them away from each other can be rather challenging (discouraging retreat). Infantry gain a 2x bonus to their combat effectiveness when they are defending cities. Cities are indicated by a flag of the controlling nation and usually have other military structures present (barracks, aviation center, etc). You cannot build new structures, another design choice that I find interesting (I would've liked the ability to construct new buildings). Each city provides constant income, which is important because each unit costs billions of dollars.
There are different game modes, including a wide-branching story mode and online matches. There are some sandbox modes that allow you to select a nation and/or starting city. These are very challenging if you do not maximize your time and resources because the AI will slowly steamroll you into oblivion.
Overall, the game plays very well for a real-time grand strategy game, and anyone interested in the genre should give it a try. Personally, however, I would wait until the game goes on sale or is bundled again.
Recommend!

I first found Copy Kitty a little over 2 years ago, but I wish I'd started even earlier because this game is an incredible experience. The flashy rainbow-filled explosive fun begins immediately and only keeps climbing from there. It offers endless satisfaction as you wipe out hordes of hugely creative and diverse (and often amusingly silly) varieties of robots, as well as explore many vibrant and colorful worlds, and do battle with numerous engaging and memorable bosses. All providing you with a constant feeling of immense power and destructive capability.
Story Mode filled me with a strong sense of curiosity and wonder that I've not felt for a game to such an extent in a long time. Every level is gorgeous to look at, a pleasure to learn and navigate, and rewarding to clear. I was always anxious and excited to see what's next. What super powerful weapon combo will I discover today? What neat mechanics will be introduced? What bosses lie ahead? What will the next worlds look like, how does the story progress through them, and what kind of lore will I uncover? There was always a reason to keep pressing forward and be pleasantly surprised by what I found. Even after discovering everything, I wasn't disappointed, because it's still a limitless joy to revisit the massive variety and enjoy each scenario again.
Most of the levels are relatively small, so a lot of progress can be made in a short time while not feeling over too soon. Even if you struggle on one, you learn a little bit each time you fail. The small areas not only make them easier to retry a whole bunch if needed, but they always make victory feel within reach too. All of the above applies to Hard Mode as well. It's always fun seeing what's familiar and what's new in terms of presentation, challenge, and enemy varieties, and how they change the circumstances. The boss upgrades are especially menacing, but all the more satisfying to conquer.
Endless Mode is also a fantastic time. Just the fact that the terrain and enemies are constantly changing around you is wondrous in itself, creating everlasting chaos and always keeping you on your toes. Weapon combos are often more situational in Story Mode, but here you'll discover unique combinations a lot more spontaneously because all of the components are provided at varying points. Each wave is super short and environment progress is checkpointed every 5 waves, so exploring everything is always an attainable goal. Dozens of environments to experience and many ever-changing conditions make each run feel different, so the replay value is immense.
Both modes are hugely fun, and picking a favorite really comes down to whether you want organized and deliberately-arranged scenarios, or much more randomized and chaotic ones, with every aspect of the gameplay being extremely well suited to both. I often find myself switching between them regularly because I'm in the mood for either at different times, and I'm unable to pick a favorite because both are just that enjoyable in their own ways. In addition to all of that, there's even a fully-functional level editor at your disposal. Even with all of the experiences present in the game, there's still the capacity to create your own scenarios as you please and even create packs to share with others. It comes packed with a vast assortment of enemies, weapons, and environmental options, so you can pretty much create whatever you can imagine in the game. You can even customize the Hard Mode of each level a lot!
This game offers a huge degree of challenges and experiences that do eventually become pretty hard, but I found it to be really simple to try out and get a feel for from the start. Control is super smooth and customizable, with tutorials that are quick and easy while doing a great job of showing everything you're capable of. The earliest levels of either mode start you off in really tame territory, so no matter when it gets tough, you always have something to fall back on to practice with and it never makes you tackle a situation until you're ready for it, even if some things take a little while. The smooth difficulty curve, replayability, and ability to alternate between modes at your leisure makes the game fantastic at training you if you give it the time and patience. The level editor's great for this too, as you can make something based around anything you struggle with at any difficulty you desire until you get the hang of it.
I can't praise this game enough or fully describe just how amazing playing the game has been and continues to be for me, and I still not sure I've done that feeling proper justice. I'd strongly recommend this to anyone who enjoys platformers, shooters, robots, lasers, cute things, cyberspace, or colorful atmospheres of any kind, perhaps even video games as a whole. Even if you're not great at platformers, the movement is incredibly generous and comfortable, and the game is far more focused on combat with the platforming really being more a way to traverse and explore rather than being a point of skill. Plus, nothing is insta-kill and you can't die from falling, and even the combat is kept nice and simple for newbies at the beginning. You can also take a lot of hits and health is pretty common, so the game isn't too punishing for individual mistakes. Definitely try this out, it deserves all the love and $10 is an absolute steal for what's given.

Copy Kitty is a damn good action-platformer-shooter hybrid, which gleefully shows its inspiration from Kirby, Mega Man, Gunstar Heroes and other classic titles in dazzling technicolour explosions. The simple premise - copy and combine up to three enemy attack types to produce well over 100 unique weapons on the main character alone - carries both the Story Mode's 120+ puzzle-maze levels and the Endless Mode's small but looping arena battles against unpredictable enemies, dynamic terrain and weather extremely well.
Both modes are punctuated by some brilliant bosses, each of which typically drops unique copy abilities so you can throw their own attacks right back at them. This leads to some absolutely brilliant moments - my favourite involved uppercut-jousting with a recurring miniboss inside a tornado, set to the most rocking music in the game. Some bosses fill the screen and use devastating, sweeping attacks - others are smaller, but their speed makes up for their lack of presence, forcing you to duck and dive around them and their attacks. I won't spoil the final and hidden bosses, but let's just say they're incredibly worth experiencing.
The amount of polish in the game is absurd for such a small team, with the variable-mix music and huge array of stage types working wonders. Little things like the bestiary listing off nearly every single enemy type and their weaknesses, or the fact that every single weapon and combination - for both characters! - has a unique name, that's care and attention to detail that just makes the experience that much better. There's even a full-featured level editor.
Boki, the lead character, is all about chaotic destruction - her attacks are mostly straightforward and blasting, if not entirely screen-devastating. Some of her powers - especially those incorporating the "Remote" weapon type - take a little to learn their quirks, but prove essential nonetheless. While you're sure to find a favourite weapon combination or two, variety is exceptionally high and you'll likely find yourself trying out nearly all of them one way or another - some stages require a little more thought, but never demand excessive precision. She double-jumps, rolls, kicks, and generally handles in a way that should feel innately familiar to fans of classic platformers, but her terrain-destroying and projectile-reflecting kicks and impressive dynamic arsenal set her apart as a unique hero.
The second character, Savant, provides a slower, more tactical pace and a whole different set of weapons using an entirely different approach - flying and warping around the stage with carefully-positioned weapons. The stages may be the same, but they play almost completely differently as a result. He only mixes two weapons at once, but the order you mix them in matters, so his weapon variety is still staggeringly high. He unlocks fairly shortly into the game, and I strongly recommend giving him a spin.
All in all, Copy Kitty has absolutely taken me by storm, and I reckon it'll do the same for you if you like games which can do both chaos and tactics at the same time. This game has both in spades, providing both delightful neon firework displays and fraught battles in which you'll be hanging on to that last flicking point of health as you overcome challenge after challenge. If you like relentlessly fun games that build on the classics but bring something unique to the table, Copy Kitty is a must-buy.

Disclosure:  I marked “received this product for free” because I won it in a giveaway.
This review is based on the early access build available on 08/11/2016.
When I first heard about Copy Kitty I wasn't sure what to think about it.  As mentioned in previous reviews, I've actively been looking for run and gun shooters.  Let's face it, Boki isn't exactly the Bill Rizer or Lance Bean I was originally looking for, but the mobility and power combination mechanic displayed in the trailer were more than enough to pique my interest.  It sort of reminded me of Mega Man and Kirby in a way, but in the end it turns out Copy Kitty does a great job of being its own game.
The general story is that the main character Boki receives a virtual reality style combat simulator game as a present for her birthday from her uncle.  Boki is sucked into the simulator where she must battle her way through each level.  Despite not being particularly confident in her abilities, it turns out she is quite powerful.  Other than her wicked kung-fu kicks, she is able to take powers from defeated enemies and make use of them herself.  Boki can hold three powers at a time and can use them individually or combine them all together for a unique power attack.  In addition to the powers, there are also power-up items that bestow assorted temporary abilities.  The various powers not only serve as weapons, but also as tools for navigating stages.
In story mode each level is divided up into roughly ten stages.  The stages are short, fast paced, and filled with combat.  Unlike some platformers where the goal is to navigate your way to the the end of each level, in Copy Kitty the objective is to destroy the enemies.  It's a game that is much more focused on combat than precise jumps with instant death pits and spikes.  As of writing this I've almost completed the game on normal as Boki and I don't recall seeing any instant death hazards at all.  Boki is easy to control (though I do recommend using a gamepad) and combat is satisfying. You can also eventually play as Boki's Uncle Savant.  I haven't experimented too much with him yet but he has a completely different play-style.  Other than story mode, the game also features a randomly generated endless mode, and a level editor to create your own stages.
As far as presentation goes, the game looks good for the most part.  The enemies are creative and there are some incredible boss battles.  During combat there are colorful explosions and rainbow bursts all over the place.  The only criticism I have regarding graphics is that I think there is room for improvement in the way some of the stages appear.  The majority of the stages look good but overall I felt that Boki, the enemies, and the bosses all seemed to be a lot more visually polished in comparison.  The soundtrack is solid and I've had a few of the songs stuck in my head since I started playing.  It's worth mention that the game features an awesome extras menu with a detailed bestiary, concept art, sound-test, and play stats.  Why don't more games have bestiaries?
Even though it's in early access, Copy Kitty is a very solid game right meow.  There is already a lot of content and the developers are planning to add two additional worlds.  According to the store page the game should leave early access about a year from now.  I'm definitely looking forward to see what will change between now and then as I feel the offered package is already strong.  The available content is certainly worth the asking price of 9.99 and I'd recommend it to people looking for an action platformer that leans more towards the action side than it does platforming.
Edit: Started hard mode, it kicked the explosions up to 11.  I was already enjoying it before but this cemented it.  What can I say? I like a challenge.  Copy Kitty is good stuff.

As of writing (12/8/2015), since this is new software, there are still a lot of kinks to be ironed out. Proper fullscreen support has only recently been added, as an example. Hammerwatch is a top down Gauntlet-esque "quarter" eater. Featuring up to 4 player co-op, sprawling levels, secrets, and at higher difficulties some really unforgiving gameplay, this dungeon crawler is a must have for those that want a throwback game with enhanced graphics and sound. While the levels aren't randomly generated, there are a variety of challenge modes and a map editor for custom content. Four distinct classes feature similar core gameplay but differ greatly at later levels when purchasing upgrades for ranged attacks or skills from vendors.
Some weaknesses include the inability to scroll the map, some unfortunate invincibility frames in certain animations, and a rather steep boss difficulty curve. Additionally during floor clearing, the lack of respawning enemies can sometimes make secret hunting rather tedious. Overall an excellent game to pick up and play with friends (assuming the broken multiplayer lobby system gets fixed).

Not a bad game. Not as good as it could be. The primary character can't do simple things (like jump) except in certain occasions, which means they had to put ramps in areas to allow access.  Seriously, what kinda crap is that? Can't even hop up in the air to look at something? Console-like key functions get boring and frustrating (to open windows, hold a key, then hit it over and over until the window opens), wasting 10 seconds on some windows, while others open after the initial space bar. Plus, why keep locking drawers Ive already unlocked if there's nothing in them the 2nd time around?  Can't skip some of the long mandatory "watch this to see how great the story is"  scenes, like the elevator ride up. Can't skip the "look how scary we can (not) be" scenes. Watching them during the first playthrough was barely tolerable. I didnt buy the game expecting Oscar-winning actors, and after the first, somewhat disappointing, disjointed ending, IDGAF about the "story line". Fine, have mandatory crapscenes the first play-through, then allow them to be skipped. Also, if I wanted to play a 2-D side shooter where I'm locked in to one course of action, I WOULDNT, because I don't. Running through collapsing buildings trying to get loot before I burn to death, dying , then trying again and again until I make it through by trial and error. Not enjoyable, no benefit to the game, I'd say someone's girlfriend or boyfriend wanted to show off his/her arcade style design skills. Also didn't enjoy wandering around trying to figure out how to get where I needed to go . Surely it wouldn't have been too hard to have a map with freaking location names on it. I'd bet that was left out so that the total  time spent searching for a way to get to a portion of the city could be counted as play time, when it's  not really. The end of-mission rewards for goals didn't make sense. Ok fine, let's have a goal like don't be detected, and then have one for 10 combat takedowns, which pretty much means one of them isn't achievable. At least if I DO 3 or 4  of the goals, why are only 2 of them shown at the end? Are the goals based on play style?  Also, have one AUTOSAVE slot of you must, but if I hit quick load, allow it to load MY last save,. On the topic of saving, what moron came up with the idea that we can't save if anyone is looking for us? Sneaking through an area for 10 minutes, get spotted by one guard and we can't save while anyone is alerted even if we're hiding and there's no way they can reach us? That's a CROCK!. Next, the restrictions on passing through the transitions where we need to move a board. Dash to an exit , get spotted by a guard, try to move through the exit and get told,no , you have to stay, wait for the guard to come up and fight him. Again, BS. On the topic of fighting, yeah, I get it, we're not supposed to fight. I guess the same moron designed the fight limitations. Hit someone with a sword, try to hit them again, nope! can't do it, gotta pause until they hit you back. Can't block, and dodging wont work if youre in a narrow area. Same thing with trying to blackjack someone to initiate a combat takedown. Sitting for 5 seconds mashing the blackjack key while the screen is prompting me to do a regular takedown, then the guard turns around and I get nailed by 3 other guards when he yells because I couldnt initiate a combat takedown. Just crappy crappy coding.
Now that I've listed (most) of the irritating and pointless parts of this game that had the potential to be great, but missed, here are the good parts.  Not many FPS games are worth a crap anymore. This one wasnt great, suffered from an attempt to make it more than it was, but it was fun when I wasn't trying to figure out how to get to a certain portion of the city if I didn't want to go on a prescribed mission. I did like being able to see what the goals were for each mission, but I and many others figured out how to by accident. I like the ability to jump from target to target in mid-air without falling. I like the bow, but it's underpowered until after it's leveled up. Shoot someone in the head or face with a bow, they should be down for the count, period. Over all, did I like the game, despite the many shortcomings? Yes. Was it worth $59? HELL NO!! Would I spent $59 on another game from the same developer? Nope, sorry. $50 and up should be reserved for top of the line, well-written games. No longer does just being New mean a game should be priced that high. I do recommend the game, but with reservations. I'd give it a 6 on a scale of 1 to 10. That might seem like a low score, but a lot of the games coming out are only 3 to 5. The main benefit is this game CAN be played for hours and hours.

Now that I have calmed down from my "nostalgic" rage, I have to admit: Thief (2014) is a decent game. I wouldn't go call it a master piece or very good, but it's fairly good and a nice experience on its own. If you start comparing it to the original versions or even Dishonored you are very likely to find a ton of things to nitpick and cry about. This was the mistake I did the first time, and although it was somewhat justified, it was in the end a bit unfair since I have to judge the game as ITSELF, not as a recreation of bygone glory days or as a rival to something else.
With that said, I personally have enjoyed this new installment. There are, like mentioned, TONS of little and bigger things to complain about, namely the very restricted movement around the small sandbox environment you dwell in, and buggy A.I. (I just love the dialogue audio problem where the guards keep repeating the same things all the time... not). I also found the new way of peeking around the corners absolutely stupid (whatever happened to good ol' Q and E?), and the cinematic cutscenes look dámn weird at times - from cinematic view, that is. The story I couldn't care less about, and the chance to roam yourself from mission to mission in the city, although cool at first, is just tedious in the long run and I find myself getting lost half the time, thanks to the pretty useless map. I just wanted to get the mission started, not to trying to navigate through the confusing city layout and pondering which rope or ladder would lead me to a window that'd took me to the right place!
And with THAT all said... I still like the game. The missions are fun to play when you adjust yourself to the game mechanics and the overall philosophy (meaning, the less you kill the more you enjoy the challenge), and some of the maps are just brilliant when it comes to gameplay, almost bringing memories from the Thieves of yore. Do I recommend this rebirth? Meh... on sale, definetely. If you loved Dishonored and unchristianly worshipped the original ones as your Lords and Saviors, I see no reason why you wouldn't enjoy this one as well... provided you play it with open mind. So, I might even recommend it. I think I will.

I have been waiting for this game since 5 years ago. It may not be the game for people who looking to murder virtual humans & monsters but its the perfect game for a sneaking gamers like me. This game is pretty much like Dishonored, but with more realistic graphics and darker color palete. Like Dishonored, you can also "ghost" the level by completing only the main objectives and leaving the NPCs alone without leaving a trace of your whereabouts. This is a must have for those who love stealth games.

The story is bland, the main appeal of the game, stealing, is tedious as you have to check every drawer, cabinet, cubby, chest or safe. In said places you will find gold which is necessary to upgrade your character. Half of the upgrades are what I would consider combat upgrades (reduced damage do more blackjack damage etc.). You should never be in combat as you will more than likely die trying to defend yourself against the enemies who have swords and crossbows while you are armed with a bow and blackjack. So why bother with these upgrades and gold after getting all the stealth upgrades? It doesn't play like a combat game which is fine but the stealth portion of the game is so boring and repetitive you kind of wish there was something else to do besides crawl from shadow to shadow in search of gold for upgrades and journals.
Stealth games need to play like puzzle games almost they need to show you a room and you need to figure out which combination of tools you need to use to get to the end goal. This game it feels like you are just crawling from button to button from drawer to drawer knocking every single enemy out because there is no threat to you if you take them all out. There needs to be consequences for doing something like knocking a guard out, guards should check on each other from time to time.
Stealth games are hard to do because the nature of them is to walk slow and wait things out but there has to be some other mechanics in between that make you think out what you are doing, keep your mind occupied with thought on solving problems and not tedium of pressing forawrd.

The new Thief is a lot better than what you've probably heard by now. Perhaps that's damning it with faint praise, but really, when the dust clears, this is a solid stealth game that's worth playing whether or not you've played any of the Thief games before. Yes, it has its faults, but all of the previous titles have. I think it's best to sum it up in terms of pros and cons:
PROS:
+ some great, spacious levels with multiple entrances and wings
+ plenty of sidequests are available to not only get more stealthy gameplay, but also gather up more money for equipment
+ very customizable, you can have as much or as little UI assistance as you like
+ regardless of what the naysayers might have you imagine, the swoop function is pretty cool and does not, in fact, trivialize stealth
+ more stealth challenges...birds and dogs can alert guards if they detect sudden movements; items can be bumped over, causing noise
+ chapters and sidequests can be replayed, if you want to revisit some earlier challenges
+ sets of loot exist for people who just gotta steal 'em all
+ traps and hidden passages make Garrett feel more rogue-like (but not roguelike)
+ I think the new engine looks pretty good. Many people have complained that it's a little too monochromatic, but The City is supposed to be a dingy, miserable place. Some of the indoor levels are more colourful
CONS:
- even though there are only a few action setpieces in the game, they feel out of place
- TOO MANY ZOMBIES, the cardinal sin of any Thief game
- the Basso sidequests are more about getting to the destination than thieving (the Ector and Vittori sidequests are much better at this, though)
- and of course, this is related to the rope arrow thing
- silently knocking out a guard should not be accompanied by a loud yell and musical sting
- could benefit from a fast travel system if the City has already been explored
What I wanted from dishonored, executed how I wanted it to be and looking how I wanted it to.

This game is truly bad. Which breaks my heart as I am a newcomer to the Thief franchise, not a longtime fan held back by the legacy of the older games. This game suffers both from a technical aspect and a creative point of view.
THE BAD
First, let's look at graphics. The textures are often low-res, muddy, and just ugh in general. Animations are generally smooth except when they are not. Lighting, perhaps the most important quality in a stealth game is lackluster, a big difference from Thief 1 where the lighting made the game.
Controls are loose and unresponsive. The much-hyped Swoop feature is sometimes very hard to trigger, leaving you in the middle of what you were trying to swoop through.
Level design is very linear. I expected better from the people who made games with interesting linear levels like Tomb Raider and games with interesting hub levels like Deus Ex Human Revolution. This is the laziest level design I have seen in a decade.
The story is the average spooky wizard cultists try to spread plague/zombies into a city and the main character, who has amesnia or was in a coma, has to rediscover what went wrong. This has been done a million times and this iteration is not any better.
Characterization is where this game really goes to new depths. Garett has always been more of an avatar for the player than a protagonist. But Erin is a horrible character, bratty and unsociable like new Dante in the DMC reboot, that makes me grit my teeth in disbelief. Let alone sympathize with her, I want her to suffer as much as possible. Which makes the whole saving Erin plot pretty useless.
THE GOOD
This game is very very customizable. If you can get past the lackluster plot, the bad graphics, linear and lazy level design, and the mindblowing stupid Erin, this game offers you lots of choices. You can cancel the HUD, the map, loot glint, turn on instant death, and loads of other interesting options.
Which is a pity because all the other aspects will turn you off the game. I could not even get through 5 hours of this game, it was that slow and tedious and irritating and I kept asking myself why I am wasting time here. What a waste of a free AMD rewards game.
TL;DR = The graphics are dated, the controls feel bad, the plot is lame, the levels are lazy, the characters are stupid, but hey you get a lot of nifty toppings on this steaming pile of ****.
