This game has:
- A power-combining system similar to Kirby 64, but greatly expanded
- Massively destructive abilities
- Very difficult platforming, with a gentle learning curve
- Two characters with unique playstyles, powers and game mechanics
- Tons of hidden game enhancers (EG; all your shots are converted to a laser version, you have only one health, you start with permanent melee abilities, etc.)
- Gameplay that rewards tactical planning and execution
- Penguin robots
This game is more than worth buying at full price. I heartily recommend it to anyone who loves platformers, especially fans of the old Kirby and Megaman games.

Holy crap, this was so much fun to play.
I've only played mission mode so far (up to world 5 as of writing), which for each level you have to shoot and destroy the enemies. You have a standard shot, but some enemies will drop weapons you can collect and shoot. You can also combine up to three weapons to make an even more powerful weapon. There are also other picks up that do things like make your shots flaming or give you a more powerfukl kick attack.
Even though it's Early Access, everything I've played so far feels complete. Can't recommend this enough.

Note : review based on the beta version, i played throught the whole game
The game is literally a blast to play! :D It manage to combine power stealing and combining from kirby 64 with highly, jumping and shooting from megaman and explosive action that would rival even the best Treasure games!
It's also sorta 2 game in one : the mission mode put you against more than a hundred stages and plenty of bosses, and all weapon available reset and change from stage to stage, leading to a tons of variety in action, especially count taken of the many ways those weapons can be combined to form really badass firepower!
The second mode, endless mode, should be called arcade mode : you keep fighting wave of ennemies in an everchanging battlefield, you keep your weapons from wave to wave and bosses will challenge after each 5 waves. Fortunately there's checkpoint after each bos so you don't have to do it all in one go!
Even in it's early access stage, there's already tons to do to challenge the player : 2 characters with radically different way of playing(Boki reminds of gunstar heroes while savant reminds of Bangai-oh), more than a hundred stage, the aforementionned endless/arcade mode(coming with it'sown set of ennemies, hasard and bosses), and a hard mode that radically change the game in every way possible and will challenge even the best of players!
There's not much minus to mention, if only that the control may takes a few minutes to get the hang of since the moveset is quite extensive(a gamepad is highly recommended!) and that it ends on a cliffhanger, since it's still an early access afterall. But there's already more than a fullgame worth of content here, both for casual and hardcore gamers.
If you remotely like 2d action games, definitely check this out! ^^

is a greenlit Visual Novel about the trials and tribulations of Scanlating (ripping and translating) manga. How the game approaches this, however, is more in the 'image' of scanlation teams, rather than trying to systemize the individual steps themselves, which is understandable due to the limited range that engines like Ren'Py can offer.
What is harder to forvgive, however, is the irony that is a
translation. It feels like this title was given a translation and three passes by a non-english speaker, who then delegated the proofreading to someone who did not understand the Russian language, and thus missed the tiny little idiosyncrasies that translating a language as accurately as possible comes with. There are censor bleeps on lines of dialogue that contain no curse words or anything that would imply a need for such a thing.
The inter-character dialgue is what suffers the most from this, as their are moments of actual, genuine humour, that get lost in the sea of cliché anime tropes. Moments of actually hilarious bait and switches are peppered throughout an experience that overall forces you to perceive it as a low-effort cash in on easy jokes and the usual sexualization of women. And when I say cliché, I mean cliché aplenty, with such corny dialogue lines as "It's not as simple as you think!" when referring to one of the many jobs available, or choosing an option and having a character literally tell you "It doesn't matter".  Which is odd, seeing as how the game's depiction of manga translation is actually fairly accurate.

Starting off, the game lets you talk to various 'teachers' (really just the other people in the group who do various jobs, e.g. Scanning, Translation, Typesetting, etc.) and decide which job you'd like to do for yourself. This is the title's first major misstep- it presumes you'll know your first time through what experience you'll require to do any given job. In general Visual Novel style, you'll get the bad end first, and then have the information available to take the route your actual interested in your second time through- which you might not actually do, as the game patronizingly prods you on after a game over to see what the rest of it has to offer. Let me tell you something, "One Manga Day", if I wanted to keep playing, I'd do it on my own; your needy-sounding justification to see the other endings just comes of as desperate rather than a selling point.

After you restart the game 4 times and eventually get a job on the team (which doesn't even effect anything in the long run), the 'game' proper begins, however I hesitate to call the length of this story a 'game'. Choices in "One Manga Day" are very vapid and shallow, with most choices throughout the experience being a 'what one line of dialogue would you like to see differently?' and the rest of the big ticket choices amounting to whether or not you'll get an impromptu Bad End or one of the two Good Ends. You'll come to find that the various characters (who have the
ridiculous names ever, by the way- what kind of parent names their baby girl 'Laiby', 'Lin', or 'Lap'????) are all pretty much the most low effort stereotypes you'd see in babby's first anime- there's about 3 tsunderes, a computer geek, a creeper nerd (which, by the way, I feel deserves mentioning is the developers self-insert), and and they're all pretty prone to violence (generally on the nerd) as the immediate go-to solution.

The various members of the team seem to have trouble with the basic functions of their jobs. For instance, the translator apparently has no idea what Esperanto is (also according to the game, 'Ne, ne' is now an Esperanto phrase), and does not know what function Lorem Ipsum serves, even though the game uses it at several points for example purposes- they missed a free opportunity to at least teach you something, but completely miss it. When you first meet the cleaner, he is complaining about FreeBSD and servers, just so you know he's the 'smart one'. It doesn't effect his 'story' or 'arc' at all, he literally talks almost exclusively in computer jive and that's his entire character. By the way, I feel it's worth noting once more that the scene that introduces this character is case-and-point proof that the foreground and background assets look absolutely horrendous on top of each other- this game was clearly made with prefab assets, which wouldn't be a bad thing in itself, but it's haphazardly thrown together at best. There seems to be no consideration for any sort of artistic direction, and when your game is text-based, you should likely try to get in ANY kind of flavour you can.

The music is functional and sounds decent- it never got on my nerves in any serious way, and a few tracks I actually enjoyed. It's a shame then, that they're all used for the most banal scenes ever. There's a nice little track (I use the word 'nice' sparingly) they use for a party to celebrate your addition to the team which has 3 whole frames of animation, all the while your terrible new 'friends' are running around in the background trying to kill each other. For at least every single scene in the game that will make you crack a small smile, there will be at least two or three that are guaranteed to make you want to quit playing then and there- which is where the skip function comes into play.

You'll play the game once for real, and after you get a good or bad ending, you'll find yourself hovering on the skip button almost out of instinct. Most visual novel games employ this, because nobody likes reading the same text over and over, which is why most games offer differing paths with changed dialogue to keep you interested. "One Manga Day" however has no such interest, and would rather change one response line that a character will parrot off to you and then continue on, exactly the same as your last playthrough- even for some of the more important, ending-altering choices! Speaking of choices, there seems to be something not explicitly told to the player. While you're contextualized as someone seeking to join a (School?) club for manga, you don't really 'say' your choices, rather than direct the other characters with them. More often than not, your choices aren't actual speech that you say, but stage directions that the other characters perform with each other, which makes the experience wildly inconsistent and a bit hard to get a grasp of.

I'd love to continue talking about this game, but I've really been writing an essay on something that does not want to be taken that seriously. If you're a die-hard Visual Novel fan such as myself, then you might get some entertainment out of it, the occasional joke that makes you actually laugh made it able to sit through for me. If you're however not one of those people, the game still holds value in that you can laugh at it with some buddies for a few minutes for the low, low price of free and then uninstall it at your leisure. I really think this game has a huge 'Mystery Science Theatre 3000' appeal in that regard, it's ripe Retsupurae material. With a little more time in translation and maybe a more serious effort, it could have been one worth remembering. "One Manga Day" is a game with a fantastically interesting premise that fails to deliver on almost all fronts.

The following comes from the eyes and mindset of a software engineer.
TyranoBuilder is a software that is extremely active and very engaging. It's easy to understand, and even if you're new to video games and the design or scripting process, it's very intuitive and the community is more than happy to help (in several languages). They have a VERY active support system, constantly coming to the rescue and explaining many aspects of the scripting and normal software that makes me feel more than comfortable going to them for help. I've even just found out that the raw source code for each project is available, so if you're like me and want to skip all the visual jazz and just program the whole dang thing, you actually can.
TyranoBuilder is a great way for people to get into scripting and programming. Every engine claims it's set up so that you don't require programming skills, but this is honestly a white lie, though in no way "bad". You ABSOLUTELY can make a game in TB without ANY programming. It is wonderfully simple and easy... But your game will be too.
When you go into TB, go in prepared to learn to script or program. If you want to create a romance sim, you're going to need variables, you're going to need branching scenes, and you're going to need to know how instantiating, declaring, and incramenting/decramenting works, especially if you want even a semblance of player interraction with your game. If you're looking to just make a visual book, you won't need scripting.
Their API (Tags Reference) for the built in language is fantastically simple to follow, if sometimes a little too simple. But in the end, if you just post a comment on steam inquiring about a tag you didn't understand, you will ALWAYS receive a kind and more-than-happy-to-assist response. The support is one of my favorite things about this. Another thing I love is their variables- they have temporary variable types that get deleted when the game is closed, game variables that are particular to each save, and system variables that stay with your computer and are independant of saves (that can be for such things as "you've gotten all the endings, have a super secret ending"). It was probably what sold the software to me in the first place.
THE BEST THING POSSIBLE about this game is that it has the ability to build the game for you for the best consoles. I'm talking Mobile, Linux, PC, Mac- the whole shebang. With a click of a button and a selection from a dropdown, it does it FOR YOU. I LITERALLY CANNOT EXPRESS how amazing that is. It might just be because trying to get UE4 to make a PC build was the death of me and an entire week/month, but this is literally the best part. SERIOUSLY CANNOT SAY I'M JUST SO HAPPY WITH THAT PART.
Overall, I like this software. For what it's worth and what you get, it's amazing and wonderful. You're not just paying for the software- you're paying also for the support, the people, the experiences, and even the game jams, which they do host.
TL;DR: If you aren't afraid of working hard, do it! But then again, that goes for anything in the game industry. Making games is NEVER the same as playing them.

I want to like Thief, mostly because the artists here put an incredible amount of love to the art, but the sub-par game design elements, lame story and overall lack of polish means that everytime I launched the game I minimized it at some point and started fooling around on the web completely forgetting the thing was even there, which is a first for me and hopefully the last.
For all of these reasons I can't recommend this game, at least not at full price. It's not the worst, but it's also not good.

I recently finished this game on the hardest difficulty with all side content complete. Here are my thoughts:
-The customizeable difficulty was a really cool idea and I enjoyed shooting for the 700 point challenge. Basically the game lets you pick a base difficulty and then set a ton of modifiers worth varying levels of points. My settings forced a game over if I was seen or touched anyone and I enjoyed having the option to do that.
-The game is completely ghostable and it doesn't rely on abusing AI patterns or using glitches. Careful observation and exploration allow for some really useful alternate approaches similar to Dishonored. I was able to able to ghost (despite what the broken post-mission rating said) every single main mission and every single sidequest in the game on the hardest difficulty so props to the devs for allowing for that.
-The swoop mechanic is a joy to use. It is incredibly handy for crossing those small gaps between the darkness when you can't take out the light or ducking back into a corner after swiping some loot while a guard's back was turned. The animation and sound effect give it this nice agile feel and it's hard not to feel like a pro thief every time you use it.
-I really liked that the best loot was tied to exploration-based puzzles. It was fun picking through documents to find clues for vault codes or searching for ways to disable traps. The sidequests really take advantage of this and some of the later ones feel quite clever.
-Thiefing in general was fun. Pickpocketing has a nice feel to it. It's risky, but not overly hard. Picking locks is simple, but trying to do it before a patrol returns can be quite tense. The animation for cutting paintings out of their frames is superb.
-The full body-awareness is nice. I love all the intricate first-person animation (though a couple get old fast) and seeing your legs is always a plus.
-The devs didn't skimp on content either. The game took me roughly 20 hours to see all the content. The Client side missions are definitely worth checking out as they take place in areas separate from the hub and are pretty involved, taking anywhere from 20 minutes to an hour.
-The AI is consistent and reads pretty well from the player standpoint which I think is the most important aspect of designing AI for stealth games. They aren't terribly clever, but they do feel like a threat.
-The art is solid. The visual variety is a bit lacking, but the style they went for works well with the theme and the character design is pleasant. Dishonored definitely takes the cake here, but Thief isn't without it's merits.
-The non-stealth segments are a bit goofy, but they make up a miniscule percentage of the game. The bridge sequence was actually pretty cool as a visual setpiece and it wasn't as jarring as the previous one had been.
-The third-person platforming stuff could have been used a lot more than it was. There were only 3-4 actual implementations of it and most of them were just there as the only way to reach a new area. I wish they had used this system to add more verticality to levels.
-The blatant streaming-in-the-new-area animations were really annoying. There are 2-3 of them that get used for the whole game and I would honestly have preferred a loadscreen if we have to compensate for ♥♥♥♥♥ier platforms. By the end of the game you never want to pry open another window for the rest of your life.
-The story execution is pretty terrible. The plot is poorly explained and important characters will show up like twice over the course of the 15-20 hour game. When I reached the end I was completely lost on why they even bothered. It's ridiculous and nonsensical.
-The sidequest organization in the city gets really old by the end due to the lack of fast travel. I would probably recommend just letting everything sit till the point of no return and then do it all then because if you do them as they become available you will be crossing the city back and forth twenty or so times. It gets really ♥♥♥♥ing old when you are ghosting the game and are creeping past the same guards for the tenth time.
-The game has a very stitched-together feel and the troubled development is obvious when playing. There are a couple segments that you can tell the guys who were trying to save the game couldn't do anything about short of completely redoing them, which wasn't an option after 5+ years of pre-existing dev time. It's a bummer.
-The pre-order bonus is one of the best missions in the game. It's a really well-fleshed out side mission where you rob a bank that has multiple levels of security. It was really fun and it bothered me that most of the people playing the game down the road probably won't be playing it.
If you hold the first two games sacred, don't bother with this entry. This game is not for you and you will be wasting your time and money. No one is asking for you to do community service and torture yourself with it. If you liked Dishonored a lot though, Thief 2014 might be worth checking out at the 15$ or less price range and you can pretend it's a spin-off from that series, because let's be honest, that is what the game feels like.

On the downside, the game's story leaves a bit to be desired. In addition, completionists will find that, aside from Steam achievements, there isn't much reward for attaining every piece of loot. Also, I found the quick-time events to be more of an annoyance than an appealing game mechanic (although picking locks was admittedly exciting). Overall though, it's a brilliant game.

Fault Milestone Two Side:Above is everything good about the first novel, plus everything that it was lacking.
It is shorter than the Fault 1, only taking a couple hours to read through, but it is also only the first half of this title. There is supposed to be a second part, hence why the ending is rather abrupt.
Keeping in line with Fault 1, the art and music are both beautifully done. With the integration of the new 3d camera system, it really does feel much more immersive. It’s a terrific addition that makes this novel feel much more engaging.
As I’ve mentioned in my Fault 1 review, this story is very focused on the use of mana, as well as social and political injustice.
While Fault 1 revolves around educating the reader on the lore, Fault 2 is able to focus on creating an emotional plot. Through the well written story, you cycle through the calm, relaxing, sweet moments to the intense, action filled, downright eerie bits. Through this emotional rollercoaster, you gain a better understanding of the characters and you are able to relate to them on a much deeper level. Halfway through, I found that I grew very attached to them.
Fault 2 is an enthralling visual novel that successfully pulls you into an intricate science-fantasy world.
If you’re a fan of the genre and don’t mind the lack of fan service, I fully recommend the Fault series.

Fault Milestone two: above picks up right where the last game ended and introduces us to new areas other than the original's Outer Pole. If you haven't played the first game you will very likely be lost straight away and even if this game features an encyclopedia detailing the world it's set in, I would still highly suggest you play the original first, mediocre as it may be. Going into this second entry of the series I honestly had my expectations set rather low since it's no secret I wasn't a fan of the original due to the massive amount of time you spend in flashbacks and being force fed the lore. Luckily now that the characters are introduced and the unique world that houses both science and magic has been explained we now have a much better flowing & coherent story. While in the original it felt like you had done very little other than get new clothes and friends, in this sequel you will go through a surprising amount of situations in this very beautiful aquatic city.
Once again it is more than meets the eye as it may appear like a simple light hearted adventure with three very young looking anime characters it actually touches upon social inequality, corruptions and other subjects you would not expect by just glancing at the game. This sequel does a very good job at hooking you in immediately and features a rather neat trick in the beginning that inadvertently caused me to face-palm when I thought the game crashed. The main villain that looks like someone just got out of a Halloween themed party, shows off her power and the threat she poses is made clear to us so she no longer seems like a joke of a character. Not much else will be shown about the villains as this sequel takes place very far away from Princess Selphine's now conquered castle. The story mostly focuses on Selphine, Rune and Ritona as they gather supplies for their journey back to the castle but things end up going really wrong for them.
They become pretty much stranded in this new land and Selphine really shines. She was your typical happy go lucky cliché type of character but under this new found stress she beats up old people, holds cops hostage and does not take no for an answer. It is no doubt funny seeing such a little girl doing all these things though she will surely hold your attention whenever she is on screen and always has a reason for her rather extreme actions. Back in our protagonist's homeland we will also briefly play as three new characters on a journey to search for the princess. Not much time will be spent with these fellows but from what little we did they seem like decent characters and I am interested in where their journey leads them. This time around there are no choices to be made and you will just be right clicking for the duration of the time. The original had a single “decision” which was completely meaningless so this feature won't be missed though it is something you should be aware of.
Unfortunately one thing that did carry over from the original game is the glitch in where the text cuts off at the bottom if there are multiple lines in the speech box. It's annoying as ever and pretty disappointing that it has not been fixed in their new game. Aside from the main story you will have an audio box to listen to the sound track and a gallery to see the artwork used in this game from the main menu. The artwork for this game is simply amazing and features far more awe inspiring locations. Everything is much improved over its predecessor and it is very much worth its asking price. Which is where the problem comes in, you pretty much need to play the original to understand this sequel and fault milestone one was indeed interesting but very lacking as well as the same price as this. Fans of the original or even those that weren't too keen on it should definitely give this a shot since it does feature a demo while those new to the series should wait for a sale on the original instead of diving straight into this. Fault milestone two: above is an extremely interesting entry to the series and if the quality of the future entries retain this potential then it's well on its way to becoming one of the best Visual Novels ever made.

This game provided me with a lot of good, fun hours.  I played for 57 hours to complete (including the DLCs), 45 of which included actual save-point-to-save-point progress through completion.  I like to explore and feel like I hit every corener though, so the game itself could probably be played through in around 30 hours.
All of the islands have enough unique features to keep the otherwise island-by-island story grind somewhat interesting.  The different player upgrades, character interactions, unlocked islands and so on along the way are all rewarding.  Having one of many companions with you is also a fun feature. The story was interesting and the quest system is handled in a way that kept all of the next (of many) objectives obvious.
From owning a ship, to building a crew, locating legendary treasure, and following a story arch to save the pirate-world from a Titan, this game is a solid pirate game.  I liked that it followed a (very different atmosphere'd) Risen 1's story, continuing with the main character, a few side characters, and the same world; while shifting from a dark warrior's temple quest (Risen 1), to a pirate captain's artifact-hunt story (Risen 2).  Defeating a fire titan in #1 and then a water titan in #2 was a nice touch, which left me looking forward to at least two more titans to defeat in the future.... ?
Cons:
-The world, while nicely broken into smaller chunks, was too big for me, as compared to Risen 1.  I hate feeling like I missed a handful of treasures becuase I failed to climb every ridge, check behind every bush and trace every shore.  I finished the game with a few unfinished legendary weapons, which I couldn't all the pieces for.
-I never really felt like combat reached its potential for me.  I went from hacking at weak monsters while wearing weak gear, to hacking at stronger ones with simply better gear.  The combat stayed hard and a bit frustrating throughout, even though I upgraded my melee combat and gear almost completely.  It wasn't overly difficult, just never made me feel like I had awesome gear and awesome skills.  The moves introduced along the way (aside from power attacks), were too hard to know how or when to use, so felt like a waste of the hard-earned booty to train.
-Load times are nuts!  This is a good game for working on art, or playing a phone game on the side, as dying (which can happen easily if careless) results in a good minute or two load time.  Thankfully each island is seamless, inside and out... perhaps the reason the loads take so long?

Back when I was a bit younger and started playing Video games on my own, I didnt start with games like Morrowind or Gothic, No I actually began with Risen. It was a very special game to me showing me for the first time how you could write an acceptable story into the game and still have a lot of fun in it. Risen was often seen as a Successor to Gothic and today i can for sure see why that is, back than it was one of my favorite games, it was hard, beautiful and still had an interesting gameplay. But enough of the past and lets get on with the Review. So when i heard that Risen 2 came out i wasnt that sure how it would come out, on one hand i heard that it was about pirates and included stuff like vodoo and guns, back then i was really into pirates and there werent that many games in first or third person about being a pirate (and please dont start with assassins creed, it wasnt out then i dont like it that much either) but on the other hand i was a bit conservative and werent that happy about the changes from which i heard of in the Gamemagazine called Gamestar. I bought the game anyway and the first few hours i was really interested. They set up an okay story so i was already happy but then the mess started. I had played Risen 1 a lot of times and i always was quite perficient with magic or another fighting style so i expected the character which i played (they say its the same guy) to at least be able to do stuff but no, he couldnt do anything and the reason why he couldnt remember the magic stuff was apparently because your character became a drunkard... sure. I digress, in any case i wasnt that blown away by the fighting system but i still felt okay, it suddenly changed when i arrived on the first island and i will go on with this review with as less spoilers as possible. So i arrived on the island and after going a bit into the island itself i found many things, a temple, pirates and even wildcats. I didnt have that good equipment when i came to that point but still enough to actually start to like the system, the special weapons like sand were funny and using them was maybe a bit tricky at first but you came to like it. Well, at the point when i was in the pirate town i came across some really weird and downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ things which made me somewhat angry. I discovered that your character wasnt a drunk no he was actually just so stupid that he didnt even know how to kick something, YES YOU HAVE TO ACTUALLY LEARN HOW TO KICK SOMEONE! But hey the story is still good right? Yes but no, the general Story might be okay, it definitely isnt a masterpiece but still good but then they throw in little things that actually straightup annoy you. At one point you enter a library in which you theoretically could find runemagic. When you do your character walks up to it and calls it old useless junk, so basically he calls that stuff which made him depending on the path in risen 1 so amazing junk. Risen 2 Dark Waters isnt a bad game, no it can definitely be fun but it also feels a bit like a teenager. They put some really stupid stuff into it and given that risen 1 wasnt the brightest of lights either i still expect though that the game is smarter than the first one. If there is a sequal i expect it to be better because if it wasnt and it couldnt show that it is really better than the original i dont see why there even is a sequal. Risen 1 wasnt a bad game and Risen 2 isnt but at some points it has just straight up flaws like, why should you use a riffle if you can throw a spear that always comes back? The combat system can become boring very fast and even if it gives many options not that many are actually helpful. The World itself is okay or even good, it is a pretty world with temples and lots of nature. The Skill and Experience system though are really bad and i would wish sometimes they were left out completely.
Pro's: A pretty World, A lot of items/weapons and an acceptable range of fighting options, Pirates, an okay Story
Contra's: Bad to Mediocre Experience System, Can become boring quickly, little sprinkles of really bad writing
Who should buy it?: If you like Western RPG's in General and like the pirate spin-off and maybe want to pick-up a game with an acceptable story and/or maybe want to try out something new you definitely should think of picking it up but rather not at its full price.
Sincerely, Lord Larker the Lurker

Its the game that started me on MMORPGs.
What brought me to it today was the nostalgia from way back in 2006 and what brought me to it back then was an interesting challenge by an friend of mine to "beat the game", in which I found the meaning of this phrase after many many  hours of playing the game means something completely different to what I originally interpreted it for single player games on my handy Playstation 2 console and nintendo handheld devices.
So in the end, my 12 year old self was drawn into awe by the anime/cartoon style graphics, including clothing/armor designs and the cute (so-called) monsters, and (at the time) amazing soundtrack. One of which, the sleepywood soundtrack which led to my first ever avatar, a low level mage, to become traped in the village of sleepywood with no clear way of getting passed the higher level creatures but left to enjoy such a calm and relaxing song while he tried all methods his little 12 year old brain could come up with.
What killed it was the amount of time needed to level up. This forced me to seek out private servers, as I began to notice the time the game was taking from my real life responsibilities. This meaning, while playing for at max 1 hour every day (sometimes every 2 days), I would go sometimes weeks without leveling up or completing certain quests.
This, coupled with the fact that I wasnt getting along with the majority of the community, mostly because the people I seemed to be getting mixed up in seemed to be closed off, isolated, EMOtional and downright rude ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, not to mention my original account was hijacked by someone I once thought was my friend, the young 12 year old boy I was back then didnt need all that drama in his life. However, I*m not going to take this review down that path, people cant control their audiences and I am not in the mood to make a lengthy, detailed and EMOtional review but I will be damned if it dosent atleast contribute to an MMO and the overall game.
Although my strongest traits growing up were my immeasurable amount of patience and persistents, the above two problems were my main reasons leading to my "ending" to the game, although not on a sour note, to seek another game to spend what little spare time I had as an active child. Having returned to the game once again as an adult, I find that I have simply outgrown it and I am unable to enjoy my time here in the Maple world as I did so many years ago.
Regardless, Maple Story will always be remembered as my first ever MMORPG. It and my brave little avatars will always hold a special place in my heart.
===================================TL;DR==============================================
These are based on what I have seen as of 2015/2016 compared to 2006.
Pros
-Cute characters and avatars
-Easy to level up (may appeal to casual players, however... *skip to cons second point*)
-Chill soundtrack
-Good place to get started if new to MMORPGs (This point might be outdated but I still stand by it)
-Game has been out for a while, seen many updates and many guides from veterens.
Cons
-Nexon store (Items may not appeal to all, perhaps I have outgrown the style.)
-Ease of level up may not appeal to all nor may it sit well with old players.
-Does questing matter anymore?
-Jump quests. Just- dont ask.
-Massive list of classes does not appeal to all veteren players.
(Potential Con - mostly unresearched or observed from other players reactions)
-The community in Maple Story has not always been great. There seems to be a bit of a change in the attitude of the community as a new generation of gamers arrive. I havnt really stuck around long enough to analyze it. The stigma of my time in 2006 still lingers.
Some complain about the immaturity of the community, "full of 12 year olds", but what do you expect from a game
appealing to that age group of which most people started playing.
-Some people have complained of the games emphasis on damage nowadays. I thought this was standard since, well, since forever.
Overall
Still a good place as any to start your adventure in the massive open world of MMORPGs. There are other options out there nowadays, however, there is no reason why you shouldnt give this old veteren among MMOs a go.
KEEP IN MIND - If you are a returning player, you may not fall inlove with this old MMO as you did back in the day. People tend to find that they will outgrow the things they once enjoyed as a child or adolescent and this may be one of those things. Come for the nostaligia, see what the Maple World has been up to since you left and adventure again if you fancy, atleast for a little while - in memory of our veteren avatars.

I am curious how this software will look and operate in a year or so. But for now, the little things can stack up and at times those of us with less-than-stellar patience may not find it worth the stress. However, if updates and fixes keep coming this product will be amazing as it grows to meet its potential.
Until then, however, it can occasianally feel like this software works against you rather than with you at every turn. Every click must be a stressful, carefully planned move or you could delete a massive block of TScript in one fell click (no undo button... I KNOW, right?!) But it is at the top of the Suggested Feature list last I checked.
It is really easy to use but can be just as easy to mess-up what you're trying to do. Until more updates are available I suggest the following...
1) Go to
and read all of the tutotial info under "Support" at least three times per lesson. Trust me, you'll need it.
2) Be patient. If you have the money, get the program and have fun messing around. If you don't... wait a bit and wait until some more bug-fixes are up.
3) If you use the program, find its folder in your Steam directory and back up any projects (by copy/pasting their folders elsewhere) as often as possible! You can't "save as" or easily duplicate projects from the program itself. So this will save your hard work from bugs or user error!
An earlier review I posted was a bit tougher on the product. I have toyed around with it another hour or so and re-read the suggested tutorials above and discovered some (but most definitely not all) of my frustration was user error. As you learn to work
TyranBuilder's quirks, you get the hang of its current eccentricities.
The question for you as the would-be buyer is; are you willing to work with said eccentricities or wait until a more...
version of this product is available?

I made my first visual novel - my first game, period - in something like 4 days using this.
I mean, granted, I am a digital artist so I can easily make my own sprites, but nonetheless. I have very little know-how when it comes to things like game development and coding.
Seriously though, like, if you tried Ren'Py but staring at blocks of code made you feel like a troglodyte who can't do basic things, this is the tool for you. It's EXTREMELY simple and intuitive. It's pretty much entirely drag-and-drop, and the only coding I had to do was a line or two for variables. Also it exports to HTML5 in like 2 seconds so anyone can quickly and easily play your games if you throw them on dropbox with zero installation. That is insane!
It feels extremely easy and natural to work with, with very little stopping and struggling to figure out how to do something. It's also a very stable program from what I've experienced, and it apparently offers Android and IOS exporting built in with the base $18 purchase, something other game development suites often charge an arm and a leg for.
My only cons are the following:
The documentation (That I could find) on the custom coding is a bit scant, I had to use a steam guide to clarify how to use variables. But you're probably not going to do much more than a few variables in your game anyway
Things can act a little weird in the HTML5 version vs the software's preview, things take longer to load, timing like putting waits between dialogue can suddenly take twice as long - but it's a pretty small beef, you can just adjust the timing to compensate, and the loading times are understandable
I was a little unsatisfied with the lack of customization for sprite movement and placement - you can't resize a sprite and put it in the background or make it bounce up and down, for instance, but maybe there's a way to do that I haven't found yet
All in all, it is A Very Good Program. If you want to make visual novels, buy the hell out of this. I wish I could go back in time and give this to my 10-year-old self, that's how easy it is to use.

I'm a fan of fun, easy to get into grand strategy games, like Superpower 1 and 2, I have Geo-Political Simulator 2 which sucks due to every tiny fraction revolting every waking minute, and Supreme Ruler games suck because they are a great grand-strategy RTS, with lots of detail, but worst economy and military system ever: every country is magically in super-debt, and you have to super-micro-manage because AI managing your army fails every time, worse than the AI that manages CPU controlled countries (Mexico's puny army easily conquers the USA for example), and even then, the units don't respond to your orders 75% of the time. Worthless software.
Now, we have WAR: THE GAME. I love the fluid feel, the graphics, the simplicity. I agree, the "globe" thing is a gimmick but it's an very nice gimmick. Better than the overly clunky maps in the Supreme Ruler series and even worst Hearts of Iron/Europa Universalis series which are a million times over-rated (seriously, they blow).
WAR: THE GAME, is not a "grand strategy" game like these. It reminds me more of an very old PC game called "COMMAND HQ". Any fellow old school gamer will know what I mean. Or, if you like games simple like DEFCON, this is kind of similar in the simplicity. But you have to be very smart. I though that first it was easy to deceive the AI but then got my butt kicked, so it's simple, but that hides it does require some thought. There is a space-war type game out there, can't rememeber the name, but operates with the same principle: simple, but you have to think it out.
I very much appreciate games like this and developers that try to go as far as they went here.
The graphics are very fluid, runs great, feels smooth, and very comfortable. Nothing to over-convolute the screen and has a somewhat relaxed feel. I would be interested to see what games the developer makes going forward. No crashes, no hiccups, there is a comfortable level of quality and I like to give credit where I think it is do.

I wil reccomend RIsen 2 to all gothic fans, because as one of them I love it.

And here we are at the first part of the second installation of fault. And what a hell of an intro this one has. Picking up where fault milestone one left off, this jumps straight back into the fray with an intro that might leave some of you thinking your computer broke. Do not worry, it didn't. That was just the visual novel being awesome.
This part of fault gives us another tidbit of the story going on behind the current story, reminding us that these people are trying to get back home despite the obvious danger upon arriving. The main story in this part of fault removes Selphine and Ritona for large chunks of time allowing us a little room to breathe and take in what else is happening. Rune to comes into her own a little and Rhegan tags into the fight, allowing us to see what Selphine could be capable of despite her frail appearance. The main cast once again find themselves in an unfamiliar territory where they must once again fix the problems that everyone else seems to have with being reasonable and their war on sensibility. Joking aside this situation seems familiar, doesn't it? No matter, the story is still just as brilliant as last time. This time we see three more characters that the story will be following as they set out to find Selphine and Ritona. They are in this part for a very short time but no doubt we will see them a lot more in the next part.
The characters are fleshed out even more this time around, showing us what Selphine could be capable of, that Ritona is not an impassable guardian and that Rune, despite being girly personality-wise, is still one hell of a machine that can kick your♥♥♥♥♥♥from one end of Rughzenhaide to the other.
Music and artwork-wise, it is just as good as last time. Nothing to add.
In conclusion, if you liked fault milestone one, there is no reason whatsoever you wouldn't like fault milestone two side:above and you will be left waiting, once again, for the next part but this time, you will have a hole in your heart. This story is much more touching than the last.

Note: You should play fault milestone one as this is a direct sequel.
TL;DR:

It’s not all that common for a game to leave me with a lasting feeling for it. A lasting impression almost like being heartbroken due to the impression it left and the feelings it left me with. Fault milestone one didn’t do this to me as much although it was a great game, just a little prolonged for my tastes but I love the story. There are no options in this, it’s a story so expect reading.
IF YOU HAVEN’T PLAYED ONE THEN PROBABLY SHOULDN’T READ PAST HERE BECAUSE SPOILERS.
So two starts where one left off being confronted by one of the badies from the start of the first game and from that point the story continues. The story of two follows the journey of Ritona, Rune and Selphine as they continue their travels. In terms of the story, it’s great and I love it. The characters get some more development and are places outside of everything they are used to and put them into a different frame of mind. Rune, from the world of science (and steampunk?) gets to see the magic world. Unfortunately we don’t get to see a lot of Ritona this chapter and I would really like to know her story but no matter. Most of the interaction in this story is between Rune, Selphine (while in Empress Syndrome you see at the end of the first game) and characters they met in their journey.
As far as the art and story goes it’s great, the sound fits the game although I turned it down a fair bit otherwise it’s just too loud for me. The art is amazing as it was and I really like the CG events in this game a lot.
Personal feelings on this are I just love the story, the pacing was better than it was in the last game and the story was something that if I had the time I could just sit down and play through in one sitting. This really left a heavy feeling in my heart and left a lasting impression emotionally. I love the concepts shown in this world and also the stark difference between the inner and outer poles. I can’t wait for the third game.

Depression Quest is a game that perfectly respects the subject of disempowerment. That crawling feeling on the back of your neck when you realize your vulnerability. Your inability to make the call for help or voice the reasons for the void in your chest. Depression Quest finds the words for all the uncomfortable, persistent nagging thoughts that keep you awake long into the night. It shows the strain of families and relationships as you struggle to maintain your outward appearance for their peace of mind, how saying you're fine is just easier for everyone in the long run. How you figure no one really wants you around already so you best not disturb them with your shameful depression any further. How sometimes, despite your best efforts, you simply lack the ability to reach out or engage with the people you care about even when you desperately want to. How disengaging from social events swiftly becomes a part of a routine that you feel helpless to change.
The game shies away from none of these facts or the tough decisions that lead up to them. It is neither fun nor necessarily reassuring to play. The game offers no swift solution to depression, no easily digestible answer that will absolve this strange self-loathing ritual because the developers understood there are none to be found. It's all of matter of how you choose to handle the road ahead. But it does provide a significant amount of insight into what it's like to suffer from prolonged depression; how easy it is to fall victim to yourself while still encouraging you to seek help and move forward whenever you can.
Honest, powerful and astute (and short enough to finish in one sitting). Whether you need help empathizing the pain of someone you care about or seek a kindred spirit through text, you're like to find yourself a compelling experience in Depression Quest either way.

This game is an amazingly accurate portrayal of depression. As such, it is not a fun game per se. But it can be comforting, seeing that other people go through the exact same things, and it can be informative, for those who may think depression is "just in your head" or something that "you should just get over." I highly recommend it, because it is certainly something worth experiencing, but I suggest that you be in a good state of mind when you play it.

This is a no brainer.  Exactly the kind of game we need sometimes just to relax for a couple of hours. And for that purpose Battle Group 2 is perfect.
We command two ships. One shoots missiles while the other does the support i.e. provides us with abilities in order to eliminate the oncoming projectiles / missiles. There is a cool down for every missile we shoot and each ability we use - this requires some tactics on our end especially towards the end game.
We have some upgrades for the ships and newer, bigger, better warships can be purchased. The currency is oil which we obtain after each and every completed mission. This is a typical game with grinding - we can repeat levels as many times as we want and we can have the best equipment before we begin the endgame.
Do note that Battle Group 2 is the port of a mobile game. It really is a simple game with simple (yet sufficient) graphics and fast-paced, exciting gameplay. For a couple of euros this is an excellent purchase.

I really want to like this game, it has so much potential. I love the different alien barbarian style enemies, the fact that some are virtually impossible to defeat early game while others are pretty simple.
However this game does have its draw backs, many of the functionality with regards to trade routes is pretty lacking. When you discover a trading outpost which is wonderful, it always ends up being right next to where you were about to drop down another city. There are AI issues in regards to alien populations when it comes to the island games, you will find no aliens on many islands and then find an island with 8 squares, all filled with aliens.
The tech tree is really hard to figure out. Whenever you complete one, you build whatever it is you just researched, there can be quests attatched to it. Do you want option A or option B which makes the research far more specialized to your game style. However only two options appear, same ones each time but no indication as to what they are beforehand so it really is an experience thing. You might be looking for a building for increased production but your health is dangerously low, so you research a health building which then gets a quest for energy or food added, however if you had researched a production building, it may have given you a quest for culture or health. Regardless, it can be rather frustrating if you are trying to min-max.
Starting a new game can also be frustrating, needing to watch where every other player lands and then wait for the hello text. Same thing actually progresses through the game with end of turn loading. It is actually the other players and aliens or computer controlled opponents but it still leaves something to be desired when it returns to your turn and you need to still wait, then you are hovering over a unit and given a quest option which then turns out to be a quest option for right next to one of your cities. So you might thing you are removing xenomass from the middle of nowhere on the far side of the map where it does not effect you but in reality, it is two squares away from your capital where it would be really handy.
However dispite all of that, it is still fun to play and kill some time with. However it has the same problem all 4X games have these days and that is the hump. Once you reach a certain number of turns, you tend to be in a position to just power through the rest of the game. You have already won but you need to go through the motions of clearing out the enemies and what not to finish. I tend to just end the game early because when you have an army strong enough to do whatever you want with, the game is pretty much over.

Battle Group 2 can best be described as a naval-themed strategy clicker, on-rails.
Take one or two ships, survive thirty-one naval patrols by destroying enemy planes, ships and missiles while keeping  your kill streak alive.  Gain rewards to upgrade and unlock better ships.  Its simple premise, fast-paced gameplay and short quick-fire sessions are sure to take you back to playing Missile Command back in the day.  The challenge is pretty easy, though gameplay is quite addictive.  Graphics are well-drawn and the music though simple, suits the pace of the game perfectly.
Reservations include not so dynamic enemy spawns and pathing.  It gets grindy towards the end.  There is no endless mode and it could really do with more content with more ships, more weapons, more levels and even more action!
Other than that despite its mobile/tablet origins, it was actually a fun port to play and is sure to be a draw for fans of casual games.
Arcade/Clicker Action-Shooter.
Naval Warfare operations.
Singleplayer with one thirty-one level campaign.
So-called replayable missions but low randomness.  Missions can be replayed if failed.
Guide your ships to the end of the level and blast every enemy seen as your fleet moves horizontally across the screen without player input.  Point and click to shoot weapons or approaching missiles.  Your ships have numerous fixed weapons and anti-fire measures such as: missiles, cannons, helicopters, flares or anti-missile guns.   Maintaining high kill-streaks provide bonus oil barrels and raises your score.  A few Boss encounters are littered through the missions.
The action is in real-time.  Timing is everything.   Better ships can be unlocked with oil barrels earned by shooting enemy aircraft, missiles, installations and ships.  Three power-ups can be purchased to assist you: Hyper-time - slows down time, EMP Blast - clears enemy missiles and Instant Recharge - circumvents the reload time.
There are a limited number of enemies, each with their own particular traits.  Kamikaze gunboats move slowly but zig-zag to avoid your fire.  Frogfoot sub-sonic planes fly slower and shoot projectiles while their Mig-type counterparts fly faster and fire homing rockets.  Forcing players to concentrate on where and when they fire.  Rockets provide a slow moving target but are fired in large numbers.  While helicopters hover and fire multiple times before fleeing off-screen.  Periodically you will see bonus aircraft.  These are harder to destroy but provide a good amount of bonus are help maintain kill-streaks.
Basic but well implemented.  Mostly due to the fact that the A.I. doesnt have to react to anything.  The illusion of a clever enemy is conjoured through the use of varied flight-paths/pathing, increased numbers, speed of movement and spawn frequency.  However its all done very well and you never quite feel in control in the final missions.  Something I imagine is intentional so iOS users spend cash on power-ups.  PC users at least wont need to worry.  (Earn enough to buy power-ups by farming oil, by repeating missions)
Very simple and robust.  Just mouse click on the target to shoot, use ships secondary equipment or activate a power-up.  Its not to hard to see why this was made for iOS.
Pristine, clean-cut and great for this sort of game.  From the detailed artwork of each of the four primary and secondary support ships to the enemy air and seacraft, all of it is pretty to look at.  As are the explosions!  Changes to ships when damaged by enemy fire is neat.  As are the animations when you fail to protect them and they sink.
Very good.  Music changes depending on the mood of the action from soft mellow _ to hard pulsating eletro rock tones when you are up against it!  Simulated battle chatter takes the overall audio experience from being good to just that bit more!
Very good again.  It has an excellently voiced female commander/co-pilot to help you through the first few missions which I thought was actually well-written and voiced.  Thought there isnt enough of it and during my playthrough she isnt used as much in the final third of the game.  Which is a shame.
Difficulty is very low to barely moderate.  The real challenge is slanted towards getting perfect or near perfect scores using high kill-streaks.  Given the speed of the moving craft, their numbers and frequency this becomes near impossible in some missions, especially towards the end.  For mere mortals like me the availability of the power-ups makes life much simple!  Overall the recipe is simple: Choose the right ships.  Have enough upgrades and power-ups and the game ceases to be much of a challenge and devolves into a click-fest!

I've been playing this game on and off for six years and I just spent real money for the first time yesterday. Maplestory is one of the few f2p's that are not pay to win. The most that real money will get you are temporary buffs to lessen the grind, better character aesthetics, and other things that in the end don't necessarily make it easier to reach level 250. Reaching level 250 is an incredibly daunting task and is something I've never actually seen happen (although to be fair I play exclusively on quiet channels of an unpopulated world). Unless you choose a character with a long backstory you'll either run out of things to do midway through or you'll hit a wall as the distance between levels prevents you from continuing their storyline. This is where the grind comes in. Eventually, leveling up becomes an arduous process that can take hours to do a single time. While the grind has prevented me from ever even getting just to 150, there are enough characters with enough backstories to ensure that whenever you feel bored, you can switch it up by creating a new character. If you have friends you can play with, this game becomes exponentially more fun, but if you don't, I'm sure you'll enjoy it anyway. At the very least give it a shot. You have nothing to lose except hundreds of hours of your life.

You will love this game. You will love it enough to completely loathe it. Here's why.
I've been playing Arche Blade for a few hours now, and when I first picked it up and started playing the tutorial and training mode, I was absolutely immersed in the action combat system. It's something that will remind you both of Dark Souls and Smite.
The problem is that it's also got some elements of an early 2000's first person shooter- that is, the games modes are centered on deathmatches and point control, which, don't get me wrong, is incredibly fun. But only for so long.  I find myself thinking that this game would be a fantastic action game for the next generation of F2P multiplayer battle games. If you've heard of Gigantic (an upcoming action game by Motiga), it'll feel something like that. If you haven't heard of it, definitely look it up.
The game also uses an old school server list system instead of the now integral "Play Now" button you find in most mobas and team fighting games today. This isn't necessarily an issue, but it lends itself to the problems that result from server lists. This would include having too many players, not enough players, not being matched with players by ELO and instead just hoping you get a good match, etc.
The characters are balanced enough to play the game, but you'll definitely run into some games that you're raving about how OP the healer character can be. (Wtf!?).
You can also play the same character as other people on your team- something you can't do in MOBAs for this exact reason: your team comp will either become completely OP, or complete trash. You can modify your server to remove this feature, but most servers don't do so.
Oh, and I forgot just one thing. There are instances in the game where a skilled player can fire off a combo to knock you up (which prevents you from doing anything to attack or defend yourself) and repeatedly *keep* knocking you up without ever getting a chance to save yourself. It's extremely annoying and unfair.
This could easily be an MLG E-Sport to contend with the next generation of team based fighters. But the devs have basically left it as it is and refused to update it for months at a time. That's why I can't recommend this game.

Creating a finished visual novel is easy, yet the program supports complex scripting for features like variables.
With the software as is, you will be able to create choose your own adventure style programs that you can give away or sell.
With variables and advanced scripting you can:
The scripting offers a deep list of possibilities for advanced users or users who don't mind learning a simple scripting language.
The forums offer quick responses normally and even has a community manager who is right on top of things.
All the cons can be addressed in upcoming updates easily, so hoping they consider the following:
Debugging system.  Currently if you exit a character without having it in the scene the game will just freeze and not go on.  If you have complex scene jumps you can easily miss something like this and I would love to see the program have a debugging option for simple issues like this.
Export Directly to Android.  Currently you have to use about 3 different programs to get an Android APK where you can export to web or Windows in 1 click.  This leads to so many issues and potential for unsupported features not to mention it is a difficult process even if you don't have any problems (such as music not playing, etc).  If you do, then you have to back track and decide which of the many steps and multiple programs has the issue.
Plugins.  Would be nice to have the ability to support community driven plug ins so battle systems, inventory etc could be looked at possibilities.
Indents or custom coloring.  I would like to be able to indent like an ordered list style layout or change colors to color code different areas (currently sections have a 'Label' header but the color is the same as other functions).
I would easily suggest this software, especially at this price point, as it is a great program for creating simple to mid-level games.
Finally the tool I've been looking for. Easy to use, stable, and versatile, this is an amazing tool for all your visual novel and kinetic novel creation needs.

I'm going to summarize the two main disadvantages to this game (note that these only apply to single player, and I have no knowledge of multiplayer at all):
1. The map is terrible.
In this game, each dungeon can last literally hours. That may not be too terrible in itself, except it takes even longer because the map screen does not allow you to see the whole dungeon that you've explored at once. The map only shows the areas nearby which you have already seen, and thus is severely limited in its usefulness. This can make exploring the full dungeon a nightmare. It can become a chore trying to find where to go next, sending you running in circles, simply because your map has practically no range beyond you.
2. The saving system and game over system are completely horrendous pieces of garbage.
You can have several save files, only one per character you start. The game works like this: you have several lives for your character, and if you lose them all, you completely game over and have to revert to your last save or revert to the very beginning of the game. That is complete rubbish. The saving works in that you have one save per character, as said before. You can't revert to old saves of that character. Any time you step on a checkpoint or go to another floor, your game is automatically saved. This hurts you, as if you find you have only one life left and critical health, this game becomes a joke between running to enemies and back to a save point, hoping to God you don't get hit even once. In my personal experience, I went into the first dungeon's boss room during single player. As a reminder, whenever you travel to another floor of a dungeon, your game automatically saves. However, this time, without any warning, the door in which I entered became locked, meaning that I was literally save-locked into the boss room. In a GOOD game, if you found the boss to be too advanced for you, you'd be given the opportunity to backtrack and get more upgrades so that you stand a chance against the boss later. However, in THIS game, since I die in literally two hits to the boss and I can't do anything about it, I have to restart an entire 2+ hours of gameplay, making sure I clear out even more of the dungeon than I did the first time. I'm sorry, game developers, but would it really kill you to take it more like a Legend of Zelda game? In LoZ, if you game over, you get sent back to the beginning of the CURRENT dungeon and all of the enemies are respawned, but you don't lose any upgrades, items, or progress throughout the dungeon. This is still a punishment for losing, but it doesn't make you redo literally hours of gameplay. Even the original Legend of Zelda on the now-archaic NES had this methodology, as Nintendo knew their audience wouldn't want to restart every detail of a long and difficult dungeon. You crazy guys instead, for the far worse, force someone to restart literally the whole game over in the case where they get save-locked into a fight they can't win. This is the kind of design people joke about from the NES era, and it seems you did not pick that hint up. Game-overing someone to the title screen is a joke. Stop using it. It's an easy way to kill a game.
Oh yeah, and remember that I haven't even tried multiplayer yet, and I've heard some terrible things about multiplayer. Since I have no experience of it, though, I'll give it the benefit of the doubt (or at least exclude it from this review).
It's a huge disappointment, as this game actually would be tremendous amounts of fun otherwise. The characters are unique, the fighting style is linear and remarkable, and the dungeons can hold many great secrets. I swear that if you simply made a better map to allow someone to see more of the dungeon at once, a better save system to allow people to revert to older saves on a character, and a better game over system that doesn't literally force you to do the entire game over again, this could easily become several times more enjoyable and popular.
Those things above shouldn't even take that much work to fix. If done with actual care, a developer wouldn't even have to edit any campaign levels.
Until the above are fixed for better enjoyability, I highly recommend that you, reader, STAY AWAY from this game. You'll find yourself addicted for a few good hours, then curse its name for such a crappy game over and save system. This game is not too old yet, so maybe the developers will take some heart and at least try to salvage it.
In short:
This game has tremendous potential, but it is horribly ruined by a bad saving and game over system, along with a map that doesn't help you get un-lost. Generally avoid unless you don't mind replaying literally hours over.

There's a bit of a learning curve to this game, but if you are able to stick with it you'll find a real gem here.
First of all, as many others have pointed out it is very similar to the core concept behind Gauntlet. At it's core, it follows the same 'find all of the keys to get to the exit' formula, but this gameplay is augmented by player progression, special abilities, backtracking, and boss fights. It's colorful, lots of great effects, and has a generally high production value.
I'd also like to express a few issues I have with the game, but at the same time point out that these should not necessarily deter you from buying/playing the game, just give you a better idea of what to expect.
First, there's no steamcloud support. To me this is a basic feature if you're going to put a game on steam.. it'd be forgivable if it were a roguelike with no persistence, but this is a long-play game. Anytime a game doesn't support steamcloud I have to copy the save to my dropbox before I go to work.
The decision to make the paladin the 'default' character for players who just start the game without changing options is questionable. The paladin takes a fair bit of skill and nuance to play effectively- not to mention that just about any other game that has a paladin gives that class some sort of healing ability. This paladin has a charge/dash. It's a great skill, but just not what people are going to expect when diving into the game for the first time. Your average player is going to start the game, get swarmed and die repeatedly. Personally I think the wizard probably would have made a better default character.
There is virtually NO onboarding in this game whatsoever. The closest you get to a 'tutorial' are these little 'hint boxes' that you have to attack, but if you happen to take a warp or staircase past the first floor (not as hard as it sounds) you'll never see them. An actual onboarding level or optional tutorial would go a long way to making the game more digestible for the average gamer. After my first 30 minutes of playing this game I nearly wrote an angry email to the friend who recommended I buy it, but I persevered and found the diamond in the rough.
The soundtrack is nice, but personally it doesn't gel with the art style. I feel like a retro chiptune style soundtrack would have fit better, but that's just my opinion. What's in the game is good, it's not distracting, so in the end it is what it is. I just feel like it's an area where they could have given the game a bit more personality.
A lot of the encounters aren't really balanced for single player. It's clear to me that they are pushing for coop multiplayer for this game, but a bit more thought could have been given to making sure the singleplayer experience didn't suffer. It's not bad, mind you- I have a singleplayer game going right now and as an example- I was able to full-clear the first 3 floors without dying once, but during the first boss battle I died 9 times. It's not so much that the fight is hard, it's just that they spawn you right in the middle of an area where you're going to take damage immediately (and a low armor class is going to die quickly). So that's just an example, but you'll see little hints of it throughout the game. Not a huge deal, still very enjoyable as a single player game.
So, TLDR version: It's fun, great, awesome. Hard, steep learning curve. Stick with it and you'll love it.

War, the Game is a deceivingly simple game at first, but as you progress you will be surprised by the circumstances and how the mechanics interact with one another and will have to carefully plan your actions in order to meet the mission objectives. Each nation that you controls has units, which can range from infantry and tanks to nuclear missiles and aircraft carriers, and production facilities that can be used to create them. You can choose what and when to build, based on the money the cities you control are generating, and on moving your forces across the map in order to engage the enemy, defeat him and then capture his urban centers. The actual battles do not require any sort of input and they are only based on the power of the units that are taking part, with both infantry and tanks contributing one level each when at full strength and with air units offering the same strength but with some special rules attached.
The systems in the game mean that small initial advantages in unit power lead to a win in the long term and most of the strategy needed to win in War, the Game is linked to knowing when and how to commit forces in order to win, even by the smallest of margins, while crippling the enemy army. The initial scenarios seem simple, but the game quickly ramps up the difficulty level and it takes a lot of tries and restarts in order to complete the later mission objectives. The best way I have found to create a solid path towards victory is to find the nearest enemy divisions and focus as many of my forces on them in a coordinated attack. The trick is to keep your own units together as much as possible, while making sure that the enemy is scattered and unable to mount a powerful counteroffensive.
What makes the entire experience more difficult than it should be is the fact that the entire game moves a little too fast and sometimes the AI, with its unlimited attention, simply makes moves that you cannot respond to in time. The game does a good job of teaching you, via a virtual assistant, how to play the game and it’s always easy for you to understand what you need to do in order to succeed.
War, the Game is a lesson on how to do more with less as the development team uses what is clearly limited resources to create a graphics engine that delivers a fluid game, interesting details and an art style that enhances the gameplay experience. Units and terrain are all abstracted and the look of the title borrows a lot from the military video feeds that show battlefields and combatants, although on a much larger scale. The user interface is easy to read and offers all the info that you need and the choice to allow you to zoom in and out at any moment manages to convey the scale of each operation, while the representation of Earth offers a sense of time. War, the Game shows that indie developers do not need to try to compete with big companies in the graphics department and only have to come up with an interesting design choice in order to capture your attention with a simple, clean, efficient look. The sound design is less impressive, but it does mesh well with the rest of the experience.
The developers at Gabber Games have created an interesting game overall, with some very cool ideas, but the game might be too niche and abstracted to appeal to gamers who are used to a view of war that’s more about spectacle than about decisions and consequences. War, the Game is a title that all strategy lovers should try out at least once in order to see how smaller teams can innovate by taking the classic concepts of the genre and turning them into something new.

This game has quickly risen to one of my all-time favorite video games. I ended up clocking in 12 hours in one weekend once I started the game. The atmosphere is intence and affects you almost immediately; you feel the weight and depression that comes with the war atmosphere. The gameplay is simple and stream-lined. Overall, the game is genuinely addicting and fun to play.
The main downside is that there is a bit of a learning curve with the game. The first couple of playthroughs were incredibly difficult and I could not figure out get through 15 nights, let alon the whole war! But after some trial-and-error and help from the internet, I was able to figure out how to play, the best strategy, etc. Pro tip: If you are having trouble with the set storymodes, just create your own story/game mode with the survivors you think are best, adjust the war settings, etc. That was the best way to get over the learning curve and become comfortable with the gameplay. After that, I felt like I could handle any of the other story modes.
Finally, the story and background is interesting, but I wish there was more! You never get a full story about the war, why it started, or in-depth details about the world outside. Any information you get is through short clips from the radio, clues found across the locations, and some comments from the survivors themselves. Honestly, this just adds to the experience! It drives home the point that war is just universally pointless and awful; it does not really matter how the war started or who is in the "right" because it is innocent people who suffer. I do wish there was more meat behind the characters: The diary entries are nice, but a lot of the characters just come off bland and forgettable. I would love if there were more diary entries that shared individual character experiences and thoughts so that they were more fleshed out. But that is just a nit-picky issue for a game that is really great.
Ultimately, this game is wonderful experience that makes you want to put so many hours into it without realizing it. I recommend it to anyone who is looking for a unique, emotional game that is sure to affect you on so many levels.
A wonderfull blend of hardcore survival, emotional gameplay and beautiful art styles. It's not something you can play for hours on end, but it's definitely worth a try.

You owe it to yourself to try it out. This is arena deathmatch done really really well.
The gameplay is fast paced, fair and pretty well balanced. Skill is the determining factor in this game. Everyone has access to all the abilities and perks (called battlerites in this game) from the get go. Learning your chosen character is key to success. You will need to be able to switch up your playstyle to suit your opponents.
Matchmaking takes very little time thanks to the high player base and short match times. Playing with random partners isn't that bad, and on the of chance you get paired with someone truly useless, you'll likely be out of there in 4-6 minutes.
This game does have loot boxes, which i don't like, but it is all cosmetic for the most part (other than a chance at champion unlocks) and this is a free to play game. I'm on the fence about loot boxes, but that's just me.
This game is very well made, not predatory with its monetisation. In game currency is earned at a decent pace. Unlocking one mid priced champion per week isn't that difficult or time consuming, and seems fair. There's two other price brackets for champions, 950 and 4250 (or so).
Overall it's worth checking out. It doesn't give objective advantages to existing players and has a decent range of ease of use characters.

On the black tide I washed ashore on these uncharted rocks. I wonder now if I had drowned and awoken in Sheol, for find myself among only devils of the abyss. In the night, I hear their drums, the arrhythmic pounding when they sacrifice to their cruel gods. I dare not venture inland. I make camp on the desolate sands, for the jungle is awash with rot. Miasmic and pulsating, it calls to me, but I will not follow. It is a festering wound. It stinks of corruption.
There are no ships on the horizon. No sails to be seen. I hunt crabs on the beach, without much success. The thirst is maddening. I crack fallen coconuts against the rocks, sucking them dry like marrow from bone. Soft flesh or putrid milk, I gag and choke it down.
I collect the shell fragments. I use them for jewelry, fashioning necklaces and armbands. I decorate my camp. I bring civilization to a place of savagery. I piled rocks by the firepit and called it a throne—for having carved out an existence here, am I not queen of this forsaken shore?
The natives grow restless. Savage shades who harbour only murder in their hearts. They know I am here. They are hunting. They are coming. From a smashed coconut I dab war paint on my face. Run my fingers down my axe, squeezing the handle. These are my rocks. These are my palms. They are coming. They are coming.
I am the coconut queen.
