There is so much hate out there for this game and i dont think that it deservese that. So i decided to make an own review and try to stay as objective as i can.
So is Beyond Earth (BE) as bad as most of the Reviews here are trying to tell you? No!
Is it a good startegy game? Sure!
Is it as good or as deep as Civ V+Expensions? Hell, no!
Should you buy it? Well...
That depends on two very big and very improtant"If"s:
First of all and most important:
With the expansions, Civ V offers a way deeper and more diversified experience. If you are not into the SiFi-Setting and like the imagination of a few refugees trying to colonize a new alien planet, there is no reason to buy this game instead of Civ V. There are just so many Gameplay elements missing like Cultures, buildings and units you actualy know, Religions, Unique Units and buildings for every Civ. and so on. While at the other hand there are only a few new elements like:
All of those quests are only written down - there are no videos or even pictures throughout the whole game, which is not only my biggest point of criticism but also the second If:
(at least in German language version)
In Civ-Games, you know exactly what you are doing, when you order f.e. the Pyramids, a Knight, or a City Wall, or research the Wheel. You know these things from your live, documantaries or from history education in school. In BE we are in a SiFi-Setting with tons of buildings, tech, units, resourses and so on you don't know. They have strange names and minimalistic Icons, that tell you absolutly nothing about how they look like, or even what they do at all. Even if you have completet a wonder, you get nothing but a lousy blueprint of that building. Yes that's right no video like in Civ IV or Civ II not even a freaking picture of how this would look like - just a STUPID BLUEPRINT! When you build the Great Wall in Civ 5, you know how it looks like from thousands of pictures and videos - you even might have visited it already in reallife. Whilst in BE you have NO IDEA what youre spending your production on, when  you build the "Tectonic Anvil", or the "Stellar Codex".
This game would have desperatly needed videos, that show you your wonders in action, or at least big 3D-Models of all your Buildings and Wonders (like in Civ 2) in your city screen or at least some FREAKING PICTURES. But there is nothing of that. So you have 2 options: You either say: "♥♥♥♥ it" and just build strange icons with strange names only for their stats, then you're not goint to enjoy this game at all - as you just cant identify yourself one bit with your Colonies. This is why many people descripe this game as "soulless" even if the developers actualy put a lot of effort into the lore of their universe. The problem is, that the only way to "find" the soul of this game, is through the descriptions.
So what I recomment you to do is to read the description of EVERY SINGLE unit, every building, every wonder just everything. This is the only way to get an Idea of the lore and the universe you're in and the only way to get attached to the game. So while this is already a lot to ask from the modern gamer, who is used to have at least 5 hours of cutszence in their CoD Story Campaign. it's getting even worse:
All the descriptions are written from a retroperspective point of view: All, or at least most of your actions through the game have already happened. It's just written like the events in BE were based on our actual history (just like the other Civ games) and we are some colonists from the year 2400 or sth like that who are replaying their own past. While this might be a cool idea they just took it over the top by putting an overhelming number of scientific special words in their descriptions. It might be conceivable, that those words might be part of general knowledge in 300 years, but for today, you almost need a universty degree in Medicne, Biolgy, and Physics to 100% understand, what they are writing in those texts. Of course u can also get the point of the descriptions without understanding every single word, but if you're not used to a certain pretty high level of scientific parlance, you're going to have struggles to understand those descriptions, even if you are already willing to read them.
The decissions of how they try to immerse the player into their game are so poorly made, that i wish the responisble designer to get eaten by angry Xenos!
But if you think, that you are fulfilling both "Ifs", and are that type of player, that likes to create the biggest part of the story in his imagination and through the gameplay, just like it is needed in games like Skyrim, other Civ games or Total War games, you are going to have a lot of fun with this game. At the moment i enjoy BE more than Civ 5 just because of the Setting and the way the actualy pretty well written and described universe fuels the biggest graphics engine that exists: My imagination.
But if you're not a fan of the SiFi-Setting or are not that guy/girl that likes to read him/herself trough tons of text just to get a better immersion, there is no way to recommend this game over Civ V. Mabey you can check it out when it is at 10 Bucks on a Steam Sale.

Such a massively disappointing Civ game that I'm having trouble even beginning to describe it.  It took 18 months in my library before I even finished my first game, just because I felt I somehow owed it to a franchise I've been playing since I was 8.  I wish I hadn't.
The goal was obviously to take the game in new directions, abandoning things such as linear tech trees, unpredictable AI, and unit obsolescece.  Credit where credit's due, those have been major complaints of the community for several iterations and they are no longer part of the game.
However, what they were replaced with seem shallow and unintuitive.  Unit customization is just a shade of what was present in Alpha Centauri (a game which inevitably became the comparison for CIV BE), offering only two options that at times seem equally unimportant.  The tech web was a difficult to navigate and harder to comprehend mess.  The AI opinions were slim, and you can easily spend the whole game without ever drawing any opponent into meaningful conflict no matter how abusive you became towards them.
Not to mention minor quibbles, like the color pallette being evocative of an oil stain on an asphalt driveway.  Or the incredibly anticlimatic "Wait timer" for victories.  Or the shifting and sometimes senseless Affinity system. Or the ... you get the idea.

A lot of the feelings fit close to home. I struggle with depression, and seeing so many of my thoughts ("I'm just sad and pathetically dealing with being an adult", "everyone else can do this but I can't because I'm a big baby", "people would be better off without me") and my own feelings -- the feelings of static, of being this creature that can't interact with people and just floats through the world untouched and untouching, even the excuses for why I wouldn't go to work -- was a relief. I'm glad the developer put it on Steam today. I'm so very glad. I won't say this is the reason I'm making my therapy appointment later this week, but I've had a hard time making the effort to schedule appointments often enough and this game reminds me why I'm trying.
I don't want depression to win. I want to fight. I'm lucky that I'm at a point in my life where I have enough energy to keep going (even though it's exhausting) and I feel hope that things will get better. Just playing a game reminded me of how much I want to get better.
Also, for real, 10/10 if only for having cats thrown into your life randomly because I've also experienced unexpected cat ownership during one of my low points and having a soft fuzzy thing to look after makes life a little easier.

As a person who has suffered from depression in real life, and come out of it, I knew exactly what to do. This game, is a brilliant glimpse into what life for a person suffering from depression is like. I highly recommend it, but also recommend that you do it with a neutral mind, that is -- try to pick options that you would realistically do, given the circumstances. (E.g: Don't take meds if you wouldn't in real life).
A bit of a spoiler below, but you can win the game:
"You've done it. You've won. You've never really thought of yourself as a "fighter" and even to say it now it sounds hokey, but looking back on the past few months to where you are now it really does feel like you've endured an immense struggle, and you look at where you are now with a sense of somethin that isn't quite pride.
With all that seems to have improved recently, it's sometimes difficult for you to think about the fact that you still have bad days - sometimes even really bad days. They serve as a stark reminder of the fact that this will be something you likely have to deal with for the rest of your life. Depression is a battle, and though you're certainly ahead in the fight, you know the battle isn't ever going to be over. Sometimes even Alex can tell when things are going rough, despite your efforts to the contrary.
While you know that your depression can never be "cured", you have a very strong support network in your friends and even Malcom, and armed with a newfound confidence in your friends and family, you accept that though the road may be rocky, it is at very least not solitary.
You meet your mom's gaze from across the table and muster up a smile.
"I'm good Mom. It's all going to be all right." You tell her.
She says nothing, but you can feel her smile from across the room.
You smile back.

Nowhere near as good as the originals, but I won't go so far as to call it not a "true" Thief game. It's Thief alright, just not a very good one. The levels are too small and too linear, the guards are too aggressive (if you're on your 127th straight night as a guard in Lord Inbred XIV's mansion, you're not going to be jumping at shadows and raising the alarm every time you hear a rat), and the City's lost most of its charm, as has Garrett.
Play it if you absolutely need a stealth game with all the shine of modern graphics, but if you want a true quality gameplay experience, pick up Thief II. This new effort did a few things right that I wouldn't mind seeing again, but the developers need to go back and look at what made the old games great. And dramatic fiery action sequences weren't on the list.
The much-hyped Bank Heist addon was designed to be an homage to the bank level in Thief II, which apparently the developers thought meant "a bank level with steampunk security cameras." The attempted homage basically comes across as more of an insult, with the bank being painfully tiny and linear compared to the sprawling, three-story building from the original, with a suffocatingly increased guard density, nonsensical arrow traps, and security cameras that are somehow candle-powered and can easily be disabled, robbing any challenge they posed.
Let's hope if they squeeze a sequel out of this, they don't include an "homage" to the warehouse level which consists of one rental box, three offices, and twenty paranoid soldiers to look after it.

Well, here we are. 16 years after the original Thief and 10 years after the last game. Just to create some quick context, I played it when it originally came out and Thief 2 is one of my favorite games of all time. I was dissapointed with Deadly Shadows, but I still played it through...twice. I've played every fan mission for The Dark Mod, some several times. I like Thief. I like the atmosphere, the world, the characters, the history. I am a Thief fan. There, now I have my pedigree out of the way and I can feel all superior about myself (sarcasm).
So, that said, I was worried about Thief 4 when it was announced. Looking Glass Studios (rest in peace you magnificent creation) was gone. There were rumblings of some of the same people from the glory days working on the current Thief project. Trepidatious anticipation. Cautious optimism. Then, tragedy! Garrett was going to be replaced, possibly by a teenage smart-talking goth chick. I have no problem with advancing the concept of new characters and new ideas in this hallowed game, but come on...know your source material and more importantly, and much more sacred, know your audience. Who were they making this game for if not the fan? Your average gamer is going to find something like Thief boring. There is no instant gratification. That comes from careful exploration, patience and cunning. Thief games have a very deliberate and esoteric design.
Then, silence. Thief 4 was in development, it was not in development, there were hints, there were rumours, Ubisoft was in turmoil over the project. I almost gave up hope of seeing another Thief game. Then, BANG! It is re-announced as though Thief 4 had never been mentioned. A reboot? Garrett returns? Sort of, not the same voice actor but the character was back. But now Garrett was goth? Whaaaat? Trepidation, cautious optimism, confusion.
Now it is finally here. Garrett is no longer goth (sort of). I pre-purchased the master thief edition the second it twas available. Even if it was going to be a disaster, I was going to be part of it. The wait was excutiating but it was finally almost over. When it came, it was met with a broad range of confused responses. Long time die hard fans mostly hated it. Newcomers didn't know what to make of it. People in between panned it as not Thief-like enough for fans and not accessible enough for newcomers. So, what was the truth?
This is only my opinion. I am no expert on game design or entertainment. I won't try to inflate my importance by stating that I have been playing video games since the days of wood-panneled pong machines or that I owned my own computer game store in the glory days of pc gaming. I won't say those things...er...anyway, but I do have a strong sense of what works and what doesn't in a modern video game. So, without rambling on too much longer...here it is:
What Thief does right:
Atmosphere. Hells ya. It nails that. I don't necessarily mean that its an exact replica of the worlds we know. Did we really want that anyway? Its been done. But, it had to adhere to certain forms and it does that admirably. The twisting streets of the city, the swirling fog lit by cold lamplight or the warm glow of a torch. Complaining guards muttering as they make their patrols. Moonlight straining through thick clouds to cast a murky gloom over a twilight maze of cobbled stone. Brilliant. The interiors, the locales, the themes of desperation and loss all intertwine to create an interesting (if somewhat generic) steampunk victorian goolash.
Stealth. Pretty good. Not great, but certainly as good as it was in any of the previous games. If it fails at all its in the "feeling" of your movements. Garrett should feel like an accomplished thief, like he is gliding in and out of the shadows or better, becoming one himself. There are times the game achieves this and there are times that it does not. When it works, its awesome. The same thrill exists now as it ever did sneaking through a level totally unnoticed. Ghost indeed. Also, it is tremendously satisfying to clobber a guard who just happened to look the wrong way. These moments of opporunity create neat little vignettes that, while they do get repetative, are still always satisfying.
Exploration. Also pretty good. Also not great. I love finding little hidden areas, little venues that have some personality. But therein are the beginnings of the cracks. Things start to feel awful samey after a while. You can only find so many silver flasks or gold cups before it gets boring to take things. You don't really get the sense that you are stealing anything because there is never anyone around who will miss it. If things are just laying around is it really stealing? I mean, you can pickpocket people which is a mild rush but, anyway, this was supposed to be the "good stuff" so I won't complain here.
What thief gets wrong:
Story. Okay, so this has been discussed to death on the internet. The story is kind of weak. A bit of a mess. This is going to sound sacriligious to hard core Thief fans but...I argue the story of Thief has never been that strong. Now, put down the torches and pitchforks and hear me out. The first Thief, lets be honest, had no real story at all. It was just a series of disconnected missions with a few threads winding throughout. The game as brilliant largely because nothing like it had ever been done. It wasn't a masterpiece because of its story. Thief 2 had a much stronger narrative, but having recently played it again I argue that it too was largely an excuse for different levels moreso than it was for a cohesive narrative. What it did better than Thief TDP was to have a theme and strong characterizations. It is legend in my mind. I barely remember the story for Thief DS and I played it twice. So, yes, the story isn't much to get excited about but its an excuse to move through the game.
A.I. Wow. For a game that is 16 years after its original I was expecting a bit more. Yes, guards notice you and pursue you and eventually give up looking for you. Guess what? They did that 16 years ago. Can't we have guards that run to a constabulary to alert them? To go bring two or three more guards? To cordone off the streets? To tell the public to go indoors until they've found the menace? How about guards that question witnesses who might even have an idea which way you went or where you might be hiding now? Imagine the panic as a citizen points right at the cubby hole you're crouched in, panting like a mad fool, and tells the guards he/she last saw you skulking around that area. How much more immersive and interesting would that have been? Lots. Is this sort of thing possible of A.I. in a game in 2014? Of course it is, and I am not even being that imaginative. Regardless, the A.I. is there for you to bonk on the head. Nothing more. They do not organize manhunts. They do not remember where you've been for more than a few seconds and they don't communicate with anyone about their situation. Also, just throwing this out there...but Garrett could use a sword. It didn't overpower him, it wasn't wise to do because it was loud and even having it drawn made you too visible. It was a last resort. What do developers have against him using a sword? But I digress.
Conclusion:
So, what are my final thoughts? I am enjoying the game despite myself. Maybe I feel sorry for it because of all the bad press or maybe the torrent of hate against it has lowered my expectations. Yes, the long game starts to feel a little pale. It loses its luster after a while and moving around the city is a boring chore. Still, I can't help but enjoy every last little escape or every cunning theft from under a guard's nose. When it works, it works. You just have to give it room. Also, what's this about the music being wrong? Does anyone remember the first game? I think they nailed that with thrumming drums and chimes. Like the rest, it is evocative if a little flawed. Recommended.

At first glance, this game felt like it was pulled from the AI for War Games but upon further inspection I found a much deeper dynamic World Domination RTS.
Gameplay: 7/10
It's a very heavy yet simple unit en masse selection reminding me of Base Defense maps from StarCraft: Brood War. There are a few modifiers here and there, like the ability of only infantry to capture bases and the instant range of aircraft. The slight history infusion with almost every battle and the encouragement almost to always play both sides is a great plus as well. And for those that like to fight real people instead of robots, there are a slew of multiplayer battles available.
Graphics: 8/10
Really digging the artstyle, calling back to the retro 80's but still keeping it smooth. There's a lot of green and a lot of glowing things. I think everyone likes green glowing things. Still, I wish there was a little more to choose from, maybe some filter pack updates in the future would be awesome -- or even DLC.
Sound: 8/10
The narration in this game uses a pregenerated voice but the amount of dialogue is amazingly helpful. The music and sound effects fit the environment perfectly but are also something else they might be able to extend via updates or DLC.
And if you're one to dislike the AI voice there is an option in the menus to disable it. :]
Overall: 8/10

War, the Game (WtG). It's an RTS about war on a global scale. Strategy games are probably my weak point when it comes to gaming, I put this down to increasing complexity and a decrease in my abilily to focus. Fortuantely, WtG offers short missions that you can replay over until you beat them, (or not in some cases). The simplificaiton of units to 1:1 hardness ratio gives you a good idea of whether you're going to get kicked hard, or, preferably the other way round.
So far, so straight forward, except it isn't like any other RTS I've played, you rotate the globe using the mouse, zoom in and out with the wheel, It's a smooth flow from say CoH, or (cough) dune 2. The consistancy in motion and the ability to skip forward a day/week make for a fast action strategy game. The whole interface makes targeting units a joy. That is once you've got your head round the basics control-wise, because there really are only a handful of controls, and that is all that is needed.
Finally, what really made this game stand out, was the atmosphere created by the glitched up view of the planet, coupled with the glitchy tutorial AI and the almost glitch-hop soundtrack, which went down very well with my ears.
What I didn't like about the game (and this is probably my own ineptitude) was the lack of direction after the initial 3 battles. It felt like there should have been an order in which to do them, but I failed to see it, and pretty much failed every mission afterwards, until the AI started to hand out advice seemingly randomly.
After giving the single player missions a good go, I decided not to get my back side fedex'd to me on a platter in the multilplayer.
Do I recommend? I reckon this game is good fun, not too frustrating, and lovely to look at. So I'll be going back to it.

Before actually playing this game I didn’t quite know what to expect. Other players likened it to Risk and while that certainly gives you a rough idea of what it’s about, it isn’t a perfect analogy. Unlike Risk, for example, “War, the Game” features a more developed economic aspect that you will have to pay attention to.
Generally speaking, the player with the larger income will win, assuming that their armies are about the same size and the terrain is negligible. However, that doesn’t mean that tactics and strategies play no role. To win it certainly is necessary to pay attention to enemy troop movements and the composition of their troops.
Relatively few things bothered me while playing “War, the Game” but one of the things that did were nukes. Equal in cost to about six infantry or five armor batallions, you’d expect more of a nuke than to only wipe out infantry, leaving naval and armored units completely undamaged.
Very bewildering is also that you cannot seem to move armored batallions across oceans with your transport ships. In other words, if you or your enemy sit on an island (e.g. Great Britain), you’ll have a hard time trying to conquer them. Even air support helps only minimally in those situations because of the games Rock-Paper-Scissors principle which makes it kinda necessary to have some of all unit types.
Were these things amended, “War, the Game” would be even more enjoyable but it’s already a solid RTS game as is.

It's an exciting and new hybridization of older games, originally based off of 1992–96 Siege of Sarajevo. The way the game operates is somewhat of a cross between Sims and Minecraft or Call of Duty and Sid Meier's civilization. Overall, it does a decent job of catpuring the niche intense and realistic war-survival market by forcing you to make tough ethical descisions while giving you the freedom of exploring different map locations and scavenging for resources that you use to survive and improve your own home. After the first play through, I would rate the game at 8.5/10.
Like life, the game has no manual. But despite how it brags about its realism, the combat is not the focus of the game and lacks versitility. And, there are a few features of the game which offer limited style of game play, such as the limited save feature which especially enforces the descisions you make, forcing you to live with the consquence of those descisions rather than giving you the choice to do so. There is also the large amounts of time it takes to simply shovel a pile of dirt or build a piece of machinery with no option to fast forward through the unimportant parts, so strap in for a while if you intend to beat the game. At this point because of the time it wastes and the fact that it is undecided between being completely realistic or moving along with its entertaining nature, I would put the game currently at 6.8/10.

This will probably get lost in the sea of positive reviews, but I had to add to them. This War of Mine is a great game, and one that's hooked me in solidly for the past two days. On my first playthrough my main scavenger was quickly killed after I tried to prevent a soldier sexually assaulting a civilian. Clearly this game is not shy about throwing you straight in, and this is one of many moments that highlights that the morally correct decision is not necessarily the one that's going to get you through the war. This, combined with overnight bandit raids on my shelter left the remaining survivors wounded and depressed. One died of sickness, and the last one was then driven to suicide by day 14.
At this point I didn't think I'd ever pick the game back up - it was harrowing and felt legitimately futile (intentionally so, I'm sure). However, on a second playthrough you'll most likely get to grips with the game mechanics and start to learn to scavenge and trade effectively, allowing you to build utilities and structural improvements to your shelter. Eventually, you'll even become self sufficient to the point that food is no longer too much of a concern when scavenging. It's not all plain sailing though, as the game progresses you'll need to traverse increaslingly dangerous areas to continue collecting supplies, and you'll face tough choices on whether you can afford to help people. You'll also inevitably be faced with the moral dilemma of whether to steal or not. And you probably will.
I have only a couple of minor negative points to mention about this game. First is that the combat is very unintuitive. Some kind of tutorial system for this aspect is badly needed, given that one wrong move will almost certainly end with your death. Second is that if you do well in the early game, the mid to late game can become a bit of a formality, You'll have all the food and meds that you need and plenty of luxuries to trade, which can result in a 15 or so day period where you're kind of just waiting for it to end. It still manages to be fun, but the variety is gone by this point.
All in all, however, the positives FAR outway any minor drawbacks and I highly recommend giving this engrossing, thought-provoking game a go.

This interactive experience (a book whose story unfolds according to the reader's actions) is extremely well polished. It's so well polished I don't even know how far they went.
After playing some runs, I've started to grasps the mechanics: There is a lot of scarcity, and getting around that scarcity requires a lot of creativity or painful choices (stealing, killing, or letting comrades die so the food consumption rate may decrease). It's extremely hard to be productive.
The AI is also very polished. The characters have proper expected behaviour: An AI charactery only protecting its own house in self-defense, althought it might hurt you badly, doesn't go as far as needlessly murder you (since you are badly hurt, and slowly fleeing). AI characters that do initiate aggression (like thieves and murderers) do will try to kill you, even if you are fleeing and can no longer pose a threat to them.
However, the game wasn't designed in order to 100%-assuredly force a miserable experience. After some runs, I've grasped that killing won't always make everyone sad. If you kill the bandits in the warehouse, no one will be sad, and you'll look like a badass (no one will be sad if you kill the soldiers in the construction site too. Screw the rebels, screw the military!).  Plus, by killing said bandits, you'll hit the jackpot, since you'll get their firearms, ammunition, protective body suit and all of the contents of the warehouse. It'll be easy to purchase what is needed, and everyone of the four people in the house will easily have the status "Well  Feed" and "Content".
In fact, on one run, by using the strategy above, my team became so wealthy that I decided to be generous and give all of our medical supplies (five bandages, three medicine bottles, four herbal meds and, as a bonus, two food cans). After giving the generous donation for the hospital (and receiving a few cigarettes), I've then resumed my business of collecting materials from the hospital debris. While walking in the hospital, I've saw someone (from his blue, pajama-like clothing, I guess it was a patient) poking around a nightstand (which, apparently, he wasn't supposed to, since it had the "private property" mark). I, still in character, felt stung by this outrageous act! My donation was to the hospital, and the doctor will decide how these medicines will be used. So I decided to give him a punch, just to stop his theft attempt. And guess what?
. And, all of a sudden, I'm a murder in the middle of the hospital, and everyone else is scared of me, and a guy with a shotgun starts to pursuit me.
Have I just overcalculated things, by being too much in character, or have the developers indeed placed a trap like that to me? This is what motivated me to do a review.

No cockpit view. Though some mods allow that. But I can't say I'd use cockpit view more than the standard view, it doesn't really make sense to not have it be here.

If I hadn't picked Battle Group 2 up in a game bundle, I likely would never have even known it existed. That said, it's actually not a bad game, considering how shallow the gameplay is.
The game's easy to complete in a couple of hours, and has exactly enough content to make it feel like it's worth finishing without being tedious. Some of the achievements are a bit ridiculous (grinding out thousands of kills), but if you're not a completionist then it's not a big deal.
The gameplay is simple: fire guns at incoming missiles and enemies, and try not to get hit. You can upgrade your ships, and there are a few power skills you can use when things start getting rough.
I
would not pay full price for this ($7.99 at the moment), but if you can get it for a couple bucks and enjoy arcade style gaming, it's worth picking up.

BattleGroup 2 plays best in short, enjoyable bursts.  You can push through the missions and make progress, or replay earlier missions for currency to unlock or upgrade ships and buy abilities.  The relatively simple gameplay can be very challeneging in later missions, with a ton of things coming at you and almost no way to deal with it all without taking a few hits and/or letting enemies slip away.
The sound is what draws me into the action most... planes, missiles, helis and almost everything has a unique sound, and the explosions and missile impacts feel solid.  The radio callouts from your mates may become reprtitive, but are not obtrusive; you will be so focused on the incoming enemies that you don't pay much attention to anything else.
The control is simple point and click with key bindings for special abilities.  It's that simple and it works well.
Honestly, I was expecting much from this game, but have come back to it again and again for a quick 15 minutes of fun.  As a relatively simple mobile port, I wouldn't spend much money here.  If you can get it on sale for a few dollars, it's certainly worth picking up if you're looking for something to play for short breaks, or as a quick change of pace between your usual fare.

So, I really liked Fault Milestone One and still like this second one, but there are a few things that I kinda feel like I need to address:
-We really need a more satisfying conclusion. This was a problem with the first one, but I overlooked it because the second one was already availiable. For a serial story, I think it would be more functional if each episode were more standalone.
-The Encyclopedia isn't as complete as it should be. A number of terms in the story that are mentioned and defined do not appear. It would really lend to the "Science" part of Science Fantasy if these things were more accessible. You've certainly put time into the mechanics of your setting, and we'd like to see them.
--On that note, I'd like to know more about the relative manakravting power of characters to others. Is a Trikravter superior to a Dualkravter? While your setting explains itself well, it doesn't address some of the major questions I have about the setting. It defines a lot of marginalia, but is hesitant about defining the overall world. Fault Milestone One worked because we could contrast the Outer Pole with Rughzenhaide, but Viscanta and New Sasary do very little to inform us about the overall world. Because of that, this second milestone feels more like an extended prologue, rather than the first chapter of an engaging novel. It's a very effective prologue, but I care about Ritona, Selphine, and Rune (I was on the fence about her, but you swung me over nicely) way more than Sol and Mil.
-While it's great that you're calling attention to social inequality (expecially gender inequality) it feels a littttle disingenous to have a semi-nude scene with a woman. Amazing Skillshot based Multiplayer Hero Brawler Arena!
It's a Multiplayer Online Battle Arena but not a MOBA. It's a team based multiplayer game (2v2 or 3v3) and everyone plays a hero but there are no creeps, no lanes, no towers and no items. You could say it's similar to a MOBA reduced to teamfights only. It however plays quite a bit different because you control your character with WASD and the whole game is very skill shot focused. A lot of people compare it to WOW Arena.
The business model consists of two parts:
1. You unlock heroes with either gold (earned by playing) or gems (premium currency).
2. You get cosmetics from lootboxes which you gain for playing the game or for gems. Lootboxes can contain duplicates which will get converted to Shards. Shards can be used to buy skins directly.
Overall it is one of the most consumer friendly implementations of a lootbox system around (cosmetics only, you get a decent amount of boxes without paying, the game is F2P) but it's still a lootbox system. I don't like lootbox systems (for various reasons) which means I will not spend a cent on the game but the implementation is not so bad that it would stop me from playing the game.

Take a MOBA, remove the parts that gives the game a high skill ceiling and complexity and you have Battlerite.
Battlerite is a f2p "MOBA" that removes everything eccept the team fighting phase. There is no last hitting to practise, you don't have to be very aware of your surroundings, and there are no real big objecive that you can take in the game eccept the orb in the center, but because that is the only objective it doesn't add much tactical depth. In the popular MOBA League of Legends as an example, you have the Baron, Dragon, Turrets, Inhibitors and finally the Nexus wich is the final goal of the game. In League of Legends you have to make sure you get the good stuff before your oponent and if you see the oponents taking dragon you can choose to stop them, take baron, try getting an inhibitor or even the nexus ++. You just have so many more options. Here you only need to get the orb in the middle, everyone knows when you get it and there is no other options to take, so the complexity is almost zero when it comes to objectives.
Another problem lies in that your objective is to kill the opponents. This works very well from a casual point of view, but for a competitive game it's not the best option. The reason for this is that it limits the complexity of the game. Take three very popular competitive games: CS:GO, LoL, and DOTA2. What all these games has in common is that the end goal is NOT to kill the enemy. That gives you way more options. In a game like CS:GO you can choose to kill the entire enemy team, or you can just plant the bomb and defend it until it says boom. While the right choice will be to plant that bomb pretty much all the time it still adds another element of strategy to the game, if the bomb is down you don't actually have to fight the enemies. You can choose to engage only when you HAVE to. However if the bomb is NOT down you HAVE to make a good play because the time is ticking down and the oponents have the advantage.
In LoL and DOTA2 it adds complexity because it allows the devs to make characters that is good at other things than just dealing damage, applying CC and healing. It allows them to make characters that can push out a lane and threaten a tower quickly, characters that excel at fighting 1v1, characters that excel at teamfighting, characters that excel at contesting big objectives and characters that can fit every role.
The champions all feel pretty similar and the battlerite tree adds little to zero depth. You have to select a tree before the game starts wich give you no option to build vs your oponents playstyle, all you can really do is build vs their champion. I think a lot of the problems with the champions come from the simple game design. There are only so much you can make original of a character when all you do in the game is hit the enemy and zone them away from the orb. In other MOBAs character depth often comes from the different stages of the game and that you have the option to buy items for your champion depending on what playstyle you have. In this game you cannot really come up with creative builds as the battlerites are champion spesific and you will almost always take the same tree every match.
Finally there is the part where I talk about toxicity. People seem to be very braggy about how this game has almost no toxic players compared to other popular games. It's pretty easy to explain why. Battlerite is a very small game compared to the games people compare it against (LoL, CS:GO etc.) Smaller community = Less toxic players simple as that.
Overall I think the game is fine for casual people, but I don't really know why anyone would play it competitively. As I said the skill ceiling/complexity is pretty low and that goes against everything that a competitive game is. This is why I give it such a low rating. If it would just call itself a casual game instead of having competitive modes and trying to be something it's not I would probably rate it much higher.

Its fun, whoever liked the first part or the Gothic series will enjoy this game.
Undeniable it has some edges, e.g parts of the combat system or the overall character animations but thats probably because of a low budget, but beneath that lies a really good RPG with nice graphics and a nice realization of the pirate scenario.
Whereas the mainstory is kinda boring, there is like a bad god and you spend the game preparing to kill that god. I don't want to spoil too much but the ending is pretty obvious after a while, so not really interesting.
Same goes for most characters, while some of them are at least good written, they are boring as hell and simple chliches, so everyone who is in search for a game with deep lore and interesting characters won't be satisfied with this game.
The fighting system is kind of fun, at least against humanoid enemies, against animals its much more simple but less fair. While you can counterattack humans there is no possibillity to do so against animals, you can not even block incoming attacks of some animals. One tip: don't use the musket that much, that makes the game even easier than it already is, at least in the latter parts. Either way, after about 20 hours you should play the game on hard,  many enemies stay the same while you become undoubtedly better.
The skill system is a fairly simple one, you get XP for every kill/quest you do, which you can then spend on one of 5 traits which are: Blades, toughness, firearms, cunning and voodoo.
The money you gain you either spend on improving your skills at special trainers or in gear like clothes, swords or pistols.
The graphics are sometimes really gorgeous, the design also. Even after 30 hours of gameplay the jungles or beaches you visit won't be boring at all. But still, the worst part of the game is part of the graphics though: the character animations, those are so unbelievable bad you should probably laugh at them rather then criticizing them.
And for everyone with a fairly good computer, you should check out the mod "AntiWarp", it removes that weird warping of the plants, it's really easy to install as well.

TL;DR:None. Seriously, if i could sum up this RTS game in as few phrase as possible i would say enjoyable, simple yet frustrating. You do have to read the whole thing and see if its the sort of game for you.
1.Introduction:What the ♥♥♥♥ is War, the game
A game of war, The game of war, Wargame. I have been pondering why exactly that the dev chose that name War, the game as oppose to something more palatable, perhaps it ryhmes with A Game of Throne then? We shall never know.
Essentially War, the game [♥♥♥♥. we shall refer it to WAME from now on.] is a simplistic RTS where player takes control of proabably a rookie commanding officer doing VR round in the newly made simulation program since the story is barebone but WAME doesnt really need story to flesh it out much since its gameplay carries it strongly by itself. Onward!
2:Graphics
WAME uses simplistic wireframe style graphic that pays homage to the VR vision of the olden days. Its functional and does not gets in the way of the battle except during the few times where plenty of units overlap with each other. Simple yet functional.
3:Gameplay

Upon starting the game you will be immedietly thrust into the VR control centre with a a floating AI head explaining some stuff to you before you are required to finish the tutorial before more scenario is unlocked. A pet peeve of mine with the menu is that we are not presented with the option menu upon starting the game but you have to press ESC before being able to access it at the bottom screen. Also flicking the mouse while the setting menu changes betwenn options probably to simulate finger swiping in a VR overlay but honestly its annoying when that accidentally happens. From the bottom screen you can also access the guide and several other options. I recommend reading the guide to get a clear handle on the capability and weaknesses of your units before you start the game.
Here's the part that divided me the most and which causes me to unable to provide a summary to this game. You see when starting the match there are several generic objectives that you might get such as hold out against the enemy assault, capture the enemy base and total annhilation style objective. Some missions allow you to build units and ship them to faraway location where the objective is located while some gives you specific number of units and expect you to deal with it.
Left click to select and the right mouse button to do anything with contextual action determine by a quick tap and a long press although it is a bit stupid to assign the attack button to long press since by the time the command is inputted the enemy has already started moving which means delays in response.
The game begins when 2 units meet on the field with a power gauge on the bottom right showing who has more of an advantage over the other although unit count, reinforcement and other stuff also factors in. It is incredibly simplistic with each game session not lasting for more than 10-15 minutes at maximum. You have the options to build units but thats pretty much the only management option you will get with this game.
The game is FUN [Subjective to individual, i use my own scale for now.] but several non-intuative controls frustrate me to no end. You cant simply draw a select box to select many units at once but instead you have to hold down the left mouse button and select them one at a time. This gives the already quick ai more time to prepare for an assault as i toss about trying to organize my forces. Also the only way to speed up time is by pressing the spacebar but that only speeds it up by 1 in game day so you might resort to tapping which i highly discourage since the game registers every single tap. So you got the units close enough to the enemy and want to begin planning an assault? Too bad since the games still plays out the last 5 spacebar tap so your units helplessly blunder straight into a fight. Judicious use of the skip time problem solve this one problem but another one pops up, the ai is a cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ since they can just order their troops straightaway while youre still busy with the clickings and such. How i wish for a pause function.
The game is also simplistic, the only tactic you need to know for basic bootcamp is stalling, redirection, sudden attack and air support strikes to thrawt the ai since ground and sea units once lock into a deadly struggle with their foes will not retreat at all so expending a tank unit to delay the enemy while the infantry unit waddle up for reinforcements is actually a good ideas at times. Why infantry instead of tanks? Because they have all the weaponry to counter everyone just not particularly strong against any.
I'll give more thoughts in the conclusion.
3.Sound
Battle sounds and simulation noise thingy are good enough although the constant stuttering of the ai voice that is blamed on bugs of the simulation got on my nerve shortly after and it doesnt help that the ai speak in the most gravel voice i have ever heard. That is a compliment masked in sarcasm btw dev.
Conclusion and final thought:
I dunno, i like the game because it focuses more on the traditional unit placement to stall and counter the enemy but the overly simplistic gameplay is definitely not for me. That and that annoying ai. But at the end of the day the game is solid enough to stand on its own 2 legs from the rest of the game on steam and it does play smoothly enough for me to warrant a positive review.
While i did only play it for an hour the game pretty much opens up fully within that timeframe which is enough for me to say that its a good game marred by a few minor annoyance.
Also i lied.
TL;DR:
A simplistic RTS game with heavy emphasize on quick reaction and fast mouse clicking with a focus on strategy more. Fans of RTS game should probably get it after viewing the gameplay on youtube but those who want base building to go along with it should look elsewhere.

I'm sorry I didn't play this game when I bought it, I've been totally addicted to it all week and played it every night... finally completing it this evening. The concept for the game is refreshing and quite frankly excellently executed. It's a survival game set in a war torn eastern European city, you must guide the fate of up to four civilians and try to keep them all alive until a cease fire is called. The focus of this game is very much on scavenging, base building and resource management. Combat is possible during the game but should be avoided at all costs because you are almost always outgunned and / or outnumbered! I've had this game for a while and I still love it, which can't be said for a lot of games.
Not only are the visuals aesthetially pleasing, they also fit the theme of the game really well. Every single time I play, I go through every single emotion imaginable. The way individual events play with your heart and how each character has their own storyline and what makes it even better is that at the end, it's not an immediate cut off; you're told what happens to them after the ceasefire. This game is one of the most dramatic, exciting and heart wrenching games on the market and is worth every penny.
Not only that, there's an additional DLC that you can buy which adds artwork to the game and the money goes to charity (you can also decide how much you spend, to a certain extent).
However, there are a few things that I would like to see improved in the future as I believe it was touched on but not competely developed. Each character has a certain personality, explained in their biography. When certain events happen, their biography is updated with how they feel about the situation that happened, for example, if you choose to kill an NPC for supplies, some don't care while others actually do. What bothers me is that even though certain characters aren't affected by these, they still become sad, depressed and broken, leaving them completely useless. I would expect a character that actually understands the concept of self defense and the fact that sometimes we must kill for supplies and even says that they understand it, to not become so depressed. Another thing is during the day, sometimes there are events in which a survivor has the choice to leave the base and help an NPC out. It would be nice to add another choice to go with them, perhaps for an extra reward where you can physically help them out, such as clearing rubble, fixing up a base, healing people etc. (You could see it as a minigame during the day).
All in all, I really recommend this game and I believe there is also room for improvement. If you're even thinking about it, buy it. You will not regret the decision and the replayability immense, with the difficulty changing every single time.

Well, how to start... ? TyranoBuilder isn't finished. There are many - and I mean it, many - features that are left to add to make it on par with Ren'Py. But the question is : is it worth buying ? Yes. I freaking, gigantic yes. Because even though it's incomplete, the interface makes everything simple and noob-friendly.
You can make your own Visual Novel even if you know absolutely nothing about coding with a very well-thought drag and drop interface. For those who know how to code, you can also do that in TyranoBuilder to make more complex VNs. Unlike Ren'Py, TyranoBuilder can be used by everyone and still result in a very honorable game, so long as you have the ressources - sprites, musics, backgrounds... The software itself does provide some of those, too ! So if you want to make a VN and can't figure out how to use Ren'Py, TyranoBuilder is a must have !

The Good
TyranoBuilder is a very good piece of software for making a basic visual novel. It has an intuitive system for setting up text, character entries/exits, and scene changes. It also has a (reasonably) simple scripting system for making variables, and other useful things for more complex games.
The Bad
What TyranoBuilder is awful at, is organization. Once you start having 40-50 Sound FX files, 30 music files, etc. it's impossible to quickly access them in the editor, as it's just organized based on when you imported them. Unfortunately, this makes it rather annoying when your game gets to even moderate size. Also, the lack of ability to organize scenes makes keeping track of what scene is what a pain (get yourself some flowcharts and label them or you'll be regretting it later).
The Ugly
I've encountered a number of bugs while working in the program, generally fixable with a restart, but they can be an annoying time-waster.
Overall
I like TyranoBuilder and will continue to use it, and suggest it to people who want to build visual novels, while it's not the most advanced, for the price it is a great 'out of the box' game creator 7/10 score.

Compared to fault milestone one, fault milestone 2 had much more of an "open world feel". Even if the characters are locked down to one area again, it's still interesting to watch as they engage in another brother-sister relationship, this time, in the making. There's also a lot more lore to be had. If Project Written would allow it, I'd want to stick my own character in there somewhere. fault has fandom-like qualities. A vast, open world for people to explore, a compelling main story that adds a lot of detail, and lore that really intrigues the reader to join in and live through. Enough about that though  you read for a review on THIS story, right? Compared to the first installment of fault, this one really improved on mechanics, even to the point of (spoilers for the first 5 minutes or so) crashing your game on purpose only to re-open to a really scary moment, only to laugh at it after clicking the "undo" button. The main characters (not including the actual main characters) had, in comparison, less story to tell than Rudo and Rune from fault milestone one,  but that's probably because of how young they are. This story also brings up controversial topics that the last one tried to do, but only a few understood (namely techies and the technological singularity and such) and the drive of a man who's lost his loved ones compared to two children who never had anything in the first place. Also, fault milestone 2 had so many tricks up its sleeves, from expanding on what we know from fault milestone one to outright changing the point of focus in two lines. There are more cliffhangers though, which (of course) makes me excited for fault milestone 3... or three... however they decide to word the number.

Which is not surprising, since the story the new Garrett is involved in is absolutely abyssmal. The concept behind the story is more or less okay, some of the characters are intriguing, but the dialogue, the feel of the world and it's inhabitants are just flat at best, and the story simply goes nowhere. At first, after seeing Rhianna Pratchett's name in the credits I thought I had the answer as to why this happened, but apparently even she wasn't really working on the game and was involved rather briefly and in the early and mid stages of development.
And the fact that this happens is really a shame, since some of the characters and some of the hooks are pretty nicely done, and visually The City looks nice. Voice actor for the new Garrett was good, reminding of Stephen Russell's delivery, but at the same time creating a different character. Music, composed by Luc St. Pierre according to credits, is actually very nicely done and reminiscent of the fantastic score of the original trilogy done by Eric Brosius. Not quite the same mix of weird creepy and industrial ambient with trip-hop and industrial metal sounding stuff, but very close and, because of the fully dynamic nature of music in the game, feels more natural and enhances the gameplay.
The gameplay itself, though, is where you start asking questions. Now, some of the ideas were nice.They did improve on the Deadly Shadows' claustrophobic City - it's bigger, has much more stuff to do, but at the same time, still fell in the same trap of pointlessly boring backtracking, "upgrades/tools" (think climbing gloves from TDS), which you absolutely have to get, and do it almost immidiately, making the idea of buying them in the first place almost redundant. And added to this a really big problem of doors and other closed things re-locking after every mission and even side-mission (client job type, not just a mini-quest thing) for no apparent reason, rather then to just waste more player time.
I also did like how now Garrett had to physically interact with everything - be it grabing loot, opening doors, flipping switches and etc. It means, no "telepathic" interactions, more thinking about where any interaction places you and how long each interaction takes when thiking about guards or other enemies around you. To somehow balance this idea out the movement became much faster and quiter, though, but actually not completely silent when crouched and on "loud surfaces", as it was in TDS. Plus, the "swoop" move is a really nice idea for the kind of gameplay the game created.
The bad thing about this swoop, however, is that it completely overrides the jump button. Instead, all the jumping in the game is context sensitive and if you understand that the jump should be easily possible, but the game doesn't want you to jump there - you just can't. It, along with a few other "context sensitive" animations restricts the game much more than one might want to. But, at the same time, it doesn't matter, because the problems with gameplay lie much deeper than that.
The actual problem with the gameplay is that, despite understanding it and getting it almost 100% right in their previous project DX: Human Revolution, the developers completely misunderstand the core idea behind Thief's gameplay. Which is not that far from what Deus Ex gameplay is, in it's core. Because Thief, even TDS, had very simple rules during missions - no cutscenes, at no point the controls are taken away from the player, all that happens in the level happens because of the set and, if not bothered or rarely scripted, never changing character routes and player interaction with it, and the level as a whole. That's it - if there's a "cinematic action moment" during the level, it's because the player screwed up somewhere and alerted the enemies, not because the script says that there is a cutscene, during which Garrett gets discovered and it cues into an actions running away scene. And, because of this "forced storytelling" approach in the new Thief, levels are much much less open ended. And, you know what - with this approach it is understandable, that jump button got cut and rope arrows work as tools with very specific use in specific places (think more Tomb Raider 2013, than classic Thief, hell even less than climbing gloves from TDS). There's no point in having normal jumping and proper rope arrows, if the levels are not structured in the same vein, as in the original trilogy, now is it?
And it becomes painfully obvious, when the game tries to directly reference those unforgettable missions from original trilogy. Sure, one of the levels does look like that incredible mission in T2 with Angelwatch tower, but the magic of the original was in how huge, varied and almost completely non-scripted that mission was. How breathtaking that run across rooftops was. Here it's just a super linear level with a forced "run away" sequence jammed in the middle for no good reason. And they try to do their own Robbing the Cradle. And it is good. But where the original in TDS was brilliant because it worked just as a normal mission, but with no enemies at the start and with almost completely silent and frighteningly deadly enemies later, the mental sylum mission in the new Thief feels more like a first person horror game, a lot of free ones of which are constantly been created lately. With jump scares and horribly banal twist to the history of the place, where the original was just a sad and scary place, which got really unlucky at some point.
Also, there are two "boss" fights. Yep. Developers who got severely burned by including boss fights in ther previous game did it again. And while Deus Ex actually had boss fight encounters from the very first game, Thief never did. Now, granted, you're not required to fight, hence the quote marks. And the second one actually works much more like the "boss" encounter at the end of the TDS - more of a stealth puzzle than anything else. The first one, however, is ridiculously badly done, especially for ones playing on highest difficulty with several custom difficulty settings. The fight can be avoided, but the boss is so erratic and his attacks have such a wide spread, that it's just painful to try and avoid him. Especially if the game does a rare reloading glitch, where the game just goes to a black screen after the loading and has to be force quit. And since I mentioned glitches - the other really bad and very noticeble glitch is AI reset when reloading - sometimes all the NPCs would just return to their starting places on the location and do the starting things they might do upon reloading, which may make some levels almost impossible to complete with full stealth/no knockouts approach.
But since I've mentioned custom difficulty - it is a nice, but, to be honest, pointless thing that will, most likely, just make your playthrough more painful. They set restrictions, which give you "points" for leaderboards, but that's it - points, not multipliers, so there is a max of 1300 and Top of the leaderboard is full of those.
So yeah. Lots of bad things, but a good stealth game.

I picked this game up some time ago in a steam sale, tried it for a couple of hours and thought... damn that's really hard. So cut to about a year later and I decided to pick this out of my game backlog!!
I'm sorry I didn't play this game when I bought it, I've been totally addicted to it all week and played it every night... finally completing it this evening. The concept for the game is refreshing and quite frankly excellently executed. It's a survival game set in a war torn eastern European city, you must guide the fate of up to four civilians and try to keep them all alive until a cease fire is called. The focus of this game is very much on scavenging, base building and resource management. Combat is possible during the game but should be avoided at all costs because you are almost always outgunned and / or outnumbered! It is possible to get weapons in the game, on my final playthrough I think that game completion was secured by getting a shotgun on about day 4 which I used to protect my home to great effect during an ensuing crime spree. The game has a great level of depth and requires micro management and resource planning. There is a strong trading and crafting element to the game and is arguably its core mechanic alongside stealthy scavenging.
The big plus point of this game from my perspective is being a mature gamer you can play this game in a day and night cycle at a time as it saves the game each morning. This effectively happens in 10 minute chunks so it's easy to pick up and put down. I'm not going to give this game a score, I will simply say that as a game from a small company the finish and stability would put some big studios to shame. The graphics and sound effects are top notch. This game is a must play, regardless of the type of game you enjoy. Pick this up and try it you won't be disappointed, the one caveat being that it is intended for a mature audience.

I've had this game for a while and I still love it, which can't be said for a lot of games.
Not only are the visuals aesthetially pleasing, they also fit the theme of the game really well. Every single time I play, I go through every single emotion imaginable. The way individual events play with your heart and how each character has their own storyline and what makes it even better is that at the end, it's not an immediate cut off; you're told what happens to them after the ceasefire. This game is one of the most dramatic, exciting and heart wrenching games on the market and is worth every penny.
Not only that, there's an additional DLC that you can buy which adds artwork to the game and the money goes to charity (you can also decide how much you spend, to a certain extent).
However, there are a few things that I would like to see improved in the future as I believe it was touched on but not competely developed. Each character has a certain personality, explained in their biography. When certain events happen, their biography is updated with how they feel about the situation that happened, for example, if you choose to kill an NPC for supplies, some don't care while others actually do. What bothers me is that even though certain characters aren't affected by these, they still become sad, depressed and broken, leaving them completely useless. I would expect a character that actually understands the concept of self defense and the fact that sometimes we must kill for supplies and even says that they understand it, to not become so depressed. Another thing is during the day, sometimes there are events in which a survivor has the choice to leave the base and help an NPC out. It would be nice to add another choice to go with them, perhaps for an extra reward where you can physically help them out, such as clearing rubble, fixing up a base, healing people etc. (You could see it as a minigame during the day).
All in all, I really recommend this game and I believe there is also room for improvement. If you're even thinking about it, buy it. You will not regret the decision and the replayability immense, with the difficulty changing every single time.

I must admit it is not an easy review to write. I've been playing Civilization games continuously since Civ II, so I thought I had seen it all. I was wrong, because BE is the proof that Civilization still has something more to say. Not everything is better, but at least many things are new!
+ New types of challenges: new planets can look like the Earth or not at all; new resources; a new, futuristic age means new technologies, buildings and units.
+ Aliens instead of barbarians: they are less aggressive than your usual hordes at the beginning, and their behaviour evolves according to your behaviour. However, they are literally everywhere at the beginning, and they will still attack you every now and then, even if you are not hostile.
+ Non-linear technology tree: imagine it like a spiderweb - you can move in every direction at any point, as long as you can reach that technology through another one you already own.
+ Affinities: three different ways to face the game, six different types of victories. Your units change according to your affinity, your relations with other countries do too, your cities look different, you can build exclusive buildings or train unique units.
- Not immediately understandable: when in any other Civ you come across the resource Horses, everyone immediately gets you're gonna use it for mounted units; the resource Grain means the area is particularly fertile; and so on. In BE, when you are first faced with this new map, it is not exactly that immediate to understand what you are supposed to do with floating, purple rocks or xenomass. The same goes for technologies: you know what you could do when you discover the gun powder, but here you are threading in a completely unknown area of science fiction. Obviously, most of the time the same is true also for builings. Consequently, you can get the impression you are doing completely random things, without having any clue on where you are going.
- A pleasant challenge at the beginning, when you are a poor, small colony and the world is wide, unexplored and hostile, covered in poisonous gas and strong aliens. Then, it gets less challenging, to the point that most choices can be automatised or left to chance.
All in all, it is worth trying! Just bear in mind that you are not playing your conventional Civ. If you come to it with an open mind, I'm sure you'll find a deep game that will keep you interested.

The sequel to fault milestone: one remarkably and convincingly builds upon the lore established to drive the story in a direction that is both unexpected, and relevant. The story is more tightly written, showing the creators had learnt much from the first outing, and is relentlessly addictive.
Unlike the first outing, fault milestone two side:above actually compelled me to finish the whole visual novel in 2 sittings. The story manages to explore the consequences of unregulated capitalism, imperialism, and moral choices through simple dialogue. And without me having to make a single choice throughout the visual novel.
Whatever the next story will be, I am hooked into the fault milestone universe, and am eagerly awaiting the sequel!

Though I have never felt the need to write a review before, after playing this game, I had a sudden, impossible-to-ignore urge to write one. This game is beautiful. The story is captivating and keeps you on the edge of your seat most of the time. The amazing character development continues from Fault Milestone 1 when we're introduced to two, new characters. I won't name both of their names because it could spoil some of the plot, but I will state one of them. A little boy named Sol became Selphine's, Ritona's, and Rune's tour guide for Viscanta. After playing the demo for this game, I honestly hated Sol for what he did to Ritona and the others. After playing through the whole game, I can happily say that Sol has become one of my favorite characters for this game along with the other character, but I won't say the name of this character for plot reasons. It takes a true masterpiece of a game to pull that off. If you enjoyed Fault Milestone 1, you'll undoubtedly enjoy Fault Milestone 2a.

I am currently debating my existance because wow. I feels so sad yet happy that I'm done. I am both satisfied and desatisfied as I really enjoyed fm2:above but, at the same time, I'm having a crisis since fb2:silence the pedant and fm2:below have not been released yet.
I assume the reason they split it up (besides the whole $15 issue) is because, even though fm2:a is a self contained story, part of it, which I can't really go into without spoilers, is overarching. Basically, the main focus of this cinimatic/visual novel is resolved, but a different, over-arching plot is not. That's what I reckon Alice in Dissonance meant on their Patreon update when they stated that it wouldn't really make sense to just make fm2 and fm3.
On that note, I highly recommend that those who enjoyed the game go support their Patreon. I noted in my review of the previous installment that the character art seemed a bit static, but this is much improved in fm2. The art is much more consistant, and the new use of 3D parallax really adds to the scenes (especially the action ones). Everything has a lot more movement, and the characters are interesting as usual. I'm sure the extra funding from Patreon really helps in improving these aspects.
AiD has a great affinity for pulling people into the stories they spin and the characters they create. I didn't cry in this one like I did in the first one, but it was still moving nonetheless. If it wasn't obvious already, I highly recommend this story to any VN lovers out there.
The VN team never fails to impress, and Ren'Py never fails to deliver. With both in hand, Visual Novel as amazing as the Fault series have been brought to life. Viss, VN makers.

No programming required! If you want to make your own visual novel, this is the fastest, easiest tool out there. All the basic stuff is integrated and you can write your own scripts and call javascript and html code for more functionality. Exports to win, mac, android, ios and web (although the exporters for mobile are very hard to use right now).

Pros:
#1 - An actual drag and drop of VN segments, such as character, background, images, choices, sound, text, etc.  Finally someting a lot easier then RenPy.
#2 - Scripting ability for those that are comfortable with that sort of way to make visual novel, like with RenPy, and to make use of advanced features.
Cons:
#1 - No manual, or no PDF instruction file.  Only link to a website in the tutorial section, that gives basic instruction to enable the creation of a basic visual novel.
#2 - No  image or sound resource.  Tyranobuilder does not come with an character or image art, or audio files.  You have to have or find these yourselves, and if you are making a visual novel for commercial purposes, you pretty much have to be an artist and create your own image files.
In short, I like TyranoBuilder, but as mentioned, it is almost not possible to create your own visual novels for legal, commercial distribution, unless you are also very skilled in art, and also have the use of a tablet, like a intous or cintiq, and also have the time to create such artwork for a quality, commercial, visual novel.
On the plus side, if you have ever wanted to create a visual novel for to satsisfy your own personal creative impulse, or to share with friends, this is a great program that can let you focus more on the actual building of a visual novel than on the learning curve itself.

War, The Game appears to be an attempt to create a very easy to learn, simplified grand strategy game that still offers challenge and meaningful content. Unlike many games that try to dumb themselves down to become accessible, War, The Game is designed from the ground up to be easy to learn, but harder to master.
The control scheme is very inventive and while counter intuitive to what strategy gamers may expect, once you get your head around the system it works reasonably well. Many of the control options feel very touch screen orientated, for example selection is not driven by a box drag, but rather a click and hold, dragging the mouse over the units you want to command. Panning of the map is done automatically as your cursor approaches the edges, and the effect is amplified if you zoom further out. While I’m not sure the nonstandard controls really add to the game, once you get used to them they work nicely and in my opinion don’t detract from the experience.
Game flow is built around a set of scenarios. Build units at cities, move them, if they encounter enemy units then a fight breaks out. As is common in GSGs, you don’t have direct control over the fight, but you can help by piling in extra units. In a very interesting twist units all have the same combat strength, but differ in terms of mobility and special abilities. For example one armoured battalion versus one infantry battalion will end in near stalemate. However armour can move much more quickly and so can be used to pin other units in place while the bulk of your forces arrive to tip the balance. This means positioning and control of multiple units is important. Infantry on the other hand double their strength when dug in at outposts or cities, and are also the only unit that can capture them. Sadly without transports they are also very slow.
Another interesting departure is that the game is in real time, and there's no pause option. Instead space bar accelerates time briefly so that your slow moving units can be shifted quickly. I’m not sure on this decision, as I like time to carefully consider my options. That said the rest of the game’s design very much feels like it’s almost rushing you. The goal seems to be rather than playing a game that lasts hours and hours, you pick up a scenario, play it, and if you want to keep playing you just play another. As such while I don’t like the absence of time controls, I will admit that the decision does seem to further a very intentional design choice, rather than being omitted by mistake. And for the most part that design choice can be summed as minimalist, and quickly paced.
And that's pretty much War, The Game's watchword- minimalism. Despite being very much a GSG, it's the bare bones of what one is. This makes the game quite hard to call for GSG fans. On the one hand they may enjoy the very basic yet functional and satisfying gameplay for a while, or it can be enjoyed as a deconstruction of the genre. On the other hand there just isn't the mechanical complexity to keep someone who's logged 200 hours in HoI engaged. That said it's £6.99, so you'll probably get your money's worth. The mission based structure is also an interesting touch. While many GSGs do offer various scenarios, War, The Game takes this one step further and some of the missions are more like puzzles than anything else. They put me in mind of those trick decks from the Magic The Gathering videogame campaign modes.
For people who don't like strategy games, there isn’t much pull here. But I think the group that really benefits from this game though are people who want to get into GSGs. War, The Game is very basic and while the control scheme is very different, the core concepts and ideas are the same. It's about meta game planning and positioning of assets, with the occasional bit of micro management when the war needs it.
There's a total domination mode that was added in after release, but for the most part the game consists of a sequence of unrelated scenarios. Again, this seems to inform a very careful choice for how the player is supposed to approach the game. Plus, the fact the developers added in something the fans really wanted is also a good sign.
The game's presentation is also worthy of note. Obviously it's not a AAA polished 4K treat with advanced rendering and lighting effects- but it has a charm of its own. The fact the game takes place on an actual globe is a nice touch, as is the fact you can navigate around without needing to actually press any buttons.
There are also three different map projection modes- there's monochromatic for people who enjoy gaming on what looks like an IR display screen (admittedly it does look cool, just not great for actual gameplay), there's colour which is what you see in most of the screenshots, and finally there's unstable. Think the technology in the Alien movies and you won't be far off. Basically it switches back and forth between monochromatic and colour, as well as adding in occasional scan lines.
All in all War, The Gameis a solid little title, well-conceived, well designed and well built. It's not going to be for everybody but I'd say anyone with an interest in the GS genre should at least check out the store page.
