Hello, I'm not sure about the game making capabilities of this application so I won't go into that. I will however, review how I used the software and what it did for me. My daughter is getting married in September and I wanted to write a romantic short story with real life people from her world in it. This software worked perfectly for that. Years ago I wrote a children's story called The Gypsy Princess. In this current project, I used that story and tweeked it with my daughter and her fiancee as the main characters and all her family and friends as the other characters. I used Gimp2 to import images of Gypsies, Kings, and Princes, etc, then used the same software to install my loved ones heads on the bodies and scenes  that I downloaded. (This video novel was for our own enjoyment so I wasn't concerned about copyright infringement of images since no one but my family will ever see it.) The images of gypsy camps, kings, princesses, etc. turned out perfectly and looked so realistic. I turned each scene into a cartoon using Gimp2 (excellent free software) and transferred each scene to Tyranobuider....super easy to do. I would preview each scene by playing it and adjust the box accordingly in Gimp if there was any distortion and was able to achieve perfect results 100% of the time.  I was able to import music of my choosing for the video book in just a few clicks which really made the book shine. I used the loop function to keep the music playing if someone took too long reading the book. Installing the text of the book was very easy too. I would install one line at a time, then press Enter, so that only one line at a time would come up each time you pressed enter. This kept the beautiful scenes I created from looking cluttered and made it nice if a child was reading the video novel since they could take their time and click at their own speed. I also did away with the box that housed the text by reducing the opacity (very easy to do). Then I adjusted the text so that it would appear towards the bottom of the page so that each beautiful scene would not be cluttered by words. (again very easy...each process using this software usually only involves a few clicks or drag and drop.) Initially, when i first started the project, I had a few problems figuring out how to change scenes with the "Jump" button, but it was a glitch...I simply restarted the process and  it worked perfectly ever since. The finished product was amazing....a true video novel that took place in a medieval fantasy world, but had all the people in my life as the characters in it. This is undoubtedly the best thing I ever purchased on Steam and a real bargain to boot since I got it at a discount of just over $12.00 USD. As a video novel maker, this thing is seamless...everything is just click and drag. Importing your images and music is the same....very very easy to do and I am not the most computer savvy person in the world. I used youtube videos to figure out how to use Gimp to alter my images before downloading them to Teranobuilder.  As I said before...I know you can make games with this too and I saw that the software includes scripting and so forth, but I did not get into that aspect of this software. A very nice product at a very affordable price and perfect for making video memories with pictures, text, music, and even sound effects.

I don't write reviews often. However in some cases where something exceptional is made i will.  Something that i can either put my time to for extremely long periods, enjoy it to a maximum extent where nothing gives me hesitation or where my very outlook on certain things change entirely. This visual novel bought out both 2 and 3 of these 3 reasons.
The art/style: The visuals are absolutly stunning, amazing barely covers it. I presonally love it and feel that it adds a lot to the visual novel with the different backgrounds, charater designs, and effects. The intro and credits are the only two "movie" cg throughout the game but are well done for how short they are both explaining the latest events from fault milestone 1 and the aftermath of whats happened in this visual novel. The CG itself is beautiful and again really shows off the skill and talent  at  Alive in Dissonance. This game is visually stunning in every detail
The story: (No spoilers) The story took me about 4-5 hours to complete. This is fairly short but don't go into it expecting to read little. In the time given the story explodes with absolute moments of intensity, moments of calm (including in the menu screen) moments of disbelief and one moment of genuine anger towards a charcter. It was filled wit a lot of emotions. Also desipte its size this visual novel can be both for casual readers and those are looking for something that truly surfices their reading needs. I will say this as well. The way the story moves forward is smooth. There are no points i felt it was rushed or needed to be sped up. Unlike the fault milestone 1 i felt i could have read this visual novel the whole way through in one sitting with no problems at all (not to say fault milestone 1 was bad because it isn't).
The characters: There are 3 main characters, multiple sub characters and the main bad group of enemies. The 3 main characters develop an ever bigger sense of self showing their personalities even more so then they already had been. Providing a new outlook on them especially with Rune and Selphine. Sadly with Ritona although we don't see much change in personality or even development in her overall character. We do get a new side of her compared to Fault Milestone 1 that is caused mainly by the events of Fault Milestone 1 as well as an event that occurs within Fault Milestone 2.
The new characters you meet as well as old characters from Fault Milestone 1 were somehow all unique and none felt they were wasted or pointless at all. One thing that was interesting is the fact that even characters who had little to no input into the story still had actual character models made for them. Hell a few characters you never even found out their name.  I'm espeically interested in what will happen with Flora, Misha and Riggs.
Next the group of "enemies" now due to my no spoiler review this will be harder to explain. We see barely anything about them again in 2 however we do get a little bit of interest from the leader. Learning her power and even her breaking the 4th wall very slightly. It gave a whole insight into what Ritona and Selphine are up against when returning home to Rughzenhide.
Replayability: Although i find it hard to replay most visual novels without having a very large gap inbetween play times. I can very easily see myself replaying this. It left me wanting, no craving for Fault Milestone 2 : below. I really cannot wait to see how the story progresses.
Music: The soundtrack and effects made are truly incredible. They push forth what the scene is trying to make you feel. Anger, Sadness, Intensity. The general mood in visual novels hinges by a pivot and the music really sets the mood into what the writers clearly wanted the mood to feel like for the reader. The soundtrack is great but doens't have anything in my mind that stood out such as The fruit of grisaia's Home (for Amane) or Holograph (for Sakaki) in Their respective routes.
Overall: I really really enjoyed this visual novel. No ifs or buts about it. It was a massive improvement on what was already a good 1st game. Although we are left with a lot of unanwsered questions I got a brilliant amount of satisfaction from the game. I would highly recommend trying it.
However  for the love of god play through the 1st fault milestone. If you do not you may be very confused as to what is going on.
Final score 10/10 At the least a must try. After reading through this visual novel i'd be happy paying for it at full price despite how short it may seem.

After putting a lot of time into this game, though not playing it at all in a couple months, I was content to just consider it a dud and move on.  Then Civ6 was announced with the usual push for pre-orders and I remembered what a waste it had been to pre-order this one.
I'm a huge fan of the Civilization franchise and have well over 10k hours logged on Civ5, so it was with much anticipation that I pre-ordered Civ:BE.
My first impression? Wait... this is just Civ5 with a new "skin" and a completely revised tech tree.  I set about to figure it out.
I quickly learned that it should say "Abandon all hope, ye who click here..." over the launch icon.  Everything can and will kill you. Quickly.  Everything AI (aliens and other civs) can and will grind you under it's boot heel without so much as getting winded.
Health is of critical importance and oh, by the way... you'll never have it.  Want to build more than a few cities? Forget it. They'll be diseased cesspools.  Think technology will help? Some will, but never enough.  Go ahead, answer every choice in how you play in such a way that it will benefit health... Still not enough. Build different buildings. Still helps, but never enough.  Social policy choices?  Sure, pursue everything related to health into the gates of hell or madness.  It's still not enough.
In the meantime, the AI civs are all 3 times your size and building every wonder before you can even research the techs to start them.
This is what game play is like on the relatively easy settings.  I've never played it beyond the "A 3 year old should beat this" difficulty setting.
Nothing makes sense, nothing works the way you think it should (or at all, really), every choice you make will just hasten the progress of the AI and in short, you don't stand a chance.
I've never bothered purchasing the expansion "Rising Tide" because frankly, even if it really improves the game, they would have to sell it for $4.99 just to make up for how much I wasted on the original game.
This, in a nut shell, is why I won't be duped into pre-ordering Civ6.  I'll wait to see whether it more closely resembles Civ5 or Civ:BE first.
Very disappointing. Even more disappointing that they're charging for the expansion, considering how poor the base game is.
An unfinished shell of a CIv game, left to rot in the mud with the development of yet another sequel to replace it. Do not buy this game.

I don't recommend this game- especially with Civ 5 sales occuring every other week and other turn based scifi games becoming avaliable (stellaris). Here's why- (and I'm going to reference civ 5 alot)
READ THIS 4 SHORT SUMMARY: Beyond Earth has a more fun early game than Civ5, but feels lack luster because of how easy it is. I have over 200 hours in Civ5 and never beaten the game. Beyond Earth with bots on the average difficulty was beaten on my first play thru, in one sitting (about 8-10 hours). Way easier to accomplish whatever you want, cool aspects of the game are lackluster-such as wonders- and the lack of any real draw to return to the game after i beat it, forces me to say don't buy, or wait to buy once its under $20. Also I'd rather play more Civ 5.
New features are gimmicky:
Aliens-
Usually nonhostile creatures who function like raging barbarians, they have nests (barbarian camp mechanic), and attack all units who get too close. Also there are giant worms that randomly roams the map causing headaches etc. Once you have a basic army, aliens don't really bother you, especially since they dont attack cities.
Miasma-
Poison gas that covers parts of the map, causing harmful effects to units normally, and healling effects to aliens. You can tech to either ignore or remove miasma fairly early, so not really the impactful of a feature come mid game.
Health-
Reworked happiness mechanic. More people, less healthy. Less healthy, less productive.
Satellies-
Structures you find or build that grants benefits to a certain area. Cool feature, but never feels needed.
3 types of civilizations-
Purity Supremacy and Harmony I think they are called. Think of them as ideologies like autocracy, order, and freedom in civ5 but in Beyond Earth, these tenets are formed by what you choose to research and tech. There is no specfic victory minded tenet, as you can pick any of then tenets and win the game however you like, but I will say that Supremacy just seems better than the others in all aspects.
Wonders-
Feel lame. I built this one wonder in which everyone's consciousness could be merged in one area- and all i got was either plus 200 culture or +10 culture per turn on top of other bonus. Now you might be saying "that's op" but realize this building took me 30 turns to build and it didnt feel as epic as the wonders in Civ5, where the music plays and you get a cool quote, and some depiction of the wonder on the map. In Beyond Earth, the presentation just feels boring after you get used to it.
Other things that annoyed me:
Lack of alien balance (one shots your ships in ocean when you first go, but 2 upgrades later you forget aliens exist)
Small selection of different leaders/governments
Lack of focus in tech tree, pretty confusing to navigate
No real feel of alien prescence in late game feels like lamer Civ 5 late game
Not sure if it exists, but I couldn't find nukes or any type of late game super wep.
Things I liked:
Energy-
Currency like gold, but way more "manipulatable". I quite liked how effective this games currency is, as i start new cites and buy huge energy boosting buildings to quickly amass wealth.
Spies-
Way more effective than civ5s spies, as the whole spying system was enhanced and reworked. You can now steal way more different types of stuff from energy to tech or even cities. Becomes a bit of a hassle late game when every other turn you seem to be managing your spies. Still cool that the game added player based rng, as players are forced to adapt to the fact that they know spies are in their cities.
Overall: 6/10

Avast ye, matey! Give up yer plunder, lest we send ye down tae Davey Jones' lockerrr!
Over the top pirate language like this contributes to our overall "enough with the pirates already"-attitude and it speaks for Risen 2 to refrain from exactly that. Yes, Risen 2 is essentially about pirates in a Caribbean-like setting, fighting each other with sabres and pistols and sailing the oceans in pursuit of treasure. All of this is more of a setpiece, though, as this game is a sequel to the first Risen, which only featured a handful of pirate-like characters. Being a sequel, Risen 2 does what Risen 1 did, only better. The combat is more refined (though still wonky, more later), the story was expanded and everything looks even better. Considering this is a low-medium budget title, the graphics are gorgeous, with the exception of character models.
Risen 2 is a classic PC RPG, third person and with a healthy balance between action-oriented combat and interactive narratives. Depending on how interested in the story and sidequests you are, you will spend most of your time talking to people. The English VO is, unliike the early Gothics or even Risen 1, not as terrible as it used to be, although you will run into various people with the same voice over and over again. Combat is definitely not one of Risen 2's big strengths, as it ofttimes feels unresponsive and flatout unfair, when fighting against multiple opponents. It turns out some of the fighting-styles just are not very good in this game. My tip would be to stay away from a purely melee-focused build and invest in firearms, throwing weapons or magic. Also be sure to have a companion with you whenever possible, as they make everything a lot easier. Risen 2 does enough to keep you interested, offering a plethora of different skills, including some for forging swords and even firearms, to alchemy and Voodoo, this game's magic. Speaking of Voodoo, at one point in the game you'll have to decide whether to ally with the Inquisition (sort of like colonial marines) or the natives (your standard, dark-skinned indigenous people), which will affect how the rest of your game is played. Not only will you have access to their specific areas of expertise (natives use throwing spears and magic while the Inquisition favours muskets), you will also have different possibilities to tackle some of the quests, with Voodoo clearly being the more entertaining choice as it lets you take over certain characters for a while and speak with their voice.
My complete playthrough of Risen 2 took me 24 hours in total, with a good amount of exploration and sidequesting, though I did skip a lot of the dialogue (your classic "I'm much faster just reading the subtitles than listening to you"-behaviour). What you can expect of the game is an adventurous experience of once reknown RPG-artisans PiranhaBytes, intendet to be a treat for those who loved Gothic I and II and were sorely disappointed by Gothic III. If you would like to relive some of those days, but do not want to go all the way back to Gothic, I would definitely recommend giving Risen a chance.

This is worth checking out if you have any interest in the subject matter. It has been released on the day Robin Williams died, one of the greatest stand up comedians of all time and sadly a man that suffered from depression during his life. He has left in his wake some of the most memorable films I have seen during my time.
Life is not always puppies and sunshine, some people struggle everyday with being content. Depression Quest shines light on what it is like to deal with the feelings that have led so many great minds to take their own lives. Before we start, just know that this is not a game but more of a story that allows you to choose the characters reactions, determining their fate.
The game is presented in a simple layout that requires you to answer a series of questions that have consequences on your characters mental health. These questions are presented with a description of the scenario you are in along with the other characters' words and actions. It then presents you with a choice that will determine your mood.
As much as I enjoy the games ideas and approach, one thing that might get annoying to some people, is that there happens to be no way to save your progress, so get ready to push through some reading in one sitting if you want to reach the ending without starting over, or leaving the program open in the background. If you don't feel like dealing with all the text, then this is not for you. The game is fairly short and possible to finish in one go leaving the reply value determined by you and how much you've enjoyed the story or want to discover another ending.
The first thing I noticed after booting it up was the love and care the developers had put into this gem. The quote that filled my screen was perfect and set the mood instantly, along with some sad piano that lingers. At first the piano is welcome, yet after awhile it becomes far too redundant. The writing itself, being the main focus of the "game" is better than expected and remains quality the entire time.
I have a lot of respect for the fact that the game warns you that if you're not feeling well, you should seek help before going any further. It even provides a link to a website that helps those with suicidal tendencies. This was a mature and honorable approach to a subject that should not be taken lightly. Now before you rush out and download this, it's not really a game but more of a story you take part in. The developers themselves state that it's not meant to bring pleasure, but was created to bring awareness to the often hused subject. In my opinion, Depression Quest is something all of Steam should be aware of.
I'll end this review with a poem by Charles Bukowski:
Cause and Effect
The best often die by their own hand,
just to get away,
and those left behind can never quite understand,
why anybody,
would ever want,
to get away from them.

Oh how I despise platform games, I blame it all on Donkey Kong you know, that game scared me for life. In all the platform games I have ever tried I have never, ever gone beyond the first level, and Bunny and Piggy, to my shame, is another brick in my wall of failures. All that timed jumping, jumping, jumping! I can never get my head around it, I am as co-ordinated as a blind, dyslexia, tightrope walker.
The story of Bunny and Piggy is a simple one, they must collect enough food before winter arrives. You get to choose who you will be Bunny, who needs to collect carrots or Piggy who needs to collect…. Um …. acorns? What!? Wait, acorns! Should in not be corn or grain or bits of other animals (Pigs are naturally Omnivores). Or maybe Piggy could have been a you know, a squirrel. Call him something like Scrillex, that’s a nice jumpy platform-ish name.
Ok, ok, I know, just get on with it. So you must do your normal, jumpy thing, and collect all your carrots/acorns (what if the pig has a nut allergy?) to advance to the next level. Jump up platforms, jump down platforms, jump onto platforms that move left and right and jump onto platforms that go up and down (really fast like a bungee jumper on red cordial).
You have other animals that will hinder your quest to collect, some that run on the ground like hyperactive snails (I think some have snorted way too many bug pellets) and what looks to be one♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off fly (hey, the pig is jumping in the sky, dose that still count as “Pigs can fly”?). Unfortunately, as far as I can tell there is no shooting or jump-on-them sans Mario style to knock these guys out of your way. Touch them and the whole level resets.
And if this was not enough of a challenge for you (Hell, it was for me, but then again so is opening child proof jars) you now need to do it within a set time (first it was speed dating, now it’s speed snacking! As if my ineptitude was not bad enough trying to time jumps, now I need to do it under time constraints, schesh!). When the timer runs out, the level resets and no, collecting your food dose not extend the timer (As far as I can tell, do not know for higher levels).
Bunny and Piggy upon the title screen offers you the ability to select your language, seven are supported including English, German, Korean, Polish and Russian. You can turn sound on or off, can choose easy or hard (only difference I can see is in the timer, 60 seconds on easy and 30 seconds on hard). There is an options button but this is only a key/button (controller) map but you can not re-map the keys/buttons.
Your movement keys are Up arrow (A) to jump, left arrow (Joystick) to move back and Right arrow (Joystick) to move forward.
Graphics in Bunny and Piggy are cartoon-ish, 90’s Mario type, but are nice and clean and Bunny and Piggy are just a square block (Yea man, your just a Square!) so the appeal of this game seems to be aimed at a younger audience of say 5yrs and up or those who like that type of graphics.
Music seems to be two tunes, the menu tune on a loop, and the game tune on a loop, so thankfully they gave you the choice to be able to turn it off in menu.
I am sure Brzezinske has made a good platformer, one that may keep your child entertained for hours or you may be a platformer who handles pressure like a Diamond (all 725,000 pounds per square inch of it) and wants that extra challenge. Then Bunny and Piggy is right up your ally.
But as for me, I’m just going over to this corner and assume the foetal position, and cry once more over my platforming impotence.

Navigate through dozens of completely awful levels trying to collect the icons of your character's choice while avoiding hoards of lazy enemies and jumping across terrible platforms that move without rhyme or reason.
In many stages, sets of vertically moving platforms oscillate in such a way as to render them impassable after the first ten seconds - both will be at their peaks at the same point in time.
Reeking of lazy, inept game design in every possible regard, Bunny and Piggy would still be a ripoff at 10% of the price.

What does Bunny & Piggy represent to me?
Here's what you got to know. Bunny & Piggy is a minimalist platformer made by Russian developer Brzezinski. To date, it's their only game. Here's how they describe their work:
And what kind of world is Bunny & Piggy? From the outside, it looks minimalistic and cute. But when you delve into the game, it becomes a metaphor for self-destruction and struggle.
You see, there's only one kind of person who will love Bunny & Piggy: people who like to die. A lot. To call this a "hard" platformer does not do this game justice. This game does not allow for mistakes. And even if it doesn't look like you're making a mistake, you'll make a mistake. Over and over again, and you'll you can't fix your mistakes because you only have 30 seconds to complete most levels.
Bunny & Piggy gives you just that little bit of hope. Yes, you'll die but should you pass just the first level, you'll find a transcendent joy that makes you feel like a god-damned genius. But it's all for naught. The next level will surely murder you over and over again. Its cuteness gives you no respite.
Let me talk about the graphics for a brief moment. If you're nostalgic for Flash games, you'll like this. The asthetic is stripped down and minimalistic. Both characters are represented as coloured squares with smooth corners. The obstacles are made up of circles and squares. You'll come across various enemies that will give you a one touch death, but they're rendered simplistically.
As for the audio? Oh boy. If you play this, mute it -- which is what I did. It deserved a better soundtrack. Something that represented its philosophy more. Perhaps something like Joy Division or The Manic Street Preachers. Something that represents the dread of dying over and over again.
This game doesn't require much as far as hardware is concerned. If you have an Intel Core 2 CPU and 1GB of RAM, you should run this fine.
Perhaps it's the booze talking, but Bunny & Piggy took me on a whirlwind journey. There were moments I felt like crying, but when I managed to win a level, it was like an injection shot of ecstasy. And just as quickly, I'd come crashing down, wondering about the futility of it all. Why do we, as humans, put ourselves through these lonely tests of mental fortitude -- and what is there to show for it?
But what is Bunny & Piggy trying to say to us? One clue is at its Steam store description:
So why exactly is a rabbit gathering carrots that are bound to spoil, and a pig gathering acorns which it *cannot* digest? And why must this be done within 30 seconds? This game is a comment on capitalism and consumer culture, how we tend to plunder for goods, looking for the quick exit.
For what end? Death. Yes, you can try again. And every so often, you'll find success. But isn't this all just a way to amuse ourselves before the inevitable? This reminds me of a quote by the great Marcel Proust:
stop now

Bunny & Piggy is a tough platformer, however it’s difficulty doesn’t come from where the designers thought it would. Perhaps the hardest thing to do in this game, is to listen to the ingame music. Unfortunately this game suffers from “restarting the music whenever you restart the level” syndrome, which in a tough platformer like this one can be as often as every 5 seconds. Luckily there is an option to turn off the ingame music, but it’s a bit of a shame because a lot of the music is pretty good (especially that groovy main menu music). Even when you don’t die, when the music loops, it ends and then restarts with a gap between (or maybe it was a fadeout, I don’t remember) and it was pretty jarring.
There are a total of 28 stages and they range in difficulty from “literally you don’t need to press any buttons” to “fffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff”, although excluding those 2 levels where you do nothing I’d say the minimum difficulty is quite hard. Only get this game if you like challenging platformers (and have a tolerance for resetting a lot).
There are a wide variety of platform types in this game. Regular floating blocks, moving donuts, grey moving blocks that kill you, blocks that looks exactly like the regular blocks but they fall when you touch them, yellow moving blocks that kill you, disappearing(only invisible, they are still there) moving donuts, donuts that explode when you stand on them, boats, some random floating pieces of terrain sometimes, blocks that looks like other blocks but arbitrarily spawn more block/change the level completely, the floor, sometimes roofs of houses, and my personal favourite: the explosions that the yellow donuts make. All in all there’s a fair amount of different platform types, however I feel like there definitely could have been more to vary up the gameplay. By about level 14 you’ve seen pretty much all the blocks the game throws at you and then you still have half the game left.
As a bit of an aside, what’s with the disproportionally detailed crabs? I think those crabs have more detail and more frames of animation than all the other game assets put together. I think maybe the other enemies need to be a bit more detailed in order to match the crabs.
Pausing the game doesn’t pause the game, if the “resume” button wasn’t there I would be fine with it, games not allowing you to stop time while in a menu is fine as long as they don’t pretend the game is paused. Also maybe you could add the controller button's that the pause menu options are linked to on the menu in game, I didn't even realise that they were mapped to buttons until I was writting this review and was complaining about how I spent the whole game switching to mouse to click restart, they controls weren't exactly the clearest to see on the control screen.
I’m going to file that under “bugs” and while I’m at it throw a couple more at you:
The explody donuts and the falling blocks trigger when you touch them from the side, they clearly shouldn’t do this.
A lot if not all of the moving platforms aren’t consistant in their movement. I feel like this is most evident in level 15. If you don’t move at all and just watch the donut on the right you will notice that it has no discernible movement pattern beyond just going left and right.
With that out of the way I can mention some of the other points of contention that I have, such as THERE ISN’T ENOUGH TIME ON THE TIMER, unless you do everything on the earliest possible cycle without messing up you aren’t going to make it to the end of the level, there should at least be enough time to miss a cycle of one of the longest cycles in each stage.
And finally my biggest point: what is the point of offering a choice between bunny and pig? As far as I could tell they were exactly the same but had different food/face. A real missed opportunity there to have the bunny be better at jumping and the pig better at… something. There certainly wasn’t enough difference between them to include both of them in the game title like that, especially because there is no co-op or using them both at the same time. It should be Bunny or Piggy.
I hope that the developers read this and maybe make a few changes based on my troubles here, as I think that this could change from being a frustratingly challenging game to a fun challenging game.
As it stands for the price I recommend it, but only to those who like challenging games and to those who are willing to forgive games for making the player die because of questionable design decisions.

Just no.  Any claims this game makes to realism is generous, and the reviews were carefully chosen.  It's mixed Metacritic rating is closer to the mark.
In 'War..', you control one side battling one or more enemy sides.  At your command is infantry, armored, fighters, bombers, carriers, battle fleets, transports and nukes.  And that's it.  With the exception of the nukes, everything has the same number of hit points, and other then a few minor tricks (aircraft in a battle don't take damage until all friendly land or sea units are destroyed, or transports and carriers don't do damage in naval battles), each one fights the same.   Take Risk, toss in a little Rock Paper Scissors, and you have this game.
You can buy new units to help your conquest, but the interface for this is a bit unfriendly, and building up the money to reach that point can take awhile.
'War' boasts some 20 odd scenarios, 3 of which make up a crash-course tutorial.   The tutorial doesn't necessarily end there however, and will constantly interrupt your battles with well meaning advice.  Incidentally, completing one part of this tutorial and advancing by a full day in game uses the same key (space bar), so if you press space too many times trying to shut the tutorial up your enemy is going to take advantage.   You CAN turn the tutorial off, but since it's trying to help you and you're obstensibly a new player, is that wise?
The scenarios range from realistic (US counterinvasion of Kuwait, China vs. Taiwan) to unlikely (Britain vs. Zimbabwe over South Africa, China vs. Russia and Japan).  There's a World War scenario I didn't try, as well as Global Domination.  From YouTube videos it looks like the last is more of a sandbox game with multiple AI factions.
The description boasts of the game using a spherical globe.  It does, and this is actually a pretty nice touch, but it's just not enough to save this game.  It's a little too simplistic (though a decent AI), parts of the interface (like building units) is God awful, and memorizing its peculiar combat rules (what will attack what) isn't worth it.
Still, the game isn't unfixable.  Fix the interface somewhat, maybe either add some more units or make the combat a little more engaging, and make a number of more realistic scenarios (or even giving players the chance to mod in their own scenarios) and you could have a fun little game here.  Not one a wargamer can take seriously, but a way to pass a few hours.
Right this second however, you can spend your gaming dollars more effectively elsewhere.

I absolutely hated this game at first, couldn't quite place my finger on why immediately. So I gave it a second chance, and a third, maybe even a fourth. I plowed through the tutorials and got to the more in depth scenarios. I am now kind of hooked on this game, even though it's not really what I expected.
This game is simple in some ways, yet deceivingly so. All of the units have the same strength, but have varying costs, speed of movement and utility. There aren't that many unit types, although the game doesn't feel like it's missing anything critical. Air, land and sea are all represented. There's no fog of war, no base building, and the economy doesn't need to be managed. It's definitely not a typical RTS in that sense.
I think I hated it at first becuase I was expecting another RTS. A typical RTS. I couldn't get past the fact that one tank unit and fighter jet unit are worth exactly the same once in combat. I couldn't get by the the interface and control scheme being unique. And I certainly couldn't get by the fact that there are no special abilities, rank ups, or customization options. I'm glad I plowed through and looked past my expectations.
This game rewards thinking ahead, the dance of tactics. It doesn't require you to click a thousand times a minute. Any ruses or strategems you create are entirely based on what you do and decide, not what some simulated fog of war or magic ability button says happens.
If you take two units and feint east, what happens? What if your opposing player doesn't even notice? Or what if he does and guesses what you're really up to? Even the AI feints and doubles back in this game.
This type of situation and depth is part and parcel to this game, all while giving the player the option to play the game their way. The game doesn't force you to use Air units. It doesn't force you to use Tanks. By all means kick out a hundred infantry in a massive stack and just plow straight ahead. A smart player will trounce you if you do, but that's the beauty of a game that rewards tactics over click fests, and has unit strength parity at all times.
Really all I can say is give this game a shot. Considering the price point it really delivers. Just try to get past the tutorials. The game gets alot better.
TL;DR
Has strategic depth without tomfoolery or magic abilities, simple controls and units while remaining versatile, no clickfest! A real gem for the price.

I was thinking...what could possibly go wrong with a game series like Thief if there´s a new game after like 10+ years. I thought nothing dramatic could go wrong, but...
It´s neither fish nor flesh and most definitely lightyears away from the original game.
I am quite disappointed with the game as it is. Should´ve read tests and such beforehand instead of wasting my money on...this
Gameplay:
Controls are somewhat wacky and will most likely drive you crazy on more than one occasion. Why they put the rope arrow in the game still puzzles me - one can only use it at predefined locations (as it is with climbing or even jumping for that matter) which frankly sucks. Oh and also forget about the water arrows, you will not need them a single time to progress. Speaking of arrows: how are chances that one survives 4 arrows to the head? Well, normally I´d say slim to none - not so with Thief, these 4 arrows leave the guard with around 80% health left - do the math. Even in Dark Project, which had a badass difficulty, guards could be snapped with one arrow if the aim was right...
So why would I want to shoot the guard, you ask? Should I not take a stealthy approach?
Yes, you could do some semi-stealthy thing but now it does not even matter on what material you walk on (apart from occasional glass clutter on the ground, which does just what I want for much more surfaces - different sound and loudness), only at what speed is of the essence, which is why there´s no moss arrow at all. And should you get caught, don´t panic, just take two or three turns, park yourself in the shadow and wait.
The fun thing about windows (no, not the OS) is, that in Thief you have to break them open from both sides (one time getting in and one time getting out)...makes sense, now does it? Well, I always use a crowbar to open my windows at home...not.
I wander the city lifting tons of stuff or doing "missions" which basically is, tadaaa, wandering the city lifting stuff...and not in an exciting manner - most (like in almost all) rooms you loot are depopulated like the zone around Fukushima NPP (as are the streets in big portions). Or, if someone actually placed some guards, you can bet that you don´t even have to confront them in one way or another, like luring them away for a quick heist in their room.
It is now possible to fast pace from shadow to shadow, if you spam spacebar hard enough. Wacky controls FTW.
The levels pretend to be open, but you´ll figure they are not...whoohoo I can choose to crawl through there or do the same thing 5 meters to *insert preferred direction here*, or simply try out all since they are so close to each other
Story:
I´ve still got no idea what the story is about (but I´d like to know at least a little something after the first/second chapter). I know there´s some illness and lots of dead people (which all look exactly the same -doh!). And then there´s a missing year in the thiefs´ life. But does he care? No. Totally ingorant of that. And there´s some female character, the name I already forgot. Can´t be that important, I guess. Since the game does not give me even the slightest clue as to WTF is going on, appart from the sometimes confusing cutscenes and the lack of lip-sync´ness in them, I´m stuck with little to no info at this point.
Graphics/Sound:
Well, I´d say the graphics are ok. Not great. Reason I say that is quite simple, my rig is beyond its second year of service and can run this game at max settings on a GTX 570 without almost any lags related to the game. So far I only came across one point the framerate dropped below 30+fps.
Squenix did some nice job with the lighting, but they used this at least one time so idiotically (the morgue with the oven) that I was really scratching my head if this is meant serious. It is a nice tech-demo of sorts, but for F´s sake, give these things at least a reasonable motivation. In plain text: you get into the morgue where the bodies are burned and you have to cross the room with two tables for cover. To make this "more thrilling" someone came up with the idea of the oven being opened and closed like every 2-3 seconds resulting in the passage way either being lit or not...Head-->Table, repeat.
I mentioned the clone NPC earlier. All nicely modelled and animated, but I´d favor a bit more diversity.
The sound has quite some issues, or rather the people who took care of that: ever heard of normalization between different audio clips?! This and the lip-sync issue makes for a bad experience - but nothing a patch might fix soon.
All in all a game with quite some potential, especially if one turns off all the overconvinient ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t helpers. This helps getting a more original Thief feeling but the game still lacks tremendous amounts of immersive depth...
Not sure if I´ll play through it, I´m not having the fun I was expecting. Or maybe it´s just me getting older...but then again, nah...it´s the games that keep getting more casual/stupid every time.
Think twice about buying Thief, watch some videos first or testplay it somewhere...would´ve saved me 60 bucks.

Im not very good at writing reviews, but what else can I say, this game is absolutely amazing. At this point in time I have over 16 hours on the game and haven't come across anybugs or glitches. The game has an absolute amazing soundtrack, and a huge amount of areas to loot and explore. Beforte I go into anymore detail, you start off as a group of survivors (the group changes depending on what group you pick) who are stuck in a war struck town full of scavengers (people like you who are just trying to get buy), Raiders (people who are also trying to get by, but will try and kill you and steel your stuff), Soldiers (they will shoot you on sight), and civilians (who are helpless but often have materials for you to steel. Note that steeling things from these people will lower morale). The game makes you ration supplies such as food and materials that can be used to craft a huge variety of things from weapons, ammo, beds, radios, medicine ect... Ontop of the big crafting aspect of the game, it also has a huge decision making aspect. Around every corner there is a tough decision to be made. These decisons range from; should I steel these supplies? should I take this person in, or leave him out on the streets? Do I help my fellow citizens or turn them away? Who in my group should I look after, and how? The list of these decisions goes on. All of these decisions will affect your group in some sort of way (either negatively or positively). The game does an amazing job of making you feel for the decisions you make, almost as if they are real decisions. Overall I would give this game a solid 10/10

Despite the name, there really is not much "navy" involved except the overall setting. What this really is is skeet shooting. You don't move, you simply mow down defenders before they can reach you, much like the good old "Missile Command" except your perspectives shift a bit: enemies can now come from the sides, top, bottom, even from behind. AND you get a secondary ship with some fancy stuff like missile decoy, escort fighters, and so on. And then there are special abilities such as satellite support (i.e. zap all the missiles or all the enemies at once), then there are the boss fights.
Basically you control this one ship (and an optional support ship) and you run into some very very fancy terrorists called Talon (clearly modeled after GI Joe's "Cobra") with a LOT of weapons and planes and ships... and you need to shoot as many of them as you can. Easy enough? Except your ammo doesn't reload instantly (your clip size is limited) and you need to "lead" the enemy fighters / missiles / ships / bombs / etc. This was originally a touchscreen game on iOS and Android, and somehow doesn't play quite as good on mouse, IMHO.
Graphics are decent for 2D sprite game, sound is a bit of "meh". it won't blow you away, for sure.
Still, if you need some arcade-y action (never mind the hokey storyline, like helo gunships 'escorting' an airliner) then give it a try. It's cheap, it's exciting, and it's a break from the FPS and RTS and such games. AND it's cheap.

In fault milestone two side:above, you follow the story of Selphine, Ritona, and Rune as they try to travel back home from the Outer Pole. They run into some difficulties, and end up with this full part revolving around their time Port/Neo Sasary. While the start and end felt quite well paced, it did feel like a massive drag in every other part.
The game does have some minor issues. Namely, some lines near the start will randomly repeat, often with a different "speaker" for them. There are also spelling errors every now and then, and on at least one occasion the entirely wrong speaker is said for a line (that wasn't a repeat). Despite that, fault milestone two side:above has a fantastic story - although I felt it had some lacking pacing issues at times - along with amazing graphics and music.
I do highly suggest reading/playing fault milestone one beforehand though, although it is possible to get through two side:above without having done so. After all, that's what I ended up doing. There'll be some bits you still end up confused on, even with the "previously on fault" and encyclopedia available, but the story is still gripping enough.

Fault has everything to make a brilliant anime. The world building, characters, story, music and the new cinematic style is exceptional. The initial girlish and pretty impressions from the screencaps belie a dark and grander storyline. This series has action, adventure, magic, mayhem, and politics (but no love, yet ;-D), you really can't ask for any more. Except maybe for the side:below to hurry up and be released...

For Mac Users Only:
I'd like to recommend Hammerwatch, but have to take issue with a few of it's key selling points being plainly false.  First and foremost, Hammerwatch claims "Controller support, supports various different gamepads".  While this may be true on other platforms, on Mac I have tried 4 different gamepads, from Logitech to Microsoft... not a one works at all.  This is fairly important since another selling point is the ability to have multiple people play local on the same machine.  Without controller support this is simply unfeasable.
It would be nice to imagine this is simply a bug that is soon to be fixed, but judging by Steam and Hammerwatch forum posts, this has been a problem since day one, which was 6 months ago.
While it is certainly possible to play with a keyboard alone, Hammerwatch's gameplay style truly begs to be played with a controller.

A marked improvement over (the already very good!) fault Milestone One in every single way!
The visuals in particular stand head and shoulders over just about any VN I've read. The CG and character art is at least as good as the first but there is now roughly twice as many CG images as Milestone One despite this installment being slightly shorter than the first (more on that further down).
But, even more than that, the clever '3D Camera' system that has been added extracts so much more from each image by the clever way it pans and zooms around the images during dialogue and action-y sequences (rather a lot of those this time!). Coupled with the typical changes in expression of the characters and other subtle changes it created a great sense of movement and pace without actual animation. You'll understand what I mean when you see it in action!
The story and dialogue itself as excellent and they have definitely addressed one of the key criticisms of Milestone One with it's unnecesery.. wordiness in a small number of scenes. Things feel a lot more punchy and to the point this time; the plot itself is generally a lot more fast paced in this installment so it suits it well.
This time Selphine and Rune take center stage and Ritona sits out much of the story for plot reasons. I feel there's some great development in Rune's character as she becomes more sure of herself culminating in one seriously epic scene that I won't spoil here. :) And you'll certainly see a very different, ah, "side" of Selphine throughout the story too...
However, Rhegan has to be my favourite character of this part. It's easy to dismiss her as just a *censored* when she first appears, but I guarentee she will grow on you as you come to understand her throughout the story; I came to respect her a great deal if not necessrily 'like' her. Her ruthlessness is certainly no facade but she has damned good reasons for being as such; that and her sharp cunning serves the girls well.
As negatives.. well the character art of the side characters is of markedly lower quality than that of the main characters. Understandable, sure, but when the quality of everything else is so excellent in contrast you can't help but notice.
Also this is only the first half of Milestone Two due to a decision to split it into two releases. As such there are rather a number of plot threads that are raised but left unresolved. Though the central plot 'side:above' centers around is concluded and it doesn't exactly end on a cliffhanger like Milestone One did it's a little frustrating knowing I'll be waiting rather a while to see certain events resolved.
Alice in Dissonance is onto something very, *very*, special with the fault series and I hope it gets the recognition it deserves so they can keep it going for a long time to come!

It's more or less a digital version of Risk. Unfortunately there appear to be a limited number of scenarios but it's not bad overall. However I do have some difficulty recommending at even this price point simply because in many ways it is extremely simple.
Now that I've had  alittle more time to fiddle with it:
Pros:
- A nice simple version of Risk (as I'm sure you noted, also a con). Units have the same strength but do move at different speeds. Easy to understand and really reduces things to how well you can strategically/tactically manage things.
- The AI isn't that bad.
- Each scenario is fairly unique (in terms of what you need to accomplish and under what constraints).
- Game does an excellent job of explaining what everthing does and how you need to do it piece by piece (each of the early scenarios introduce something new and how to use it).
Cons:
- A nice simple version of Risk (as I'm sure you noted, also a pro). As all units have the same strength there isn't a ton of variety in what you see scenario to scenario.
- There are a few minor bugs I've noticed (it seems to love to minimize when I click things).
- The UI is a bit clunky and a little bit of work could have streamlined it considerably (you have to click on individual barracks/airbases/etc to generate units). Essentially you have to go to each place to build something new (although there isn't a ton of new unit generation - at least early on) which involves going to each city, finding the barracks/airbase/etc around the city, then clicking on what unit you want to build rather than from a nice menu.
- It's all scenarios, I assume they run out at some point but no global conquest type thing that I've seen.
I'll update it a bit more as I can accross other items of note.

Now, by no means am I an experienced maker of anything but arts, writing, and odd conversation, so that stands to either aid my review or hinder it.
But, dang, do I already love TyranoBuilder.
When the download finalized, which was really fast, I hopped in and was instantly greeted by a screen offering some help to inexperienced players. For someone like me, it was a beauty to see. The tutorial over on the TyranoBuilder site was helpful, if a bit Engrish in places, and I managed to build my own Visual Novel from the loose-in-a-good-way instructions.
After the tutorial, the menus and building have treated me well, and I've continued the simple test VN I developed into a rather large piece about the usual stuff (friendship, romance, dream-walking, et cetera). The easy to grasp drag and drop system gives way into a more advanced, specific numbers-and-references bit where all the fine block-edges mash together to spin those giant cogs of VN.
Further beyond the D&D layout is a scripting option, with Javascript and the program's own TyranoScript branch. I took a class in scripting a while back, so I'm no wizard, but I understood the deal well enough. It seems like a very nice alternative to other VN Studio's methods, in both D&D and scripting, though Python was never my strong suit.
TyranoBuilder does require you to find your own assets, but I found some easy enough with the aid of a Google Search AND the developers' help. They're really pushing forward with assistance on the forums, and seem rather active on the hub itself. A suggestion, though: use some kind of translator software to find what you're looking for, Japanese sites are, unusually, in Japanese.
There's no royalties to be paid, either. No watermarks or any permanent sign that a game built with TyranoBuilder was built with TyranoBuilder than the scripting, I suppose. Only be careful about the assets used, since not all of that stuff is up for commercial.
The games can be developed and published for a variety of platforms, as well. I'm on Windows, of course, but I see Mac, iOS and Android, too, not to mention browser-based versions for Firefox, Chrome, Safari, and IE.
Long story short, I recommend TyranoBuilder. It's been nice to me, it's very supported, and the mascot is absolutely adorable.
Now i can make visual novels although it's a pain to make characters but its totally worth it 10/10

The original Thief games set a new standard for stealth gaming, and although the new Thief lacks many features of the originals (like putting rope arrows anywhere you wanted) It delivers solid stealth gameplay, freedom to choose how you progress through a mission and a wide range of optional content, and it does this better than I had expected.
After seeing all the overly negative reviews I went in to the game expecting it to be terrible, well it was not and this is probably a touchy subject after the initial negative response the game got on launch, the gameplay requires a heavy dose of patience which some may dislike and find the game boring, it is also best played on a harder or custom difficulty to get a really good experience. movement is fluid, visuals are excellent and the environment can be your greatest enemy as well as your best weapon, getting spotted because of a bird in cage becoming alarmed is frustrating, kill or knock it out with a gas arrow to facepalm when a guard spots the bird is dead raising the alarm anyway, frustrating but you have to give them thumbs up for it. Unfortunately sometimes guards become stupid when pulled out of their patrol routes leaving themselves open to attack and when you know how to exploit them, have very predictable responses to distractions, it would have been nice to see more randomness and variety with the guards.
But if this game is so good why does it have such a low score? Ignore the meta score (hard to trust them these days), most negative reviews either dont reflect the game at all or expect it to be completely free roaming like skyrim or assassins creed, I found this game should easily have been rated 80+ and it is unfair to compare Thief to other games including its predecessors, not perfect by any means but certainly one of the best stealth games I have played in a while. The game world has boundaries but it is set in the city, Garrett barely ever leaves the city outside of missions and it would make no sense to leave the place he is so familiar with, so yeah the story may be linear but the way you go through missions is open to how you play the game and between each major story chapter there is the chance to do side missions in the open city or client missions in their own replayable instances. More than 30 hours of gameplay and only on chapter 6, many collectables are well hidden, and though optional, completionists will want to find everything. The bigger side quests are repeatable to hit achievements, earn more cash and pick up loot you missed first time around, as are the main storyline quests, yes you can replay any main story mission, the city is packed with random loot and secrets including the collectables you display back at your hideout. Garrett can upgrade his gear with a few buyable extras opening up more ways to play, trinkets to boost abilities and spend focus points obtained in some missions, secrets and by donating gold to an npc which improve existing or add new abilities.
Difficulty? Dont bother with easy mode, most of the games appeal especially enemy AI is dumbed right down to make it a story mode (it even warns you of this) probably for quick playthrough, this way it does not reflect how complicated situations can be if you intend to complete the game purely pacifist for the "moral victory" achievement, custom game option lets you choose how realistic you want the gameplay if you are a true stealth gaming masochist. The game suggests 3 playstyle paths to follow, Ghost (for pure stealth, all pockets picked and none the wiser), Opportunist (using stealth and the environment to get what you want even if something "accidentally" drops on a guards head) and finally Predator (getting the job done by any means, kill em all and loot the bodies) for the longest time I was playing opportunist but when replaying maps for the extra rewards/items predator became the easiest method to use...plus its bloody funny.
my biggest gripe with the game, the in game menus and especially the map....its functional but they could have improved this by adding place names, points of interest, map transitions and replayable mission locations, thankfully some nice players have put these on their guides but the in game map is just lazy. the rest of the menu system is a pain to navigate though when you want to find specific documents for a lock combination or to track the objectives in an area.
My final verdict, excellent game for any fan of the originals or stealth games in general, If you are concerned about the cost wait for a steam sale but Master edition is well worth the extra cost for the additional content it gives. Otherwise watch some gameplay vids on youtube or Twitch, see what you think and if this game is ever half price, its a steal (pun intended)
One last thing, if you plan to get the game, dont read or watch anything from the Moira Asylum in chapter 5: The Forsaken, if you played Thief deadly shadows and remember the Shalebridge Cradle, you are in for a treat, play in a dark room with the sound up. You're welcome. ;)

So I got thief on a special deal and decided, before i play it, to play Thief Gold. Thief Gold is the original and features many great things. It has a range of arrows that the player can use to do a lot of things from putting out torches to causing distractions on the other side of the room. It is older than me so my hopes were not that high but it is still a very challenging game.
But anyway, to the game in question. The first thing I noticed was the fantastic PC port. I was not expecting this but you can change almost everything including controls, audio, graphics etc. Jumping into the game I found myself in a world of grim beauty. The artwork creates a very good atmosphere along with the eary music that keeps you on edge.
Those are all nice things but after completing a couple missions I realised the city/hub world was an "always on". The guards will always want to kill you and that makes getting around to the shops quite annoying. I read some reviews of people saying they liked this as it was good for practising but I found it more of a nuisance. Another unneeded nuisance is that, as far as I know, the only way to increase arrow holding capacity is to buy three extra DLCs all 79p each. It seems cheap but I do not want to pay money for something they could neatly add as the player gains more focus points. That leads me on to the skill points in thief called focus points. They are gained from completing certain missions and by paying in game gold to "The Queen of Beggars" for an ever increasing price. This is fine. I am perfectly happy with the gaining of focus points but not so happy with the usage. The skill "Trees", even though they are barely branches, consist of two perks; one will read something along the lines of "Slightly encrease your ability to..." the second one will be along the lines of "Majorly encrease your ability to...". I do not see a point in having them if they barely do anything. Even the first branch gets given a point already allocated to it before you get given an open map, leaving one space left for upgrade that early on in the game.
The puzzles were another thing that stood out to me. They all seemed so forced like a cry of attension reminding everyone you bought a game with more than stealth. THey never really fit into place and delay the proper gameplay.
At the end of each level you are "rewarded" for how you played. I say "Rewarded" because I have yet to see what it does besides XP. The three wins you can get are Opportunist, Predator and Ghost. I put them in order of how good it feels to get them, Opportunist being last. Opportunist is where you steal a lot of things and put out the most light sources but doesn't feel as rewarding as the others. In the first mission it teels the that the main character, Garrett, is against killing people then lets you get rewarded for killing as many people as possible. The game should strive towards making people want Ghost or Opportunist, not just Ghost.
Another thing that made me want to steal less was the fact houses had around 2 things to loot in them and some even had really oddly placed traps that make their houses unsusable and just dumb thief killing machines.
The combat was actually quite clever. In the original you were given a sword and blackjack, but in this game you do not get a sword. This makes people want to do more stealth than if they could just complete the game with stabing everyone under the sun. The blackjack is still used for takedowns ,although in an animation format instead a 'Click to hit' way, but you can press 'r' (by default) to hit with your blackjack. One verse one battles are easy enough with correct dodging along with one verse two battles, but any more and you are certain to loose life.
Overall Thief was still a good game, it has an immaculate stealth system and an atmosphere that keeps you on edge with the chance of guards always being around the corner. I will compare it to the original and say it clung to it like it should. So I will give this game 7/10 as it seems completely finished just could be better in all the above stated reasons. :3

I can finally write a review for Thief, as I've beaten the main story and the client jobs. My total playtime was about 24 hours, as I dicked around a bit and explored the city hub as much as I could, as there is quite a bit to do in "The City".
If you played the original games, you'll recognize a few things which hints at this game taking place several years after the originals, as in there are ruins of the Keeper's library, the old Cathedral from the first game is in ruins, and a few other places pop up as well. The city hub should be familiar too, if you played Deadly Shadows, as the names of various sectors are the same, like South Quarter, Stonemarket, Auldale, Docks, North Quarter, Old Quarter, and a few more. Point is, the developers kept the openness of The City that is seen in Deadly Shadows, as well as a similar layout.
Now, about the game. It's a good game, at least I thought so. I know there's been plenty of negativity, but a lot of that is, to me, whining about it not just being exactly what Thief: TDP, or Thief II: TMA is. The game is more Deadly Shadows than anything. And that's doesn't make it bad by any means.
One of the biggest complaints is about the predictable story and mediocre writing, but looking back at the first two Thief games, no one talks about the story or the writing, they talk about the atmosphere and open level designs. So the fact the story is just as predictable as the original Thief and has mostly mediocre writing doesn't make it bad, that's not what a Thief game is about. A Thief game is about atmosphere, level design, and lore. The Thief reboot has atmosphere, a lot of it, fog and eerie areas. It has some good level designs, as in, they tried. They didn't give their all, but the levels, as in the story levels, because the City hub is pretty big. But the story levels are like half linear, half kinda open to "wow, this is awesome". Two or three levels in particular are awesome, they come in during the last four missions, so I won't talk about them, because of spoilers and♥♥♥♥♥♥ (The fifth mission is this game's horror level, it's probably the best level)
The story, well, you play a Thief, your prodigee dies....or does she? Well, it's a little complicated, a little predictable. It was enjoyable, but it wasn't mind blowing like The Last of Us or Assassin's Creed II or Bioshock.
I think I got design and story out of the way, beside graphics, which are stunning. I mean, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ that lighting, I could look at that lighting all day. It's glorioius.
There's a lot to do besides the main missions. In between missions, you can complete client jobs from your old pal Basso, who's featured a little bit in Thief: TDP and Thief II. You can also grab side jobs from an inventor named Ector and a carnivale manager type person, Vittori. Most of the game I spend doing these client jobs and, even though they have no story in them, they're just as enjoyable as the main game.
Because I pre-ordered the game with GMG (I got it for like $30.) I got the Bank Heist DLC, which is undoubtedly a huge thank you to Thief II, has a wide open bank with a lot of security, the steampunk cameras. A big♥♥♥♥♥vault. It's pretty sweet.
I think that's all I have to say. I'll probably give it another playthrough later this year after Eidos Montreal patches the game even more (it still has a few bugs in it, you'll notice the AI is kinda messed up)
But I give this game a 8/10

My review of Fault Milestone One wasn’t particularly positive, and neither will this be. But having said that, Milestone Two is better than I dared hope. It takes big steps forward in quality from the first one, and though I still can’t recommend it, it shows the creators learning and improving rapidly.
My problems with Fault Milestone Two start with the opening. It doesn’t smoothly draw you into the story of the lives of the characters, instead it slams you right into an action scene without knowing what’s going on. There’s just too much information too fast, without giving you time to latch on to something human to care about. They kind of wrote themselves into this corner by ending Fault Milestone One with the start of this scene. The sequence is creative and impressive in its production quality. But I wish they’d rolled back the story, to give us some time to get reacquainted with the cast, and to know where they’re going. All it needed was a couple minutes of calm before the storm. Because as it is now, when the opening scene ends, the air goes out of the story. It takes a good while before it builds up momentum and feel like it’s going somewhere.
The marketing describes Fault Milestone Two as a “cinematic” visual novel, and it lives up to that moniker, both in good ways and bad. The positive is that the developers went to town with production values. Part one already looked good, but this takes it to another level, using multiple angles and simple animations during key scenes. The audio is also way above average for a visual novel, with both music and ambient sound doing a lot to heighten the sense of presence and mood.
I’m not sure if it was an intentional stylistic choice in order to make it feel more “cinematic”, but the writing feels distant from the characters. You rarely get any insight into what the viewpoint character is thinking or feeling inside. For much of the episode the primary viewpoint character is Ritona, the personal guard of a princess, who are on the run after enemies conquered their country. The viewpoint is so distant I often forgot that she, and not the camera, was the viewpoint. This harms some scenes quite bad.
For example, at one point the cast arrives at the port of a new city and are approached by a boy claiming to be a tour guide. His appearance doesn’t suggest he is anything other than what he claims to be. Ritona is suspicious of the boy, but because the scene is told entirely though dialog, she comes across as hysterically irrational. I wish Fault would make more use of the fact that it’s told through text. The dialog writing and portraits aren’t good enough to make up for it. Something made her suspicious, but without getting even a little hint of what it was, she just acts rude for no apparent reason. Movies have a hell of a time trying to convey people’s inner thoughts visually, while novels can easily move inside a character’s head and show us what’s going on in there. Fault Milestone Two does that a few times, so it isn’t averse to doing it. I wish it’d do it more often so I wouldn’t sit there trying to figure out whether a character is a racist, hates children, or if I’m an idiot who missed something.
Another problem I had is that it suffers from “RPG side quest syndrome”. I.e., it feels like the characters should be doing more important things than what they’re doing. There are multiple story threads, and they aren’t balanced as well as they could. One of them is underlined clearly as “the main story”, “urgent”, and “seriously, this is important” for the characters. And instead of relentlessly pursuing that threat, they go off and do something else. I wish they’d deemphasize the story threads that won’t be resolved within the episode you’re in, and just keep them simmering in the background for later.
It’s well worth playing this in fullscreen, as the default window doesn’t convey how high rez the artwork actually is. The passion that went into it is clearly visible. Almost every minor character gets their own sprite, and there’s tons of backgrounds and alternative angles to break up the traditional visual novel aesthetic. It’s a big story, with many moving parts, some marching forward to some goal we’ll only see in future installments. I’m interested in seeing what happens next, but I’m a bit worried about where it will end up. There’s so much going on already, that I hope future installments calm down a bit and don’t introduce anything new, for at least one episode. As it is now, the pace is glacial.
Fault Milestone Two is close to ok, but not quite there. I noticed myself skimming past the many lore exposition scenes, and some of the dialog is diabolically bad. Parts of the story hit like they should, and I certainly enjoyed the lavish production values. But it still feels like it’s written by amateurs, who don't inspire enough confidence that they know what they're doing. But at the rate they're improving, they might get it right next time, or the time after that. We'll see.

After the first episode that moved me to tears, the second episode is just as good. Just be careful of the character which res-

fault milestone two side: above returns with another story, directly following the events of milestone one, and like the first episode, it eschews the adventure fare for a more human story, which it pulls off nicely, though it keeps feeding us hints of the overall big picture journey.
This time around, there were less 'fantastic' elements, in that the magic presented corresponded more closely to conveniences we have with present-day technology (such as long-range communications, without spoiling anything specifically). And per its pedigree, rather than dwelling too much on the details of such magic itself, the story uses them to explore what people would do with such tools at their disposal, and the effects on both personal relationships and society in general, making a few not-so-subtle parallels to things people do in the present-day.
The presentation continues to be well done, including the music which was appropriate and enjoyable, and the artwork which felt quite improved over the first installment. The backgrounds for different locales seemed more diverse this time around as well. And though the basic themes of the story are ones that have been retold many times before in other places, a solid execution of the storytelling counts for much in my estimation, without necessarily having to create anything unique or complex (after all, what story *hasn't* been told over the last few thousand years of human history anyhow?), and fault delivers in this respect.
I found side:above's story to be less elaborate than milestone one's, which started playing out a number of different threads, giving hints of how they are weaved together here and there, and then finally completing and showing off the pattern at the end when all the pieces of the puzzle fall into place in an emotional crescendo. The sequel is a bit of a different style, more straightforward, with less mystery but more emotion sprinkled throughout, though certain threads are left hanging at the very end. This chapter is half a chapter it seems (with side:below to be forthcoming), and is thus unfortunately even shorter than the first episode.
So as with my review of milestone one, I continue to wait with anticipation for the next installment...

If you like Gauntlet-types, you'll like this.
Your fingers won't, though.

On the whole, this is a great tribue to Gauntlet style gaming.
Level design:  Complex well thought out levels make you think about how to best handle a situation.  Secrets abound, but are very cleverly hidden.  You will likely miss some.  Lack of random level generation is a minus, but one could be added at a later date.
Graphics:  Very nostalgic feel, but very good detail at the same time.  You even have the option to make it look like you are playing on an arcade machine or old CRT if you wish.  They did an excellent job of adding good graphics while keeping the same feel.
Sound:  The music is good, but didn't really stand out to me.
Gameplay:  Plays very well with a controller.  Could have been better though if you used the right analog for directional fire instead of having a hold to strafe key.  Also the campaign lacks a save feature.  This disappointed me.
Multiplayer:  If a player disconnects, they can recconect right to your game starting back at the last check point.  Lives are shared however, so if one player lags and gets killed by a trap repeatedly, it could eat all of your lives quickly.  However this is made up for by the fact that money isn't split, it's duplicated for both players, allowing both to buy all the upgrades they need, including more lives.
Final words:  There is a level designer you can use, but I don't see a way to share them with the community or for people to vote on them.  If there was, or if there was a map mutator for randomized level design in the options, this game would be perfect.  Still I highly reccomend this game as I like it far too much already, I couldn't stop playing.

The levels are designed, not randomly generated, which might hurt when it comes to replay value. The levels are very large, but are mostly empty. Most of the time you are smashing near-endless amounts of containers that primarily contain coins. The rest of the time is spent on effectively killing hordes of enemies in bullet-hell type of situations. There's a littlebit of puzzles and secrets sprinkled around, but not a whole lot it would seem. Checkpoints allow you to try again if you die, but you have limited lives. Reaching a new floor saves your progress.
You can select from a few different classes that behave quite differently. You can bring some friends with you in co-op mode if you wish. Sound-wise, there's not much to go on, but the art style is cool. Shops spread out in the dungeon allow you to purchase upgrades.
What I find to be the issue with this game is than it's simply not a lot of fun. With an addition of randomly generated, faster-paced levels and more interesting things to do, the game would look a lot more interesting. I think it has potential, but the experience, as it is, doesn't allow me to recommend this game. If you still think you'll like it, or just want to show your support to the developers, consider getting it during a sale. The regular asking price is rather high.

Virtually everything good about Far Cry 4 is riding directly on the coat tails of Far Cry 3.  It neither innovates or changes anything in terms of game play.  With that said it was really up to Ubisoft to give us an ultra polished and killer story, a few new tools to play with and exceptional presentation to sell us what is basically Far Cry 3 on a new map with new characters.  They fail to do this and it's a step backwards in nearly every category from it's predecessor, Far Cry 3.
The story wasn't all that engaging, lip synching was way off in certain parts during dialogue [Far Cry 3 was stellar, like playing a movie], some things you do don't even make sense/matter/have a point at all [Yogi & Reggie?], none of the characters really tie into one another like they were all written by different people in a silos and outside of a few new welcome events game play is virtually completely recycled content from Far Cry 3, and not even recycled well.  In Far Cry 3 I would cringe going into radio towers, in this it was nothing. That was my experience with nearly everything in this game.  The magic just isn't here.
I don't recommend it to anyone at full price.  Hold off till this is $20 or less.  What you're getting with Far Cry 4 is basically exactly what Blood Dragon did to Far Cry 3 and even that was more entertaining/original then this.  It's a decent enough game on it's own, I guess, but held next to Far Cry 3...  this is rather disappointing.
If you're starting the Far Cry franchise with this game, you're going to like it.  Do yourself a huge favor though and check out Far Cry 3 afterwards and everything I've said here will make perfect sense.  That title came out years ago and is superior in nearly every single way.
