Thief is a troubled reboot of an excellent stealth franchise. Garrett explores claustrophobic, circuitous city hubs that are linked together with frequent loading screens. Side quests are exercises in tedium as you search for the indirect route into treasure rooms. Once inside you’ll comb through empty drawers and watch Garrett grab every item. Missions take you outside hubs into more focused situations. The Northcrest Manor mission is one of few highlights, with numerous routes of infiltration and flames that encourage the use of water arrows.
When creeping around you’ll be disheartened to learn how the ground surface has little impact on stealth. Moss is gone too; so you have to crawl over endless puddles of broken glass that you can’t jump over because Thief only allows contextual mantle. Don’t try to grab anything when on glass because Garrett will crunch the shards and you’ll be heard. Luckily you can hear guards from far away, but they sound like they are inside your ear canal and will never call you taffer. The sound systems are worse than the original and this is compounded when guards repeat quips or copy each other’s lines.
Stealing loot and sneaking around guards can still be satisfying. The swoop mechanic has some merit and the focus blue hue is actually useful in the dull, foggy interiors. Unfortunately the story brushes over themes from the previous games as though the Trickster himself wrote it. It ends with an unresolved finale that does no favours to the jumbled story. This was not the way things were supposed to go. 6/10

TL:DR It is so close to a good, online, MTG game that is makes me sick, because it isn't a good, online, MTG game.
WTOC missed another chance to get this right. The UI in MTGO is terrible, crunched card text and clunky controls... it is a mess. So you think this game will fix that problem and that has to be a good things right? Nope. Sure, it looks better and some things work a lot better, but the game isn't the same. You don't get to play MTG, you get to play a toned down version on the game. It is a good game, but it isn't quite MTG.
Then we come to the constant animations. The UI improvement is much needed over all, but the excess art work bumping into one another is a nightmare.
The good news is you can get a lot of cards without spending real money, if you have a lot of time to play the story mode for those cards. I played two of them, I didn't hate them, but I was always a little ticked off that I had no idea what cards were in my deck, that I had no idea how to play this deck and so on, because it was a random deck given to me with no way to look at the cards before hand. That might be a complaint that the new player wont know to have, but for me it was a big deal, I'm used to playing TCGs and knowing what you hace in the deck matters. Clearly the answer was, "you are just supposed to put the biggest thing in your hand on the board and swing with everything every turn." and that is really boring. MTG has a lot more to offer than that.
I would love to see a real MTG game work well. Hearthstone does an insanely better job at being an online CCG. Which brings me to my last point. With digital card games, they get to control if you can trade your cards. If you can't trade them you HAVE to buy them, if you can't buy the 1 or 2 you want, you have to buy random packs to get the cards you need. The system for Magic Duels is pretty loose with the gold right now, but if you really want to jump in and start playing and enjoying yourself you are going to want to win, and Magic has been pay to win since the mid 90s. I could probably write an article on how WTOC evented pay to win, and MTG was their launching point.
In closing, it isn't terrible. You can probably play is casually without going nuts. Eventually you will find that you either are, or are not the kind of person that MTG is designed for. If you find you love MTG, Magic Duels will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off the moment you look at the real game, because you will see the short comings and the way it sort of abuses you. If you find that MTG isn't for you, then you will likely just forget about this and move on.
If you already know MTG pretty well, my advice would be to stay away. You could spend your money on the real game and have something real you can really do things with. I found that my MTG background pulled me to research the cards and try to form a deck and then track those cards down... and that is where is stopped. Spend a ton of cash, or a ton of time and pray that you open what you need because I've played with the game for 3 hours, and haven't seen anything about trading. If you can't trade there should atleast be a way to purchase 1 card, or craft it Hearthstone style.

Overview:
Highschool (sic) Romance is a visual novel set at a private school.  The main character is a boy sent to the school by his parents, only to find out the admission policy changed, and that the school is now an all-female institution of learning.  For reasons unknown, the principal of the school decides to admit the main character, but transvestize him to fit in for whatever reason.  Along the way, the main character encounters two other girls in addition to the principal.  Expecting more people to be encountered?  I know I was.
Graphics and sound:
Highschool Romance cuts so many corners, the programmers would be better suited for making globes.  The main thing that really stood out to me, was that gym class was being held outdoors, and yet the graphic on screen was the stock picture of the gymnasium:
I should have taken a closer look at the graphics when I got Highschool Romance, but for some odd reason, it wasn't until I got in game, that I noticed that every female in the game looks like they have a Hapsburg jaw.  In fact, the jaws are even more pronounced on the females than the male character, which may explain why the principal thought the main character could pass for female.
I was also disappointed by a scene in which another character attempts to put makeup on the main character, yet all you're treated to, is the same stock picture of the main character and his Plain Jane face.  Not even the tiny picture of the main character features him wearing makeup, yet you would think that such a scene was big enough to warrant a full sized screenshot.
The sound is nothing special.  The music isn't my style, but it's a letdown in the sense that it doesn't help set the mood of the game, which should be the be all, end all for a game's soundtrack.  There's very little sound effects to speak of, and none that stand out.
Positives:
Although the idea of transvestized (and sex changed) anime boys is nothing new, I did have a lot of fun with the concept of this game earlier on.  I was really humored in the beginning when the principal takes the main character shopping for girl's clothes.  It's obvious that shopping trip was designed by a man, because there was a lengthy trip for lingerie shopping.  (My personal favorite part of the game.)  But absolutely no mention was made of buying shoes.
Negatives:
The main character is in a school full of girls, and yet only three other people seem to exist.  The only interesting thing about the trio, is that they have Hapsburg jaws.  They're merely just stock characters masquerading as major characters with no interesting details or personality quirks about them.  The athletic girl in the game has the same physical attributes as every other athletic girl in Anime (including warrior women):  Her arms and legs are just as lacking in muscle as every other female in the game (or movie), and her breasts have the same amount of fat as every other non-athletic girl.
I'll admit to being suckered into those tags on Steam that infer Highschool Romance has nudity and mature content.  Both of these were lacking.  I was thinking that maybe I should play through the game again and see if there's any other path that offers nude scenes, but I lost interest in the game soon afterwards.  Just as well, because I noticed that all of the "interesting" pictures from the game are online outside of Steam, anyway, and I saw none that contained nudity.
Adult content aside, when a game has the word "Romance" in the title, I don't expect anything less.  The kissing I saw in the one path I took was just that; kissing without substance.  I felt no sort of attachment to the girl that the main character was kissing, and I'm sure the rest of the girls would have been equally disappointing.  No dialogue to infer how much in love both characters were with one another, zero passion in the pictures involving "love," and really, absolutely no sense of beauty in intimacy.
Conclusion:
The game would have been more aptly labeled "High School Transvestism," since it's an even bigger point of the game than the romance.  But I've learned my lesson:  Don't pay more than a dollar for a game that has only four achievements!

This game is difficult to write a review for. It ranges from brilliant to extremely obnoxious and in the end manages to be a flawed, okay game that really could have been great. It took me about 22 hours with quite a bit of exploring, not killing or knocking anyone out, and doing all of the side missions. If you rushed through the main story it would be MUCH shorter than that.
First things first, the actual thieving is great. The missions are, for the most part, well designed, and they have a good variety. Attempting to steal as much loot as possible without being detected really does have its thrills. Swooping in, stealing something while a guard's back is turned, and swooping back to the shadows feels immensely rewarding. The stealth is well done, and there is a variety of tools and upgrades (if you choose to use them) at your disposal. Most of the levels have quite a few different paths you can take. The Bank Heist DLC / preorder bonus is also quite fun, but probably not worth 5 dollars.
Many kudos to the game for the wide variety of difficulty options, graphic options, HUD options, etc. Pretty much every HUD item can be turned off, and you can adjust the difficulty and change various things (knockout/kills not allowed, no focus, no reticle for your bow, expensive resources, etc). There's even an iron man mode (die and it's over). Really, I can't give them enough props for this. Well Done.
On to the bad. The City, or the 'open world' portion of the game, is tedious at best and absolutely annoying at worst. I feel like this was tacked on due to the popularity of open world games, and in the end it really suffers for it. The game would have been better off without the entire city. It's neat that there is random hidden loot everywhere, but trust me, by the end of the game you'll be really tired of running across the same strange paths, dodging the same guards walking the same paths, and hearing the same dialogue lines. If I have to hear about why that one guard doesn't reek of ♥♥♥♥ anymore... Oh, and if you decide to turn on 'expensive resources', get ready for side missions to be pretty obnoxious to do. Expensive resources makes rope arrows 450g, and you often need one to get to an uninteresting side mission that will net you 50-100g.
Speaking of guards, the guard AI is, in a world, terrible. I can't hold this against them too much, as stealth games sort of thrive on terrible enemy AI (WHERE DID HE GO? ~5 seconds later~ IT WAS PROBABLY NOTHING), but I think it's worth mentioning.
I didn't experience any crash to desktops or graphical problems, but the game does have a few audio bugs. Sometimes guards would say the same piece of dialogue twice in a row, on top of each other, so you'd hear it twice. Othertimes the audio would go out of sync during a cutscene, or other audio would be playing when it shouldn't have been. There was one mission where I couldn't hear Garrett's voice over the sounds of the game. Again, not serious, but worth noting.
So overall, would I recommend this? Maybe-- To the right person. If you can slog through the city and the other undesirable parts, there really is some fun to be had. The story isn't fantastic, but the setting is interesting enough and the thieving is fun.
And finally, this game really isn't anything like Dishonored. Really, it's not. Corvo is a highly trained magical assassin who specializes in murdering dudes as quickly as possible. Garrett is a thief. He steals things. He says, during the prologue, something like "I don't just kill people." People will want to compare the two because they're both first person stealth games, but they really are not similar games. I cannot stress this enough. Do not expect this to be like Dishonored.

Im not very good at writing reviews, but what else can I say, this game is absolutely amazing. At this point in time I have over 16 hours on the game and haven't come across anybugs or glitches. The game has an absolute amazing soundtrack, and a huge amount of areas to loot and explore. Beforte I go into anymore detail, you start off as a group of survivors (the group changes depending on what group you pick) who are stuck in a war struck town full of scavengers (people like you who are just trying to get buy), Raiders (people who are also trying to get by, but will try and kill you and steel your stuff), Soldiers (they will shoot you on sight), and civilians (who are helpless but often have materials for you to steel. Note that steeling things from these people will lower morale). The game makes you ration supplies such as food and materials that can be used to craft a huge variety of things from weapons, ammo, beds, radios, medicine ect... Ontop of the big crafting aspect of the game, it also has a huge decision making aspect. Around every corner there is a tough decision to be made. These decisons range from; should I steel these supplies? should I take this person in, or leave him out on the streets? Do I help my fellow citizens or turn them away? Who in my group should I look after, and how? The list of these decisions goes on. All of these decisions will affect your group in some sort of way (either negatively or positively). The game does an amazing job of making you feel for the decisions you make, almost as if they are real decisions. Overall I would give this game a solid 10/10

COMPARING BEYOND EARTH TO CIV 5:
Having played Civ II, III, IV, V and BE before and after the Rising Tide expansion, there are pros and cons to each. Civ 5 is currently the most popular game in the franchise, and as such, I'll be comparing Civ BE to it.
Pros of Beyond Earth:
*Building wide (many cities) is viable, and even preferable. "Health" replaces happiness as the population limiter that was in Civ 5, and it is much much easier to deal with. For starters, health is more of a spectrum. There are bonuses to having extra health while the penalties for negative health are less intense and more gradual. I've always enjoyed being very expansionistic in the Civ games and was disappointed that this is less accessible in Civ 5. If you enjoy playing wide, ruling a vast empire, and have a thing for manifest destiny, Beyond Earth will certainly fill that more than Civ 5.
*Combat and tactics is the best it's ever been. Civ 5 made great progress in removing the ability to stack units, but my biggest complaint about it is the lack of unit diversity until around the WWII era. In Beyond Earth, you can get your infantry, cavalry, ranged, siege, air, naval, submarines, etc. all relatively early in the game. In Civ 5, you're stuck with only about 3 unit types for over half the game. There are also several special units for each "affinity." Each unit can be upgraded with different promotions selected as you level up your affinity. There are also sattellites that can be launched. These orbital units range from simple solar collectors that give you extra energy (gold) on the affected tiles to lasers that can bombard cities from space.
*Affinities. These are essentially the ideologies Civ 5 added in it's Brave New World expansion. You have one of three affinities to choose from which will dictate how humanity will progress through the game. Purity focuses on perfecting the human form. Supremacy merges humanity with machines. Harmony merges humanity with alien life. Your affinity can affect win conditions, unit types, available buildings/wonders, and diplomatic relations. It also functions as a great narrative device.
*Tech web. In Civ 5, you start in the ancient era and research technologies through a tree. In Civ BE, you start in the near future at the center of a tech web. The end-game techs are on the outside of the web, but you still choose which techs you want and when you want them. Though this can be a lot to take in, this does allow much flexibility in the way you build your empire.
You may have more things you like, but these are the large selling points for me.
Cons of Beyond Earth.
*Few victory conditions. You have a choice of domination, contact (similar to science victory), or an affinity-based victory. Though I personally go for domination victories regardless of which Civ game I'm playing, it is nice to have more options. Civ 5 allows you domination, cultural, science, and diplomatic victories, all of which have a fairly deep way of obtaining them. Beyond Earth basically has a domination victory and two separate science victories. (Your affinity victory will be largely dictated by your science and production.)
*Culture is shallow and there is no religion. Religion was added to Civ 5 via the Gods and Kings expansion. Though there was no religious victory, religion could influence your civilization greatly and influence diplomatic relations as well. Culture exists in the way of virtue trees, similar to the social policies of Civ 5. These virtues are well-worth gunning for which does add value to culture, but there is no way to "win" with culture. Focusing on culture would allow more virtues thus resulting in a stronger civ, but again, you can't win on culture alone anymore.
*Civ leaders are relatively stale. The passive buffs to each civ are interesting, but the personalities of each leader are pretty dry. Honestly, I think the biggest reason for this is that they are not representations of historical figures. Rather, the leaders are entirely fictious. This makes it more difficult to develop and flesh out an impressive persona. I find the leaders and their dialogue to be just as animated and dramatic as previous games in the series. The difference, however, is that when meeting Genghis Khan in a Civ 5 game, I have historical knowledge to draw on and it helps bring the character to life. Meeting the leader of Space Africa, I only have what I experience in-game.
I've also left out several aspects of Beyond Earth that others may enjoy. The Pros listed are simply the reasons that bring me back to BE. The game gets a bad rep, but there are things about Civ 5 that make me want to play it, and there are other things about Civ BE that make me want to play that instead.
At the end of the day, Civ 5 is the deeper game. There are more victory types allowing in different ways to focus on building your empire. All yields are critical in Beyond Earth, but not all of them result in victory. There are more leaders to choose from in Civ 5 as well. Despite this, I keep finding myself coming back to Beyond Earth. Both games feel different to me, and I highly enjoy playing them both. I personally have always loved having a massive army and empire while fighting wars with other superpowers. That experience is a rarity in Civ 5 whereas it's a promise in Beyond Earth.
I've left any mention of the Rising Tide DLC out of the review as I have not had ample time to play it. These are all my assertions on the base game. If you like civ, outer space, and are looking for a new experience then give Beyond Earth a shot. It's worth the price tag, but sales never hurt either. GRID 2 is an arcade racing game where you are the main star of the WSR, a tournament that goes around different parts of the world looking for reputation to grow and be a worldwide fenomenon. It's your responsability to win races and be the pretty face of WSR.
Let's start with some criticism, as this game has more positive things than negative ones, but it's always worth talking about these too. The menus are nothing special, and can be clunky sometimes. Soundtrack has it's moments but sometimes it feels really bland, repetitive and generic. The narrator can be very irritating sometimes, as the trigger for his voices don't seem to work very well, and his phrases repeat a lot. I can see how many people could find this game repetitive.
But where GRID 2 really shines are the driving physics. It's fast-paced arcade racing is easily one of the best I've ever played - The game achieves the feeling of intensity and speed very well. With it's absolutely gorgeous environment, challenging tracks and incredible atention to detail, GRID 2 gets you to the edge of your seat in a heartbeat. Every turn is a new challenge with new possibilities, and the thrill of speed is represented perfectly through very well recorded sounds, fantastic lightning and post-processing. In fact, the graphics have aged very well, and still are more beautiful than some AAA games out now. Each stage is very interesting and it has it's own personality - Some stages are incredibly hard and tense, and the representations of the cities were absolutely mindblowing to me.
Considering it's little flaws that can be somewhat irritating sometimes, GRID 2 does very well in places that haven't been done in ages. With all that this game has to offer, it's really hard to find another good arcade racing game like it, specially on PC. Definitely a must play for the fans of the genre.

Alright. So let me tell you why Hammerwatch is awesome. Like most of my games I bought it some time back because it was on sale and after watching the trailer I decided that one day I'd like to play it. So in my infinite quest to get more badges I thought it was about time to see if this game was actually any good or if I'd drop it as soon as I got my three cards and left. Boy was I surprised by this one. I soon as I started playing it I could tell the diffrence, this was a game that had the classic spirit of the Rouge-like gerne to it with all the things that made it fun. First off, it was visually very appealing with it's classic 16-bit style of graphics which I felt only added to it's retro theme. Next, was it's simple yet intence combat system, ok I know what you're thinking and running up to a guy and hitting him in the face isn't very complex but when there are hundreds of enemies on screen and dodging them is just as important as getting a super long combo chain of destruction combat becomes just as thrilling as it is desperate. Lastly, the game is full of secrets. I don't know if I spent more time trying to find my way, killing all the monsters, and looting every thing that wasn't nailed down or combing the levels making sure I hadden't missed anything. Also this game is challenging. The first few playthroughs I did were just to figure out how to not die on the first level. All-in-all I like this game. I brought me back to a better time in my life where I played games not to get achivements nobody else had or get a badge saying I spent more time and money on it than others, but because it was not just a game good enough to waste a few hours on and leave once I got what I wanted; but insted actually play it all the way to the end, beat it, and still want to keep playing. Even if it was the same stuff I had just played. This is one of the rare few games I've encountered that not only did I have more fun that I ever thought I would have gotten out of it, but that I know I'll still get every time I come back to play it. 5 Stars all the way.

It's fair to say that when one sees an Indie game (especially when for sale cheaply) one can lower one's expectations a bit. You might forgive some length of the game, or quality, or clunkiness in mechanics. This is one of those rarer games where NONE of that applies. It's extremely polished.
As others may well have commented, there's obvious parallels here to the old classic Gauntlet. I'm probably going to commit gaming heresy here, but I'll confess that Gauntlet was rather a mixed bag to me. As an arcade game that certainly popularised hack'n'slash (and there was so very little DnD related stuff in the arcades up until then), I loved it. I also loved the merits and fun in having 4 players crowd round the unit, each with their own controls, and I also loved the fact you could stick another 10p in to just add HP to your character, extending your progress.
However, I disliked that it was obviously an arcade game, written with the emphasis of milking coins from you as quickly as they could get away with. You would often think "that was a fairly good and long game" only to realise you'd stuffed a quid's worth of 10p's in, where you'd probably get the same amount of game time on another game for half the price. This ias the main reason why I felt it never really translated well to home conversion.
Thankfully, Hammerwatch takes the best bits of Gauntlet, throws away the coin-stuffing problem, and improves on a few things too, making it very much it's own unique thing. It is, of course, very retro in nature - older, large-pixelled graphics, 2D view, low HP and more old-fashioned gameplay. However, these are not done for the sake of nostalgia - they perfectly fit, and are indeed designed very much around these premises.
Where the game truly shines are in mechanics - it's not-too-fast offers fluid movement, and solid nimble attacks. You soon pick up the distance from enemies which are best for bashing them, and the time-honoured tradition of funneling enemies works so very well here. In a nutshell, it just plays so beautifully.
There's no levelling up of character through XP. However, your character can be improved through amassing the tons of coins thrown around the place (you'll need them), and by visiting specific vendors. One quite lovely trick of the game is utilizing where these vendors are - a 2D map can easily fall prey these days to being quite old-fashioned and tired. Thankfully, due to where these vendors are, and that there are several exits and entrances to each level, you'll need to dart back and forth quite a bit, and it never really feels like a chore.
Put simply, this game does very much "what it says on the tin", and does it brilliantly. It does adopt a traditional 3 lives system (extra lives can be earned), but you really feel that it is well-balanced, appropriately challenging and I never once felt that a death was cheap or anything other than my fault.
If that were not enough credit to it, then there's one massive one that is very dear to my heart, and that concerns difficulty. I openly admit to being an older gamer (I'm nearly 50) and disabled. A lot of the time, it doesn't really hinder my gameplay too much, although my reactions have naturally slowed a bit over the years. But I do have bad days, and there's nothing worse than starting a game, getting many hours into it and then having a bad day which means you simply cannot progress in that game because you're finding it too hard that day (and nothing takes your mind off the bad days better than gaming).
So, I'm a fan of the theory that you can NEVER have too many difficulty options. If you select the "vanilla" easier option when starting a game, you'll find Hammerwatch still quite challenging, and if you're used to the standard of what easy mode truly means, then you won't get to the end, most likely.
However, you can tweak the difficulty even further, with "crutches" (strangely appropriate for me) - regenerating HP, double-damage just to name two main ones. Conversely, there are also the opposite - tricks to make the game harder still, such as no earning of extra lives and more. So, a number of options for anybody.
It's often a situation that I'll end up modding the INI files of some games due to inadequate difficulty settings, but the downside of this is it can often be a balancing act to get it just right for you without it destroying interest in the game. I found that these "crutches" were perfect for me - they made the game much easier, but kept it interesting enough even though only the stupidest of mistakes will leave you in trouble.
In summary, I can't recommend this game highly enough. It offers what you'd expect and much more. It is so very well polished and designed extremely well. With those added thoughtful difficulty settings, that really makes it a cherry on one delicate, but utterly more-ish cake.

So Far Cry 4... My short answer is sure its worth the money (for me) but is it worth it for you?
Storyline: So obviously the storyline is no where as good as Far Cry 3s, but that does not mean its bad. Throughtout the story your fighting with the Golden Path with the two real annoying leaders who never can agree on♥♥♥♥♥♥ I wish the story had a little more meaning to fight for rather then, I need to kill all these people so I can spread my Mother's ashes. I find myself enjoying myself more when I am just exploring then actually doing the Main Quest. Also to note there is some copy and paste missions from far cry 3. However still a pretty good Story, not Far Cry 3 status but still better then any Call of Duty. I do wish that you heard more from the main antagonist Pagan more often as he just disappears intill almost the end of the story.
Side Missions: In Far Cry 4 there is a ton of side missions to do, lighting your map up. Some of the side missions get real tedious after a while, but they give good money and karma so its worth it. With all these missions you will be busy for hours after you complete the main quest.
Graphics: The graphics in the game are real amazing... Well when your standing still atleast. When just walking arounrd the graphic look stunning with himalayas in the background. The second you get yourself into a car or start wingsuiting the graphics become a blur and you begin to see the real flaws with in the graphics. That is still an issue in Far Cry 3, but thinking out of a Far Cry setting it seems a bit annoying. Most (almost all) textures in the game are amazing looking for being an open world. However there are some ugly looking textures when it comes to the rocks and the water. But in all still a jaw dropping experience.
Audio: The audio in the game is by far the best I have heard in any game. When running through the forests of Kyrat I feel like I am in the world, hearing all the sounds of nature ( deers, monkeys, elephants, etc). The sound track is done so nice, with all the ambient sounds and entertaining mixes to listen to. Speaking of mixes however I did found the Radio station a bit annoying at times. When you constantly hear the radio talk host Rabi Ray Rana repeat the same damn things over and over again. Which I know it would take forever to make enough dialogues to not hear repeats but when Playing GTA V I dont hear them repeat as often. My last and only gripe with the Audio is that you never get to really hear the protagonist Ajay Ghale. As he only speaks a couple of words at a time.
New Features: The game has done a real good job at making it feel fresh without making the game loose its purpose. The saying, "Don't fix something that's not broken" is present in Far Cry 4, at the base, but they have added some many new things to the Far Cry series that its amazing. Some features that they have added that are worth noting are; being able to throw meats to get animals attention, the ability to throw knifes, being able to purchase the wingsuit instead of waitin half way through the game to obtain, gyrocopters, hovercrafts, being able to call in backup, a refined map editor, actual good co op, and a pleather of new vechicles to choose from along with some old favorites from Far Cry 3. There is of course a lot of other features but those are just the ones worth mentioning.
A.I.: I feel they did a good job at A.I this time around, the bots are noticably harder and smarter compared to Far Cry 3, but it makes it more enjoyable and satisfying when you get a kill. The animals on the other hand is kind of a mixed bag. They do do a good job at being animals I guess, but they always seem to come and attack at the worst times, like that its in the code for them to just ♥♥♥♥ you other when you're already in♥♥♥♥♥♥ Overall A.I. is pretty good.
Problems worth to Note: There are some issues in the game that I will note now; bad optimization (I feel it is no where as good as far cry 3s optimization), steam overlay does not want to work (for me atleast), cutscenes are unskipable, you have to wait through a long boring slide of things when you launch the game up everytime. Money in the game is way to easy to obtain and that I see myself always waisting money on things so my wallet isn't full. And lastly that it uses uPlay.
Conclusion: In conclusion it diffently has its spot in your library if your new to the Far Cry series or if your a veteran. At this very time I give the game a 7.5/10. If ubisoft come through and change most of the problems (being) textures, cut scenes. and optimization then heck I would change my rating to 9/10. However at the end of the day it is your choice to make the decession to buy not me. Happy Gaming. IGN 9/10- Went into a heavy guarded fortress and murded everyone with myself and my elephant.

First off you have to install Ubisoft's UPlay client.  I guess Steam's DRM isn't good enough.  More accounts and more passwords to remember.
Before I even got to play I was annoyed at the long cut scenes.  I paid for the game already, why does Ubisoft insist on forcing me to watch long, obnoxious scenes?
Once I actually got to start playing I noticed mouse lag - some of the worst I've ever experienced.  A combination of config file fixes found online and turning down the graphics quality got me past that.
Next came the dark shadows.  Anything covered by a shadow was black - I couldn't see anything.  After spending hours testing every video setting imaginable, I finally figured out it was SLI (I'm running a GTX 690).  I found another fix (hack) using NVIDIA inspector and SLI compatibility bits.
Next was flickering.  If you use SMAA anti-aliasing things flicker everywhere.  Ultimately to get decent performance and visual quality I've turned off AA all together.  Even still I occasionally see flickering shadows.
Much like Far Cry 3, this game can't seem to figure out what I'm pointing at.  Sometimes I have to re-position myself several times to search a dead enemy or skin an animal.
Did I mention the obnoxious, long cut scenes that interrupt the game that you can't skip?
There's not much new here; this feels like an expansion to Far Cry 3 with better graphics (though you'd better have dual GTX 980's if you want to run at that highest settings).  Overall it's still a fun game, but until they clean up some of the issues I wouldn't recommend paying full price for it.

The game is good but if you have Performance issues please read below.
(This guide is for Ultra but can be applied to other configs as well.)
The game has a few issues performance wise. these can be, for the most part, suppressed. In the graphical settings I recomend setting SHADOWS to HIGH, AA to SMAA, AMBIENT OCCLUSION to SSBC, TREES RELIEF to OFF, and maybe GEOMETERY to VERY HIGH/HIGH. also try these in GamerProfile.xml: DisableLoadingMip0="1" (I don't use this because of texture degredation) , AlphaToCoverage="0" (barely noticable in-game and gives a pretty good FPS boost), and GPUMaxBufferedFrames="3" (this should help with stuttering). With these settings and a 280x the game is stable and looks almost identical to Maxed settings. I hope this will help some people with performance.

With this installment Fault Milestone becomes arguably the best Visual Novel series on Steam. Not only that but Alice in Dissonance could even be compared to the VN kings Nitro+ and MAGES. in terms of overall quality. Keep up the fantastic work Alice. From the opening minutes to the closing credits this VN is an incredibly well written, well directed, and well paced journey all the way through.
Picking up at the exact moment the original left off you're greeted with surprise after surprise on the journey along with mystery, suspense, lots of feels, and wonderful wonderful character development. Even the end credits are wonderfully done and will leave a lasting impression. The rise in production quality from the first is immediately apparent even in the first few lines of the VN, and that is saying something considering the level of polish the first one had. Although this installment also follows the same anime-ey/manga-ey (it was supposed to be a manga originally) "come to a new place, meet new people, move on" story arc style (similar to One Piece for a popular example) the characters and pacing are leagues ahead of anything similar I've seen especially considering this is from an indie studio.
Also much like the first the overall plot regarding the journey home gets touched mostly at the start, and any scenes regarding the overarching story after are sprinkled throughout allowing the urgency of the situation to still be clear even as the VN is in the middle of the story arc for the new location. Those who have played the first will also be pleased to know that the great art from the first has somehow improved along with a lot more backgrounds and transitional effects that really make this VN stand out from many others I've played. The OST for this game is also one of the best I've heard in a VN, and thankfully the opening movie is slower than the first which moved so fast it was fairly difficult to read it all.
The only cons I can think of are:
-This game is too great not to get Voice Acting, but the lack of any voice actors allow for the higher quality of everything else. I can only hope that they will one day be able to patch some Voices in.
-Some of the art for the one-off characters is of noticeably lower quality than of everything else. While this isn't exactly a problem the level of polish this VN has definitely makes the disparity in quality stand out more.
Overall:
9.5/10
I can only hope the rest of the series continues to be as great as this release was.

Highschool Romance is a slice-of-life visual novel developed and published by Dharker Studio. After moving to a new city, it's the start of Shoji's final year of high school but because of a crazy mix-up by his parents, he is due to attend an all girls school. Backing out now would be a costly process that would delay him from graduating on time with his class, fortunately, the principal has a solution to this strange crisis...pretend to be a girl in order to attend. You soon discover that what would have been a "dream-come-true" to many a male student is actually a lot more complicated. In this unusual situation, can you survive, make friends, or even find love? Highschool Romance is a light hearted V.N. full of teen angst and hilarious situations.
Graphically, this visual novel is a wonderful delight to the eyes and has a top notch presentation just as all of Dharker Studios V.N.'s do. It has a manga-inspired artstyle that is extremely gorgeous and filled with bright colors as well as beautiful effects. Also of note is the fantastic audio quality and a quite memorable soundtrack which is delightful and fits the story perfectly. In summary, the excellent visuals and terrific aurals do a great job of complimenting the outrageous yet intriguing plot of Highschool Romance.
This novel was a great read with endearing art and a very well written if not whimsical story. There are many decisions to make and multiple endings so the replayability is fairly high. Also, this V.N. offers a few options such as an image gallery to unlock as the narrative progresses, there are also Steam Achievements and Steam Trading cards to collect. In the end, Highschool Romance is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to fans of the visual novel genre and anyone in general who likes "fish out of water" stories.

Make no mistake, this certainly isn't a terrible game, but I've played better, and it's got a lot to do with how it's only difficult due to poor design choices.
Simply put, those new ships and upgrades you can buy and upgrade over the course of the game? Not optional. Not in the slightest. You're going to notice early on that your performance is kind of hamstrung by the fact that ALL of your ships have an absolutely abysmal reload rate, and the only way you're going to remotely keep up with the increasing onslaughts that the enemies throw at you is to upgrade your clip sizes and reload rates to the max as early on as you can - and when I say reload rate, I don't mean the reload rates for your main gun, which you cannot upgrade the reload rate of by any means.
Well, that's not so bad, you may say, doesn't that add to the challenge of the game?
It does. Right up until you start realizing that you are literally having too many enemies and missiles thrown at you to shoot down unless you buy a lot of expensive single-use powerups, and I mean expensive as in "you will have to grind entire early-to-mid-game missions at least once to buy a single pack of the only truly useful one", and that's not even factoring what it's going to take to get the late-game ships and upgrades that, again, you're absolutely going to NEED in order to stand a chance.
Basically, you can't beat this game without grinding like crazy, and that's not challenging. It's a timesink and nothing more. It's really too bad, because there's really not much wrong with the game itself - it's simple, good, lead-the-target fun that allows you the chance to negate all damage if you're quick and accurate enough... at least until the game starts throwing too much at you to handle without the need for powerups. I did beat the game, but I didn't four-star every mission, and the ending isn't worth it. I have my doubts that 100%ing the game is worth the time it'll take to beat it, and I personally can't recommend this game unless you wait for a rather hardcore discount; it's not worth eight dollars.

The best way I can think to describe this game is as a top-down scrolling 'Missile Command' style game.  You click on a spot, and a missile flies there, making you have to lead your targets a bit so you hit them.  The challenge of the game comes from racking up hit streaks to increase your score.

The game is a basic arcade shoot-em-up. You are in control of two ships, a primary vessel geared towards attacking and a secondary vessel with a variety of support options.
The game's story is Command and Conquer with you playing as the UN versus NOD, for some reason. The dialogue is a bit simple and nonsensical.
The gameplay is standard fare except for the nature of your weapons. There is a delay between when you fire and when you hit so for fast moving enemies (all of them) you have to lead. A lot of enemies also bob and weave meaning you have to be good at predicting their next position. The levels themselves are largely samey and are very short in length. There are some gimmicks in levels, such as your vessels getting split up, having to defend civilians and night battles but its really the same thing again and again. At least for me, the combat was satisfying because of that delay and it is satisfying to blow up enemies and watch the debris fall into the water.
The sound design is steller. You get nice ambient radio chatter, satisfying explosion sounds and distinctive noise made by each enemy and missle type.
On the whole, I'd say its a nice short arcade blaster worth its budget price.

So, the new Thief game has come and a lot of people have a lot of oppinions on it. Personally, the old Thief games are some of my all time favourites and I gladly place Thief 1 & 2 at some point in my Top 10 list of best games ever. I am also a big fan of the more recent Dishonored game, really hoping for a sequel there, and I hold it as the true spiritual successor to the old Thief games. So how does this new, actual THIEF Thief game hold up?
I am glad to say that I enjoyed it! When judges on it's own merrits, it is a very enjoyable experience with some great gameplay throughout. The story is a bit simplistic, especially when compared to the old games stories, but there are a lot of layers to the story and the universe that you really have to dig for to get a glimpse of. For example, there is a very interesting theory circulating that this Thief game actually takes place in the same universe as the old games, only set about 800 or so years into the future, with this games Garret being a sort of reincarnation of the old games Garret. There is a theme about the cyclical nature of time in the game, and there's a side-quest in particular that discusses the idea of all parts of time existing at the same time all the time (sorry if it sounds a bit confusing from my explanation), but it would make sense that this story could be a continuation as well as a reboot at the same time.
The best part of the game is clearly the gameplay, and stealing things really takes the main stage, as is appropriate. There is almost always something to steal in any part of the environment, and sometimes you happen upon special loot that is especially valuable. A lot of it is also hidden or contained in special places where you actively need to find the loot or figure out how to unlock it in some very intricate ways, which gives a thorough player a great sense of rewarding the dedicated playstyle. The addition of the "swooping" mechanic to Garrets moveset is also really enjoyable, and it works as a sort of counter to the "Blink" ability that was the absolute best part of the stealth system in Dishonored.
It is very interesting to observe the evolution of the first person stealth genre visible here, as the original Thief games so strongly influenced the development of Dishonored, where they borrowed elements very hevily and used them to an extremely good extent, whereupon the developers here for the new Thief game were very heavily inspired by the style and development of Dishonored in turn. A great example is the three-part introduction to the world of the game that both Dishonored used (Tales from Dunwall) as well as Thief (Stories from The City).
There are some aspects that detract from the overall experience of Thief, however. There are a couple of times when bugs can ruin the immersion, however they were fairly infrequent and none of them were really game-breaking. The worst one I ran into was durring a chapter where you ride in an evelvator and at the end of the ride have to climb out through a hatch in the top of the elevator. Upon trying to climb up, Garret got caught in a hanging-animation from the hatch and refused to climb up. After trying to climb, and then letting go and trying again, I was finally able to get on top of the elevator on my third or fourth try, so the problem solved itself after all. Problems like this, however, are rather frustrating to run into, even if they never ruin the experience completely.
The navigation system can also be somewhat frustrating at times, due mainly to the fact that there is no real "jump" button in the game. The player can only perform a leap of some kind at certain points, like near an edge to jump accross to another platform. At times this jump can behave unexpectedly, however, and sometimes even gets the player killed. An example is any situation where you need to jump to a hanging rope, where you need to be perfectly aligned with the rope and do the exact kind of jump the game asks you for. If you don't, Garret won't aim for the rope and can sometimes instead just jump of the platform and throw himself to his death. This happened a couple of times durring my playthrough and it got very frustrating at some points.
Overall, however, I would possitively recommend this game to everyone. If you're an old Thief player, or if you enjoyed Dishonored, you will be able to get a lot of enjoyment out of this game if you are able to judge the game based on it's own merrits rather than only comparing it to how great the originals were. Even though I absolutely love the old games, as I said, I was able to accept the changes the developers had made to the mechanics and I ended up enjoying the new Thief game a whole lot. And if you're a gamer that hasn't yet experienced this type of game, I would also recommend it, as it is a pretty nice introduction to stealth mechanics with a very well designed game. However, for these types of people I would probably also suggest that you give at least Dishonored a try before hand, as it is the most well designed stealth game of the modern era. While I would also suggest the old Thief games, they can be very challenging to a newer player, but if you are brave enough (both figurativelly and litterally), you should definitely give them a try as well, you won't regrett it!
As a final touch, I have to compliment Thief on being a ridiculously well ported/optimised game with some amazing graphical options on all fronts. Running the game at max settings is also a true treat for the senses as the world is strictly beautifull to behold both visually as well as through it's audio. Finally, I have to say I really enjoyed the new voice actor for Garret. While not as amazing as the originals Stephen Russell, the new voice actor manages to capture the feeling of Garrets personality and his internal monologues really well. At times, his delivery made it feel like I was playing the old games again, which is a really nice thing indeed.

I...do not know how to describe this game.....I am....conflicted. it is a fun game. It really is. But.....
To begin with, I have never played the original thief series. I know nothing of the characters, story, or lore up to this point. I only know what this game showed me. It was.. an interesting experience. I feel as though the start was a bit rocky. The game, for being a reboot, expected me to be attached to characters that I had hardly even known their name before trying to make me feel sorry for them...but besides a slightly rushed beginning, the story itself is interesting enough to catch attention.
The stealth mechanics are, while not unique, fun. You feel like you're outsmarting the opponents half the time, and when you mess up it feels like it is your own fault....however....There are...moments. The open world stealth mechanic, where there are guards on every corner, and you need to wait a couple of minutes for the patrol to move on make the game play come to a screeching halt.
It is...it's like the game is flowing, as you go through stealing items, outsmarting guards, and making it work out. during story quests, the story was driven home by the guards chatter. But...once again the entire open world hub where you go from mission to mission didn't have much to offer in this. No interesting characters talking about anything, nothing to warrant having to go between it or even to explore when there wasn't a mission going on.
The collectables were interesting enough, and I have a weakness for finding journal entries in every game so those both added another layer of interest...that being said, this isn't the type of game that I would purchase right of the bat at full price. Even with the challenge mode, it, in my humble opinion, isn't worth a full price purchase. But if you have some disposable income, and are looking for a reasonably fun experience I would purchase this game. If not, wait until its on sale and buy it up, it would be worth it for a bit less....but this is just this Pider's personal opinion.

A fun and immersive diversion that could have been so much more but ultimately failed to grow further and improve, especially since the developers themselves threw in the towel and abandoned the game. Potential lost but on a positive note, people can still play and battle amongst each other, just don't expect any balance changes or glitch fixes. With that said, I still recommend it; but for me, I fail to see why I should keep it in my hard drive.

The drag & drop system is way more easier to use than the complicated syntax and text placement in Ren'Py.
You can directly and easily customize the title screen layout and look, as well as the settings menu, the size of the buttons, message windows, texts, ...
There's no template to create a Gallery though, but it can be done easily with a bit of time by using image buttons for thumbnails and placing everything in a separate scene.
Talking about gallery, the softare doesn't come with images nor music (just a sky background for the title screen, an alternate message window and some buttons) so you'll have to mount your own library (well, it's a given of course, but having placeholders could have been useful).
The use of coloured tags makes things pretty clear and legible but I'm not sure how helpful it will be for very long scenes (on my laptop, it begins to lag at around 300 items but it would require a very long scene to need that much, I think). But the ability to preview the work at any point is great.
Note : You might want to write the dialogues in wordpad or something because the text window in Tyrano Builder is quite small.
Lastly to place flags and whatnot, you'll have to use Javascript.
Edit 1.7 : Finally a backlog. Also, the new features are good, but be careful when using some of them (like the UI customization) with your existing projects because it could mess up your layout. The positioning tool has never been better, too, and thus, all my past grievances disappeared with this new patch.

Tyranobuilder,
Is, basically, like the big brother of Novelty; a freeware Visual Novel engine that does the same, but in a somewhat more complex way.
What TyranoBuilder makes stand out is the thing they promote so much. The GUI is super easy to use and very, very straight forward.
The only thing that TyranoBuilder does NOT do for you is to come up with a good story and personal artwork. Which is a pretty important aspect when it comes down to this.
So, would I recommend it? I give it a yes, because I do have some experience in designing VN's through other applications and TyranoBuilder is by far the "fastest" to get a presentable result. Ofcourse, the quality of your production all comes down to your own creative / writing skills and you won't puff out a quality product in just 10 hours. But, besides of that it's a very good product; just the tool to get started; especially if you're not good at coding.
Winning in this game requires luck. Too bad I don't have it.

I have been playing Magic The Gathering since its creation by Richard Garfield.   I love this game, and this game Magic Duels is the best Online Game for Magic I have played in a very long time.  The only thing I think would improve this game is if it were possible in the Deck Builder to search for specific cards. I.E. Were Wolves, or Creatures with Life Link, etc.  I just personally think a text field where you can type what you are looking for in your collection would greatly steamline the Deck Building Experience...

-Its a free to play magic game, with versus and 2-headed Giant.
-There are cards out of 5 different sets (Origins, Battle of zendikar, oath of the gatewatch, Shadows over Innistrad and Eldritch Moon).
-There are about 45 kampagne missions. (Where you play a fix deck)
-The KI plays ok, but after getting a few better cards it is really not a challange anymore. Its pretty bad in 2-headed against Ai.
-You get Gold through winning
(Against Ai: 5-Easy, 10-Middle, 15-Hard  -- 30 - 2 Headed Giant
(In Versus: 30 (In 2 headed & solo))
-One Booster costs 150 Gold(or 1,80 Euro). So it will take quite a while to get all the cards (about 10k Gold if the progress bar is correct)
Positiv:
++Free-to-Play
+Realtiv good AI with many different decks
+Only about 10 secs search time for an opponent
Negtiv:
- Deck building is bad. There is no search function, no keywords,... All you can do is sort by color, by rarity, by mana costs and by set. Still quite lacking.. plz at least put keyword search in... like Sacrifice /Discard / Madness ....
- Takes quite a bit of time to gather enough cards to build a fun deck.
-No ranked matchmaking (or at least not visible)
-Leaver
All in all a nice free to play Magic game with some problems.
My wishes would be the keyword search and better Ai!

This game is a really great VN. The story flows and the characters are just as engaging as they were in the first one. The graphics are some of the most beautiful I have ever seen in a game and the soundrack is equally amazing. My computer is a little old so some of the CG scenes lagged for me but I am sure that on a better computer they will run just fine. It is really important that you play the first Fault Milestone before you play this one because the story won't make as much sense to you if you just start with this one(the first game is a little slow and expostion heavy but develops a really compelling world and characters over time with a story that will grip you and leave you wanting more by the end of it.). The real plus to this game though is the character development; they are not just the awesome protagonists that we grew to love in the first game but they start to grow in such a way that will make you root for them even more than you had before (Selphine and Rune's relationship in particular is a highlight).
As for the negavtives there are a couple. The first being a few side characters that had a little more screen time than I personally cared for. In my review of the demo I mentioned Flora, Misha and Riggs and how their story kind of bored me a few times but I gave it a pass assuming their arc would develop into something really interesting but by the time I finished the game I was a little dissapointed. Their story did not really go anywhere and felt like wasted time. I know there is a sequel already in the works and that they will probably somehow play into the main plotline but honestly their side story felt like kind of a drag to get through (especially since I had to watch it twice because for some reason I wasn't allowed to skip past the parts I had seen in the demo).
The other major gripe I had is connected with my previous point in that the story in this one kind of felt like filler for things to come. I do not want to spoil anything but the first couple hours of the game was wonderful in how it set everything up and immediately pulled you in. The game unfortunately does not really capitalize on that too much and there are a lot of loose ends left by the time the game ends. I was legitmately surprised when the game ended and not because it had a great cliffhanger (it doesn't) but because it felt a little incomplete (I actually said out loud "Wait...that's it?").  For a little background; Fault Milestone 2 has been split into two games "Fault Milestone Two: Above" and "Fault Milestone Two: Below" and it definetely shows. I'm sure there is a perfectly good reason for splitting the game but after finishing Above it feels very much like an incomplete game which is a little dissappointing.
Despite my gripes this game is still worth your time; especially if you enjoyed the first game. It, for the most part imporves on the first one and despite my personal problems with the story "Fault Milestone Two: Above" has a great story that will make you impatient to discover how everything pans out for Selphine, Ritona and Rune.

I started playing Maplestory way back since Patch 1.83. Or 2007....The game has certainly changed much over the years...and will always keep changing, don't ever expect it to be the same for more than 3 months.
My main character has been level 200 for many years now and I have a 200 NPC In Kradia. So take my word for it, the game is now, just as playable as it ever was.  Many of the things we know and love are gone, like the challenges, or Temple of time being the most difficult location in the game (most players walk over pink bean now like he's a snail)..The direction of the game has changed, and is much more story driven now. Before you just made a character and made it your own story. But you can choose from several. AND I MEAN SEVERAL...different classes with a pre-determined story. And advance them to lv 250 (new level cap)  by grinding on monsters or doing party Quests.
The game seems overwhelming at first, but once you get the world map down, you'll be navigating like a pro in no time. The 2D anime style chibi art makes the game much more social than any 3D MMO so feel free to take a break and grab a chair..(literally a chair) that you can buy or collect from events...and sit down and make some cyber friends! Or go gear up and be the God of Damage and solo every boss in the game and wow your friends.
My major complaint about the game (and it's been this way forever) is that many ways to grow are all based on luck....nothing makes a person more angry than to spend Hard earned cash on a scroll, that ends up failing. It's always better to let other people do it....but on the other hand...you can sell sucessful gear at a higher price.
This game used to be VERY ADDICTING...fortunately I was able to break off of it and do other things with my life after I hit 200, but the new update and all still hasn't pulled me back in. If you plan on getting into this game....you will certainly have a blast...all the confusion at the beginning is worth it and it has something for everyone!

GRID 2 offers a balance of arcade and simulator racing. How you want to race is up to you, choosing the damage model and how much of a challenge your opponents will be. The single player follows a plot of you aspring to be a multi-disciplined and world renowned racer, becoming a top driver in standard closed circuit racing to one on one Togue racing. As you progress you'll earn cars for your racing career and you get to personalise each one with choosing the livery, racing number and sponsors. Just don't get too attached to your paintwork. The AI in this game has a bit of a road rage mentallity. That being said, take care when slowing down for corners. Especially if one of them's right up your behind.
I recommend this game if you're looking for a racer to play on PC.

This game moves at a glacial pace. Things develop very slowly without any sort of excitement. I found myself going through the motions, turn after turn, without feeling any attachment to my settlement. After I while, I realized that I was not enjoying any of it.
As a new player to the Civilization games, I started of with a single player match with random settings and the tutorial enabled. I found that the tutorial was very weak and it failed to explain many of the basic concepts of the game. Help files, while extensive, are blue text on dark blue background in a tiny font and extremely unpleasant to read. User interface suffers from the same problem. Resource displays are very small and difficult to read. The game fails to clarify how various resources work.
Technology trees are vast and complicated, and with the poor state of the tutorial and help files it would take months of game-play to fully understand them fully.
Combat is boring, and like everything else in the game, slow. Exploration is not very interesting and notifications of what you found are very anticlimactic.
As far as strategy games are concernt, I'm used to playing games like Age of Empires and XCOM, and if you are like me and enjouy games like that, you probably won't like the glacial pace and lack of excitement in Civilization: Beyond Eart.

Only drawback that I can see is that there is no "Quit" button, but hitting the [esc] key is their substitute for one (gives you the option to quit).  Not mentioned anywhere, but hey, now you know...

Into the Void
Mozg Labs
Mozg Labs
Space Fleet Simulator
It’s hard to pin Into the Void to one single, predominant genre and I consider this a very fortunate exception from the rule. Far too many Sci-Fi themed video games focus on just one gameplay aspect and leave other parts, less developed. This title mixes near flawlessly the strategic elements with those more commonly found in roguelike RPGs while the randomly generated campaigns maintain the sense of mystery between each new playthrough. The cel-shaded graphics engine is a welcome change from most strategic space sims and the soundtrack didn’t disappoint either. A tutorial could have been more fleshed out but I was  never overwhelmed by Into the Void’s difficulty. Sure, some choices lead to inevitable losses within you fleet but I consider that an important lesson on the many compromises you must endure as a leader. Onto the subject of the ships themselves you have a rich variety of armaments and technological advancements, giving you an edge over competing factions. I never understood some of the reviews claiming the unresponsive controls or the inflated price tag. I stand behind none of these claims since I consider the game decently priced, given its scope and replay value and I was never hindered by the control scheme (in truth I wouldn’t have known Into the Void is a PC port, until I read it in some reviews). Some repetitive combat animations and several non-game-breaking bugs are the only cons I will acknowledge. You have a competent fleet and space exploration simulator, also offering strategic and personal choices. What more could you ask?
+ Beautiful art style and sound effects.
+ Rich story and diversified missions with freedom of choice.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- A few bugs and glitches.
- Some repetitive animations.

Into the Void is yet another clone entered into the gaming world. While it has Great Idea for how the game should be it sadly falls far short. Your fleet from what I have played is 6 ships of your choice (when classes unlocked and buildable) from battlecruisers to your typical Super Capitals these types of games have.
The Combat gets stale quickly as the same visuals are seen in near all the fights. Any Intense fighting it advertised I did not encounter in its Turn Based Combat. Issue Order to each ship individually as its turn arrives, choose which guns to fire, at which ships, click end, wait for next ships turn. Each animation has the ships turn the guns at each other.... Each and Everytime and then they open fire. After your 10th time broadsiding the enemy (all you do is Broadside) you would think the crew would keep the guns trained instead of aligning them back across your Bow. But, nope, Each shot... Guns turn towards the ship you have been engaged with for over 8 minutes... fire its volley, and recenters itself forward. Maintain Targetting solution does not exist in this game.
While you can Colonize planets and take over bases, that is about as far as it goes. When you have Resources Click the upgrade on the Structure you put on the planet for mining, harvesting antimatter, farming, or Entertainment centers. Each of these assists in its obvious areas. You get One Structure Per Planet. Your Resources gather each day, click and forget. No setting up supply chains, gaurding transports that might get under attack, nothing further to manage. They might come under attack havent had it happen yet.
Research and Manufacturing are Instant if you collected enough points. These are gathered from Raiding enemy fleets, bases, or probing planets. Once you have enough points, you click what you wanted and you have it. The same goes for building any ship, If you have the points Its Insta built.
Fitting the ships is done in a few clicks. Drag whatever weapons onto the matching Colored box and you have it equipped, upgrade it if you can fit it. Each module has mass and power outputs. Get to heavy and respond slower in turns, Have to little power and you cant fire. Modules of course Exist to boosts anything from Damage to power generation. Larger classes can use fleet boosting modules.
Your missions are a few multi choice questions, then go and enter combat somewhere. Use Autocombat (which cant kill anything quickly) or manually select your choices as mentioned before. After you complete the final missions you automatically return to base. You can return to base at anypoint you want, Even when low on fuel, your magically refilled and made the multiple refuelling trip back in a single click.
This game could become something if it made the combat more exciting, expanded on planet management or even let you run multiple fleets. Some others have mentioned this game was a Mobile game and it would fit in well with those style of dumbed down content that exist on the mobile platform. But when you can get other games like this for cheaper or equal pricing that offer better, its hard to suggest to anyone to purchase this.

TLDR: Great Warriors game with a surprisingly great plot, improved gameplay mechanics and power portrayals of the historical characters.
Dynasty Warriors and Samurai Warriors has always been favourites of mine. Its Asian history glorified through legend, mindless action and it always gave you that epic feeling as you cut down thousands of men at a time. The Sengoku period is a very popular period in Japanese history as the events that transpired and the men behind them became legend, none more than Sanada Yukimura.
When you think of Samurai Warriors, the plot is usually secondary as the mindless gameplay and terrible voice acting has always been the main selling points. Samurai Warriors: Spirit of Sanada flips that upside down as the plot now takes the focus with the Sanada Clan as its centre. The game goes through the efforts, feats and events that allowed the Sanada Clan to survive throughout the entire Sengoku period and still be revered as legend, almost all throughout it. Never before as a Samurai Warriors game ever put in a story like this before, bringing the epic legend of these men of history into an even more grander light. I really enjoyed how the story played out and how it was portrayed, more so than the usual 'Next Stage, Next Characters you can use' format they usually follow. The cinematics and music were done well along with its portrayal of the characters, with usually big characters have more or less cameos and smaller characters with more of an appearance based on how they interacted with the Sanada Clan in history.
The gameplay is outstanding, but it has its fault. The new Multi-Battle system is incredible, as it uses the progress of the previous maps to affect what special commands you can utilise in the next. The new 'Sanada Coin' system triggers certain events that provide strategic value, but only if you have enough of them to use. The coins are generated based on battle ratings along with achieving objectives, which brings in a rather great sense of achievement when you are able to pull them off. The downside however was the 'exploration' system, which made the characters go through smaller maps to collect items used in crafting. I personally found them boring but it did help move the plot forward at times. The combat animations, Musou moves and the rage system were definite highlights - which realy brough the epic feeling of being legendary warriors to life. Never before have I ever seen Yukimura appear as the greatest warrior of that period before this game.
All in all, the game is fantastic and any person who loves the Warriors series should play this game. I would have to say that this is my favourite warriors game by far.

I believe that this game is completely underrated. It's a wonderful game, perfect the way it is. I've seen people complain that "It's not like the other thief games" or "I wish if I were playing a different game that was exactly like this". It's not fair to rate a game by comparing it to other games that were a lot like this game, and it's also not fair that this game has to be rated based on how the previous thief's played. Think of it as it's own game. I've played Deus Ex, and I heard that Thief was a lot like it. It was true, Thief is a lot like Deus Ex. If I compared the two, I enjoyed Deus Ex a bit more because I could kill people without worrying much about dying. But that's a different game, and therefore, comparing it is completely unfair. Thief is perfectly good the way it is; You steal, it's open world, you can kill if you have to, stealth is more important than other stealth games (meaning your play style should be based on stealth without the option of murdering everybody with great efficiency), and over all fun. I couldn't ask for more from this game. Basically, the score of 68 is not fair, don't believe it, and get the game. If you play it, you will know how good it is. One last addition: I've heard that the ending was disappointing, and that partially drops the score, but I believe that it's the game play in between that should determine the score, and not the ending.

For reference on where I'm coming from, I am a huge, HUGE fan of the Thief series.
The short version of my thoughts; better than I feared, worse than I hopped. It was a mixed bag. I will say wait till it goes down in price before getting it.
Now for more detail. The game was better than I was worried it would be. This is, at least in the way I played it, a stealth game for sure. I did play it on master difficulty with only non-lethal take downs enabled, as well as no objective markers, but still like that this DOES feel like a stealth game.
The things I liked.
The city hub was actually quite well done and had a good number of things to do and see (and steal, of course) with a good number of side missions to do. I found the game was at it's most fun when it just let you do some straight up thieving, and thankfully there are plenty of activities that are just that. The stealth mechanics work well, using light and sound effectively, as well as the various ways you can create distractions. I also appreciate how many difficulty options there actually are, as well as hud customization so I could turn off objective markers, threat markers, the mini map, etc etc.
The three best missions I'd say is the first one, the one in the House of Blossoms Brothel (Not for the reason you think), and the Northcrest Manor, because they actually felt like they had a sense of openness and exploration to them, and I didn't constantly feel like I was being lead down a path like the others. This, along with the various side missions and my exploration in the city, is when this felt the most like a Thief game to me.
There's also more than enough collectibles to put into a collection Garrett has at his hideout so, it certainly scratches that itch well.
Things I didn't like.
Too many of the main story missions felt overly linear for a Thief game. They do have multiple paths but usually, it feels less like you are choosing your own strategy and more like you are choosing from one of two or three predetermined paths. The missions were broken into different sections like Dishonored, which wouldn't be bad, except you could not go back. This became a real annoyance to me.
Also, I did not like how rope arrows are contextual, only working on specific spots rather than any wooden surface. Also, the story was, honestly, crap. One problem was Garrett would get caught in almost *every* chapter, to the point to where it almost made him seem like a crappy thief, when he is supposed to be a master. This lead back into the mission structure in that it almost always ended with an escape sequence. This was annoying because part of the fun of the old Thief games was getting in and out quietly without anyone ever knowing you were there. And, Garrett just doesn't feel as lovably cynical in this as he used to. There are elements of it there, but there's just not enough. Plus he kept going on too much about the character of Erin which, honestly I just could not care about despite how much the game wanted me to. Frankly I cared more about Basso, Garrett's friend and fence, than Erin. I said this before, but I also didn't like how cartoonishly evil the guards were, were as before they were just guys on a job.
Also, no one ever said the word "taffer", the made up swear word from the old games.
So, over all, it was a mixed bag. I did enjoy it, but, I can't say I'd give it a strong recommendation. And, if they do make a sequel (which I honestly doubt), I can't say I'd want it to continue in this direction.
But yeah I'd say you'd be better off getting the old trilogy on Steam or GOG for now. Or the Dark Mod since it's free.

And of course the same pretty solid story that I've come to expect from this  series.

For you that just want a quick review, i say this as simple as possible. This kinetic novel story, is the best that i have ever read. The character development, the plot, the art, the music, its all done professionally and beautifully craft. You should buy and read the first one and also buy and read the second one. Now, if you still need more reason, Let me tell you in this long wall of text.
First thing first, the character development is.. wow. Its very good, you will know, care, and feel connected with the characters after you done with this kinetic novel. Usually in a lot of anime or visual novel, the way they tell the ruthless character to soften up is to change their personality instanly once they soften up, but this kinetic novel managed to make the ruthless character stay ruthless, but giving her a deep and logical reason of why she is ruthless. There is no one dimensional characters in this kinetic novel. It managed to makes me care with every characters even the evil one, and also makes me curious about others characters that the kinetic novel still didn't tells. Every characters have a reason to do what they do, even though it feels wrong at first, that is the best part of the characters.
The plot is well done as well, because it depends on the characters and as i said above, the characters development is really good. Although the plot didn't have the "Unique" stuff like the first one have, it is still engaging and also fun while also very touching and might makes you cry. I have to say this however, this one is also leaving a lot of unanswered plot point while didn't really answered the first one. Unlike the first one however, the plot give the main character a better reason of why they do what they do, why they help the people along the way even though their freaking kingdom is in danger !
The art and the visual as you see on the store page is very nice and beautifully drawn, it what makes me even try this title when it first came out. Like i said on my fault milestone 2 demo review, they have a freaking battle cutscene !! In a kinetic novel !!! All the battle CG feels alive and engagging which is really good, not a lot of visual novel could do that to me, to make my imagination fill in the blank. In my mind, the battle CG plays out like an anime instead of still pictures.
I don't know how to comment about the music, but i know when a background music is good and did their job well, and this novel background music did that both. they help me connect to a scene, like a sad scene or a fight scene. One of my dissapointment however, its the lack of voice acting. A lot of jokes felt flat because of it, because i know i would have laugh out loud if i heard the intonation of the characters when they said this funny stuff.
Soo, yeah ! Recommended to the highest degree. If you enjoy visual novel and reading, be sure to buy this. If you enjoy an epic and touching story, be sure to buy this. Just buy this already ! Steamkravter, buy this ! ^-^
